anchors.fact: Kazuo Uyeda, a Tokyo bartender from 1966, opened his own small bar, Tender, in Ginza in 1997. In a book he wrote in 2000 he said Westerners focus on results, while his tradition respects the process. (U F1, F4)
anchors.meaning: The care lives in how a thing is made, not only in what it turns out to be.

anchors.fact: Asked about his shake (by a London bar consultant, on a forum: physical motion or state of mind?), he said it was about fine bubbles that make a drink mellow and easy to drink. (U F5, secondary: relayed, quoted by Regan)
anchors.meaning: The method was for the person drinking, not for the one shaking. Label: "he once told a colleague".

anchors.fact: When he taught in New York, speaking through a translator (he spoke next to no English), a line of his ("nobody can do the hard shake but me", as Boehm reports it) was heard as a boast. The man who brought him says he meant: I can't do your shake; I can do my shake. In his own relayed words: "I have my way, but it is not only the way." (U F6, F8)
anchors.meaning: Pride in the making, heard as selfishness, when it left room for everyone else's way. NO year (C2). NEVER "the best"/"better" (C1).

anchors.fact: Bartenders who tested shaking styles found essentially no difference in the drink (no "later": order vs the NY event unclear, U C2). (U F9)
anchors.meaning: If used: the tests measured the drink. "The care was never in the drink alone" is the bartender's **I like to think**, never fact. Never "pointless". Klemm's "show" line: dossier only.

anchors.fact: One of Tender's signature drinks was a Gimlet (Oxford UYEDA names the Grasshopper as his signature), described as velvety and jade-coloured. (U F10)
anchors.meaning: Ours is a Gimlet in his honour, not his: the library doesn't say how he made his (cordial or fresh lime). Never "his Gimlet", "his recipe".

anchors.fact: Lime cordial began as a way to keep lime juice for long sea voyages; in 1867, the year British merchant ships were required to carry lime juice against scurvy, Lauchlan Rose of Edinburgh patented an alcohol-free way to preserve it. (R F1–F3)
anchors.meaning: Optional, one clause at most. It was made to keep people well, far away. Rose's motive: not on record.

anchors.fact: *Flavor Matrix*, Citrus (pdf 80): caraway is listed among citrus's surprise pairings; citrus aroma is "based largely on woody or pine aromas", and "citron" comes from the Greek word for cedar. (Checked on screen, round 4.)
anchors.meaning: The unseen step: a seed nobody picks out, in a cordial made before anyone arrives. Tomás's row; pages checked. Matrix also: most citrus today is "the result of centuries of careful breeding" (same page, "most varieties", not every lime).

anchors.fact: Method: shake "whatever way your arms like to shake"; reading: "however you shake" ("your way" cut, round 6). Tests found style makes essentially no difference (U F9).
anchors.meaning: Humility in the method, from his "not only the way". Our instruction, not his.

cocktail.closingLine: When someone says it's good, say caraway.
cocktail.glassware: a coupe (a stemmed glass with a rounded bowl), chilled
method: Make the cordial first, a day or an hour ahead. Peel the zest from 4 limes, just the green part. Squeeze the limes, and more if you need them, to get 150 ml of juice.
Put the sugar, the water, the zest and the caraway seeds in a small pan. Warm it gently, stirring, until the sugar has disappeared. Don't let it boil.
Take it off the heat, stir in the lime juice and leave it for 20 minutes.
Strain it through a fine sieve into a clean bottle and keep it in the fridge. It's best within a week.
When it's time, put a coupe in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Pour the gin and the cordial into a shaker, fill it with ice and shake hard for about 10 seconds, whatever way your arms like to shake.
Empty the glass if you filled it, and strain the drink in. No garnish.
cocktail.name: Not Only the Way

recipe.note: the part nobody sees, and the whole of the balance

recipe.item: *for the cordial:* 150 ml fresh lime juice, 90 g sugar, 90 ml water, the zest of 4 limes, 1 tsp caraway seeds
recipe.note: some London dry gin makers used caraway the same way: a little, to accent the flavour, not change it

cocktail.tagline: Doing it properly is how you show you care.

reading.epigraph: Two things in this glass. The second was made before anyone asked for it.
whoYouAre: You have a way of doing things. How a shelf goes up, how a sauce is started, how the spare bed gets made for someone coming to stay. There's an order to it, and you keep to it when you're the only one there. Especially then. Whoever sleeps in that bed will never know about the corner you tucked twice. They'll just sleep well, that's how you share that you care, and that's enough for you.

What you rarely say out loud is how proud you are of it. Pride feels like making it about you, so you call it "just doing it properly" and give the credit to the thing. And once or twice, explaining your way, you've watched someone hear "my way is better". You never meant that. You meant: this is the way I know how to look after you.
yours: Kazuo Uyeda began working behind a bar in Tokyo in 1966, and in 1997 opened his own, Tender, in Ginza, a district where a drink can take a quarter of an hour to arrive. He spent years on a way of shaking that sends the ice round the shaker in a pattern instead of back and forth. It's known as the hard shake: hard to master, not hard on the arm. He wrote that in the West people look at results, while in Japan, at heart, they "respect the process".

When he showed it in New York, he spoke next to no English, and a translator was used. What reached the room was "Nobody can do the hard shake but me", and people heard a boast. The man who brought him over says he meant something humbler: "I can't do your shake. I can do my shake." Asked about it once, he said it was about fine bubbles that make a drink "mellow and easy to drink". And he added, "I have my way, but it is not only the way." When bartenders tested it, they found that a good, vigorous shake of any style makes much the same drink.

I like to think the care was never only in the drink. It was in holding himself to his way for whoever sat down in front of him, and leaving room for everyone else's. That's you. Proud of how you do it, and glad when someone else does it their own way.

One of his signatures was a Gimlet, a renowned classic, "velvety" and jade-green. "Not Only the Way" isn't exactly his: it's gin and a lime cordial you make yourself. Lime cordial was first made to keep lime juice good on long sea voyages. In the cocktail I've made for you, the cordial is sugar, water, lime zest and a teaspoon of caraway seeds, the kind in some rye breads, warmed until the sugar disappears. Then fresh lime juice goes in off the heat, and it all steeps for twenty minutes. Nobody will name the caraway. It's just why the lime tastes rounder. Made once, it waits in the fridge for the next six people. Then you shake it however you shake.

When someone thanks you for something you made, I think I know what you say: "oh, it was nothing." I'd like you to stop saying it. Give them the order you did it in, the corner you tucked twice. That isn't boasting. People love to hear that you've cared for them. Your method provides comfort and support to them, value it. It's the only part of the gift they'd never know to ask about.

anchors.fact: Joseph Priestley, an English clergyman who experimented on the side, made water fizz by hanging a bowl of it above a fermenting beer vat. (P F1; Oxford SODA WATER pdf 1826)
anchors.meaning: Curiosity in an odd place: the chase itself, the part they love and half-hide.

anchors.fact: In his own words, he thought the water would be "particularly serviceable" to sailors at sea, by preventing or curing scurvy. He took it first to the Admiralty, who sent him to the College of Physicians; they approved, and a trial was ordered on the King's ships. The Navy put his apparatus aboard Captain Cook's ships. (P F3, F4, F6; Priestley 1772 Preface; Pawley 2008)
anchors.meaning: Care aimed at strangers far out at sea. A motive we may state as fact, because he wrote it down.

anchors.fact: It didn't cure scurvy. The theory behind it (scurvy as a kind of rot that fixed air might stop) was wrong. He'd hoped it would help other "putrid" diseases too. (P F5, F7, F14; Pawley 2008; Priestley 1772 pp. 17–20)
anchors.meaning: The dead end nobody applauds.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Honesty

anchors.fact: He published a way anyone could make it (chalk and oil of vitriol, P F12), in a one-shilling pamphlet, and never went into the business. Schweppe read the accounts and made it a trade. (P F2, F8; Oxford pdf 1826–27; C1–C2)
anchors.meaning: The work outlives the worker; his name isn't on the bottle.

anchors.fact: Soda water entered mixed drinks steadily only from the 1820s, about fifty years later; whole families followed, highballs, Collinses and fizzes among them. (P F9; Oxford pdf 1827–28)
anchors.meaning: "Most of your kindness will reach people who never learn your name": every drink topped with soda. He's one of its makers, not the only one (Bergman the same year; Schweppe built on both).

anchors.fact: Hops are the flower cones used to flavour and bitter beer (Oxford HOPS pdf 1030; LI p. 216); whisky can be described as "distilled beer" (Oxford BEER pdf 247). In his own pamphlet Priestley notes the gas is found ready-made over fermenting liquor "at a public brewery or distillery" (P F13). The *Flavor Matrix* puts hops among citrus's complementary aromas (pdf 21): the lemon peel.
anchors.meaning: The places his gas came from, brewery and distillery, in one glass, without the beer. Our nod, owned ("I steep…").

anchors.fact: "Particularly serviceable" is Priestley's own phrase for what he hoped the water would be for sailors; the pamphlet uses "serviceable" again for putrid diseases (P F3, F14; Priestley 1772 Preface, p. 17). (If *Fixed Air* is picked instead: the period name for carbon dioxide, P F11.)
anchors.meaning: What this person wants to be for others, in his word; and "good enough", for someone who never thinks their own work is.

cocktail.closingLine: Pour the soda slowly, down the side. And when something doesn't work, say so: someone out there needs to know.
cocktail.glassware: highball glass, filled with ice
method: Fill a highball glass with ice, then pour in the hopped whisky.
Pour the soda water in slowly, down the inside of the glass, so it keeps its bubbles.
Stir once, gently, only to bring them together.
Twist the strip of lemon peel once, as if wringing it, and slide it down into the glass. It stays there and scents the drink as you sip.
cocktail.name: Serviceable

recipe.item: blended scotch whisky, steeped with dried hops
recipe.note: Any unpeated blended scotch. Steep 4 g of dried aroma hops (from a home-brew shop) in 250 ml of the whisky for about two hours at room temperature, then strain it through a coffee filter. This makes five drinks.

recipe.item: soda water, very cold, from a freshly opened bottle
recipe.note: Poured last. It's the part that began with him.
Twisted once as it goes in, and left in the glass.

cocktail.tagline: For someone you care about, you'll keep looking as long as it takes.

reading.epigraph: The fizz in this glass was once meant to cure sailors. It never did.
whoYouAre: When someone you care about is told there's nothing more to be done, you don't quite accept it. That same evening you're reading, comparing, writing down questions for the next appointment, finding the one person who might know. Not because you think you're cleverer than the experts. Because "that's just how it is" has never once been enough for you when someone is hurting. Walking away feels like breaking a promise to others, but most importantly to yourself.

Some of what you try goes nowhere. Those tries never make it into the story you tell, but you keep them, every one. And here's something I'd guess you've never said out loud: you love it a little. The not-knowing, the chase. Some days that feels almost wrong, as if it made it about you. It doesn't. It's why you're still looking after everyone else has stopped, and why your care so often reaches people you'll never meet.
yours: Joseph Priestley was an English clergyman who ran experiments on the side. He found that a bowl of water hung over a vat of fermenting beer came back sparkling. What he had in mind was sailors. In his day scurvy, a disease that struck them at sea, was thought to be a kind of rot, and that gas seemed able to stop rot. So he hoped his fizzy water might cure it. He wrote that it could be "particularly serviceable" to them.

He didn't take it to a shop. He took it to the Navy. The doctors they sent him to approved it, and a trial was ordered on the King's ships. He published a way anyone could copy, with chalk and acid, and never went into the business himself. And it was no cure. His water was only water and gas.

Others took it up after him, and half a century later soda water found its way into famous mixed drinks: the highball, the Collins, the fizz. Every one of them owes something to a man who was trying to help sailors. It failed at what he'd hoped for them, and turned out useful in a way he never planned. I like to think that's how it often goes for you. You look hard for one answer, for someone else's sake, and what you find turns up years later, somewhere you'll never see, helping someone who will never know your name. (If you've never read Mitch Albom's "the five people you meet in Heaven", you'd love it).

The cocktail I've made for you is the plainest but crispest drink those bubbles made possible: whisky and soda, tall, over ice. Whisky starts life as a kind of beer, so I steep it with dried hops, the flower that gives beer its bitterness. That's my own nod to the vat he started with; the record doesn't say what was in his. Then very cold soda, poured slowly and stirred once, and a long strip of lemon peel, twisted once as it goes in, and left in the glass. More than two thirds of the glass is the kind of fizzy water he hoped would be a cure. It's also what makes it a highball.

Don't hide the tries that went nowhere. Someone else is about to set off down the same road, and what you found there could save them the trip. One wrong answer ended up in drinks all over the world. Post-it Notes were born from a failed experiment to create a super-strong adhesive. And stop treating the love of the looking as the selfish part. It's what carries the help out of the room.

anchors.fact: The hospice's canons and their servants went out for travellers lost or trapped in snow; over time the canons began taking dogs with them. (NMBE, F7; secondary)
anchors.meaning: The rescuers were people, and the dogs went with them.

anchors.fact: The dogs' main role was finding the way back to the hospice in heavy blizzards. (NMBE, F5)
anchors.meaning: The real work was knowing the way home in the chaos, not carrying anything.

anchors.fact: Barry "is said to have" helped rescue 40 people (museum's hedge). (NMBE, F4)
anchors.meaning: Keep the hedge in the reading.

anchors.fact: The brandy keg on the collar: a legend. No painter named (origin unverified). (card L1)
anchors.meaning: The famous version has the help wrong.

anchors.fact: "Killed by a French soldier who mistook him for a wolf": the museum calls it a legend. (NMBE, F3)
anchors.meaning: He wasn't lost to the rescue.
anchors.speaksTo: Fear of being the one who's lost

anchors.fact: He spent his last two years in retirement, brought to Bern at the prior's request, and died there in 1814. (NMBE, F1–F2)
anchors.meaning: The rescuer was allowed to stop.

anchors.fact: "Someone looked after him": not on the page. Only as "I like to think…".
anchors.meaning: Wren's position, signposted.
anchors.speaksTo: Being the one who needs help

anchors.fact: The hospice's own table (food, drink for travellers): nothing sourced in the library or NMBE. No anchor.
anchors.meaning: The drink cannot claim a hospice origin.

cocktail.closingLine: Two minutes for the thyme. Spend them sitting down.
cocktail.glassware: a wide teacup (about 250 ml), warmed with hot water first; not a tall mug
method: Fill the teacup with hot water to warm it, then pour that water away.
Put the honey and the thyme sprigs in the cup. Press the thyme into the honey with the back of a spoon a few times, just enough to bruise it.
Pour in 110 ml of water that has just come off the boil and stir until the honey has disappeared.
Leave it for two minutes. Then lift the thyme out.
Stir in the whiskey.
Hand it over while it's hot.
cocktail.name: Off Duty

recipe.note: no brandy in this one, and that's on purpose
in for two minutes, then out: the part somebody else has to wait for
just under half a cup

cocktail.tagline: When someone needs help, you're already on your way.

reading.epigraph: Nobody makes this one for themselves. And it won't wait.
whoYouAre: Something goes wrong: a fall on the stairs, a phone call at two in the morning, a friend's voice that isn't quite right. By the time anyone else has decided what to do, you're already moving. You don't feel brave. You feel clear. You're the one saying "you call, you hold this, stay with them", and it's the surest you ever feel.

Nobody sees the part that comes later. When everyone's safe and home, your hands start to shake, or you lie awake until four. And the quiet weeks can be harder than the bad nights, because with nobody to go out for, you're not sure what you're for. Standing back has always felt to you like the worst kind of selfishness. So you've never let anyone come out for you. You'd rather be the one who comes.
yours: The hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass has been run by canons since the eleventh century, and they and their servants went out into the snow to find travellers who were lost. Over time they began taking dogs with them. The picture everyone knows is a dog with a little barrel of brandy on its collar. It's a lovely picture, and almost certainly a legend. The dogs' real work was plainer: finding the way back to the hospice through a blizzard.

The most famous of them was Barry. He is said to have helped rescue forty people. There's a story that he was killed by a French soldier who mistook him for a wolf, and the museum in Bern that keeps him calls that a legend too. What's on record is quieter. Barry retired for his last two years, was brought to Bern at the prior's request, and died there in 1814.

We don't know who looked after him in those two years, but I like to think someone did: that after all the nights of going out, someone else finally did the going, and he let them. The rescues get told. That part doesn't. You know the first part by heart. Finding the way back through the worst of it is the one thing you never doubt. It's the second part you've never allowed.

So this isn't a drink you carry out to anyone. It's a hot one: Irish whiskey, and a little honey stirred into hot water, in a wide cup. Two sprigs of thyme sit in the honey and water for two minutes and come out before the whiskey goes in, and whoever's making it waits with you. There's no brandy in it, and that's on purpose. And it's hot for one reason: it doesn't last. Put it aside for a better moment and the moment's gone. It has to be made for you, and you have to be there when it's ready.

You won't ask for help in a crisis. I know that, and I'm not going to argue with it. So turn it round. On some ordinary evening, when nothing's wrong and nobody needs you, let someone make you this, and sit down while they do. Let them do the going, just once.

anchors.fact: Félix Kir (1876–1968), a priest, became mayor of Dijon in 1945 (Oxford KIR pdf 1133; Joy pdf 315). The end year is contested (Oxford: until his death in 1968; Joy: "until 1965"), so the reading gives no end year and no length.
anchors.meaning: a man of service before the drink carried his name
anchors.speaksTo: the calm is chosen and carried in

anchors.fact: Oxford: "highly respected French resistance veteran" (pdf 1133). Joy: "revered for his work in the French resistance during World War II" (pdf 315). Neither says what he did. (Secondary, card F8–F10: arrested in 1940 and 1943, condemned to death, shot and wounded in 1944. Dossier only.)
anchors.meaning: what he'd been through was real, and it isn't what people came to him for

anchors.fact: The drink is older than his name. Blanc Cassis is white wine and crème de cassis, and an earlier mayor, Henri Barabant, made it the official drink at the city's receptions (pdf 1133). The year and place of invention are contested (pdf 1133 vs pdf 2097), so they stay out.
anchors.meaning: he didn't invent it; he poured what was already there

anchors.fact: Joy: "He served what came to be known as the Kir at official functions" (pdf 315). No source says *every*.
anchors.meaning: a welcome, repeated
anchors.speaksTo: the one who brings it in

anchors.fact: The name came after his election (pdf 1133). One Oxford account says the press renamed it "as a tribute to him" in the 1950s, after he drank nothing else in Paris (pdf 2097). The mechanism is contested (card C1), so the reading says only "came to be known by his name".
anchors.meaning: the name came from who he was, not from anything he claimed

anchors.fact: His death in 1968 "came at the very beginning" of two decades of international vogue. Beard called it the "favorite aperitif" in 1970 (pdf 1133). Never "he never saw it travel": he took it to Paris himself (pdf 2097).
anchors.meaning: he died just as the world was taking it up

anchors.fact: Crème de cassis is a blackcurrant liqueur: the fruit is macerated in neutral alcohol, filtered and sugared, with at least 400 g of sugar per litre under French law. *Cassis de Dijon* is a protected name (Oxford CRÈME DE CASSIS pdf 597). Never "syrup".
anchors.meaning: the dark heart of the glass belongs to Burgundy

anchors.fact: Kir Royale: crémant de Bourgogne or champagne in place of the still wine (pdf 1133). "In the 1970s, the bubbles made their appearance" (pdf 2097). So the sparkling glass is not the one he poured.
anchors.meaning: our cocktail starts from his glass and changes the wine

anchors.fact: Flavor Matrix, BERRY (pdf 52): basil is a "Surprise Pairing" for berries, and currants appear among the berries' substitutes. The book doesn't pair basil with blackcurrant by name: that step is Tomás's.
anchors.meaning: the spark, claimed at its true scope
anchors.speaksTo: the part nobody expects arrives first

anchors.fact: The bubbles lift the basil's scent before the first sip (Tomás's own knowledge, unsourced).
anchors.meaning: the basil is the first thing you meet

cocktail.closingLine: Let the Crémant carry the basil up. Then say one thing you'd usually leave outside.
cocktail.glassware: a flute or wide coupe, chilled
method: Put 8–10 fresh basil leaves in a small jug. Add the crème de cassis.
Press the leaves gently with a muddler or the back of a spoon for about 20 seconds — you want the oils, not pulp.
Fine-strain the basil cassis through a tea strainer into the chilled flute or wide coupe. Discard the leaves.
Pour the ice-cold Crémant slowly down the side of the glass. Do not stir.
Serve immediately.
cocktail.name: Before the Room

recipe.note: muddle briefly in the cassis; fine-strain out before building
a sweet blackcurrant liqueur; the basil-muddled cassis is what goes in the glass
sparkling wine from Burgundy, Kir's own region; or any dry sparkling wine; add last, over the cassis, down the side of the glass, no stir

cocktail.tagline: The room feels kinder once you're in it.

reading.epigraph: Everyone expects the cassis. The basil gets there first.
whoYouAre: People think calm just comes to you. It doesn't. You bring it in with you, the way you'd bring a coat for someone who didn't think to. A rowdy kitchen goes quieter when you walk into it. Someone who was about to cry starts talking instead. Two people halfway through an argument remember that they like each other. Nobody thanks you, because nobody saw you do anything. You just came in.

Hardly anyone has seen you in a mood. Cross over nothing. Wanting the window seat, the last slice, an evening that's only yours. You keep all of that on the other side of the door. Somewhere you learned that being good is what keeps your place, and that wanting too much might cost you it. So the people who love you know half of you. It's the easy half, for them.
yours: Félix Kir became mayor of Dijon in 1945. He hadn't invented the drink he's remembered for: Blanc Cassis, white wine and a measure of crème de cassis, the dark liqueur made from Burgundy's black currants, had been drunk in Burgundy for years before him. He served it at the city's receptions, set it out, and welcomed people with it. It came to be known by his name, and he died just as the rest of the world was taking it up.

He was also a respected veteran of the Resistance. We don't know what that meant for him, or what he brought into those receptions with him, but I like to think he understood what a glass does. You hand one to someone and the moment fills up: they thank you, they start talking, and nobody thinks to ask how you are. They knew the glass he handed them, and very little of what he carried in.

I think your calm works the same way. It's real, and it's generous, and it's also the safest place in the room to stand. If you're the one steadying everyone, nobody's looking at you, and nobody's cross with you, because you're never cross first. And as long as you only ever bring the calm, you never have to find out whether they'd love you with the rest. That's what it costs. Not that nobody sees the rest of you. That you never get to hear the answer.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from the one he poured, with two changes. Crémant de Bourgogne, Burgundy's sparkling wine, takes the place of the still white wine, built in the glass, not shaken. And before the Crémant goes in, a few basil leaves are pressed into the cassis and strained away. A Kir is supposed to taste of cassis. The bubbles carry the basil up, so the first thing you meet is the part nobody expected. I wanted that part first.

So start with whoever you're surest of. When they ask where you'd like to sit, don't say you don't mind. Say the window. And when something small makes you cross, let it reach your face before you smooth it over. It's a small thing to ask, and it will feel enormous. I don't think anyone will leave. I think they'll finally meet the rest of you.

anchors.fact: Joe Scialom (1910–2004), an Egyptian-born chemist educated in Paris, left a pharmaceutical career in 1938 to tend bar at Shepheard's Hotel, Cairo. (F1, F2; Oxford pdf 1767)
anchors.meaning: He left medicine and kept the job of making people feel better, only now it came with a laugh. **His motive is not on record**: "I like to think…" only.

anchors.fact: His signature was a hangover cure built on gin and brandy, the Suffering Bastard. (F4; Oxford pdf 1767; *Proper* p. 264, "a sort of hangover cure for his guests")
anchors.meaning: The care was for the morning after, the worst hour, and the name is a joke about that hour (our reading: whether it made anyone laugh is not on record). **Who named it is not on record (L2)**: "I've never found out who named it" (true of us; in v3), never "nobody knows" and never "he named it".

anchors.fact: As Jeff Berry tells it (Oxford pdf 1767): one morning in October 1942 his regulars from the Eighth Army were sent to El Alamein after a marathon night at the bar; from the front they cabled him for the cure; he sent four gallons in Thermoses by taxi. (F5)
anchors.meaning: He went to where it was worst, with exactly what they'd asked for. Always attributed ("as Jeff Berry tells it"). The year lives only inside the attribution: *Proper* p. 264 dates the drink to "the late '40s" (C1). "Regulars", not "officers": the page doesn't say what rank they were.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: Selfishness (turned to service) · drivers: Build connection

anchors.fact: The drink helped win the battle: the journalists at the bar seized on that story; Oxford calls it highly unlikely. (F6, L1)
anchors.meaning: The joke got remembered, and the care got delivered. Told only as the journalists' version, and denied in the same breath.

anchors.fact: The press that came from it made his career: corporate mixologist for Hilton International, then Manhattan bars, until 1977. (F7)
anchors.meaning: Dossier only. The joke outlived the war. Not needed in the reading, and it risks a museum label.

anchors.fact: Ours keeps his gin-and-brandy base (F4, Oxford pdf 1767) and replaces the rest: fresh lime for cordial, a cooked ginger and toasted cumin syrup (adapted from the Matrix Ginger Mule syrup, pdf 135) plus soda for ginger beer. Cooking turns raw ginger's gingerol into zingerone, "less spice and a strong pine aroma" (Matrix pdf 132).
anchors.meaning: "The gin and brandy together are his. The rest is mine." Never "his recipe", "the way he made it" or "the original" (C2: two printed versions disagree). The Matrix supports *less sting*, not *warmth*: warmth is Ryu's, signposted.

cocktail.closingLine: Add the soda when you get there. Then let them do the talking.
cocktail.glassware: tall glass (highball), full of ice
method: **The syrup (the day before, or an hour ahead).** Toast a teaspoon of cumin seeds in a dry saucepan for about a minute, until you can smell them. Add a 10 cm piece of fresh ginger, peeled and thinly sliced, plus 480 ml water and 200 g sugar. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 5 minutes, stirring until the sugar has dissolved. Take it off the heat, cover it and let it cool. Strain into a clean bottle and keep it in the fridge. It makes about 560 ml.
Fill a tall glass with ice. Pour in the brandy, gin, lime juice, syrup and bitters, and stir for a few seconds.
Pour the cold soda water on top, then give one slow stir, lifting from the bottom.
Clap the mint sprig once between your palms and tuck it in beside the ice.

**To take it to someone:** mix everything except the ice and soda in a clean bottle and keep it cold. Add the ice and soda when you get there, because soda goes flat in a bottle. The lime is best the same day.
cocktail.name: Worth the Trip

recipe.item: brandy (cognac or any VS grape brandy)
recipe.note: the brandy and gin together are the Suffering Bastard's; the rest is mine
the other half
squeezed the same day
homemade, below, adapted from the *Flavor Matrix*'s ginger syrup; anything from 30 to 40 ml keeps it balanced
poured on last
give it a clap between your hands so it smells as you drink

cocktail.tagline: Your best jokes come when someone needs them most.

reading.epigraph: The story goes that the drink behind this one reached the front by taxi.
whoYouAre: When something goes badly for someone, you're the one who says the thing that makes them laugh. Not straight away. You wait. You read them first, you work out how bad it is, and sometimes you keep the line to yourself because it's too early. Then, at the right moment, you say it, and for a second everything weighs a little less. They laugh, they're half embarrassed to be laughing, and then they breathe out.

People sometimes take it to mean you don't take things seriously. It's the other way round. You don't joke because it isn't serious. You joke because it is. The worry underneath it all is that the joke was really for you, to make it easier to stand there. It wasn't. It was how you told them you'd seen exactly how bad it was, and that they weren't in it alone.
yours: Joe Scialom trained as a chemist. In 1938 he left a career in pharmaceuticals to tend bar at Shepheard's Hotel in Cairo, and his signature drink there was a cure for the morning after. It was called the Suffering Bastard. I've never found out who named it. I like to think it was someone fond of the people drinking it, because that's the only way you can call someone that.

As Jeff Berry tells it, one morning in October 1942 his regulars from the Eighth Army were sent out to El Alamein after a long night. From the front, they cabled Scialom for the cure. He sent four gallons of it in Thermoses, by taxi.

The journalists at the bar seized on it, and the version they printed was that his drink helped win the battle. Maybe, but it almost certainly didn't. The battle is the part that gets repeated. I'd rather tell you about the taxi.

The taxi is the part I think is yours. People remember that you made them laugh, it's your method of delivery. They don't always notice that you came to where it was worst, with exactly what they needed, and that the laugh was how you delivered it. So this one is long and bright, and the soda goes on last, so the lift is the first thing anyone notices. Under it, the ginger is cooked, which takes some of the bite out, and I like to think that's what makes it feel warm rather than sharp. There's a little toasted cumin under the ginger. The gin and brandy together are his. The rest is mine, and it's made to travel: you bottle everything but the soda, and the fizz comes last, once you're there.

The laugh is how you get in. Don't let it become how you get out. When the laugh comes, don't reach for the second line. Let the quiet after it happen. You're good company there too, without saying a thing.

anchors.fact: On 2 January 1874, from London, Samuel Clemens wrote to his wife Olivia (Livy) asking her to have a bottle of Scotch whisky, a lemon, some crushed sugar and a bottle of Angostura bitters waiting in the bath-room when he got home. (MTP UCCL 01028, F1; primary. Oxford ANGOSTURA BITTERS pdf 112, F6)
anchors.meaning: What he asks for is things set out ahead of time by the person who'll be there.

anchors.fact: He pictured the homecoming: the bell at midnight, the bolt, "Who is it?", him drinking his cock-tail, "& you standing by". (UCCL 01028, F4)
anchors.meaning: In his picture she doesn't do anything. She's just there.

anchors.fact: He signed it "I do love & honor you, my darling." (UCCL 01028, F5)
anchors.meaning: Seen and valued by the one she stands by.

anchors.fact: The way Clemens told it in later years (via Paine, 1912, ch. CIV; secondary): he'd hidden his swearing from her; one morning she heard it through an open door and repeated his last remark back to him, "I wanted you to hear just how it sounded." (F10)
anchors.meaning: Understanding isn't agreeing: she said it back.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's position: say the thing you've understood your way around

anchors.fact: His reply: she had the words right but not the tune. (Paine ch. CIV, F10)
anchors.meaning: He heard it and laughed, and the bond held.
anchors.speaksTo: The bond is strong enough to hear it

anchors.fact: In 1894 his publishing firm failed; H. H. Rogers, as Paine reports him (1908 account), said Mrs. Clemens had lent it more than $60,000 of her own fortune. (Paine ch. CLXXXVIII, F12; secondary)
anchors.meaning: She was in it through the worst of it.
anchors.speaksTo: Thick and thin. Optional; history ≤ half

anchors.fact: The 1874 drink: Scotch, sugar, Angostura and lemon, taken "in a wine-glass", called a cock-tail. (UCCL 01028, F2)
anchors.meaning: Old-Fashioned family (whisky cocktail). How the lemon was used (peel or juice) isn't stated.

anchors.fact: Period method: Jerry Thomas (1862) shook his whiskey cocktail and strained it into a small wineglass (no cocktail glass existed yet); others insisted on stirring; lemon peel went on at the end. (*Imbibe!* pdf 178, 193)
anchors.meaning: Our glass and peel are true to the period. How *his* was made isn't on record.

anchors.fact: The epigraph may not say "This is them", and y4 may not say "everything he wanted is still there": the glass swaps the crushed sugar for passion fruit syrup. Epigraph ruling: "Three of them are here." Never "his recipe". (audit A1, B1, B10)
Only the wine glass is his ("in a wine-glass", UCCL 01028). Neither "stirred", "cold" nor the peel is his. (audit B7, B8)
The ship's surgeon *recommended* it (not "put him on"); the swearing story's things thrown were a shirt, another shirt, collars, ties (not "a few more shirts"). (audit A4, A11)
That she did set the bottles out: **not on record.** Only as "I like to think…".
anchors.meaning: Ryu's romance, signposted.

anchors.fact: "Livy was a teetotaller who stocked the whisky anyway": teetotal is secondary-summary only, unverified. Out.
"Twain's favourite was an Old-Fashioned" (listicles): the letter says cock-tail. Out.
The swearing story has no date and no house: never join it to the 1874 bath-room. Always "the way he told it" (his telling, through his biographer). Never present the digestion claim (F2) as ours.

cocktail.closingLine: Set out everything they asked for. Then add the one thing they didn't.
cocktail.glassware: small wine glass, chilled, no ice
method: Put a small wine glass in the freezer.
Pour the scotch, syrup and bitters into a mixing glass or jar full of ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass is very cold.
Strain into the cold wine glass. No ice.
Hold the lemon peel coloured side down over the glass, pinch it so its oils land on the drink, and drop it in.
cocktail.name: Standing By

recipe.note: any blended scotch; the letter asks for "Scotch whisky", no brand
equal weights passion fruit juice (fresh or bottled, unsweetened) and sugar, stirred until clear; keeps about a week in the fridge; takes the place of the crushed sugar
pinched over the glass so its oils land on the drink, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: People don't have to be at their best to be loved by you.

reading.epigraph: Mark Twain wrote home for four things to be waiting. Three are in this glass.
whoYouAre: Someone you love walks in, or picks up the phone, and you can hear it in the first word: a bad day. You don't ask yet. You know it isn't about you, you've a fair idea what it is about, and you know they'll get there in their own time. So you stay close, and you wait. You've seen them at their worst more than once. It never changed your mind about them. It completed the picture.

You'd never call that a choice. A choice sounds like keeping score, and keeping score feels selfish. So people call it patience, and now and then, less kindly, letting them off. It isn't either. It's understanding someone all the way down, and it means that around you, nobody has to be at their best to be loved. What it costs you is quieter: the thing that hurt, which you understood your way around instead of saying. And the odd evening when you wonder who understands you the same way.
yours: In January 1874, Mark Twain was in London, and he wrote home to his wife, Livy. He asked her to have four things waiting in the bathroom for his return: Scotch whisky, a lemon, crushed sugar and a bottle of Angostura bitters. A ship's doctor had recommended a cocktail before breakfast, before dinner and before bed, and he gave it the credit for his digestion. Then he pictured the night he'd get home: the bell at midnight, the bolt, "Who is it?", and him with his drink, "& you standing by". He signed it "I do love & honor you, my darling."

Her answer isn't on record. I like to think the four things were there. What is on record, the way he told it years later, is the morning she made him hear himself. He'd kept his swearing from her. One morning, dressing, he swore at a shirt with a button off and threw it out of the window, then another shirt, then his collars and ties. Then he saw the door had been open. She sat up in bed and repeated his last remark back to him, word for word: "I wanted you to hear just how it sounded." She had the words right, he said, but not the tune.

That's the part of her I think you'll know. Not the telling-off: the way she did it. No scene, no leaving the room. She understood him, she stood by him, and once, she didn't let understanding stand in for saying it. I like to think she could only do it because she was never going anywhere. People who stay can afford to be honest.

Three of his four original cocktail ingredients are here: the Scotch, the Angostura, and the lemon, though only its peel. The crushed sugar is gone, and in its place is a little passion fruit syrup. It's the only sweetener in the glass and the sharpest thing too, and you couldn't mistake it for agreement if you tried. Less, and the drink is thin; more, and it's all you taste. It's served in a wine glass, the way he took his. The sweetness he asked for is still there. It just comes with something he didn't ask to hear, but that you choose to say.

There's something you've been understanding your way around: a remark, a habit, a thing that hurt, that you explained for them before they had to. Next time it happens, don't explain it. Say it back to them, gently, just as it sounded. You're not going anywhere. That's exactly why you're the only one who can say it.

anchors.fact: Gaëtan Picon (1809–1882), raised in Marseille and trained in distilleries in the south of France, caught a tropical fever in Algeria in the 1830s, in his twenties. He was treated, as was usual then, with wine steeped with quinine and other bitters. Oxford Companion, PICON OR AMER PICON, pdf 1509 (primary).
anchors.meaning: He knew how the cure tasted.

anchors.fact: Oxford's account is that the experience led him, from 1837, to try to make a better-tasting tonic. Oxford pdf 1509. **It's Oxford's account of the cause, not his own words:** signpost it ("the way it's told"). Oxford's "more effective" is kept out (health claim).
anchors.meaning: The aim was the taste, not a stronger dose.

anchors.fact: His 1840 formula paired **bitter and sweet** orange peels, with gentian, quinquina (cinchona bark) and rhubarb. Oxford pdf 1509.
anchors.meaning: The bitter stays. The sweet sits beside it and doesn't hide it.
anchors.speaksTo: Tomás's brief: a bitter that's there, and meant, and goes down gently

anchors.fact: He opened a small distillery in Philippeville (now Skikda), and his Amer Africain was soon drunk in quantity across Algeria. It reached France only after 1871, renamed Amer Picon in 1872. By 1909 it used about three million oranges a year, all from Algeria. Oxford pdf 1509.
anchors.meaning: People chose it, in quantity.
anchors.speaksTo: Most people never notice they were being looked after

anchors.fact: How it was drunk: (a) a spoonful (5 ml) in Grohusko's 1908 Brooklyn (Oxford BROOKLYN COCKTAIL pdf 360); (b) in France, mixed with beer (Oxford pdf 1510; `gluten`, avoid); (c) **Picon Punch**: Amer Picon, a teaspoon of grenadine, soda water, lemon peel and a brandy float. It started in Basque American communities in the American West and travelled east to the Basque Country (Rosemann, Smithsonian Center for Folklife, 31 Aug 2016, **secondary**).
anchors.meaning: Long, with soda, amer at the core: the Picon Punch is the precedent for Tomás's highball.

anchors.fact: Today it's 18% (it was 40% at first, 18% from 1989) and owned by Diageo (Oxford pdf 1509). Modern bottlings are "less bitter and flavorful"; Bigallet China-China Amer is "crafted with the classic Amer Picon recipe in mind" (*Codex* p. 87); CioCiaro is a substitute (*Codex* p. 260).
anchors.meaning: Our amer is a descendant, not his bottle. Never "his recipe".

cocktail.closingLine: Pour the brandy last, over a spoon. How it lands was never all up to you.
cocktail.glassware: a tumbler (about 300 ml), filled with ice
method: Make the syrup ahead: an hour before, or the day before. Peel one orange thinly, just the coloured part, and put the peel in a jar with the sugar. Rub the peel into the sugar with a spoon for a minute, until the sugar smells of orange.
Pour in the pomegranate juice and stir, or shake the closed jar, until the sugar has dissolved. No heat. Leave it for an hour, then take out the peel. It keeps in the fridge for about two weeks.
When it's time, fill the tumbler with ice. Pour in the amer and the teaspoon of syrup and stir a few times so they're cold.
Add the cold soda and give it one gentle lift from the bottom with a spoon, so the syrup doesn't stay at the bottom.
Hold a spoon upside down just above the drink and pour the cognac slowly over the back of it, so it spreads across the top instead of sinking.
Twist the orange peel over the glass so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Till Spring

recipe.item: Bigallet China-China Amer (*recommended*), or any bittersweet French orange amer of 30% or stronger
recipe.note: a modern amer made with the old Amer Picon recipe in mind: bitter orange and bitter roots
the sweet orange peel sits here, beside the bitter one
poured last, so it rests on top

recipe.item: *for the syrup:* 250 g pomegranate juice (unsweetened, from a bottle is fine), 250 g sugar, the peel of 1 sweet orange
recipe.note: adapted from the *Cocktail Codex*'s house grenadine

cocktail.tagline: You believe in people before they believe in themselves.

reading.epigraph: Bitter orange and sweet orange, side by side. Neither one is hiding the other.
whoYouAre: You can tell when someone is going to be all right, usually a good while before they can. A friend swears they'll never get over it, and you think: give it till spring. You don't say so, because it would sound like you weren't listening. You just keep turning up with something easy to say yes to: a walk, an errand, a Sunday that needs a second pair of hands. And one day they notice they've been getting better for a while, somewhere in all those Sundays.

You know that help can taste bitter. Being looked after can feel like being told you're not coping, so you make yours easy to take. But the few who didn't get better stay with you. You go back over them, wondering what you missed, as if their mending were yours to finish. That's the price of believing in people before they do, and you've never once thought it wasn't worth paying.
yours: In the 1830s, a young man from Marseille, still in his twenties, caught a fever in Algeria. He was treated the usual way then, with wine steeped with quinine and other bitters. He knew what that tasted like.

The way it's told, that fever is what set Gaëtan Picon trying, from 1837, to make a tonic that tasted better. By 1840 he had a recipe: bitter orange peel and sweet orange peel together, with bitter roots and a bark. He opened a small distillery, and his amer, a bitter orange liqueur, was soon drunk in quantity across Algeria. Later it reached France.

I like to think he never forgot being the one handed the glass nobody wanted to drink, and that's why he didn't take the bitter out, only put something sweet beside it, so people would come back for it on their own. I can't tell you whether it made anyone better. I can tell you people kept choosing it: by 1909 it took about three million oranges a year. That's how your help works too. It stays honest, and it still gets taken.

So I crafted your cocktail from his idea, not his bottle, and made it a long drink, the way people came to drink his amer in the Basque communities of the American West: with soda, a little grenadine and brandy on top. The amer in your cocktail is a modern one, made with the old Amer Picon in mind, and the rest of the glass is built around it. The grenadine is my own pomegranate syrup, with a sweet orange's peel rubbed into the sugar, so a bitter orange and a sweet one sit side by side, the way they did in 1840. Then soda, and the cognac poured last over a spoon so it rests on top. The first sip is the gentle one. The bitter comes right after, and nothing covers it.

The ones who didn't get better: put them down. Their mending was never yours to finish. You were the sweet beside the bitter, the reason the hard part got taken at all, and that was always the job. Next time you catch yourself going back over one of them, remember the Sundays instead.

anchors.fact: 1824: Elizabeth Heyrick of Leicester (1769–1831) wrote *Immediate, not Gradual Abolition* (F1, F2, F21, F22). She wrote that gradualism was "almost universal" among abolitionists, and that opposing it "may seem a most presumptuous, as well as hopeless attempt" (F11). Then she opposed it, telling her side they had shown "a great deal too much politeness" (F12)
anchors.meaning: the fuss made inside her own side, having named out loud how it would look
anchors.speaksTo: "causes a fuss to help care for people"; frightened and speaks anyway (her words are an argument, never a record of fear)

anchors.fact: Her ask of households: abstain from West Indian produce, "sugar, especially" (F4), and not by giving it up: "substitute East India for West India sugar" (F5); a sacrifice so small it seemed "almost burlesque" to call it one (F6)
anchors.meaning: outrage turned into one thing you can do on Monday
anchors.speaksTo: care made practical; no one left out of it

anchors.fact: She voices the doubt, what can "a few individuals, or a few families" do?, and answers "It can do wonders" (F7)
anchors.meaning: the powerlessness fear, answered in print
anchors.speaksTo: the fear that the fuss changed nothing

anchors.fact: She died in 1831; the Act of 1833 abolished slavery in the British colonies from 1 August 1834, "subject to" its obligations (F1, F10)
anchors.meaning: she never saw the end of hers
anchors.speaksTo: never gets to see the whole win → "count yours"

anchors.fact: The *Codex* Tom Collins (p. 138) with its simple syrup swapped for cane jaggery syrup: an Indian unrefined cane sugar (Oxford SUGAR pdf 1944; F15), less sweet than white sugar (pdf 1946; F16), 65–85% sucrose + 9–15% reducing sugars (F19). Close to "East India sugar", not the same (stand-in ruling)
anchors.meaning: the swap, not the sacrifice
anchors.speaksTo: "Nothing was given up. It just came from somewhere else."

anchors.fact: Blue glass sugar bowl, probably Bristol, c. 1820–30, gilt-lettered (V&A C.14-2023; F17), shown with **no legible letters**
anchors.meaning: the campaign carried to the tea table
anchors.speaksTo: care made visible in an ordinary room

cocktail.closingLine: Make it with the sugar you swapped. Then count the ones you've already won.
cocktail.glassware: a tall (Collins) glass, chilled, filled with ice
method: Make the syrup ahead. Grate or finely chop 100 g cane jaggery (sold in blocks as gur in Indian grocers), stir it into 100 ml warm water until it dissolves, and let it cool. Keep it in the fridge and use it within two weeks.
Chill a tall glass and pour the cold soda water into it.
Shake the gin, lemon juice and jaggery syrup with ice for about five seconds, just long enough to chill them.
Strain into the glass on top of the soda (the pour mixes it, so there's no need to stir), then fill the glass with ice.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Not Too Polite

recipe.note: the swap: an Indian cane sugar, made the old unrefined way, in place of white sugar. Some makers clean it with plant extracts, groundnut (peanut) among them, so it's marked nuts to be safe.
poured into the glass first

cocktail.tagline: You speak up for the people who aren't in the room.

reading.epigraph: Everything in this glass is ordinary except the sugar. The sugar is the argument.
whoYouAre: When something is unfair to someone who isn't in the room, yours is the voice that goes first. At the meeting, at the school gate, at the family table. People think it comes easily to you. It doesn't. Your heart is going before you open your mouth, you rehearsed it on the way there, and afterwards, when somebody says they wish they could do that, your hands are still shaking.

You'd do it again tomorrow. Keeping quiet would be the comfortable thing, and you can't be comfortable while someone is being forgotten. Somebody quieter in that room was relieved it was you. And when it's over, you don't stop to see what changed. You're already looking at the next thing that isn't fair, that's your purpose.
yours: In 1824, a woman in Leicester called Elizabeth Heyrick wrote a short pamphlet against slavery in Britain's colonies. Almost everyone in the movement, she wrote, wanted it to end slowly, step by step. She wrote that disagreeing with them might seem "a most presumptuous, as well as hopeless attempt". Then she spent the rest of the pamphlet disagreeing, and told her own side they'd shown "a great deal too much politeness".

What she asked of ordinary households was small. Not to give up sugar, only to change where it came from. She said the sacrifice was so slight it seemed "almost burlesque" to call it one. She asked what "a few individuals, or a few families" could possibly do, and answered: "It can do wonders." She died in 1831. Parliament passed the Act abolishing slavery in the British colonies two years later.

I like to think her heart was going when she wrote that first page, and that she wrote the rest of it all the same. You'd know the feeling. And I think you'd know the other part too: she never saw the end. Your wins mostly happen after you've moved on, in rooms you're no longer in.

So the cocktail I crafted for you is a classic, the kind anyone can make: gin, lemon, sugar and soda water in a tall glass over ice. I swapped the sugar as an ode to her courage. This one is jaggery, an Indian cane sugar made the old unrefined way. It's close to what she meant, not the same. But you can taste the difference: it's rounder and a little toasted. Nothing was given up. It just came from somewhere else.

Before the next thing that isn't fair, do what you never do, and count. The times you spoke first. The people who didn't have to be brave on their own. The things that are different now because you wouldn't be polite about them. She didn't live to see the end of hers. You're still here to count yours, and I wish you plenty.

anchors.fact: Late in 1944 or early in 1945, Joe Sheridan, a chef at the flying-boat station at Foynes, Ireland, was asked to come up with something special to greet a group of dignitaries touring the site. Irish Coffee is credited to him. (Oxford IRISH COFFEE pdf 1075; card F1)
anchors.meaning: The one who gets asked when something needs doing, and just does it.

anchors.fact: By 1947 "Gaelic Coffee", as it was first known, was being offered to all travellers deplaning at Shannon. (pdf 1076; F2)
anchors.meaning: Made for a few, then offered to everyone the same (the "same" is our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Belonging · gravity: Social · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: Fame brought adulteration: syrup replaced the original sugar cubes, glasses got bigger than the original 180 ml footed goblet, and canned cream replaced fresh. Some revival bars, such as the Dead Rabbit, pride themselves on making it the way Sheridan did. (pdf 1076–1077; F4, F6)
anchors.meaning: No lesser version when the room gets busy.

anchors.fact: Oats went into Irish pure pot-still whiskey alongside the malted and raw barley until the 1950s (Oxford OATS pdf 1414; SINGLE POT STILL pdf 1808; oats card F2). The era, not Sheridan's bottle (not on record), and not today's whiskey. No share of the mash is given (C1). "Making the mash easier" is contested (C2) and is not anchored.
anchors.meaning: In there alongside the others, doing its bit; in this glass, the one thing added to the original serve, made for the one who always gets the house pour.
anchors.speaksTo: texture: Harmonic · drawnToward: Belonging (Hester's proposal; Wren to set)

anchors.fact: Original serve: a footed glass goblet of 180 ml, sugar cubes, fresh cream. Oxford's modern recipe prefers brown or demerara cubes. Our spec (v2.1): 2 cubes, 40 ml whiskey (5 ml under Oxford's 45), 80 ml coffee, 30 ml cream steeped with toasted rolled oats, strained, whipped fresh; the numbers and the oats are ours. (pdf 1076–1077; F7)
anchors.meaning: Two cubes for all; the small care is the warm glass and the cream whipped fresh.

cocktail.closingLine: Two cubes for everyone. For one person, ask how they take it.
cocktail.glassware: a footed glass goblet, about 180 ml, warmed with hot water first (or any heatproof stemmed glass or small handled toddy glass of about that size)
method: **The oat cream, for two glasses.** Put 2 tablespoons (about 10 g) of rolled oats in a dry frying pan over a medium heat. Stir them all the time for 3 to 4 minutes, until they're golden and smell like warm biscuits. Tip them onto a plate and let them cool right down.

Stir the oats into 80 ml of cold heavy cream in a jar and leave it in the fridge for at least two hours (it keeps until the next day). Pour it through a sieve, pressing the oats with a spoon to get the cream out, and throw the oats away. You'll have about 65 ml. Keep it cold.
For each glass, put 30 ml of the oat cream in a cold bowl and whisk it by hand until it thickens and just starts to hold soft peaks, about double its volume. Stop before it goes stiff.
Fill the goblet with hot water, leave it a minute, then pour the water away.
Drop in two brown sugar cubes and pour in 80 ml of hot coffee. Stir until the sugar has gone.
Add 40 ml of Irish whiskey and stir once more.
Spoon the cream gently onto the top, over the back of the spoon, so it floats and covers the coffee right to the rim. Don't stir after this: it's drunk hot through the cool cream.
For the next person, whip the cream again.
cocktail.name: Everybody's

recipe.note: cubes, not syrup: syrup came in when it got famous

recipe.item: hot fresh coffee (filter or drip, not espresso)
toasted-oat cream, whipped by hand just before
recipe.note: heavy cream steeped with rolled oats toasted in a dry pan, then strained; 80 ml of cream and 2 tablespoons of oats make enough for two glasses

cocktail.tagline: You make strangers feel as welcome as old friends.

reading.epigraph: First made for a few important visitors. By 1947, everyone off the plane was offered one.
whoYouAre: Something small goes wrong in a room full of people. Someone arrives soaked, a glass goes over, somebody's aunt doesn't know a soul. Before it's become a thing, you're there with a towel, a dustpan, a chair and a name. You didn't wait to be asked. Sitting there watching would have felt stranger.

And everyone gets the same you. The friend of twenty years and the new neighbour, the boss and the person clearing the plates: the same question about their week, the same cup, made the same way. Having favourites feels a bit selfish to you, a bit unfair, so you don't. What you'd rarely admit is that the people closest to you get exactly what everyone gets. Not a bit more. They'd never say so.
yours: Late in 1944, or early in 1945, Joe Sheridan was a chef at Foynes, in Ireland, a station for flying boats, the planes that landed on water. He was asked to come up with something special to greet some important visitors. He made hot coffee with Irish whiskey and sugar, under a head of cream, in a small glass on a foot.

It started as a welcome for a few. It didn't stay that way. By 1947 it was being offered to every traveller getting off a plane at Shannon: not only the important ones. Everyone. Later it reached San Francisco, got famous, and fame did what fame does: syrup instead of sugar cubes, bigger glasses, cream from a can. Some of the bars that brought it back pride themselves on making it the way Sheridan did.

I like to think that was the part that was really his. Not the recipe: that it went to everyone the same, the visitor with a title and the next passenger off the plane. You'd have done it exactly that way. You don't keep a better version for the people who matter. Everyone who comes in gets the real one.

The cocktail I've made for you keeps the shape of his: a small glass on a foot, sugar cubes, hot coffee, Irish whiskey and fresh cream. The glass is warmed with hot water first. The cubes are brown, two of them: it began with cubes, and the syrup only came with fame. There's a little less whiskey than today's usual recipe, so the coffee under the cream stays gentle. What I've added for you is in the cream. Rolled oats go into a dry pan until they smell like warm biscuits, sit in the cold cream for a couple of hours, and are strained out, so only their taste stays. Oats had their place in Irish whiskey: until the 1950s, they went into the old pot-still Irish whiskey alongside the barley. I like to think that's you: in there alongside everyone, doing your bit. Then the cream is whipped by hand until it only just holds, and spooned on so it floats.

Don't change a thing about how you treat everyone. But being fair to everyone was never meant to mean that nobody gets to be special. Somewhere there's someone close to you who has been getting the same you as the new neighbour, and has never once complained. Give them something nobody else gets. Not more work: an evening, a call that isn't checking in, the good cup. The first of these drinks was made for a few particular guests. Let someone be yours.

anchors.fact: In 1740 Admiral Edward Vernon, commanding the Royal Navy's West Indies station, ordered that his sailors' daily rum ration, until then drunk neat, be issued mixed with water. That was the start of grog. His stated concern was the "pernicious custom" of the men drinking their allowance in drams, "often at once". Oxford gives the danger as men who had to climb high into the rigging. (F1, F2, F3; Oxford GROG pdf 951, SPIRITS IN THE MILITARY pdf 1868)
anchors.meaning: The no nobody else would say, said for the people who have to climb. That it cost him anything to say it isn't on record: signpost it.
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: A reality check · texture: In control

anchors.fact: Four parts water to one of rum (half a pint of rum to a quart of water), split into two servings a day rather than one. The ratio later changed (two to one from 1937 until 1970). (F4; C1)
anchors.meaning: He didn't take it away. He made it last: "one now, and one later." The rule is about pace, not punishment.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The best version of me · drawnToward: Peace

anchors.fact: The order let men who were thrifty buy lime and sugar (out of savings on their provisions) to make it more palatable, which effectively turned it into punch. Palatability was the stated reason. The scurvy benefit is Oxford's later observation, not Vernon's motive. (F5; C2: don't quote "husbandmen")
anchors.meaning: Inside the rule he left room for their own taste. Structure with room in it: scaffolding, not a cage.

anchors.fact: The order had the mixing done in a scuttled butt (Oxford's gloss: "a repurposed barrel half") and served out openly, so the men could be sure they weren't cheated of their full allowance. (F6. "On deck" and "the lieutenant of the watch" are secondary: wordorigins.org)
anchors.meaning: Authority done in plain sight. Anyone can check that the rule is fair.

anchors.fact: The daily tot, always mixed into grog, stayed a formal ritual (the bosun's call "Up spirits!"). When the last ration was issued, on 31 July 1970 ("Black Tot Day"), sailors held mock burials at sea and wore black armbands. (F9, F10; Oxford RUM, NAVY pdf 1701–1702)
anchors.meaning: **Our reading, signposted:** the rule they were handed became something they mourned. Grog was issued for 230 years (1740 → 1970, checked), though the measure itself was cut twice (1824, 1851) and the ratio changed: never "the same measure". Never claim that the 1740 sailors liked it or hated it (L1).
anchors.speaksTo: lens: My future self · drawnToward: Belonging

anchors.fact: Our drink keeps Vernon's first proportion: one measure of rum to four of cold water (F4, 1740 only), with no ice. It's our build, not his recipe: the rum is navy-strength (a style today; the Navy's 54.5% dates from 1866, F11), and it's made as a still highball ("A Highball can be effervescent or still", *Codex* p. 201).
anchors.meaning: The measure is the Nanny's, and nothing melts behind anyone's back: the ratio poured is the ratio drunk (Tomás's physics). Fair, and seen to be fair, the way the cask was.

anchors.fact: Lime juice and a demerara syrup, half a measure each: the two things Vernon let the men buy to make it taste better (F5).
anchors.meaning: The room for someone else's taste, inside a fixed measure. It's fixed in the spec, never "to taste", because a free-for-all isn't this person.

anchors.fact: Sherry vinegar in the syrup. The *Flavor Matrix* lists sherry vinegar among the best pairings for cane syrup and molasses (pdf 240; the entry is about those syrups, not demerara sugar). Vinegar is "the only common food acid that is aromatic" (*LI* p. 59, pdf 63).
anchors.meaning: **Tomás's reading, kept or cut by Wren:** a little sharpness inside the sweetness, care that doesn't only soothe. No historical claim: Vernon's men never had it.

anchors.fact: Reportedly, Vernon wore a coat of grogram, a gum-stiffened waterproof cloth, was nicknamed "Old Grogram", and the drink took the name. Oxford says "reportedly" both times. (F7)
anchors.kind: name (legend; in the reading as "Legend has it", y2)
anchors.meaning: Told only as a legend ("Legend has it", reading v3 y2; changed from "the story goes" for lint). No anchor meaning rests on it. "Old Grog" (the reading's form) is the Abbey's wording (secondary); Oxford has "Old Grogram".

anchors.fact: Don the Beachcomber's Navy Grog (in print 1942: rum, grapefruit, honey) is a punch, not a grog. (F12)
anchors.meaning: Keeps us from calling any tiki "grog" ours.

cocktail.closingLine: Four of water to one of rum. The lime and the sugar are theirs.
cocktail.glassware: tumbler or highball glass (about 300 ml), no ice
method: Make the syrup ahead, an hour or a day before. Warm the sugar and water in a small pan, stirring, until the liquid turns clear. Don't let it boil. Take it off the heat, stir in the sherry vinegar, let it cool, and bottle it. It keeps for about two weeks in the fridge.
Put a jug of water in the fridge so it's properly cold.
Use the same jigger for everything. Pour one jigger of rum into the glass.
Add four jiggers of cold water.
Add half a jigger of lime juice and half a jigger of syrup, and stir a few times. No ice: as it melted, it would change the measure.
cocktail.name: Fair Measure

recipe.item: navy-strength rum (57%; any navy-strength rum, 54.5% or stronger)
recipe.note: strong enough to still taste of rum at four to one
four to one: Vernon's measure, 1740

recipe.item: demerara and sherry vinegar syrup, homemade (below)
recipe.note: the sugar, with a little sharpness kept in it

recipe.item: *for the syrup:* 200 g demerara sugar, 100 ml water, 30 ml sherry vinegar
recipe.note: makes about 250 ml, enough for ten

cocktail.tagline: You think about tomorrow so everyone can enjoy tonight.

reading.epigraph: Most of this glass is plain water. In 1740, that was an order.
whoYouAre: It's late, everyone's having a good time, and you're the one who says "one more, then home." You're the one who checks what's left in the account before the trip gets booked, who asks for a text when they're home, who keeps the Sunday call going long after the others have let it slide. Some people hear a rule. It isn't one, not really. It's what keeps the good thing there tomorrow.

People call you the sensible one, and on worse nights, something less kind. It stings more than you show, because you were never against the fun. You're the reason there's any left in the morning. Everyone else gets to forget the time because you never do. And somewhere under the plans is a fear you wouldn't say out loud: that if you stopped holding it all, it would come apart, and it would be your fault for wanting one night off.
yours: In 1740, Admiral Edward Vernon, in command of the British ships in the West Indies, put a stop to the way his sailors took their daily rum: in drams, often all at once, with work waiting for them high in the rigging. From then on it was mixed with water, at first four parts to one, and served in two portions a day instead of one.

What I like is what he didn't do. The rum stayed. He let the men buy lime and sugar to make it taste better. And he had it mixed in the open, in a half-barrel, so nobody could think they'd been given short measure. Legend has it he was called Old Grog, after the stiff, gum-proofed coat he wore, and the drink took his name.

The ration outlived him by more than two centuries. When the navy poured its last one, in July 1970, sailors held mock burials and wore black armbands. I like to think some of what they were mourning was the order of it: the call of "Up spirits!", the measure, the hour, every day. That's how you hold a line. You don't take the good thing away. You make it last, you leave room for everyone's own taste, and you do it where everyone can see it's fair.

The cocktail I've crafted for you is his order made into a long drink, with something he never had. One jigger of a strong rum, bottled well above the usual strength so the rum isn't lost at four to one, and four jiggers of cold water, measured with the same jigger. Then half a jigger each of fresh lime and a demerara syrup made ahead. There's no ice, because ice would melt and quietly change the measure. What's poured is what's drunk. The thing I added is in the syrup: a splash of sherry vinegar, a vinegar made from sherry, which you can smell as well as taste. So even the sweet part, the part that's handed over, has a little sharpness in it. I don't think you can help that, and I wouldn't want you to.

Next time you set the limit, set it, and then let the rest be theirs to make. Don't check how they did it. Focus on enjoying the fun yourself. The taste was always theirs. It'll still hold, and you might even get that night off.

anchors.fact: David Wondrich, a drinks historian: distillers who were trying to bring back lost spirits often turned to him for the know-how (*Proper* p. 241; W F1).
anchors.meaning: The one who knew. "Had the directions but couldn't drive the car" is Simonson's phrase: paraphrase it or attribute it, never as Wondrich's words.

anchors.fact: An old friend of his had started a distillery in Oregon (Ransom), which had been making brandies and eaux-de-vie. The friend had been thinking about making a gin for a while (*Proper* p. 241; Seestedt in Tales of the Cocktail, 2016, secondary; W F2, F10).
anchors.meaning: The friend's own plan, the one he was hoping to hear was fine. NAME: see C1. Safest is "an old friend with a distillery in Oregon".

anchors.fact: Wondrich advised him to make an Old Tom instead, a sweeter gin from the 1800s. In the friend's own words, "David suggested an Old Tom." He had never heard of it (*Proper* p. 241; Tales 2016; W F3, F10).
anchors.meaning: A plan met by someone who knew something the planner didn't, and said so. VERBS: "advised", "suggested", "told him about", "offered". NEVER "refused", "said no", "talked him out of", "stopped", "saved", "spared". No motive for Wondrich is on record: any "why" is "I like to think".

anchors.fact: "He did." (*Proper* p. 241). Ransom Old Tom reached the market the year after Hayman's (2007), so in 2008. Oxford names the two among the old spirits the revival brought back, and by its writing at least a dozen gins called themselves Old Tom (Oxford OLD TOM GIN pdf 1438; W F5).
anchors.meaning: The advice was taken, and what he pointed to came to exist, with others following. NOT "the first" or "the only" on Oxford's word: Oxford names two and ranks neither. The only sourced "first" is the *Codex* p. 68: "Hayman's was the first to reach the United States", so "the first of the revived Old Toms reached America" is fine (audit v4, R6). Also "essentially unavailable" by the late 1900s, never "gone for decades" (R5). NOT "saved his distillery": nothing says what a plain gin would have done.

anchors.fact: Gary Regan, writing on the Martinez, gives Ransom as the Old Tom he "highly" recommends (*Joy* pdf 336). The *Codex* describes it as lightly aged (p. 68) (W F7, F8).
anchors.meaning: Someone with no stake vouches for it. Use as "a bartender who had no part in it recommends it", or leave it in the dossier.

anchors.fact: In his own book, Wondrich recommends Ransom for an older-style Old Tom and adds a "fair warning" that he had a hand in developing it (*Imbibe!* pdf 68; W F6).
anchors.meaning: He tells you what he knows and what his stake is in the same breath. That's the Sage side's fear of being deceived, answered. Paraphrase it: "fair warning" is his phrase, so quote only those two words if at all.

anchors.fact: Wondrich is the editor-in-chief of the *Oxford Companion*, and he signs its OLD TOM GIN entry (pdf 1439).
anchors.meaning: If the reading uses any Oxford fact about Old Tom, own it in one plain clause ("the same man later wrote the encyclopedia entry on it"). He is also quoted as an authority in *Beside the First* and *As It Was*: that's fine, because here he is the person, not the citation.

cocktail.closingLine: Twist the lemon over it. Then tell someone what they haven't heard of yet.
cocktail.glassware: a small stemmed cocktail glass, chilled, no ice
method: Put the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Pour the gin, the vermouth and both bitters into a mixing glass or a jar. Most Martinez recipes add a little maraschino, a cherry liqueur, here. This one leaves it out, and nothing goes in its place.
Fill it with ice and stir with a long spoon for about 30 seconds, until the outside is very cold. The melting ice is part of the drink: it adds about two-fifths to what you poured.
Empty the serving glass if you filled it, and strain the drink in. No ice in the glass.
Cut a strip of lemon peel, just the yellow part. Twist it over the glass so its oil falls on the drink, then rest it on the rim.
cocktail.name: Instead

recipe.item: Ransom Old Tom gin (recommended), or any Old Tom gin
recipe.note: the gin from the story: an old, slightly sweet style, this one with a little time in barrel

cocktail.tagline: You care enough to ask the difficult question.

reading.epigraph: Someone wanted to make a gin. A friend knew an older one worth making.
whoYouAre: Someone tells you about a pain they've had for weeks, and before they've finished you've asked "since when?" You won't tell them it's probably nothing. Not until you know it's nothing. And when a friend comes to you hoping you'll say the plan is fine, you ask the one question they were hoping nobody would. Kindly. But you ask it, because you know to ask from experience.

Yes would be so much easier, and for an evening they'd like you more for it. You say no anyway, and then you go over it all the way home, wondering if you were too hard. You weren't. You'd just rather be the one who said no than the one who said yes and was wrong.
yours: In the 2000s, some distillers set out to bring back spirits that had simply disappeared. A few had the will but not the know-how, so they went to David Wondrich, a drinks historian. (Later he edited the *Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails* and wrote its Old Tom entry, so some of what I tell you is his.) He knew the way to things he couldn't make himself. One of his old friends had started a distillery in Oregon called Ransom, and wanted to make a gin.

What Wondrich gave him wasn't a verdict on the plan. It was an instead: make an Old Tom, a sweeter, older style of gin that bars used in the 1800s, and by the late 1900s all but impossible to buy. His friend had never heard of it. He made it. Ransom's Old Tom came out in 2008, a year after the first of the revived Old Toms reached America, and at least one bartender's book recommends it by name. In his own book, Wondrich points you to it, and in the same sentence warns you that he had a hand in developing it.

You know the moment before that. A friend tells you the plan, and you can already see the trouble in it. You're good at the question, and you ask it even when it costs you the evening. But I like to think this is the part of you people keep: not the question itself, but that you already knew what to do instead, and you handed it over, and told them what you had riding on it.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from that gin. It's a Martinez, one of the Martini's early names, in print by 1884 and believed to have been made with Old Tom from the start: twice as much Old Tom as sweet vermouth, the way one bartender suggests for today's taste, and two dashes of bitters, stirred until cold. Old Tom is the sweeter kind of gin. But among the sweetened gins of the 1800s, it was the strong one, the one they added the least sugar and water to. That seemed right for you.

Go on asking the question. It's the right one. But the next time a friend's plan isn't fine, don't leave them with only the no. Tell them what you'd make instead. They may never have heard of it. That's exactly why it has to come from you.

anchors.fact: Ada "Coley" Coleman went to work at Claridge's after her father died in 1899. She started in the hotel's flower shop, making buttonholes for gentlemen, before she was moved to the bar, where the wine butler taught her to make a Manhattan. From 1903 she worked the Savoy's American Bar, where customers took her for the head bartender (her title is contested, C6). Oxford judges her the most famous woman bartender in Britain in her 1920s heyday. (F1, F2, F3; Oxford, COLEMAN, ADA, pdf 554)
anchors.meaning: Small things made by hand for other people to wear, long before she made a drink. The hands came first; the bar came later.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Beauty · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: Charles Hawtrey, actor and impresario, one of her regulars, came in worn out from overwork and asked her to make him "quite alive" again (the *Sphere*, 1926). She told the *People* (1925) that she spent hours experimenting until she had a new cocktail for him. (F4, F5)
anchors.meaning: The hours are a fact, in her own words. *Why* she spent them isn't on the record: fondness, pride and duty are all our reading, so signpost them ("I like to think…"). The shape we can state: his answer wasn't a word, it was a thing made for him alone.
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: Comfort · drawnToward: Mastery · texture: Quiet

anchors.fact: Gin and sweet vermouth, with a small measure of Fernet-Branca: one of the first cocktails to use it. In that small dose it adds depth without making the drink plainly bitter. (F6, F9)
anchors.meaning: What made it his was the smallest thing in the glass. The care is in the measure, not the size.

anchors.fact: Oxford gives the Fernet as a range, 5–10 ml (F6; C2 for other proportions). Tasting off the spoon and adding only what the person needs is **our method**. No source says Coleman made it that way.
anchors.meaning: Made to measure: her hours for one tired man, done in a minute for someone you know. (Pitfall: modern technique as origin. Never say "as she did".)
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · texture: In control

anchors.fact: It's the only one of her drinks known to survive, and the first canonical cocktail definitively credited to a woman bartender. The cocktail revival took it up again for its early, unusual Fernet. (F8, F10)
anchors.meaning: Of everything she made, the one we *know* lasted is the one made for one person (some *Savoy Cocktail Book* drinks may be hers: say "known to survive" (or the bartender's "I know of"), never "the only one"; no "we", per the one-voice rule). That's a fact; what it *means* is ours. Own the coincidence plainly.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · drawnToward: Belonging

anchors.fact: In 1920s slang, "hanky panky" meant trickery or conjuring, not its modern sense. (F7)
