anchors.meaning: **Not in the reading** (Wren: tricks belong to *No Accident*, and here it would make her care look like sleight of hand). Kept here so nobody "explains" the name wrongly.

anchors.fact: In December 1925 she and her colleague Kitty Burgess were retired from the Savoy bar, and Harry Craddock took over. (F11; C5)
anchors.meaning: **Not in the reading.** It's a different story (being displaced), and the reason is only Oxford's "it appears".

cocktail.closingLine: Look up before you pour. That's the recipe.
cocktail.glassware: coupe (a stemmed cocktail glass), from the freezer
method: Put a coupe in the freezer.
Pour the gin and the vermouth into a jar or mixing glass, then add one barspoon of Fernet-Branca (about 5 ml).
Fill it with ice and stir for about thirty seconds, until the outside of the glass is very cold.

Taste a drop off the spoon. Then look up at the person it's for. Are they worn out tonight, and do they need the bitter? If they do, add another half spoon and stir a few more turns. Never more than two spoons in all.
Strain it into the cold glass. Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, and drop it in.
Hand it to them yourself.
cocktail.name: Quite Alive

recipe.item: Fernet-Branca (recommended; or any dark, minty Italian fernet)
recipe.note: the measure is the person

cocktail.tagline: You say “I love you” in things people can hold.

reading.epigraph: The smallest thing in this glass is what made it someone's.
whoYouAre: When someone you love is having a hard time, you rarely know what to say. You know what to make: a meal from scratch, a card you started three times, a present you were still finishing at two in the morning because one small thing wasn't right yet. People call it perfectionism. It isn't. To you, a shortcut says "you weren't worth the time". So you never take one.

What they're really holding is proof that someone looked closely at them. What you rarely let anyone see is what it costs you: the evenings you vanish into it, sometimes away from the very person it's for. And the quiet hope, each time you hand it over, that they'll understand what it was saying.
yours: In the 1920s, the most famous woman bartender in Britain was Ada Coleman, known as Coley, at the Savoy in London. She didn't start behind a bar. She began at another London hotel, in its flower shop, making buttonholes for gentlemen to wear. Small things, made by hand, for someone else.

One of her regulars was the actor Charles Hawtrey. He came in once worn out from overwork and asked her to make him "quite alive" again. By her own account, she spent hours experimenting until she had something new for him: gin, sweet vermouth and a little Fernet-Branca, a dark, bitter Italian digestif, the kind once sold in pharmacies. It became the Hanky Panky.

Coley made drinks at the Savoy for more than twenty years. Of everything she made, the only drink of hers known to survive is the one she made for one tired man. That's a coincidence, and I won't pretend it's more. But I like to think she understood what you understand: you can't really tell someone "I can see how tired you are". You can make them something, take the time it takes, and let it say that for you.

So the cocktail I've made for you is her drink, made to measure: gin, sweet vermouth and a barspoon of Fernet, stirred with ice until it's very cold. In a small dose, the Fernet gives it depth without making it plainly bitter. Then you taste a drop off the spoon, and look up at the person it's for before you decide whether they need a little more.

You do your best work alone, out of sight, and hand it over finished. Next time you make something for someone, this or anything else, don't vanish to do it. Make it where they can see you. Let them watch you taste, look up, and add a little more because of the day they've had. They've always had what you made. Let them have you, making it.

anchors.fact: Angostura began in the 1820s as a stomach medicine, made by a surgeon serving with Bolívar's forces in Venezuela, and sold abroad as a remedy. It found its way into drinks "off-label", and most recipes that call for it still use a few dashes. Only gentian and "other spices" are on record: the recipe is secret.
anchors.meaning: A thing used for what it was never meant for, and used well. That's this person with everything they touch. Say "warm spice", never "cinnamon" or "clove".
anchors.speaksTo: lens: One of my many selves · drawnToward: Change · soughtFor: Ideas

anchors.fact: In Brooklyn, Giuseppe Gonzalez made a sour with an ounce and a half of Angostura as its base and only half an ounce of rye.
anchors.meaning: Asking what happens with an ounce of what everyone uses by the dash. It's finding out, not defying anyone. No year (sources give 2008 and 2009), and never "he took it from" anyone.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Wonder · soughtFor: A little chaos

anchors.fact: By his own telling, it didn't win the competition he made it for, he was told nobody would drink it, and he kept making it.
anchors.meaning: Failure barely touches them. Always signposted ("he says", "the way he tells it"). The menu reprint stays out: it's disputed, and it reads as rule-breaking.

anchors.fact: It wasn't an immediate hit. It spread onto menus and spawned many variations, and the *Oxford Companion* uses it as its example of a drink that looks absurd on paper and works in the glass.
anchors.meaning: It didn't stop at one recipe. Other people made their own versions, which is how this person would want their work treated. Never "never settled".
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Freedom · lens: My inner child

anchors.fact: In the printed recipe the whiskey is the small part, half an ounce. Here that slot is the guest's: any unsweetened spirit. The *Cocktail Codex* says a swapped spirit keeps a sour balanced but can't promise it'll taste good.
anchors.meaning: Never the same drink twice. The recipe is ours (lemongrass replaces his orgeat): keep his ounce and a half, never "his recipe". "Balances", not "works".
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Change · soughtFor: A little chaos · texture: Excited

cocktail.closingLine: It'll balance whichever spirit you pour. Whether you like it is the experiment.
cocktail.glassware: coupe (a stemmed cocktail glass), chilled
method: Put a coupe in the freezer.
Pour the Angostura, the lemon juice and the lemongrass syrup into a shaker. Yes, all 45 ml of the bitters.

Now pick the accent: any unsweetened spirit on your shelf, such as rye, gin, mezcal, rum, brandy or whisky. Not a liqueur; it would make the drink too sweet. Try one you haven't used here before. Add 15 ml.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold.
Strain it into the cold glass.
cocktail.name: Off-Label

preparations.text: (makes about 250 ml; keeps two weeks in the fridge): slice 2 lemongrass stalks thinly and bruise them with the back of a knife. Warm them in a pan with 200 g sugar and 200 ml water, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Take it off the heat, leave it for 30 minutes, then strain it into a clean bottle.
preparations.title: Lemongrass syrup

recipe.item: Angostura aromatic bitters (recommended; or another aromatic bitters)
recipe.note: yes, the whole measure

recipe.item: the accent: any unsweetened spirit you have open (rye, gin, mezcal, rum, brandy, whisky)
recipe.note: yours to change, every time

cocktail.tagline: You've never made the same thing twice. Not even when you tried.

reading.epigraph: Bitters usually come by the dash. This drink is built on them.
whoYouAre: Hand you instructions and you'll follow them, right up to the moment you don't. You start things before you know what they'll be. That isn't a hole in the plan. It's the part you like best: finding out.

Some of what you try doesn't work, and you honestly don't mind. You rarely mention those ones, and there are more of them than anyone guesses. What gets under your skin is the opposite: something works, and everyone wants it exactly like last time. Being asked to repeat yourself feels like a door closing. Stand next to you long enough and people start saying what you say: "let me try something." You've shown them that something that didn't work isn't a disaster. It's just the next thing to change.
yours: You've probably seen the bottle behind a bar. Almost nobody pours more than a few dashes of it. It's Angostura, and it began in the 1820s as a medicine: a surgeon in Venezuela made it for soldiers' stomachs. It was never meant for drinks. Bartenders borrowed it anyway, and in their hands it stayed a seasoning, hardly ever the main thing.

Then a bartender in Brooklyn, Giuseppe Gonzalez, made a sour (spirit, citrus and sugar, shaken) with an ounce and a half of it. The bitters became the base. The whiskey, just half an ounce, became the accent. The way he tells it, the drink didn't win the competition he made it for, and he was told nobody would drink it. It wasn't an immediate hit. But it spread, and the *Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails* now uses it as its example of a recipe that looks absurd on paper and works in the glass.

He wasn't trying to be clever, I like to think. He just wanted to know what would happen. That's the question you ask about everything, and like him, you'd rather find out than be told. And it didn't stop at one recipe. Bartenders went on to make their own versions of it, which is exactly how you'd want something of yours to be treated.

So the cocktail I've made for you keeps his ounce and a half of bitters and his lemon, and changes two things. His almond syrup is gone. In its place is a syrup of lemongrass, which sits beautifully beside warm spice and citrus. And his half ounce of whiskey is now yours to choose: any unsweetened spirit you have open. Gin, mezcal, rum, a smoky whisky. Every one balances, and every one makes a different drink. It's shaken hard and served in a wide, shallow stemmed glass. The bitters stay. Only the accent moves.

It didn't win, Gonzalez says, and he kept making it anyway. Somewhere you've got something you left half-tried: a recipe, a plan, an idea you walked away from just as it started working. Go back to it. Not to make it the way it was. To find out what it turns into when you stay.

anchors.fact: In the 1890s a New Orleans saloonkeeper, Henry Charles Ramos, put two existing drinks together, a Silver Fizz and a Cream Lemonade, and made it his way: shaken with the soda already in, until the ice had vanished into the drink. He called it the "One and Only One". Year of invention not established. (F2, F3, F4; C1)
anchors.meaning: Something new made from two old things, on the condition that it be made fully.

anchors.fact: Beside each bartender stood one or two young Black men hired only to shake (Mardi Gras, 1899–1909). By Mardi Gras 1915 there were thirty-five men doing nothing but the shaking, each working until his arms gave out, then passing the shaker on down the line. The 1915 source gives no age or race for the thirty-five. (F6, F7)
anchors.meaning: He didn't shorten the shake when demand outgrew one pair of arms. He added arms. A vision this size is never one person's. (That he never *considered* shortening it is **our reading**.)
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Mastery · soughtFor: Courage · texture: In control

anchors.fact: Ramos had always given his recipe out, which helped the drink spread; when Prohibition shut his bar he went on giving it, and in 1925 he dictated it to a newspaper. In San Francisco, Duncan Nicol kept his Pisco Punch mix secret, and it died with him. (F10, F11, F12; Oxford pdf 1609)
anchors.meaning: The handover: clear enough for someone else to carry on. His motive isn't on the record, so any "why" must be signposted ("I like to think…").
anchors.speaksTo: lens: My future self · soughtFor: Honesty

anchors.fact: He died in 1928. The drink came back after Repeal, and it is still a test of a bartender's skill. A century of bartenders keeps inventing ways to meet his standard (the dry shake, even paint-can shakers), and his formula still works. (F13, F14, F15)
anchors.meaning: Still being carried on, by strangers, to a standard he set. Not finished: kept.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Mastery · lens: The best version of me

anchors.fact: It's the only great classic named for the bartender who made it. (F16)
anchors.meaning: Not used in the reading: the Visionary's mirror is the chain, not the signature (Wren: the name belongs to the Auteur). Kept as a sourced fact for the dossier.

anchors.fact: His own 1925 formula calls for three or four drops of orange flower water. A New York recipe of 1895 for the same drink left it out. (F9)
anchors.meaning: Kept, "as written in the recipe he gave away": dropping it would be making his drink smaller to suit our evening. Robin cleared it (2026-09-25: "completely fine"); it is now in the ingredient table with no allergen.

anchors.fact: In 1925 he told the reporter to keep shaking until no bubble was left and the drink was smooth and snowy white: a standard, not a time. The printed recipe says only "well shaken and strained". (F18)
anchors.meaning: The finish is set by the work, not the clock: the foam has to be earned. Whatever epigraph the rework picks, if it says "earned" it rests on this row.

cocktail.closingLine: Pass the shaker when your arms give out. Just don't let it stop.
cocktail.glassware: tall glass (a highball or Collins glass), no ice
method: Put a tall glass in the freezer.
Pour the gin, both juices, the syrup, the cream and the orange flower water into a shaker. Add the egg white last.
Close the shaker and shake it hard with no ice for about fifteen seconds, until it froths.
Fill it with ice and shake hard for five minutes. That's longer than you'll want to. If someone is with you, hand them the shaker halfway, and don't let it stop.
Strain it into the cold glass through a small sieve. No ice in the glass.
Pour in the soda slowly, a little at a time, tapping the base of the glass on the table now and then, until a firm white cap of foam stands on top.
No garnish. Serve it while the foam stands.
cocktail.name: Down the Line

recipe.note: as written in the recipe he gave away

cocktail.tagline: Your dreams have gravity. People want to be part of making them real.

reading.epigraph: Anyone can have the recipe. The foam has to be earned.
whoYouAre: You see the finished thing first. Long before anyone else can, you can describe it: its size, its shape, what it will change. And you describe it so clearly that people want to help build it.

What they don't see is the arithmetic you do alone: how far away the end is, what it will cost, whether you're the one slowing it down. Some nights you doubt the whole thing. You never do it out loud, because other people are building on your belief. What frightens you isn't that it won't get finished. It's that you'll make it smaller so it can be.
yours: In New Orleans, more than a hundred years ago, a saloonkeeper named Henry Ramos served a gin fizz unlike anyone else's: gin, lemon and lime, sugar, cream and egg white, shaken until the ice was gone and the drink had turned into a soft white cloud. It was slow to make. Then it became famous, which meant more of them, every one just as slow.

The obvious thing would have been to shorten the shake. He didn't. He hired more hands instead. Beside each bartender stood one or two young Black men hired only to shake. By Mardi Gras in 1915 there were thirty-five men doing nothing but the shaking, each one working until his arms gave out, then passing the shaker down the line. The drink was never one man's work, and it couldn't have existed without theirs. And Ramos had always given the recipe away to anyone who asked. When Prohibition closed his bar, he went on giving it, and in 1925 he dictated it to a newspaper. He died three years later.

I don't know why, but I like to think he knew what you know: the recipe was never the hard part. The hard part was refusing to make it smaller, and keeping it whole even when it needed more hands than he had. And when he couldn't carry it any further, he left it clear enough for other people to carry on. They still are. A century later, bartenders are still inventing ways to reach his standard, and his formula still works.

So this is his drink, made to his standard: gin, lemon and lime, a little sugar, cream, egg white, three drops of orange flower water as written in the recipe he gave away, and soda to finish. Bartenders today shake it once without ice, to build the foam, and then hard with ice for five minutes, far longer than anyone expects. The soda goes in slowly, until a white cap forms on top. If someone is with you, hand them the shaker halfway. It can't be made halfway. It can be handed on.

So, a proposal. Think of the thing you've been quietly trimming so that it fits: your time, your budget, other people's patience. Put it back to its real size, and write it down that way, not the version that sounds reasonable: clear enough that someone else could pick it up and carry on. Then give it to them. Things this size are never finished by one person. But someone has to hold out for the whole of it.

anchors.fact: By the end of the 1970s the ordinary Margarita was mostly sour mix, cheap triple sec and not much tequila. At the family restaurant where Julio Bermejo tended bar in San Francisco, a plain neighbourhood place, the Margaritas used fresh lime but also sour mix and cheap blended tequila.
anchors.meaning: The crowded, mediocre version was the norm, and nobody there was asking for anything else.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: A reality check

anchors.fact: In the mid-1980s he tasted a 100% agave tequila and decided to sell only tequila made that way (100% agave), though it cost about four times as much and he raised prices by 75 cents. He described it as a decision made as a young person with no authority. People were slow to notice.
anchors.meaning: The first cut cost him and nobody applauded. The unseen work (Wren): leaving out is harder than putting in. His own words may be paraphrased; anything more about *why* is signposted.

anchors.fact: He threw out the sour mix. Later, once agave syrup reached the US, he used it in place of the orange liqueur. The drink came together slowly, over years: tequila, fresh lime and agave syrup, nothing else. Year not established.
anchors.meaning: Nothing added, three things taken out. What's left shows the spirit instead of covering it.

anchors.fact: He called it the house Margarita. Other people gave it the restaurant's name.
anchors.meaning: He didn't sign it. Nobody credits what isn't there, and he didn't ask them to.

anchors.fact: Because it's so simple it turns up in ordinary places: in 2014 a Denny's in New York offered it.
anchors.meaning: Not in the reading (Wren, v1; I agreed in round 4: read cold it's the sting, and the reading is the shortest in the set). Kept for Robin.

anchors.fact: He thins his agave syrup with an equal amount of water so it pours cleanly and none is left clinging to the spoon or jigger.
anchors.meaning: The one habit of his that goes in the glass. Never "his recipe": the measures are Tomás's (Bermejo's own run out of range on acid).

anchors.fact: Tequila is by law made from blue agave; agave syrup is commonly made from blue agave too. This recipe names blue agave syrup, so the syrup and the tequila come from the same plant.
anchors.meaning: The spark was already in the drink: one choice that made another thing unnecessary. **Only true if the recipe names blue agave syrup.** Never claim it of Bermejo's own drink.

anchors.fact: Clear ice made at home: water freezes slowly from the top of an open, insulated cooler; the growing crystals push air and impurities into the last water to freeze, which is drained or cut away (*Liquid Intelligence* pp. 68–70).
anchors.meaning: Not in the reading (cut in v2); lives in the recipe, method step 1 and the closing line. It's clear because of how it froze; the cut only removes what the freezing pushed out. Never "clear because it was cut" (audit X4). Tomás's gesture from *Liquid Intelligence* p. 69, never Bermejo's or Tommy's.

anchors.fact: The Margarita is traditionally served with a salted rim. Some bartenders salt only half the rim so the guest can choose each sip or skip it, and a properly balanced drink doesn't need the salt.
anchors.meaning: The one thing kept that isn't needed: there for the drink's history and for the guest's choice. It's the ending's proof. Never "he salted half".

cocktail.closingLine: Cut the cloudy part off the ice. Then stop cutting.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass (a short, heavy tumbler), salt on half the rim, one large clear ice cube
method: A day or two ahead, make the clear ice (above).
Rub the cut side of a squeezed lime half around the outside of the rim (the outside only), halfway round the glass only. Roll that wet half in a saucer of salt. The other half stays bare.
Put your clear cube in the glass.
Pour the tequila, the lime juice and the thinned agave syrup into a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold.
Strain it over the clear cube. Nothing on top.
cocktail.name: Half a Rim

preparations.text: stir equal parts blue agave syrup and water until they're one. Keeps two weeks in the fridge. (He thins his so none of it stays behind in the measure.)
preparations.title: Thinned agave syrup

preparations.text: (a day or two ahead): fill a small picnic cooler with hot tap water, leave it on the counter to cool, then put it in the freezer with the lid off. It freezes from the top down, pushing the air and the cloudiness into the last water to freeze. Take it out before it's frozen solid, tip the block out and cut away the cloudy part. Let the block sit until it looks wet and clear, not frosty. Then score it with a bread knife and tap the back of the blade with a rolling pin until one large cube splits off. Keep the spares in a bag in the freezer.
preparations.title: Clear ice

recipe.note: the same plant as the tequila
made a day ahead, with the cloudy part cut off

recipe.item: kosher salt, for half the rim
recipe.note: not needed; there if you want it

cocktail.tagline: You take things away, and somehow there's more.

reading.epigraph: Its maker called it the house Margarita. Other people named it after the restaurant.
whoYouAre: You rewrite a message three times, and every time it gets shorter. The last version looks like it took a minute. Most of what you make is what you said no to.

You don't want less. You want to feel each thing properly, and too much of anything drowns it out. Some people mistake the quiet for coldness, or for plain. The ones who know you know it's room: what you make leaves space, and people find their own meaning in it.
yours: In the mid-1980s, Julio Bermejo was back behind the bar of his family's restaurant in San Francisco, an ordinary neighbourhood place, pouring Margaritas the usual way: fresh lime, but sour mix too, cheap tequila, orange liqueur. Then he tasted a tequila made only from agave, and decided the bar would pour nothing but tequila made that way, at about four times the cost. He made that call, he says, "as a young person with no authority".

Over the years the sour mix went, and then the orange liqueur, with agave syrup in its place. What was left was tequila, lime, a little agave, and nothing to hide behind. He called it the house Margarita. Other people gave it the restaurant's name.
I like to think you'd recognise those years: all that work, to end up with less. Nobody thanks you for what isn't there.

So this one keeps his three ingredients and his habit of thinning the syrup with water, so none of it clings to the spoon. The measures are mine. The syrup is blue agave, the same plant the tequila comes from.

Sometimes you cut one thing too many, and it's usually the one that was only there because you loved it. The salt on this glass isn't needed. It's there on one side, in case you want it. Leave one thing like that in whatever you make next. Not because it's needed. Because you like it.

anchors.fact: In 1886 four men named Nix imported tomatoes from the West Indies into New York and paid the 10% duty on vegetables, under protest, because fruit came in free, and sued to get it back. In 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled that botanically the tomato is the fruit of a vine, like cucumbers, beans and peas, but that in the everyday speech of the people who buy and sell food it's a vegetable, so for the tariff it was taxed as one.
anchors.meaning: The Court saw both and picked the dinner table's word, for a tax. Nobody was wronged and nothing was misfiled by mistake; the everyday name won over the botanical one, for a tax, the way it usually does. **Not a horoscope** (Wren): the guest isn't the misfiled tomato.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Ideas

anchors.fact: At trial both sides read dictionary definitions into evidence (the importers: "fruit", "vegetables", "tomato"; the collector: pea, egg plant, cucumber, squash, pepper), and two witnesses who'd sold fruit and vegetables for thirty years gave evidence.
anchors.meaning: Everyone reached for the book. *I like to think* the guest would have skipped the dictionaries and served it for dessert (Wren's sideways leap; our reading, signposted, never history).

anchors.fact: The Court's reason was where it's eaten: tomatoes are served with or after the soup, fish or meat, not like fruit, as dessert.
anchors.meaning: Where a thing sat at dinner decided what it was called. The glass simply moves it to the other seat: say what you see before anyone rules on it.

anchors.fact: Botanically a berry is a fruit that encloses its seeds. By that definition the tomato is a berry; the strawberry isn't (it's an aggregate fruit).
anchors.meaning: The fact that sounds made up and is true: the guest's "this is going to sound weird, but…", correct a minute later. Always "botanically".

anchors.fact: *The Flavor Matrix* lists strawberries as a substitute for tomato (pdf 244) and tomato as one of vanilla's surprise pairings (pdf 256). Here cherry tomatoes are crushed with sugar and a split vanilla pod into a syrup, made the way the *Cocktail Codex* makes its cold-blended strawberry syrup (equal weights of fruit and sugar, blended, sieved, p. 47), tomatoes in the strawberries' place, and shaken into a daiquiri (rum, lime, syrup; pp. 105–106).
anchors.meaning: Tomás's build, not a historical recipe. The strangeness is in the recipe, not in a trick: it tastes of ripe red fruit and vanilla before it tastes of an idea. Served straight-faced, like the guest's odd remark.

cocktail.closingLine: Tell them it's tomato before they taste it.
cocktail.glassware: coupe, chilled
method: A day ahead, make the syrup (above).
Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Pour the rum, the lime juice and the syrup into a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold.
Empty the glass if it's full of ice water. Strain the drink into it through a small sieve, so no bits of tomato get through.
Cut a small slit in the bottom of a cherry tomato and sit it on the rim, where the strawberry would go.
cocktail.name: The Other Berry

preparations.text: (a day ahead; makes enough for a dozen drinks or more): put 250 g ripe cherry tomatoes and 250 g white sugar in a blender and blend until completely smooth and the sugar has dissolved. Don't heat it. Push it through a fine sieve into a jar, pressing the pulp to get all the liquid out, and throw the skins and seeds away. Split a vanilla pod lengthways, scrape the seeds into the jar and drop the pod in. Leave it in the fridge overnight, then take the pod out. It keeps up to two weeks in the fridge. Taste it before you use it, and if it fizzes at all, throw it out. (No pod? Half a teaspoon of vanilla extract instead.)
preparations.title: Cherry-tomato and vanilla syrup

recipe.note: made the way you'd make a strawberry syrup

recipe.item: small ripe cherry tomato, for the rim
recipe.note: where the strawberry would sit

cocktail.tagline: You make people laugh at things they'll never see the same way again.

reading.epigraph: Made like a strawberry daiquiri. There isn't a strawberry in it.
whoYouAre: You've started a hundred sentences with "this is going to sound weird, but…". Then you say what you saw: the thing that looks like something else, two ideas nobody thought belonged together. There's a pause, then a laugh. About a minute later, it doesn't sound weird at all.

None of it is a performance. You're just saying what's there. You laugh along, but you meant it, and it stings a little when it's taken as only a joke. So the strangest things you see, you mostly don't say. What you can't stand is the sensible version: an idea sanded down until it fits in. What you give people is a second look at things they thought they knew.
yours: In 1886, four men named Nix brought tomatoes into New York from the West Indies. They paid the tax on vegetables, under protest, because fruit came in free, and sued to get the money back. At the trial, both sides read dictionaries aloud. The importers looked up "fruit", "vegetables" and "tomato"; the other side looked up "pea", "cucumber" and "squash". Two men who'd sold produce for thirty years gave evidence.

The case reached the US Supreme Court, and in 1893 it answered. Botanically, the Court said, the tomato is the fruit of a vine. But the people who buy and sell food call it a vegetable, because it's served with the soup, the fish or the meat, not as dessert. So for the tariff, it was a vegetable. And botany goes further than the Court did: the tomato is, botanically, a berry. The strawberry isn't.

My guess is you'd have skipped the dictionaries. You'd have looked at it, red, its seeds kept on the inside the way a berry keeps them, and served it for dessert. It's what you do with everything: you go by what a thing is, not by where it usually sits.

So this is a daiquiri (rum, lime and sugar, shaken), made the way you'd make a strawberry one, with the tomato in the strawberry's seat. The syrup is made the way a strawberry syrup is: ripe cherry tomatoes blended cold with sugar, plus a vanilla pod, because vanilla and tomato, surprisingly, go well together. It tastes of ripe red fruit and vanilla first, and only then of an idea. There's no trick in it. It's the tomato, served where it looked like it belonged.

You apologise in advance for things you'll turn out to be right about. Drop the "this is going to sound weird". It gives people a way to laugh it off before they've looked. Say what you saw, plainly, the first time. Then let them catch up. They usually do, about a minute later.

anchors.fact: In 1993 Ted Breaux, a research scientist in the Louisiana petroleum industry and not in the drinks trade, heard a colleague call absinthe the green liqueur that made people crazy. He'd seen the word in New Orleans, where he grew up, without knowing exactly what it was. He read Barnaby Conrad's book on it three times, got in touch with the author, and tried distilling it himself.
anchors.meaning: *Our reading:* he fell for something he knew from a sentence and a book. Nobody asked him to; the thing itself was enough.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Ideas

anchors.fact: Then he got two old bottles of absinthe, still sealed, called them the Rosetta stones, tasted them, and said they were a lot better than what he was making.
anchors.meaning: *Our reading:* the moment he could taste the difference was also the moment he was alone with it (Wren). His motive on record is setting right an injustice; the love is ours to say, signposted.

anchors.fact: He kept going. In 2004, still unable to make it in America, he went to a distillery in France and began producing his own absinthe, a couple of thousand cases a year.
anchors.meaning: More than ten years from the sentence to the bottle. Not practice for mastery: he went back to the same thing because he loved it (Wren's line against the Old Master).

anchors.fact: *Louche* is French for cloudy, shadowy, and so disreputable. It's the word for the opal cloud that forms when water meets absinthe, as the anise oil drops out of solution. A good louche is one of the tests of a well-made absinthe.
anchors.meaning: The same word names its bad name and its beauty. What looked disreputable from outside is, from inside, the proof of care.

anchors.fact: The traditional drip: ice-cold water added slowly, about five parts to one, so the oils come out fully; drunk slowly, like wine. In the early 1800s it was sweetened with syrup in the glass; the spoon and sugar cube came later.
anchors.meaning: Ours is richer than five to one, with a cranberry syrup where the old syrup went. The cloud only comes for whoever waits for it: a thing you love opening up a little at a time.

anchors.fact: Anethole gives anise and fennel their flavour (Oxford LOUCHE; *Flavor Matrix* pdf 116); the Matrix gives fennel a surprise partner in Vaccinium, the cranberry's genus.
anchors.meaning: Tomás's build, not Breaux's. Carrying the fennel pairing over to absinthe through anethole is our inference. A love affair between two things nobody introduced.

cocktail.closingLine: Wait for the cloud. Then bring the red up into it.
cocktail.glassware: a stemmed water goblet or a large wine glass (240 ml or more)
method: Put a jug of water in the fridge with plenty of ice, so it's as cold as it gets.
Pour 15 ml of cranberry syrup into the bottom of the glass.
Pour the absinthe in slowly, down the inside of the glass, so it floats on the syrup instead of mixing into it.

Hold the jug just above the glass and let the iced water fall into the absinthe in the thinnest trickle you can, a few drops at a time (no ice in the glass). Take a minute or two. The cloud comes up from where the water lands, and the red stays underneath.
Look at it. Then stir it once, all the way to the bottom, and drink it slowly.
cocktail.name: Rosetta

preparations.text: (makes enough for a dozen drinks or more; keeps two weeks in the fridge): weigh 200 g unsweetened, 100% cranberry juice (not cranberry "cocktail") and 200 g white sugar into a jar. Close it and shake, then leave it a few minutes and shake again, until the sugar has completely dissolved. No heat.
preparations.title: Cranberry syrup

recipe.note: in the glass first, the way absinthe was sweetened before the spoon

recipe.item: Lucid absinthe (recommended), or any absinthe verte of 55% or stronger
recipe.note: Lucid is made to Ted Breaux's recipe
added slowly, a few drops at a time

cocktail.tagline: The things you love become worlds you never finish exploring.

reading.epigraph: The French word for the cloud in this glass also means disreputable.
whoYouAre: There's one thing you keep going back to. A song, a recipe, a drawing you've started over so many times that nobody else can see the changes any more. People think you're repeating yourself. You're not. Every time, you notice something you missed. When someone asks why it matters so much, you explain the details, the how, the history, because "I love it" sounds like too much.

And when you finally show it to someone, you watch their face. You're not waiting for praise. You're waiting to see if they felt it too. The word that hurts you most isn't "no". It's "nice". Still, spend enough time near you and people start to care about things a little more than they planned to. You make loving something that much look like what it is: a pleasure.
yours: Ted Breaux grew up in New Orleans seeing the word absinthe, without ever knowing quite what it was. In 1993, working as a research scientist in the Louisiana oil industry, with nothing to do with bars, he heard a colleague call it the green liqueur that made people crazy. That sentence was enough. He bought a book about absinthe, read it three times, got in touch with its author, and started trying to distil it himself.

Then two old bottles of absinthe, still sealed, came into his hands. He called them his Rosetta stones. He tasted them and said plainly that they were a lot better than what he was making. He didn't stop. It was more than ten years from that first sentence to the absinthe he began making at a distillery in France in 2004. He says he did it to set right an injustice. I believe him. I also don't think anyone reads the same book three times for justice. I think you have a pair of sealed bottles of your own: the first time something got you, and you've held everything up against it since.

So this glass is mine, not his. Absinthe is made with wormwood, anise and fennel, and a book of flavour pairings gives fennel an unlikely match: cranberry. The cranberry syrup goes in first, the way absinthe was sweetened before the spoon and the sugar cube came along. The absinthe goes over it, then iced water, a few drops at a time. As the water falls, the clear green turns to a pale, shifting cloud. The French call it the louche, and the same word means shady, disreputable. Its bad name and its beauty share one word. A good cloud is one of the ways you tell it was made with care. Then one stir, and the red comes up through the white and turns it rose. The feeling doesn't spoil the careful part. It's what gives it colour.

Next time you show someone the thing you love, leave out the how. Tell them what got you, the way one sentence got him. They may never taste the difference you can. But they'll hear it in your voice, and that's the part you've been waiting for them to feel.

anchors.fact: Milk punch (in general, bowl or bottle) is on record from 1688; the earliest written recipe is from 1711. Oxford doesn't date the curdled kind to 1688; our earliest curdled recipe on the page is Franklin's (1763). In the bottled kind, milk is curdled and strained out, and what's left is smooth and stable. It kept without a fridge: bottles were found in Charles Dickens's cellar after his death in 1870 (no age given).
anchors.meaning: A makeover that holds (Wren). The after wasn't a trick for one evening; people put it in the cellar.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Change · lens: The best version of me

anchors.fact: Benjamin Franklin wrote a milk-punch recipe into a 1763 letter: boiling milk goes into the punch, it stands two hours, then it's run through a jelly-bag "till it is clear" (his words; for the dossier, not the reveal word), then bottled.
anchors.meaning: The ruined-looking middle is written into the recipe as a wait. Nobody panics in a recipe. Franklin wrote it down; he didn't invent it.

anchors.fact: Dave Arnold made alcoholic Arnold Palmers for a film crew in 2012, and everyone agreed they weren't very good. Afterwards he washed tea vodka with milk: the astringency fell away, the tea flavour stayed strong, and the drink went on his bar's menu.
anchors.kind: the turn (before and after, on the record)
anchors.meaning: Not turned into something else: more like itself. The harsh edge goes and the tea stays. "That's so you", said of a drink.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The best version of me · texture: Bright

anchors.fact: The curds are what do it: the milk's casein binds the harsh, astringent compounds and leaves with them. You stir the curds gently so they gather the free casein, and don't break them up.
anchors.meaning: The mess is the method. The part that looks like failure is the part doing the work, and only the one who's seen it before can stand there calmly.

anchors.fact: Arnold found an "unintended side benefit": the whey stays behind, so the washed spirit comes out silky. It fades over about a week.
anchors.meaning: The Magician's fear is unintended results; here the unintended result is the best bit. Said lightly.

anchors.fact: Tamarind: a brown, sticky pulp whose sour is mostly tartaric acid, reputed to be both the most acidic and the sweetest fruit; the *Flavor Matrix* gives it as a surprise partner for dairy. Jerry Thomas printed a Tamarind Punch in 1867. In ours (v2) it gives most of the sour (about 60%, Tomás's arithmetic), with 10 ml lime; together they break the milk.
anchors.meaning: Tomás's build, not history's milk punch. The least glamorous thing in the pantry given the lead, and it still tastes of tamarind at the end (Wren's guard).

cocktail.closingLine: Leave it overnight, and don't fix what you find.
cocktail.glassware: a small tumbler (rocks glass), chilled, no ice
method: Put the tea in the rum in a jar, shake it, and leave it 20 to 30 minutes, until it's as dark as strong tea. Strain out the leaves.
Make the tamarind water.
Mix the tea rum, tamarind water, lime and demerara syrup in a jug. Taste it. It should be too sour to enjoy: the milk softens it. If it isn't, add lime a little at a time until it is.

Pour the milk into a large bowl. Pour the punch into the milk slowly, stirring gently as you go (the punch into the milk, never the milk into the punch). Within a minute or so the milk breaks into soft curds, like scrambled egg in cloudy liquid. It looks ruined. That's right.
Stop stirring. Leave it an hour.

Set a sieve lined with a paper coffee filter over a clean jug, and pour everything in, curds and all. The first cup runs cloudy: pour it back over the curds. Once the curds have settled on the filter, they do the cleaning. Leave it to drip in the fridge overnight. Don't press it.
Bottle what came through and keep it in the fridge; it's at its silkiest in the first week. Throw away the curds.
Pour it cold from the bottle into a chilled small tumbler, about 125 ml. No ice.
cocktail.name: Overnight

cocktail.tagline: You see what makes someone themselves, and change everything around to let it shine.

reading.epigraph: Last night, this drink looked like a mistake.
whoYouAre: Show you almost anything and you see what it could be: the chair someone put out on the pavement, a friend's flat, the haircut they've had since school. Once you start on it, you'll change nearly everything, except the one thing that makes it theirs. You find that part first, and build the rest around it. So the words you're hoping for at the end aren't "I'd never have recognised it." They're "That's so you."

What nobody sees is the middle. There's always a point where it looks worse than when you started: the room stripped to the walls, the paint half on, a friend at the mirror not sure what you've done. You're the only one who isn't worried. You've been through enough middles to know the mess is part of how it works. What worries you comes later, once you've gone: that it all slides back, or that it turns out in some way you didn't mean. What stays is how you looked at them: as if the best of them was worth moving everything else for. Most people have never been looked at like that.
yours: In 2012, Dave Arnold was asked to make Arnold Palmers, iced tea and lemonade, with alcohol in them, for a film crew. He made several. Everyone agreed they weren't very good. Afterwards he tried something that sounds like a way to make it worse: he poured his tea-flavoured vodka into milk. The milk curdled, which looks exactly like a mistake. But the curds do the work. They catch the harsh, drying edge of the tea and carry it off with them, and what comes through is smooth. The tea flavour, he wrote, was still very strong. It went on his bar's menu. It had also come out silky, which he hadn't planned at all. He called that an "unintended side benefit".

He wasn't the first to curdle a drink on purpose. Milk punch is on record from 1688, and by 1763 Benjamin Franklin was writing the curdled kind into a letter: pour boiling milk into the punch, leave it to stand for two hours, then strain it. The part where it looks ruined is right there in the recipe, written as a wait. And made that way, it kept. Bottles of it were found in Charles Dickens's cellar after he died.

Here's what I see in it, and it's only my reading. Nobody turned that tea into something else. The harsh part went, and what was left tasted more like itself. And the part that looked like failure was the part doing the work. You've known that for a long time. It's how you can stand in the middle of a mess and not flinch.

The one I'd make you starts with tamarind: a brown, sticky pulp, about the least glamorous thing in a kitchen. It's most of the sour in the drink, with a little lime, and together they break the milk. With them go aged rum steeped with black tea, and a little brown sugar. It's made a day ahead: all of it stirred into milk, left to curdle, and strained back through its own curds. What comes through is smooth, softer than what went in, and it still tastes of tamarind. It's poured cold, from the bottle. Whoever drinks it never sees the middle.

Next time something you've changed comes out differently from the picture in your head, don't fix it straight away. Give it a night. Look at it the way you'd look at that chair on the pavement. Arnold was only trying to get rid of a harsh edge, and he got silk. Some of your best work will be the part you didn't mean.

anchors.fact: A drink called the Cosmopolitan was already around San Francisco: a newspaper writer met it in 1987 as a Kamikaze with cranberry, and Cecchini remembers it as cheap vodka, bottled lime and grenadine (accounts differ). Most likely in 1988, at the Odeon in New York, he remade it: a lemon vodka new that year, the fresh lime and Cointreau the bar used in its Margaritas, and a little of the sweetened cranberry it kept for another drink.
anchors.meaning: He didn't invent something from nothing to be first. He fixed a thing he didn't think much of, for himself, with what was to hand.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Taste

anchors.fact: He made it as a staff drink, and was puzzled when customers started ordering it.
anchors.meaning: Going first is private before it's public. The Trend Setter isn't launching anything; they're just liking it.

anchors.fact: Other downtown bars began making it, "wrong and badly" in his words. By 1990 it was all over New York, and it became the one cocktail of its era that was a household name.
anchors.meaning: Once it's everyone's, it's usually done a bit worse. Said plainly, no bitterness.

anchors.fact: The young craft bartenders who came after rejected it (the flavoured vodka and the sweetened cranberry), and some bars wouldn't stock cranberry so they'd never have to make it. For years bartenders gave him grief for it and he'd say sorry. He shirked the credit, and in 2014 he said that five years earlier he'd have asked to be "unshackled" from it.
anchors.meaning: The real wound: not the crowd, but the people you respect rolling their eyes, and the pull to disown your own thing. Wanting out still lets them decide.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Courage

anchors.fact: "That changed" (Simonson). As of 2026 (Lascelles, secondary) he still makes it at his own Long Island Bar in Brooklyn: 2:1:1:1, in a saucer coupe, with a lemon twist, and he likes it "shrill".
anchors.meaning: Take it back and make it your way, even now it's everyone's. Nothing on record says he ever stopped making it, and that's the point: he stopped letting others decide how he felt about it.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: My future self · texture: In control

anchors.fact: Three basil leaves, shaken with the drink and strained out. The *Flavor Matrix* gives basil as a surprise pairing for the berry family, cranberry included (pdf 52). The proportions stay his (2:1:1:1).
anchors.meaning: His spine, your mark. Keeping something and still making it yours: a seasoning, not a correction.

cocktail.closingLine: Shake it hard, keep it sharp, and serve it to whoever rolls their eyes.
cocktail.glassware: a saucer coupe (a wide, shallow stemmed glass), chilled
method: Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you make the drink and tip that out before you pour.
Drop three basil leaves into the shaker. Add the vodka, orange liqueur, lime juice and cranberry.
Fill the shaker with ice, close it, and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is almost too cold to hold.
Pour it into the glass through the shaker's strainer, with a small tea strainer held underneath, so no bits of basil or ice get through.
Hold the lemon peel over the drink, coloured side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the surface. Then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Still Yours

recipe.note: the lemon vodka that came out the year he most likely made it

the part that's yours

cocktail.tagline: You love what you love, and somehow everyone else starts loving it too.

reading.epigraph: It was made for the staff. It didn't stay there.
whoYouAre: You rarely set out to start anything. You just like what you like a little before everyone else does: a song, a way of dressing, a word, a place nobody goes yet. You wear it or play it or order it because it's yours. Then, a while later, you notice other people doing it too, and it honestly surprises you every time.

The part you keep to yourself comes next. Once it's everywhere, it's usually done a bit worse, and the people whose taste you respect start rolling their eyes at it. Quietly, you go off it. You've let go of things you loved just because too many people started loving them. Nobody gets to tell you what to like. That includes telling you to stop. And without meaning to, you hand people something they rarely name: the nerve to love a thing before anyone else does.
yours: Most likely in 1988, at the Odeon, a restaurant in lower Manhattan, a bartender named Toby Cecchini heard about a drink from San Francisco called the Cosmopolitan. By his account, it was cheap vodka with bottled lime and grenadine, and he didn't think much of it. So he remade it: a lemon vodka that was new that year, fresh lime and Cointreau the way the bar made its Margaritas, and a splash of the sweetened cranberry juice the bar kept for another drink. It was for the staff.

Then customers started asking for it, which puzzled him. Other bars began making it, "wrong and badly", he says. By 1990 it was all over New York, and it became the one drink of its time that nearly everyone knew by name. The bartenders who came after turned against it, flavoured vodka, processed cranberry and all. Young ones would give him grief for it, and he'd apologise. For years he played it down. In 2014 he said that five years earlier he'd have asked to be "unshackled" from it.

Then that changed. Last I read, in 2026, he still makes it at his own bar in Brooklyn, and he likes it, in his word, "shrill". I like to think he found out what you keep finding out: going off something because of who else has it is just another way of letting them choose for you.

He fixed it mostly with what was already behind the bar. The cocktail I've made for you keeps his proportions, two parts lemon vodka to one each of orange liqueur, fresh lime and sweetened cranberry, and takes one thing from the kitchen: three basil leaves, shaken with it and strained out, leaving their scent and a little of their taste. They add nothing he'd measure: no sugar, no sharpness, no strength. That part is for you. Basil and cranberry are an unexpected match, and basil and lime are old friends. It goes into a wide, shallow glass, with his lemon peel squeezed over the top.

The next time something of yours turns up everywhere, and the eye-rolling starts, don't quietly let it go. Wear it, play it, order it anyway, out loud. You never gave something up because everyone else did. Don't give it up because everyone else found it.

anchors.fact: Hugo Ensslin, a German-born bartender who had trained as a painter and photographer before he came to New York at sixteen, worked the bar of a hotel in Times Square. In 1916 he published *Recipes for Mixed Drinks*. It never caught on, and he was never one of the city's celebrated bartenders. One cocktail historian judges that no other book records as exactly what New York's bars were actually serving just before Prohibition.
anchors.meaning: He kept an ordinary season, the drinks people actually ordered, in plain detail. The book never caught on, and that's where his part ends: what lasted is the record, not the man.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Honesty · drawnToward: Belonging

anchors.fact: Nobody can say which of the drinks in his book he created. The Aviation's first printed recipe is in it, but the name was already in a newspaper in 1911, and several different drinks shared it.
anchors.meaning: He made nothing up. The keeping was the whole of the work. Never "his drink" or "he invented": the drink is "as his book gave it".
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: Honesty · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: The Aviation as his book gives it has gin, lemon, maraschino and two dashes of crème de violette, which tints it a pale sky blue. A far more famous London cocktail book of 1930 printed it without the violette, and that colourless version is the one that survived and was revived. The liqueur itself fell out of cocktail use by the 1930s and was gone from the US for decades. Why the 1930 book left it out is not on record.
anchors.meaning: The famous version lost the colour that was really there. Only the plain record had kept it. That it was "the detail that made it true" is our reading, signposted ("I like to think"). Never say why it was dropped, and never call it careless.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Beauty · soughtFor: Honesty · texture: Soft

anchors.fact: His book resurfaced in 2003, and in 2007 crème de violette came back to the US. Since then bartenders have split between the version without it and the version with it.
anchors.meaning: The colour came back from the everyday record, not from the famous copy. The return belongs to the record, not to him: no vindication ("finally credited") and no "one day they'll see".
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Wonder · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: His book names a brand of gin, El Bart, in the Aviation recipe, and El Bart was a sponsor of the book. The historian who reprinted the recipe suspects that, rather than taste, is why that gin is named.
anchors.meaning: Even the honest record had an advert in it, and nobody retouched it out. The reason is only a guess, so the reading says "probably".
anchors.speaksTo: lens: My inner child · soughtFor: Honesty · texture: Relaxed

anchors.fact: His book gives two dashes of crème de violette, which one historian reads as about a teaspoon. His full recipe has no sweetener and fails our balance checks, so the glass is a modern build, with a teaspoon of violette put back: the colour is his, the balance isn't. At that dose the drink is a pale sky blue, not purple.
anchors.meaning: Only the colour is his, and it's the part that was really there. Never "made as he made it" or "his recipe". The noticing is the guest's: hold it up to the light.

cocktail.closingLine: Hold it up to the light first. The colour was always there.
cocktail.glassware: a stemmed cocktail glass (a coupe or any small stemmed glass), from the freezer
method: Put a stemmed glass in the freezer.
Squeeze the lemon.
Pour the gin, lemon juice, syrup and maraschino into a shaker. Add one teaspoon of crème de violette. No more than that.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is frosty.
Strain it into the cold glass.
Hand it over while the glass is still frosted.
cocktail.name: As It Was

recipe.item: simple syrup (equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear)
crème de violette (Rothman & Winter recommended; or any crème de violette, a violet liqueur around 20%)
recipe.note: Ensslin's two dashes, about a teaspoon

cocktail.tagline: You see the moments worth keeping in the days nobody thinks to remember.

reading.epigraph: The truest record of this drink is a book that never caught on.
whoYouAre: "Hold on, don't move," you say, at the kitchen table, on an evening nobody planned. People laugh, because nothing's happening. You know something is: the light across the table, what everyone ordered, the thing someone said that they'll have forgotten by Friday. Other people wait for something worth remembering. You notice it's already here.

Ask you about it and you'll shrug: it's nothing, just a picture. Making a fuss of it would feel like showing off. The shrug covers a fear you don't say out loud: the blur. A whole year going by and looking like one day. Keeping the ordinary is how you make sure it counted. And the people around you get to see their own everyday life the way you saw it: worth keeping.
yours: In 1916, a bartender at a hotel in Times Square published a book of drinks. His name was Hugo Ensslin, and before he came to New York at sixteen he had trained as a painter and, of all things, a photographer. The book never caught on, and he was never one of the city's famous bartenders. But what he wrote down was plain and exact: the drinks New York's bars were really serving, just before Prohibition closed them. One of the best cocktail historians says no other book shows it as faithfully. He even named a brand of gin in a recipe, El Bart, probably because El Bart helped pay for the book. Nobody tidied that out either.

One of the drinks he wrote down was the Aviation: gin, lemon, a cherry liqueur called maraschino, and a violet liqueur called crème de violette, which tints it a pale sky blue. In 1930, a far more famous London cocktail book printed the Aviation without the violette. There's no record of why. But that colourless version is the one that survived. The colour only came back after his book turned up again in 2003, and the violet liqueur returned to America in 2007.

I like to think the violet was the detail that made it true. It wasn't a flourish. It was part of the drink as his book gave it, and it was that plain record that kept it. That's what you do. You don't make things prettier than they are. You keep them as they were, colour, advert and all.

So the cocktail I've made for you has his violet put back: a teaspoon of the violet liqueur, about what his book's two dashes come to. The rest is a modern balance, not his: gin, lemon, a little sugar and a teaspoon of maraschino, shaken and poured into a stemmed glass straight from the freezer. Only the colour is his. It isn't purple. It's a pale sky blue. And many London dry gins carry orris, the root of an iris, whose scent has long been compared to fresh violets, so the violet isn't a stranger in the glass.

Stop calling it nothing. Somewhere in everything you've kept this year there's an ordinary day that someone else has already forgotten. Print it, and give it to the person in it. They don't know yet what their Tuesday looked like. You do.

anchors.fact: Asked to run Pegu Club in New York (it opened in August 2005; the year of the pitch isn't given), Audrey Saunders was clear about what she wanted, in her own words: "I want a project where I'm making the calls." Every detail was worried over (the logo alone took months, she said), and nothing reached the menu, classic or new, until it had survived her testing. (F1, F2, F3, F5)
anchors.meaning: The whole of it, or not at all: the calls, not the credit. Her motive is on the record, so it may be told as fact.
anchors.speaksTo: texture: In control · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: Toby Maloney, her first head bartender, describes her testing: she gave the specs, sipped, set the glass down, gave new specs, and they made another, with little tiny tweaks each time. She gave the **answer** each time: new measures, not a ratio to work from. (F8)
anchors.meaning: She didn't remake it herself; she sent it back and said what she tasted. That she *chose* this over doing it herself is **our reading**, signposted.

anchors.fact: Jim Meehan, on the opening staff, later named the flaw in that method: palates differ, "There is no perfect drink." In the same account: "That is the way I develop cocktails now." (F9)
anchors.meaning: The standard outlived the admission that it can't be perfect. What passed on was the sending back, not a perfect drink. Nothing about the bars her staff later opened (Visionary's chain: dossier only).
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: Courage · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: Her own account of her Tantris Sidecar: starting from a Sidecar ratio ("say" ¾ lemon, 1 Cointreau, 1½ Cognac) she split parts inside it, lemon with pineapple, Cognac with Calvados, some Cointreau with Chartreuse, to riff "but to stay within the parameters"; then she added simple syrup. (F10) Our drink holds those three amounts (45 / 30 / 22.5 ml) and makes its own swaps inside them. Holding them to the millilitre is **our** rule, not hers.
anchors.meaning: Invention inside a structure you set yourself. The frame is hers; the swaps are ours: never "her recipe", never "her Tantris".

anchors.fact: *Flavor Matrix*: honey's best pairings include citrus and alcohol, and olive is listed among its surprising pairings (pdf 148); the table-grape entry lists honey among grape's best pairings (pdf 140; Cognac mapped to Grape by the studio's rule, check 3). Brine values in our table are unsourced; plain, unstuffed green olives only.
anchors.meaning: One unexpected element, given a job (rounding the edges) and measured: nothing in the glass without a reason. Tomás's row; I've checked the pages.

cocktail.closingLine: Make the first one to the millilitre. Then set it down, name what you'd change, and let someone else make the second.
cocktail.glassware: a coupe (a stemmed glass with a rounded bowl), chilled
method: Put a coupe in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Stir a teaspoon of honey into a teaspoon of warm water until it runs. Let it cool. You'll use 7.5 ml.

Measure everything into a shaker: Cognac, orange liqueur, honey syrup, lemon, and one dash of the brine from a jar of plain green olives. Measure it, don't guess: the drink holds a strong-sweet-sour frame to the millilitre.
Fill with ice, shake hard for about 10 seconds, strain into the cold glass.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Making the Calls

recipe.item: honey syrup (honey and warm water, 1:1, cooled)
recipe.note: inside the sweet part

recipe.item: brine from a jar of plain green olives (not stuffed)
recipe.note: works like a pinch of salt

cocktail.tagline: You'd rather answer for every detail than take credit for just your part.

reading.epigraph: There's one dash in this glass you'll never pick out. The rest tastes brighter for it.
whoYouAre: You have the picture before anything starts: how the evening runs, how the room looks, what comes first and what comes last. After that, every piece has to match it, and you can't leave one that doesn't. You send it back, with a note, and then again, until it's right.

People say you're hard to please. The ones who stayed know it's simpler than that: it's the whole of it you care about, never only your part. What you rarely admit is the other habit, the one after everyone's gone home: quietly redoing someone else's part yourself, because fixing it felt quicker than explaining. Nobody asked you to take it all on. You just can't bear to see it come out ordinary. And the people beside you end up doing the best work they've ever done, sometimes without knowing why.
yours: Before Pegu Club opened in New York in 2005, a bartender named Audrey Saunders was asked to run it, and she was clear about one thing. In her words: "I want a project where I'm making the calls." The logo alone took months. Nothing reached the menu, not even a classic, until it had passed her tasting.

The people who worked there remember how that went. She'd give them the measures and taste what they made. Then she'd set the glass down and give them new measures, and they'd make another. "Little tiny tweaks," one of them called it. The book that tells the story says an eighth of an ounce could turn into a federal case. Later, another of her bartenders named the flaw in working like that: there is no perfect drink. And in the same breath: "That is the way I develop cocktails now."

I think you'd have known that bar the moment you walked in. Not for the fuss. For what sat under it. The part I keep coming back to is who made the next drink. It wasn't her. She tasted, she gave new measures, and they made it again. I like to think that's how, for one of them at least, her way of tasting became his.

This drink borrows the frame of one of hers. She started one of her drinks from her own measures for a Sidecar (brandy, orange liqueur, lemon), and split what went inside each part. This one keeps those measures to the millilitre; what's inside them is mine. Cognac. Orange liqueur, with a little honey inside the sweet part. Lemon. And one dash of brine from plain green olives: too little to taste as salt, enough to make everything else sit right. Nobody will ever name it.

Next time someone's part comes back not quite right, you'll feel the old pull to stay late and redo it yourself. Leave it on the table instead. Point to exactly what's wrong, and let them make it again. You'll still be making the calls. You just won't be the only one who knows why.

anchors.fact: Jerry Thomas's *How to Mix Drinks* (1862) was the first book to give the Cocktail a section of its own: thirteen recipes, among them the plain brandy, gin and whiskey Cocktails that Wondrich calls the three "standard" ones. (F1; *Imbibe!* pdf 173, 179)
anchors.meaning: He wrote down the standard. He didn't invent the Cocktail: it was defined in print by 1843 (F18).

anchors.fact: In 1876 the book was reprinted with a supplement of new drinks. In it Thomas added three "Improved" Cocktails: orange curaçao out, maraschino in, a dash of absinthe, and Angostura allowed. Absinthe was the fad bottle of the 1870s and 1880s, "everywhere" (Wondrich). (F2, F3, F18)
anchors.meaning: The master went back to his own standard fourteen years on and changed it. **Why** he did it isn't on record ("I like to think…" only). Absinthe was fashionable, not new.
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: Courage · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: The 1862 recipes stayed in the book; the Improved ones were added in a supplement at the back of the same book (Wondrich: "that groundbreaking 1876 Appendix"). (F5, *Imbibe!* pdf 17, 179)
anchors.meaning: Refusing to settle, and respecting the structure: the old version is left standing. "Beside" means *in the same book*, not on the facing page. "On purpose" is our reading.

anchors.fact: Wondrich calls the improvement "a subtle one" and reads the Sazerac as the Improved Whiskey Cocktail; Oxford agrees it was "virtually identical" apart from the absinthe rinse. The Sazerac, first in print 1899, is New Orleans's official cocktail (since 2008). (F6, F7, F16, F17)
anchors.meaning: His correction outlived him (d. 1885) under another name. "Better" is Wondrich's word, never ours stated as fact. The Sazerac's origin story stays out.

anchors.fact: Green Chartreuse, 55%, 130 botanicals, made under Carthusian monks to a formula a handful of them know. It grew out of the order's intense, medicinal "long life" elixir (sold since at least 1764); green was first sold in 1840. It reaches cocktail books only in the 1880s. (F14, F19; Oxford pdf 439)
anchors.meaning: Our change, in his dash slot: a teaspoon of the herbal liqueur where his absinthe went. Never "his".

anchors.fact: Orange liqueur in place of the maraschino: Wondrich's own suggestion for the Improved Cocktail (*Imbibe!* pdf 180, F9), taken because maraschino is nuts in our table. Thomas used curaçao in his 1862 plain brandy and gin Cocktails, "but not" in his Whiskey Cocktail (*Imbibe!* pdf 176).
anchors.meaning: The historian's swap, not the bartender's change: the one change of ours stays the Chartreuse.

cocktail.closingLine: Taste it next to the one you already know. Then decide.
cocktail.glassware: a small coupe, chilled, its rim wiped with lemon
method: Put a small coupe in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Empty the glass if you filled it, and run the cut side of a lemon wedge around the rim.
Measure the rye, the syrup, the orange liqueur and the bitters into a shaker. Add the teaspoon of green Chartreuse last, on its own.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Strain into the cold glass.
Twist the strip of lemon peel over the glass to spray its oil onto the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Beside the First

recipe.note: instead of the cherry liqueur of 1876
where he put his dash of absinthe

recipe.item: strip of lemon peel, plus a lemon wedge for the rim

cocktail.tagline: What everyone else calls finished, you call the first edition.

reading.epigraph: Its first author came back fourteen years later and added an 'Improved' one.
whoYouAre: People bring you what they've made so you can tell them it's right. Often it is, and you say so. But alone with something you made years ago, the one people still quote back to you, you keep asking whether it could be better. Not because it failed. Because it didn't, and everyone stopped looking.

What you dread is settling into being right, becoming the way it's always been done, with everyone too respectful to mention it. So you question it yourself, first. And because you'll do that to your own best work, the ones who work with you feel free to do it to theirs.
yours: In 1862 a bartender called Jerry Thomas published *How to Mix Drinks*, the first book to give the cocktail a section of its own: thirteen recipes. In 1876 the book came out again, and Thomas had gone back to his own cocktails. He added three new ones and called them "Improved", with a cherry liqueur and a dash of absinthe, the fashionable bottle of the day.

He didn't tear out the old recipes. The plain ones stayed where they were, and the improved ones went in at the back of the same book. The historian who wrote the book on his drinks calls the change "a subtle one". It outlasted him, though. That historian reads the Sazerac, now New Orleans's official cocktail, as Thomas's improved whiskey cocktail under another name.

I like to think nobody would have blamed him for leaving it alone, since it was his book and it worked. That's what I see in you. You'd rather ask the hard question about your own work than wait for someone else to find the courage. And you never throw the old one away. You put the new one next to it, so anyone can see what changed, and why.

So this drink starts from his improved whiskey cocktail: rye, plain syrup and bitters, with half a teaspoon of orange liqueur instead of his cherry one, the same swap his historian makes. It's shaken hard with ice and strained into a small chilled glass whose rim has been wiped with lemon. There's one change of mine, and it sits where he made his. Instead of his dash of absinthe, a full teaspoon of green Chartreuse, a herbal liqueur that grew out of a monks' medicine and is still made under Carthusian monks, to a recipe only a few of them know. American cocktail books only took it up in the 1880s. His change was a whisper. This one you can taste.

Take the thing you're best known for, the one everyone says not to touch, and change one thing in it. Don't replace it. Show the two side by side, and let people choose. You'll learn the most from the ones who choose the old one.

anchors.fact: Each agave flowers once, on a stalk that can grow 20 cm a day, then dies; its pollen and nectar come at night, and bats do most of the pollinating (Oxford, AGAVE pdf 74).
anchors.meaning: The plant's one flower is its whole life's spending: a thing that's there once, and then gone.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: grief in advance; "gone"

anchors.fact: As tequila grew, producers stopped letting agaves flower; that took a main food from the nectar bats, whose migration paths shifted, and thinned the crop's genetic diversity (Oxford, AGAVE pdf 77).
anchors.meaning: What everyone else was enjoying (more tequila) was quietly thinning something out.
anchors.speaksTo: sees what's thinning while others enjoy it

anchors.fact: A flowered agave is lost to the still: the sugar goes to the flower's nectar and the plant "is no longer useful for tequila production" (Univ. of Gothenburg, 2024, on *Environmental Research Communications*); the ecologist Rodrigo Medellín said letting it bloom is "considered a waste", since it can't be harvested for tequila (*Edible Philly*, 2016).
anchors.meaning: Holding back isn't free: the flower is paid for with the harvest.
anchors.speaksTo: the pull to take; it cost them

anchors.fact: David Suro-Piñera, who produces tequila (Siembra Azul, "Produced by David Suro", *Codex* p. 164) and co-founded the Tequila Interchange Project, helped start the Bat Friendly programme with Medellín: at least 5% of the agaves left to flower, bats seen feeding (batfriendly.org; *Natural Areas Journal* 36(4), 2016).
anchors.meaning: Someone inside the trade chose to leave some of the harvest standing.
anchors.speaksTo: not taking; hands places back whole

anchors.fact: One of his own tequilas, Siembra Valles Ancestral, is on the programme's first list, 2016 (batfriendly.org).
anchors.meaning: He held his own bottle to it, not only other people's.

anchors.fact: His reason, in his words: bringing back the bats' food came from "the necessity of genetic strength", healthier plants (*PhillyVoice*, 2023).
anchors.meaning: Care for the wild and for the plant's future are the same act.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: keeps a thing going for later

anchors.fact: He has given "more than we can afford" to the project, and wants it "totally independent… run by new people" (*Edible Philly*, 2016, his words).
anchors.meaning: He built it and won't own it.
anchors.speaksTo: loves things they refuse to own

anchors.fact: The lesser long-nosed bat came off the US endangered list in 2018, the first bat removed for recovery (EDF, 2018); it had many causes, and tequila is never credited. A second pollinator, the Mexican long-nosed bat, is still endangered (BCI, 2021).
anchors.meaning: Something is still alive, and not all of it is safe: no doom, no rescue.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: coming back to find it gone

anchors.fact: "The bats came back and the flowers were gone" is our reading of Oxford's "shift in their migratory paths". Signpost with "I like to think".
anchors.meaning: The persona's own fear, handed to the bats.

cocktail.closingLine: Nothing goes on top. Drink it while it's cold: you can miss it later.
cocktail.glassware: a copita (a small tulip-shaped tasting glass), chilled, no ice
method: Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Pour the tequila, the vermouth and the spoon of peach liqueur into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir with a long spoon for about 20 seconds, until the outside feels very cold. The melting ice is part of the drink: it adds about two-fifths to what you poured.
Empty the serving glass if you filled it, and strain the drink in. No ice, no peel, and nothing on top.
It's at its best in the first few minutes, while it's at its coldest.
cocktail.name: Left Standing

cocktail.tagline: You'd rather know it's there than have it.

reading.epigraph: The plant behind this glass flowers once in its life. Most are harvested first.
whoYouAre: Every time you return to a place you love, you're bracing before you arrive. The café that might have closed. The field that might be houses now. The woods at the end of the lane, with a car park where the gate was. Everyone else sees the view. You're counting what's left.

You start missing things while they're still here. So you touch them as little as you can. You don't pick the flower. The stone stays where it was. The path looks the way you found it. People sometimes take that for strictness, and you'd rather they did. It's easier than saying how much it hurts to watch something thin out while everyone around you is still enjoying it. And easier than admitting the fear under that one: that some day you'll be part of the reason it went. When other people arrive, your care means there's still something there for them to love, whether anyone thanks you or not.
yours: The agave, the plant tequila is made from, grows for years before it flowers, and it flowers only once. A stalk shoots up from its heart, sometimes twenty centimetres in a day. It makes its nectar at night, and bats come for it and carry the pollen. Then the plant dies. As tequila grew, producers stopped letting their agaves flower. A plant spends the sugar in its heart on that one flower, and once it has flowered it's no use to the still. Stopping the flowers took away a main food of the nectar bats, and their migrations shifted.

David Suro-Piñera produces tequila. With a bat scientist, Rodrigo Medellín, he helped start a programme that asks growers to let some of their agaves flower, at least five in every hundred, and to show that bats have fed from them. Letting them bloom, Medellín said, is "considered a waste": a plant that flowers can't be harvested for tequila. One of Suro-Piñera's own tequilas was on the programme's first list. And his reason, in his own words, wasn't only the bats. It was "the necessity of genetic strength": plants left to flower make the crop stronger for later. The lesser long-nosed bat, one of the agave's bats, came off the US endangered list in 2018, the first bat ever taken off because it had recovered. Its recovery had many causes.

The bats, I like to think, came back one year to the fields they'd always fed from and found the flowers gone. That's your fear, exactly. What Suro-Piñera asked for is what you already do everywhere you go: leave some of it standing, even when taking it would make perfect sense, so there's something there for whoever comes next. His reason is yours too. You don't hold back only because you're soft about wild things. You hold back because you feel responsible for what a place will be long after you've left it.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Martini, the drink with more poems and jokes to its name than almost any other, made with blanco tequila: the clear kind that never sees a barrel, made from agave alone. I'd pour Suro-Piñera's Siembra Azul, though it isn't the bottle on that first list. A delicate, herbal blanc vermouth goes with it. No peel, no garnish, so nothing is laid over the plant's own smell. Then one teaspoon of peach liqueur. When an agave flowers, its sugar goes to the nectar instead of the still, and I like to think that spoon is the sweetness the still never got. I chose fruit rather than a flower. You'd leave the flower where it grows, and a peach is there to be picked. It's served small and very cold, without ice, so it's at its best in the first few minutes. It asks you to pay attention while it's there.

You don't have to be the only one watching. The next place you're afraid of losing, don't go alone. Take someone and show them what you see: the thing that's thinning out, the one nobody else has noticed yet. Then there are two of you who'd notice if it went. And I think you'll find that watching it with someone feels less like grieving and more like what it really is: loving it while it's here.
