cocktail.closingLine: Make it a day ahead. Then the evening is for your guests, not the blender.
cocktail.glassware: a large stemmed goblet (about 350 ml), chilled, no salt rim
method: A day ahead, stir the tequila, Cointreau, syrup, water and vanilla together in a jug.

Pour half into each of two freezer bags or wide lidded containers, about 450 ml each. Each one makes two drinks. Seal them and lay them flat in the freezer for a day. The alcohol and sugar keep the mix from freezing hard: it sets thick and icy.
If it's still liquid after a day, your freezer isn't quite cold enough. Add the lime (75 ml to each bag) three to six hours before you serve, and it will set.

To serve two, put two goblets in the freezer for ten minutes. Squeeze 75 ml of lime juice, unless it's already in the bag from step 3. Break up one bag with your hands through the plastic, tip it into a blender with the lime, and blend just until smooth and thick, a few seconds. Blending longer only warms it.
Pour into the chilled goblets. No salt and no garnish. The second bag makes the next two, and they'll come out the same.
cocktail.name: For Good

reading.epigraph: One idea behind this glass came from a convenience store.
whoYouAre: Somewhere in your life there's the proof of how you work: a thing that used to jam, drip or stick, until one afternoon you'd had enough of it. You took it apart there and then, and it hasn't jammed since. And you regret none of it.

What you keep quiet is how it starts. It sounds like moaning: the queue that's slow for no reason, the form that asks for the same thing twice, the way something has always been done that has never quite worked. You've tried sighing and getting on with it. It doesn't take. It stays with you until you've found a way round, and the way round usually comes from somewhere nobody thought to look. The sentence you can't bear is "it's always been like that". The one that frightens you is hearing yourself say it, and meaning it. And the things you fix stay fixed. People stop having the problem, forget it was ever there, and get their afternoons back. That's what your restlessness gives them, and it's worth far more than the grumbling it started with.
yours: By the early 1960s, some people were already making the Margarita in a blender. About ten years later, in Dallas, Mariano Martinez was making frozen ones at his own restaurant, and they weren't working. They kept coming out different, and not even cold, his customers complained. His bartenders were threatening to quit. The restaurant was burning out blenders, he said later, as fast as it could buy them.

The answer wasn't in a bar. It was at a 7-Eleven, in the Slurpee machine. He took a soft-serve ice cream machine and bent it to the job: through trial and error, as he tells it, they made it spin faster and gave it a bigger compressor, so the drinks came out colder. Before long, frozen Margarita machines were a fixture, and many versions came onto the market. The original is in the Smithsonian now. He never meant to invent anything, he said; he was just trying to make his customers happy.

The complaints bothered him long before any machine did, I like to think. You'd know that feeling. You hear the grumble everyone hears, and you're the one who can't let it go. Then you find the fix somewhere nobody thought to look: a restaurant's answer, sitting in a convenience store. And once it works, you're happy for it to disappear. I doubt many people ordering a frozen Margarita today think about Dallas, or burned-out blenders. They just get a cold drink. That's how you look after people: they never have to find out there was a problem.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Margarita, one of the most famous cocktails there is, made frozen, with blanco tequila and Cointreau, the orange liqueur Martinez's father always insisted on. It's built the way you'd build it: most of the work happens once. A day ahead, you mix everything but the lime, water and all, and freeze it in two bags. By coincidence, the book I took the method from describes it as making a 7-Eleven-style frozen treat. After that, every two glasses are one bag from the freezer and the juice of two or three limes, then a few seconds in the blender. There's no ice added and nothing to guess at, so it comes out the same, and properly cold, every time. And there's a little vanilla in the batch, just half a teaspoon. Orange and vanilla always makes me think of the ice-cream counter, so I borrowed it from there, the way he borrowed a machine. It's served thick in a big chilled stemmed glass, with no salt.

So trust the annoyance. It isn't moaning, and it isn't ingratitude. It's usually the first sign that you've found something worth fixing. The next time someone tells you it's always been like that, take it as directions: they've just shown you where to start. And when it works and nobody says a word, enjoy the quiet. You made it.

cocktail.closingLine: Take the sugar off at amber. And when they ask, let them hear how close it came.
cocktail.glassware: a small tumbler (about 200 ml), chilled in the freezer, no ice
method: Make the caramel syrup ahead. Put 1 tablespoon of water in a small heavy pan and pour 200 g of white sugar on top. Heat it on medium without stirring, just swirling the pan now and then, and watch it the whole time. It goes clear, then pale gold, then deep amber. Take it off the heat at deep amber, as soon as it smells toasted and before any smoke rises: past that point it turns bitter in seconds. Stand back and slowly pour in 200 ml of hot water. It will spit and boil hard, and the caramel will set into lumps. Put the pan back on a low heat and stir until everything has dissolved, then let it bubble gently for a minute or two more, until it's about as thick as runny honey. Let it cool and keep it in a closed jar in the fridge. It makes enough for about 25 drinks.
Put a small tumbler in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.

Read the strength on your bottle's label. Up to 47.5% (95 proof), use 60 ml of bourbon and no water. If it's stronger, the bourbon and cold water together make 60 ml: up to 51.5%, 55 ml of bourbon and 5 ml of water; up to 57%, 50 ml and 10 ml; up to 63%, 45 ml and 15 ml; up to 70%, 40 ml and 20 ml. If you're between two, take the one with more water.

In a mixing glass or jar, pour 1½ teaspoons of caramel syrup, 2 dashes of Angostura, then the bourbon (and the water, if you need it). Fill it with ice and stir steadily for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
Strain into the cold tumbler. Don't add ice.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top, skin side down, so its oils fall on the drink. Rub it once around the rim, then set it aside.
cocktail.name: Nothing to It

cocktail.tagline: You went first, so they knew they could.

reading.epigraph: One barrel, bottled alone, used to stay inside the trade. Then someone put it on sale.
whoYouAre: The top of the high board, the whole pool gone quiet, everyone looking up. Years later it's a microphone, or a first day in a place where you don't know a soul. You've gone through it so many times in your head that you know every step of it. From the outside, it looks as if you were made for this.

You're scared every time. Nobody's ever been able to tell. What gets you up there isn't a lack of fear. It's a bigger one: the day you could have gone and didn't, and knowing it for the rest of your life. So you go. And afterwards, when people ask, you make it sound like very little. That isn't modesty. You've seen what happens when something looks impossible: nobody tries. So you make it look possible, and somebody behind you decides they could do it too. Hardly anyone knows you do that on purpose. It's one of the most generous things a person can do for whoever comes after them, and you do it every time.
yours: Most whiskey is poured together from many barrels before it's bottled, sometimes a great many, so every bottle tastes the same. A single barrel doesn't get that. Whatever that one barrel became is what goes in the bottle. In Kentucky, Albert Blanton, whose name the distillery in Frankfort once carried, used to bottle one particularly good barrel on its own, for himself or as a gift to people in the trade. Other distillery bosses of his time did it too. It stayed with him and the people he gave it to.

Elmer T. Lee had joined the same distillery in 1949, and worked under Blanton. When new owners asked Lee for a premium bourbon, the idea, he said, was what he'd learned from Colonel Blanton. In 1984, Lee and his staff did it in front of everyone: barrels bottled one at a time, and sold. It was the first single-barrel bourbon brand. Other fine bourbons had been launched before and taken off the shelves for lack of interest. This one's audience gathered slowly, and then, as Lee told it, the other distillers followed, three or four years later. "I had no idea," he said, "it would become as worldwide as it is." When the owners asked if a bourbon could carry his own name, he said yes, provided he could pick the bourbon that went in it. At ninety, he was still picking.

I don't know if Lee was nervous. I like to think he was, a little, and that nobody could tell. This is the part of the story that's about you. Years of learning something where it was safe. Then one day doing it on a shelf, where anyone could judge it. And twenty-five years later, still no speech: "I had no idea." You know that shrug, because it's the one you use. And it did what it always does for you: it made the thing look possible, and the others followed.

The cocktail I've made for you is an Old-Fashioned, the oldest shape a cocktail has and one of the best loved, made with one single-barrel bourbon and no other whiskey. I'd pour Blanton's, or any single-barrel bourbon. The sugar is my change. Every bourbon barrel is charred inside, and the charring turns some of the wood's own sugars to caramel. So instead of the usual sugar, I do the same to it: it's cooked in a pan to deep amber, taken off the heat before it can turn bitter, and loosened with water, to bring out what the barrel already has, not to cover it. I did that for you, because you know exactly how far to go, and when to stop. Two dashes of Angostura, a long stir over ice, and it's poured, small and cold, into a tumbler from the freezer, with no ice. Last, the oil from an orange peel, for its scent, and the peel set aside.

After the next thing everyone watched you do, don't make it sound like nothing. Find the person who's thinking of going next, and tell them you were terrified, and that you went. Your steadiness showed them it could be done. Your fear will show them they don't have to be fearless to do it. And you get back something you've been giving away every time you shrugged: how much it took.

Pour the rum, the vermouth, the Madeira, the curaçao and the grenadine into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir with a long spoon for about 20 seconds, until the outside feels very cold. The melting ice is part of the drink: it adds about two-fifths to what you poured.
Empty the serving glass if you filled it, and strain the drink in. No ice.
Hold the strip of orange peel over the glass, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the drink. Then drop it in.

cocktail.tagline: The smallest things can stop you in your tracks. You let them, they're here for a reason.

reading.epigraph: Someone once put drinks like this in bottles for years, to see what time would do.
whoYouAre: On any walk, you're a few steps behind. Something stopped you: frost that's stayed only in the shadow of a fence, a bee climbing into a flower the wrong way round, a sign you've passed a hundred times and have only now read properly. Somewhere up ahead, someone says "come on". You've been hearing "come on" for as long as you can remember.

You were never dawdling. You wanted to see what it would do. You don't often say how much a small thing can make your day, because it can sound naive, and there's an old, faint guilt about holding everyone up. It isn't being slow that scares you. It's getting busy, and sure, and one day walking straight past something without feeling the tug, and not even missing it. The people who walk with you see more than they would on their own. The ordinary comes back to them new. That's what your slowness gives them, and every so often the thing you stopped for turns out to matter to everyone.
yours: A Manhattan is usually drunk within minutes of being made. Around 2004, in London, a bartender named Tony Conigliaro started putting some aside instead: Manhattans, and a Cuban classic called the El Presidente, in glass, for years. His question came from wine. Wine changes slowly as it ages, and he wondered whether a mixed drink could be helped by ageing too, if it was done with the same care. For years he tried to interest his customers in the idea. Nobody paid it a bit of attention, he said.

In 2009 he opened a bar of his own, a small one on a side street in Islington. That October, a bartender from Portland, Oregon, Jeffrey Morgenthaler, was in town, and was told to ask for the Manhattan that wasn't on the menu. It was five years old. Conigliaro told him the years had brought its flavours together. Morgenthaler, by his own account, thought it tasted like a Manhattan. He went home and tried the idea anyway, in a small wooden barrel, where it takes weeks instead of years. His first batch was gone in a week or two, and before long bars across the world were ageing cocktails in barrels.

I like to think Conigliaro gave that bottle its years because he trusted there was something in it, while nobody else was interested yet. That's you. You give an ordinary thing more time than anyone else would, before there's any sign it'll be worth it. And look at what travelled. Not the taste: the man who took the idea home could hardly tell. It was the idea, and the question under it: what happens if you don't hurry? You hand people that question all the time, and some of them take it further than you'd ever have guessed.

The cocktail I've made for you is an El Presidente, a Cuban classic that became popular far beyond Havana, and a stirred one: white rum and a sweet white vermouth, with a little orange curaçao and half a spoon of grenadine for its colour. My real change is in the wine. I've swapped part of the vermouth for Madeira, a wine the law won't let anyone sell until it has had years, because Conigliaro's question came from wine. So some of the time he was asking about is in there already. It's stirred cold and served in a little stemmed wine glass, chilled first, with an orange peel twisted over it, and it's ready the moment it's made. You're usually the one giving things time. This once, somebody else did the waiting for you.

Busy comes for everyone, and the stopping goes first. You won't hear it go. So have one thing going that can't be hurried: a cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a question you haven't looked up yet. Look in on it now and then. And when someone up ahead says "come on", take the minute. It's usually the best one of the walk.

anchors.fact: In colonial American taverns a hot drink was often a flip: beer or cider, rum and molasses or sugar, heated by plunging in an iron rod heated in the fire until it glowed. The red-hot metal caramelised the sugars and toasted the grain. (F1, F16; Oxford pdf 812–813; *LI* p. 177)
anchors.meaning: The long way was once the ordinary way. "Often", never "usually" (A3). Taverns only, never sailors or shipbuilders (F15).

anchors.fact: As Arnold tells it, eggs came in around the Civil War, boiling water replaced the iron, and "something crucial was lost". (F2; *LI* p. 177)
anchors.meaning: The easy way won and took something with it. The whole sentence carries his channel (A4).

anchors.fact: Arnold decided to bring the poker back to taste what had gone missing. He tried a soldering copper (sometimes a penny taste), cast iron, steel and hot stones (which he thought better of serving), then built his own electric pokers for the New York bar he opened with David Chang in 2012. (F3, F6, F7; *LI* pp. 45, 177, 179–180; *Proper* pp. 225–226)
anchors.meaning: The deliberate long way, with the pot right there. Motive on record: taste. One laugh only (the penny). No duration ("a winter", struck, A8). Past tense for the bar; never "he opened" alone (B1). Never "invented" the poker (F10).
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: the long way is the fun; drawnToward: Originality

anchors.fact: One writer on the cocktail revival (Simonson) described a kid-like "why not?" enthusiasm in everything he did. (F12; *Proper* p. 224)
anchors.meaning: Simonson's portrait, never Arnold's quote, and never "knew him" (A7). "Charlatan" stays out.

anchors.fact: When somebody is making a poker drink, "everybody perks up a bit". (F5; *LI* p. 177)
anchors.meaning: The gift: people lean in. "Perk up", never "turn round" or watching (A9; *The Entertainer*).

anchors.fact: To his taste the poker beats the pan; Oxford independently records that the iron caramelised the sugars and toasted the grain. (F4; *LI* p. 177; Oxford pdf 813)
anchors.meaning: "He was right about the iron" is our reading on Oxford's page; "better" is his taste (A10, A11). Caramelises *some* of the sugar.

anchors.fact: His best faux-poker for a kitchen burns the sugar in a pan (then flambés the liquor; we keep only the sugar). (F8; *LI* p. 184)
anchors.meaning: Our glass. "The part I've kept" (A13). No flame, no "amber", no edge-of-burning beat (*Nothing to It*). "Arnold doesn't assume you will either", never "neither does Arnold" (A13). Never hand anyone the hot pan (S2).
anchors.speaksTo: drink: burnt sugar instead of a syrup you could just pour

anchors.fact: He serves hot drinks in wide teacups, because tall cups concentrate the alcohol vapour. (*LI* pp. 182–183)
anchors.meaning: His reason, not "the smell reaches you first" (A14).

cocktail.closingLine: Get someone to pour the ale in while you stir. Then you both built it.
cocktail.glassware: a wide china teacup (about 200 ml), warmed with hot water first
method: Fill the teacup with hot water to warm it. Measure everything else and set it beside the stove, because once the sugar is ready the rest goes in quickly.
Put the sugar in a small heavy pan over a medium-high heat. Don't stir: swirl the pan now and then as it melts, and let it go dark brown and smell toasty.

Take the pan off the heat and pour in the water. It will spit and steam, and the sugar will seize into a lump, so keep your face and hands back. Put the pan on a low heat and stir until the lump has melted again.
Pour in the ale while you stir (this goes best with two people, one pouring and one stirring). Warm it until it steams, but don't let it boil.
Take the pan off the heat and away from the flame. Stir in the rum, lemon, bitters and salt.
Empty the teacup and pour the drink in. Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Why Not?

cocktail.tagline: There's an easier way, but it just isn't as much fun.

reading.epigraph: Taverns heated drinks like this with a red-hot iron. This one burns its sugar instead.
whoYouAre: There's a perfectly good way to do it, and everybody knows it. Then there's your way: three extra steps, a part you made from something at the back of a drawer, and someone in the doorway asking what on earth you're doing. It lit you up the moment you thought of it, and that was reason enough.

Some of it falls over. You laugh first, and loudest. What you don't laugh at is the kind voice that says "you could just buy one". It's said with a smile, as common sense, and it lands harder than any collapse, because it turns the best part of your week into a waste of time. What you'd hate most is a life with nothing left to build. Here's what your long way gives people: the kitchen gets louder when you start, and an ordinary job becomes the most interesting thing in the house. When it works, nobody is more surprised than you, and the surprise is catching.
yours: In the taverns of colonial America, a hot drink on a cold night was often a flip: ale, rum and sugar, heated by plunging in an iron rod that had sat in the fire until it glowed. The red-hot metal did more than warm the drink. It caramelised the sugar and toasted the grain. Then, as Dave Arnold tells it, eggs came into the flip around the time of the Civil War, boiling water took the iron's place, and something crucial was lost.

Arnold, who happens to have written one of the books I mix from, decided to bring the iron back, to taste what had gone missing. A pot would have heated the drink. He tried a soldering copper first, which sometimes made the drink taste, as he put it, like sucking on a penny. Then cast iron, then steel, then hot stones, which worked, though he thought better of serving people drinks with stones in them. In the end he built his own electric pokers, for the New York bar he opened with David Chang in 2012. One writer on the cocktail revival described a kid-like "why not?" in everything he did. And when a poker drink was being made, Arnold wrote, everybody perked up a bit.

The pot was never really an option, I like to think. You'd know. There's always a pot: the easy way, right there, that would do the job well enough. And there's the other way, the one that takes trial after trial, and leaves everybody perking up. You take the second one because it's the fun one. What makes me smile is that he was right about the iron. It does something a pot doesn't: it caramelises some of the sugar and toasts the grain, right inside the drink. The long way wasn't only more fun. To his taste, it was better. Not every time. But more often than the people who say "you could just" would like to admit.

The cocktail I've made for you is a hot flip, the kind colonial taverns served before the eggs came in, and a popular one: a malty abbey ale and rum, the taverns' own spirit, here an aged one, with a teaspoon of lemon, three dashes of orange bitters and a little salt added. I don't expect you to keep an iron in the fire, and Arnold doesn't assume you will either. His own stand-in for a kitchen, the best he's come up with, starts by burning the sugar dark in a pan, and that part I've kept: it gives a toasty, burnt-sugar taste a plain syrup doesn't have. It's the long way round to sweetening a drink, when you could just pour the syrup, and it's there as a nod to the poker and to everyone who'd rather build it. It comes in a warm, wide teacup, the way he insists, because a tall mug traps the fumes, with a strip of orange zest pinched over it.

So when you next hear "you could just…", don't explain. Explaining makes it sound like a defence, and it was never one. Hand them the other end instead: the spanner, the bit that needs holding, the ale to pour. Let them be there when it works. I'd bet they'll want to do the next one with you.

anchors.fact: Bradsell grew up on the Isle of Wight (Oxford pdf 335).
anchors.meaning: The place the taste took him back to.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: a taste that takes them somewhere whole

anchors.meaning: One taste, of three, took him somewhere whole, at once.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing; hidden: how hard a sensation hits

anchors.fact: He made a British drink with gin, lemon and sugar when "the scene was totally vodka", with a blackberry liqueur hardly anyone thought of (Proper pp. 25, 31).
anchors.meaning: He went with the taste, not the fashion.
anchors.speaksTo: goal: freedom, an appetite nobody has to approve

anchors.meaning: The taste gave the drink its fruit.

anchors.fact: *Flavor Matrix* BERRY: vinegar among the best pairings (pdf 52); balsamic on the Berry chart (pdf 53). Our riff: half a teaspoon in the drizzle.

method: Fill the glass with crushed ice. A tea towel and a rolling pin will crush it fine.

cocktail.tagline: You find something wonderful and want someone else to feel it too.

reading.epigraph: The cider man also brought three liqueurs. One of them tasted like an island.
whoYouAre: Someone opens a jar, and before anyone has said a word you're standing in a kitchen you haven't been in for years. A smell on a stairwell, the first bite of a plum, and you're somewhere else, completely. You can't always remember what year it was. You can remember exactly what the bread tasted like. And whatever is in front of you now, you're really tasting it.

What you play down is how hard it hits. You say "mm, lovely", because you've seen the eyebrow go up across the table: it's only bread. It's never only bread to you. What frightens you is a life with the senses turned down, on a menu somebody else chose. Or a meal with someone who isn't tasting, which is lonelier than eating alone. And look what you do with good things. You tear off the warm end of the loaf and hand it over. You crush a leaf under someone's nose: "smell this". Years later, the taste that takes them somewhere has you in it. That's a lovely thing to leave in someone's life.
yours: A man who supplied cider to the London bar where Dick Bradsell worked once brought in three liqueurs: a blackcurrant, a raspberry and a blackberry. It was the blackberry that did it. As soon as he tried it, he said, he was "back in that blackberry patch on the Isle of Wight", the island where he grew up. "It was spot-on, that flavour."

He made a drink around it, with gin, lemon and sugar: a British drink, at a time when, as he put it, the scene was totally vodka. He started from a drink he already had, a Singapore Sling he'd made at another club, and cut it down into a short one. The blackberry gave it its fruit, and he gave it a more British name: the Bramble, the wild bush that blackberries grow on. At Fred's, the Soho members' club where he worked, it was popular straight off, and before long it had crossed the Atlantic.

Hardly anyone was thinking about blackberry liqueur then, and he went with it. I like to think that, for a second, people at Fred's stood in a blackberry patch on an island they'd never seen, and nobody had to tell them. That's how it is with you. A taste doesn't only please you. It takes you somewhere, and you can't help wanting to take someone along.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Bramble, now a modern classic: gin, lemon juice and a little sugar, shaken and poured over crushed ice, then the blackberry liqueur poured slowly over the top, so it runs down through the ice in dark threads, and a fresh blackberry to finish. My change is in that pour. Into the blackberry liqueur I stir balsamic vinegar, no more than half a teaspoon, the dark, sweet Italian kind: a cook's pairing for berries. I like to think the berries he remembered were the ones eaten warm off the bush at the end of summer, soft and almost like wine, so the vinegar is there to make the blackberry taste riper and darker, the way those do. It's the sort of thing that raises an eyebrow. Then people taste it.

Find the taste that takes you somewhere, the one you could never quite explain, and give it to someone you love. Cook it, pick it, track it down. Don't tell them the story first. Just hand it over, and then let them tell you where it took them. You've been taking people into your places for years. This time you'll get to go into one of theirs, and you'll know that the person across the table is tasting too.

anchors.fact: In 1973, new to New York and nervous at the bar, he began arriving at least an hour before his shift, eating dinner alone and then sitting on, taking in the room (Joy pdf 119; card F2, F4, F5).
anchors.meaning: A small thing done on an ordinary working night, on purpose, before it had any name.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: something ordinary already working

anchors.fact: He looked back and called it "in effect, meditating", "though I wasn't really conscious of that at the time. I just knew it worked." (Joy pdf 119; F6)
anchors.meaning: Our reading: the search gave words to something an ordinary night already held.
anchors.speaksTo: recognition: a practice for years you'd never call one

anchors.fact: The idea of mindfulness for bartenders came to him while attending mindfulness workshops; he gave presentations in Moscow, London, Paris and Beirut, and said he wasn't a qualified teacher (Joy pdf 115; F8).
anchors.meaning: Passing it on without a sermon.
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: the line handed on, no lecture

anchors.fact: In his book: "don't ever take things too seriously" (Joy pdf 116; F12); setting up a bar alone for the first shift of the day, loud music "can be a form of meditation" for him (Joy pdf 120; F11).
anchors.meaning: The thing kept doesn't have to look holy, or quiet.

anchors.fact: He wrote *The Negroni* (Oxford pdf 1635; F15); in *The Joy of Mixology*, his best-known book (Oxford pdf 1635), the Negroni is "BUILD in any order in an ice-filled rocks glass" (Joy pdf 351; 2003 ed. too, F19). Not verified in *The Negroni* (C10).
anchors.meaning: No ritual in the method.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; epigraph and y4 (name: *Just Knew*, from F6)

anchors.fact: Throughout his career he stressed that a bar relies on "the happiness of its patrons" (Oxford pdf 1635; F14).
anchors.meaning: What changes inside shows in how people are met.

cocktail.closingLine: Take the bay leaf from the jar you never think about. Then name one habit that's quietly kept you going.

Put in the torn bay leaf, the gin, the Campari and both vermouths, in any order.
Stir for a few seconds.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

cocktail.tagline: You're always looking for a little magic to carry into everyday life.

reading.epigraph: A famous bartender's recipe for the classic behind this drink: build it in any order.
whoYouAre: There's a shelf somewhere in your home that would surprise people. Very old books next to very new ones, and a couple you'd rather nobody picked up. You've gone further than the shelf, too: the silent weekend, the long walk, the course your friends teased you about. Each time you return with one thing, a line or a habit, and you want it to last through an ordinary week.

Nobody sees how often it slips. By Wednesday the inbox has it, and part of you decides the real answer must be somewhere else, so you start looking again. What would scare you is a life that stops asking what it's for. But some of it has been working for years without your noticing. The walk you take before a hard day. The song you play in the car before you go in. You'd never call those a practice, and they've been holding you up the whole time. People feel it, too. You arrive more present than most, and sometimes you hand someone exactly the line they needed, with no lecture attached. That line was worth every retreat.
yours: In 1973 Gary Regan, a young bartender from a small English seaside town, started a new life in New York, where the customers seemed larger than life and made him nervous. So he began arriving at least an hour before his shift. He ate dinner alone at a table, then sat on, taking in the room, telling himself the night would go well.

The customers stopped intimidating him, and they still teased him, which he said was how he liked it. Years later he looked back and called that hour meditating, in effect, though he hadn't known it at the time: "I just knew it worked." The idea of mindfulness for bartenders came to him at workshops, and he gave talks on it, saying plainly that he was no qualified teacher. Writing about it, he told bartenders never to take things too seriously, and said that when he was setting up a bar alone, loud music could be his meditation.

I like to think the part of his story that belongs to you isn't the workshops. It's the hour before them, when he had no name for what he was doing. The search mattered, I think: it gave him words for it, and with words he could pass it on. But what he was doing was already there, on a working night like any other, doing its job. I'd guess something in your week does that for you, and you've never given it a name.

He wrote a book about the Negroni, a renowned classic. In his best-known book, he printed it with the Campari first, then sweet vermouth and gin, the same measure of each, and one odd instruction: build it in any order. The recipe doesn't say why. I like to think there's a whole outlook in those three words. In the cocktail I've made for you, his instruction stays. I've changed two things, so the gin leads and half the vermouth is dry, which makes it brighter and less sweet. Then one addition: a dried bay leaf, torn in half, out of the kitchen cupboard. I put it in for that hour: something ordinary you already had, doing more than anyone gave it credit for.

Keep going away. It's where you find the words. But before you plan the next retreat, look at what already carries you through an ordinary day, the walk, the song, the hour you keep for yourself, and give it its proper name. It counts. You're further along than you think, and I'm glad of it for you.

anchors.fact: Lee came to bartending from IT work ("an IT administrator", one of two "refugees from the tech world"). Proper p. 165 (F1).
anchors.meaning: Came in from outside the trade, without credentials.

anchors.fact: Lee did not invent fat-washing (Proper p. 275, F12). Eben Freeman told him about the technique (Lee and Deragon, PUNCH 2019; Proper p. 231). Where and who first fat-washed at WD-50 stays out (C2, C3).
anchors.meaning: He took a route someone else had found; what he added was putting it on a menu.

anchors.fact: A regular at PDT had bacon fat he didn't know what to do with (Tien Ho, "a regular of ours", Proper p. 275). Lee asked about it, as a joke at first, then asked for some: "Hey, can I have some of it?" (Lee, PUNCH 2019, F19). Chang: "Don would always ask for things" (F19).
anchors.meaning: Asking for the odd thing nobody wants, half as a joke.

anchors.fact: Lee took the concept to Jim Meehan, who was wary (Lee, PUNCH). Meehan was worried about the barbacks' time and consistency, so Lee could put it on the menu only if he did all the infusions himself: "In true Don Lee fashion, he did." Meehan: "definitely his idea" (PUNCH 2019, F20). Meehan's intent beyond that worry isn't on record, so any "meant to put him off" is signposted.
anchors.meaning: "Only if" heard as a way in: carrying the whole load instead of waiting.

anchors.fact: It became PDT's best-known and best-selling cocktail (Proper p. 275, F15). It inspired a whole genre of fat-washed drinks (Proper p. 275); PUNCH names nuts, chorizo and olive oil (2019).
anchors.meaning: The route stayed open, and others took it their own way.

anchors.fact: Freeman, given a sample early on, said Lee's version was better than his own and that he was impressed (PUNCH 2019, F22).
anchors.meaning: Credit runs both ways: no timid foil.

anchors.fact: Lee is proud of the drink and also troubled by it: he said it's the drink that will "probably" follow him to the grave (Proper p. 276, F17).
anchors.meaning: The fear: being known for the one thing.

anchors.fact: Later, an environmental cocktail group (Trash Tiki) held it up as a sustainability drink. Lee granted you could say that, but said it "certainly was not what we were thinking" (PUNCH 2019, F23).
anchors.meaning: The route goes places the maker never meant.

anchors.fact: Printed recipe: 2 oz Benton's-bacon-fat-washed Four Roses bourbon, ¼ oz Grade B maple, 2 dashes Angostura, orange zest; one large cube, stirred. Wash: 1½ oz fat melted, combined with 750 ml bourbon, 4 h at room temperature, 2 h in the freezer, fat lifted, strained through cloth (Proper pp. 275–276, page images, F18, F25). Bottle printed as "Four Roses bourbon"; "Yellow Label" is Lee's word in PUNCH, and not today's name on record.
anchors.meaning: Meehan's terms are in the glass: the guest does the washing.

anchors.fact: Benton's bacon is dry-cured by hand with salt, brown sugar and black pepper, about three weeks, then smoked two to three days over hickory in a wood-stove smokehouse, Madisonville, Tennessee (maker's product page; Heritage Foods; F26).
anchors.meaning: The smoke and the pepper, for Checks and the spice question.

anchors.fact: No year (2007 vs 2008, C1). No "a regular at WD-50" (C2). No "first", no "introduced fat-washing". No "didn't ask". No "Freeman never served it" (Wren r3: kept-inside-then-sold shape). No speakeasy, no phone booth. No "Yellow Label" as a current bottle. "Trail-blazing" is WD-50's word (p. 230), never Lee's.
anchors.meaning: Keeps the reading inside the record and off sibling ground.

cocktail.closingLine: Wash the whole bottle yourself. And when it starts following you around, let it.
cocktail.glassware: a tall highball glass, packed with ice
method: **Wash the bourbon (about 6 hours, the same day).** Cook the bacon slowly over low heat until the fat has run clear and the edges are crisp, not burnt: fat from overcooked bacon tastes bad. Measure 3 tablespoons (45 ml) of the melted fat. Stir it into a 750 ml bottle of bourbon in a wide container that can go in the freezer. Cover it and leave it at room temperature for 4 hours, then put it in the freezer for 2 hours. The fat sets into a solid layer on top. Lift it off, then pour the bourbon through a clean cloth or a coffee filter back into its bottle. It keeps in the fridge for up to 2 months.
In a tall glass, stir together 45 ml of the washed bourbon, the maple syrup and the bitters until the maple has dissolved.
Fill the glass with ice and stir for 3 seconds.
Pour in the cold cider and stir once.
Twist the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

cocktail.tagline: You hear “only if” as a yes with instructions.

reading.epigraph: The bourbon in this glass owes a lot to someone's leftover bacon fat, and a joke.
whoYouAre: Somebody once told you, "You can, if you do all of it yourself." They thought that would be the end of it. You said fine, and spent your own evenings on it without a word of complaint, because a hard yes is still a yes. You ask for odd things too, half as a joke, and you're often the only one who comes away with them.

You suspected the "only if" was meant to put you off. You took it anyway, in plain sight, with a grin. What frightens you comes later, when the thing you made becomes the thing you're known for, and everyone expects you to keep making it. But here's what your stubbornness gives people: because you carried it the first time, nobody after you has to. They get the yes for free. That's a generous thing to leave behind.
yours: Don Lee came to bartending from a job in IT. Eben Freeman, a New York barman, told him about fat-washing: stir a melted fat into a spirit, freeze it, lift the fat away, and the flavour stays behind. You may have heard Lee invented it. It's often told that way, but he didn't.

A regular at PDT, the bar where Lee worked, had a lot of bacon fat and no idea what to do with it. Lee asked about it, as a joke at first, then asked for some. When he took the idea to Jim Meehan, who ran the bar, Meehan was wary, and fairly: infusions take staff time. Lee could put it on the menu if he did all the infusions himself. In Meehan's words, "in true Don Lee fashion, he did." Early on, Freeman tried Lee's version and said it was better than his own. It became the bar's best-selling drink, and it set off a whole run of fat-washed drinks, made with nuts, chorizo, even olive oil.

Whatever Meehan expected, I like to think Lee heard a yes, and got to work. So would you. The rest of it comes later. Lee is proud of the drink, but it nags at him too: he once said it's the one that will probably follow him around for the rest of his life. Years on, an environmental cocktail group even held it up as a sustainable drink. He granted you could see it that way, but said it certainly wasn't what they'd been thinking. I'd guess you know that feeling, of watching something you started go places you never meant it to.

The cocktail I've made for you starts where his did: bourbon washed with bacon fat, the way his recipe is printed, with Benton's bacon from Tennessee and Four Roses bourbon if you can get them, or a smoky dry-cured bacon and any straight bourbon. You make it yourself, so the washing is yours to do: warm the fat, stir it into the bourbon, wait four hours, freeze it for two, lift the fat off and strain. A little maple, Angostura bitters and a twist of orange peel, as in his Old-Fashioned. Then I take it somewhere his recipe doesn't go: a tall glass packed with ice, topped with a crisp, dry sparkling cider, so the apple meets the smoke and the maple. I did that as a nod to everyone who took his idea their own way.

So let it follow you. Being known for something isn't a fence around you. It's the mark you meant to leave, even if you'd never say so, and it carries on without you holding it up. Walk on to the next odd thing whenever you like, and be glad, out loud, that you made this one.

anchors.fact: Ron Cooper was in Oaxaca on holiday with friends (Oxford, COOPER, RON pdf 573); in his own telling, a New Year's trip through Mexico that friends invited him on and he led, in Oaxaca "to drink a little mezcal" (VinePair 2021; F13).
anchors.meaning: Company and a way back from the start: a trip, not an exile.

anchors.fact: A policeman at a roadside checkpoint said his uncle made mezcal in the mountains; Cooper asked if he could get some ("Really, can I get some?"), and was told to come back the next day; it was unlike anything he'd had (VinePair 2021; F14). "He came back" is our close inference.
anchors.meaning: The step past the usual: someone asked, and came back for it.

anchors.fact: He brought a couple of litres home and tasted them with friends: "Everyone went crazy for it"; a chef friend asked when he could bring in more (VinePair 2021; F15).
anchors.meaning: The trip finished at his own table, told to friends.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing; yours y2

anchors.fact: "I wanted to bring them back to the U.S. to share with friends, but I wasn't allowed" (JBF 2016; F16; the reading quotes only "but I wasn't allowed"); he got the licences "to make it available for me and my friends" (VinePair 2021; F18).
anchors.meaning: Sharing was the reason, in his words, not our reading.

anchors.fact: When he went back (a three-month trip to make art, with the mezcal hunting alongside; never "for more"), the border let him keep only a little, and he poured most of a jug of Chichicapa mezcal away (VinePair 2021, his account; F18; no number, C4).
anchors.meaning: Stuck = a find you can't bring home. He fixed the way back, not the trip.

anchors.fact: He named the first mezcals after the villages where they were made, Chichicapa and San Luis del Río (Proper p. 248; Oxford pdf 573); sold as it is, not blended to suit a brand (Oxford, DEL MAGUEY pdf 638).
anchors.meaning: He came home with the address: the credit goes to the place.

anchors.fact: Slowly placed in bars, and many drinkers took it straight (Proper p. 248); a cult following, then bartenders "clamored" (Oxford pdf 573).
anchors.meaning: It came to be loved at home. No scale.

anchors.fact: He calls it "a famous Mexican dicho": you don't find mezcal, mezcal finds you (VinePair 2021; F22). In English it's a popular expression in the drinks trade (*Fortune*, 4 Aug 2019); I found no Mexican source for it independent of him, and Oxford's two recorded dichos are others (pdf 1288, 1291).
anchors.meaning: The villages' answer to "discovered". Cold epigraph: "They say", not "in Mexico"; in the reading, "in Mexico" only as his ("a Mexican saying he quotes").

cocktail.closingLine: Buy the honey on a street near home you've never walked down. It still counts.
cocktail.glassware: a tall highball glass (about 300 ml), filled with ice
method: Make the honey syrup ahead. In a small jar, stir 1 tablespoon of runny honey into 1 tablespoon of warm (not boiling) water until smooth, then let it cool. If your honey has set hard, stand the jar in hot water first so it runs. Keep it equal parts: a thicker syrup makes the drink too sweet. This makes enough for two drinks, and the rest keeps in the fridge.
Squeeze the grapefruit and the lime.
In a tall glass, pour the honey syrup, 1 teaspoon of lime, the grapefruit juice and the mezcal, then add a small pinch of salt. Stir until the honey and the salt have disappeared.
Fill the glass with ice. Top with the cold sparkling water, then lift the drink once from the bottom with a long spoon.
Set a grapefruit wedge on the rim.
cocktail.name: Brought Home

cocktail.tagline: Every good find makes you think of someone.

reading.epigraph: Two places go into this glass: a village in Mexico, and wherever you live.
whoYouAre: You're halfway through the best meal of the trip, down a street the guidebook didn't mention, and you're already working out who you'll tell. You'll come home with the name of the place, what to order and who to ask for.

Truth is, you like the guidebook. Around people who brag about never booking anything, you leave the return ticket out. Softer still: the best night of a trip is sometimes the one after it, at your own table, telling it. Not because you didn't love being there. Because a find isn't finished until someone you love has heard about it. So the one trip you'd never book is the one with no way back: stuck somewhere, even somewhere beautiful, with no one to tell. You bring it home instead, and everyone who stayed gets to go a little. That's what you give them: the world, handed round, with directions.
yours: Ron Cooper had been drinking mezcal for years, the everyday kind, and he'd always bring a bottle back for his friends. Then one New Year he led some friends on a trip through Mexico. At a checkpoint in Oaxaca, in the south, he told a policeman they'd come "to drink a little mezcal". The policeman said his uncle made mezcal up in the mountains. Cooper asked if he could get some. The uncle was coming down the next day: come back tomorrow, and there'd be some. Cooper came back. It was, in his words, "mind-blowing", unlike anything he'd had.

He bought a couple of litres, took them home and poured them for his friends. "Everyone went crazy for it." Coming home from a later trip, he was told at the border he could bring in only a little, and he had to pour most of a big jug away, a jug from a village called Chichicapa. He did it "tearfully". He'd wanted to bring it home to share with friends, he said later, "but I wasn't allowed". So he got the licences to bring it in properly, and he named the first mezcals after the villages where they were made.

He quotes a Mexican saying: you don't find mezcal, mezcal finds you. The villages had it all along. What he did is what you do with every good find: he didn't keep it, and he didn't pass it off as his. He brought it home and put the village's name on the bottle, and anyone who loved it knew where to send their thanks. And I like to think what hurt at the border wasn't the mezcal going down the drain. It was the friends at home who'd never taste it. You'd feel it the same way.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Paloma, the long, bright drink people say Mexico orders instead of the Margarita, made here with mezcal instead of tequila, so it's smoky as well as sharp. I'd pour Del Maguey's Chichicapa: the village on that jug he had to pour away, and one of the first two he named on a bottle. Fresh grapefruit and a little lime give it its edge, and it's built in a tall glass, then filled with ice and lengthened with sparkling water. The sweetening is my change. Many bartenders make their own grapefruit soda, with sugar. I use honey, and I'd ask for a honey from near where you live, a jar from one place rather than a blend. Most of the drink's sweetness is that honey, so the glass doesn't work without it. That's for you. Home is half the trip for you, so it goes in with the same respect as the village. Two places, both named, and neither one the lesser. Any runny honey will do.

You don't need a ticket to go one street further. Away, you give a place everything: the market, the side street, the tip from someone who lives there. At home, you take the same road to the same shop. Try the street after it. Ask the person behind the counter where they'd eat. I'd bet there's a find twenty minutes from your door that nobody you know has heard of yet, and you're the one who'll tell them. That's a whole trip, and you'll be home in time to tell it.

anchors.fact: On the night of 6 January 1909, at 88° 7′ S, Shackleton admitted it must be the last outward march with the sledge, saying nature and too little food had beaten them. Two days in the tent in a blizzard followed. On 9 January they left the sledge and pushed on to 88° 23′ S, about 180 km from the Pole (SPRI: "within 180km"; our sum is 179.6 km). They raised the flag, turned their backs on the Pole, and he wrote that failure was theirs, though they had done their best to avoid it. (F7–F10, S1)
anchors.meaning: He called it failure; the Scott Polar Research Institute calls it "the brave decision to turn for home". The guest files their own turn-rounds the same way.

anchors.fact: At New Year 1909 (the passage isn't pinned to the day), he wrote that he made himself consider the lives of the men with him, and that going too far would make getting back impossible. He kept going south for days afterwards. (F3, F5, F23)
anchors.meaning: Only "he made himself consider". "He turned back for them" and "one sum since New Year" are the bartender's **I like to think**.

anchors.fact: Same passage: the science was done, "But all this was not the Pole. And how sadly I realised that I need not say." (F4)
anchors.meaning: The want he swallowed, on his own page.

anchors.fact: Two days in the bags in "shrieking blizzard", the food going without marching, fearing the tracks to the depot would drift over. (F8)
anchors.meaning: Stuck, with other people's lives on your count.

anchors.fact: The Bluff depot was "the one which I had told Joyce to lay out" (Ernest Joyce, in charge of dogs and sledges), "the one ray of hope". Without it they hadn't food enough to reach the ship. Joyce stocked it in two journeys, and it held luxuries in plenty and an ample supply. (F11, F21, 526)
anchors.meaning: The sum only worked because he'd laid down the way home before he left.

anchors.fact: Marshall's illness grew worse. Shackleton left him in Adams's care and pushed on with Wild, found the hut empty, and reached the ship on 1 March: "the load which was suddenly lifted from my shoulders". That same afternoon he set out again to bring in Adams and Marshall. On 4 March the entire expedition was safe on board (date only: the book gives 1 a.m. and 2 a.m.). Dossier only: Adams nearly went over the ice edge within sight of the ship. (F12–F18, F22)
anchors.meaning: Everyone home is the only summit that counts, and he went back out for it the day he could have rested. Never "no man left behind".

anchors.fact: Joyce's party left Carlsbad plums at the depot: a preserved plum sweet, sold boxed as a luxury (1891 London cookbook, 1900 German exhibit, 1952 analyst). Never "candied" or "stuffed". (P1–P5)
anchors.meaning: Our fresh-plum syrup is a stand-in, owned in one clause: a nod to what was waiting and the planning behind it. Never "the plums they found".

anchors.fact: Antarctic Heritage Trust conservators found crates of Mackinlay's in the ice under his 1908 hut at Cape Royds (no find year). Whyte & Mackay, which owns the brand, recreated the whisky as a limited edition, then (April 2017) launched Shackleton, a blended malt "inspired by" him and using the recreation as its "foundation". (W1, W4, W5, W8, W10)
anchors.meaning: The link, never the mirror. Say "a blended malt named for him and built on a recreation of the whisky his expedition left under its hut", never the hut whisky, never "his whisky".

anchors.fact: Plum is on the *Flavor Matrix*'s Grain wheel (pdf 137, rendered), not in Grain's listed pairings (pdf 136). The syrup is adapted from the *Codex*'s Blended Strawberry Syrup (p. 47). (card)
anchors.meaning: Craft, not story.

anchors.fact: The famous ship: *Endurance* was trapped in the pack ice and "finally crushed by the pressure" (SPRI). (S2)
anchors.meaning: One clause in y1, to set it aside. Never in the image.

cocktail.closingLine: Drink to the top you turned round from. It was still the right place to turn.
cocktail.glassware: a heavy double tumbler, one large clear cube
method: **The plum syrup (about 20 minutes; makes about 220 ml, enough for about 35 drinks).** Stone 100 g of ripe plums and throw the stones away whole; don't crack them. Blend the flesh, skins and all, until smooth. Put it in a small pan with 200 g of white sugar and warm it gently, stirring, just until the sugar has dissolved; don't let it boil. Press it through a fine sieve and let it cool. It keeps in the fridge for about a week; if it ever tastes fizzy, throw it out.
Put the plum syrup and the bitters in the tumbler, then the whisky, and stir to mix.
Add one large ice cube and stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Twist the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Far Enough

recipe.item: Shackleton blended malt Scotch whisky (40%), recommended, or any Highland blended malt Scotch, 40-43%
recipe.note: a blended malt named for him and built on a recreation of the whisky his expedition left under its hut

recipe.item: rich plum syrup, made at home from ripe plums
recipe.note: a nod to the preserved plums waiting at the last depot on the way back; fresh plums stand in for them

cocktail.tagline: People go further with you because they trust you to bring them home.

reading.epigraph: They turned round 180 km from the South Pole. This glass is for the way home.
whoYouAre: It was your idea in the first place: the hill, the all-day walk, the trip nobody else would have booked. Then, a couple of hundred metres below the top, the cloud comes down, someone has gone quiet, and you hear yourself say it: "Right. Turning round." The groan. The long way down. In the car park you count heads, and nobody notices you're counting.

You'll go as far as everyone can get back from, and not a step further. You wanted that top more than any of them. You swallow it on the spot, so nobody has to feel they cost you anything, and later, privately, you file the day under "didn't make it". The fear is getting stranded somewhere you led people, with no plan that gets every one of them home. And that's what your turning round gives the people with you: they go further in your company than they'd dare alone, because they know you'll turn round in time. You earn that trust every time you turn.
yours: You may know the story of Ernest Shackleton's ship, crushed in the ice. Years before it, he walked towards the South Pole with three others, Frank Wild, Eric Marshall and Jameson Adams, hauling sledges onto the high plateau. At New Year 1909, short of food, he wrote that he made himself "consider the lives of those who were with me": go on too far, and they could never get back. He kept going south for days afterwards. On 6 January he admitted, that night, that it had to be their last march south with the sledge. Then a blizzard pinned them in their tent for two days, with the food going. On 9 January they left the sledge, pushed on to about 180 km from the Pole, planted the flag, turned their backs on the Pole, and started home. He wrote that failure was theirs, though they had done their best to avoid it. The Scott Polar Research Institute calls it "the brave decision to turn for home".

The way home was hunger and storms, from one store of food to the next. He had told one of his men, Ernest Joyce, to lay out the last big store, and he called it the one ray of hope in front of them. When they reached it there were plums and plum puddings waiting. Then Marshall's illness grew worse. Shackleton left him with Adams and pushed on with Wild to catch the ship, and found the hut empty. When they finally got aboard, he wrote of the load suddenly lifted from his shoulders. That same afternoon he set off again, to bring in the other two. On 4 March the whole expedition was safe on board.

I like to think Shackleton had been doing one sum since New Year: how far four people could go and still all get back. He gave the weather and the food as his reason, and both were real. But I think the food was the road home, and he turned while it could still get them all back, with that last store counted in. That's you. You go as far as everyone can get back from, you hold your own wanting until the last possible moment, and then you turn. "But all this was not the Pole," he wrote. "And how sadly I realised that I need not say." You know that sentence. You've just never said it out loud.

The cocktail I've made for you is a whisky Old-Fashioned, as great a classic as there is. That classic is built from things that keep: whisky, sugar, bitters and water. I've added one that doesn't. The plums at Shackleton's depot were preserved ones, a boxed luxury; mine are fresh and blended into a rich syrup: a nod to what was waiting at that last store, and to the planning that put it there. I'd pour Shackleton, a blended malt named for him and built on a recreation of the whisky his expedition left under its hut in Antarctica, or any Highland blended malt Scotch. It's built over one big cube in a heavy tumbler, the kind of glass that stands steady wherever you set it down, and orange peel finishes it.

So stop keeping that file. Every turn-round in it is a reason people still say yes when you ask them to come. And one of these years, choose a top that's only for you, take people strong enough to get there and back, and go. They'll all come home, the way they always do with you. This time, I hope you stand on it.

anchors.fact: At twenty-one, in 1979, he asked Ray at the Tiki-Ti "What's in this drink?" and, "no matter what the drink", heard "Rum and fruit juice", "everywhere I went" (Proper p. 258). (F2)
anchors.meaning: An answer that is true and explains nothing. *Our reading:* it wasn't even a lie.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: can't rest inside an answer that explains nothing; fear: entrapment, stuck with an answer they can't get behind

anchors.fact: Ray Buhen had worked at the original Don the Beachcomber; Beach had told him (not "his staff") never to reveal trade secrets, lest competing tiki bars adopt them, and he "was only acting on ingrained instincts" (Proper pp. 258–259). (F3)
anchors.meaning: Nobody was hiding anything from him in particular. The answer was a habit, not a villain.

anchors.fact: Many recipes, "including the Zombie", were lost by the time Berry started asking (Proper p. 259); in 1998 he put it in print that nobody seemed to know what went into the Zombie (Oxford pdf 260, Curtis quoting him). (F3, F8)
anchors.meaning: The one question that stayed open.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: how long it's been. Guard: paraphrase the 1998 line (*The First Guess*); never "he asked about the Zombie in 1979" (C2); never "the one nobody could explain" or "the one he still couldn't answer" (many were lost; he decoded many others, pdf 260; A8, my shorthand struck)

anchors.fact: By day he wrote film trailers and poster copy (Proper p. 259), later "his day job as a screenwriter" (Oxford pdf 259); through the 1980s, "I was working completely in isolation" (Proper p. 259). (F4, F5)
anchors.meaning: Held alongside an ordinary life, for years, without telling anyone.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: they've stopped mentioning it. Guard: one clause, "a day job in films"; no Home Alone; the guest is never called lonely

anchors.fact: He interviewed retired bartenders, and their children where the bartender was gone; many recipes were "written in code" (Oxford pdf 259); off-hours he read microfilm in libraries and hunted former Beachcomber and Trader Vic barmen (Proper pp. 260–261). (F6, F7)
anchors.meaning: Evidence from the people who made the drinks, not anyone's say-so.
anchors.speaksTo: goal: understanding; trusts evidence. Guard: the code gets one clause, no secret-recipe romance

anchors.fact: Ted Haigh, a "fellow cocktail historian" (Oxford pdf 259; not "friend", A16), "Gregarious and bombastic", "was the opposite of Berry" (Proper p. 259). Alone Berry got "rum and fruit juice"; with Haigh "he walked away with a recipe"; "The first Don the Beachcomber recipes I got were because of Ted" (p. 260). They met in the 1990s (Oxford pdf 259). (H1, H2, H4)
anchors.meaning: The door opened when he took the question to the person least like him.
anchors.speaksTo: the proposal (Wren's y5 candidate). Guard: Beachcomber recipes in general, **never the Zombie**; no Corpse Reviver, "skeleton key" or "Dr. Cocktail"

anchors.fact: Berry said it took "ten years and three books" to nail down the Zombie's origins (Oxford pdf 260). (F9)
anchors.meaning: The years were his own count, and he didn't stop.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: how long it's been. Guard: always "he said"; no arithmetic from 1998

anchors.fact: In *Sippin' Safari* (2007) he revealed "an early recipe" from a self-published 1950 three-ring-binder cookbook whose author thanked Don the Beachcomber for his "generous assistance"; he later turned up a 1934 Zombie Punch and a 1956 recipe in *Cabaret* (Oxford pdf 260). (F10, F11)
anchors.meaning: Pieces, each on paper, none the whole answer yet.
anchors.speaksTo: evidence wins, not charm. Guard: the binder is never "the original" (C1)

anchors.fact: In the ZOMBIE entry he signed himself, Berry writes that the original formula Beach "took to his grave" was found by him in 2006 in the notebook of former Beachcomber's headwaiter Richard Santiago (Oxford pdf 2229). (F12)
anchors.meaning: The day he finally knew.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: they love the day they know. Guard: "what he calls the original"; no order against the binder (C1); no "as he tells it" frame (*Worth the Trip* y2)

anchors.fact: He printed the whole recipe in that entry, every part named and measured, including "Don's Mix", spelled out as two parts grapefruit to one part cinnamon syrup (Oxford pdf 2229); Regan reprints it from Berry's site (Joy pdf 409). Codex p. 179: Donn's Mix No. 1 is "a classic tiki syrup made with grapefruit juice and cinnamon syrup". (F14, F19)
anchors.meaning: Handed over whole, so nobody has to take it on trust.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: hand over the whole answer, plainly. Guard: never "the old recipes hid" grapefruit and cinnamon (A12); our glass is *a* Zombie, not *the* (A10)

anchors.fact: Seven books "featuring definitive recipes" (Oxford pdf 259); Smuggler's Cove and Three Dots and a Dash "owed a debt to Berry" and were "near-instant successes" (never "hugely", A6), and Three Dots is named after a lost tiki drink whose recipe he uncovered (Proper p. 262); he "made a convincing case" that tiki drinks were among the original craft cocktails (Oxford pdf 259). (F1, F17, F18)
anchors.meaning: Something everyone had written off is seen properly again.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: things written off get seen properly. Guard: no "Eighty percent", no "shamed" **Not in the reading since 2026-10-06** (Q054 cut y2's last sentence); dossier only.

anchors.fact: Craft cocktail people "didn't want to touch tiki with a ten-foot pole" (Proper p. 257); "the mavens… paid him little heed" for many years (p. 261). (F16)
anchors.meaning: Standing didn't move him. The evidence did, in the end.
anchors.speaksTo: Sage: authority that can't explain itself. Guard: no villains, no grievance

anchors.fact: The glass: the parts of the Zombie as Berry printed it (Oxford pdf 2229), shaken and poured over crushed ice as the Codex's own Zombie is (Codex p. 127), with Tomás's proportions.
anchors.meaning: Every part named, in the glass. The proportions and the shake are ours.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof. Guard: never "Beach's recipe", "his recipe" or "the notebook's recipe" for our glass

anchors.fact: Falernum: "recipes vary"; rum, sugar and lime, with cloves, ginger and nutmeg; "Almonds are sometimes added" (Oxford pdf 761). Berry went "gathering ferns and Falernum recipes" from the old barmen (Proper p. 261). (F20)
anchors.meaning: A bought bottle is the one part you'd take on trust. Ours is made at home, with every part known. *Our riff.*
anchors.speaksTo: gift: nothing taken on trust. Veto: bought falernum counts as nuts

anchors.fact: "6 drops Pernod" (Oxford pdf 2229; Joy pdf 409). Regan lists Pernod among the absinthe *substitutes* (Joy pdf 64) and treats Pernod and absinthe as two bottles (Joy pdf 395); the Codex's own Zombie uses "Pernod Absinthe" (p. 127), which the Codex counts among its absinthe bottlings (p. 34). (C5)
anchors.meaning: Drink only, no story.
anchors.speaksTo: Guard: if kept, "Pernod (the anise liqueur)", never "absinthe" (*Rosetta*'s bottle)

cocktail.closingLine: Write everything that's in the falernum on its bottle. Then ask your oldest question out loud.
cocktail.glassware: a tall Zombie glass, filled with crushed ice
method: **The falernum (10 minutes, then a day; makes about 375 ml, enough for about 20 drinks).** With a vegetable peeler, take the green zest off 4 limes, leaving the white pith behind. Put the zest and 12 whole cloves in a clean lidded container with 150 ml of the gold Jamaican rum, and leave it at room temperature for 24 hours. Strain it. In a small pan, warm 200 g of sugar with 100 ml of water, stirring, just until the sugar dissolves, then let it cool. Stir the syrup into the strained rum and pour it into a clean bottle. Write everything that went in on the bottle. It keeps in the fridge for a few months.

**The cinnamon syrup (5 minutes, then 30 minutes off the heat).** Warm 200 g of sugar in 200 ml of water with 3 cinnamon sticks, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then let it simmer for 2 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it for 30 minutes, then strain. It keeps in the fridge for about two weeks.
Fill the tall glass with crushed ice so it chills while you mix.
Put everything except the mint in a shaker. The grapefruit juice and the cinnamon syrup go in separately: together they're "Don's Mix", two parts grapefruit to one of cinnamon.
Fill the shaker with ice cubes, close it and shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Strain over the crushed ice, and top the glass up with more crushed ice.
Slap the mint sprig once between your palms to wake its scent, then stand it in the ice.
cocktail.name: Show Your Working

recipe.item: falernum, made at home: a lime and clove syrup with rum in it, as they make it in Barbados, but with no almond, no nutmeg and no ginger
