cocktail.tagline: You'll follow a question for years, then share every part of the answer.

reading.epigraph: Once, if you asked what was in drinks like this, you'd hear: rum and fruit juice.
whoYouAre: Years ago, someone gave you an answer that was perfectly true and told you nothing. You nodded, and kept the question. It has come along ever since, at the back of an ordinary week, and now and then another piece falls into place. Nobody would guess that one of your questions is older than some of your friendships.

You've stopped mentioning it, because people expect a question to be settled or dropped by now. Some take you for a know-it-all. It's nearly the opposite: you can't rest inside something you aren't allowed to understand. What frightens you is being stuck for good with an answer you can't get behind. And once you do understand, you lay all of it out, plainly, so nobody else has to take it on trust. People get the whole answer from you, free, and every year it cost you was worth it.
yours: In 1979, at twenty-one, Jeff Berry started going to tiki bars on his own. At the Tiki-Ti on Sunset Boulevard he asked the old barman, Ray Buhen: "What's in this drink?" Whatever the drink, Ray gave the same reply: "Rum and fruit juice." Berry heard it in bar after bar. Ray wasn't being difficult: he had once worked for Donn Beach, who created the Zombie at his Hollywood bar, and Beach had told him never to give away the bar's trade secrets, in case rival bars copied them. So by the time Berry started asking, many of the old tiki recipes, the Zombie's among them, had become a mystery.

Berry had a day job in films. His off-hours went on the question. He read microfilm in libraries, tracked down retired barmen, and their children when the barmen were gone, and learned to read recipes written in code. In 1998 he put it in print that the Zombie's recipe was still unknown. Getting to the bottom of the Zombie took ten years and three books, he said. He found an early recipe in a self-published cookbook from 1950, and in a former headwaiter's notebook, what he calls the original. And he printed a Zombie with every part named.

The answer that kept Berry going, I like to think, wasn't a no. He could have lived with a no. It was "rum and fruit juice": polite, true, and empty. You've been handed that answer too, more than once. A shrug doesn't end a question for you. It starts one. And his narrowed the way yours do, from every drink on the menu down to one: the Zombie, and then he stayed with it for years, beside an ordinary job, until he could write the whole thing down.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Zombie, the first famous tiki drink and still one of the great ones. Every part Berry printed is in it, and your recipe names each one. Two of them, grapefruit and cinnamon, travel under one old name, Don's Mix, a classic tiki syrup. Here they go in one at a time. The balance is mine: more of the lime, the grapefruit, the cinnamon and the falernum, so it's brighter and fresher. And I make the falernum myself (a sweet syrup of lime, cloves and rum that goes into many tiki drinks), as a nod to all the years he spent asking what was in things: with a bought bottle, you'd have to take the maker's word for it. It's shaken, then poured into a tall Zombie glass full of crushed ice, and topped with mint. It's a big drink and a strong one, made to be taken slowly.

One more thing from Berry's story. On his own, he got "rum and fruit juice". When he went in with Ted Haigh, a loud, sociable fellow historian whom one writer called Berry's opposite, he left with a recipe. "The first Don the Beachcomber recipes I got were because of Ted," Berry said. So take the question you've carried longest, and ask it out loud to the person you know who's least like you, the one who'd ask a stranger anything. Ask before you're sure it's a good question. You may get there years sooner, and on the day it all falls into place, you won't be the only one who's glad.

anchors.fact: Less than four months after the wartime ban took effect (30 June 1919), and before national Prohibition, the Greenwich Village Inn that Barney Gallant ran was raided, and he was arrested with half a dozen of his waiters (*Joy* pdf 59).
anchors.meaning: An ordinary working night. The trouble landed on the people carrying the trays.

anchors.fact: He agreed to plead guilty on condition that the waiters were set free (*Joy* pdf 59).
anchors.meaning: A trade made calmly, with a condition: his name on the record, theirs off it.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: takes the cost for specific people ("put it on me"); In control, Controlled

anchors.fact: He was sentenced to thirty days in jail and served far less (*Joy* pdf 59).
anchors.meaning: It cost him something real, and it wasn't martyrdom. The plain size of it takes the halo off.

anchors.fact: At his later club (West Third Street, from 1924) the house rules told guests not to overtip their waiter ("Why be a chump?") and to check the bill (*Joy* pdf 59–60).
anchors.meaning: One act, not a saint. Good business and a good deed sat in the same man.

anchors.fact: His name was Gallant (*Joy* pdf 59).
anchors.meaning: A coincidence owned once, about him, never pointed at the guest.

anchors.fact: In the saloons of the 1870s–80s, acquaintances drank in rounds, taking turns to pay (or rolling dice for it), so few stopped at one, and a strong Cocktail was too much. Oxford reads vermouth as "one solution": by the early 1880s, spirit and vermouth half and half (the Manhattan and its siblings) (Oxford, COCKTAIL pdf 490; MANHATTAN pdf 1221). Not dated to 1919 or to Gallant's bar.
anchors.meaning: The round is the bar's own ledger. The Saviour always gets the next one in.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: owing; position: let one stand unpaid

anchors.fact: Whether the waiters went free is implied by the condition, not stated. When (never "that night": the page dates neither the plea nor any release) and what they felt or owed are nowhere on the page.
anchors.meaning: Only as signposted wonder ("I've always wondered…"), never as a claim about them or him.

cocktail.closingLine: Let someone get this one. Don't get the next.
cocktail.glassware: tall glass (highball, about 350 ml), filled with ice
method: Fill a tall glass to the top with ice.
Measure 45 ml of rye into the glass. Then fill the same jigger to the same line with sweet vermouth and pour that in too.
Shake in the Angostura (two dashes) and stir five or six turns with a long spoon, just to chill.
Top with the cold soda water, then lift the drink once, gently, with the spoon.
Squeeze a strip of lemon peel over the top of the glass so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Next One's Mine

recipe.note: the same measure as the rye: half the weight is the vermouth's
added last

cocktail.tagline: People breathe easier when you say, “Leave it with me.”

reading.epigraph: The vermouth in this glass is there because hardly anyone stopped after the first.
whoYouAre: The bill nobody can split, the call nobody wants to make, the mistake that was only half theirs: it's landed on someone near you. You don't rush. You weigh it up, quietly, and then you say it: "Put it on me." And they go home lighter. That's the kindness in you, and it counts for more than you'll ever let anyone say.

The other half is harder. Someone does you a small kindness, a lift, a meal, an evening of their time, and it's paid back within the week, with a little extra. Owing anyone, even briefly, feels like weakness to you, like leaving a door open that someone could walk through. So your books are always in credit. Plenty of people owe you something. You've never asked for any of it back.
yours: In 1919, months before national Prohibition began, a wartime law had already made selling drink illegal. That year, the Greenwich Village Inn in New York, which a man named Barney Gallant ran, was raided, and he was arrested along with half a dozen of his waiters. Barney agreed to plead guilty on one condition: that his waiters were let go.

He was sentenced to thirty days in jail, and he served far less. Yes, his name really was Gallant. You could say it was his place to answer for, and maybe it was simply good business. But I like to think it was more than that: that he looked at his waiters, who'd only been carrying the trays, and decided the cost was his.

You'd have made the same decision, and you'd have called it only fair. What I've always wondered is how it felt for those waiters, going home owing someone that much. You've stood where Barney stood more times than you can count. You've never let yourself stand where they did.

The cocktail I've made for you comes out of the old saloons, where people at the bar drank in rounds, taking turns to pay, and hardly anyone stopped after the first. A strong drink was too much for that, and one answer was to split the whisky half and half with vermouth, a wine flavoured with herbs: that's where the Manhattan, a renowned classic, and its family come from. So I kept the equal split, the way the Manhattan's early recipes often had it: rye and sweet vermouth, poured to the same line twice, with bitters, then let it run long over ice with soda and a twist of lemon. The rye dry, the vermouth dark and bittersweet, all of it cold and bright. I kept the split for what you won't allow yourself: something else carrying half the weight, so everyone can keep going.

So when someone does something for you, don't pay it back. No dinner in return, no bigger present, no "I'll get you back for this". Every time you square it straight away, you take something from them: the feeling you get every time you say "put it on me". Let them keep that. And for once, you get to be the one who's let off.

anchors.fact: With Repeal coming in 1933, the *New York Sun* gave G. Selmer Fougner a series to help readers find their way around legal wine and spirits, which were unfamiliar to them. His daily column began on 20 October 1933 and ran until he died in 1941 (Oxford pdf 833; F4).
anchors.meaning: He didn't make a speech. He made a thing that came out daily, with his name on it, and he kept it up.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: they argue in what they make, not across the table; fear: going quiet when it matters (answered by the record, never claimed of him)

anchors.fact: Before him, wine writing tended to be high-toned and mystifying, and cocktail writing jocular and even aggressively vulgar. Oxford: "Fougner was neither." He didn't talk down to people who drank cocktails or beer (pdf 833; F6, F8).
anchors.meaning: The belief is shown in how the thing is made. Never "he didn't argue": he did, in print, "gently (usually)" (pdf 834; F11, G3).
anchors.speaksTo: Leave a mark; the made thing *is* the argument

anchors.fact: He answered readers' questions patiently, however silly: one asked whether all scotch was made in Australia (pdf 833; F9). Not "every" question.
anchors.meaning: Nobody gets talked down to: that's what the guest's made things give. The humour is the reader's question, not Fougner's wit (F7).
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: nobody talked down to

anchors.fact: When he didn't know an answer, he put the question to his readers, nationwide. Many of them had first-hand knowledge of how famous drinks began, and the column "seems to have been" especially popular with former bartenders. Their testimony still lights up the history of famous drinks, the Ward Eight among them (pdf 833–834; F10).
anchors.meaning: The made thing lets other people say what they know, together. It's a door he opened, never a man stuck for an answer (that's the Problem Solver's ground).
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: others get words and room to join in

anchors.fact: In 1934, while Fougner was seeking more about the Ward Eight, a reader sent the *Sun* a recipe: a whisky sour made to fix "certain objectionable features" of it, with bourbon, grenadine, orange bitters or (as "many prefer") half an orange's juice, plain water or seltzer, in a large, heavy, round-bowled beer glass over "a rather large piece of ice". Fresh mint, when there was any, went in place of crème de menthe, bruised and added with the orange slices ("This is an improvement"). Wondrich prints this letter rather than the only pre-Prohibition recipe, then gives his own build with rye (*Imbibe!* pdf 243–244; W1–W5).
anchors.meaning: The recipe exists because the column asked and someone answered: the made thing still working decades later. Never "the original Ward Eight" (the origin is legend, W8), and never "the books don't print it" (Wondrich prints the letter).
anchors.speaksTo: the made thing carried beyond him

anchors.fact: Spec v1: 75 ml bourbon (40–46%), 30 lemon, 30 orange (half an orange), 15 ml grenadine of pomegranate juice and sugar only, short-shaken for about 5 s (*Codex* p. 138's Collins method), over one large piece of ice in a heavy round-bowled beer glass, topped with 45 ml seltzer, then the mint (bruised), orange half-slices, pineapple and a cherry. **The letter's:** bourbon, lemon, orange juice, grenadine, seltzer, the ice, the glass, the mint and the fruit (pdf 243–244). **Ours:** the shake (the reader built it in the glass), the measures (the letter gives none that convert: "three-quarters full" of a whisky glass), a fixed grenadine dose, and the sugar left out.
anchors.meaning: Every ingredient comes from someone who wrote to the column, or from Fougner. Only the method and the measures are the bartender's. Never "his recipe".
anchors.speaksTo: the made thing carried beyond him; brought others in

anchors.fact: The reader: "The amount of sugar should be regulated to taste, and likewise the grenadine" (pdf 244). Spec v1 leaves his barspoon out, and the orange and grenadine carry the sweetness (balance.py: with the spoon it's 8.00 g, OUT).
anchors.meaning: The letter left room for the drinker, so the drinker's choice is on the page. Say "his letter leaves the sugar to taste", never "he said to leave it out".

anchors.fact: In June 1936, after Repeal, when American commercial grenadine was imitation, Fougner wrote of "innumerable products masquerading under that name" and claimed the reputable French makers used real pomegranate juice. Oxford: it "took some decades to sink in" (pdf 947–948; G2–G4). Grenadine was in the Ward Eight from the start (pdf 2120). He gave no home recipe (G3).
anchors.meaning: Where he did argue, he argued in the column, and the point landed slowly. No cause claimed. Our syrup is our choice, tied to his line, never "as he made it", never "fakes", never "the argument", never "my own pomegranate syrup" (*Till Spring*).
anchors.speaksTo: put the finished thing out; it lands later

anchors.fact: *Flavor Matrix* pdf 200: pomegranate is "mostly fruity" but "also characterized by sharper aromas such as anise and mint". Mint isn't on its pairings list, and the page describes the fruit and its juice, not a syrup.
anchors.kind: pairing (Checks only; one clause in y4)
anchors.meaning: The reader's 1934 mint and Fougner's 1936 pomegranate share an aroma. Wording: "pomegranate has a note of mint of its own" or "pomegranate's own aromas include mint". Never "hint" or "faint" (strength words the page doesn't give; "hint" was my own r3 shorthand, struck), and never "the Matrix pairs them".

anchors.fact: The reader adds the mint "with the slices of orange, &c.", after the glass is filled (pdf 244): last.
anchors.meaning: "Mint in last, the way the reader wrote it" is on the page. "Wrote", not "did".

cocktail.closingLine: Mint in last, the way the reader wrote it. Then see who writes back.
cocktail.glassware: a large, heavy, round-bowled beer glass (about 400 ml), with one large piece of ice
method: Make the grenadine ahead. Put the pomegranate juice and sugar in a jar, close it and shake (or blend) until the sugar has dissolved. Keep it in the fridge.
Put one large piece of ice in a large, heavy, round-bowled beer glass.
Pour the bourbon, lemon juice, orange juice and grenadine into a shaker. Fill it with ice and shake briefly, about five seconds. That leaves room for the seltzer.
Strain it into the glass, over the ice.
Top up with the cold seltzer (soda water).
Press the mint sprig once between your fingers to wake it up. Tuck it into the glass with the orange half-slices, the pineapple and the cherry, the way the reader wrote it.
cocktail.name: The Long Answer

the reader said many preferred it to orange bitters
real pomegranate, which Fougner wrote the reputable French makers used
the reader wrote "plain water or seltzer"; I chose the seltzer

*for the grenadine:* 250 g pure pomegranate juice (unsweetened; a bottle is fine) and 250 g sugar

cocktail.tagline: What you make gives people the words they were missing.

reading.epigraph: This glass starts from a reader's letter to a New York paper, in 1934.
whoYouAre: When something matters to you and the arguing starts, you're rarely the loudest person there. Often you go quiet. The right words turn up later, on the way home, and you can lose sleep over the ones you didn't say. Losing an argument, you get over. Staying quiet when it really mattered, you don't.

Then you make something: a page, a song, a picture, a menu, a message that took all evening. In that, you say all of it, plainly, and you mean every word. Sometimes you wonder whether making things instead of arguing is just a nicer way of hiding. It isn't. An argument changes one mind, if you're lucky. What you make travels. It gives people the words they were missing, and room to join in without anyone being talked down to. That's your way of standing up for something, and it brings people together.
yours: In the autumn of 1933, with Prohibition about to end, the *Sun*, a New York newspaper, gave a writer named G. Selmer Fougner a daily series to help its readers find their way around legal wine and spirits. Wine writing then tended to be grand and mystifying, and cocktail writing jokey, even crude. Fougner was neither. He didn't talk down to anyone who liked a cocktail or a beer, and he answered readers' questions patiently, however silly. One wanted to know whether all scotch was really made in Australia.

When he had a view, he gave it, gently, usually. In 1936, when the grenadine sold in America was mostly imitation, he wrote that the reputable French makers used real pomegranate. And when he didn't know an answer, he put the question to readers all over the country, many of whom had been there when famous drinks began, and they wrote back. The column ran daily until he died in 1941.

This was his way of standing up for something, I like to think: not with a speech, but with a daily column, where nobody was laughed at for asking and anyone who knew better could say so. It's your way too. And look at what came back when he asked. More than one reader wrote to him about a single Boston drink, and one of those letters holds the recipe behind the cocktail I've made for you.

It's the Ward Eight, Boston's best-known cocktail, built from that reader's 1934 recipe: bourbon, lemon, grenadine and half an orange, squeezed, which he said many people preferred, over a rather large piece of ice in a heavy, round-bowled glass "of the type generally used for beer". Fresh mint goes in with the orange slices, pineapple and cherry he listed, in place of a mint liqueur. "This is an improvement," the reader wrote. He allowed plain water or seltzer; I chose the seltzer. His letter leaves the sugar to taste, so I left out the spoon, because the orange and the grenadine carry the sweetness. The grenadine is made from real pomegranate, for Fougner's column of 1936. Pomegranate's own aromas include mint, so the reader's improvement and the columnist's point share a scent. It's long, bright and tart, a hazy rosy orange, and strong: the reader called his "highly potent".

Somewhere there's a thing you made about what you believe, and never put out: the page, the song, the long message sitting in drafts. It's ready. But sending it is the argument, so it waits. Send it, where anyone can see it. Then ask people what they think, and mean the question. Some of the answers will surprise you, and you'll find you were never standing up for it alone.

anchors.fact: Simonson calls him perhaps "the most mild-mannered person in the cocktail industry", soft-spoken, "in a world of brassy characters", and says there was "nothing safe or boring about his business" (*Proper* p. 240; F1).
anchors.meaning: The quiet one who goes anyway, in the book's words, attributed. Never that he was afraid (G1).
anchors.speaksTo: doesn't look the part; the drive is inside

anchors.fact: As a student in Austria (Vienna, says Oxford) he met Alpine pine liqueur, and thought it would sell in Colorado's ski towns. He went back to Austria "to find an example" and brought over Zirbenz, made for two centuries (*Proper* p. 240; Oxford pdf 975; F2–F3).
anchors.meaning: He went after a kind of drink he'd met abroad. He found the bottle when he got there: never "went for Zirbenz" (G2).
anchors.speaksTo: needs something named to go after

anchors.fact: Zirbenz is made by the Josef Hofer family distillery in Austria, since 1797 (Haus Alpenz catalogue 2026; *PUNCH* 2015; F14).
anchors.meaning: Say who made it, plainly. He found it; they made it (G7).
anchors.speaksTo: gives: brings back what nobody near could get

anchors.fact: He could afford only one pallet, sixty cases; none of the big distributors were interested, so a one-man wine outfit carried it. Sold as an après-ski tradition, "the product struggled, but there were places where it did well" (*Proper* p. 240; F5–F6).
anchors.meaning: The risk is real and his own; the counterweight always comes with it (G3, G4).
anchors.speaksTo: fear: a comfortable life that asks nothing of them

anchors.fact: Of bartenders meeting Zirbenz: "warm, if bemusing"; "the conifer is hardly an essential bar ingredient" (*PUNCH* 2015; F13).
anchors.meaning: He knew how odd the prize was, and went anyway. Usable as a light touch; not a fear.
anchors.speaksTo: the prize matters a little less than they say

anchors.fact: "With the Alpine liqueur under his belt", he asked Aspen's best liquor store what they would be interested in carrying, and that "would become his modus operandi"; he asked bartenders on both coasts what he should be importing or creating (Meehan asked for Batavia arrack) (*Proper* pp. 240–241; F7–F8).
anchors.meaning: The first prize became a way of never running out of things to find. "Missing" is our gloss (G5).
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: finished scares them more than far

anchors.fact: In the decade before 2016, a visit by Seed to a cocktail bar "was always an occasion": nobody knew what rare bottle he'd "pull from his bag" (*Proper* p. 240; F11). Oxford: Alpenz imported things "long absent from the American market", "in response to demands from bartenders", until they became a "near necessity in serious cocktail bars" (pdf 975; F10).
anchors.meaning: Others' wants became his next map. He mostly imported what existed abroad: never "revived" (G6).
anchors.speaksTo: gives: makes far-off things feel reachable

cocktail.closingLine: Pine first, then a spoon of what came next. Then ask someone what they'd like you to find.
cocktail.glassware: heatproof glass mug with a handle (about 250 ml), warmed with hot water first
method: Fill the glass mug with hot water and leave it for a minute to warm, then tip the water out.
Pour in the stone-pine liqueur first, then the rum.
Add the teaspoon of allspice dram, the lemon juice and the demerara syrup.
Top with the hot water and stir a few times so it all comes together.
Squeeze the strip of lemon peel over the top of the mug so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in. Drink it while it's hot.
cocktail.name: Someone Else's Map

recipe.item: Zirbenz Stone Pine Liqueur of the Alps (recommended)
recipe.note: or any Alpine stone-pine liqueur (Zirbenlikör) of about 35%; made in Austria by Josef Hofer, a family distillery since 1797
any aged rum of 37.5 to 45%

recipe.item: hot water, just off the boil

cocktail.tagline: Every summit gives you a better view of what you could do next.

reading.epigraph: Sixty cases of the pine in this glass were all one importer could afford.
whoYouAre: The medal's still round your neck, or the last exam's handed in, or the record you hunted for two years is finally on the shelf. Everyone's pleased for you. And by that evening you're quietly reading up on the next one.

People call it restless. It isn't, quite. What you dread is finished: a comfortable life that asks nothing of you, a map with nothing left on it. Going after something far away and hard to get is how you find out what you're made of, and once you know, you need something new to find out about. And you never return empty-handed. You turn up with things nobody near you could have got, and you make far away look like somewhere people can actually go. Everyone you know lives a bigger life because you went. No prize on your shelf is worth as much.
yours: Eric Seed was a student in Austria when he first came across the pine liqueur of the Alps, and he thought it would sell in Colorado's ski towns. One writer calls him perhaps the most mild-mannered person in the cocktail business, soft-spoken among loud characters, and then adds that there was "nothing safe or boring about his business". Seed went back to Austria to find a pine liqueur he could bring over, and returned with Zirbenz, which the Hofer family distillery has made since 1797.

He could afford one pallet: sixty cases. None of the big distributors were interested, so a one-man wine business carried it, sold as a drink for after skiing. It struggled, though in some places it did well, and a Denver bartender took it on. Years later Seed said the conifer "is hardly an essential bar ingredient". Back then, with that first bottle behind him, he walked into the best liquor store in Aspen and asked what they'd like to carry. That became his way of working. He asked bartenders on both coasts what he should bring over, and went and found it: one asked for Batavia arrack, a rum-like spirit from Indonesia. For a decade, by one writer's account, a visit from Seed to a cocktail bar was an occasion, and nobody knew what rare bottle he'd pull out of his bag.

The pine was never the whole point, I like to think. It took him somewhere, it showed him he could, and then came the question you know well: what now? As I see it, his way out was to stop waiting for something new to find him, and to ask other people what they'd like him to find. That way, the map never runs out. You've had that flat evening more times than you'd admit, and his way out is one you can borrow.

The cocktail I've made for you is a toddy, the classic warm winter drink, for the end of a cold day. The pine goes in first, Zirbenz or any Alpine stone-pine liqueur, three parts to one of aged rum, a pairing its importer suggests for toddies. Then a teaspoon of allspice dram, the kind of bottle Seed might pull out of that bag. I added it for the find that comes next, so the first prize and the one after share a glass. A little lemon, a touch of brown sugar syrup, hot water, all in a glass mug warmed first, and last, lemon zest twisted above the steam, for its scent. It takes a reddish tint from the pine, and it smells of pine, with spice underneath.

So the next evening you arrive and it goes flat, don't go looking for a bigger mountain straight away. Ask a friend what they've stopped hoping to find: the book that's out of print, the song they half remember, the place they always meant to see. Then go and get it. You'll never be short of somewhere to go, and a friend gets the thing they'd given up on. I hope your list stays long.

anchors.fact: For six years from 1978, at a Los Angeles hotel bar, DeGroff learned spirits and cocktails on his own; one book says it was so he wouldn't lose a good job he knew was beyond his qualifications. Perhaps his regulars noticed; the wider world didn't (*Proper* p. 10; card F16; A1).
anchors.meaning: The private certainty with no proof yet, and the fear of being found out. The motive is the book's narration: "the way one book tells it".
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: sure there's more in them, no proof

anchors.fact: Baum auditioned him to run a classic cocktail bar at Aurora. His instructions were oblique; he mostly said right or wrong. DeGroff: "Joe never told me anything" (*Proper* p. 11; Oxford pdf 633; A2).
anchors.meaning: Trusting a teacher who gives no reasons. Baum is never softened or made a trickster.

anchors.fact: Baum tasted DeGroff's beef-broth drink: "There's something wrong with it. Fix it." DeGroff: "I couldn't figure it out" (*Proper* p. 11; Oxford pdf 374; A3).
anchors.meaning: The verdict from the one person you wanted to impress, with no clue attached. "His beef-broth drink"; "fix" only in Baum's quote.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: asked for real, having nothing

anchors.fact: At a Chinese restaurant he saw beef with orange on the menu. The lemon and lime came out, orange went in, and Baum said OK (*Proper* pp. 11-12; Oxford pdf 374-375; A4).
anchors.meaning: The answer is his own, found away from the teacher. Only what both tellings share.
anchors.speaksTo: turn: find it wherever it turns up

anchors.fact: More than thirty years later the orange is still in the recipe DeGroff gives: a little fresh orange juice, and orange peel over the top (Oxford pdf 375, 2021; A5).
anchors.meaning: What you find yourself lasts. Ours is built on it, never "his recipe".
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; both orange touches

anchors.fact: One drinks historian's own 2017 Bullshot uses lemon juice and a lemon wedge (Wondrich, *Daily Beast*, 10 Apr 2017; A6). The Matrix's beef wheel says only "citrus", which covers orange and lemon alike (Matrix pdf 45, 80; M2-M3).
anchors.meaning: The orange stayed his own choice, not the standard. One writer's recipe; never "everyone uses lemon", never "off the chart".
anchors.speaksTo: the answer was his, not the standard one

anchors.fact: Baum insisted on fresh juice, no soda guns, no ready-made sour mix. DeGroff hesitated (what if it got busy?). Baum: if it was too much for him, someone else would get the job. The book says he decided to work it out (*Proper* p. 12; Oxford pdf 1598; A7).
anchors.meaning: The safety net refused, and the fear of being replaced. Order-neutral ("Baum also…"), no bar named.

anchors.fact: When Baum reopened the Rainbow Room he made sure DeGroff ran its bar, for a decade (Oxford pdf 633; A8). By one account it became the centre of a change in how cocktails were made (Oxford pdf 1598; A9).
anchors.meaning: The test held: a decision, never "Baum believed in him". No year; never "grew from".
anchors.speaksTo: the hard word, worked on, held

anchors.fact: From 2005 he taught and influenced thousands of bartenders; Oxford calls him generous to his younger peers (Oxford pdf 636, 264; A10).
anchors.meaning: The one who listened becomes one people learn from. Date the present tense to 2021; "younger" out.

anchors.fact: The Bullshot was soon a favourite of ad men, movie stars and anyone after something flashy and different (Oxford pdf 374); one of the most popular drinks of the late 1950s and '60s, surprisingly tasty when made with care, faded after the 1980s (Wondrich 2017; A11).
anchors.meaning: Lets a beef-broth drink sound worth having: "once everywhere, now half-forgotten". No Monroe line.

cocktail.closingLine: Squeeze the orange peel over it last. When nobody will say what's wrong, read every menu you're handed.
cocktail.glassware: tall highball glass (about 400 ml), filled with ice
method: The day before, make the broth: put about 1 kg of beef shin on the bone, one onion cut in half and one carrot in a large pan with 2 litres of cold water. Bring it slowly to a bare simmer and keep it there for about 3 hours, skimming off the grey foam as it rises. Strain through a fine sieve, add no salt, let it cool and keep it in the fridge (it keeps 3 days, or freeze it). Lift off the fat once it's cold.
If the broth has set to a soft jelly in the fridge, that's a good broth. Warm it just until it pours again, then let it cool to room temperature.
Fill a tall glass to the top with ice.
Put the vodka, 90 ml of broth, the orange juice, the sherry and a small pinch of salt in a shaker with plenty of ice.
Shake hard for about ten seconds, then strain into the glass.
Squeeze a strip of orange peel over the drink so its oils fall on it, then lay the peel on the ice.
cocktail.name: Work It Out

recipe.note: any vodka, 37.5% or stronger

recipe.item: plain beef broth, made at home
recipe.note: beef shin and bones, onion, carrot and water; no salt, no stock cube; made the day before; made with beef: not for vegetarians

cocktail.tagline: You know there's more in you, and keep working until it shows.

reading.epigraph: Vodka, beef broth, and an orange someone found on a Chinese menu.
whoYouAre: Someone you look up to tries something you've worked hard on and says, "Not quite." Nothing else. You smile, say you'll have another go, and that night you're still turning it over, long after they've forgotten they said it. You'd never admit how much one sentence from the right person can move you. Or why: you're sure there's more in you than anyone has seen so far, and you don't have the proof yet.

What you dread is the day it's for real: being asked for it properly, in front of the very person you wanted to impress, and having nothing to show. So you listen to people who know more as if every word might be the key. It's also your gift to them. People love teaching you, because you take a hard word home and come back with something. But part of you is still waiting for them to hand you the answer. Some answers nobody can hand you.
yours: In the mid-eighties, a legendary New York restaurateur named Joe Baum was opening a new restaurant, Aurora, and he tried out a bartender called Dale DeGroff to run its cocktail bar. DeGroff had spent six years behind a hotel bar in Los Angeles, learning spirits and cocktails on his own; the way one book tells it, so he wouldn't lose a good job he knew was beyond his qualifications. Perhaps his regulars noticed. The wider world didn't.

Baum rarely explained himself. He mostly told DeGroff whether he was going the right way or the wrong way. "Joe never told me anything," DeGroff said. One day Baum tasted his beef-broth drink and said: "There's something wrong with it. Fix it." DeGroff couldn't work out what. Baum also wanted fresh juice behind the bar, never a bottled sour mix, and when DeGroff asked what they'd do if it got busy, Baum told him that if it was more than he could manage, someone else would get the job.

The answer turned up somewhere else entirely: at a Chinese restaurant, where DeGroff saw beef with orange on the menu. He took the lemon and lime out of his drink and put orange in, and Baum tasted it and said OK. Baum never pointed him to the orange. I like to think he couldn't have: he could taste that something was wrong, but the answer had to be DeGroff's, and it stayed his. More than thirty years later, the orange is still in the recipe DeGroff gives for it. You treat the people you learn from as if they're holding the answer and deciding when to let you have it. The answers that make you who you are come from somewhere nobody pointed you, and they're yours for good.

The cocktail I've made for you is built on the Bullshot, as DeGroff prints it: vodka shaken with beef broth. It was once everywhere, from advertising men to film stars, and it's half-forgotten now, which is a shame, because one drinks historian calls it surprisingly good when it's made with care. So I make the broth at home the day before, slowly and plainly, then shake it cold with the vodka, a splash of medium dry sherry, a little salt and a little fresh orange juice, and squeeze an orange peel over it at the end. I left out his hot sauce and pepper, and there's no lemon or lime anywhere in it. I kept both touches of orange, because the orange is the answer he found for himself. It comes out a warm amber, savoury and deep, and the orange lifts it.

So if someone whose opinion matters to you says "not quite" and stops there, don't hold out for an explanation. Take it home, and let the answer come from wherever it turns up: a conversation on a train, a shop window, something you read for another reason. When you bring it back, it'll be yours, and so will everything you build on it. Nobody is going to tell you when you're good enough. You'll know it the day your answer is one they hadn't thought of.

anchors.fact: He liked to tell people a shark had eaten his leg (Difford's, Sutcliffe, secondary; F7), and as his fame grew many believed it (Beyl 2015, secondary; F8).
anchors.meaning: The hard thing, told as an adventure, and people leaned in. His telling rests on one page: "he liked to tell people", never "always" or "everyone".
anchors.speaksTo: they tell their struggles as adventures so the struggle doesn't win

anchors.fact: He lost a leg as a boy (Oxford pdf 258; Beyl; Difford's; F2). No cause, no age (C1, C2).
anchors.meaning: Said once, plainly. The mirror is the telling, never the loss.

anchors.fact: After leaving school, a run of jobs that didn't last, selling paint and tyres among other things; then in 1934 a barbecue shack in Oakland, Hinky Dink's, where he was owner, bartender and cook (Oxford pdf 258; F3–F4). He opened it with $800 borrowed from an aunt, and at first it held about thirty workers from the neighbourhood (Beyl; F4).
anchors.meaning: The life without the shark was already worth telling.
anchors.speaksTo: a plain life, told plainly, that nobody remembers

anchors.fact: "Trader" came from his habit of trading meals for goods and services, and he renamed the shack Trader Vic's (Beyl, secondary, single source; F6).
anchors.meaning: The big name grew from a plain habit, and the plain root is the better tale. Never "the Trader was a fake".
anchors.speaksTo: make life larger in the telling

anchors.fact: In later years, sitting with a special customer, he liked to pull the artificial leg out from under the table and tell them not to get one unless they really needed it (Beyl; F9).
anchors.meaning: The same man could tell it plainly, with a joke in it, and it still held the table. Touches the leg itself: Wren decides if it's safe for a reader who has lost a limb.

anchors.fact: In 1938 the shack became Trader Vic's; by his death in 1984 there were more than twenty, across North America, Europe and Japan, and his bar guide is still counted a classic of its kind (Oxford pdf 258; F12).
anchors.meaning: The legend was never the whole person.

anchors.fact: His Mai Tai, as he told it: 1944, the service bar of his Oakland restaurant, aged Jamaican rum, fresh lime, orange curaçao, rock candy syrup and almond orgeat, shaken hard with shaved ice, half the lime shell and a branch of mint; he gave two to friends from Tahiti, and the name came from what Carrie Guild said (*Joy* pdf 327; Oxford pdf 1210–1211; F13–F14). A rival's 1933 Mai Tai tasted almost nothing like it, and it was Vic's formula that rose (Oxford pdf 1211; F15).
anchors.meaning: The one thing he made that everyone still knows: "his Mai Tai", "the drink he said he created". Never "he invented the Mai Tai" flat.

anchors.fact: By 1955 the name had spread through the islands while his recipe stayed a secret, so rivals mixed rum and juice under it; by the 1970s the only place making it properly was Trader Vic's (Oxford pdf 1211–1212; F16).
anchors.kind: provenance (the epigraph only; y4's sentence cut, Hester r4)
anchors.meaning: The name travelled; the real thing underneath was better. Provenance only, never a second reveal.
anchors.speaksTo: the real thing doing the work underneath

anchors.fact: Our orgeat is made at home from almonds toasted first; the *Flavor Matrix* says nuts should be toasted to bring out their flavour (pdf 184). Vic's own orgeat was a bought French one, "for its subtle almond flavor" (*Joy* pdf 327; F18). Before the Trader, he was owner, bartender and cook of the shack, and drew on his cooking skills for his drinks (Oxford pdf 258; F4, F11).
anchors.meaning: The cook's step from the plain record, signposted as our reading ("I like to think…"). Never "he toasted his almonds" or "his orgeat".
anchors.speaksTo: the real thing doing the work underneath

anchors.fact: Appleton Estate became part of J. Wray and Nephew Ltd. in the early twentieth century (Oxford pdf 132; F19); the firm runs more than one distillery (pdf 1698), and Vic's seventeen-year Wray & Nephew is long defunct (pdf 1212).
anchors.meaning: From the firm whose name was on his bottle; never "the same rum" or "the same distillery".

cocktail.closingLine: Take the almonds to gold before anything else: that's where the taste is.
cocktail.glassware: double old-fashioned glass (about 350 ml), packed with crushed ice
method: Make the almond syrup a day ahead, or that morning. Spread 150 g blanched almonds on a baking tray and toast them in the oven at 180°C for 8 to 10 minutes, until pale gold and smelling toasted. Let them cool. Blend them with 300 ml cold water for a minute, leave it 30 minutes, then squeeze it all through a clean cloth into a bowl. Weigh the almond milk, pour it into a pan with the same weight of white sugar, and warm it gently, stirring, until the sugar has gone (don't let it boil). Off the heat, stir in ¼ teaspoon orange flower water. Bottle it: about 400 ml, two weeks in the fridge.
Make crushed ice: wrap a tray of ice cubes in a clean tea towel and bash it with a rolling pin.
Squeeze the lime, measure 30 ml of juice, and keep half the shell.
Put the rum, lime, curaçao, almond syrup and sugar syrup in a shaker with a big scoop of the crushed ice. Shake hard for about ten seconds.
Pour everything, ice and all, into the glass. Pack more crushed ice on top until it mounds over the rim.
Push the half lime shell into the ice, cut side up. Squeeze the mint branch once in your hand so it smells, and stand it up beside the shell.
cocktail.name: Hold the Shark

recipe.item: Appleton Estate 12 Year Old Rare Casks Jamaica rum (43%), recommended, or any aged Jamaican rum, the oldest you can find
recipe.note: Vic's seventeen-year Wray & Nephew is long gone. Appleton Estate became part of J. Wray and Nephew, the firm behind Vic's rum, in the early twentieth century.

recipe.note: measure it: a big lime's juice pushes the drink too sharp

cocktail.tagline: Your worst days become everyone's favourite stories.

reading.epigraph: Its name went round the islands long before its recipe did.
whoYouAre: A flat tyre on the motorway, in the rain, with no signal. By Friday it's the best thing anybody's heard all month: there's a tow-truck driver who sang the whole way, a hailstone the size of a plum, and a lorry that people ask you to do again. All of it happened, more or less. You simply know which version deserves to be the one people keep.

What nobody at the table knows is that the bigger the story, the worse it really was. The forty minutes on the hard shoulder, cold, and sure nobody was coming, never make it in. Told plainly, a bad day might sound like weakness. Worse, it might sound like nothing much, and be forgotten by the weekend. So you tell it larger, until the bad day is the small thing in it. The people listening go home believing their own bad week will pass, and might even be funny one day. That's a real kindness, and it's why they keep asking for another.
yours: Victor Bergeron lost a leg as a boy. Years later, when people knew him as Trader Vic, the man behind a chain of South Seas restaurants and the Mai Tai most people know, he liked to tell them that a shark had eaten it. As he got famous, plenty believed it. Maybe a shark really did. The odds are against it.

The plain version goes like this. He left school, then tried one job after another, selling paint and tyres among other things, and none of them lasted. (Yes, tyres. I didn't make that bit up.) In 1934, in his early thirties, he opened a barbecue shack in Oakland with $800 borrowed from an aunt, and ran it as owner, bartender and cook. One writer says that's where the nickname began, with his habit of trading meals for goods and services. Four years later the shack became Trader Vic's, and by the time he died there were more than twenty, across North America, Europe and Japan.

I like to think he knew the shark was the better line at a table. But look at the plain version again: the jobs that didn't last, the borrowed money, a cook paying his way in meals, and a name that grew out of it. None of it needs a shark. It's a terrific story as it stands, and it was his all along. So is your own. The version you tell is a gift, and it does people good. The one you leave out would hold the table just as well.

The cocktail I've made for you is his Mai Tai, the renowned classic. I built it on his own account of making it, which he dated to 1944: aged Jamaican rum, fresh lime, almond syrup, orange curaçao, a dash of sugar syrup, all shaken hard with shaved ice, then half the squeezed lime shell and a branch of fresh mint standing up out of the glass. This one keeps close to his formula, and the main change is mine. He used a French almond syrup. I make mine at home and toast the almonds to pale gold first, the way a cook would, as a nod to the cook he was before anyone called him Trader. I like to think the cook in him would have approved. It's golden and cold, sharp with lime first, then round and nutty underneath.

So keep telling them. The shark stays: people need it, and you're good at it. But once, tell one exactly as big as it was. I'd bet the table goes just as quiet. And what they'll remember afterwards won't be the shark. It'll be you.

anchors.fact: The Vesper (gin, vodka, Lillet, once sold as Kina Lillet) is the first cocktail James Bond orders in Fleming's first novel, *Casino Royale* (1953). Fiction, owned in one clause (Oxford VESPER pdf 2099; F1).
anchors.meaning: The guest may know the name; the part they don't know is the gift.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me; gravities: Classic

anchors.fact: He asks for "a dry martini", then "One. In a deep champagne goblet.", and gives the measures himself: three of Gordon's, one of vodka, half a measure of Kina Lillet, shaken very well until ice-cold, then a large thin slice of lemon peel (novel, archive.org OCR highlights of two printings; Oxford pdf 2099; F2–F3).
anchors.meaning: The style is the precision: one drink, specified to the half measure.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Mastery; gravities: Controlled; texture: Sharp

anchors.fact: The drink is presented as his invention on the spot and at first has no name; later he borrows his colleague Vesper Lynd's name and christens it the Vesper (Oxford pdf 2099; F4).
anchors.meaning: Our reading: the drink takes its name from a person.

anchors.fact: Oxford: after her death at the end of the book, he never drinks it again. The book closes on her death, so this covers Fleming's later books; films out (Oxford pdf 2099; *Shaken Not Stirred*, OCR highlight; F5, C1).
anchors.meaning: Our reading, signposted ("I like to think"): the feeling shows only as something he stops doing.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me; texture: Quiet; fear: Weakness

anchors.fact: Fleming inscribed his longtime friend Ivar Bryce's copy "For Ivar, who mixed the first Vesper"; Bryce recalled making the cocktail with Fleming's help (Oxford pdf 2099; F6–F7, C4).
anchors.meaning: In print the drink is the character's; in the inscription, the credit goes to a friend.

anchors.fact: Bryce's account (Oxford: "apparently"): the name came from a drink of frozen rum with fruit and herbs, served at a country house in Jamaica and announced by the butler as Vespers. The page names no rum style or origin; our Jamaican rum is our choice for the place (F7).
anchors.meaning: The teaspoon under the order is our ode to where the name was served, tied in one clause.

anchors.fact: "Kina" (French for quinine) left Lillet's name in 1986; the cut in bitterness came in 1917 (Oxford pdf 2099–2100). *Codex* p. 74: Kina Lillet had a bit more cinchona than today's (F8, C3).
anchors.meaning: Today's Lillet Blanc makes the order; never "can't be made", never "the same bottle".

cocktail.closingLine: The rum goes in first, under the order. Once, tell one of them they're the reason.
cocktail.glassware: deep champagne goblet (about 200 ml), chilled
method: Chill the glass: half an hour in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you work.
Pour the teaspoon of rum into the shaker first.
Then make the order exactly as it was given: three measures of gin, one of vodka, half a measure of Lillet.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake it very well, until the outside of the tin is ice-cold (about 10 to 15 seconds).
Empty the glass, and strain the drink into it.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: One Line

recipe.note: not spiced, not sweetened; goes in first. Jamaican is my choice, for the island where the drink behind the name was served
the gin the order names; or any London dry gin
any plain vodka

cocktail.tagline: You keep your cool so the people you love can breathe.

reading.epigraph: Ordered down to the half measure, shaken ice-cold, then named after one person.
whoYouAre: The car slides on an icy bend with a friend beside you, and by the time it stops you've got them laughing. The wedding speech goes missing an hour before, and you've written a new one, with a joke about the old. People say nothing seems to touch you. They're wrong about why.

It's never for the room. It's for one person in it. The more someone matters, the cooler you get, because if the feeling showed, it might look like weakness. So you love in exact, unspoken ways: you know the date they'd rather not mention, and you never let on that you noticed. It was never the danger you were hiding. It was them. Around you, anyone you love gets to feel light, because the fear in the room comes to you and goes back as a joke. That's how you protect people. It matters more than the style ever could.
yours: In Ian Fleming's first novel, *Casino Royale* (1953), James Bond asks the barman for a dry Martini. "One," he adds. "In a deep champagne goblet." Then he gives the measures himself, down to the half: three of Gordon's gin, one of vodka, half a measure of Kina Lillet, shaken very well until it's ice-cold, with a large thin slice of lemon peel. It's fiction, of course. The drink is real, and it's still on cocktail lists.

In the book, the drink is Bond's own invention, and at first it has no name. Later he gives it one: Vesper, after Vesper Lynd, a woman he works with. After he loses her, at the end of the book, he never drinks it again in any of Fleming's books. I like to think that was the only way he'd let it show.

I recognise you in that order. The precision, three and one and a half, shaken until it's ice-cold, is the part everyone sees. The name is the part meant for one person. And if you've ever lost someone, I'd guess you kept it to yourself. There's just a place you stopped going back to, or a thing you quietly stopped doing, and nobody near you knows why.

The cocktail I've made for you is built on Bond's order, word for word: Gordon's, the gin the order names, then vodka and Lillet Blanc, the aperitif wine once sold as Kina Lillet, in his three, one and a half, shaken hard, in a chilled champagne goblet, with that large slice of lemon peel. Under it is the one thing that's mine: a teaspoon of rum, poured in before anything else. In the story Fleming's friend Ivar Bryce told, the name came from a frozen rum drink served at a country house in Jamaica, which the butler announced with "Vespers are served". The rum is my nod to that frozen rum drink, and I chose a Jamaican one for the place. It starts from a famous classic, and it's bone-dry, very cold, bright with lemon peel, and the rum only shows at the very end, to someone who knows to look for it.

No speech required. In his friend's copy of the book, Fleming wrote: "For Ivar, who mixed the first Vesper." So pick one of the people all that cool is for, and give them their line, plainly, on a day when nothing's gone wrong. It'll take more nerve than anything you've ever made look easy. And I'd bet it's what they keep of you.

anchors.fact: By the late 1930s he had wealth and some fame beyond Cuba, yet each morning he still put on the white jacket and went behind the bar to mix drinks (Oxford pdf 1655; F7). This ran until 1950, when ill health took him from behind the bar (pdf 1657; F12): never "to the end".
anchors.meaning: Our reading, signposted: he kept choosing the working side when he no longer needed to. Whether the jacket or the famous man was the disguise is the bartender's question, not the record's.

anchors.fact: Oxford calls him plain to look at, quiet and reserved in manner (pdf 1655; F6).
anchors.meaning: The ordinary side is on the page. Paraphrase only.

anchors.fact: He squeezed every lime by hand, fingers only, and in the same sentence was a pioneer of electric mixers (pdf 1655–1656; F8).
anchors.meaning: Plain handwork, kept by choice beside the newest tools, not a refusal of them.

anchors.fact: He told an American journalist in 1935 that he made up a new drink every day, as self-discipline (pdf 1656; F9). His words, through the journalist.
anchors.meaning: Keeping the edge daily: the fear of going weak, answered in his own words. Never "hours" or "in secret".

anchors.fact: He bought the bar in 1935, and by the late 1930s was rich and known abroad (pdf 1655; F5, F7).
anchors.meaning: A setting only. No "king", no superlative (C3), no famous customers.

anchors.fact: Oxford counts the Floridita (rum, red vermouth, white crème de cacao, lime, a little orange curaçao and grenadine) among his lasting creations (pdf 1656, 821; F10, F13).
anchors.meaning: His, on two entries. Oxford's recipe cites only Vic's 1972 guide and is in no booklet of his, so never "his recipe".

anchors.fact: For reasons nobody knows, it isn't in any of the souvenir recipe booklets he put out for the bar (pdf 821; F14), though he did reprint praise of himself in them (*Imbibe!* pdf 216; F17). No booklet years (C2).
anchors.meaning: The one thing of his that wasn't put forward. Any why is "I like to think". Never "he left it out".

anchors.fact: Trader Vic came across it on a visit in 1938, put it on the first menu of his own restaurant, and later printed it in his bar guide; Oxford's writer says it would have been lost otherwise (pdf 821; F15).
anchors.meaning: The part never put forward is the part someone else carried home: the answer to "would they still call?". One clause, owned; no leg, no shark, no Mai Tai, no "loved".

cocktail.closingLine: Half the lime, squeezed by hand. When you're next introduced, bring up something the introduction doesn't cover.
cocktail.glassware: nick-and-nora glass (about 150 ml), chilled
method: Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes.
Before you cut the lime, take one wide strip of peel off it with a vegetable peeler, green only, none of the white underneath. Set it aside.
Cut the lime in half. Squeeze one half over a jigger with your fingers, nothing else, until you have 15 ml.
Put the rum, vermouth, crème de cacao, curaçao, grenadine and lime juice in a shaker. Fill it with ice and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold.
Strain it into the cold glass.
Hold the strip of peel over the drink, green side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top. Lay it on the rim.
cocktail.name: Day Job

recipe.item: white rum, Cuban style (light and dry, unaged or lightly aged), 40% or stronger

recipe.item: fresh lime juice: half a lime, squeezed by hand

cocktail.tagline: You make difficult things look possible, and leave people feeling capable.

reading.epigraph: Its first maker put out booklets of the bar's drinks. This one's in none of them.
whoYouAre: Most days you're easy to miss: quiet in a meeting, with a joke that lands a second too late. Then something turns up that only you can sort out, like a friend's figures that won't balance the night before they're due, or a letter that has to be exactly right. For an hour you're someone else entirely. Afterwards you go back to being easy to miss, and that part is on purpose. You'd rather nobody near you felt outshone.

Ask which of the two is the costume, and you'd hesitate. Years ago, without quite noticing, you decided the quiet one was the disguise, and the ability was the real you. So you keep it sharp, every day, because going rusty would feel like disappearing. The people you're with get someone who could make them feel small and chooses, every time, to make them feel capable instead. That's worth more to them than the ability.
yours: Constante Ribalaigua came to Havana from near Barcelona as a child. At sixteen, as he told it later, his father, a bartender himself, asked if he'd like to learn the trade, and he said yes. He made his name at La Florida, the Floridita. In 1935 he bought it, and by the end of that decade he was rich, and known abroad too. He's remembered as quiet and reserved, and not much to look at. And every morning he still put on the white jacket and went behind the bar to mix drinks.

He squeezed every lime by hand, with his fingers only, though he was one of the first to put electric mixers on a bar. He told a journalist in 1935 that he made up a new drink every day, "as self discipline". Among the drinks he created was the Floridita: rum, red vermouth, a little chocolate liqueur and lime. He put out booklets of the bar's recipes, and for reasons we don't know, that one isn't in any of them. A visiting bartender, Trader Vic, came across it in 1938, put it on the first menu of his own place, and printed it years later. Without him, it might have been lost.

I like to think the jacket was the point: he no longer needed it, and he chose it anyway, morning after morning. I recognise you in that. You'd probably call the ability the real you. I'd call it the jacket: you put it on for other people. Who you are is the one who keeps choosing to. And of everything he made, one of the drinks that lasted is the one that isn't in any of his booklets.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from the Floridita, with two changes of my own. It's white rum, red vermouth, a little crème de cacao (a chocolate liqueur as clear as water), and grenadine and orange curaçao, one spoonful of each, shaken hard and strained into a slim stemmed glass that's been in the freezer. My first change is half a lime instead of a whole one, because a whole one makes it too sharp. Squeeze it with your fingers, the way he squeezed his limes. The second change is the twist: the lime's own peel instead of orange, so the lime that balances the drink scents it too. You'd only notice it if you knew, and that felt like you. It tastes of chocolate and lime, and it's a delicious one.

People will keep introducing you by what you can do: "this is the one who can sort anything out." When it happens again, let them, and then add something about you that has nothing to do with it: the song you can't stop playing, the town you'd move to tomorrow, something you're hopeless at. Watch which one they ask about. And let the quiet one be introduced too. It was never the disguise.

anchors.fact: In 2003 LeNell Smothers opened a wine and liquor shop at the far end of Van Brunt Street in Red Hook, Brooklyn, almost on the waterfront. Her chronicler jokes that you could hardly pick a better spot to hide a business. Bartenders came out to it anyway. (*Proper* p. 237; F1–F3)
anchors.meaning: It looked like the worst bet on the map, and the people who needed it made the trip. The doubtful look and the dependable thing are both true at once.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · texture: Risk taker

anchors.fact: In her own words (to Simonson, 2014), she knew how hard many things were to find if you were into classic cocktails. While friends in the trade worried about buying big cases of Hennessy at a good price, she went after odd cases of Italian amaro. (*Proper* p. 238; F7, F9)
anchors.meaning: She stocked for the people who needed it, not for the easy sale. Her reason is hers, on the record; nothing beyond it is claimed.

anchors.fact: Her shelves held bourbons not distributed in New York, rye at a time when hardly anyone stocked it, rye from Kentucky barrels she chose herself, amari and cachaça. Other liquor stores didn't bother with slow-selling stock like this, though much of it could be bought. (*Proper* pp. 237–239; F4, F8, F18)
anchors.meaning: What you came for was there, without fuss. Never "nobody else had it"; never "she lost money".

anchors.fact: She broke local liquor rules to stock Peychaud's and Underberg bitters, which counted as food, so grocery-store goods. (*Proper* p. 237; F5)
anchors.meaning: A small rule, bent to have what her customers needed, never for show. One clause, never glamour.

anchors.fact: The shop became famous among drinkers, and so did she, often as much for her temper as for her shelves (Simonson's word: "cantankerous"). Being told off by her became almost a rite of passage for regulars. (*Proper* p. 238; F11, F14)
anchors.meaning: Grant the bad name first, with a grin: it's other people's view, and it's half true.

anchors.fact: On his first visit, Damon Boelte started unwrapping the tissue paper round a bottle of the Red Hook Rye and she yelled at him on the spot. She later hired him; he went on to design the cocktail programmes at two Brooklyn bars. (*Proper* p. 238; F12–F13)
anchors.meaning: Two plain facts side by side. The page never links them; any link is "I like to think…".

anchors.fact: Boelte says that when he tells people he worked at LeNell's, they're amazed. (*Proper* p. 239; F17)
anchors.meaning: The place with the bad temper became the name people were proud to have on their record.

anchors.fact: Underberg is a bitters that a bar book gives as an example of a digestif, a drink meant to help digestion. Its country and recipe are not in our books (unsourced). (*Joy* pdf 419; F19)
anchors.meaning: The odd, bitter bottle the rules filed with the groceries, in the glass because she stocked it anyway.

anchors.fact: Sorghum syrup is made by pressing the stalks of sorghum, a grass related to sugar cane, and boiling down the juice (Oxford pdf 1834). A flavour reference book pairs syrups of this kind with grain (*Matrix* pdf 240). In her own words, her Southern background meant bourbon had to play a major role (*Proper* p. 238). (F7, F20, F21)
anchors.meaning: Our touch, chosen with her own words about where she came from in mind. That the syrup is Southern is not on any page we hold: say it as the bartender's choice ("I chose…"), never as the syrup's history.

cocktail.closingLine: Stir the sorghum in first: once it's cold, it clings. Then tell one person you'll be there, ahead of time.
cocktail.glassware: small rocks glass (single old-fashioned, about 200 ml), one large ice cube
method: Spoon the sorghum syrup and the Underberg into the glass.
Pour in the rye and stir with a bar spoon until the syrup has disappeared into the whiskey, about fifteen seconds. Do it before the ice: once it's cold, the syrup clings to the spoon.
Add one large ice cube and stir for another twenty to thirty seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Squeeze the strip of orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: No Promises

recipe.note: any straight rye at that strength; stronger bottles run too hot over one cube
pure sorghum syrup; or pure cane syrup. Measure it: half a teaspoon either way tips the balance
recommended; or another digestif bitters

cocktail.tagline: You never said you'd come. You always do.

reading.epigraph: This glass holds grocery-store bitters. A Brooklyn liquor shop wasn't supposed to sell them.
whoYouAre: A friend asks if you can help on moving day. "Probably," you say, with a grin that convinces nobody. On the day you're the first one there, with a van you borrowed from someone you won't name, and you leave after the last box is in. People introduce you with a warning: don't believe a word they say. You've never minded the warning.

You don't say you'll be there, because saying it out loud is a leash to you, and breaking it would be worse than anything they could call you. So you keep the bar low and clear it every time. You'd rather surprise them than let them down. When something really matters, your friends stop asking who's sensible and call you. You're the proof that someone can be rough round the edges and completely dependable, and to them that beats a good name any day.
yours: In 2003, LeNell Smothers opened a wine and liquor shop at the far end of Van Brunt Street in Brooklyn, almost on the waterfront. One drinks writer jokes that if you wanted to hide a business from its customers, you could hardly have picked a better spot. Bartenders found it regardless. She'd filled it with what they were looking for: bourbons not distributed in New York, rye when hardly anyone stocked it, a rye bottled from Kentucky barrels she'd chosen herself, bitter Italian liqueurs, and bitters that local liquor rules said belonged in a grocery store. She stocked those anyway.

Most liquor shops didn't bother with bottles that sold slowly. She told that writer, in 2014, that she knew how hard many of those things were to find if you loved classic cocktails, and while friends in the trade worried about buying Hennessy by the case at a good price, she went after odd cases of amaro, the bitter liqueur Italy makes from herbs. She was famous for her shelves, and often just as famous for her temper. Being told off by her became almost an initiation for her regulars. The first time Damon Boelte walked in, he started peeling the tissue paper off one of her bottles of rye, and she yelled at him on the spot. Later, she hired him. He says people are amazed when he tells them he worked at LeNell's.

The shop, I like to think, was a lot like you. It looked like the last place you'd count on, with a sharp word waiting at the counter, and it had exactly what you came for. And the people she told off were the ones most devoted to the place. That's you, as far as I can see. You give people every reason to expect nothing, and then you're the one who's there. You never ask them to rely on you. They just find out they can.

The cocktail I've made for you is a straight-rye Old-Fashioned. That's the great classic of whiskey, sugar and bitters, here with rye, the whiskey she stocked when hardly anyone did. I swapped the usual bitters for a teaspoon of Underberg bitters, as a nod to the rule she bent so her customers could have it. The sweetness is a spoon and a half of sorghum syrup, the pressed juice of sorghum stalks boiled down into syrup, because its sweetness sits well with rye. It's stirred over a single block of ice in a short, heavy glass, with orange peel twisted above it for its oils. Deep, dark, bitter at the edges, and exactly what you'd drive to the end of the street for.

Next time someone you'd go anywhere for has a big day coming, skip the grin and the "probably". Say yes, plainly, the week before. You won't lose an inch of your freedom: you were always going to go. What changes is theirs. For once they get to know, instead of hope. And you might find the warning was never what they believed about you.

anchors.fact: At an upscale Mexican restaurant (p. 72 gives no city; the chain had Seattle and Portland branches, so guest text says "the Pacific Northwest", audit v1 H10), he worked his way up from busboy to bartender, mostly making frozen drinks, "and liked it" (*Proper* p. 72; P1).
anchors.meaning: An ordinary job, done gladly. Never "frozen Margaritas" (*For Good*'s).
anchors.speaksTo: the everyday side; no solo genius

anchors.fact: A customer ordered a Singapore Sling. He asked two senior bartenders, and nobody knew how to make it. The book says that "didn't sit right": he bought his first cocktail book at Powell's in Portland and "kept going back" (p. 72; P2). The night itself isn't placed (H10).
anchors.meaning: Someone asked, and nobody behind the bar could answer: that's the guest's mirror. Not his failure, and never the seniors' fault. The page doesn't say he later made that Sling, or found it in the book: "I like to think" at most. No year, no outcome for that guest.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: being the one who isn't enough when someone's counting on them; hides the hours nobody saw

anchors.fact: His collection grew to hundreds of volumes (three hundred on p. 60; he said 350 in 2010). In 2010 he said he'd learned more from watching other people work than from his books; asked about mentors: "Probably dozens… I take something from each person." (FoodGPS 2010; P3, P4).
anchors.meaning: The hours were real, and he hands the credit to the people around him, in his own words. Say "hundreds", never either number.
anchors.speaksTo: shares all the credit, keeps all the fear

anchors.fact: His own words, of a Friday night in the rush: sixteen drinks going, "a lot of it is still muscle memory", keeping track of who's next; "That moment where: I got this." (p. 75; P6).
anchors.meaning: The rush is the day that counts, and it comes every week. The drill is why it feels ordinary. It happens every week: never "the one night".
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: what looks like calm is rehearsal; the practice holds

anchors.fact: Asked what he'd like to be known for: "making consistently excellent cocktails" (FoodGPS 2010; P5).
anchors.meaning: The same good drink every time, not the best one once.
anchors.speaksTo: anyone would have done the same; gives: the people near them are all right on the bad day

anchors.fact: Simonson says he could have become his city's star bartender but "didn't seize the mantle or seem to want it"; by the 2010s he stayed for years at one bar, long after its original staff had moved on, and "seemed most contented simply being a bartender" (p. 75; G1, G3).
anchors.meaning: Attributed, hedges kept. He stayed in the place; the crew left: never "stayed with his crew". His early cocky years get one clause at most (X1) and are never read onto the guest. No line says he never wanted attention.
anchors.speaksTo: being singled out feels like being left out; belonging

anchors.fact: Born Mark Johnson, he moved to Seattle at twenty-one and changed his name (the page dates the move, not the change); the surname came "from Greek mythology" (p. 71; N1). Dionysos is the ancient Greek god of wine (Mark Cartwright, *World History Encyclopedia*, 2012; secondary). He spells it Dionysos (N2).
anchors.meaning: Wren's ruling: one plain clause. He chose it, from the god of wine this place is named after. Never luck, never a joke, and nothing of his character read into it (the page's "more extroverted" reading stays in the dossier). **"God of wine" isn't on p. 71**: the page says only "Greek mythology", so the gloss rests on the encyclopedia, and the page gives no reason for the choice.
anchors.speaksTo: — (flag for Robin: second name coincidence in the family)

anchors.fact: The Sling is gin, liqueurs, citrus and soda, made across British Asia with plenty of latitude in the recipe. Its earliest recipe we have is a bar order printed in 1913, from the Singapore Cricket Club: "one Cherry Brandy, one Domb [i.e., Bénédictine], one Gin, one Lime Juice", ice, soda water, a few dashes of bitters (Oxford pdf 1803; *Imbibe!* pdf 122; S3, S11). From 1974 a Singapore hotel remade it with less Bénédictine and cherry, and added pineapple, orange and Cointreau; Oxford calls the result "sweet, rather sticky" (pdf 1804; S6–S7).
anchors.meaning: "The older way, before a hotel sweetened it in the 1970s." Never "the original", Raffles or Ngiam Tong Boon. Who ordered it: Oxford says "a member", *Imbibe!* says the younger members, so no number. One order that names the parts, never "one at a time" (my shorthand, struck, audit v1 H7). The club's refusal stays out.

anchors.fact: Spec v1: 30 ml each of London dry gin, Cherry Heering, Bénédictine and lime, built over one large cube in a large rocks glass, stirred, 90 ml soda, 3 dashes Angostura on top, no garnish. **The order's:** the four "one"s, ice, water, bitters (pdf 1803 / 122). **Wondrich's:** reading each "one" as 1 oz, the Singapore measure (*Imbibe!* pdf 122). **Ours:** the rocks glass and single cube (he says a Collins glass over ice), 90 ml soda (his 1–2 oz), three dashes, no garnish.
anchors.meaning: "I kept it at one measure of each": the equal measures are ours by Wondrich's reading, and the order itself says "one" of each. Never "his" Sling: p. 72 never says Dionysos made one.
anchors.speaksTo: practice so ordinary it needs no book; one of the crew

anchors.fact: Bénédictine is "essential" to the Singapore Sling among other classics (Oxford pdf 256); in the period it was "often replaced or supplemented by curaçao" (pdf 1803–1804). It's made from 27 plants and spices, nutmeg among them (pdf 256), so it counts as `nuts` on the safe side (S10).
anchors.meaning: "Goes into the Singapore Sling", never "always". The 1510 monk is company legend: out.

cocktail.closingLine: One of each, so anyone can learn it. Someone beside you already has.
cocktail.glassware: large rocks glass (about 400 ml), one large ice cube
method: Pour the gin, Cherry Heering, Bénédictine and lime juice straight into a large rocks glass: 30 ml of each.
Add one large ice cube and stir for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Top up with the cold soda water and give it one gentle stir.
Shake three dashes of Angostura bitters onto the top. No garnish.
cocktail.name: Anyone Would Have

recipe.note: one of each: that's the whole recipe

recipe.item: Cherry Heering (recommended), or another red cherry liqueur
recipe.note: the red cherry brandy Singapore drank then; it's what turns the drink pink

recipe.item: Bénédictine (recommended), or another sweet herbal liqueur
recipe.note: a French liqueur of herbs and spices, finished with honey
on top, last

cocktail.tagline: When it counts, you've already done it a hundred times.

reading.epigraph: Gin, cherry, herbs and lime. One day, nobody behind the bar could make it.
whoYouAre: The lights go out in the middle of a party, and you already know where the fuse box is. The car won't start on the way to the airport, and you've got the number saved. Afterwards, you shrug: anyone would have done the same. But you know that isn't quite true. You found the fuse box the week you moved in. You drove the route the day before. You don't trust yourself to be at your best on the day, so you don't leave anything to the day.

What you'd never say is why. It isn't pride. You're afraid of being the one who wasn't enough when someone was counting on you. So you practise, quietly, for things that may never happen, and when it goes well you hand the credit to everyone else. Being singled out has always felt a bit like being left out. But everyone near you gets through a bad day more easily because of a hundred ordinary ones you never mention. That's how you care for people, and it deserves more than a shrug.
yours: At a Mexican restaurant in the Pacific Northwest, Marco Dionysos worked his way up from clearing tables to the bar. (He chose that surname himself, after the Greek god of wine: the same god this place is named after.) There he mostly made frozen drinks, and liked it. Then one day a guest ordered a Singapore Sling. Marco asked two senior bartenders, and neither of them knew the recipe. As his story is told, that didn't sit right with him. He went to a bookshop in Portland, bought his first cocktail book, and kept going back.

His books ran into the hundreds, though he said he learned more from watching other people work. He moved to San Francisco and tended bar there for years. He once described a moment on a busy Friday night, with sixteen drinks going at once, a lot of it muscle memory, and the part he loved: "I got this." One writer says he could have become the city's star bartender, but "didn't seize the mantle or seem to want it". Asked what he'd like to be known for, Marco said "making consistently excellent cocktails". Asked about his mentors, he said: "Probably dozens."

That guest at the bar, waiting for a drink nobody there could make: I like to think he never quite forgot them. Nobody had done anything wrong. Someone had simply asked, and nobody was ready. I think that's the moment you practise against: not failing, but being the one who wasn't enough when it mattered. So you put in the hours nobody sees, and when the day comes and goes fine, you shrug. Like Marco, you'd rather be known for getting it right every time.

The cocktail I've made for you is that Singapore Sling, the older way, before a hotel sweetened it in the 1970s. The earliest recipe on record is a bar order from 1913, at a club in Singapore: one cherry brandy, one Bénédictine (a sweet herbal liqueur), one gin, one lime juice, then ice, soda water and some bitters. I kept it at one measure of each, so it's the kind of recipe you'll never need a book for. It's built straight in the glass over one big ice cube and stirred, with no shaker and nothing to show: a deep, rosy pink-red, a little cloudy with lime, the bitters just starting to bleed in from the top. I made it properly, for the guest who asked for it that day, and for every day you've got ready so nobody's left waiting.

You've spent years getting ready for other people's hard days. What you forget is that the others have been getting ready too, and some of it was for yours. Being enough was never meant to be your job alone. So before the next day like that, practise as much as you like. Then look at who's around you, and trust their hours the way they've always trusted yours. You were never the only one who was ready.

anchors.fact: After Katrina, Neal Bodenheimer, a New Orleanian then bartending in New York, felt he should be back in New Orleans (many from the city who lived elsewhere felt that if they didn't go home, it might not survive), so he came home, with the idea of being one of the first there with a stand-alone cocktail bar (as he told Robert Simonson, *A Proper Drink*, 2016, p. 284).
anchors.meaning: He went back because the place needed people to go back.

anchors.fact: He and his partner, Matt Kohnke, opened Cure in 2009 in the lonely Freret neighbourhood, far from the French Quarter (*Proper* p. 285; *The Gannet*, 3 Dec 2015). At least ten to twenty people tried to talk him out of it (p. 285).
anchors.meaning: Going first into a place people warned him off.

anchors.fact: In a 2015 interview he said they were a little nervous about the location at first, and that they couldn't afford to be anywhere else (*The Gannet*, 3 Dec 2015).
anchors.meaning: The doubt is on the record, and it passed; the choice was partly money.

anchors.fact: He handed the drinks to his bartenders, but gave the bar a dress code: no shorts, no flip-flops, no baseball caps. Cure never quite lived it down (*Proper* p. 285).
anchors.meaning: He kept a standard for the room, one the bar never quite lived down.
anchors.speaksTo: drivers: provide structure; Control; fear: Revolution / Chaos
