anchors.fact: For the first nine months to a year, he said, they had to persuade people to drink cocktails and that they weren't just being pretentious; in 2015 he granted that craft cocktails' label of pretentious was not without justification, and said they had to work on their service (*Proper* p. 285; *The Gannet* 2015). The bar did well from the start (*Proper* p. 285).
anchors.meaning: Keeping the standard, and fixing what the doubters were right about.

anchors.fact: Short of cash, for the first two weeks the bartenders poured from his own bottles from home (*Proper* p. 286).
anchors.meaning: It cost him, quietly. One clause only.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: Failure **Not in the reading since 2026-10-06** (Q153); dossier only.

anchors.fact: Looking back, he said that in a way it had been a decaying city, where people started over (*Proper* p. 287).
anchors.meaning: Order kept while everything around was starting over.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: Revolution / Chaos; drivers: provide structure

anchors.fact: The Crusta, a New Orleans drink of the mid-1800s by the bartender Joseph Santini, is known for how it's dressed: a sugared rim and a long lemon peel lining a small wine glass; its name is the crust the sugar makes (Oxford CRUSTA pdf 610; SUGAR RIM pdf 1953).
anchors.meaning: A drink that dresses properly by definition, from the city of the story.

anchors.fact: Its 1862 printed recipe ends with two words: "Then smile." (*Imbibe!* pdf 234).
anchors.meaning: The standard and a light face go together.

cocktail.closingLine: Fit the peel inside the glass, then take your hand away: it stays.
cocktail.glassware: small stemmed wine glass (about 200 ml), chilled, fine sugar on the outside of the rim, lined inside with a collar of lemon peel, no ice
method: Put the two tea bags in the cognac in a jar and leave them 20 minutes. Taste from 15 minutes on and lift them out, without squeezing, when the tea shows as a dry edge behind the brandy. Left too long, black tea turns harsh.
Chill a small stemmed wine glass (step 3 does it).

About an hour ahead, run a cut lemon around the outside of the rim, roll the outside of the rim in fine sugar so none falls into the glass, and put the glass in the fridge: the sugar sets and won't run.
Pare half a lemon in one long strip, the way you'd peel an apple, yellow only. Curl it and fit it inside the glass so it lines the bowl like a collar.
In a mixing glass, put the tea cognac, syrup, curaçao, lemon juice and bitters. Fill with ice and stir for about 20 to 30 seconds, until the outside of the mixing glass is very cold.
Strain into the glass, inside the collar. No ice.
cocktail.name: Dressed for It

recipe.note: 2 ordinary black-tea bags in 150 ml cognac (any VS or VSOP, 40% or stronger), 20 minutes, then lift the bags out; enough for two drinks
2 parts white sugar to 1 part water, by weight, warmed until clear (100 g sugar and 50 g water make about 110 ml, enough for about 20 drinks; it keeps about two weeks in the fridge)
or a triple sec
measure it: a full teaspoon makes it too sharp for a stirred drink

recipe.item: lemon peel, pared in one long piece
recipe.note: the collar
for the outside of the rim

cocktail.tagline: You keep life's small rituals steady when everything else gives way.

reading.epigraph: The Crusta is named for its sugar crust. Its 1862 recipe ends with two words: "Then smile."
whoYouAre: The week everything goes wrong, you still put a proper dinner on the table. You still turn up on Monday ironed and on time, and you'd quite like everyone else to as well. People roll their eyes. Someone always asks whether this is really the moment.

It is, and you know why, even if you seldom explain it. In a crisis, people watch whoever's in front to see how serious it is, and a rule that's still being kept tells them it isn't over. You rarely admit that the rules hold you up too, or that some nights you've agreed with every person who told you it was a terrible idea. What you guard against is wobbling in front of them. But look at what your rules give people: in their worst week, someone still expects something of them, so they still count. That's respect, and most people never think to offer it.
yours: After Hurricane Katrina, Neal Bodenheimer, then tending bar in New York, felt he should be back in New Orleans. Many people from the city who lived elsewhere felt that if they didn't go home, the city might not survive. So he came home. His idea was to be one of the first there with a cocktail bar standing on its own, not inside a hotel or a restaurant. He bought a building in Freret, a lonely neighbourhood far from the French Quarter, and his partner, Matt Kohnke, loved it. At least ten to twenty people tried to talk him out of it: a terrible idea, they said. Years later he admitted that at first they'd been a little nervous too, and that they couldn't afford to be anywhere else.

Cure opened in 2009. He handed the drinks over to his bartenders. What he did give the bar was a dress code: no shorts, no flip-flops, no baseball caps. It gave the place a reputation it never quite lived down. For the first nine months to a year, he said, they spent their time persuading people that they should drink cocktails, and that the bar wasn't just pretentious.

Then comes my favourite part. Years later, talking about Cure's first days, he didn't say the critics had been wrong. He said craft cocktails had partly earned that label, and that they really had to work on their service. So they did. Cure did well from the start, and later he and his partners opened more bars. I like to think the dress code was never really about shorts. In what he called, in a way, a decaying city, where people started over, it said: this place still expects something of you. That's you. And the rest is you at your best: he granted the part of the criticism that was fair, worked on it, and kept going.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Brandy Crusta, a New Orleans classic from the mid-1800s. It's famous for how it's dressed: its name means the crust the sugar makes around the rim, and a long lemon peel lines the glass like a collar. Inside go cognac, a teaspoon apiece of dry curaçao (orange liqueur) and syrup, Angostura, and lemon, just half a teaspoon, all stirred until icy and strained into a little wineglass from the fridge, no ice in it: deep amber and rich. My main change is in the cognac. It sits for twenty minutes with ordinary black tea, so the firm grip at the end comes from the tea, not from more lemon. I did that as a nod to you: firm, without ever raising your voice. By 1908, one New York newspaperman was already sneering at sugar rims as old-fashioned. I kept the crust anyway.

Next time you're keeping a standard and someone calls it pretentious, or too much, don't hear it as all or nothing. Find the part they're right about, admit it plainly, and fix that part. You'll worry it looks like wobbling. It doesn't. That's how the rest of what you stand for holds, and people will trust your rules more for it.

anchors.fact: The family story goes that Cox, with American visitors to serve, found he had no gin left (Oxford pdf 621; Puig to Wolfe, 1970).
anchors.meaning: The plan broke with people there to see it.

anchors.fact: He had a local rum, but the family says he feared the visitors wouldn't like it (Oxford pdf 621).
anchors.meaning: A doubt about the answer before anyone tasted it; the worry is the family's report, so the reading signposts it.

anchors.fact: So, in the family's telling, he picked limes from his own garden tree and added juice and sugar to soften the rum, and swizzled it in a pitcher with shaved ice (Oxford pdf 621).
anchors.meaning: He solved it with what was within reach, and the fix for his worry is the drink's balance.

anchors.fact: Oxford says he made the first Daiquiri or at least oversaw its making, long after Caribbean people had mixed rum, lime and sugar (pdf 621).
anchors.meaning: A renowned classic; his part is the occasion, not the invention of the mix.

anchors.fact: One of his engineers recalled in 1935 that it was more a group effort among Cox and his crew (Oxford pdf 621).
anchors.meaning: One clause of honesty; not the point.

anchors.fact: Later newspaper accounts say that for years he gave it no name and called it his rum sour (Oxford pdf 623; no number, C3).
anchors.meaning: The fix worked and he never stopped to name it.

anchors.fact: Meanwhile he kept introducing it to bars in Santiago, where a bartender made a single-glass version (Oxford pdf 623).
anchors.meaning: He didn't drop the answer; he kept handing it out unnamed.

anchors.fact: Bacardi moved distilling to Puerto Rico in 1936 and left Cuba after the revolution; Wondrich writes of the lack of true Cuban Bacardi (Oxford pdf 182; *Imbibe!* pdf 241).
anchors.meaning: Cox's bottle isn't on today's shelf; the recipe names a style.

anchors.fact: Year (1896 vs 1898), who named it and when, the clock, his pleasure: contested or absent (C1–C3; card "Not on any page").
anchors.meaning: Keep out, or signpost as the bartender's reading.

anchors.fact: *Codex* lists makrut as a different lime from the juicing limes; its juice is harsh and its fragrant leaves are the part recommended for muddling (*Codex* p. 117; Oxford pdf 465).
anchors.meaning: The spark comes from another tree, and on that tree the leaf is the useful part; never "thrown away", never "the same tree".

anchors.fact: Oxford counts kaffir lime leaves among garnish leaves that may work only on the nose (pdf 865); *Codex* says a Daiquiri needs adjusting because citrus varies fruit to fruit (p. 105).
anchors.meaning: The leaves bring scent; exact ml fixes the volume, not the fruit.

cocktail.closingLine: Pour all six in one go, along the row and back. And the next time the plan falls apart, admit you're having fun.
cocktail.glassware: six small tumblers (about 180 ml), chilled in the freezer; a pitcher (about 1.5 litres)
method: Put six small tumblers in the freezer for 10 minutes.
Pour the lime juice into the pitcher, add the sugar, and stir until no grains are left on the bottom: about a minute.

Tear each makrut leaf in half and drop the halves into the lime. Press them against the bottom of the pitcher with a muddler or the end of a rolling pin, five times each, until they smell strongly of lime.
Add the rum.
Fill the pitcher about two-thirds with the crushed ice. Swizzle for 30 seconds by the clock: push a long spoon down to the bottom and work it up and down through the ice, turning it as you go.
Lift the leaves out with the spoon.
Pour straight away into the six tumblers, ice and all, along the row and back, so every glass gets the same.
cocktail.name: Leave It With Me

recipe.item: white rum, light and dry (Spanish-style, unaged or lightly aged, 37.5-45%; not spiced, not sweetened)
recipe.note: the kind of rum that was there when the gin wasn't

recipe.item: fresh lime juice (about 3 to 4 limes), measured
caster sugar (granulated works, it takes longer)
recipe.note: dissolved in the lime, no syrup: rum, lime and sugar, nothing else

recipe.item: makrut lime leaves, fresh or frozen
recipe.note: lime's scent, without more sour; they come out before you pour

recipe.item: crushed ice (a bag of cubes in a tea towel, hit with a rolling pin)

cocktail.tagline: The plan's gone. Now it gets interesting.

reading.epigraph: The first was made in a pitcher, a family story goes, when the gin ran out.
whoYouAre: The oven gives up an hour before twelve people arrive. Someone says the evening's ruined, someone else starts looking up takeaways, and you're already at the open fridge, asking what you've got. You'd never wish it on anyone. But when the plan breaks and every face turns to you, a small part of you lights up. You keep that quiet. It hardly seems fair to enjoy someone else's emergency.

The bit you never mention is the blank before the answer comes. They're all looking at you, and there's nothing there yet. That blank is your nightmare, and somehow the whole fun of it too, because a puzzle that couldn't beat you wouldn't be worth solving. So you keep a level face through it, and no one learns how close it felt. The moment you ask what there is to work with, the room stops panicking and starts looking. Everyone gets something to do with their hands, and a little of your nerve. That's a real gift, and most people never notice who started it.
yours: In the 1890s, Jennings Cox ran an iron-mining company near Daiquirí, a port town in the east of Cuba. The family story goes that he had some American visitors to serve, and found he'd run out of gin. He did have rum, from a distillery in Santiago, under thirty miles away. But he worried, the family says, that it wouldn't suit the Americans' taste.

So, in the family's telling, he picked limes from a tree in his own garden, added their juice and some sugar to soften the rum, and swizzled it all in a pitcher with shaved ice. It went down well at once, the accounts say. One of his engineers later remembered it as more of a group effort among Cox and his crew, and maybe it was. People in the Caribbean had been mixing rum, limes and sugar for two centuries by then, but the Daiquiri, a renowned classic today, goes back to him: he made the first one, or at least oversaw its making. And for years afterwards, the old newspaper accounts say, he simply called it his rum sour, and kept taking it to the bars of Santiago.

I like to think none of his visitors saw the worry the family remembered. They saw a man with a pitcher and a handful of limes. I recognise you in that: the answer arrives with a level face, and the doubt stays behind it. And then there's the name. He'd solved a problem with visitors to serve, and for years he went on handing the answer round as just his rum sour. Whether he enjoyed that day isn't known, but I like to think he did. You'd do the same: you hand the answer over plainly, and nobody hears how much you loved finding it.

The cocktail I've made for you is built like that pitcher, for six: a Daiquiri in the shape the family story gives it. White rum and fresh lime, with sugar stirred into the lime until it's gone, swizzled on crushed ice for thirty seconds and poured straight away into six small chilled tumblers, so nobody waits longer than anyone else. A Daiquiri always asks for some quick thinking, because limes vary in sourness from one fruit to the next. I've measured everything a measure can fix, and the limes are yours to judge. My only addition is four makrut lime leaves, pressed into the lime and lifted out before you pour. Makrut is a different lime, with harsh juice but fragrant leaves, so the answer comes from the part of the tree you'd never think to squeeze. The leaves bring lime's scent without making the drink any sharper. They're there as one more answer to his worry, and as a nod to the question you always ask first: what else is there? It's icy, bright and fresh, and the lime carries right through it.

When every face next turns to you and nothing has come yet, tell them the truth, smiling: this is the bit you love most. Watch what that does. They stop waiting for you to produce an answer and start hunting with you, and the blank isn't yours alone any more. It becomes a game the whole room is playing, and you can love it in the open.

anchors.fact: Sherry barrels for fino aren't filled to the top, and in the space left, a layer of yeast called flor grows on the young wine: a protective barrier that keeps the air off it (F1, F13, C1; Codex p. 245, sherry.wine). No fraction.
anchors.meaning: a cover over the smaller one, kept there all the time
anchors.speaksTo: the smaller hand at the crossing

anchors.fact: It forms by itself, from yeasts native to the region and already in the air there (F4; sherry.wine "indigenous ambient yeasts", Luyten). Never "nobody adds it" (G6).
anchors.meaning: the care came by itself (our reading; never "before anyone asked", Not Only the Way's epigraph)
anchors.speaksTo: a reflex from childhood that never switched off

anchors.fact: There's always air at the top of the barrel, and a little more comes through the wood; the flor sits between it and the wine and uses up most of the oxygen itself, so the wine stays protected (F13; Luyten "consuming most of it"; F5 scoped: the Consejo's breathing sentence is about oxygen from moving the wine).
anchors.meaning: effort, not being used up: the air that would change the young wine reaches the flor first (our reading, signposted)
anchors.speaksTo: it gets to you first, and by the time it reaches them it's smaller

anchors.fact: Its work stays in the wine: the Codex credits the flor with fino's dry, yeasty character, and much of its dryness comes from its years under the flor, and the flor makes most of the compound behind its almond aroma and its sharp nose (F8, F14, F15; Codex p. 247, *Molecules* 2022, sherry.wine). Never "bread" (G5) or salt (fino's own, Codex p. 245) as the flor's; never apple (G3).
anchors.meaning: what you gave goes on with them
anchors.speaksTo: some of them are calm now and couldn't tell you where they got it

anchors.fact: It stays over the wine for years: every sherry ages at least two years, and a five-year-old fino was sampled still under an intense white film (F6 all sherry, F7; no fixed fino term, C2).
anchors.meaning: a watch kept over time, not one rescue: every day, for years

anchors.fact: The Bamboo: sherry at the core and "the vermouths surround the sherry" (Codex p. 91, printed with amontillado); *Imbibe!* pdf 210 says "a fino or an amontillado"; on record by 1886 in St. Paul; a staple by 1900. Origin contested (Boothby/Eppinger, Wondrich's hedge, Codex's Japan): none in the reading. Fino "can be lost" among spirits (Codex p. 246).
anchors.meaning: the young one kept at the centre, with nothing loud around it

anchors.fact: Chamomile honey: the *Flavor Matrix* lists honey among grape's best pairings (pdf 140; sherry maps to Grape); the *Codex* says honey "loves chamomile" and that lemon, honey and chamomile together are "warming and, for some people, tinged with nostalgia" (p. 92).
anchors.meaning: the nights the watch was kept (our reading; never that it calms or helps sleep)
anchors.speaksTo: staying awake because someone littler was frightened of the dark

cocktail.closingLine: The fino needs only quiet company. Let one of them know you were scared too.
cocktail.glassware: a small stemmed cocktail glass, chilled, no ice
method: Make the syrup ahead. Pour the just-boiled water over the chamomile and leave it for 5 minutes, then take the tea out and squeeze it. Stir the honey into the warm tea until it's smooth, and let it cool. Keep it in a closed jar in the fridge and use it within about two weeks.
Put the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Pour the fino, both vermouths, the syrup and the bitters into a mixing glass or a jar, and give it a stir so the syrup dissolves.
Fill it with ice and stir with a long spoon for about 30 seconds, until the outside is very cold. The melting ice is part of the drink: it adds about a third to what you poured.
Empty the serving glass if you filled it, and strain the drink in. No ice in the glass.
Cut a strip of lemon peel, just the yellow part. Twist it over the glass so its oil falls on the drink, then drop it in.
Cork the fino and put it back in the fridge. Once it's open it fades quickly, so use it within a week or so.
cocktail.name: Night Light

recipe.note: from the driest end of sherry, made under the flor. Look for a recent bottling date. A manzanilla (a fino from the seaside town of Sanlúcar) works too
fino is so dry that a little honey gives the drink more body

recipe.item: *for the syrup:* 50 ml just-boiled water, 1 chamomile tea bag (or 1 tablespoon dried chamomile flowers), 50 ml light runny honey (acacia or a light clover)
recipe.note: makes about 100 ml, enough for about twenty drinks

cocktail.tagline: You find your courage in making someone else feel safe.

reading.epigraph: Part of the taste in this glass comes from something that stayed behind in the barrel.
whoYouAre: You were small too. People forget that part. You were the one holding the smaller hand at the crossing, saving the last biscuit, staying awake because someone littler was frightened of the dark. No one had asked. It just seemed obvious that anyone you loved should be safe, and if nobody else was watching, you would. You were never less scared of the dark. You just had someone to be calm for.

You still do it. When something goes wrong, the calm voice comes out before you've decided anything. And underneath it, whenever someone you love gets hurt, part of you is already asking what you should have seen, as if it had been your watch. The ones who grew up near you learned from you that the dark can be got through. Some of them are calm in it now, and they couldn't tell you where they got it.
yours: Fino sits at the driest end of sherry, and it's made in a way I still find surprising. Its barrels aren't filled to the top. Once the young wine is in the barrel, a pale layer of yeast grows across its surface. It forms by itself: the people who make sherry say it comes from yeasts already in the air of that part of Spain. It's called flor, and it stays over the wine for years.

What it does is keep the air off. There's always air in the space left at the top, and a little more comes through the wood, and air would turn a fino into a different wine, darker and heavier. The flor sits between that air and the wine and breathes up most of the oxygen itself, so the wine underneath stays protected. The air that would change the wine reaches the flor first. I like to think that's the whole job. Not a rescue. Just being the one it reaches first, every day, for years.

That's what you've done since before you were tall. The fright, the bad news, the thing that would have spoiled their night: it gets to you first, and by the time it reaches them, it's smaller. Most of the time they never knew it was there. That's how you've always cared. Everyone close to you has felt safe without ever having to think about it, and that was you.

The cocktail I've made for you is built on fino. It's delicate, and beside anything loud it can get lost, so no spirit goes in with it, just a little dry and a little sweet white vermouth around it, the way the Bamboo is built, a famous classic already on record by 1886. The flor itself is left in the barrel, but you can still taste its work: the dry, yeasty edge and the hint of almond in the smell are mostly the flor's. I sweetened it with a teaspoon of honey stirred into chamomile, the tea people make at bedtime, for all the nights you stayed awake so someone smaller wasn't alone in the dark.

Pick one of the people you watched over, one who's grown now, and tell them about one time back then when you were scared too, while you were the one being calm. They can carry it now. I think they'll be glad to know what reached you first, and prouder of you than you'd guess.

anchors.fact: The Kalimotxo is red wine and cola in equal parts, usually over ice, and immensely popular in the Basque Country. Oxford's recipe: a tall glass of ice, stir (F1; Oxford pdf 386). Called a Basque-country classic (F9, Schaap 2013).
anchors.meaning: something plain and obvious that the people it's for love as it is

anchors.fact: Spaniards were probably mixing wine and cola decades before it had this name, since the 1920s at least (F2, Oxford "likely"; F11 council, flat). Its older names include "Rioja Libre" (R1). So say **named**, never **invented**.
anchors.meaning: it was always obvious to the people drinking it; nobody needed permission (our reading)
anchors.speaksTo: "It hasn't crossed your mind that there's a proper way to do it."

anchors.fact: The name "Kalimotxo" spread through the Basque Country and Navarre and was popular by the early 1980s, then spread across Spain (F11, F14; council account via EFE 2022, secondary). Its root is **a friend's nickname** and nothing more (C1). Elsewhere it's *bambus* across much of the former Yugoslavia, *vadász* in Hungary (F5, F13; never Chile's name, which is contested).
anchors.meaning: a thing made for the people nearby that travelled on their love for it alone
anchors.speaksTo: "the people it's for can always tell"

anchors.fact: An undated scene, told by a writer in the *Guardian* (2012): in a Granada tapas bar, his partner poured cola into a glass of the good local red, and the barman came down the bar pointing. The house wine from the barrel is the one you mix, this bottle isn't (F10, F15). Craft agrees: nobody puts a grand wine in it (F8, *Codex* p. 18). The knowing's wider verdict: Oxford files it among drinks with "no baggage and no rules" and says many felt they gave up complexity and elegance (F6, pdf 1332, scoped to the whole canon).
anchors.meaning: the rule, explained, pointing, to someone who didn't see the problem
anchors.speaksTo: "Someone explains, kindly, how it's usually done. You nod."

anchors.fact: The version of its history considered the most reliable comes from a book edited by a Bilbao artists' collective, Funky Project. Oxford admits the name doesn't sound authoritative, and takes them at their word because Bilbao takes the drink seriously (F4, pdf 386; paraphrase only, never "not very authoritative-sounding").
anchors.meaning: the people it's for are the authority, and the big book deferred to them
anchors.speaksTo: "You still don't see what was wrong with it."

anchors.fact: Its taste has been likened to sangria (F12; Oxford pdf 386, Schaap 2013).
anchors.meaning: worth having as it is, with no wink (our reading)

anchors.fact: Ordinary ice dilutes a drink as it chills it: no chilling without dilution (*LI* p. 84, Tomás). Cubes frozen from the same equal parts melt into more of the drink, not into water. The cola in the tray goes flat, so the fizz comes from the fresh pour (Tomás's spec, pending).
anchors.meaning: what you make should stay as you made it, to the last sip (our reading, said to the guest in y4)
anchors.speaksTo: "It looks like how the thing felt"

cocktail.closingLine: Stir once, over its own ice. How it's usually done can wait until they've tasted it.
cocktail.glassware: tall glass (about 400 ml), filled with the frozen Kalimotxo cubes
method: **The cubes (at least 6 hours ahead).** Stir 150 ml red wine and 150 ml cola together in a jug until the fizz settles, so the tray doesn't foam over. Pour into an ice-cube tray (a silicone one is easiest: the cubes come out soft) and freeze on the coldest setting. They freeze softer than water ice, a bit like an ice lolly.
Put the wine and a fresh bottle of cola in the fridge, so both are cold.
Fill a tall glass to the top with the cubes, straight from the freezer.
Pour in the wine, then the cola, slowly: it foams up on the cubes.
Stir once, gently, and serve it straight away.
cocktail.name: The Way It Felt

recipe.item: young Spanish red wine, unoaked (a young Rioja or Garnacha, the kind poured by the glass)
recipe.note: fridge-cold; never a grand bottle
fridge-cold, freshly opened: the fizz comes from this pour

recipe.item: cubes frozen from the same half and half
recipe.note: made first, below; they melt into more of the drink, not water

cocktail.tagline: Your creations get the feeling right before the rules get a say.

reading.epigraph: Half red wine, half cola. There's a right bottle to mix, apparently.
whoYouAre: What you've made, you hand over straight away: a cake iced the colour the day felt, a card you drew instead of buying one, a birthday song with one verse too many. It's obviously lovely. It hasn't crossed your mind that there's a proper way to do it.

Then someone explains, kindly, how it's usually done. You nod. You still don't see what was wrong with it. The day you'd dread is the one when the explanation starts to make sense. Because what you make rarely looks like the thing. It looks like how the thing felt, and the people it's for can always tell. That's rarer than getting it right, and it's worth more.
yours: In the Basque Country, people pour red wine and cola into a tall glass of ice, half and half, and call it a Kalimotxo. Spaniards had probably been mixing the two since at least the 1920s. The name, the story goes, came at a festival in Algorta in 1972, after a friend's nickname, and within about ten years it had caught on through the Basque Country and Navarre. In much of the former Yugoslavia it's bambus; in Hungary, vadász.

People who know wine have their doubts. A writer in the *Guardian* once remembered a tapas bar in Granada where his partner started pouring cola into a glass of the good local red. The barman saw it and came down the bar, pointing: the house wine from the barrel is the one you mix, and this bottle, you don't.

In Bilbao, they take it seriously. The most trusted account of its history was put together by an artists' collective there called Funky Project. The *Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails* admits that doesn't sound much like an authority, then takes them at their word anyway, for that very reason.

I like to think you'd have done what the Basques did: looked at the wine and the cola, and not seen the problem. So the cocktail I've made for you is a Kalimotxo, the way they pour it: red wine and Coca-Cola, half and half, stirred. My red is a young Spanish one, the kind poured by the glass. It's a Basque classic, dark, cold and fizzy, a little like sangria. I haven't corrected a thing. The one change is the ice. It's the same drink, frozen into cubes first, so as it melts it turns into more of itself, never into water. The fizz comes from the fresh pour. That's for you: something you make should still be what you made, right to the last of it.

So when someone next explains the proper way, listen. Some of it will be useful. Then make the next thing the way it looked to you, and hand it straight to whoever you made it for, before anyone else sees it. They'll see what you meant. And you'll get to enjoy making it again, the way you did before anyone explained.

anchors.fact: In 1872 Antonin Baudoin, a pharmacist in Cognac, drew two botanists' attention to a black, sooty growth on walls and roof tiles near the distilleries (F2; Scott et al., *Mycologia* 2007). It *looked* like soot, and nobody is recorded as taking it for soot (L1).
anchors.meaning: someone who wouldn't leave a strange thing at "it's nothing"
anchors.speaksTo: "drew two botanists' attention to a black growth"

anchors.fact: He printed his own short study (1878, 15 pages, titled for "the nostoc of the walls of Cognac"): blue-green algae. He was wrong (F4; BnF record; Scott "incorrectly"). Never "first" for his answer (C4: the botanists' suggestion came in 1872).
anchors.meaning: asking out loud, and getting it wrong, in print
anchors.speaksTo: "offer your guess, even if you suspect it's wrong"

anchors.fact: In 1881 Richon and Petit described it and filed it as *Torula compniacensis*, "from Cognac" (F5, F6). *Torula* was a catch-all: more than 300 kinds have been put in it over its history, and nearly all have since been moved out (F7, Scott citing Crane 2001). Never glossed as a yeast (G3).
anchors.meaning: the label that closes the subject
anchors.speaksTo: "The worst answer, to you, is a label"

anchors.fact: For decades the science went almost silent (one 1961 study). Industry-commissioned studies on three continents kept naming the same ordinary everywhere-fungi (F8).
anchors.meaning: "it's just a…", said to close the subject

anchors.fact: More than a century later (no decade: C1), a team showed it didn't fit the group it had been put in (*Torula*), or any similar one (Scott: in a known order, Capnodiales), and gave it a group (genus) of its own, and named that *Baudoinia*, "in honor of Antonin Baudoin" (F10). Rogers' account of their reason: he first brought it to scientists' attention (F11, secondary). The species name was kept.
anchors.meaning: being wrong didn't keep the asker's name off the answer
anchors.speaksTo: "the people who finally got it right put his name on it anyway"

anchors.fact: Its nearest known relatives live on rock in Antarctica (F12; never "only", C2). It feeds on alcohol escaping ageing barrels but is believed to live on something else too, being millions of years older than any barrel (F1, F13; Oxford pdf 238 "it is believed"). No simple formula predicts its growth (F14).
anchors.meaning: the answer that opens the next question

anchors.fact: Two regional bottles from around Cognac. VSOP cognac: by law at least four years in wood (Oxford pdf 546), and cognac's wood is oak (pdf 1404). White Pineau des Charentes: fresh grape juice stopped with young cognac from the same farm before it becomes wine (Oxford pdf 1518, 1315; *Codex* p. 74), 16–22%, at least 18 months' ageing with at least 12 in oak (INAO).
anchors.meaning: the strange thing is in what's already here

anchors.fact: Sichuan peppercorns steeped in part of the cognac (Tomás). Grapes pair with "spices with citrus notes" like these (Matrix pdf 140). A faint tingle on the lips is Tomás's taste claim. **Dossier only, never in the copy:** *Zanthoxylum*, citrus family, not related to black pepper (D6, secondary).
anchors.meaning: a small question in the glass
anchors.speaksTo: "a small question in the glass, the kind you've never been able to leave alone"

cocktail.closingLine: Ask what's in it before anyone tells you what it is.
cocktail.glassware: a small tulip-shaped glass (about 180 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Beforehand: lightly crush 1 level teaspoon of Sichuan peppercorns with the back of a spoon. Leave them in 60 ml of the cognac for 20 minutes, then strain them out. That makes enough for four drinks, and it lasts.
Put the glass in the freezer for 10 minutes.
Pour 30 ml cognac, 15 ml of the peppercorn cognac and 35 ml Pineau into a mixing glass or jar.
Fill it with ice and stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the jar is very cold.
Strain into the cold glass. No ice in the glass.
Hold the lemon peel over the drink, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the surface. Then set the peel aside.
cocktail.name: The First Guess

recipe.note: any VSOP: by law it has spent at least four years in wood
made beforehand (see Method); it gives a faint tingle on the lips
the Cognac region's own aperitif: grape juice stopped with young cognac before it could become wine, the cognac from the same farm, then rested in oak; any white Pineau
squeezed over the top, then set aside

cocktail.tagline: Your questions are how everyone else starts looking.

reading.epigraph: From around Cognac, where something growing on the walls was misnamed for over a century.
whoYouAre: When someone says "actually, nobody's really sure", most people sigh. You light up. You ask why: why the form needs that box, why a thing is called what it's called, why everyone does it this way. You're not making a point. You'd honestly like to know, and you're secretly hoping the answer will be stranger than you expected. It usually is.

Not everyone hears it that way. Over the years a few of your questions got you told off: "because I said so", the sigh, the look across the table. So now you ask lightly, with a smile, as if it hardly matters. It matters. The worst answer, to you, is a label: "oh, it's just a…", handed over to close the subject, so that nobody looks again. And yet around you, people do look again. With you, "I don't know" stops being embarrassing and becomes the start of the fun, and people need that more than they'll ever tell you.
yours: In 1872, a pharmacist in Cognac named Antonin Baudoin drew two botanists' attention to a black growth on the walls and roof tiles near the distilleries. It looked like soot. A few years later he printed his own short study of it. His answer was that it was a kind of blue-green algae. He was wrong.

Others filed it under a catch-all name that more than three hundred kinds of fungus have been put under over the years, nearly all of them moved out since. Then for decades the science went almost silent, and the studies that did look kept calling it the ordinary sort of fungus found everywhere. It wasn't. More than a century after Baudoin's first look, a team of scientists showed it didn't fit the group it had been put in, or any similar one, and gave it a group of its own, named after him, as the man who first brought it to scientists' attention. Its nearest known relatives live on rock in Antarctica. It feeds on the spirit that escapes ageing barrels, yet it's millions of years older than any barrel, so it's thought to live on something else too. Nobody is quite sure what.

I like to think Baudoin felt what you feel the moment someone says "it's just…": that it wasn't, quite. He wrote fifteen pages on it, and guessed wrong in print. Then the people who finally got it right put his name on it anyway. That's what your questions do. Even the ones that land wrong get other people looking, and what they find is often stranger than anyone guessed.

The cocktail I've made for you is stirred over ice until it's icy, then poured without it, the way a Martini is, from two bottles from around Cognac. One is a cognac aged for years in oak. The other is Pineau des Charentes, the region's aperitif: sweet grape juice stopped with young cognac from the same farm before it could become wine, then rested in oak too. Into part of the cognac I've steeped a few Sichuan peppercorns. You'll feel them as a faint tingle on your lips before the warmth comes through, a small question in the glass, the kind you've never been able to leave alone. I've poured it into a tulip-shaped glass, narrow at the top, to keep the scent with you. I like to think of it as a little of what escapes the barrels, kept for you this time.

So when a question next comes to you, don't make it small. Ask it properly, and offer your guess, even if you suspect it's wrong. Being wrong didn't keep Baudoin's name off it. It got the whole thing looked at. And I'd bet the real answer turns out stranger than your guess. That's the part you'll enjoy most.

anchors.fact: The day after seeing the Tom Cruise film *Cocktail*, in 1994, he asked the boss of the village pub he worked in to buy him a cocktail shaker (*Proper* p. 206, F1–F2).
anchors.meaning: The road starts with one plain request, not a plan to win.
anchors.speaksTo: They never set out to win anything; they set out to get a bit better at the work.

anchors.fact: In the late 1990s he barbacked at a formal Prague bar every weekend, five hours each way by train, and ran a restaurant in Slovakia during the week (*Proper* p. 206, F5).
anchors.meaning: The long honest road, shown in hours, with no shortcut.
anchors.speaksTo: Got there with nothing but the work.

anchors.fact: The Prague bar's owner asked "What about the hair?", and he trimmed his dreadlocks back a bit (*Proper* p. 206, F4).
anchors.meaning: Someone wondered if he belonged; he answered by adjusting, not arguing.
anchors.speaksTo: Being doubted, and going on anyway. (The fear of being called a cheat stays the guest's: C3.)

anchors.fact: At Paparazzi in Bratislava the menu changed with every trip he took; when he wasn't travelling he studied in internet cafés and translated articles into Slovak (*Proper* pp. 206–207, F6–F8).
anchors.meaning: Learning in the open, from whatever he could reach.
anchors.speaksTo: Study, never borrowing: the work is visibly theirs.

anchors.fact: On a whim he posted that menu to a new award in New Orleans; at its first ceremony Paparazzi won Best Cocktail Menu, and two months later a package came. He didn't know his bar had won until he opened his mail (*Proper* p. 205, F10–F11; year 2007 per Tales' archive, F12, never told: C1).
anchors.meaning: Everyone in that room knew before he did.
anchors.speaksTo: "Everyone else could see how far you'd come. You were the last to hear."

anchors.fact: Of all the places around the world where the cocktail revival took hold ("all the crucibles of the cocktail revival the world over"), Robert Simonson gives Vadrna "the prize for obscure and improbable", for the destination bar he built and the bartenders he trained (*Proper* p. 205, F13).
anchors.meaning: The recognition comes from outside, in someone else's words; his place, not a life story (audit v2 R4).
anchors.speaksTo: Others see the distance; they don't.

anchors.fact: No year, no trophy, no "for years", no "got the shaker", no Trnava population, no "overnight", no "nobody believed in him" (C1, C2, F2, F5, F11; Wren r1).
anchors.meaning: Accuracy is the kindness for a guest who fears being caught in something not quite true.

anchors.fact: After a visit to London he threw out Paparazzi's thick glassware and simple garnishes and brought in tropical fruits imported from Holland (*Proper* pp. 206–207, F7); the day after the film he had asked for a shaker (p. 206, F2). Paparazzi already served Daiquiris when he started (p. 206, F6).
anchors.meaning: A thin chilled coupe, a shaken sour and tropical fruit carry the story. The Daiquiri shape was the house style, and the recipe is ours, never his or Paparazzi's. The bare rim is the *Codex* Basic Sour's (p. 106), ours, never his London lesson (audit A1). Mango is our pick, not named on the page (A2).
anchors.speaksTo: What he learned abroad is in the glass as study, not a reward.

anchors.fact: Borovička is "the Czechoslovak version of gin" (Oxford pdf 1710); one Slovak borovička has its own geographical indication, *Spišská borovička*, 39.7–40.3% vol (Slovak IP office GI dossier). Nothing says he poured it.
anchors.meaning: Any tie to where his road began is "I like to think", and never makes Zemné his home (F3).

anchors.fact: The *Flavor Matrix* pairs mango with dill "thanks mainly to the woody, piney aromas of both" (pdf 251); juniper's oils give "piney-camphorous notes" (Oxford JUNIPER pdf 1123).
anchors.meaning: The fruit he went out and learned shares a piney note with the juniper spirit (never "its strongest note": A4).
anchors.speaksTo: What they learned on the road tastes as if it had always been theirs: the answer to "borrowed".

cocktail.closingLine: No garnish. And when good news comes, let it in first.
cocktail.glassware: a thin stemmed coupe, chilled in the freezer
method: The day before, or up to two weeks ahead, make the mango syrup. Weigh 250 g ripe, peeled mango flesh and 250 g white sugar, blend until smooth and the sugar has dissolved, then press it through a fine sieve. Keep it covered in the fridge.
Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes.
Pour the borovička, lime juice and mango syrup into a shaker. (Some borovičkas have a little sugar added: if yours tastes sweet on its own, use 15 ml of syrup.)
Fill it with ice, close it, and shake firmly for about twelve seconds, until the outside of the shaker is frosted.
Strain into the cold glass, through a small tea sieve to catch the ice chips. No garnish.
cocktail.name: Straight Up

recipe.item: borovička (a juniper spirit from Slovakia and the Czech Republic)
recipe.note: Or, if you can't find it, a juniper-led London dry gin.
Tropical fruit, the kind he brought into his drinks after a trip to London. Mango is related to cashew and pistachio, so if nuts are a worry, leave this one aside.

cocktail.tagline: You keep getting better, and never need someone else to lose.

reading.epigraph: Mango and juniper, from far apart, have a note in common. It was always there.
whoYouAre: You never set out to win anything. You wanted to get a little better at the thing in front of you, then a little better again. So you rarely turn round to see how far it has taken you. Other people do, and when they mention it, you're honestly surprised.

And when something good comes your way, there's a moment before the happiness. You replay how it happened, checking it was all fair, as if someone might ask. Somewhere along the road you learned that good things can be taken back, and you couldn't bear anyone thinking you hadn't got there honestly.

What you don't notice is that you never suspect anyone else. When someone you know gets the job or the prize, you're simply glad, and sure they got there fairly too. Not many people manage that, and it's a gift: people watch you take the straight road and start to believe it goes somewhere.
yours: It starts with a cocktail shaker. In 1994, the day after he saw the Tom Cruise film *Cocktail*, a Slovak named Stanislav Vadrna asked the boss of the village pub where he worked to buy him one. Later he wanted to work at a formal cocktail bar in Prague. He had long dreadlocks then, and the owner asked, "What about the hair?" He trimmed it back a bit. Then every weekend he rode the train five hours to Prague to work there as a barback, the bartender's helper, while running a restaurant in Slovakia during the week.

At Paparazzi in Bratislava, the bar he later ran, the menu changed with every trip he took: after London, out went the thick glassware and in came tropical fruit. When he wasn't travelling, he sat in internet cafés, translating articles about cocktails into Slovak. Then, on a whim, he posted his menu to a brand-new award in New Orleans. Two months after its first ceremony, a package arrived. He didn't know Paparazzi had won Best Cocktail Menu until he opened his mail.

A room in New Orleans knew before he did. Of all the places around the world where the cocktail revival took hold, the writer Robert Simonson calls Vadrna's the most improbable. I don't think any of it was luck. He learned from everyone he could reach, and the menu he sent was one he'd made himself. If it had been you opening that package, I suspect you'd have checked it twice, looking for the mistake. There wasn't one. That's your road too: no shortcut and no plan to win, only the next thing, done well, until other people notice.

The cocktail I've made for you is a sour, of the same family as the Daiquiri, one of the most famous drinks there is. It's shaken, because the day after that film he asked for a shaker, and it goes into a thin, chilled glass. The base is borovička, a juniper spirit from the country he was born in. With it go lime and a mango syrup, as a nod to the tropical fruit he brought into Paparazzi after London. And here's what I love about it: mango and juniper have a piney note in common. The fruit comes from far away, and it tastes as if it had always been there. That's what happens to anything you learn by doing the work: it ends up yours.

So when something good finds you again, don't search it for the catch. You remember how you got there, and nobody handed you any of it. Someone near you is watching to see whether the long way pays off. Show them it does. The checking can wait, and I'd bet it never finds anything.

anchors.fact: In 2001 his family opened a cocktail bar called Ginger in Fitzroy, Melbourne. Most who went remember it as innovative and odd; Jason Crawley, a London bartender who moved to Australia, remembered "lots of orange plastic", like "a psychedelic spaceship" (*Proper* p. 144; F1–F3).
anchors.meaning: A whole room built for the fun of it.

anchors.fact: Sebastian Reaburn, who worked there, said the menu "read like a comedy script". For one week every drink on it shared Jägermeister, and that menu was never seen again (p. 144; F4–F5).
anchors.meaning: The fun was the point, and nobody was its butt.

anchors.fact: Jacob Briars said that at Ginger "there was no such thing as the idea anything might be wrong" (p. 144; F6).
anchors.meaning: The guest's laugh is how they check a room is safe; Ginger was a room that had already said yes.

anchors.fact: Its "anything-goes frivolity" didn't go down well with everyone, particularly Sydney bartenders. Reaburn: it was so "tongue in cheek" that "there was a credibility gap" (pp. 144–145; F8–F9).
anchors.meaning: Being told off for delight, on the record, from outside the room. Reaburn's words with his name; never "taken seriously" in our voice.

anchors.fact: The Paper Plane: equal parts bourbon, Nonino Quintessentia amaro, Aperol and lemon, shaken, in a coupe. He made it for the opening menu of a new bar in Chicago where he never worked. The first recipe had Campari; Aperol soon replaced it and became the norm (p. 288; F11–F13). No year (C1).
anchors.meaning: Fun made for a room he'd never stand in.

anchors.fact: It was named after a song by M.I.A. that he was listening to while he tried to come up with the recipe (p. 288; F14).
anchors.meaning: Named for whatever was playing. Any paper plane sailing across a room is "I like to think".

anchors.fact: He calls it his second most well-travelled drink. It's especially popular in Toronto, for reasons that remain a mystery to him: "essentially the official drink of Toronto", he said (p. 288; F15–F16). The quote is undated: Simonson interviewed him in August 2014 (p. 331) and published in 2016, so tell it in the past tense, with no year.
anchors.meaning: Delight travels further than anyone can explain, the way a room follows a laugh.

anchors.fact: Aperol is an Italian aperitivo from 1919 Padua, vibrantly orange, less bitter and much lower in alcohol than Campari (Oxford APEROL pdf 125; F18).
anchors.meaning: The brightest thing on the bar is the first thing you see.

cocktail.closingLine: Five drops of salt water before you shake. And when something's funny, laugh out loud.
cocktail.glassware: a coupe (about 180–200 ml), chilled
method: Make the salt water once: stir 1 level teaspoon of fine salt into 4 teaspoons of warm water until it's clear. It keeps in the fridge for months.
Put the coupe in the freezer to chill.
Pour the bourbon, the Nonino, the Aperol and the lemon juice into a shaker. Add five drops of the salt water.
Fill the shaker three-quarters full with ice, close it and shake for about 12 seconds, until the shaker's too cold to hold comfortably.
Strain into the cold coupe. No garnish.
cocktail.name: There It Goes

recipe.note: 43% or stronger
an Italian bitter herbal liqueur made on grappa (a brandy distilled from what's left after winemaking); or any other bitter herbal liqueur made on grappa
or any bright orange Italian bitter aperitif of about 11%
a touch less than the printed recipe's ¾ oz, so it's bright, not sharp
1 level teaspoon fine salt stirred into 4 teaspoons water; or a small pinch of fine salt

cocktail.tagline: You find it funny first. Then everyone does.

reading.epigraph: Behind this drink is one named for whatever song was on. One city adopted it.
whoYouAre: A friend is halfway through a story, and you've already gone. Not a polite laugh: the real one, eyes watering, trying to say "sorry, go on" and not managing it. You're hardly ever the one telling the joke. You're the one who can't stop laughing at it, and that's usually the moment it gets funny for everybody else.

What people don't see is how many you hold in: in meetings, at the serious dinner, anywhere someone might think less of you for it. A laugh held in sits in your chest all afternoon. You've heard "you'd laugh at anything" more times than you can count. You wouldn't. You just find more of it funny. Now and then there's the second when you're the only one laughing and the room doesn't follow, and it stays with you longer than you let on. And the fear underneath is being told off for it so often that one day you stop. Please don't. When you laugh at something someone said, they leave feeling funny.
yours: In 2001, Sam Ross's family opened a cocktail bar in Fitzroy, in Melbourne, and called it Ginger. Most people who went remember it as inventive and odd: "lots of orange plastic", one bartender remembered, like "a psychedelic spaceship". Sebastian Reaburn, who worked there, said the menu "read like a comedy script". And Jacob Briars said the thing I love most about it: at Ginger, "there was no such thing as the idea anything might be wrong".

Not everyone was charmed, Sydney's bartenders least of all. In Reaburn's words, the place was all "so tongue in cheek", and "there was a credibility gap". Some years later, Ross made a drink for the opening menu of a new bar in Chicago, one where he never worked. It's called the Paper Plane, after a song by M.I.A. he had on while he was working it out. It became, he said, the second most travelled of his drinks, and Toronto took to it so completely that years later he called it "essentially the official drink of Toronto". Why Toronto, he couldn't say.

I like to think that's the Ginger in it. A whole city's bars joined in, and not even the man who made it could explain why. That's how your laugh works too. Nobody in the room decides to follow it. They just do. And I like to think the name suits it for one more reason, though it came from the song: a paper plane is the thing that sails across a room where everyone's being very serious, and somebody always smiles.

The cocktail I've made for you is the Paper Plane, a modern classic, with two small changes of mine. It's bourbon, Aperol (a bright orange Italian aperitif, gently bitter), Amaro Nonino (an Italian bitter herbal liqueur made on grappa, a brandy distilled from the grape skins, stems and seeds left once the juice is pressed out for wine) and fresh lemon. It's shaken until the shaker's uncomfortable to hold, and poured off the ice into a coupe that's been waiting in the freezer. I've taken a little of the lemon out, so it's bright rather than sharp. Then I've added five drops of salted water. It isn't meant to taste salty. It brings nothing of its own; it makes everything around it come forward, and it takes the frown off the bitter. I put it there for you, because that's what your laugh does for other people's jokes.

Next time something's funny in a room that's gone stiff, don't hold it in. Look round first: there's nearly always someone else trying not to laugh. Let yours go, and you'll have given them theirs. Then enjoy it. It really was funny.

anchors.fact: Many drinks have been called the Brooklyn Cocktail; most of their inventors wanted one to rival the Manhattan and the Bronx (Oxford BROOKLYN COCKTAIL pdf 360; *Imbibe!* pdf 211). F1
anchors.meaning: A borough wanting its own drink, the way its neighbours had one. The rivalry is one light clause (condition 2).
anchors.speaksTo: love for a place, said out loud

anchors.fact: July 1910: Maurice Hegeman, a Cincinnati man living in Brooklyn, told a New York paper he couldn't sleep one night, thought up a cocktail for Brooklyn that would compare with the Manhattan and the Bronx, and got up to make it at a café by the Brooklyn end of the bridge (hard cider, absinthe, ginger ale, in a long glass). Reprinted in Kansas City and Cincinnati (*Cincinnati Enquirer* 7 Jul 1910 p. 4, crediting the *New York Telegraph*; *Kansas City Star* 4 Jul 1910 p. 7). F7
anchors.meaning: Someone who made a thing for the place he loved and put his name to it in print. The night and the café are the paper's report of his account: "he said".
anchors.speaksTo: the note, the playlist, said first

anchors.fact: Asked his excuse for calling a pint of liquid a cocktail, he answered that a cocktail is meant to be small "but there is no law about it", and that he wanted Brooklyn to be known by a cocktail (same papers). F8
anchors.meaning: **His own words, on the record:** the motive may be told as fact ("he said"). He heard the teasing question and answered it straight. Paraphrase "known by" in the reading (*Before the Room* has "known by his name"). Who asked: not said.
anchors.speaksTo: knows how it looks, says it anyway

anchors.fact: September 1910: a lawyer offered his own Brooklyn with a florid tribute (it fit the throat "like a velvet flame"); bartenders at the Hoffman House and the Waldorf-Astoria scoffed at its syrup, one saying all he forgot was the ice cream, and another said that if he lived in Brooklyn he'd stick to beer. Reprinted in the *Washington Post* from the *Kansas City Star* (6 Sep 1910 p. 6). F9
anchors.meaning: **The ridicule Oxford names (F6), with its words.** The papers printed it; bartenders said it. It was aimed at this drink, never at Hegeman's. The lawyer stays unnamed. The jokes are told as theirs; the bartender never calls anything silly (Wren's trap 4).
anchors.speaksTo: being laughed at for meaning it

anchors.fact: Less than two months after Repeal, on 28 Jan 1934, the *Brooklyn Eagle* printed a reader's letter asking: there's a Manhattan and a Bronx, why not a Brooklyn? The column offered a competition (*Eagle* 28 Jan 1934 p. 55; Repeal 5 Dec 1933, *Joy* pdf 62). F10
anchors.meaning: **One reader asked first; the paper took it up.** Truer than Oxford's "the Eagle wondered why". The reader is initials only: no name, no gender.
anchors.speaksTo: the big words said first **Not in the reading since 2026-10-06** (Q061); dossier only.

anchors.fact: Recipes came in for weeks, from readers and barmen: one named for Brooklyn's Dutch past, Jamaica Avenue and Pineapple Street; the column joked of boycotting Bronxes and Manhattans until Brooklyn's had equal standing. In December 1934 its Broadway columnist crowned one (a Gage & Tollner's house drink) (*Eagle* Jan–Mar 1934; 20 Dec 1934 p. 12). F11, F12
anchors.meaning: Saying it again, and having fun doing it. **Fence:** a paper crowned one and it still didn't catch on (F13): never "nobody chose one", never "finally caught on". No recipe for the crowned drink (C2).
anchors.speaksTo: the whole volume **Not in the reading since 2026-10-06** (Q061); dossier only.

anchors.fact: In December 1945 the Bronx borough president, in an open letter, said Brooklyn had no cocktail and offered one with vinegar, raspberries, DDT, part of a tree, vodka and "Durocher Bitters", good enough for "Dem Bums" (*Eagle* 9–10 Dec 1945, quoting his letter; Oxford pdf 360). F14
anchors.meaning: The teasing came back, in print, from a neighbour. Told as fun (condition 3). Durocher and the Dodgers: unsourced here, so not glossed.
anchors.speaksTo: the smirk on the way home

anchors.fact: Within days Brooklyn answered: a party leader sent him a recipe, a restaurant sent its own, a hotel manager challenged him to a contest (bring your own bartenders and start shaking), and the *Eagle*'s columnist heard thirty-three recipes in a day and soon gave up the subject because so many were coming in (*Eagle* 10–14 Dec 1945). F15
anchors.meaning: **Said again, by many, louder than the laugh.** Some answers were politics and publicity: never "nothing to gain" (condition 2).
anchors.speaksTo: say it again, the same words a second time

anchors.fact: The Bronx man then wrote that there is such a thing as a Brooklyn Cocktail (*Eagle* 13 Dec 1945). F16
anchors.meaning: **Not a vindication beat** (Naive Artist's ground; Wren's "out" list). The *Eagle*'s "abjectly" is the paper's word: never ours. Use only if Wren wants it, as "even he wrote back".

anchors.fact: The Brooklyn Club's drink: Oxford dates the earliest Brooklyn to 1883 and says it apparently never left the club (pdf 360). In 1945 the *Eagle*'s columnist, after asking the club, printed it as half Jamaica rum (100 proof), half Italian vermouth and a dash of Angostura, and its bartender said he didn't get many calls for it (*Eagle* 13 Dec 1945 p. 3; the column Oxford cites, pdf 361). F2, F17
anchors.meaning: **For Tomás:** the rum Manhattan now has a recipe on record, as served in 1945 (never "the 1883 recipe"; the method is garbled, so not sourced). The bridge-opening reason is the club's 1945 story: **legend, labelled** ("the story the club told"). A drink kept in one room, which fits Wren's tie: the cocktail made for this guest is the one that leaves it.
anchors.speaksTo: kept indoors, never said out loud

anchors.fact: Jack Grohusko, bartender at a downtown New York restaurant, printed a rye Brooklyn in his 1908 book; Wondrich calls it by far the closest anyone came to making one stick (Oxford pdf 360, 952; *Imbibe!* pdf 211). F3, F5
anchors.meaning: Grohusko's drink was praised, not laughed at: he's never the one ridiculed. Never "the first Brooklyn" (C1): "one of the first", or "in his own book, in 1908".

anchors.fact: Grohusko never lived in Brooklyn; the restaurant's owner, Victor Baracca, did (Oxford pdf 952). F4
anchors.meaning: **Two plain facts, side by side.** No page says the drink was named for Baracca. Tell them as a juxtaposition, or signpost the link ("I like to think…"). Never "named for his boss" or "for someone else's home" as fact.
anchors.speaksTo: loving out loud on someone's behalf (our reading)

anchors.fact: Today bartenders make Grohusko's again and invent riffs named after Brooklyn's neighbourhoods, probably more popular than the Brooklyn itself: "back to square one", Oxford says (pdf 360). F18
anchors.meaning: Still being said. Neighbourhoods unnamed (Red Hook and the rest are siblings' ground). Never "it finally caught on".

anchors.fact: Out of guest text: the lawyer's name and his later court case (F9); Hegeman's other details (the Follies line is OCR-garbled; the reporter's "Herr" and "back yard" teasing); Craddock/Straub; Picon as a story; maraschino; any recipe for Gage & Tollner's (C2); the 1944–45 restaurant and hotel Brooklyns (publicity).
anchors.meaning: Counterweights kept in the card.

anchors.fact: Sibling wording: "known by" (*Before the Room*), "first, then everyone does" (*There It Goes*), vindication (*The Way It Felt*), reply-now / "careful" / hurt (*Wide Open*), "fall for" (*Rosetta*), "anyway" (*Anyway*). Absinthe is *Rosetta*'s base; cider with rum is a held Stone Fence in the family plan.
anchors.meaning: Grep the reading for each before round 3.

anchors.fact: The earliest Brooklyn on record was a rum Manhattan (Oxford pdf 360); the 1945 *Eagle* printed the club's drink as equal parts Jamaica rum (100 proof) and Italian vermouth with a dash of Angostura (F17). Ours: aged Jamaican rum at about 50%, 2:1 with sweet vermouth, a dash of Angostura and a spoon of amaro (Tomás, v3).
anchors.meaning: The style, the strength and the dash are the tie. The proportions and the amaro are ours: never "the club's recipe", "the 1883 recipe" or "the same rum".
anchors.speaksTo: the one that leaves the room

anchors.fact: Grohusko's Brooklyn had a dash of Amer Picon, a French digestive bitter made from bitter and sweet orange peels (Oxford pdf 1509, 360–361); Oxford and *Imbibe!* name Amaro CioCiaro as the stand-in (pdf 361; *Imbibe!* pdf 212), and *Codex* p. 260 says it tastes of burnt orange.
anchors.meaning: A stand-in, never "Grohusko's bitter". Picon is an ingredient here and never the story (Till Spring's).

anchors.fact: The flamed orange twist, now out of the drink (Wren's ruling, Tomás agreed), kept here as a record: the peel's oils are squeezed through a lit match, which caramelises them before they land (*Joy* pdf 136–137); it takes a little practice (*Joy* pdf 136), and if it doesn't work the fruit may be too old or dry (DeGroff, Oxford pdf 800). DeGroff calls it "a highly theatrical technique" (pdf 800). A chilled 22.5% drink doesn't catch (Oxford pdf 801: 40% spirit burns readily only above 28°C).
anchors.meaning: Not in the pour. The top is an unflamed peel squeezed high. "Often fails the first time" is on no page. **Fence:** the Flame of Love story (Chasen's, Dean Martin) is the lover-ruler backup's: technique only, never that story.
anchors.speaksTo: knows how it looks, does it anyway

cocktail.closingLine: Squeeze the peel from high up, so nobody misses it. If they laugh, keep the words the same size.
cocktail.glassware: a cocktail glass (about 180 ml), chilled
method: Put the cocktail glass in the freezer for 10 minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
With a small knife, cut a wide strip of peel from a fresh, thick-skinned orange, about 2.5 cm across, leaving a little of the white underneath so it holds its shape.
Fill a mixing glass or a jar with ice. Pour in the rum, the vermouth, the CioCiaro and the dash of bitters.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass is very cold.
Empty the cocktail glass and strain the drink into it.
Hold the peel by its edges, orange side down, high above the glass (about a hand's width), and squeeze it sharply so its oils fall in a fine spray over the drink.
Rub the orange side around the rim and drop the peel in.
cocktail.name: The Big Words

recipe.item: aged Jamaican rum, about 50% (any aged Jamaican rum from 40% to 57% works; not spiced)
recipe.note: the style and strength of the rum in the Brooklyn Club's drink, as the *Eagle* printed it in 1945
the club poured as much vermouth as rum; at half the rum the drink stays bright

recipe.item: Amaro CioCiaro (*recommended*), or any dark, bittersweet Italian amaro (herbal liqueur) with a burnt-orange taste, about 30%
recipe.note: in place of the 1908 Brooklyn's French orange bitter, Amer Picon; the stand-in Oxford and *Imbibe!* both name
the club's dash

recipe.item: wide strip of peel from a fresh, thick-skinned orange, about 2.5 cm across
recipe.note: squeezed high over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: You've never loved anything a little.

reading.epigraph: Manhattan has a cocktail. So does the Bronx. Brooklyn is still asking.
whoYouAre: When you love something, people hear about it. A person, a band, a team, the town you grew up in: it gets all of you, out loud, usually before anyone has asked. You're the one who makes the playlist, writes the birthday card that runs onto the back, and says the big words before anyone else dares to.

People assume you don't notice how it looks. You do. Nobody knows the pause after the big words better than you: the half-second before the room decides whether to smile with you or at you. You step into it regardless. The part you hide is the walk home afterwards, going back over the one face that smirked. What stings is being laughed at for meaning it, because it tempts you to say it a little smaller next time. Still, there's a gift in it: everyone you love has proof. Most people go their whole lives without being loved out loud, in front of others. Whoever you love never has to wonder.
yours: Manhattan had a cocktail, and so did the Bronx, so for well over a century Brooklyn has wanted one of its own. The earliest on record is from 1883, a rum Manhattan made at the Brooklyn Club, and it apparently never left the club. In 1908 Jack Grohusko, a Manhattan bartender, printed a Brooklyn in the book he wrote. He never lived in Brooklyn. The man who owned his restaurant did.

In the summer of 1910, the papers reported, a man living in Brooklyn couldn't sleep, so he got up and mixed a new one: a long glass of cider, absinthe and ginger ale. Asked what excuse he had for calling a pint a cocktail, Maurice Hegeman said there was no law about it, and that he wanted Brooklyn to have a cocktail people would recognise it by. That September, papers from Kansas City to Washington printed another Brooklyn, someone else's, offered with a very flowery tribute, and bartenders had their fun with its recipe. One of the Waldorf-Astoria's bartenders said all it was missing was the ice cream. A bartender far from Broadway said that if he lived in Brooklyn, he'd stick to beer.

Brooklyn kept at it. In 1945 the Bronx borough president teased that Brooklyn still had no cocktail, and offered one made with vinegar and DDT. Brooklyn answered so fast that within days the *Eagle*'s columnist heard thirty-three recipes in a single day, and gave up on the subject because more kept coming. Bartenders today are still naming new ones after Brooklyn's neighbourhoods.

That, to me, is you. Not the winning, because no Brooklyn has ever really stuck. The not stopping. I like to think Hegeman knew exactly how a pint of cider and ginger ale sounded when he called it a cocktail, and said it plainly because he meant it. When someone laughed, sooner or later somebody else in Brooklyn picked it up, at full size.

The cocktail I've made for you is a close relation of the Manhattan, that renowned classic so many other cocktails grew from. It starts from the Brooklyn Club's drink as the *Brooklyn Eagle* printed it in 1945: strong Jamaican rum with Italian vermouth, plus Angostura bitters, just one dash. The club poured equal measures of the two; mine is an aged Jamaican rum, two parts to one of vermouth, so it stays bright. Where Grohusko's had a little French bitter made from orange peel, mine has a bar spoon and a half of a dark, bittersweet Italian liqueur that tastes of burnt orange. It's stirred cold, rich and warm from the rum, with a bitter-orange edge, poured into an ice-cold cocktail glass. The last touch is mine too: a wide orange peel, squeezed high over the top, so the orange arrives before anything else. As a nod to you, a drink built on the club's quiet Brooklyn now announces itself.

Whenever you say the big words and somebody laughs, don't take them back, and don't trim them for next time. Same words, same size. Somebody usually joins in. In Brooklyn, it was thirty-three recipes in a day.

anchors.fact: On a day out trout fishing with his father-in-law, sitting in Tasmania's highlands, the two of them talked over what the island already had: water they thought among the best in the world, good barley, a climate that seemed fine for whisky. And nobody was making any. (SB, Lark; no year, C5)
anchors.meaning: Our reading: the hope was built from what was in front of them, not wished from nowhere. It was a conversation between two people.
anchors.speaksTo: The one true thing (a hope built from things noticed, close by); test limb (1)

anchors.fact: Lyn arrived and said, in effect, let's try it. (SB, Lark quoting her; never her exact "give it a go", which echoes the Have A Go Hero)
anchors.meaning: The first answer the idea got was a yes, from his wife, who had just arrived. Lyn is in the story from the first day, never "he alone".
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's Lyn condition; the gift (someone keeps the hope going)

anchors.fact: Neither of them had distilled before: he was a land surveyor, she a survey draftsman. (SB, narration)
anchors.meaning: Our reading: the hope came well ahead of any proof.

anchors.fact: The island had whisky distilleries by the late 1820s and early 1830s. (Oxford pdf 171)
anchors.meaning: What they hoped for had been there before.
anchors.speaksTo: Test limb (2) (about something near, already there)

anchors.fact: From 1901 the law required a licensed distiller to run a very large still, so for most of the century only big industrial firms distilled. After the 1970s, Australians turned to cheaper imports and away from local brands, and the big whisky makers stopped. (pdf 172; stopping date conflicts, pdf 172 vs 2173, so no date)
anchors.meaning: The "no" on the page is a rule and a market, not a person. "A country had stopped hoping its whisky could be good" is our reading: signpost it.
anchors.speaksTo: Test limb (2); the guest's "don't get your hopes up" stays in the guest's half

anchors.fact: "Stymied by regulation", in his words. In 1992 he persuaded the government to rewrite the rule on how big a still had to be (pdf 2173; pdf 172 "lobbied"). As he tells it, politicians helped "instantly". (SB)
anchors.meaning: A rule from 1901, still standing in 1992 (no page says whether anyone had questioned it before him). Nobody on the page scolded him: as he tells it, the help came at once.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's position direction ("an old rule nobody has checked")

anchors.fact: "Lyn and I were the first ones to get a licence." (SB, 1992)
anchors.meaning: Shared, again. No "first in N years" (C4).

anchors.fact: Within two weeks, a phone call at 10 at night: John Grant of Glenfarclas in Scotland, offering to help them make good whisky. His reason, as Lark remembers it: someone's first whisky should be a good one, so they'll go on to explore the rest. (SB, Grant relayed by Lark)
anchors.meaning: Someone far away kept the hope going for them before there was any whisky.
anchors.speaksTo: The gift (keeping hope for others); bridge to limb (3)

anchors.fact: "As other producers came along, I thought I should help them as well" (SB, Lark, with Grant's words in mind). Oxford: several craft distillers soon followed in his footsteps (pdf 172). Most of Australia's distilleries are now in Tasmania (pdf 2173).
anchors.meaning: The help he was given, he passed on, on his own record: the hope opened a door for others, and he held it open.
anchors.speaksTo: Test limb (3); Wren's question "did he help the ones who followed?" (yes)

anchors.fact: Tasmanian distillers tend to use local brewing malt; the local peat gives different aromatics; wine and fortified-wine casks, often small (pdf 2173). Craft spirits there are often much dearer (pdf 172).
anchors.meaning: For Tomás: island-grounded material (malt, peat, small fortified casks) that isn't honey; and a sourced Makeable flag on price.

cocktail.closingLine: The Glenfarclas goes in last. Then find out what's really in the way.
cocktail.glassware: a tall glass (highball, about 300 ml), filled with ice
method: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the Lark, then the cold water, and stir a few turns, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Add the two teaspoons of Glenfarclas last, over the top, and give it one more turn.
cocktail.name: Let's Try It
