cocktail.tagline: You notice the little signs that make a big hope feel possible.

reading.epigraph: Tasmania's new whisky began on a fishing trip: good water, good barley, and nobody making any.
whoYouAre: Little things add up for you. The friend who lights up whenever baking comes up. The job advert you know would suit someone perfectly. The two people at a party who keep ending up talking to each other. Put enough of them together and you can see how something could turn out, well ahead of everyone else. To you, that isn't wishing. It's where the signs point.

But you learned early to keep it quiet. "Don't get your hopes up" was nearly always said kindly, by people who loved you. So now every hope comes with a little "probably not" in front of it, said first, to beat everyone else to it. What you dread is the look afterwards, and worse, someone telling you that you got their hopes up.
And still you don't stop. When a person close to you puts a hope down, you quietly pick it up and keep it for them until they're ready to have it back. Most people just tell them to be realistic.
yours: Tasmania, the island south of mainland Australia, owes its whisky today to a fishing trip. Bill Lark and his father-in-law were sitting up in the highlands, talking over what the island already had: some of the best water in the world, as they saw it, good barley, and a climate that seemed fine for whisky. And nobody was making any. Then Bill's wife, Lyn, arrived, heard the idea and said, more or less, that they should try it. Neither Bill nor Lyn had ever distilled.

What stood in the way was an old rule. Since 1901, Australian law had asked for stills so big that only large industrial firms could distil, and by then even the big whisky makers had stopped: Australians had turned to cheaper imports and away from their own brands. I like to think a whole country had been told not to get its hopes up about its whisky. In 1992 Bill persuaded the government to rewrite the rule, and, as he tells it, the politicians helped at once. Lyn and Bill were the first to get a licence.

Within two weeks of the licence, the phone rang at ten at night. It was John Grant, of the Glenfarclas distillery in Scotland, offering to help them make good whisky. His reason, as Bill remembers it: if somebody tastes whisky for the first time from the Larks' distillery, it should be a good first time. As others on the island started distilling, Bill decided he should help them too.

The idea that day wasn't a wish. They'd looked at what was in front of them and added it up. The "no", when it came, wasn't a person at all, just a rule that had stood since 1901. And once the door was open, Bill held it for the ones coming after him, the way a distillery in Scotland had held it for him. That's what you do with other people's hopes. You keep them going until they can carry them again, and some of them come true because you did.

The cocktail I've made for you is a whisky highball, one of the great simple drinks, made still: a Tasmanian single malt, Lark's own if you can find it, with cold water over ice, for the water and barley they talked about that day. The last thing in is two teaspoons of Glenfarclas, the Scotch from the distillery whose call came at ten at night. It's there for the help that turns up before there's anything to show for it, and for the hopes you keep for other people.

Whenever you can see how something could go, for yourself or for someone close, drop the "probably not". Say what you've added up, plainly, and then find out what's really in the way. It's often smaller than the hope: an old rule, a form, one person nobody has thought to ask. And sometimes the first answer is a yes.

anchors.fact: Thoreau wrote that the wild apples of old pastures, the ones a farmer leaves out as unsalable, are the walker's choicest fruit in late October and early November (W5, W6).
anchors.meaning: What everyone else passes over as not worth gathering is, to the one who walks there, the best thing in the field.

anchors.fact: He wrote that the same apple, brought into the house, often tastes harsh and crabbed, and that one he took from his desk indoors was unexpectedly crude, sour enough to set a squirrel's teeth on edge; indoors you miss the November air, which is its sauce (W7). Thoreau's claim, not a fact about apples.
anchors.meaning: The fear of being brought indoors and turning sour, in someone else's words: nothing in the apple changed, only the room.

anchors.fact: He applied it to himself: one thought for the field, another for the house; his thoughts, like wild apples, were food for walkers and not warranted palatable in the house (W9). He also wrote that "our wild apple is wild only like myself" (W2).
anchors.meaning: The mirror is his own, on the record, not ours: what he was is right in its own air and wrong in someone else's room.

anchors.fact: Thorny pasture apple bushes, he joked, have "no malice, only some malic acid"; when the tree finally rises, it lets the cows that cropped it into its shade (W3, W4). Same pages also use fighting words ("foes", "defeats").
anchors.meaning: Sharp, not angry. Something that held its ground for years and, once grown, let them in to shade and fruit.

anchors.fact: His friend Emerson wrote that Thoreau kept his freedom "at the cost of disappointing the natural expectations of his family and friends" (E2), and counted it "a fault in him that he had no ambition": instead of engineering for all America, "the captain of a huckleberry party" (E6).
anchors.meaning: The cost spoken by someone who loved him, and he meant it ("if, at the end of years, it is still only beans!").

anchors.fact: Emerson's next sentence calls these "foibles, real or apparent", and says Thoreau's study of nature made his friends curious to see the world through his eyes (E7). He was always ready to lead a huckleberry party with the young people he loved (E8).
anchors.meaning: The disappointment and the love sit in the same paragraph; the friend half grants it may only seem a fault.

anchors.fact: Emerson: "He chose to be rich by making his wants few, and supplying them himself." (E4). Emerson also hedged it: "Perhaps he fell into his way of living" (E5, C3).
anchors.meaning: Enough, called riches by the friend who doubted him. Quote Emerson's line as his; "chose on purpose" stays the guest's, not a fact about Thoreau.

anchors.fact: He once tempted a companion, keeping a straight face, with one of the sour apples; once frost and thaw had turned them sweet, "Now we both greedily fill our pockets" (W11, W12). The page doesn't say who brought whom, or when the tease happened.
anchors.meaning: He didn't carry the apples in to convince anyone: the companion was out there with him, where they taste right. (Winter, not October; "cheated" is his word, so it's a tease, not a lesson; never "he brought/took" the companion.)

anchors.fact: The Stone Fence (also Sampson, recorded from 1750) is spirit and cider in roughly equal parts, "originally rum, and then whisky", hard cider preferred (S1). Jerry Thomas's 1862 version: bourbon, sweet cider, "2 or 3 small lumps of ice" (S2).
anchors.meaning: The old country drink the bar made from the apple: the apple arrives as cider. Ours goes the older way, with rum and hard cider (never "the original recipe", C1).

anchors.fact: Wondrich notes that as late as 1869 a bar manual said a tart, full-flavoured crab-apple cider was often preferred to ordinary cider in the Stone Fence (S3, a relay). Thoreau wrote that small, high-coloured wild apples "are thought to make the best cider" (W10), and Oxford says today's best cider apples are high in tannin, sugar and acid (S5).
anchors.meaning: The sharp apple the market skips is what the cider and the old drink wanted, and still want. That's the clause that keeps "still best where it was left" true today (S5 is present tense).

anchors.fact: Wondrich: by the Civil War the Stone Fence was "a ghost of its former self"; Jerry Thomas's 1862 version (if his testimony is to be believed, Wondrich's hedge) was bourbon with sweet, non-alcoholic cider, which Wondrich calls "suave and smooth, but comparatively feeble"; the older drink was hard cider and New England rum (*Imbibe!* pdf 160, S2). **Dates:** the tart crab-apple cider (S3) is 1869, seven years *after* Thomas's 1862 book.
anchors.meaning: The sharp version didn't come before the soft one and vanish: it carried on beside it. Someone in 1869 still preferred the tart cider while the fashionable glass had gone smooth. Never "before it was softened" (wrong order); "feeble" is Wondrich's judgement, credited to him.

anchors.fact: Right before "best cider", Thoreau wrote: "I still begrudge them to the cider-mill" (W10). He drank no wine (E10); nothing says he drank cider.
anchors.meaning: Own it in one clause if the reading names cider at all: he'd rather have eaten them in the field. Never "Thoreau's drink".

cocktail.closingLine: Carry it out of doors before you taste it. Whoever follows you out will understand.
cocktail.glassware: a heavy tumbler (about 300 ml), two or three small lumps of ice
method: Keep the cider cold in the fridge until you need it.
Drop two or three small lumps of ice into a heavy tumbler and pour in the rum.
Pour the cider in slowly over the ice, and give it one turn with a spoon.
Cut one thin slice from the sharpest apple you have, skin on, and slip it into the glass last.
cocktail.name: Fresh Air

recipe.note: rum was the Stone Fence's original spirit, before whisky

recipe.item: raw sharp apple, skin on (a crab apple, or the sourest apple to hand)

cocktail.tagline: You know what enough feels like, and make it look like freedom.

reading.epigraph: In 1862 a famous bar book printed this drink with sweet cider. Others kept pouring it tart.
whoYouAre: At a wedding or a birthday, someone asks what you're up to these days. You tell them: the same place, the work you like, your usual walk in the morning. Then you watch them wait politely for the rest. There isn't any rest. Years ago you stepped out of the race everyone else is running, quietly, and you don't miss it.

Living with less was easy. Being loved by people who think you're wasting yourself is harder. "You could do so much more." They mean it kindly, which is why you don't argue. And under that sits a quieter fear. No one will drag you back in. But someone kind might ask, with a job you'd be good at or a favour "just for a while", and once you're back indoors, the part of you they liked would turn sour.
After an afternoon with you, they go home wanting a little less, and lighter for it. You make "enough" look like a choice, not a defeat, and you show them someone can say no and stay kind.
yours: In late autumn, the writer Henry David Thoreau went into old pastures for the small, sharp apples farmers left out as unsalable. To someone out walking, he wrote, they were the choicest fruit. Indoors, he wrote, it tasted like another fruit: one he took out of his desk was "sour enough to set a squirrel's teeth on edge". There, he wrote, you miss the November air, "which is the sauce it is to be eaten with".

He knew he was describing himself: "one thought for the field, another for the house". His friend Emerson couldn't help "counting it a fault in him that he had no ambition": instead of engineering for all America, he was "the captain of a huckleberry party". Emerson meant it. In the same sketch, Emerson also wrote: "He chose to be rich by making his wants few, and supplying them himself."

As Thoreau tells it, nothing in the apple changes when it's carried in. Only the room does. You know that about yourself, so you keep turning down the bigger room, however kindly it's offered. Emerson wrote that it cost Thoreau nothing to say no. It costs you something every time, because you like the people asking. You're not hiding from anyone. You simply know where you're at your best. And I like to think the ones asking are curious about the world as you see it, and don't know how to say so.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Stone Fence, a drink from colonial America, on record under another name by 1750. I went back to its older pairing of rum and hard cider, and kept it sharp: aged rum and a dry, still farmhouse cider, the sharpest you can find, over two or three small lumps of ice, with no sugar to soften it, because sharp was never a fault that needed fixing. Thoreau wrote that wild apples like his were thought to make the best cider, though he still begrudged them to the cider mill. So, for the apples he'd rather have eaten in the field, a thin slice of raw, sharp apple goes in at the end.

You don't owe anyone a bigger life, or an explanation of this one. Thoreau once kept a smooth face while tempting a companion with one of those sour apples. By winter, when frost and thaw had turned them sweet, the two of them were filling their pockets together. So stop defending your life to the ones who worry about you. Have one of them come along. Some will taste what you taste, and you'll have someone to fill your pockets with.

anchors.fact: Punch was the first mixed drink based on spirits to become popular around the world. English traders in India were making it by the 1630s, sailors spread it, and from the 1670s to the 1840s a shared bowl was the drink of choice for much of the world. It's the ancestor of the Daiquiri and the Margarita.
anchors.meaning: Everyone's drink, before it was anyone's.

anchors.fact: The popular story says "punch" comes from the Hindi for "five" (five ingredients, Fryer, 1676). But around 1630 the English merchant Peter Mundy recorded its name as *chaar bakhra*, Hindi for "four shares". Origin not established.
anchors.meaning: The truer name counts the people, not the ingredients (interpretation).

anchors.fact: Oleo-saccharum: sugar left with lemon peels pulls out their oil and becomes a fragrant syrup (about 12 hours sealed). It was considered a pillar of proper punch from the late 1700s.
anchors.meaning: Care that takes time, done in advance for others.

anchors.fact: Punch was shared from bowls. Small "sneakers" were passed from person to person, at both humble and grand gatherings, with no restriction on who drank.
anchors.meaning: Nobody at the edge of the room.

anchors.fact: Some punch bowls carried inscriptions inside that appeared as the bowl was emptied, like "Drink Fair" and "One Bowl More & then".
anchors.meaning: Messages for the ones who stayed until the end.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Peace · lens: The real me

cocktail.closingLine: Ladle it out, and keep one cup back for yourself.
cocktail.glassware: a punch bowl with one big block of ice, ladled into small cups
method: The night before: bury the lemon peels in the sugar in a sealed jar and leave them alone. By morning the sugar will have pulled the oil out of the peels and turned into a fragrant syrup.
Stir the lemon juice into the jar until the sugar dissolves, then remove the peels.
Pour the lemon syrup, the rum and the cold tea into a punch bowl over one big block of ice. Stir.
Ladle into small cups.
cocktail.name: Four Shares

recipe.item: lemons, peeled in long strips (no white pith)

recipe.note: made the night before

cocktail.tagline: You make belonging feel as simple as pulling up another chair.

reading.epigraph: This drink was never poured for one.
whoYouAre: You believe the best of people, and you'd rather be disappointed now and then than live any other way. You forgive quickly. It isn't that you don't notice. It's that holding on to it costs more than it's worth. When things go wrong for someone, you don't make a speech. You just stay. People feel safer around you, and they often couldn't tell you why, they just do.
Here's the part you struggle to show: you worry about being the one left out, the one who said the wrong thing, the one who let somebody down. So you make sure nobody else ever has to feel that way.
yours: Nobody knows exactly where punch was born. What we do know is that in the 1600s, English traders in India were mixing the local spirit with water, sugar, citrus and spice, and that sailors carried the habit to every port they reached. For almost two hundred years, a shared bowl of punch was the drink of choice across much of the world. It was the first mixed drink with spirits to travel the globe, and it's the ancestor of drinks you know, like the Daiquiri and the Margarita.

Even its name is a small mystery. The story most people tell is that "punch" comes from the Hindi word for five, for its five ingredients. Maybe. But one of the first Englishmen to write the drink down, a merchant in India around 1630, recorded it under a Hindi name that means "four shares". I like to think that's the truer name: not what goes into it, but how many people get some.

Punch was never a drink for one. It was made in a bowl and passed around. Small bowls went from hand to hand, in taverns and grand houses alike, and anyone in the room could drink. Some bowls even had words painted inside that only appeared once everyone had had their share: "Drink fair." "One bowl more." That's you, isn't it? You're the one who makes sure the bowl comes round to everybody, and that nobody is left standing at the edge of the room.

So I made your punch the old way, the way that takes time, to honour the time you give to others. It starts the night before: strips of lemon peel buried in sugar and left alone until the sugar has drawn out all their oil and turned into a fragrant syrup. You can't rush it. You can only give it time. Then lemon juice, a bottle of aged rum and cold black tea, poured over one big block of ice and ladled into cups. It isn't clever. It's generous. It's a drink that says "I was thinking of you yesterday."

Here's what I'd ask of you. Make this one day for people you love, and don't wait for a reason. And the next time you're the one who's struggling, let someone pass the bowl to you. You've spent a long time making sure nobody is left out. You're allowed to be looked after too.

anchors.fact: Boadas opened in 1933 as hardly more than a corridor with a bar; after the civil war it gained a few metres and became a small triangle, and by its own page it hasn't changed since (Oxford pdf 303; bar page; F1).
anchors.meaning: It grew once, by a little, and then stayed the size it was. Nobody tried to make it bigger.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: not measured by size

anchors.fact: It sits a few steps off Barcelona's most crowded street, yet Oxford calls it the opposite of a tourist trap (Oxford pdf 303; F2).
anchors.meaning: The world's crowd went past the door; what was inside didn't change for it.
anchors.speaksTo: grown-ups' numbers and titles don't move them

anchors.fact: Maria Dolors grew up in the bar: she learned to walk there and did her homework to the sound of the customers; she left school early to help her parents after the war (bar page; F4–F5).
anchors.meaning: The small world wasn't chosen later in life. It was hers from the start.

anchors.fact: By 1956 she was looking after the bar alongside her father, and a photograph shows her throwing a cocktail behind that bar around 1965 (bar page F6; Oxford pdf 2049 caption, F7).
anchors.meaning: She was doing the daily work years before the bar was hers. Active tending, not inheritance.

anchors.fact: From 1967 she ran it, a skilled bartender in her own right, keeping her father's eye for detail and warmth, for nearly fifty years (Oxford pdf 303; F8; "nearly fifty" is our arithmetic).
anchors.meaning: Decades of the same small room, done carefully.

anchors.fact: As she told a writer, her best teachers were always the guests, from the look on their faces after the second sip (bar page, relayed and likely translated; F9).
anchors.meaning: She judged her work by whether it was right for this person today, not by a measure.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: "is it all right today"

anchors.fact: The throw: poured from an ice-filled tin into an empty one, back and forth, until the drink is cold and diluted just right (Oxford pdf 301; method pdf 1671; F12, F14).
anchors.meaning: Its job on the record is the drink's cold and its water, not the show.
anchors.speaksTo: care for the drink, never a show

anchors.fact: Oxford elsewhere calls throwing "often theatrical" (MIXOLOGY pdf 1335); Xavier Olivé, a Barcelona bar connoisseur, told the writer she was "like a show" behind the bar; the next sentence on the page qualifies it: no spectacle, a highly professional person (bar page; F10).
anchors.meaning: The show reading exists, and on the page it is qualified at once. Any "it was care, not show" line is ours, signposted.

anchors.fact: Her father and his successors, among them Maria Dolors and her husband, kept the throw going after it had fallen out of use, which paved the way for its revival; Oxford names Barcelona as the last place it was still done (Oxford pdf 301, 1671; F13–F14).
anchors.meaning: Something nearly lost lived on in one small room because people kept doing it. Never "she alone"; "paved the way", not "caused".
anchors.speaksTo: clause 4: it came through because of them

anchors.fact: The throw can now be seen at many of the city's other bars, and an apprentice from 1970, Jerónimo Vaquero, owns Boadas and still throws (Oxford pdf 303, as of 2021; F15–F16).
anchors.meaning: What they tended is now sturdier than any one keeper.

anchors.fact: Nothing on record names what Boadas throws; no house Martini (card, "Not found").
anchors.meaning: The drink is the room's own; never "her recipe" or "the Boadas Martini".

cocktail.closingLine: Four or five throws, then stop while it's cold. Make it for someone, and watch their face at the second sip.
cocktail.glassware: a small wine glass (about 120 ml), chilled in the freezer, no ice
method: Put the wine glass in the freezer for 10 minutes. Take the dry vermouth from the fridge.
Fill one shaker tin three-quarters with ice and fit the strainer on it. Measure in the gin and the vermouth with a tablespoon.

Stand over the sink. Hold the empty tin low in one hand and the full one just above it in the other. Pour the drink through the strainer into the empty tin, lifting the full tin a little as you pour, so the stream gets longer. A forearm's length is plenty. The ice stays behind the strainer.
Bring the tins back together and pour the drink straight back through the strainer onto the ice.
Do it four or five times in all, until the tin with the ice is cold to hold.
Strain it into the cold glass. Squeeze the strip of lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Whole World

recipe.note: any London dry gin of 40 to 47%
from a bottle opened recently and kept in the fridge; a full tablespoon, not less
about 5 cm, no white pith

cocktail.tagline: You look after a little world as if it were the whole one.

reading.epigraph: Thrown tin to tin. Barcelona, it's said, was the last place still doing it.
whoYouAre: Someone asks what you've been up to, and you say "nothing much, just the usual". You mean the herbs on the windowsill, the friend you've rung every week since school, the old bike you keep running. To anyone else it looks small. It has never once struck you that small makes it matter less. Other people ask how big it is. You ask whether it's all right today.

You keep the small jobs small by doing them early: the drip seen to the day it starts, the hurt feelings sorted out before dinner. Nobody notices those. They aren't meant to be noticed. And you never mention the fear. Miss one day, and it feels as if all of it could slip. So you shrug and call it your little thing, because the seriousness gets smiled at. Whatever you're looking after is safe, and anyone close to you learns that a small thing taken seriously is worth more than a big thing taken lightly. With you, nothing small is ever only small.
yours: Boadas opened in 1933, a few steps from the Ramblas, Barcelona's most crowded street. It was barely more than a corridor with a bar in it. After the civil war it gained a few metres and became a little triangle, and it has stayed that size ever since. Maria Dolors Boadas, the owner's daughter, grew up in it: she learned to walk there, and did her homework to the sound of the customers. By 1956 she was looking after the bar alongside her father, and from 1967 she ran it herself, for nearly fifty years.

Boadas threw its drinks: poured them from a tin full of ice into an empty tin and back, in a long stream, until they were cold and watered down just enough. The technique had come from Cuba, and elsewhere it had fallen out of use; for a time, it was said, Barcelona was the last place still doing it. The family, and the bartenders after them, kept it going, and paved the way for its return. A Barcelona bar connoisseur once said watching her was like a show. A writer who knew her put it more exactly: no spectacle, just a highly professional person. Her best teachers, she told him, were always the guests, and she read it in their faces after the second sip.

I like to think the throw was never about the stream, but about the second sip: the drink being right, for this person, tonight. That's how you measure things too. Not by size, or numbers, or who's noticed, but by whether it's all right today. And there's something in her story for the part of you that's scared. A gesture that had fallen out of use almost everywhere was kept alive in that small room, and as of 2021 it could be seen in many of the city's bars, and an apprentice who started there in 1970 owned the place. In the end, what she looked after grew sturdier than any one keeper, and all the days she gave it are part of why.

The cocktail I've made for you is a dry gin Martini, the great classic, made with the throw Boadas kept going. Three tablespoons of gin and one of dry vermouth, measured with a spoon as a nod to a bar whose founder shunned the jigger, as its bartenders still did in 2021, then thrown between two tins four or five times, till it's cold, and poured through the strainer into a little wine glass, with a thin curl of lemon peel dropped in. We don't know which drinks Boadas throws, so this one is mine. I kept it to two bottles because, for you, the care should be the whole of it: nothing in it is there to impress. It's bright, cold and clean, and it tastes that way because someone paid attention.

You look after it so closely that you mostly look for what might be going wrong. Next time, before you check what needs doing, stop and look at it the way someone new would, as if you'd never seen it. It's been all right for years now. That isn't luck. It's every one of those days, and you're allowed to take pleasure in what they built.

anchors.fact: In his book on bartending, Regan tells newcomers to expect mistakes and to learn from them, and gives one of his own as the example (*Joy* pdf 133).
anchors.meaning: He told it on himself, for the next person's sake. Whether he was glad is not on the page: any warmth is the bartender's, signposted.
anchors.speaksTo: why it's you; the gift is safe to receive

anchors.fact: Once he was working behind a bar, he made Scotch Sours "for a while" whenever Whiskey Sours were ordered: where he'd come from, England, asking for whisky gets you Scotch (*Joy* pdf 133).
anchors.meaning: An honest mistake, made by following the rule he'd learned somewhere else, and repeated until someone said.

anchors.fact: A waitress caught it, and only then did he learn what he was doing wrong. She is unnamed; "caught" is the only thing the page says she did (*Joy* pdf 133).
anchors.meaning: Being caught was how he learned. Nothing about her manner, words or rank.

anchors.fact: His doubt has two halves: maybe the customers never noticed; maybe they did and didn't tell him (*Joy* pdf 133).
anchors.meaning: He can't know which, and either way the mistake went on in the glass until she caught it. Keep both halves; never "their silence" alone.
anchors.speaksTo: whoYouAre; the fear of being humoured

anchors.fact: The Whiskey Sour in his own book: bourbon or rye, fresh lemon, simple syrup, shaken, a chilled sour glass (or a rocks glass on ice), cherry and half an orange wheel (*Joy* pdf 406; chart pdf 219).
anchors.meaning: The correction made right. Any change from this is ours, never "his recipe".

anchors.fact: The sour is an American drink of the 1850s (first in print in 1857), and the Whiskey Sour is one of the few that kept the old name (Oxford SOUR pdf 1837–1838).
anchors.meaning: A renowned classic, with its family on record since the 1850s.
anchors.speaksTo: let the drink sound worth having

anchors.fact: The sour glass was given a stem so the hand wouldn't warm the drink (Oxford SOUR pdf 1838).
anchors.meaning: Tomás's glass has a reason in the record.

anchors.fact: In the same book he advises muddling lemon wedges with granulated sugar for a Whiskey Sour: he says the sugar works the zest and makes a much fresher-tasting drink (*Joy* pdf 151).
anchors.meaning: The touch is his own later advice, so the correction is made right by the man who made the mistake. "Fresher" is his claim, told as his. Ours muddles the squeezed shell, not wedges: owned.
anchors.speaksTo: the twist tied to the story

anchors.fact: Sugar muddled with citrus is also *Good as It Is*'s method (lime, Caipirinha, citing *Joy* pdf 173 and 151).
anchors.meaning: Technique shared, not taken; no "grind the oil out of the skin" in guest text, and never "new".

anchors.fact: Ready-made sour mix was nearly universal in bars from the 1960s through the 1980s (Oxford SOUR pdf 1838–1839).
anchors.meaning: Fresh lemon is our "made right". Never a claim about what his Scotch Sours held.

cocktail.closingLine: Press the sugar into the peel until it smells of lemon. One little step, and the whole glass is fresher.
cocktail.glassware: a small stemmed sour glass (about 180 ml), chilled in the freezer, no ice
method: Put the sour glass in the freezer for 10 minutes.
Cut a lemon in half. Squeeze one half and measure 20 ml of juice into the shaker.

Cut the squeezed half into four pieces and drop them in with the sugar. Press them with a muddler (or the end of a rolling pin) until the sugar is wet and smells of lemon. Press, don't grind: shredded white pith turns bitter.
Add the bourbon, fill the shaker with ice and shake well for about 12 seconds.
Strain into the cold glass through the shaker's strainer and a small kitchen sieve, so no peel or sugar grains get through.
Hold it by the stem, so your hand doesn't warm it.
cocktail.name: Just So You Know

recipe.note: any bourbon of 40 to 46%; not bottled-in-bond or barrel proof
from half a medium lemon, measured
granulated, pressed into the squeezed lemon half

cocktail.tagline: You tell people what you'd want to be told.

reading.epigraph: A Whiskey Sour, as it was ordered. For a while, one bartender made it with Scotch.
whoYouAre: There's a crumb on someone's chin at dinner, or a typo on the first slide that everyone has already read, or a colleague whose name someone has been saying wrong for a year. Most people saw it. Maybe they thought it wasn't their place, or that it was kinder to leave it. You go over, quietly, and say so, to that person and nobody else. It never felt brave to you. It just seemed like what you'd want, if it were you.

There's a second after that you never mention. You've said it, and for a second you wait to see whether you're in trouble. At some point someone told you the truth was rude, and part of you still listens for it. And what hurts more is the reverse: finding out that people you trust watched you get something wrong and said nothing, to be nice.
Your way hands people the chance to fix it while it's still small, and it counts for a lot. Being told by you never feels like being caught out. It's being trusted to take it.
yours: Gary Regan was a bartender from England who later wrote a book on making drinks. He turns up more than once in my stories; this one I keep for you. In the book he tells newcomers to expect mistakes, and gives one of his own. Once he had a job behind a bar, for a while, whenever someone ordered a Whiskey Sour, he made a Scotch Sour. In England, ask for whisky and you get Scotch. The Whiskey Sour is an American classic, and in his book it's made with bourbon or rye.

No customer put him right. Maybe none of them noticed, he writes, "Or if they did, they certainly didn't tell me." A waitress caught it. That's all he says about her: no name, no words. Only that until she did, he hadn't learned what he was doing wrong.

Whoever else noticed, if anyone did, let him carry on. I like to think she did him the kind of favour you do, and treated him as someone who could take it. "Caught" is his word, but he doesn't use it as a complaint: he set the story down in print, against himself, for anyone starting out. That's what you rarely get to see after you've said it: the mistake fixed, then handed on to whoever comes next.

The cocktail I've made for you is the drink that was ordered, a Whiskey Sour: bourbon, sugar and fresh lemon, a renowned classic, served chilled, in a small stemmed glass. It borrows one tip from the same book: granulated sugar pressed into the lemon. The sugar works at the peel, he wrote, and the drink tastes fresher for it. I did it as a nod to what follows a catch like hers. He was put right, and then he passed on something better. Telling someone doesn't end with them being fixed. Sometimes it's how they get good.

So when you spot the next one, say it, and don't stand there waiting for the verdict. I'd bet most people are glad, even if it takes them years to get round to saying so. And you've done this for plenty of people without ever asking for it back. Pick someone close and ask them to do the same for you. It's your turn to be told.

anchors.fact: On a Sunday afternoon in the first months of 1917, in St. Louis, Clara Bell Walsh gave the first party Oxford finds planned as and called a cocktail party. A newspaper of the time said she was "responsible for the innovation" (Oxford pdf 512).
anchors.meaning: Somebody decided a Sunday could have a new shape, and gave it a name.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: makes the fun on purpose and gives it a shape

anchors.fact: About fifty guests came, and the cocktails ran from noon to one (Oxford pdf 512; Curtis 2025 agrees on the hour).
anchors.meaning: The hour is the rule of the game: a start and an end, so anyone could join in.
anchors.speaksTo: PROVIDE STRUCTURE; gives: a way in

anchors.fact: Before that, she had tried out other party themes. One had the guests dress up as babies and drink from bottles, and it didn't last the way the cocktail party did (Oxford pdf 512).
anchors.meaning: The tally. The one that didn't take is on record, and it came first.
anchors.speaksTo: hides: the list of flops; fear: being the one who couldn't lift it

anchors.fact: Among the drinks on offer were a few Sazeracs (and Mint Juleps) for the older guests set in their ways (Felten's phrase, Oxford pdf 512). The page doesn't say who chose them.
anchors.meaning: "I like to think" she made sure the hardest guests to win over had something too. Signposted, always.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: even the hardest person gets something; say the kindness out loud

anchors.fact: Oxford calls her cocktail party the "enduring success" the baby theme wasn't (pdf 512). Felten, in 2007, calls the cocktail party "that most essential of American institutions" (*WSJ*, 6 Oct 2007).
anchors.meaning: The one that took is still how people gather. That's our reading: never "she started it", never "everyone copied her".
anchors.speaksTo: position: the ones that didn't take are how you found the one that did

anchors.fact: No gloom, no motive and no count of her flops are on record.
anchors.meaning: Only as "I like to think…". The tally belongs to the guest, never to her.
anchors.speaksTo: trap: stating the gloom as fact

cocktail.closingLine: Muddle the whole wheel, peel and all. Then tell the story of the one that didn't take.
cocktail.glassware: stemmed wine glass (about 250 ml), chilled
method: Put the wine glass in the freezer for ten minutes.
Cut a thin wheel from an orange, about half a centimetre, and cut it into eight pieces. Leave the peel on.
Put the orange pieces and the coriander seeds in a shaker. Press them firmly with a muddler (or the end of a rolling pin) until the peel smells strongly of orange and the juice runs.
Add the gin, both vermouths and the bitters. Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds.
Pour it through the shaker's strainer and a small tea strainer held over the glass, so no seeds or pulp get in.
Nothing on the rim. The orange is already in it.
cocktail.name: Anyway

recipe.note: coriander is one of the usual botanicals in a London dry gin
more of the sweet than Oxford's recipe: it puts back the sugar a pour of orange juice would bring

recipe.item: fresh orange, about ½ cm thick, cut into eight pieces, peel and all
recipe.note: the peel is where most of an orange's flavour is; the thin wheel gives only a splash of juice
one of the usual flavourings in London dry gin, with a lemony note of its own; strained out before serving

recipe.item: Peychaud's bitters, recommended (or another bright-red New Orleans-style aromatic bitters)
recipe.note: the Sazerac's bitters, for the guests who'd rather have had a Sazerac

cocktail.tagline: You decide it's going to be a good night. Then you make it one.

reading.epigraph: People tried everything to fix the orange in the Bronx cocktail. This is one more try.
whoYouAre: It's a grey week, or a long wait, or a birthday nobody's quite in the mood for, and you've decided it's going to be good anyway. So you think of something: a silly game with proper rules, a theme, a time to turn up. Half the fun is that you took it seriously. People who would never start anything themselves find they've joined in, and even the one who swore they wouldn't ends up laughing.

There's a list, though, and only you have it: the ones that didn't take. The quiz nobody got into. The evening that stayed flat however hard you pushed it. Everyone else forgot them by the next morning. You didn't, because under all the fun is the thing you dread most: a gloom nobody could lift, and you the one who couldn't lift it. Even on the flat nights, people could tell that someone wanted the evening to be good for them. That's what your fun was for all along, and it matters more than whether the game worked.
yours: Early in 1917, on a Sunday afternoon in St. Louis, Clara Bell Walsh had about fifty guests over for something new: an hour of cocktails, from noon until one. A newspaper at the time gave her the credit for the idea. It's the first party on record that was planned as a cocktail party and called one.

It wasn't her first idea. She'd tried other party themes before it, and in one of them the guests dressed up as babies and drank from bottles. That one didn't catch on. The cocktail party did, and more than a century later it's still one of the ways people get together. I'd have gone to both.

It's the cocktail party people remember. But it might never have come without the ones before it, and I like to think she knew it. It's the same with the list you keep. The flat evenings on it aren't the opposite of the good ones. They're how you learned what people will join in with, and what they won't. And among the drinks that Sunday there were a few Sazeracs, served to the older guests who were set in their ways. I like to think that was someone making sure even the hardest ones to win over had something there for them. That's you, too.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from the sensation of her day, the Bronx: gin, two kinds of vermouth and orange. It was on her menu, and it was famously hard to get right. Put in enough orange juice to taste it, and the drink goes weak, so people kept trying new answers. The version I start from doesn't pour juice at all: one thin slice of orange is crushed in the shaker, peel and all, because the peel is where most of an orange's flavour is. You can taste the orange without drowning the gin. Then I added mine. A pinch of cracked coriander seeds goes in with the orange: coriander is one of the usual flavourings in London dry gin, with a lemony note of its own. And in place of the Angostura there are two dashes of Peychaud's, the Sazerac's bitters, for the guests who'd rather have had a Sazerac.

So keep the list. Just stop reading it as a record of what went wrong. Every idea on it that didn't take is part of the one that will. When something you've planned falls flat, laugh about it with them, and start planning another. Throw it anyway. I'd come to both.

anchors.fact: Harry McElhone, a Scot from Dundee who left school at fourteen, owned and ran Harry's New York Bar in Paris from 1923 until his death in 1958. (F1)
anchors.meaning: One address and one odd identity, for a whole working life.

anchors.fact: He advertised the bar's address, 5 rue Daunou, in Paris's American newspapers spelled out as "Sank Roo Doe Noo". (F3)
anchors.meaning: A made-up spelling, used until it became how people said it. **Reading:** "so an American could say it". Never the taxi (*Worth the Trip*). The spelling is still on a later IBF booklet's cover (F22).

anchors.fact: Among the paper jokes Oxford lists are "self-deprecating" postcards. (F2)
anchors.meaning: He was the joke first. "First" is **our reading**: signpost it or drop it.

anchors.fact: As his bar's 1927 book tells it: in autumn 1924 the columnist O. O. McIntyre wrote a "mournful" magazine piece calling Paris's regulars "barflies". A Montmartre club man then advertised his Christmas Eve takings for the "needy barflies", and Harry answered with an advert calling a meeting. Around Christmas 1924, the International Bar Flies, Trap 1, was organised at his bar. (F5; C1)
anchors.meaning: He took up someone else's joke and made it real, then kept it. The joke on the page is **the club man's advert**, not McIntyre's piece, which the book calls mournful. The meeting gets one clause (Wren). **Label:** "the way his own book tells it". **Never** "co-founded with McIntyre" (C1) or "Harry coined barfly" (L5). "Barflies" is glossed once, kindly (Wren): the regulars who never seem to leave.

anchors.fact: The presidency was "foisted upon" McIntyre as the "unconscious inspirer", as "Big Blue Bottlefly". The book lists Harry as vice-president, "Little Blue Bottlefly". (F6)
anchors.meaning: Always "listed as", never "he gave himself" (Wren).

anchors.fact: McIntyre's middle name really was Odd: Oscar Odd McIntyre (Library of Congress). Friends called him Odd. (F10)
anchors.meaning: One plain clause, owned as a coincidence. Never explain the name.

anchors.fact: The book prints the society's emblem, a housefly on a sugar lump lettered "I.B.F." (printed p. 94). (F17)
anchors.meaning: The fly is the society's own image. **No sugar lumps with dead flies in guest text** (Wren). The coffee beans are sambuca's custom (see spark).

anchors.fact: By 1927: over five thousand members and branches called "traps" all over the world, and it kept growing for years (Oxford). The book's list starts at Trap 1, his bar, and includes a Trap 17 in Shanghai. Its chapter has members greeting each other "in Shanghai or Liverpool, Madrid or Pittsburg". (F4, F7, F20)
anchors.meaning: The daft thing became part of the world. Reading v2: "members, from Shanghai to Pittsburgh, and its branches were called traps". That's the chapter's own range for the members (p. 85). Pittsburgh isn't on the list of traps (F20), so never "traps from… Pittsburgh". No rules quoted (Wren).

anchors.fact: In 1940, with German troops closing in, he locked his papers in a safe, buried it outside Paris and left for London. After the war he came back and "picked up where he left off", running the bar until his death. (F14)
anchors.meaning: The serious stretch came, the joke was put somewhere safe, and he came back. **Scope:** Oxford's line is about the *bar*. No son, no bomb, no Café de Paris (Wren).

anchors.fact: A later IBF membership booklet (a dealer dates it 1953) lists "President: Exalted Blue Bottle Fly Harry Mc Elhone", with three more McElhones on its committee, and Harry signs its membership card as President. (F22)
anchors.meaning: The flies came back too, and he'd gone from "Little" to "Exalted" ("He'd been promoted": our joke, true of the two listed titles). "A later booklet", with no date (1953 is the dealer's). Its contents are post-1934, and its place after the war sentence rests on the dealer's date. Never "his sons".

anchors.fact: Cameron's Kick, a sour of scotch and Irish whiskey with lemon and orgeat, first appeared in his 1922 *ABC of Mixing Cocktails* (Oxford). His 1927 book prints it as one third each whisky and one sixth each lemon juice and orgeat. In 1922 he was "Harry of Ciro's", not yet at the Paris bar. (F12, F18)
anchors.meaning: Two countries' whiskies in one glass, on his own page. Ours changes it, and v2 owns that in words ("a little more lemon than his 1927 book does, and a touch more almond"). Only the 1927 proportions are known to us, so it's "his 1927 book". "First appeared in his book", never "his invention" or "his Paris bar's drink" for 1922.

anchors.fact: Sambuca is usually served "con la mosca", with coffee beans that with a little imagination look like houseflies. Oxford gives "one or three". (Oxford pdf 1723)
anchors.meaning: A borrowing, owned in one clause: "the way sambuca is often served". **Never "old" and never "an Italian way":** Oxford contrasts Rome's frozen sip with the fly served "around the world" (F26, D7). No luck lore.

anchors.fact: Roasted coffee beans are lighter than water: 438–755 kg/m³ against 1,000 (Rodrigues et al. 2003, Table 2). (F23)
anchors.meaning: That they float is our inference from the measured density, labelled ours. Never "never sink".

anchors.fact: Oxford's Espresso Martini is garnished with three coffee beans (pdf 739). (F25)
anchors.meaning: A look-alike to own in Checks. The image stays pale and never reads as an Espresso Martini.

cocktail.closingLine: Three flies, every time. If you ever stop, start again at three.
cocktail.glassware: coupe, chilled
method: Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes.
Pour the scotch, the Irish whiskey, the lemon juice and the orgeat (the almond syrup) into a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds.
Strain it into the cold coupe.
Drop three coffee beans onto the middle of the drink. They float on the thin froth the shaking leaves. They're there for the eye and the nose. Bite one if you like.
cocktail.name: For Kicks

recipe.note: one country
and another, half and half, the way Harry's book has it
a little more than his book's sixth, which leaves the drink short of sour
his book's own note says it's made from almonds
the fly: floated on top, never stirred in

cocktail.tagline: You take a joke further than anyone, until everyone else is in on it.

reading.epigraph: Three coffee beans float on top. They're meant to be flies. It's a long story.
whoYouAre: Somebody once said something daft in passing, and you didn't let it go. You took it one step further, then another. Now there's a word people use without knowing it started with you, a thing you always wear, a little ritual nobody remembers agreeing to. It started as a joke, and it's still a joke. You just never saw a reason to stop.

At every age, someone has expected you to grow out of it. What you don't say is that you could. Normal isn't a mystery to you: you could do it tomorrow, and nobody would stop you. That's the part that frightens you, more than any look across a room: how quietly it could happen. Meanwhile, next to you, other people get to be a bit ridiculous too, and they are. They feel freer around you than they'd ever think to tell you. That's a bigger gift than being taken seriously.
yours: The way a Paris bar's own book tells it, it started in 1924 with a gloomy piece by a New York columnist, who called the regulars of the Paris bars barflies: the ones who never seem to leave. His name, and this is true, was Oscar Odd McIntyre. Then a nightclub owner joked about it in an advert: his Christmas Eve takings would go to the "needy barflies".

Harry McElhone, a Scot who ran that bar, Harry's New York Bar, answered with an advert of his own, calling a meeting, and around Christmas the International Bar Flies was founded there. The book lists McIntyre as president, "Big Blue Bottlefly", and Harry as "Little Blue Bottlefly". By 1927 it had over five thousand members, and branches, called traps, from Shanghai to Buenos Aires. My guess is they joined for the reason people join in with you: someone had gone first, and was clearly fine.

The joke wasn't his. He just wouldn't let it end where most people would have, which is exactly what you do with a joke. And he kept it going. In 1940, as the war closed in, he locked his papers in a safe, buried it and left. After the war he returned to the bar and picked up where he left off, and a later booklet lists him as the society's president: "Exalted Blue Bottle Fly". He'd been promoted. I like to think the silliness was one of the things he kept safe.

The cocktail I've made for you is my take on Cameron's Kick, a forgotten classic, a whisky sour that first appeared in Harry's 1922 book. It's half Scotch whisky and half Irish whiskey, shaken with lemon and orgeat, a sweet almond syrup. Two countries' whiskies in one glass sounds like it shouldn't work, and it plainly does. I've given it a little more lemon than the old printed recipe, and a touch more almond, so it tastes brighter. Then I added the flies: three coffee beans floated on top, the way sambuca, an anise liqueur, is often served "with the fly", because with a little imagination the beans look like houseflies. Here they're for the Bar Flies. They add a little roasted-coffee scent as the glass comes up, and if you bite one, a bitter crunch against the almond.

Some stretches of your life will need you to be serious, and when one comes, you'll manage it. It doesn't get to take the silliness with it. When it's over, pick up where you left off: the word, the ritual, the thing you always wear, all of it. You won't be the only one who missed it.

anchors.fact: A Chicago bar opened in spring 2011 with no counter to stand at; an Old-Fashioned (one of the most familiar cocktails, Oxford pdf 1429) arrived sealed inside a ball of ice that was cracked open at the table, and the drink ran out into the glass (*Proper* pp. 234-235, F1, F5, F10; *Reader* 2011, F7).
anchors.meaning: One of the most familiar drinks, in a form nobody expected.
anchors.speaksTo: They play with what the room expects to happen next.

anchors.fact: About a month in, a critic described the ice cracked by the server and counted it among the drinks played, more quietly, for comedy (*Reader*, 26 May 2011, F7).
anchors.meaning: Someone saw the joke from the start.
anchors.speaksTo: The one laugh they want: the unrehearsed one.

anchors.fact: Chicago's cocktail crowd received it "rather coolly at first" (*Proper* p. 235, F11); the 2011 critic said the servers had little time to talk about the drinks, and that in the wrong mood they might seem "chilly, impersonal" (*Reader*, F13).
anchors.meaning: Cleverness without company reads as cold.
anchors.speaksTo: Their hidden fear: that the strangeness reads as cold, people left outside it.

anchors.fact: Charles Joly, who took over the drinks in August 2012 (*Time Out* 2014, F15), said later it had "lacked a sense of hospitality" (*Proper* p. 235, said in 2014, F12).
anchors.meaning: The criticism came from the man who would run it, looking back.
anchors.speaksTo: Caring whether it lands, and admitting it.

anchors.fact: With Joly the drinks stayed every bit as strange, but now came with a bartender's joke and a conversation (*Proper* p. 235, Simonson's narration, F17). Joly: "hospitality, the booze and a good time" (*Time Out* 2014, F18).
anchors.meaning: Explaining didn't break it; leaving people alone with it did.
anchors.speaksTo: The position: keep the strange, stay for the chat.

anchors.fact: Nothing says the change answered the cool reception: it came with a new person (*Proper* p. 235, F16; F15).
anchors.meaning: Any link is the bartender's "I like to think".

anchors.fact: The ice-sealed drink began as an Old-Fashioned (*PUNCH* 2017, F9; *Proper* p. 235, F5). No spirit is named.
anchors.meaning: Our Old-Fashioned is a riff on the idea, never their recipe.

cocktail.closingLine: Crack it in front of them. Then don't leave the table.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass (about 300 ml), holding a shell of ordinary cloudy ice frozen in a plastic cup
method: Fill the plastic cup almost to the top with water and put it in the freezer. Leave it for three to four hours, until the sides have frozen hard, about a finger's width thick, with a skin of ice across the top and water still liquid in the middle. Freezers vary, so check from the third hour: press the top with a spoon.

While it freezes, mix the drink in a small jug or jar: rye, rum, demerara syrup, bitters and the cold water. Put it in the freezer beside the cup. It's too strong to freeze at home, so it'll just get very cold.

When the shell is ready, break a hole in the top with the handle of a spoon, about the width of a thumb, and pour out the water that hasn't frozen. Squeeze the plastic cup gently and slide the shell out.
Stand the shell in the rocks glass, hole up, and pour the cold drink in through the hole, right before you take it to the table. If a little doesn't fit, keep it and pour it in after the crack.
At the table, in front of the person it's for, tap the shell firmly with the back of a spoon. It cracks, and the drink runs out into the glass over the broken ice.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, and drop it in.
cocktail.name: Unrehearsed

recipe.note: 50% is ideal; anything from 40% works
or any aged Spanish-style rum, not spiced, about 40%
demerara sugar and water, equal weights, stirred until dissolved
measured in now; it does the job stirring with ice would
squeezed over after the ice is cracked
a cup that fits inside your rocks glass; ordinary tap water, cloudy ice is fine

cocktail.tagline: Your favourite laugh is the one nobody saw coming.

reading.epigraph: The most familiar cocktail there is, sealed inside ice. Nobody tastes it until the ice breaks.
whoYouAre: It's a birthday, and you've been asked to say something short. You do: one sentence, read slowly from a very long sheet of paper. There's a second where nobody knows whether they're allowed to laugh. You let it run a little longer than is comfortable. Then it goes, and it's a laugh nobody planned, not even you. The evening where everyone laughs on cue, at the punchline they could see coming from the door, bores you to tears.

You're watching every face. You'd never explain one of your jokes, because explaining feels like taking it apart while everyone watches. So when one doesn't land, you keep a straight face and take it home with you. What you'd least like to hear is that it came across as cold, that someone thought it was on them, or felt left outside it. It almost never is. And it's a rare thing you give people: a real reaction instead of a polite one. For a second nobody has to know how to feel, and the night everyone's still describing weeks later is usually one you were at.
yours: In the spring of 2011, a bar opened in Chicago with no bar in it. There was no counter to lean on: the drinks came to the table, from stations at the back that looked more like a laboratory. The chef behind it, Grant Achatz, said they wanted to mix the newest techniques with tradition in a way they thought hadn't been done. One writer picks out an Old-Fashioned as perhaps the finest: the most expected cocktail there is, sealed inside a ball of ice, set in a rocks glass. At the table the ice was cracked, and the drink ran out over it.

Chicago's cocktail crowd didn't warm to it at first. A critic that first spring watched the server crack the ice and counted it among the drinks played, quietly, for laughs. The same review found the drinks could feel a little cold, because nobody had time to talk about them. Funny and cold, in the same week. In the summer of 2012 Charles Joly took over the drinks, and he said later it hadn't felt like a bar: it lacked a sense of hospitality. He didn't make the drinks ordinary. They stayed every bit as strange, but now a bartender came with them, to joke and to talk. It had to be, in his words, about "hospitality, the booze and a good time."

I like to think that critic put a finger on exactly the thing you worry about. The strange part was never the problem. The joke was there from the first week, and somebody laughed. What was missing was someone staying in the room with it. You know that second better than anyone, the one where people don't yet know whether they're allowed to laugh. It's a better second with someone beside them in it.

The cocktail I've made for you brings that idea home. Inside is the renowned classic, a rye Old-Fashioned: rye, demerara sugar, Angostura bitters and orange peel. It's a drink with as many recipes as bartenders, and the whole craft of it is restraint, so it's made exactly. It waits, cold and already diluted, in a shell of ordinary cloudy ice from your own freezer. A home freezer can't freeze a drink that strong, so plain ice holds it like a cup. Whoever made it cracks the shell at the table with one tap of a spoon, while whoever it's for looks on, and the drink runs out over its own broken ice. Nothing in the bottle is strange. The joke is all in how it arrives, which, if you ask me, is you exactly.

So keep every strange thing you had planned. Don't explain it beforehand, and don't make it sensible. Just don't disappear straight after. Stay for the second that follows, and for the conversation after that. Nobody needed the joke taken apart. They needed someone in it with them. The ones who weren't sure the first time are the ones who'll come back for whatever you try next.

anchors.fact: In April 1843 the fortress of Perote, Mexico, held prisoners from Texas taken in the 1842 raids each way: about fifty Bexar men, captured when Woll's army seized San Antonio on 11 September 1842 (Green pp. 29–30, 39, 235; App. I p. 447; TSHA "Perote Prison"), Trimble among them (App. I p. 448); and Green with fifteen Mier men, taken after the Texan raid on Mier in December 1842 (pp. 74–82, 243; TSHA "Mier Expedition"). All hands came to the bowl (p. 259). They were months from home ("five months" is the Mier party's figure, p. 256), in chains, in cold quarters (pp. 256–258; F2–F3, C5).
anchors.meaning: A hardship that lasted: the long middle, not one bad day. They weren't innocents: men taken in raids both ways, told once and without a side.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: still funny on the fortieth day; limb 1

anchors.fact: They stood round their bowl in rags with chains riveted on their ankles, which they called their "jewelry" (Green p. 259, F7).
anchors.meaning: The room's own refusal, in one word.

anchors.fact: For their celebration they bought mezcal ("vino mascal"), ass's milk, thirty dozen eggs and a loaf of sugar, and used all their cooking utensils and water jars to make egg-nog; three officers beat the eggs, another pounded the sugar (Green p. 259, F5–F6).
anchors.meaning: The drink is on the same page as the joke.

anchors.fact: Their shouts alarmed the guards, who feared a riot; the captain of the guard came round to know the cause, was answered, said "Bueno" and started to go (Green p. 260, F9).
anchors.meaning: The threat walks in on the one good evening.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: the bad thing showing through

anchors.fact: Then they gave the wink to Trimble, who could mimic an owl: he rolled his eyes over, twisted his head "clean round" and whooped. The captain turned, frowned, hesitated whether to laugh or swear, said "Tecolote" (screech-owl) and moved on, to a roar of laughter from the room (Green pp. 260–261, F10). Told by a witness who wrote it down in 1845: "as he tells it".
anchors.meaning: Make the threat a little ridiculous; the threat itself names the joke.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing; method: make it ridiculous; limb 3–4; everyone checks their face

anchors.fact: The nickname stayed with Trimble to his grave (Green p. 261, F11).
anchors.meaning: The mark: the others repeated the joke.
anchors.speaksTo: driver: LEAVE A MARK; bonus limb

anchors.fact: At a later roll call, "Tecolote" delivered the cover line for two men lying on the floor ("Here is two muy malo"), "with an admirable mixture of confidence and sympathy", and the officer left. The line was the group's plan; the delivery was his, with a straight face (Green pp. 314–315, F12).
anchors.meaning: The same nerve without the laugh: being there for others.
anchors.speaksTo: position: on the day the joke won't come, turn up anyway; gives: dignity in the middle of it

anchors.fact: Another night, the sentinel at their door was made good-natured with mezcal passed through the grates in an eggshell: nothing larger could pass (Green p. 316, F13).
anchors.meaning: Even the man guarding the door got a sip: the half-shell beside the cup.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink's touch; joke on the situation, never on the guard

anchors.fact: Eggnog is on record from 1788 (Oxford EGGNOG pdf 702; *Imbibe!* pdf 127); the *Codex* calls it "the classic example" of egg with dairy (p. 256); the classic ends with nutmeg (*Codex* p. 256; Oxford pdf 703). A mezcal egg-nog is on record (*Imbibe!* pdf 127). Ours: joven mezcal, whole egg, cow's milk for the ass's milk, rich syrup for the sugar loaf, no nutmeg because none was on their list (p. 259).
anchors.meaning: A renowned classic, made from their list. Never "their recipe": the milk and syrup are ours.

cocktail.closingLine: Fill the shell for whoever's on watch. On the days nothing's funny, show up all the same.
cocktail.glassware: a small plain earthenware cup (about 300 ml), chilled in the freezer; any small tumbler will do
method: Put the cup in the freezer for ten minutes. Make the syrup ahead: stir two parts sugar into one part warm water, by weight, until it's clear, then let it cool.
Wash the egg. Crack it cleanly into the shaker, keeping one half of the shell whole, and rinse that half under the tap.
Add the mezcal, the milk and the syrup.
Shake hard without ice for about fifteen seconds. That beats the egg, which was the job three of them did by hand.
Add ice and shake again, hard and loud, for about twelve seconds.
Strain it into the cold cup. Nothing goes on top: no nutmeg, no cinnamon.
Stand the half-shell up beside the cup and pour a teaspoon of mezcal into it.
cocktail.name: The Wink

recipe.note: any unaged mezcal of 40% or stronger; no particular village needed
wash it before you crack it, because half its shell gets used. It's raw, so use a pasteurised egg if the drink is for anyone pregnant, elderly or unwell
theirs was donkey's milk. Use milk, not cream, so it stays light
for their loaf of sugar: two parts sugar to one of water, by weight, stirred until clear

recipe.item: more mezcal, in half the eggshell
recipe.note: not in the drink: it's for someone else

cocktail.tagline: Things get bad. You get funnier.

reading.epigraph: Mezcal, eggs and milk, once mixed in prisoners' water jars. Nobody stopped them.
whoYouAre: It's been bad for a while now. Not one bad day: weeks of it, the kind where everyone has run out of things to say. And you're still funny. Not loud, just there every morning with something, the way some people bring coffee. When it gets worse, people glance at you before they decide how worried to be.

People say nothing gets to you. It all gets to you. You've just decided it doesn't get the last word. What you don't mention is that each day the next joke takes a little more finding, and that you sometimes wonder about the morning nothing comes, when everyone looking at your face sees what you've been holding off. And what you give them is the thing they need most: while someone's still laughing, they're still themselves, not just people something is happening to.
yours: In April 1843, the fortress prison at Perote, in Mexico, held prisoners from Texas: men taken in the raids the two had been making on each other the year before, months from home now, with chains riveted round their ankles. They called the chains their jewellery. For a date that mattered to them, they got hold of mezcal, eggs, donkey's milk and a loaf of sugar, and made eggnog with every cooking utensil and water jar they had.

It got loud enough that the guards feared a riot. Their captain came round, was told it was how the prisoners kept their saints' days at home, and turned to go. That's when they gave the wink to a man called Trimble, who could do an owl. He rolled his eyes right back, twisted his head clean round and whooped. As one prisoner's journal tells it, the captain turned, frowned, and couldn't decide whether to laugh or swear. Then he said "Tecolote", screech-owl, and walked on, with the whole room roaring behind him. The name stuck to Trimble for good.

Everybody there knew whose face to turn to. The owl didn't make the chains any lighter. It let a roomful of prisoners be themselves for a minute, inside a fortress's walls, and even the captain who'd come to find out what the noise was ended up naming the joke. Later, at a roll call, it was Tecolote who covered for two of the others lying on the floor, sure of himself and kind with it, with a straight face. I like to think it was the same nerve the owl was made of. That's you: the laugh and the nerve, from the same place.

The cocktail I've made for you is that eggnog, made for one: joven mezcal, a whole egg, whole milk in place of the donkey's, and sugar, shaken until it's light and thick. Eggnog itself is a classic, on record since 1788, and the classic ends with nutmeg grated on top. This one doesn't, because there was none on their list: nothing goes in that wasn't on it. Crack the egg cleanly before you shake, keep half the shell, rinse it, and when the drink is poured, put a teaspoon of mezcal in it. On another night at Perote, the prisoners kept the guard at their door in a good mood with a sip of mezcal passed through the bars in an eggshell, because nothing bigger would fit. I kept the shell as a nod to that: even the man guarding the door got a sip.

Some day the joke won't come. That isn't the day it wins. On the morning you've got nothing, let it not come. Go in anyway, unfunny, and just be there. My guess is that on that morning someone else will find the joke for once, because you've been showing them how every day. I'd love you to be there to laugh at it.

anchors.fact: In a Wodehouse story first printed in 1924, Bertie Wooster tags along, as a friend, when a stern older man takes Bertie's friend round the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley to broaden the friend's mind. The older man leads and the two young men trail behind (W2, W3; C1).
anchors.meaning: The improving afternoon, being herded. The broadening was meant for the friend. Fiction, owned in one clause. (fear: being made to sit still)

anchors.fact: At lunch, every time Bertie started a joke, the older man stopped him with a stare. The one he got to the end, a borrowed one about Wembley, earned a waggled eyebrow, and he felt like rubbish (W1a, W1).
anchors.meaning: The hush, on the page. (hidden: "not now" lands as "be less of yourself")

anchors.fact: He says plainly that exhibitions have never been his thing: the crowd, the shuffling, and a stuffed fish and a jar of seeds that others find thrilling, but not him (W4).
anchors.meaning: Boredom, in his own voice. (fear: boredom)

anchors.fact: The older man had rushed them past a bar where a man was stirring tall glasses with ice in them, using a stick. That small sight was what Bertie wanted to see more of (W5).
anchors.meaning: One small, ordinary thing takes all the attention. (one true thing)

anchors.fact: He and his friend slip off to it. The barman is kind, seems to know what they want, and tells them the drinks are called Green Swizzles. As soon as he has the name, Bertie vows that any son of his will be registered as Green Swizzle Wooster (W6–W8; C2: paraphrase only).
anchors.meaning: A small pleasure taken with total seriousness, which is why it's funny.

anchors.fact: The Green Swizzle was a real West Indian drink. In 1924 it was one of the two drinks featured at the West Indies pavilion at Wembley (Oxford pdf 756, F3).
anchors.meaning: The part that sounds invented happened. (second thing)

anchors.fact: It was long believed to be fiction, until old newspapers showed it had been real and, for a time, popular at least in the Caribbean (Oxford pdf 945, F2). The page names no one who believed it.
anchors.meaning: Taken for a story, and it was real. Never "everyone" or "the experts". One sentence of fact; never on the guest.

anchors.fact: The recipes of the time differ, but they agree on gin or rum, a sweet base, bitters made by steeping wormwood in strong spirit, and ice, whisked with a stick rolled between the palms (Oxford pdf 945, 1963; *Imbibe!* pdf 124; F4, F5, F8). In Trinidad the sweet base was Carypton, a bottled mix of rum, lime, sugar and West Indian herbs, trademarked in 1907 and long discontinued (Oxford pdf 112; *Imbibe!* pdf 124).
anchors.meaning: Ours is rebuilt from the parts that Trinidad bottle listed. That's my build, never "Carypton's recipe" and never "the glass Bertie drank".

anchors.fact: For the wormwood bitters, which have to be made, Wondrich's own stand-in is a wormwood-forward absinthe (*Imbibe!* pdf 125). Absinthe is a spirit made with wormwood, aniseed and fennel. It's green from the leaves' chlorophyll, and a small amount works in cocktails much like bitters (Oxford pdf 48–50). Wondrich credits the tip of tangerine peel in the *bitters* to Eleanor Early's 1937 Caribbean travel book (pdf 125). Steeping the tangerine in the absinthe for two days is ours (Tomás, v2).
anchors.meaning: The one part made slowly, by hand, for one small thing. The tangerine is the bright note. Never "Early's way with absinthe", and never "sounds made up".
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: A little chaos; texture: Bright

anchors.fact: You stop swizzling when the outside of the glass is well frosted (Oxford SWIZZLE pdf 1963).
anchors.meaning: The glass tells you when to stop, not an audience. Frost is a method word only.

cocktail.closingLine: Spin the stick between your palms until the glass goes white. Then go back for whatever you were hurried past.
cocktail.glassware: tall Collins glass (about 350 ml), crushed ice, the swizzle stick left standing in it, no straw
method: **Two days ahead, make the tangerine absinthe.** Peel one tangerine thinly with a vegetable peeler, orange skin only, none of the white. Put the peel in a small clean jar with 100 ml green absinthe (the wormwood-forward kind) and close it. Leave it two days somewhere cool, and shake it once a day. Strain it and bottle it. A barspoon makes one drink, so the bottle makes about twenty.
Make crushed ice. Wrap a tray of ice cubes in a clean tea towel and bash it with a rolling pin until it's nearly snow.
Pour the rum, lime, syrup and one barspoon of the tangerine absinthe into the tall glass.
Fill the glass about four-fifths with crushed ice.

Stand the swizzle stick in the drink with its prongs at the bottom. Hold the handle between flat palms and rub your hands back and forth so the stick spins, moving it slowly up and down. Keep going until the outside of the glass turns white with frost, about 20 to 30 seconds.
Pack more crushed ice on top until it mounds over the rim. Dash the Angostura over the ice. Leave the stick in the glass.
cocktail.name: Off the Tour

recipe.note: Wondrich's advice for this drink: "a flavorful white one"
measure it: 30 ml makes it too sharp

recipe.item: simple syrup (1:1, white sugar and water)
green absinthe steeped with tangerine peel (method, step 1)
recipe.note: the green in the Green Swizzle. Use one barspoon, no more

recipe.item: Angostura bitters, dashed on top at the end
recipe.note: a dark-red band over the green

recipe.item: wooden swizzle stick, left standing in the glass
recipe.note: no stick? a bar spoon does the same job

cocktail.tagline: Nobody believes your stories. They all happened.

reading.epigraph: A Green Swizzle, Wembley, 1924. In a story, Bertie Wooster vowed to name a son after it.
whoYouAre: You're somewhere you're meant to sit still: a hotel breakfast with its little rules, a waiting room, the long middle of a speech. Ten minutes, and something small has caught you. The sachet that won't tear. The toaster that sends the bread round twice. You give it all your attention, because right then it's the only problem in the world. It all goes sideways, and nobody there forgets how. You look up, and that's when you find the room.

You never set out to be funny. The part you laugh off is the hush: the "not now", the hand on your arm. Being told to sit still has always sounded like being told to be less, and what you dread is managing it, and nothing happening at all. Hushing you would cost everyone else their best stories, the dull mornings they still tell, fondly, years later. And after you, nobody needs to pretend the rules made sense.
yours: In 1924, at Wembley, the West Indies pavilion of the British Empire Exhibition poured the Green Swizzle. P. G. Wodehouse put Bertie Wooster there that year, in a story, tagging along with a friend who was being taken round to have his mind broadened. At lunch, every joke Bertie started had been stopped by a stare, and the one he finished got a waggled eyebrow. Now it's a stuffed fish and a jar of seeds, and exhibitions, he admits, have never been his thing.

Then, rushed past a bar, he spots a man stirring long, icy glasses with a stick, and the urge to see more of him won't go away. He and his friend slip away to it, and the moment the barman tells him what they're called, Bertie vows that any son of his will be named Green Swizzle Wooster.
For years, the Green Swizzle itself was taken for fiction. It wasn't: old newspapers show it was real, and for a while quite popular in the Caribbean.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Green Swizzle, a Caribbean classic, rebuilt from the parts listed for an old Trinidad bottled base, discontinued decades ago. Mine are white rum, fresh lime and sugar. The green comes from a barspoon of green absinthe, a spirit made with wormwood, that I steep with tangerine peel for two days. The tangerine is a travel writer's tip for the old wormwood bitters, passed on by a drinks historian; I borrowed it for the absinthe, and I put it in for you: the bright thing that turns up in the middle of something grim. Then the stick does the stirring. You give it your whole attention for about half a minute, and the glass tells you when to stop. It comes out tall, pale and very cold, with four dashes of Angostura on top, and it gets gentler as you go.

I like to think you'd have seen the man with the stick before anyone else on the tour did, and stopped. Next time you're being steered past the one thing you'd actually like to see, look round for the other person who's had about enough. There usually is one. Go together. Give it all your attention, and if something wonderful comes of it, make a promise far too big for it. Somebody will be telling that afternoon for years, and it'll all be true.

anchors.fact: Café Brûlot's roots are a nineteenth-century French café drink, coffee and eau-de-vie simply mixed and set alight; in New Orleans it became a coffee service made at the table, in several intricate steps (Oxford pdf 381; F1, F3).
anchors.meaning: A simple café drink was turned into an event served at the table. That's what the Tease does to an ordinary evening.
anchors.speaksTo: Fear: "the moment the spell turns into routine"; gift: an ordinary thing made worth looking forward to

anchors.fact: In the classic recipe the coffee comes in at the end, and pouring it puts the flame out (Oxford pdf 382; Commander's via *Joy* pdf 262; Antoine's 1978 cookbook and Brennan's 1961, OCR highlights; F9–F12; one unsigned web account differs, C2).
anchors.meaning: The thing everyone came for arrives last, and nobody is fooled: they can see it coming.
anchors.speaksTo: "they give away a little, hold back the rest and enjoy every second of the effect"

anchors.fact: One classic recipe, the Oxford Companion's, has most of the ingredients steep for several hours before anything happens at the table (pdf 381; F7, C4).
anchors.meaning: The waiting starts long before anyone sits down. Tell it as "the recipe I follow", never as Antoine's.
anchors.speaksTo: "the best … is the wait" (persona; the phrase "best part" is *Curtain Call*'s, don't reuse it)

anchors.fact: Its invention has been ascribed to Jules Alciatore, son of the founder of Antoine's, which still runs on St Louis Street (Oxford pdf 381; F2, C3).
anchors.meaning: "It's said", no decade. Whoever brings it enjoying the faces is our reading, signposted ("I like to think…"). No page records anyone's enjoyment.
anchors.speaksTo: "relish the effect they have on you" (signposted only)

anchors.fact: Kirsch, a clear eau-de-vie distilled from cherries and their pits, with almond-like notes, goes into the classic (Oxford pdf 1135, 698; F14).
anchors.meaning: The surprise bottle in a coffee: the drink sounds worth having. Pits on the page carry the `nuts` veto.

anchors.fact: Galatoire's (opened 1905) and Commander's Palace make it too; to many it's part of eating in New Orleans (Oxford pdf 381, 332; F4, F5).
anchors.meaning: A renowned classic, not one house's oddity.

cocktail.closingLine: Run the brandy down the peel. Then give someone else the coffee, and let the timing be theirs.
cocktail.glassware: two demitasse cups (small coffee cups, about 90 ml) on saucers, warmed with hot water first
method: A few hours ahead (3 to 4 is plenty), put the lemon and orange peel strips and the broken half cinnamon stick in a small jar with the cognac and kirsch. Close it and leave it.
When you're nearly ready, make the coffee and keep it hot. Fill the two cups with hot water to warm them. Cut the orange spiral and push the 6 cloves into it.

Lift the peels and cinnamon out of the jar. Pour the spirits and the syrup into a small pan and warm them over a low heat until they just steam, under a minute. Never let it bubble, and never light it.
Empty the cups. Hold the clove spiral over the first cup on a fork and pour half the warm spirits slowly down it, so they run over the peel and the cloves. Do the same over the second cup.
Hand the coffee to someone else. They pour 50 ml into each cup, whenever they like. Stir once and drink it hot.
cocktail.name: I'll Tell You Later

recipe.note: steeped a few hours ahead with the peels and cinnamon
steeped with the cognac; two parts cognac to one of kirsch, as in Oxford's recipe

recipe.item: lemon peel and orange peel, no white pith
recipe.note: steeped in the spirits, then lifted out
steeped in the spirits, then lifted out

recipe.item: demerara syrup (equal weights demerara sugar and water)
recipe.note: warmed with the spirits

recipe.item: orange-peel spiral (half an orange, cut round in one long strip), studded with 6 cloves
recipe.note: the warm spirits run down it into the cups
