recipe.item: hot coffee with chicory (New Orleans style; or any dark-roast filter coffee), freshly made
recipe.note: added at the end, 50 ml a cup, by someone else

cocktail.tagline: You know how to make the waiting part of the pleasure.

reading.epigraph: A New Orleans coffee that keeps you waiting for the coffee.
whoYouAre: You've had the best news of your week since lunchtime, and you haven't said a word. It can wait until the plates are cleared. The present comes out last, after a decoy that gets a groan. Someone asks why you're smiling, you say "I'll tell you later", and they lean closer. The real pleasure is watching it reach their faces.

You choose the moment with care, and you light up when it comes. It isn't a no that you dread. It's a flat "just tell me" from someone who's stopped playing along, or the day your little delays become what everyone expects. And there's one seat in the game you never take: the one where you're the one waiting.
You give people something to look forward to. With you, an ordinary evening gets a reason to linger, and a tease is an invitation into the game.
yours: In nineteenth-century France, cafés served a plain little drink: coffee and a spirit, simply mixed. New Orleans took that café drink and turned it into Café Brûlot, a coffee prepared at the table over several careful steps. It's said Jules Alciatore first made it at Antoine's, the restaurant his father founded, which still serves on St Louis Street. Galatoire's and Commander's Palace make it too, and to many people it's part of eating in New Orleans.

One classic recipe soaks cinnamon and peels of lemon and orange for hours in cognac and kirsch, a clear cherry brandy. Then the warm brandy runs down a long spiral of orange peel studded with cloves. Only then, in the classic recipe, comes the coffee, the very thing everyone ordered, and pouring it in puts out the brandy's flame.

Nobody is fooled. Everyone there knows the coffee is coming. And I like to think the person carrying it out enjoys every face while choosing the moment. That's you, teasing, exactly. Coffee after dinner is about the most ordinary thing there is, and New Orleans gave it a build-up. You do that to an ordinary evening.

The cocktail I've made for you follows the classic recipe's order, in my own measures, for two little coffee cups, and it's never lit. Cognac and kirsch sit for a few hours with the peels and cinnamon. Then they're warmed gently with syrup made from demerara sugar, and run down a clove-studded orange spiral into the cups. It's warm, dark and spiced, with the cherry as the surprise. The coffee, made with chicory the New Orleans way, comes in at the end. And one more change, just for you: someone else pours the coffee, whenever they choose.

So, one evening soon, let someone else decide when. Let them keep their news until the plates are cleared, or hand you the present after the decoy. Sit in their seat for once and enjoy not knowing. You'll feel what you've been giving people all along, and you'll find the game is even better with two. I hope someone keeps you guessing.

anchors.fact: Brian Shebairo owned a hot-dog shop in New York and was turning the bubble-tea lounge next door into a bar; he had first planned a rock-and-roll bar (Proper pp. 269–270, F1–F3).
anchors.meaning: Someone with no stake in looking clever, in a scruffy everyday place.

anchors.fact: The phone booth door was Shebairo's idea; he called it "a little Get Smart" (Proper p. 270, F5). The page gives him the idea, not the building.
anchors.meaning: The joke was his, planned into the place, and played straight: a phone booth that is also a door.

anchors.fact: *Get Smart* was a 1960s American TV spoof of spy films (NBC, then CBS, 1965–70), starring Don Adams as Maxwell Smart, whose hero steps into a phone booth and dials a number (Nash 1976; *Cinefex*; FTS highlights, G1–G4).
anchors.meaning: Explains his joke plainly: a grown-up's spy-comedy gag built into a real wall.

anchors.fact: The bar opened in 2007 (Oxford pdf 521; Proper pp. 229, 242), and Oxford's edition (© 2022) still says it is reached through a phone booth at the back of the shop, with a photo (pdf 1854–1855, F7–F10).
anchors.meaning: It lasted: more than a decade later the joke was still the bar's door, working without him there.

anchors.fact: Simonson calls it "arguably the most famous bar entrance in the world" (his "arguably", Proper p. 270, F5).
anchors.meaning: The small joke left a mark far bigger than a prank.

anchors.fact: The Oxford photo: a narrow wooden booth with glass-panelled folding doors in a brick-walled shop, stools at a ledge, a wall phone inside (pdf 1855, F9).
anchors.meaning: What the door looks like, for the image brief: an everyday booth; no sign is visible in the one photo (that is all the page shows).

cocktail.closingLine: Label the bottle before it goes in the fridge. Then plant your next surprise somewhere it's still going once you've left the house.
cocktail.glassware: a plain everyday tumbler (about 300 ml), filled with ice
method: Make the rich syrup: warm 200 g sugar with 100 g water, stirring, until it's clear. Let it cool.

Make the bottle (six drinks): pour 270 ml apple brandy, 120 ml dry vermouth and 30 ml rich syrup into a clean 500 ml bottle. Close it and turn it over a few times. No water and no soda go in the bottle: vermouth in a watered-down cocktail changes within a few hours.
Label the bottle: the drink's name, "apple brandy, strong", and "70 ml over ice, top with soda". Keep it in the fridge. Use it within about a month; it's at its best while the bottle is still full.
To serve, fill a plain tumbler with ice and pour in 70 ml from the bottle.
Top with 110 ml cold soda water (130 ml if your apple brandy is stronger than 50%) and stir once, gently.
Squeeze a strip of lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: The Kind You'd Want

recipe.item: apple brandy, oak-aged (a Calvados, or an American straight apple brandy, not applejack, 40-50%)
recipe.note: from the bottle in the fridge
from the bottle; kept cold and undiluted, it lasts longer

recipe.item: rich syrup (2 parts sugar to 1 part water, by weight)
recipe.note: from the bottle
added in the glass, never in the bottle
squeezed over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: Your mischief makes grown-ups feel like they're allowed to play.

reading.epigraph: Poured from a bottle in the fridge, like anything else. It isn't anything else.
whoYouAre: Somebody's keys are in the fruit bowl, under the bananas, and you're helping them look, very seriously. This morning every mug in the cupboard was turned to face the wall. They call it trouble, and they keep letting you in anyway.

Nobody spots the rules. Every trick fits one person, and everything can be put right in seconds. The mugs go back. The keys turn up before anyone's late. For every trick people see, there are a few you decided against, because of who'd be on the end of it. What you're afraid of is the trick that lands wrong and becomes somebody's bad day. So you keep them small, and gone by teatime.
You make a house a place where being surprised is safe, and around you, grown-ups still get to play.
yours: In the 2000s, Brian Shebairo owned a rough-and-tumble hot-dog shop on St. Mark's Place in New York, and was turning the bubble-tea lounge next door into a bar. His first plan was a rock-and-roll bar. It became a cocktail bar instead, and the door to it was his idea: a phone booth, at the back of the hot-dog shop. "A little Get Smart," he called it, after the 1960s TV spy spoof whose hero steps into a phone booth and dials a number.

The bar opened in 2007. More than a decade later, that phone booth was still its door, and one writer calls it, with a careful "arguably", the most famous bar entrance in the world. It's the same bar as another of my stories, but that one belongs to someone else.

I like to think that's exactly the joke you'd make, and exactly how you'd make it: played completely straight. No wink, just a phone booth in a hot-dog shop, where a phone booth has every right to be. Nobody gets hurt. The worst that can happen is you open a door and find a bar. But there's one difference from yours. His wasn't put back by teatime. It stayed. And I like to think it went on catching somebody new on a quiet weeknight, years after he first thought of it, without him there to watch it land.

The cocktail I've made for you is built on the same joke. It's a highball: apple brandy, dry vermouth and a spoon of rich syrup, mixed in a bottle that waits, labelled, in the fridge. Whenever someone wants one, they pour a little over ice in a plain tumbler, top it up with cold soda water, then squeeze a lemon peel over it. It looks like any fizzy thing you'd find in a fridge. It tastes like a proper cocktail: dry and bright, apple first, with lemon over the top. Nothing in it is hidden, and the label says what it is. The only trick is that it's there, ready, long after whoever made it has gone out, as a nod to a phone booth that kept being a door.

Keep your rules. They're why people let you in. But make one that stays. Not a trick for this afternoon: a surprise built into something that lasts. A note in the pocket of a coat they won't wear until winter. A line written inside a book you lend. You won't be there when it lands, and that's the point. Months from now someone will find it, grin at nobody, and know exactly who it was.

anchors.fact: Croswell, a newspaper editor in Hudson, New York, was convicted of libel for publishing an article alleging that President Jefferson had paid a writer (James Callender) to attack Washington and Adams (MTSU, M1). Whether it was true: not ours to say (C4). No year in guest text (C2).
anchors.meaning: He printed it about the most powerful man in the country, and paid in court. The reading says "he printed that", never whether it was so.
anchors.speaksTo: story test: aimed up, price paid

anchors.fact: At his trial he was not allowed to prove the truth of what he'd said, or his intent in publishing it (MTSU, M2).
anchors.meaning: He wasn't allowed to show it was true, or why he'd said it. Note: intent was shut out too, so never "they only asked whether he should have said it".
anchors.speaksTo: fear: the gasp absorbed, the question never asked

anchors.fact: On appeal, Alexander Hamilton argued that a free press meant the right to publish the truth "with good motives, and for justifiable ends" (MTSU, M3). A judge, James Kent, agreed that truth should be a defence; the court split and the conviction stood (M4, M6).
anchors.meaning: Truth told for a reason should count.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: turn "how dare you" into "is it true?"

anchors.fact: By Hamilton's own rule, true words said with bad motives could still be punished (MTSU, Vile's gloss, M5).
anchors.meaning: The rule doesn't cover the nights it's only for the gasp, and this guest knows which nights those are.
anchors.speaksTo: hides: some nights it's only the gasp; position: keep the ones you'd stand behind

anchors.fact: In May 1806, after the conviction, his paper printed a mocking ledger of a losing candidate's election drinks, "Gain: Nothing", among them 25 glasses of cock-tail (*Imbibe!* pdf 169, F3).
anchors.meaning: A joke at the other side's voters, made in print, and partisan: the reading takes no side and can say gently it was for the gasp too.

anchors.fact: A reader wrote in to ask what a cock-tail was. Croswell's answer: spirits of any kind, sugar, water and bitters. Then he added that people said it suited a candidate of that party, because once you'd swallowed a glass you were ready to swallow anything else (*Imbibe!* pdf 169, F5–F6; Oxford pdf 493, F9). It's the first time we know of that the name and the recipe were printed together (Oxford).
anchors.meaning: The drink is defined by a jibe: the line he's remembered for is the cheek. Manners as swallowing things is Wren's reading, signposted.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing; story test: the line outlived the price

anchors.fact: Eleven days later a rival paper in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, printed a letter attacking him, with a swipe at him for "publishing grog stories" (*Imbibe!* pdf 169, F8).
anchors.meaning: The gasp is on record, in print, from the other side.

anchors.fact: Wondrich calls the answer one of the most famous and often repeated quotations in American drinking; with small changes, the definition described the cocktail for four generations (*Imbibe!* pdf 169, F7).
anchors.meaning: The jibe outlived the trial: people still quote it.

anchors.fact: Oxford's Cock-Tail: a raw sugar cube muddled with a little water and bitters, a spirit, cold water to taste, stirred, in a small Old-Fashioned glass (pdf 494, F10). The 1806 formula says "spirits of any kind"; our aged rum is ours, not his (C5).
anchors.meaning: Nothing hidden: four things, named up front, as he printed them.

cocktail.closingLine: Name the banana as you pour it. Then ask who else thinks so, while everyone's still at the table.
cocktail.glassware: small tumbler (about 200 ml), chilled in the freezer, no ice
method: At least two hours ahead, put the rum, banana liqueur and bitters in a small jar or plastic bottle (not filled to the brim), close it, and put it in the freezer. Put the tumbler in the freezer too.
Just before serving, fill a jug with water and ice and let it stand for a few minutes.
Pour the cold mix into the frozen tumbler. Measure in 30 ml of the ice-cold water from the jug, and none of the ice.
Stir a few turns with a spoon.
Hold the orange peel skin side down over the glass and squeeze it, so its oils fall on the drink. Drop it in.
cocktail.name: Quote Me

recipe.note: the sugar, given as banana, out in the open

cocktail.tagline: Rooms get more honest around you. Rarely politer.

reading.epigraph: The cocktail's earliest known definition in print comes with a dig at the other side.
whoYouAre: Dinner, eight of you, and everyone has spent the starter praising something nobody there actually likes. You put your fork down and say so, in the bluntest words available. There's a gasp. Somebody laughs and turns it into a cough. Then you watch for whoever will say it back.

Hardly anyone hears it right. It comes out like a verdict, but you mean it as a question. You enjoy the gasp, and you won't pretend you don't. And often you go too far on purpose: once you've said the outrageous version, the honest one everybody's been sitting on suddenly sounds mild, and someone dares. What wears you down is good manners doing their quiet work: the gasp smoothed over, someone offering round the potatoes, and the same people agreeing with you afterwards, by the coats, where it doesn't count.
You take the blame for the first line so the honest conversation can happen in the room. You turn "how dare you" into "hang on, is that true?" Not everyone thanks you for it. They should.
yours: In May 1806, in Hudson, a river town in New York, a newspaper editor called Harry Croswell printed a mocking ledger of a losing candidate's election drinks. Under "Gain", it said "Nothing". Among the losses were twenty-five glasses of "cock-tail". A reader wrote in, never having heard of it. Was it local? Was it new?

Croswell's answer is the earliest known definition of the cocktail in print: spirits of any kind, sugar, water, bitters. Then came the dig. It was said, he added, that the drink suited a candidate of that party, because anyone who'd "swallowed a glass of it" was "ready to swallow anything else". A rival paper printed a letter attacking him, with a swipe at his "publishing grog stories". His answer is still among the most quoted lines on American drinking.

By then Croswell had already been convicted of libel, for printing that the President had paid a writer to attack Washington and Adams. Whether that was true isn't mine to say, and at his trial the court wouldn't let him prove it, or explain why he'd printed it. Alexander Hamilton took his appeal and argued that a free press meant the right to publish the truth "with good motives, and for justifiable ends". The judges split, and the conviction stood. I like to think you'd have recognised Croswell at once: he put in print what was being said behind hands, and I'd bet he enjoyed the cock-tail line enormously. Hamilton's rule has a catch you know too: true words said with bad motives wouldn't have been covered. Some nights it's only for the gasp, and you can tell which ones. The others, the ones with a reason behind them, you'd stand behind anywhere.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from Croswell's four things, with a spirit of my choosing: aged rum from Jamaica, a little bitters, and a measure of water, as his definition has it, poured in ice-cold, all served without ice in a glass frozen beforehand. Last comes a bright pinch of orange oil, with its peel dropped in. My one change is the sugar: it arrives as a banana liqueur, a liqueur whose recipes only turn up about a century later. Many aged Jamaican rums already have a taste of stewed banana in them. I put it in plain sight as a nod to Croswell's line: the banana that's often already in the rum, said out loud. Expect something rich, round and smooth, and far better than it sounds when you say "banana" at a dinner party.

Keep saying it. A room needs someone who will. But when the gasp next gets smoothed over and the potatoes start going round, don't reach for a bigger line. Ask it as the question it always was, out loud, and then wait. Someone usually answers. Then you get the conversation you came for, there and then, while it still counts.

anchors.fact: Scots and Irish drinkers already washed a whisky down with beer or ale. American drinkers chased whisky with iced water and thought beer an outlandish substitute. (F3)
anchors.meaning: What's ordinary on one side of the sea is odd on the other. **Reading:** "In Scotland and Ireland it was already ordinary" (Q1). The oddness was American, not one saloon's (C3b). Never "whole countries" (A11) or "all along".
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: what feels like one person's oddity is already ordinary somewhere; drawnToward: Belonging

anchors.fact: About fifty years later the *New York Herald* printed a story about a man who ordered beer and whisky together in a New York saloon, and the consternation it caused the bartender and the regulars. One of the regulars says they've heard of strange drinks in their time. (F5; Oxford pdf 306, citing 5 Apr 1896)
anchors.meaning: One person orders, in front of the regulars, and they find it strange. It rests on Oxford alone (C1): no plot, no "comedy", no gloss on "A False Alarm". "Dismay" is fine (A5). No inner state ("what felt natural", A10), no gender for the regular (A6), no "queer", no "side by side".
anchors.speaksTo: the guest is the 1896 man: early, not odd; fear: Exclusion, being the only odd one; position seed (say "I do this")

anchors.fact: Habits changed, the pair became less outlandish, and by the 1930s it had a name that stuck. (F6, F8)
anchors.meaning: Early, not alone. "Within a few decades" is fine. Never "common enough to need a name" (A11). The 1930s date is said once (Q2 note).

anchors.fact: The first form of the name was "Boilermaker and His Helper", after a skilled metalworker and the extra muscle working beside him; by the 1940s it was just "Boilermaker". (F8)
anchors.meaning: A name taken from ordinary work. No namer (C4; the union says nobody knows, F15).
anchors.speaksTo: texture only; trap: "His Helper" is the Straight Man's shape; no namer

anchors.fact: In December 1933 a Yonkers columnist, William A. Spring, under the subhead "The Bartenders Guyed", wrote up about sixty of his town's bartenders by name, each with a specialty and, for most, a one-line joke or compliment. The column hedges "if the licenses come through". One line reads only: "Dave Ray—Boilermaker and His Helper." (F14, OCR; C2)
anchors.meaning: At the table, naming everyone, with the joke on all of them at once, and the plainest drink gets the one line with no joke ("I like to think" carries why). Spring is named before any "his" (A9). "Every bartender in town", never "a whole town" (A13). "December 1933", no day. Never "first". No word "Prohibition".
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing in a person: at the table, not the head of it; names what everyone sees, with the joke on all of them at once; soughtFor: Honesty; gravity: Social, Grounded; "fondly" signposted

anchors.fact: The revival brought it back as a menu item, with spirits and beers paired in creative ways, some still a shot of rye and a glass of lager. (F11)
anchors.meaning: The ordinary order is worth having now. Paraphrase Oxford; "renowned" is ours and isn't used; "good" is the bartender's word (A14).

anchors.fact: In 1948 Billy Rose explained the name to his readers as straight rye with a beer chaser. (F9)
anchors.meaning: Rye is the story's own whiskey, and it comes first, then the beer (the closing line, D8). Spec: 45 ml of straight rye, 50% if possible, never under 45%.
anchors.speaksTo: drink: straight rye, the name's own whiskey

anchors.fact: The *Flavor Matrix* lists beer as a surprise pairing for stone fruit, with apricot among its main subtypes (pdf 236). The *Codex* starts dried fruit at 1:4 by weight to the spirit (p. 99) and has you taste an infusion often, strain it and refrigerate it (pp. 94–95). Spec: 60 g of chopped dried apricots to 250 ml of rye, six to eight hours, strained.
anchors.meaning: Something from the cupboard, inside the plain order. **Reading:** "you find it when you taste it" (Q3), never "only". The effect on taste is Tomás's or signposted (A15). Apricot with rye is his craft call, and so is the 6–8 hour room-temperature steep (D2). No aroma claim for dried fruit. Not "an afternoon" (D3), "overnight" or "a day ahead".

anchors.fact: `gluten` (undistilled beer). `nuts` ruled out 2026-10-06 under Robin's evidence rule (no source says dried fruit is packed with nuts; *Codex* p. 37's "botanically related" is a flavour note).
anchors.meaning: Guest text says only "If you avoid nuts, check the pack for a nut warning": the guest's own pack label is the evidence that counts. Never "dried fruit is often packed with nuts" as fact.

cocktail.closingLine: A sip of the rye, then the beer. And when you tell your story, start with "I".
cocktail.glassware: small stemmed glass (about 90 ml) for the rye, room temperature; tall pilsner glass (about 400 ml), chilled, for the beer
method: Chop the dried apricots and put them in a clean jar. Pour the rye over them, close the jar and shake it.

Leave it at room temperature for six to eight hours, shaking now and then. From the fourth hour, taste a drop every hour or so. Strain it when the rye tastes clearly of apricot but still tastes of rye.
Strain it through a sieve lined with a paper coffee filter into a clean bottle. Keep it in the fridge, and take it out a little before you pour.
Chill the pilsner glass in the freezer for ten minutes. Tilt it, pour the beer down the side, then straighten the glass at the end so it finishes with a finger of foam.
Pour 45 ml of the apricot rye into the small glass. Set the two down next to each other.
Sip the rye, then the beer. Nothing goes in either glass.
cocktail.name: Is It Just Me

recipe.note: straight rye whiskey, 50% if you can find it, nothing under 45%
a pale, crisp, bitter lager; any brewery
the whiskey the name meant in 1948: "straight rye with a beer chaser"
straight from the kitchen cupboard; strained out before serving. If you avoid nuts, check the pack for a nut warning.

cocktail.tagline: Your most embarrassing moments make people feel better about theirs.

reading.epigraph: A whiskey with a beer. In 1896, a newspaper thought that was worth a story.
whoYouAre: You're the one who says it. Not the clever thing, the true one: that everybody waves back at someone who was waving at the person behind them, that everybody answers "you too" when the waiter says "enjoy your meal". There's half a second of quiet, then the whole table laughs, and somebody says, "I thought that was just me." That's the sound you're after. An evening where everyone stays polite and nobody admits to anything is your idea of a very long night.

You keep one part quiet. Every one of those starts with you. You're the one who waved back. You say "everybody does this" because it's kinder, and safer, than "I do". So you're always in the joke, and hardly ever what it's about. Somewhere under the laughing is a small worry that one day you'll say it and the table will go quiet, and it really will be only you. It hardly ever is. And people go home feeling a little less strange than when they came. You did that, with one true sentence.
yours: A whiskey with a beer beside it looks too simple to have a history. In America, though, it came late. Scots and Irish drinkers already followed their whisky with a beer, but Americans used iced water, and thought beer an odd thing to chase it with. Then a newspaper, the *New York Herald*, ran a story in 1896 about a man who walked into a saloon and ordered both, and about the dismay of the bartender and the regulars. One of the regulars said they'd heard of strange drinks in their time.

He was early, not odd. Habits changed, and by the 1930s the order had a name that stuck: "Boilermaker and His Helper", after a skilled metalworker and the extra muscle who worked beside him. In December 1933, a Yonkers columnist named William A. Spring, whose town's bars were still waiting for their licences, wrote up about sixty local bartenders by name, each with a specialty and, for most, a one-line joke or a compliment. One line reads, in full: "Dave Ray—Boilermaker and His Helper." There's no joke on it at all, and I like to think Spring knew the plainest drink in town didn't need one.

I like to think of that man in 1896 as someone you'd get on with. He ordered it at the bar, in front of the regulars, and they found it strange. It wasn't only his. That's what you do at a table. You say the thing everybody does, and it stops being one person's oddity and becomes everyone's. Spring did it to every bartender in town in one column, with the joke on all of them at once.

The cocktail I've made for you is that order, done properly: a straight rye, which is what the name meant in 1948, and a very cold German-style pilsner, a pairing that's back on bar menus now. Two glasses, nothing in between, as plain as Dave Ray's line. My one change comes from the kitchen cupboard: a handful of dried apricots, chopped and left in the rye for several hours, then strained out. Beer is one of stone fruit's surprising partners, and I like to think the cold, bitter beer brings the apricot forward. The apricot is inside the rye, and you only find it by tasting. That's how your best lines work: they sound like everybody's, and underneath they're your own.

So swap one word. When you catch yourself saying "everybody does this", say "I do this" instead. The laugh still comes, I promise, and this time you're inside it, not telling it. People enjoy you for the joke. They feel close to you for the confession. And you'll find what that order in 1896 turned out to show: it was never just one person's.

anchors.fact: The Rickey (whiskey, half a lime, soda, ice, no sugar) caught on at Shoomaker's, a Washington, DC, bar known as "Shoo's", in the late 1880s, and from there spread through the city. It carried the name of a regular, the lobbyist Joe Rickey (Oxford RICKEY pdf 1661, 1663; *Imbibe!* pdf 118).
anchors.meaning: The loud name on the drink.

anchors.fact: Oxford names two people as the drink's popularizers, side by side: Rickey and the bar's head bartender, George Williamson (1849–1915), who worked there for much of the bar's life and had a long association with the drink (Oxford pdf 1661, 1663, SHOOMAKER'S pdf 1789). Wondrich has Rickey getting Williamson to start making them for him (*Imbibe!* pdf 117).
anchors.meaning: The steady one behind the bar is in the record beside the famous one.
anchors.speaksTo: Confidence; drivers: provide structure; Build connection

anchors.fact: In 1893 Rickey told the *New York Herald* he "was not the author" of the drink, only the man who brought it east, and gave an account of its origin that put it down to a friend in St. Louis. At least three of his accounts were published while he lived (Oxford pdf 1662–1663).
anchors.meaning: The famous name on the drink was himself the first to say the drink wasn't his invention.

anchors.fact: The tellings differ on the lime. In Rickey's own account, as Oxford relays it, he had used lemon, and the lime came in at Shoo's through one of the bartenders, "more than likely" Williamson. In a 1930 history by George Rothwell Brown, a stranger gave Williamson limes, and Williamson made one for Rickey, who is said to have approved (Oxford pdf 1663). Wondrich has lime from the start (*Imbibe!* pdf 118).
anchors.meaning: Told only as "the story goes": only Rickey's own telling puts the switch to lime on a bartender; in Brown's, a stranger hands Williamson the limes.

anchors.fact: In 1895 Rickey wrote out his recipe by hand for a Syracuse newspaper: a large glass, ice, whiskey or gin, lime juice, soda water (Oxford pdf 1662; *Imbibe!* pdf 118).
anchors.meaning: Whatever its origin, by then the lime was in the recipe the famous name wrote down himself.

anchors.fact: Shoomaker's sold whiskey under its own name, a rye that was often the base of the whiskey Rickey (Oxford pdf 1789). Rickey's own whiskey was reportedly a bourbon, Belle of Nelson, and the water he preferred, reportedly, was Apollinaris, a sparkling mineral water (Oxford pdf 1663).
anchors.meaning: The bar's whiskey, and the water the colonel was said to favour: one choice from each side.

anchors.fact: Whether or not Rickey drank it, his friends did, and they tied it to him; the name itself is put down to two friends who came back asking for "a Joe Rickey" (Oxford pdf 1663).
anchors.meaning: The friends kept ordering it by his name.

cocktail.closingLine: Lime first, no sugar, not a word. Next time, let them catch you laughing.
cocktail.glassware: large plain tumbler (about 350 ml), three ice cubes
method: Squeeze half a lime into a large tumbler, then drop the squeezed half in after the juice.
Add three ice cubes, then the rye.
Top up with the cold mineral water, poured gently so it keeps its bubbles. Stir once.
No sugar, and nothing on top.
cocktail.name: Don't Look at Me

recipe.note: ideally about 50%; 43% at the least
half a normal-sized lime, squeezed; the squeezed half goes in too
recommended, plain (unflavoured), cold; or any plain sparkling mineral water with a noticeable mineral taste
ordinary cubes, not crushed

cocktail.tagline: Your straight face brings out everyone else's funniest side.

reading.epigraph: Named after a regular, mixed by the bartender. The regular denied being its author.
whoYouAre: Everyone around you thinks the funny one is your friend: the one who waves both arms through every story, gets the order wrong on purpose and starts the singing. You're sitting beside them, saying very little. You let them run, then one quiet word, or just a look, and the whole table goes. They get the laugh. It comes off you. Most of them take you for the serious one, and you go along with it, since that's part of the act.

How much you're enjoying it is the bit you hide best. You'd never say it, but you need them to be ridiculous. Put you in a room where everyone behaves and you're bored within the hour. People think you put up with the loudest person at the table. You picked them. Your fear is being taken at face value, as the grown-up who doesn't get the joke. You get it before anyone. And that's a gift to everyone near you: next to you, they're at their funniest, because someone steady is there to play it against.
yours: By the end of 1889, at a Washington bar everyone called Shoo's, a new drink had caught on: whiskey, half a lime, soda water and ice, and no sugar at all. It carried the name of a regular, a lobbyist known as Colonel Joe Rickey, who, it's said, showed bartenders how to make it wherever he went. Mixing it was the head bartender, George Williamson, who worked there for years and stayed with the drink a long time.

Then the comedy starts. In 1893 Rickey told a New York paper that he wasn't the drink's author at all, and at least three of his own accounts of how it began were printed in his lifetime. A later writer named Williamson as the real inventor. Even the lime has its stories: in Rickey's own, the switch to lime came from one of the bartenders; in another, a stranger handed Williamson the limes. Whether or not Rickey drank it himself, his friends did, and ordered it by his name. And in 1895, when he wrote his recipe out by hand for a newspaper, the lime was in it.

George Williamson, I like to think, loved it, and heard each new version of how the drink started, said nothing, and poured it again. The colonel had the name and the stories. The bartender had the drink. It doesn't work without both of them, and the steady one knows that better than anyone. So do you. You don't want the name on it. You want the act to work, and the act works because of you.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Rickey, a renowned classic, made with whiskey, the way it caught on at Shoo's: long, very cold and bone dry. Each partner puts something in. From the bar, a straight rye, because Shoo's sold its own and it often went into this drink. From the colonel, his water: he reportedly preferred Apollinaris, a sparkling mineral water, and I like to think it makes the lime taste a little brighter. The half lime belongs to both of them, whoever started it. The water is there as a nod to him, and the rye to the bar where Williamson poured, because I couldn't make it with only one of them.

You give everyone their best moment, and the one person nobody's watching is you. Once in a while, let it show. Let the loudest person at the table see you laugh. They've been playing to you from the start, and your laugh is the one they wanted most. The act survives it. They'll know you were having fun all along, and you get to have it with them, out in the open.

anchors.fact: After the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, several clergymen called the destruction divine retribution for the city's sins (Minnick 2024, F4).
anchors.meaning: The thing people were asked to swallow: that those who had just lost their city had deserved it.
anchors.speaksTo: the lie everyone pretends to believe; limb 1 (on the city's side, never against faith)

anchors.fact: The Hotaling whiskey warehouse survived, and people saved it: its own staff, with the fire department and the Navy (Minnick 2024, F5); its employees moved thousands of barrels to an empty lot (Wikipedia citing SF Heritage, F6).
anchors.meaning: Not providence: people did it.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's condition 4; the whiskey is the punchline, never a miracle

anchors.fact: Charles K. Field, a journalist and poet, is credited with four lines (one version, V1): "If, as they say, God spanked the town / For being over frisky, / Why did He burn the churches down / And save Hotaling's whiskey?" (Minnick 2024; attributed to him in 1962 too, F8–F10).
anchors.meaning: The contradiction turned into a question; the joke does the arguing.
anchors.speaksTo: wit that tells the truth; what they give: the line that lets everyone breathe out

anchors.fact: The verse was still being retold more than a hundred years after the fire (Minnick 2024; also a 1962 *ABA Journal* essay, as Wikipedia quotes it; F11). Its own year is on no page (L6).
anchors.meaning: People kept the line. Never "the whole city", never "at once", never "in 1906" for the poem.

anchors.fact: Two decades after the fire, from 1927 to 1940, Field hosted *Cheerio* on NBC: poetry and inspirational talks (OAC Stanford M1533; Wikipedia, F12–F13).
anchors.meaning: The hope under the jibe, on record, in the same life.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: a disappointed idealist who never stopped hoping; driver: seek paradise

anchors.fact: He went on air as "Cheerio", a made-up name; no press photographs were allowed, and his fee went to charity (OAC, F14; Wikipedia, F15). Passive on the page: who decided isn't recorded.
anchors.meaning: The hope went out nameless and faceless; the hope itself was broadcast, never hidden. His choosing it is "I like to think".
anchors.speaksTo: hides belief; position: the other way round, once

cocktail.closingLine: Take the peel away once its oil is on. Then, for once, say the hope first and the joke second.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail glass (about 180 ml), chilled, no ice
method: The night before, make the pear syrup. Stir the chopped pear and the sugar together in a jar, close it and leave it in the fridge overnight. In the morning, press it through a sieve and keep only the syrup. Keep it in a closed jar in the fridge and use it within a week. If it comes out thin, use 10 ml in the drink.
Put the cocktail glass in the freezer.
Pour the bourbon, the dry vermouth, the pear syrup and the bitters into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir with a long spoon for about 30 seconds, until the outside is very cold.
Strain into the cold glass.
Hold the strip of lemon peel over the drink, shiny side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the surface. Then take it away.
cocktail.name: Against My Better Judgement

recipe.note: any straight bourbon, about 45%; no particular bottle
French-style dry (white, not sweet)

cocktail.tagline: You make fun of the world because you haven't given up on it.

reading.epigraph: Bourbon, stirred dry. A four-line poem about San Francisco's 1906 fire ends on whiskey.
whoYouAre: The letter says the changes are "for your convenience". You have a line about it before anyone's finished reading it, and the table groans, then nods, because it's true. People assume you expect the worst of everything.

Here's what they miss. You only notice the gap because you still know how it should be. Under every joke is a picture of something better, and you've never quite given it up. You keep that part quiet. A joke is hard to laugh at; a hope is easy. What wears you out is the pretending: a dinner where everyone agrees to call it fine, and it goes on and on. Further down sits a fear you rarely say: that one day it won't be funny any more.
When something's absurd, you make it possible to laugh at it without giving up on it. After your line, everyone breathes out.
yours: After the earthquake and fire of 1906 in San Francisco, several clergymen said the destruction was divine retribution for the city's sins. A city that had just lost so much was told it had deserved it. A whiskey warehouse, A. P. Hotaling's, came through the disaster. People had saved it: its own workers among them, with the fire department and the Navy.

A journalist and poet called Charles K. Field is credited with four lines about it:
*If, as they say, God spanked the town*
*For being over frisky,*
*Why did He burn the churches down*
*And save Hotaling's whiskey?*
I love that it never argues. It asks one question and lets the whiskey answer. It isn't laughing at anyone's faith. It's laughing at the idea that a city in that state had it coming. People were still quoting it a hundred and more years after the fire.

Then his story turns. Two decades after the fire, from 1927 to 1940, Field was on NBC radio with a programme of poetry and inspirational talks, under a made-up name: Cheerio. No press photographs were allowed, and his fee went to charity. The joke is remembered as his. The hope went out under another name. I like to think he wanted it that way.

I think you'd understand him. The jibe and the hope have one root: caring how it turns out. Making fun of the claim stood up for the city. The poetry was the same care, without the joke. Usually only one of the two gets seen.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from a classic that was already on record in the 1800s: a Manhattan made with dry vermouth. Mine is stirred with ice till the mixing glass frosts, then poured, with no ice, into a chilled stemmed glass. Two-thirds of what I pour in is bourbon, because the whiskey is the punchline. Dry vermouth and Angostura, just two dashes, keep it lean. Its lemon is just the oil from the peel: the peel itself comes out. Stirred into all that dryness are one and a half teaspoons of syrup made from a ripe pear, left overnight in sugar. It's in every sip, and nothing on the glass gives it away: a nod to the hope Field sent out under another name, with no face on it. It's a sharp, clean drink with something soft running all through it.

Keep the jokes. Plenty of people get through the week because of them. But once, say the hope out loud, as yourself, before a joke can get there first. Tell someone how you think things could be. It might get laughed at. I'd bet it gets listened to, and I'd love you to find out.

anchors.fact: One of the stories people told about his memory: a guest sailed to England, stayed ten years, and walked back into the bar. Willard greeted him by name, recalled his old room number and remarked "how quickly ten years roll away" (Oxford, WILLARD, ORSAMUS pdf 2193, which frames it as one of the common stories of his memory).
anchors.meaning: Someone had kept him in mind the whole time he was gone. That's the feeling of being expected.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: the feeling of being expected

anchors.fact: At the City Hotel the bar was also the front desk: guests checked in at the bar (Oxford pdf 2192; *Imbibe!* pdf 20). Among the stories told of him: he almost never left the hotel (Oxford pdf 2193, "stories of his eccentricities").
anchors.meaning: He was always the first thing a guest met, and always already there.
anchors.speaksTo: the care lives in the getting ready; staying put, having it ready

anchors.fact: His own house back in Massachusetts had numbers on every room door (Oxford pdf 2193–94, "number plates on every room door"; *Imbibe!* pdf 22, "room numbers on every door").
anchors.meaning: I like to think he was still getting rooms ready for guests (our reading, signposted: the page gives no reason). The same kind of number he'd remembered for a guest.
anchors.speaksTo: the empty table; a place ready for people who might not come

anchors.fact: Willard left no book of recipes and no account of his life, and even the basic facts took a historian "a great deal of digging" (*Imbibe!* pdf 22).
anchors.meaning: He kept everyone in mind, and almost nobody wrote him down. That's attention running one way (our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: fear: attention that only runs one way; few think to know them back

anchors.fact: A British army captain who drank at the City Hotel printed a short list of drink recipes in his travel book, *Transatlantic Sketches* (1833). The Apple-toddy is the one he credits to Willard by name, "the bar-keeper of the City Hotel, who never forgets the face of a customer" (J. E. Alexander, 1833, vol. 2, p. 300, read on the page).
anchors.meaning: A guest wrote him down, and that's how his toddy reached us (never "the only reason"). The care came back (our reading, signposted; the captain's motive isn't on record).
anchors.speaksTo: the care came back; gives, and rarely asks back

anchors.fact: Willard's Apple-toddy, in his reported words: the fairest apples rolled in brown paper wetted with water, buried in live embers until thoroughly roasted and quite soft; then a fourth part each of apples, brandy and water, a lump of ice, "rich" with a fourth part of sugar (Alexander 1833, vol. 2, p. 300).
anchors.meaning: Everything is done before anyone arrives. When a guest walks in, there's only the stir and the ice.
anchors.speaksTo: the love happens before anyone arrives

anchors.fact: The captain's page says only "brandy". "Plain grape brandy" is Wondrich's reading of Willard's preference (*Imbibe!* pdf 139). "VSOP cognac" is Wondrich's modern advice, not Willard's.
anchors.meaning: The spirit Willard would have poured, as far as the record reaches.

anchors.fact: Loved in America "from the beginning of the Republic… until the turn of the last century", and early on "something of a signifier of Americanness" (*Imbibe!* pdf 138). The Apple Toddy was, with the Cock-Tail and the Mint Julep, one of the canonic drinks that made the American bar famous abroad (Oxford, COCK-TAIL pdf 494). It was enjoyed in the eastern US for over two hundred years (Oxford, TODDY pdf 2035). After Repeal, "Apple Toddy was seen no more" (*Imbibe!* pdf 139).
anchors.meaning: A renowned classic that people stopped making. Worth bringing back for someone.
anchors.speaksTo: let the drink sound worth having

anchors.fact: Wondrich thinks Willard "probably made do" with four or five kinds of glass: small and large tumblers, small and large wineglasses, perhaps cordial glasses, and something for hot drinks (*Imbibe!* pdf 55).
anchors.meaning: A small wineglass is a kind of glass his bar would probably have had. That's Wondrich's estimate, so no "his glass".

anchors.fact: "The apples go in first, then you call the one you're hoping will come": the roasting as the invitation.
anchors.meaning: The guest's ask, never Willard's. The record has him being lured back, never asking.
anchors.speaksTo: position: ask; ends on what they gain

cocktail.closingLine: Roast the apples. While they cool, call the one you'd most like to see.
cocktail.glassware: a small wineglass (about 250 ml), one plain lump of ice
method: An hour or more before anyone comes, peel and core the apples, half an apple for each drink. Wet a sheet of brown paper (a brown paper bag soaked under the tap works), wrap each apple in it, and roast at 180°C (350°F) for 30 to 45 minutes, until the apples are completely soft. Willard buried his in the embers of a fire. Let them cool.
Put half a roasted apple and the sugar in the glass, and mash them together with a spoon.
Add the brandy and the cold water, and stir until the sugar has gone and the apple is loose in the drink. Do this before anyone arrives, in the glass or in a jug for several. It will wait.
When they come, give it a stir, add one lump of ice, stir a few more turns, and serve with the spoon in the glass.
cocktail.name: Hoping You'd Come

recipe.item: roasted apple (roughly half a medium apple, peeled and cored)
recipe.note: wrapped in wet brown paper and roasted until soft, as Willard's recipe has it. Then left to cool.

recipe.item: brandy (grape brandy: a VSOP cognac, or any aged grape brandy of about 40%)
recipe.note: the captain's page says only "brandy"; Wondrich reads it as the grape brandy he preferred
Willard used as much sugar as brandy; I cut it to a teaspoon and a half, or it would be more than four times too sweet
ordinary ice, one piece

cocktail.tagline: You make room for people before you ask them to come.

reading.epigraph: A captain wrote this toddy down from a barman who, people said, never forgot a face.
whoYouAre: Someone's coming over. Long before they get there, you've been at it: the chair moved nearer the heater for the one who always feels the cold, the music down to where people can talk, the light just so. By the time they walk in, it looks as if it all happened by itself. That's the idea. Nobody should feel they put you to any trouble. They should just feel expected.

What you'd never tell them is: I was hoping you'd come. All that getting ready is how you hope without asking. A room made ready can't be turned down, and a plain question can. The thought you don't let yourself stay with is the ready room with nobody in it. People leave your evenings with the feeling that someone had them in mind before they arrived, even when they couldn't say why.
yours: In New York, back when hotel guests checked in at the bar, the City Hotel's desk clerk and its bartender were the same man, Orsamus Willard. People told a story about him. A guest sailed to England, stayed ten years, and walked back into the bar. Willard greeted him by name, and remembered his old room number.

They said he almost never left the hotel, and that he'd do anything he could to make a guest comfortable. He left no book and no account of his own life, and even the plain facts of it are hard to find. When he went home to Massachusetts, his house had a number on every room door. I like to think he was still getting rooms ready, for guests who might or might not come.
That's where I see you in him. Not the famous memory. The rooms made ready anyway.

One of his guests did write his toddy down. A British army captain who drank at his bar printed a few recipes in his travel book, and credited one of them to Willard by name: the Apple Toddy, one of the renowned drinks that made the American bar famous abroad. After Prohibition, it all but disappeared. The cocktail I've made for you is made after Willard's: the best apples rolled in wet paper and roasted until soft, then equal measures of apple, brandy and water, as he had them, and one lump of ice. His called for as much sugar as brandy, far too sweet by today's taste, so I kept it to a teaspoon and a half. For the brandy, I took the grape brandy the historian David Wondrich believes Willard preferred. Nearly all of it happens before anyone arrives: the apples roast, cool and wait. I kept it that way as a nod to you, because that's where your care always starts.

So next time you're getting a room ready, add the one thing you always leave out. Ask. Not "come by sometime": the plain sentence, to the person you're hoping will come. Getting ready is how you hope. Asking is how they find out they were hoped for. And I wish you a full house.

anchors.fact: Fitzgerald modelled Dick and Nicole Diver in *Tender Is the Night* partly on Gerald and Sara Murphy, as well as on Scott and Zelda. (F12)
anchors.meaning: The version of him that travelled is a character in someone else's book. We grant it first.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: loved as an idea rather than known · story: name rarely on the cover

anchors.fact: At the Murphys' evenings, "just the juice of a few flowers" was what Gerald called his cocktails. (F1)
anchors.meaning: A line people repeat as charm: the idea of the man.

anchors.fact: A card titled "Juice of A Few Flowers" is in the Gerald and Sara Murphy Papers at Yale's Beinecke Library. The published caption calls it Gerald Murphy's recipe, and the article says he copied his recipes out by hand. It gives 1 oz orange, 1 oz grapefruit, ½ oz lime, ½ oz lemon and 1 oz gin, shaken, poured into a glass whose rim is wet with lemon and dipped in coarse sugar. It is undated. (F3)
anchors.meaning: Behind the line people quote there's a real recipe, written down to the half-ounce: the maker behind the idea.

anchors.fact: He exhibited at the Salon des Indépendants in Paris from 1923 and painted for only a few years. Seven of his fourteen paintings survive. In *Cocktail* (1927; Whitney Museum, 95.188) the cigar-box lid alone took him four months. (F7, F8, F10, F14)
anchors.meaning: He made things, not only inspired them, and the work survives under his own name. Say "a few years" and give no reason.
anchors.speaksTo: story: creates as much as they inspire; name rarely on the cover (answered)

anchors.fact: In a 1939 letter to Alexander Woollcott he listed a cocktail he called a Bailey, "invented by me as were a great many other good things": gin (Booth's House of Lords), grapefruit, fresh lime, **fresh mint** and a great deal of ice. There are no measures and no method. (F2)
anchors.meaning: The mint comes from a cocktail he said in writing he'd invented. "Invented by me" is said of the Bailey only. The glass is "two of his recipes", joined by the bartender, never "his recipe". The Bailey's page gives no method, so the mint syrup is ours, and so is keeping the rim's sugar on the outside (F13).
anchors.speaksTo: Creator: authenticity · fear: loved as an idea

cocktail.closingLine: Pour both glasses. Hand one over with something you've made, and put your name on it.
cocktail.glassware: two nick-and-nora glasses (small, stemmed), chilled, each rim dipped in coarse sugar on the outside
method: Make the mint syrup: blend the sugar, water and mint leaves until no grains are left, then pour it through a fine sieve and chill it.
Put two small stemmed glasses in the freezer.
Cut a lemon in half. Wet the outside edge of each glass with the cut side, then dip that edge into a saucer of coarse sugar. Keep the sugar on the outside, so none falls into the drink.
Squeeze the orange, grapefruit, lime and lemon fresh, and measure them into a shaker with the gin and the mint syrup.
Fill the shaker right to the top with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds.
Pour it through a fine strainer, half into each glass.
cocktail.name: In Your Own Hand

preparations.text: 250 g white sugar, 250 ml water and a big handful of fresh mint leaves (about 20 g, stalks off). Blend until the sugar has dissolved, then pour through a fine sieve.
preparations.title: Mint syrup (makes about 400 ml, keeps a few days in the fridge)

plus the cut lemon for the rims
