cocktail.tagline: You see something worth finishing in the things people barely dare to show.

reading.epigraph: 'Juice of A Few Flowers' sounds like a joke. The handwritten card says otherwise.
whoYouAre: Friends show you things first: the song before it has words, the first chapter, the dish they've never cooked for anyone else. Something in the way you pay attention makes them want to finish it, and often they do. People are braver with their own work when you're around. Sometimes you even turn up in it: a line in the song, a character who talks the way you talk.

You make things too, and there's usually something of yours, half done, that nobody has seen. It's lovely to be someone's reason, and it feels safer than being judged on your own work. But the you in their songs is their idea of you, and an idea is easy to love from a distance. People have made beautiful things out of you. Very few have asked what you're making.
yours: In the 1920s, an American couple, Gerald and Sara Murphy, had a favourite little beach near Antibes, and it became a gathering place for their friends: Picasso, Hemingway, the Fitzgeralds. When F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote *Tender Is the Night*, he drew its main couple partly from the Murphys. And Gerald had a line about his cocktails: they were "just the juice of a few flowers". It sounds like a charming man's joke. Maybe that's all it was.

But among the Murphys' papers at Yale there's a card in Gerald's handwriting, headed "Juice of A Few Flowers". An ounce of orange, an ounce of grapefruit, half an ounce each of lime and lemon, an ounce of gin, shaken, in a glass with its rim wet with lemon and dipped in coarse sugar. He was a painter in his own right, too. He showed in Paris from 1923, and seven of his fourteen paintings survive. In one of them, *Cocktail*, the lid of a cigar box alone took him four months.

The charming version is the one that travelled: the man in the novel, the lovely line. The exact part, the half-ounces and the four months, was his, and you have to go looking for it. I like to think that card is what he'd most have liked someone to ask him about. I suspect you have a card like that too.

The cocktail I've made for you keeps every one of his measures, and his sugar on the rim. But I keep that sugar on the outside of the glass, where it sweetens your lips and not the drink, so it needed a little more, inside. I made that a mint syrup, and the mint comes from a cocktail he called the Bailey. In a letter, he wrote that he'd invented it, "as were a great many other good things". So this drink comes from two of his recipes, and joining them is my idea: I put the mint in as a nod to that sentence, where he simply says he made it. It's light, bright and properly sharp, four fresh juices and a little gin, and it fills two small glasses.

So when someone shows you what they're working on, show them something of yours back. Not the polished version, and not so they'll praise it: the unfinished one, in your own hand. Let one person see the maker, not the reason. That's how you get known up close. And since hardly anyone asks, I will: what are you making?

anchors.fact: The son of the postmaster of Skunk Hollow, New York, he made millions on Broadway, starting with *Within the Law* in 1912: "a twenty-five-year career encompassing 150 plays" (Oxford, GAIGE, CROSBY, pdf 861).
anchors.meaning: His trade was nights that end. Every play has a closing night (our reading, Wren's reframe, signposted).
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: it's never the bill, it's the lights coming up

anchors.fact: His true passions, fine vintages and cooking, "lay outside the theater" (pdf 861).
anchors.meaning: His true passions weren't the show. They were the table.

anchors.fact: After the 1929 crash he looked to those passions "for livelihood": a monthly Cellar and Pantry column in *Country Life* (pdf 861). He kept producing into the mid-1930s (*Othello* and *Macbeth*, 1935: Shaw 2019, relaying the *NYT* obituary).
anchors.meaning: When the big party stopped, what he loved all along carried him. It changed the party's shape, not his whole life.

anchors.fact: In 1937 NBC broadcast his daily radio programme, *Kitchen Cavalcade* (pdf 861, citing *Radio Daily*, 16 Sep 1937).
anchors.meaning: He shared the pleasure every day with strangers he'd never meet. The party went out on the air.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: permission to enjoy things without apologising

anchors.fact: His cocktail guide (1941: M. Barrows imprint in the *J. Am. Dietetic Assoc.* review, Aug 1942; "Copyright 1941" on the 1946 fifth printing) had celebrity contributions and was one of the vectors through which the Bloody Mary spread (pdf 861). Gaston Lauryssen, host at the St. Regis, gave it the Red Snapper: 2 oz tomato juice to 2 oz vodka, with Worcestershire and salt among its seasonings (the OCR cuts off after them) (guide p. 57, OCR of the 1946 fifth printing, F17). Joy says it was served straight up as a cocktail (pdf 249). Oxford: the Red Snapper is "the more genteel name" for the earliest Bloody Mary at the St. Regis (pdf 1624, F18).
anchors.meaning: Equal parts, short, no ice to keep it going: a drink that has an end (Tomás's physics; our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof: an ending chosen on a good note

anchors.fact: His home was Watch Hill Farm, Peekskill (UP obituary, *Kingston Daily Freeman*, 8 Mar 1949). His private press was in the barn, "overlooking the loveliest of flower gardens", and it printed dinner menus among its dozen books, one of them for the Wine & Food Society of New York's tasting at the Waldorf-Astoria on 29 April 1941 (*Print* 2:2, Summer 1941).
anchors.meaning: Even his press printed invitations to the table.

anchors.fact: *Dining with My Friends* (Crown, 1949) came out after his death in March 1949. *Saturday Review* calls it "posthumously published". Its contents run as dinners, his first, then his friends' (OCR of the contents page; the text is unread).
anchors.meaning: The company outlasted the host (our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: fear answered: the people don't vanish

anchors.fact: *Curtain Call*. The theatre was his trade (F1), and the cheer at a show's end belongs to the guest. The name makes no claim about his count or his curtains.
anchors.meaning: An ending people applaud.
anchors.speaksTo: the turn: the ending loved, not feared

anchors.fact: The glass is served up with no ice (spec; the guide's drink was served straight up, Joy pdf 249).
anchors.meaning: Nothing keeps it going, so it ends (Tomás's physics).

cocktail.closingLine: There's no ice in it, so it ends. Choose the night's ending yourself, before the coats come out.
cocktail.glassware: a stemmed wine glass (about 250-300 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Fill the wine glass with ice and water to chill it while you mix.
Pour the vodka, tomato juice, manzanilla and lemon juice into a shaker, and add the celery salt and the salt.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake for ten seconds. No longer: tomato goes thin and frothy if you keep shaking.
Empty the glass and strain the drink into it. No ice in the glass: it's served up, as a cocktail.
cocktail.name: Curtain Call

recipe.note: any plain vodka
a good plain bottled one, not a Bloody Mary mix: as much tomato as vodka, as in his cocktail guide
or any fino: bone-dry, and it brings the savoury depth the Worcestershire used to
leave it out if your tomato juice is already salted

cocktail.tagline: Your appetite for life makes other people say yes to it.

reading.epigraph: The Bloody Mary once had a politer name, and no ice at all.
whoYouAre: You say yes first, every time. Yes to the cold sea in May, to the dish nobody else at the table dares to order (and then everyone wants a forkful), to walking on somewhere after dinner because the night's too good to end there. You enjoy things properly, out loud, and it's catching. With you around, people stop feeling guilty about the long lunch on a weekday, or the second pudding.

It's never the bill you mind. It's the lights coming up. You can feel the end of a good night coming long before anyone reaches for a coat, sometimes right in the middle of the best part, and that's partly why you enjoy things so hard. Nobody's there for the ride home, when everyone goes back to their own lives and the noise stops all at once. The fear under it is a plain one: that when the music stops, you'll be the one left in the quiet. Still, you make enjoying things feel safe, and people remember who did that for them.
yours: Crosby Gaige was the son of the postmaster in a place called Skunk Hollow, New York, and he became one of Broadway's leading producers, in a career that took in some 150 plays. But his true passions lay outside the theatre: fine wine and cooking.

After the crash of 1929, he started making his living from those two loves too. He wrote a monthly column called Cellar and Pantry, and in 1937 NBC started broadcasting his daily radio programme, *Kitchen Cavalcade*. There was a printing press in the barn on his farm, and among the things it printed were dinner menus.

I like to think that after some 150 plays, he knew what every good show knows: it ends while people still want more, and that's why they come back. You'd have understood each other. The big party of the Twenties stopped in 1929, the moment you'd dread most, and what he did was lay a longer table, one that people he'd never meet could join every day on the radio. His last book is called *Dining with My Friends*. His own dinners come first, and then his friends' follow.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from a recipe in his cocktail guide of 1941, a witty book with recipes sent in by famous names, and one of the ways the Bloody Mary spread. Gaston Lauryssen of New York's St. Regis hotel sent him his hotel's version, under the politer name it went by there: the Red Snapper. It had as much vodka as tomato juice, with Worcestershire sauce and salt among its seasonings, and it was served straight up, as a cocktail, not over ice. The equal parts and the glass without ice both stay. I took out the Worcestershire and put in a splash of manzanilla, a bone-dry Spanish sherry, so his cellar and his kitchen share the glass. With fresh lemon and a pinch of celery salt, it's savoury, bright and properly cold. And because it's served up, it's short, and it has a real ending. I wanted that for you.

One night soon, when it's at its very best, the table loud and nobody watching the time, be the one who ends it. Not because you're tired, and not to be sensible. Say it out loud: this was perfect. Then name the next one, and the date. You'll leave on the best note instead of the last one, and you'll find out what happens when the music stops. Nobody vanishes. They ask you when. And may the next one be even better.

anchors.fact: Jules and Mme Verne sent "a special letter" asking her to stop and see them, if she could. She thought she'd have to decline (Bly, ch. III; card F2). Why they asked isn't on the page (I1; audit X7).
anchors.meaning: I like to think they wanted nothing but your company. (Our reading, signposted.)

anchors.fact: Her promise was public: seventy-five days (ch. IV; F10).
anchors.meaning: You make the promise first, and where everyone can see.

anchors.fact: It could be done only by going without sleep and rest for two nights. Once she knew she'd miss no connection, she said not to think about it (ch. III; F3; audit X2).
anchors.meaning: The distance has never frightened you.

anchors.fact: Her own record: 179½ miles out of her way, the hours starred in her table (ch. XVIII; F13).
anchors.meaning: You count the cost and go anyway.

anchors.fact: It hung on a special mail train ("that will not give us time to see Verne"), and at Amiens they were locked in the carriage and feared being carried past (ch. III; F4–F5). **The mail train is dossier only** (cut from y2, Robin 2026-10-06, F3); the locked carriage stays in y2.
anchors.meaning: Up to the last second, it might have come to nothing.

anchors.fact: On the platform, she wondered "if my face was travel-stained, and if my hair was tossed" (ch. IV; F7).
anchors.meaning: It was never the distance. It's the second before you see their face.

anchors.fact: They "stood on the platform waiting our arrival", and the welcome made her forget how untidy she was. Indoors, Mme Verne lit the fire with her own hands (ch. IV; F6, F8, F17).
anchors.meaning: They weren't waiting for a rescue. They were waiting for you.

anchors.fact: "Contrary to his regular rules", Verne took a glass of wine to drink to her success. Glasses clinked; "Good luck, Nellie Bly" (ch. IV; F9–F10). y4 now says he "raised a glass of wine to her success" (F3 cut, 2026-10-06); the "wine and biscuit" and the clinking glasses are dossier only.
anchors.meaning: Someone broke his own rule to raise a glass to you.

anchors.fact: He'd applaud with both hands at seventy-nine days, and she knew he doubted her seventy-five (ch. IV; F10).
anchors.meaning: Being loved isn't the same as being believed. They wished you well anyway.

anchors.fact: Bareheaded, they followed her into the cold courtyard and waved from the gate (ch. IV; F11).
anchors.meaning: The cold was real. So was the warmth that came out into it.

anchors.fact: She feared the visit had "jeopardized the success of my tour" (ch. V; F12).
anchors.meaning: The doubt on the way back, never about the journey.

anchors.fact: She finished in 72 days. The Vernes' cable was to reach her "the moment she touches American soil", and at Jersey City she cheered because she was "home again" (chs. XVII–XVIII; F14–F16).
anchors.meaning: You kept it, and they had kept you in mind the whole way.

anchors.fact: A whisky sour with a float of red wine is a drink of the 1880s, first attested in Chicago in 1883. In saloon talk any red wine was "claret". New York Sour is the name that lasted (Oxford pdf 1387; *Imbibe!* pdf 96; NY Sour card F1–F4). **Dossier only** (cut from y4, Robin 2026-10-06, F3); the rye's reason stays in Checks › Pairings.
anchors.meaning: Whiskey and red wine already belonged together in her decade (audit Y1: never "rye and red wine" for the 1880s). Never "her drink".

anchors.fact: Until the 1840s, when New Yorkers began icing them, Cock-Tails were "drunk at room temperature" (Oxford pdf 1049; audit D3).
anchors.meaning: Warm the old way: the warmth was people, and nothing in the glass is cold. (Our reading.)

cocktail.closingLine: Raise it to someone first. When one's raised to you, you've brought enough.
cocktail.glassware: stemmed red wine glass (about 250 ml), at room temperature, no ice
method: Keep everything out of the fridge: the rye, the wine, the water and the glass all stay at room temperature. A cool room is best. No ice, at any point.
Pour the syrup, the bitters and the rye into the glass and stir for a few seconds to mix.
Add the wine and the water, then stir gently three or four times.
Hold the orange peel over the glass, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the drink. Set the peel aside, so nothing is in the glass when it's raised.
cocktail.name: Out of Your Way

recipe.note: "Claret" is the old English name for red Bordeaux. Any dry, medium-bodied red works if it isn't oaky or sweet. The story names no wine, so this one is my choice.
any straight rye, 40-50%
1½ teaspoons: equal weights of demerara sugar and warm water, stirred until dissolved, then cooled. Use up to 10 ml if your wine is firm and grippy.
at room temperature, not from the fridge
squeezed over the top, then set aside

cocktail.tagline: Some people send their love. You bring it.

reading.epigraph: This cocktail is made at room temperature. Some things shouldn't arrive cold.
whoYouAre: Someone you love says it's a shame you can't make it. It's three hundred miles away, in the middle of the week. You don't argue. On the night, you're there, on time, in your good coat, and the whole room turns round. That's how you love. Not a card, not a call. You said you'd come, so you come, the whole way, with everyone watching. Anyone you love never has to wonder whether you'll be there, and everyone around them can see how loved they are. Nobody forgets being loved like that.

It was never the distance. It's the second before you see their face, when you don't know yet whether they're glad you came, or whether they'd have been fine without you. You'd never admit it, but somewhere along the way, being needed started to feel like the proof that you're loved. It isn't the only proof. Most of the time, it isn't even the best one.
yours: In November 1889, a reporter called Nellie Bly set out to go round the world faster than the hero of Jules Verne's novel, who took eighty days. She had promised seventy-five. When her ship reached England, she heard that Verne and his wife had written to ask her to visit them at home in Amiens. It was out of her way, and she'd assumed she would have to say no. It would mean two nights without sleep. If she missed no connections, she said, "don't think about sleep or rest."

It nearly came to nothing: at Amiens they were locked in their compartment and thought they'd be carried past. Then she stepped onto the platform, and the Vernes were standing there, waiting for her. What she wrote about that moment isn't the miles or the lost sleep: "I wondered if my face was travel-stained, and if my hair was tossed." A second later, she wrote, the welcome had made her forget all about it.

That's the second I mean. You'd make the whole journey without a thought and still feel it on the platform. And look at who was waiting. I like to think they wanted nothing but her company. When it was time to go, they came out into the cold courtyard without hats and stood at the gate waving, the wind blowing their white hair about. Nobody there was worried about anyone's hair.

Before she left, Verne, against his own rules, raised a glass of wine to her success and managed the toast in English, for her: "Good luck, Nellie Bly." Her book never says what the wine was, so the wine in the cocktail I've made for you is my choice: a young red Bordeaux, and it's more than half the drink, because the toast was the wine. With it goes straight rye. Then a little dark sugar syrup, Angostura bitters, a splash of water, and the scent of orange peel. Ice never comes near it. It's made and served at room temperature, soft, deep and warming: a good red with a spine of rye. I made it warm for the fire Verne's wife lit with her own hands when they arrived, and for the two of them standing bareheaded in the cold courtyard to wave her off.

So go and see someone who's doing perfectly well without you. No occasion, nothing to fix, nobody to rescue: just because you'd like to see them. You'll feel that second at the door, the same as always. Let it come. When their face lights up, it won't be for anything you've done. That's what being wanted looks like, and you've had it all along.

anchors.fact: A Scottish doctor's daughter, Rita Cowan, married the young Japanese chemist who lodged in her mother's house while he learned whisky-making in Scotland (Oxford pdf 1975, landlady's daughter; pdf 2156, "one of its young chemists"; pdf 1391, "Scottish wife"; Ross 2017, Kirkintilloch doctor's daughter; Itoh 2001, lodged with a doctor's widow, married January 1920; both secondary OCR fragments).
anchors.meaning: She said yes to all of it, the move to Japan included (our reading; her reasons aren't on record).
anchors.speaksTo: love given whole; no keeping score

anchors.fact: They went to Japan together and arrived to find the firm that had sent him under administration, and its plans for a whisky distillery on hold (Oxford pdf 1975, 2156).
anchors.meaning: The work he'd been sent to learn for wasn't there when they got there, and she was there to see it (our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: the bruises; sees the risk and chooses anyway

anchors.fact: In Japan she taught English and piano (Ross 2017, OCR fragment, secondary, single source).
anchors.meaning: After the letdown she made her own place there (our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: the decision made again after the hurt

anchors.fact: In 1934 they moved north together to Yoichi, Hokkaido, and lived in Hokkaido for the rest of their lives (Oxford pdf 1391, 1975; Itoh: in Japan forty years until her death).
anchors.meaning: Loving by staying: she didn't take any of it back.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: turning guarded; ours loves by staying

anchors.fact: His company, founded at Yoichi as Dai Nippon Kaju and later named Nikka, grew into Japan's second-largest whisky producer (Oxford pdf 1391, 1975). The bottle: Nikka From the Barrel, recommended; its strength and price are unsourced (no library page; web budget spent): open item for Robin.
anchors.meaning: The whisky comes from Masataka's company, the one that began when they moved north. "One of Japan's biggest" is a fair softening of "second-largest".

anchors.fact: A Flip is "booze, sugar, and whole egg, served cold" (*Codex* p. 240); the whole egg gives the yolk's fat and the white's froth, and is "probably the most common approach" for egg drinks wanting richness (p. 253). Proportions: the *Codex*'s Brandy Flip, 1½ oz spirit, ¾ oz demerara gum syrup, 1 whole egg (p. 252).
anchors.meaning: The whole egg is simply the Flip, not a rule broken: never set against other drinks.

anchors.fact: Whole eggs can be infused in their shells overnight on a bed of lavender in a sealed, refrigerated container; the white absorbs the aroma (*Codex* p. 94, p. 253).
anchors.meaning: Whole, and still letting something in (our reading, signposted in y4: "I like to think that's you"). Never "can't be separated".
anchors.speaksTo: the decision made again after the hurt; still open

anchors.fact: In 2014 NHK built a morning drama, *Massan*, around what Oxford calls "Masataka and Rita's love story" (Oxford pdf 1975).
anchors.meaning: It was worth it: decades later Japanese television told it as a love story (our reading). Nothing about how the drama ends (unread).

cocktail.closingLine: The egg goes in whole. And when you want to reply, reply now: that's what they love you for.
cocktail.glassware: coupe (about 180 ml), chilled
method: The night before, line a small lidded box with kitchen paper and scatter a tablespoon of dried culinary lavender over it. Lay the eggs on top, whole, close the lid, and put the box in the fridge. Use the freshest eggs you can get, clean and uncracked, and keep them cold until you use them: the alcohol doesn't make a raw egg safe. If the drink is for anyone pregnant, elderly or unwell, use pasteurised eggs, though the lavender may come through more faintly. The shell lets the scent through to the white.
Chill the coupe in the freezer.
Crack one egg into the shaker, yolk and white together. Add the whisky and the demerara syrup.
Close the shaker and shake hard with no ice for about fifteen seconds, until the egg is light and fully mixed in.
Fill it with ice and shake hard again, a little longer than you would for most drinks, until the tin is ice-cold.
Strain it into the coupe through the shaker's strainer and a small sieve held over the glass. Leave the top bare: no nutmeg.
cocktail.name: Wide Open

recipe.note: Nikka From the Barrel recommended, or any Japanese blended whisky of 45% or stronger
one part demerara sugar to one part hot water, stirred until it dissolves, then cooled
the freshest you can get, clean and uncracked, kept cold; left overnight in its shell beside dried culinary lavender (see Method)

cocktail.tagline: You make it safe to love without pretending to care less.

reading.epigraph: A Japanese whisky, a whole egg, and a love story that began in Scotland.
whoYouAre: You say it when you feel it. "I missed you", at the door, instead of "long time no see". You answer a message the minute it arrives, because you were glad to get it, and you can't see why you'd hide that. When you love someone, they know. Usually within the week.

Most people call it innocence. They assume nobody's ever hurt you. Somebody has, more than once, and every time you knew exactly what you were risking. You've heard all the advice: be careful, make them wait, don't show your hand so soon. You decided long ago that being hurt costs less than being careful. The bruises stay private, because showing them only brings the advice back. The thing you're quietly afraid of is the evening you notice you've waited three hours to reply, on purpose. And next to you, nobody has to pretend to care less than they do. They say it back. Love you don't have to earn is the rarest kind, and you give it to everyone you love.
yours: A young Japanese chemist, Masataka Taketsuru, was lodging with a doctor's widow in Scotland. His firm in Osaka had sent him to learn how whisky is made. In January 1920 he married her daughter, Rita Cowan, and she went to Japan with him.

When they got there, the firm that had sent him was in the hands of administrators, and its plans for a whisky distillery were on hold. The work he'd been sent to learn had nowhere to go. We don't know how Rita took that. What she did is plainer: she taught English and piano. He found work making whisky for another firm, and later the two of them moved north together, to Yoichi in Hokkaido, where he started his own company. Today it's called Nikka, one of Japan's biggest whisky makers. They lived in Hokkaido for the rest of their lives.

I like to think she knew exactly what she was risking, and said yes anyway. And when the plan fell through, she didn't take any of it back. That's the part I recognise in you: not the yes, which anyone can admire, but the staying open when it didn't go to plan. In 2014, Japanese television made a morning drama of their story, and told it as what it was, a love story.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Flip, a renowned classic: spirit, sugar and a whole egg, white and yolk, the yolk for richness and the white for froth, shaken hard, then served cold. The whisky is Nikka, from Masataka's company, the one that began when they moved north. My one addition happens the night before. The eggs sit in a closed box on a bed of dried lavender, and the shell, whole and uncracked, lets the scent through to the white. I like to think that's you: nothing broken, and still open. It's silky and rich, with just enough demerara sugar, a light amber-beige, with a faint breath of lavender, in a chilled coupe.

My advice is the opposite of everyone else's: don't learn the lesson. When it goes wrong again, and sometimes it will, someone will tell you to be more careful. Hear them out. Then love the next person exactly as you would have before, and if you ever catch yourself waiting three hours to reply, on purpose, reply now. Not because it's safe. Because that's how everyone near you learns to say it too. And I hope the next one says it back before you've finished saying it.

anchors.fact: Someone Harrington knew came into the Townhouse and asked for a drink he'd never made before (Proper p. 58; request is Proper only).
anchors.meaning: An invitation to play, not a dare.
anchors.speaksTo: the opening move: someone throws the ball

anchors.fact: Harrington says he thought for about twenty seconds, swapped Campari in for the bitters and lemon in for lime, and made it once (Proper p. 58; Oxford pdf 1099).
anchors.meaning: Quick, light, made for one person on the spot.

anchors.fact: One of the first two people to taste it told him he'd invented grapefruit juice; in both tellings the joke opens as praise (Proper p. 58; Oxford pdf 1099). Who said it and the exact words: contested (C2).
anchors.meaning: Our reading, signposted: the tease was the compliment.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing (teasing is how they compliment); someone played back

anchors.fact: He named the drink after the man he made it for, Matt Jasmin (Proper p. 58; Oxford pdf 1099).
anchors.meaning: Our reading, signposted: the plain compliment said out loud. No motive on record.
anchors.speaksTo: letting the compliment out of the tease

anchors.fact: Years later he realised he'd spelled the name wrong: one letter too many, an "e" the real name doesn't have; Proper adds it was by then too late (Proper p. 58; Oxford pdf 1099 for the misspelling).
anchors.meaning: The sincere thing, given a little clumsily, and kept.
anchors.speaksTo: the second fear: getting the real thing slightly wrong

anchors.fact: His 1998 book carried the drink to bartenders across the country and abroad; Oxford names it a candidate modern classic and a drink used to introduce people to gin and Campari (Proper p. 58; Oxford pdf 473, 971). Told beside the misspelling, never sequenced with it.
anchors.meaning: The name, extra letter and all, is the one people order.

anchors.fact: A riff on the Pegu Club (Oxford pdf 1099, 971; Proper p. 58).
anchors.meaning: One owned clause or nothing (*Making the Calls*).

anchors.fact: Year (1990 vs mid-1990s, C1); who teased (C2); "architecture school" (C3); Chez Panisse (C5); "dared" (plan shorthand, mine).
Tomás adds 12.5 ml of jasmine tea syrup to Harrington's four measures (spec v1). The printed recipe has no jasmine (Proper p. 58; Oxford pdf 1099).
anchors.meaning: The misspelled name played back: the "e" spells the friend's name the way English spells the flower (Jasmin is the French and German spelling). Our riff, never "his recipe".
anchors.speaksTo: playing back; the compliment let out, a letter off

anchors.fact: The Matrix's OLIVE + JASMINE row gives benzyl acetate (fruit, honey, jasmine), also shared with tea (Matrix pdf 296, rendered).
anchors.meaning: Tea carries a compound the book lists among jasmine's aromas; nothing more (no gin or Campari pairing on the page).

anchors.fact: Explorer's reserved "jasmine and frangipani, per Baker" was a backup never poured (grep of every pour file).
anchors.meaning: Jasmine here comes through the name, not Baker; owned in one clause (audit J1).

anchors.fact: The Townhouse Bar & Grill was in Emeryville, an industrial East Bay area near Oakland (Proper p. 54).
anchors.meaning: Setting only.

anchors.fact: Proper p. 55 says the Jasmine would become a modern classic; Oxford pdf 473 lists it among candidates for becoming a classic (audit r4, W2).
anchors.meaning: The label is attributed ("went on to be called"), not asserted.

cocktail.closingLine: Put in the jasmine Harrington's spelling promised. Then pay one compliment with no tease around it, even if it comes out a letter off.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail glass (about 180-200 ml), chilled
method: Make the syrup first (it keeps about a week in the fridge): pour 100 ml of water just off the boil over 2 teaspoons (about 5 g) of plain jasmine green tea, leave it 3 minutes, strain, and stir in 100 g of white sugar until it dissolves. Let it cool.
Put a cocktail glass in the freezer.
Measure the gin, lemon, Cointreau, Campari and 2½ teaspoons (12.5 ml) of the jasmine syrup into a shaker.
Fill the shaker three-quarters with ice and shake hard until the outside is too cold to hold.
Strain into the cold glass.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then rest it on the rim.
cocktail.name: Only Half Joking

recipe.note: any London dry, 37.5% or stronger
squeezed today
as the recipe prints it; or any clear orange liqueur (triple sec) at 40%
as the recipe prints it; it brings the pink and the bitter
homemade: plain jasmine green tea and sugar, equal weights (see Method)
a wide strip, for the top

cocktail.tagline: Every tease is a compliment. The fun is seeing who catches it.

reading.epigraph: Named for a friend, with one letter too many. This glass finally has jasmine in it.
whoYouAre: You don't tell people you like them. You tell them their coffee order is a cry for help, that they've clearly been practising that walk, that you'll allow the hat, just this once. Then you watch. If they grin and send one back, something starts between the two of you that nobody nearby can quite follow.

Every one of those was a compliment. You just couldn't hand it over plain, because plain is too easy to turn down. Said as a joke, a no costs nobody anything, you included. What stays with you is the one who takes it at face value and looks a little hurt, or smiles politely and lets it drop, and the joke left hanging with only you holding it. And being teased by you feels like being picked. People walk away from you funnier and better-looking than they came in.
yours: At a bar called the Townhouse, in Emeryville near Oakland, a friend asked the bartender, Paul Harrington, for a drink Harrington had never made before. He says he gave it twenty seconds' thought. He took a classic he loved, put Campari in place of its bitters and lemon in place of its lime, made it once, and handed it over. In his words, it was a beautiful pink.

One of the first people to taste it told him he'd just invented grapefruit juice. The praise came first, then the joke. I like to think that's the whole trick, and it's your trick too: the compliment, sent sideways, to see if it's caught. Harrington also did the thing you find hardest. He said it outright, with no joke around it: he named the drink after his friend, Matt Jasmin.

And Harrington got it slightly wrong. Years later he realised he'd been spelling the name with an "e" on the end, a letter Matt's name doesn't have. By then, it was too late. His 1998 book carried the drink to bartenders around the world, and it went on to be called a modern classic, extra letter and all. I recognise you in that: when you finally say the nice thing out loud, you're sure it'll come out a little wrong. His did. It still carries his friend's name, near enough.

The cocktail I've made for you is built on that Jasmine. It's gin and squeezed lemon with small measures of Cointreau and Campari, shaken hard and poured very cold into a frosted stemmed glass, with the oils of a lemon peel misted across it. All of Harrington's measures are there. My one addition is a little syrup made from jasmine tea. That extra "e" spells his friend's name the way English spells the flower, and the recipe Harrington printed has no jasmine in it. I've put some in, years late, as my tease played back to him. The syrup softens the tartness, so it ends up bright, a little bitter and softly scented.

Next time someone plays back, don't send another tease. Tell them what the last one was hiding: that they're funny, that they're good company, that the hat is actually great. Once, plainly. It may come out clumsy. Harrington's came out with a letter too many, and it stuck. Plenty of people you like have no idea how much, and the ones you tell will play back hardest of all.

anchors.fact: Angel's Share, East Village, New York: second floor, behind a door at the back of a Japanese restaurant; opened in 1994 "without notice" (Simonson's narration). F3, F5
anchors.meaning: You had to find it. Nobody on the page is quoted choosing the quiet opening, so the design rests on F4, not on this.

anchors.fact: The owner wanted it "small, intimate, and formal", Tokyo-style, with perfect drinks and service; no small talk, no standing, no large parties. F4, F9
anchors.meaning: The reserve was a plan for doing something well, not a trick.

anchors.fact: The quiet was "partly" because many of the bartenders had limited English. F9
anchors.meaning: Only part of the reason. The rest was the house's own style. Never the guest's reason.

anchors.fact: Ikeda came from Japan to play music; two years after opening, the owner told him to run the bar, and "somehow, he knew" Ikeda had tended bar in Japan. Ikeda's own account (2015). The page also says the bar didn't know how to run itself then. F6, F7
anchors.meaning: Someone knew what he hadn't put forward, and told him to run the bar (Ikeda's verb: "told"). The owner also needed him; tell both. "The card he hadn't played" is our reading.

anchors.fact: Ikeda had the bartenders stir Martinis and Manhattans as he'd learned in Japan, and added classics and originals "with Japanese ingredients like shochu and shiso leaf" to the menu (examples; never both in one drink on the page). F8
anchors.meaning: Our glass joins two things on his menu. No shochu Martini is on the page: "made with what he brought", never "his drink".

anchors.fact: The movement it helped inspire largely eclipsed and forgot it; it stayed inward-looking, with no expansion, no book, no star bartenders (but Gokan is "arguably the best-known"). F2, F10, F12
anchors.meaning: Holding back kept the work whole and kept the bar out of the story.

anchors.fact: Gokan, from Tokyo in 2006: for his first six years of eight, no friends who were bartenders; "We were always outside." (2014) F13
anchors.meaning: The cost in one man's words, and he says "we".

anchors.fact: Simonson: the refusal to reach out went both ways. F11
anchors.meaning: The door was shut from both sides; nobody in the story is to blame.

anchors.fact: Simonson ranks no 1990s New York opening more important to the future of the cocktail revival. F1
anchors.meaning: What was kept back mattered more than anyone outside saw. Scope: "to the revival".

anchors.fact: Shochu: clear Japanese spirit, usually 25%, either neutral (kōrui) or aromatic pot-still (honkaku); in US shops often mislabelled "soju". S1–S3
anchors.meaning: For the substitute line: ask for shochu, not Korean soju.

anchors.fact: Oldest explicit mention of shochu (1559): graffiti two carpenters apparently hid under a shrine roof, grumbling the priest never gave them any. S4
anchors.meaning: A hidden line, found later. Comic, not tender: epigraph seed only, keep "apparently".

cocktail.closingLine: Put the leaf on the table as you serve it. Then give away the thing you'd have kept for last.
cocktail.glassware: small stemmed cocktail glass (about 150 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Put a small stemmed cocktail glass in the freezer.
If you don't have rich syrup: stir 100 g of white sugar into 50 g of hot water until it's clear, and let it cool (it keeps about a month in the fridge).
Tear one green shiso leaf once across and drop it into a mixing glass or a jar.
Add the shochu, the gin, the blanc vermouth and ½ teaspoon of the syrup.
Fill the mixing glass with ice and stir steadily for about 30 seconds, until the outside is very cold.
Strain into the cold glass. Nothing goes on the drink.
Lift the leaf out of the strainer and put it on a small plate beside the glass as you serve the drink, before anyone asks what's in it.
cocktail.name: Worth Finding

recipe.note: Japanese barley or rice shochu, about 25% (25% or stronger); ask for shochu, not soju, which is a different Korean spirit
any London dry; 45% or stronger keeps it fully in range (40-43% makes it a touch softer)
the pale, lightly sweet style first made in Chambéry, France (also sold as bianco), not a dry vermouth
homemade: 2 parts white sugar to 1 part hot water, by weight
torn once, stirred with the drink, strained out, and set on the table beside the glass

cocktail.tagline: Getting to know you feels like finding something nobody else has found.

reading.epigraph: It starts at a bar upstairs, behind a restaurant. Its shiso hides behind the gin.
whoYouAre: You're easy to talk to and hard to finish. After an evening with you, people have said more than they meant to, and know a little less about you than they'd like. So they come back. Each time you give them a bit more: a story you don't tell at work, a look that says you noticed, a door left slightly open.

You don't keep something back to be chased. You keep it back so there's still a reason to stay. At some point you decided that once someone has seen all of you, the finding is over, and they'll go. So there's always one thing you haven't said yet. And it works: people feel they've found something in you that no one else has. They're right. That's what you hand them: a sense of discovery most people never get from anyone. It's worth a great deal. But behind that last thing, you're on your own.
yours: In 1994, on a second floor in New York's East Village, behind a door at the back of a Japanese restaurant, Angel's Share opened. Its owner wanted a Tokyo-style bar: small, intimate and formal. There was no small talk, partly because many of the bartenders had little English, and no standing or big groups. If you found the door, you'd found something.

Two years in, the people there didn't really know how to run it. Shinichi Ikeda had come over from Japan to play music. He'd been a bartender back home, and one day the owner told him to run the bar. Ikeda said the owner somehow knew. I like to think that's the moment you'd notice: someone saw what he hadn't put forward, and put it to work.

The writer who told its story says no New York bar opening in the 1990s mattered more to the cocktail revival's future. Yet it didn't expand or put out a cocktail book, and the movement it helped inspire largely forgot it. Shingo Gokan, who came from Tokyo in 2006, worked there six years before he had a single friend who was a bartender. In his words, they were always outside. The same writer is careful to add that the door was shut from both sides. I recognise you in that. What you hold back stays whole, and it keeps you just outside.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Martini, the renowned classic, built from two things Ikeda brought to that bar: Martinis stirred the way he'd learned them in Japan, and new drinks with Japanese ingredients like shochu and shiso leaf. Joining them in one glass is my idea. Shochu is a clear Japanese spirit with less alcohol than gin, so gin takes the lead, with a pale vermouth. A torn green shiso leaf is stirred with them, then lifted out and set beside the glass as it's served, as a nod to that door at the back. Shiso and juniper share a compound with a cedar-and-pine scent, and in the glass the shiso slips in behind the gin, and what you get is clean, cold and green in a way you can't quite place. The leaf is there to be handed over.

So tell one person what you've been saving. Not when they've earned it: before. You're afraid there'll be nothing left to stay for. I don't think that's how it works with you. Being known completely is the one kind of closeness you've always kept from yourself, and it's the kind that doesn't need a reason to stay. They'll stay anyway. Let yourself find out.

anchors.fact: Early in 2004 Dushan Zaric and Jason Kosmas left Schiller's and took its bar manager with them; two colleagues from Pravda, the same owner's bar, joined them. The owner, Kosmas said, "was not happy with us." (*Proper* p. 155; Oxford pdf 721: five partners)
anchors.meaning: They didn't leave alone. Others came with them.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: under the "come on" is "please come"

anchors.fact: They opened that autumn in a former pastry shop in the West Village. From the first day, whoever was still there when the bar closed was given homemade chicken soup, free. (*Proper* pp. 155–156; Oxford pdf 721)
anchors.meaning: The care went to whoever was still there.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: kept only for the noise

anchors.fact: The food was partly business (Zaric had seen hungry customers leave Pravda) and partly where they came from: a European background, where eating and drinking went together. No page gives a reason for the soup itself. (*Proper* p. 155)
anchors.meaning: Told plainly, as food, partly business.

anchors.fact: Some of the other cocktail people, Kosmas said, looked at them as if they couldn't be serious "because people are having too much fun there". Among the cocktail elite the bar never had a name for the best drinks. (*Proper* pp. 156–157)
anchors.meaning: The cost: written off for the fun.

anchors.fact: Zaric was plain about it. By his own account they weren't the best mixologists: "We chose to play a different card in order to provide experience." (*Proper* p. 157)
anchors.meaning: They never claimed to be the serious bar in disguise. The experience was the point.

anchors.fact: The staff stayed. Zaric put the very low turnover down to one thing: "they feel they had a hand in creating this", and he meant the waitresses and busboys too. Some of its bartenders have never worked anywhere else. (*Proper* p. 156)
anchors.meaning: People stay where they had a hand in it.

anchors.fact: Simonson writes that the customers could sense how close and content the staff were. (*Proper* p. 156)
anchors.meaning: The guests felt what the staff had.

anchors.fact: A colleague remembered Zaric as deep and intense and Kosmas as happy and easy-going; Simonson says they put both into one bar. (*Proper* p. 153)
anchors.meaning: The loud room had both in it from the start.

anchors.fact: When other serious bars measured with jiggers, they poured by eye, served food and didn't shun vodka. (Oxford pdf 721; Kosmas, *Proper* p. 157)
anchors.meaning: The rules they broke were the scene's, and they broke them together.
anchors.speaksTo: Outlaw limb. Near *Who's In?*: Wren's call

anchors.fact: Oxford notes the bar's Manhattan adds curaçao. Curaçao turns up in some of the Manhattan's earliest printed recipes (Jerry Thomas's guide, 1887). (Oxford pdf 533; *Imbibe!* pdf 195; *Joy* pdf 330)
anchors.meaning: Only if Tomás keeps curaçao; never "the original", never their measures.

cocktail.closingLine: Slice the beetroot yourself and leave the red on. Then ask someone to something dull, and keep whoever comes.
cocktail.glassware: coupe (about 180 ml), chilled
method: Peel and slice the beetroot with your bare hands. Your fingers will go red. Leave them.
Steep the slices in the sweet vermouth for about 12 hours, covered, then strain. It keeps in the fridge.
Put a coupe in the freezer.
Pour the rye, the beetroot vermouth, the curaçao and the bitters into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass is very cold.
Strain into the cold coupe.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Accomplices

preparations.text: 50 g peeled raw beetroot, thinly sliced, in 250 ml sweet vermouth. Cover and leave at room temperature for about 12 hours, then strain and keep it in the fridge.
preparations.title: Beetroot sweet vermouth (makes enough for eight)

recipe.note: any straight rye; proved from 40% to 50%
sweet vermouth steeped with raw beetroot (below); the change I made
Employees Only's Manhattan adds curaçao; the measure is mine

cocktail.tagline: Around you, people drop the act and like who they find underneath.

reading.epigraph: A New York bar put curaçao in its Manhattan. This one adds beetroot. It stains.
whoYouAre: Two hours into a polite evening, you lean over and whisper, "Coming?" Twenty minutes later the two of you are sitting on a kerb with chips, laughing too loudly. Then they tell you something they've never told anyone. You weren't getting them into trouble. You were getting through to them.

People call you a bad influence, and you let them, because it's half true and it makes a better story. The rest of it: polite feels lonely to you. It keeps everyone at arm's length, you included. You don't want an audience. You want accomplices. Under every "come on" there's a "please come", and you'd rather raise the stakes than say that plainly. What you dread is being kept for the noise: loved as the wild one and never really known, or made sensible and quietly dropped. Around you, people drop the act. They say the honest thing, the funny thing, and they like who they are when they're with you.
yours: Early in 2004, Jason Kosmas and Dushan Zaric left their jobs at Schiller's, in New York, taking its bar manager with them. Two more colleagues joined them. The owner, Kosmas said, wasn't happy with them. That autumn the five opened Employees Only. They broke the scene's rules together: they poured by eye while other serious bars measured, and they served food.

Some of the other cocktail people, as Kosmas felt it, looked at them as if they couldn't really care about their drinks "because people are having too much fun there". Zaric was plain about it. They weren't the best mixologists, he said, and they "chose to play a different card in order to provide experience".

And from opening day, whoever was still there when the bar closed was given homemade chicken soup, free. The food was partly business: Zaric had seen hungry customers leave a bar he'd worked at before. Partly it was their European background, where food and drink belong together. And the staff stayed. Very few ever left. One reason Zaric gave: they felt "they had a hand in creating this". I like to think that's why your people stay too. Not for the noise, but because with you, they got to help make it. The dare is what they talk about. What they remember is that you wanted them there.

The cocktail I've made for you is a rye Manhattan, a classic the whole world knows, with curaçao (an orange liqueur), which Employees Only added to theirs. My change is the vermouth. It's steeped for about twelve hours with raw beetroot that you peel and slice yourself, and your fingers will go red. I put it there as a nod to that hand in it: you can't make this drink without it marking you. Stirred over ice, it goes into a coupe, a glass they used too. It tastes rich and smooth, earthy and sweet beneath the rye, with orange oil on top.

You don't have to keep raising the stakes to keep people. Some time soon, plan something with nothing to dare in it: a Sunday food shop, soup on the stove, a film you've both seen twice. See who's glad to be there. Those are your accomplices, and they always were. They'll still be around when nothing's happening, and you get to be known for more than the noise.

anchors.fact: Siegal was one of the few friends Petraske made at Stuyvesant, his high school (*Proper*, p. 86). Petraske had talked about the bar for a few months before he told Siegal the plumber was coming and he had no money. Siegal's own gloss: it wasn't a request to invest; it was "I ran out of money" (*A Proper Drink*, p. 88, Siegal's account). Undated: the late 1990s, before the opening on New Year's Eve 1999.
anchors.meaning: He heard "help" in a sentence about plumbing. Nobody asked.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: hears the ask nobody made

anchors.fact: For months, Siegal handed over all the cash he made at the restaurant where he worked (p. 88). Proper calls it lending seed money (p. 96). A couple of other school friends took on credit-card debt too (p. 88).
anchors.meaning: Slow, dull, costly, and for one friend. Not a rescue, not a speech.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: nobody they love has to ask properly

anchors.fact: Early 2002: Petraske went to London for six months and left Milk & Honey in the hands of Siegal and Joseph Schwartz (p. 95).
anchors.meaning: He minded the thing his friend loved while his friend was away (our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: there for as long as it takes

anchors.fact: When the *New York Times* wrote the bar up in May 2000 (Chaplin, 7 May 2000; Oxford MILK & HONEY bibliography, pdf 1304), Petraske was livid and thought it made him look bad. Siegal didn't agree: "I bought thirty copies" (p. 93).
anchors.meaning: I like to think that was the sentence he never said out loud (our reading, signposted: the page gives no reason, and doesn't say what he did with them).

anchors.fact: The Gold Rush: Siegal asked Petraske for "one of those whiskey sours" with the honey syrup instead of the sugar: "It was as simple as that" (p. 96). He had the idea sitting at the bar after a long shift; his usual was a Bourbon Sour "on the rocks, without egg or garnish", as on many nights before (*PUNCH* 2021).
anchors.meaning: A blunt standing order, one change, and it came out rich (p. 96's own judgement, in our words).
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof: blunt order, full-size feeling

anchors.fact: Siegal named it: "He christened it the Gold Rush." He likes names that bring a feeling, a thought or a chuckle, with no hidden meaning (*PUNCH* 2021).
anchors.meaning: Even his names don't make speeches.
anchors.speaksTo: voice: short, dry, allowed to be funny

anchors.fact: Proper: Siegal is "not a drink creator", and his role was "largely unheralded" (p. 96). The Gold Rush was an early hit, soon made at other bars (p. 96); Oxford lists it among Milk & Honey's modern classics (pdf 1304). Around 2012 he found it chalked up at Union Square Cafe under "Classic Cocktails", last after the Old-Fashioned, Manhattan, Sazerac and Martini; he was "a little bit shocked, a little bit suspicious, and a little bit giddy" (*PUNCH* 2021).
anchors.meaning: A renowned modern classic from a man nobody credits. Worth having.
anchors.speaksTo: let the drink sound worth having; the unseen deed

anchors.fact: The honey syrup: Petraske started making it (Siegal, p. 96) for an old drink, the Honeysuckle; Toby Maloney had a hand in the 3:1 house syrup (*PUNCH* 2021). Our syrup: 3:1 by volume (*Codex* p. 45), with clover, the commonest grocery honey (*Codex* p. 45), "spiced" in the Matrix's word (pdf 148).
anchors.meaning: His friend's work, in Siegal's telling, in the one change he asked for.

anchors.fact: Bourbon: Proper recommends Elijah Craig (p. 96, "single batch"); *PUNCH* has Knob Creek for the first and Elijah Craig 12-year-old as the house bourbon after. That 12-year-old was sold as Elijah Craig Small Batch until its age statement came off in January 2016 (*The Spirits Business*, 2016; our inference that it's the same bottle). The *Codex*'s own Whiskey Sour uses Elijah Craig Small Batch (p. 130). Arnold's own Gold Rush (LI p. 133) uses a 47% bourbon, no bottle named.
anchors.meaning: The bottle a guest can buy under the name the house poured. Never "the same whiskey".

anchors.fact: Proper prints a 30-second shake (p. 96). Arnold: 8 to 12 seconds gives about the same drink; past 12 "almost nothing additional happens" (LI pp. 97–98; chilling and dilution). Reading y4: "After about twelve seconds, the drink barely changes." Closing line: "The cold's done by twelve", never "needs twelve".
anchors.meaning: The seconds past the cold are hands busy, back to the room.
anchors.speaksTo: position: say it while your hands are busy

anchors.fact: Proper prints ¾ oz honey syrup (p. 96, page image). Ours is ½ oz (15 ml against 22.5), a third less: the printed measure reads OUT on Arnold's sugar range for sours (12.19 vs 8.9 g/100 ml, `balance.py`; LI pp. 129–130), and ½ oz lands (8.73). Arnold's own Gold Rush (LI p. 133) uses ¾ oz of his thinner, by-weight honey syrup.
anchors.meaning: "So the bourbon gets a word in": our choice, stated as ours. Never "his recipe".
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; the position (a word in)

anchors.fact: "The thirty seconds and the thirty copies" (coincidence).
anchors.meaning: Owned in one plain clause if both appear; otherwise "half a minute" (Tomás).

cocktail.closingLine: Thirty seconds of shaking. The cold's done by twelve. Say it in the other eighteen.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass, one large plain cube (the biggest cube your freezer makes; not clear, not cut)
method: Make the honey syrup: three spoons of light runny honey and one of water in a jar, lid on, shaken until it's smooth.
Put one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Pour the bourbon, lemon and honey syrup into a shaker and fill it three-quarters with ice.
Close it and shake hard for thirty seconds.
Strain it over the cube. Nothing on top.
cocktail.name: Any Day

recipe.note: Elijah Craig Small Batch recommended, or any straight bourbon between 40% and 50%
squeezed the same day
three parts light runny honey (wildflower, or a light clover) to one part water, shaken in a closed jar until smooth

cocktail.tagline: Nobody you love ever has to ask you. They only have to mention it.

reading.epigraph: Ordered after a long shift: the usual, with honey instead of sugar. Now it's a classic.
whoYouAre: Someone you love mentions that the car's making that noise again. That's all. They'd never ask, and they don't need to: you heard it, because it's exactly how you'd have said it. By Saturday you're flat on your back underneath it, and neither of you makes a thing of it. A mention is enough. What comes back isn't a card or a speech. It's the thing done, for as long as it takes.

The sentence you've never quite managed is the other one, the one that says why. The feeling's there, full size. Said out loud, it sounds like someone else's words, so it stays put, and you tell yourself they know. Mostly they do. But now and then, on a long drive home, you think about the day it'll be too late to check. The people you love never have to find the words to ask, and they never owe you a thank-you. They always know where they can lean. That's worth more than any speech.
yours: In the late 1990s, Sasha Petraske was turning a tiny former tailor's shop in New York into a bar, and he ran out of money. He told T. J. Siegal, one of the few friends he'd made at school, that the plumber was coming and he didn't have any money. Siegal was clear, years later: it wasn't a request to invest. It was a friend saying he'd run out.

So for months, Siegal handed over all the cash he made at the restaurant where he worked. When the *New York Times* wrote the bar up, Petraske was furious; he thought it made him look bad. Siegal's answer, as he tells it, is four words: "I bought thirty copies." Maybe it was just good for business. I like to think it was the closest he came to saying he was proud of his friend.

You'd have heard it too. Not a money problem: help, from someone who hadn't asked. And you'd have answered in the same language: no speech, just months of turning up. And when you're proud of someone, you'd rather buy thirty copies than say so.

Sitting at the bar one night after a long shift, Siegal asked for his usual bourbon sour, with the honey syrup Petraske had started making instead of the sugar. "It was as simple as that," he said. He named it the Gold Rush, and years later found it chalked up under classic cocktails, last on a list that began with the Old-Fashioned and the Manhattan. It made him "a little bit giddy". The cocktail I've made for you starts from his order, as the recipe prints it: bourbon, lemon and honey syrup, shaken hard, over one large cube of ice, no egg, nothing on top. I've used a third less honey syrup than the printed recipe, so the bourbon gets a word in, the way I'd like you to. It's shaken for thirty seconds, as the recipe says. Thirty again: a coincidence, nothing more. After about twelve seconds, the drink barely changes.

Forget the speech. Nobody who loves you is waiting for one. You need one line, said while you're busy with something else. Under the car. Halfway through the job. On the drive home, eyes on the road. "I'd do this for you any day" is plenty. They've always known where they can lean. Now they'll know why.

anchors.fact: Born Gladys Louise Smith. When Belasco cast her at 15 he recommended a more star-like name. "Mary Pickford" came from a surname in her mother's family and a fib: she told him her middle name was Marie, not Louise, then turned it into Mary. The page doesn't say who picked "Pickford". (PBS, P4)
anchors.meaning: Even the name was put together.

anchors.fact: The public called her "America's Sweetheart" and "the Girl with the Golden Curls"; fans said "our Mary". (PBS, P1; Regan, *Joy* pdf 341, "America's Sweetheart")
anchors.meaning: The wanting came with names other people gave her.

anchors.fact: She saw that film needed a new kind of acting: smaller, more intimate, with the feeling in the eyes, not in big gestures. (PBS, P6)
anchors.meaning: The effect was worked out, not luck.

anchors.fact: Griffith offered five dollars a day, three days a week. She asked for ten a day and more for extra work, and he agreed. She kept moving company for higher pay, with her mother's encouragement. (PBS, P5, P7)
anchors.meaning: She named her price, and got it.

anchors.fact: In 1919 she and three other filmmakers (Chaplin and Griffith among them) founded United Artists, to distribute their own films and break the distributors' hold on the money. She called the satisfaction, in a word, freedom. (PBS, P8)
anchors.meaning: She built the structure so the work stayed hers to run.

anchors.fact: Her own company's money needs pressed her into the roles her fans loved; *Pollyanna* (1920) fixed the little-girl image even harder. (PBS, P9)
anchors.meaning: The trap was the success: the thing she built kept her in the curls.

anchors.fact: In 1928, the year her mother died, she cut off the famous curls, and fans attacked her for it. She said later it was as if she'd killed someone, but only so the one who came next could live. (PBS, P10; her motive on record is grief plus that line, C6)
anchors.meaning: She ended the image so the person after it could live. Any "strategy" reading is ours, signposted.

anchors.fact: A Prohibition-era drink of white rum, pineapple and a little grenadine was named for her. By one 1928 account a Havana bartender made it for her visit, most likely in December 1922. Reportedly one of the three most-ordered drinks in Cuba then. (Oxford pdf 1252; maker contested, C1)
anchors.meaning: The drink was made for the famous face.
anchors.speaksTo: the tie (Wren): that one for the star, this one for the one running things

anchors.fact: No page says she drank it. Two library books name two different makers (Kaufman, Oxford/Woon; Woelke, Regan), so no maker's name in guest text. Oxford's own recipe has no maraschino; its MARASCHINO entry and Regan's have it, so no "original recipe". (C1–C5)
anchors.meaning: Keep the drink lines to "named for her".

anchors.fact: Bacardi set up in Puerto Rico in 1936 and left Cuba after the revolution; today's bottle isn't made in Havana. (Oxford BACARDI pdf 182)
anchors.meaning: "The rum the drink's entry names" is true; "the same rum" isn't.

cocktail.closingLine: Make the grenadine yourself, the day before. Then choose your next version before anyone asks for the old one.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail glass, chilled
method: The day before, make the grenadine. In a clean jar put 250 g of pomegranate juice (100% juice), 250 g of white sugar and 6 sprigs of thyme, crushed lightly in your hand. Close the lid and shake until the sugar has dissolved, which takes a few minutes. Leave it in the fridge overnight, then strain out the thyme. It keeps about a week in the fridge.
Put a cocktail glass in the freezer.
Measure the rum, pineapple, lime and 2½ teaspoons (12.5 ml) of the grenadine into a shaker.
Fill the shaker three-quarters with ice and shake hard until the outside is too cold to hold. The pineapple will foam a little, and it should.
Strain into the cold glass. No garnish.
cocktail.name: By Design

recipe.note: unaged or lightly aged, not spiced or sweetened; labelled 50% ("100 proof" in the US) or a little stronger; anything from 50% to 63% works
or an unsweetened, not-from-concentrate juice
squeezed today
homemade, the day before: pomegranate juice, sugar and thyme (see Method)

cocktail.tagline: Your charm has an author, and it's you.

reading.epigraph: Named in Havana for America's Sweetheart. This one's for the one behind the curls.
whoYouAre: You know what you do to people, because you worked it out. The voice, the pause before you answer, the one thing everyone remembers you wore: none of it is an accident, and you'd be quietly proud if anyone asked. They don't. They think you were simply born like that.

People fall for what you made. Very few ask to meet the one who made it. That part is lonely, and you almost never mention it, because to everyone else it seems like having it all. And when you're steering, with no credit for it, an evening can turn warm, even daring, and never tip into trouble. People feel more alive around you, and safe. That's care too, though it looks like a show.
yours: Before she was America's Sweetheart, she was Gladys Smith. A producer suggested a more star-like name, so one was made, partly from a fib about her middle name. When D. W. Griffith offered her five dollars a day, she asked for ten, and got it.

In 1919, with Chaplin, Griffith and others, Mary Pickford founded United Artists, so its founders could distribute their own films. The satisfaction, she said, was in one word: freedom. Then the twist: the company needed money, and the money was in the girl with the golden curls. The thing she built to be free kept her in them.

In 1928, the year her mother died, Pickford cut them off. Her fans were scathing. Looking back, she said people reacted as if she'd killed someone, and maybe she had, to give the one who came next a chance. I like to think she knew who that was: the one who'd been running things all along.

That trap may sound familiar. You built the effect, and it works, and that's exactly what makes it hard to change: people come for it, and you're good at it. A bartender in Havana, by one account, named a cocktail for the star, light and sweet, a drink for the curls. The cocktail I've made for you is for the one behind them. The rum leads now, the lime keeps it dry, and the grenadine is homemade, from real pomegranate with thyme steeped in it. It's made at home, by you, as a nod to the one who made the image.

A hard year shouldn't be what makes the change for you. Choose the next version of yourself while the choice is still yours, and let a few people watch you choose. Some will miss the old one for a while. The ones who stay will be the ones who wanted you, and that's the company you've been missing.

anchors.fact: Chris McMillian (b. 1961) settled in New Orleans in 1984, researched early cocktails and old bars, and shared what he found freely with bartenders and customers, before cocktail history was popular (Oxford pdf 1273)
anchors.meaning: he gave away what he'd studied to whoever was at the bar
anchors.speaksTo: the gift: taking what others love seriously, and passing on the long version

anchors.fact: At the Ritz-Carlton's small library bar he'd pound the julep's ice in a canvas bag with a big mallet, in rhythm, while reciting the julep ode Oxford credits to Soule Smith (Oxford pdf 1273)
anchors.meaning: he said a long, old piece of writing out loud in a hotel bar, with no sign anyone had asked for it
anchors.speaksTo: the risk the guest doesn't take: offering the long version without choosing who hears it

anchors.fact: He recalls starting with the mallet around 2000, while reading Gerald Carson's 1963 history of bourbon (ICE MALLET pdf 1066; interview 2020)
anchors.meaning: his julep began with reading
anchors.speaksTo: the Sage half: love that starts in a book

anchors.fact: The ode is prose, printed by January 1907 (Wilmington *Morning Star*), "late nineteenth-century" per Oxford; author dates unknown; credited to J. Soule Smith in a 1956 Kentucky anthology, signed "M. B." in 1907
anchors.meaning: someone long dead wrote far more than a recipe needed, about a drink
anchors.speaksTo: the long letter: written at full depth, for whoever would read it

anchors.fact: It calls bourbon and mint a pair made for each other, grown from the same land and stream (1907 printing)
anchors.meaning: the drink is itself written as a match
anchors.speaksTo: the Lover's hope of being met in kind (our reading; never quoted)

anchors.fact: Its own method: rich sugared spring water, mint crushed round the glass then thrown away, cracked ice, bourbon, then the sugar poured over, no stirring, mint sprigs round the brim, sip slowly (1907 printing)
anchors.meaning: the ode is also a recipe, so a drink can answer it
anchors.speaksTo: Tomás's spark, if he takes one from its words

anchors.fact: He has said making drinks is only 10 percent of what he does; the rest is host, concierge, tour guide (Oxford pdf 1273; undated)
anchors.meaning: the drink was never the whole of it

anchors.fact: *A Proper Drink*: before Katrina he was one of the few in New Orleans trying anything adventurous, piecing his trade's history together "one drink at a time" (p. 284; 2014 conversation)
anchors.meaning: he worked at it largely alone, in a city that wasn't yet listening
anchors.speaksTo: the fear: being in company and unmet (our reading)

anchors.fact: The ode was reprinted and quoted for decades before him (printings 1907, 1929, 1933, 1956; one fictional recital, a colonel in Cobb's 1929 novel *Red Likker*)
anchors.meaning: he answered a text that was already known; he didn't rescue a lost one
anchors.speaksTo: keeps the answer honest: an answer, not a resurrection

cocktail.closingLine: Pound the ice loud enough that someone asks. Then give them the long version.
cocktail.glassware: julep cup (pewter or stainless steel; any metal tumbler of about 300 ml at home)
method: Put the cup in the freezer for ten minutes.

Put the ice cubes in a clean canvas bag (or fold them into a tea towel) and pound them with a wooden mallet or a rolling pin until they're fine and snowy. The canvas soaks up the meltwater, so the ice goes in dry.
Take the cup out, holding it by the rim. Press a few mint leaves round the inside with the back of a spoon, every side, then take the leaves out.
Fill the cup halfway with pounded ice. Pour the bourbon over the ice, then pour the syrup over the top.

Still holding the cup by the rim, churn the ice with a long spoon for about ten seconds. Add ice to two-thirds full and keep churning until the outside of the cup is frosted all over. The ice gives the drink about 30 ml of water as you go: that's part of it.
Heap more ice on top in a mound above the rim. Push a short straw in at one side, and set the mint bouquet in the ice right beside it, so the mint is under your nose at every sip.
cocktail.name: In Kind

preparations.text: 100 g sugar and 50 g cold water in a jar. Close it and shake until the sugar has gone and the syrup runs thick and clear (a few minutes; fine sugar goes faster). Fridge, about a month.
preparations.title: Rich sugar syrup

recipe.note: any straight bourbon at that strength; the story names no bottle
the ode's sweetener: sugar mixed into cold water until it's thick as oil
pressed round the inside of the cup, then taken out, as the ode asks

recipe.item: ice cubes, pounded in a canvas bag
recipe.note: the way Chris McMillian pounded the ice for his juleps; a clean tea towel works too
