Before long the coffee, beer and ale stopped being the heart of the business, and the place was known simply as the London Punch House. Of the four things he'd planned, one became what the house was known for.

Then the bit I can't help smiling at. In the 1750s he handed the bar to his son and turned to dealing in spirits from his cellars. When he died, in 1776, he was back running the bar, with his son. Maybe his son asked him to. I like to think he missed holding it. You'd understand that. And I like to think you'd see what I see in his house: the pieces he didn't hold himself, the hands at the counter and the trade that outgrew the other three, were what made it famous.

His recipe is lost, so the cocktail I've made for you is mine, built from what's known of his: one part spirit to two of everything else, which was his standard, and, it seems, a Seville-orange shrub. The spirit is Batavia arrack, from Java, distilled mostly from cane and rice: pungent, full of flavour, and the dearest spirit he made punch with. I chose it as the loud piece, the one with a will of its own. What holds it is the shrub: orange peel rubbed into sugar until the oil comes out, then the juice, bottled and kept cold, with a bottle of water beside it. Arrack, shrub and cold water go straight into the cup, a few turns of a spoon, no ice. It's sharp, bright and warm at once, and the arrack still sounds clearly through it. The order doesn't quiet the loud part. It gives it somewhere to stand.

Keep holding it all: everyone near you is lucky you do. But next time a piece moves by itself, a guest you didn't plan for or a change you weren't warned about, don't put it back at once. Give it the evening. What you built is stronger than you fear, and the piece that moved may turn out to be the part everyone remembers. And you'd finally get to be surprised by your own world, like everyone else in it.

anchors.fact: Until the early 1990s grappa was much ridiculed outside Italy as rough "moonshine" made from the "dregs" of winemaking (Oxford GRAPPA pdf 936; F3).
anchors.meaning: What others had already decided about. The ridicule is quoted as the ridicule, never our view. Abroad only.
anchors.speaksTo: sees a part still to play where others have decided there's none

anchors.fact: Pomace had been distilled since at least the eighteenth century, out of thrift; by tradition, for pomace brandies in general, it was buried until the wine was made and only then distilled (Oxford POMACE BRANDY pdf 1548; F2). Grappa was made in Italy before 1779 (Oxford BORTOLO NARDINI pdf 319; F12).
anchors.meaning: Nobody threw it away: everybody used it, late and all together. The difference was in how she looked at it, not in rescuing it.
anchors.speaksTo: changes nothing; sees what was already there

anchors.fact: In 1973 Giannola and Benito Nonino distilled picolit pomace on its own; Oxford says only freshly and lightly pressed pomace was used. The house says the custom was to distil all the grapes' pomace mixed (Oxford GRAPPA pdf 936, POLI pdf 1544; house account H3; F4–F5).
anchors.meaning: Two plain choices: one grape, and the leftovers taken fresh. The reasons were small and physical. Credit both, or "Giannola Nonino and the house"; never "inherited" (C1), never "she alone".
anchors.speaksTo: reasons that sound like nothing out loud

anchors.fact: Giannola, in her own words (relayed by the house): she and Benito "selected the best Friulian winemakers", with the finest picolit vineyards, for their pomace (H4).
anchors.meaning: She chose where to look. What she saw in it is ours to signpost ("I like to think she could…").
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: seeing the part

anchors.fact: In 1967, the house says, its single-variety "Aquavitae Optima" carried the year, the amount distilled, the litres made and the bottle's number on its label, the first of the tests that led to 1973 (H2). The house says it was single-variety pomace: conflict C6, so it's never called "single-grape" in the reading (audit v2 W2).
anchors.meaning: They put the working on the bottle, not only the verdict. Wren's bridge to the position, from the house's account ("the family says"). Never that a label named the grape (C3).
anchors.speaksTo: proposal: give the reason, not just the verdict

anchors.fact: Giannola says Isi Benini (no gloss: who he was isn't on the page) was at first "skeptical" and later one of their strongest supporters (H5).
anchors.meaning: One doubter, in her words, who came round. **Not** "everyone laughed"; no other mockery is on record.
anchors.speaksTo: what they hide: how unprovable the reasons are

anchors.fact: The ridicule abroad lasted into the early 1990s, nearly twenty years after 1973 (pdf 936; our arithmetic; C5). Others followed: Poli among them, with grappas "shockingly clean" (POLI pdf 1544).
anchors.meaning: A long wait before the world caught up. It is grappa's wait abroad, not a wait for her own success: never "nobody believed her".
anchors.speaksTo: the part seen long before anyone else

anchors.fact: Production has stayed fairly flat, mostly drunk in Italy (GRAPPA pdf 937); the traditional style has come back (POLI pdf 1544; F8–F9).
anchors.meaning: Right, but not all the way: the world took the idea, not the whole picture. A soft version of the fear, owned.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: what they hoped vs what came

anchors.fact: The house says the Noninos found old Friulian vines (schioppettino, pignolo, tazzelenghe) dying out because growing them was forbidden, and in 1975 founded a prize to have them recognised; they cite a 1977 decree allowing them. Their own stated reason: they wanted to distil those grapes (H8; L2).
anchors.kind: the part still to play (Wren's call)
anchors.meaning: Vines everyone had let go, seen for what they still had. Their own reason was self-interest, and it's told with it. House account only: "the family says", or dossier.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: nobody is ever finished in their eyes

cocktail.closingLine: Steep the leaf and leave the figs. When you see where someone's heading, give them your reasons too.
cocktail.glassware: small tulip-shaped grappa glass with an open rim (about 150 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Steep the fig leaf in the blanc vermouth at room temperature. Taste it after half an hour, and lift the pieces out by about an hour. The vermouth keeps in the fridge; this makes enough for ten drinks.
Put the tulip glass in the freezer to chill.
Pour the grappa, the fig-leaf vermouth and the syrup into a mixing glass or a jar. Fill it with ice and stir for about fifteen seconds.
Strain into the chilled glass. No garnish: the grape is what you should smell first.
cocktail.name: Already There

recipe.note: young, not wood-aged, made from one named grape; or any young, not wood-aged single-varietal grappa, 40% or stronger

recipe.item: blanc vermouth with fig leaf, homemade (below)
recipe.note: French blanc vermouth (Dolin Blanc style): pale, sweet and herbal
equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear

recipe.item: *for the fig-leaf vermouth:* 1 medium fresh fig leaf, 200 ml blanc vermouth
recipe.note: tear the leaf into three or four pieces, leave it in the vermouth at room temperature for about an hour, then lift it out. Keep the vermouth in the fridge. Fig-leaf sap can irritate skin: rinse your hands after tearing it

cocktail.tagline: You see who someone could become in the little things they do today.

reading.epigraph: The grappa here comes from one grape variety. Grappa made that way began in Friuli.
whoYouAre: There's someone in your life that everyone has quietly made up their mind about. You haven't. You noticed something once: the evening they stayed behind to fix a thing nobody would ever have checked. Since then you've talked about them as if their turn is coming. Usually it comes. And when people ask how you knew, you can't really say.

That's the part nobody hears. Your reasons are so small that, said out loud, they'd sound like nothing, so you hand over the conclusion and keep the reasons. It's also why you can seem a little mysterious. Underneath sits a worry you seldom admit: that what you saw in someone was only what you hoped to see, and they went ahead because you said so.

In your eyes, nobody is ever finished. People grow into the place you kept for them, and plenty never find out who kept it. Most people only get that kind of faith from someone who loves them. You hand it out on far less.
yours: Grappa is the spirit Italy distils from the wine press's leftovers, once the juice has run off. Italians have made it out of thrift since the 1700s or earlier. With spirits like it, the custom was to bury the pressed grapes until the wine was made, and only then put them in the still. Outside Italy, people laughed at it for years as rough "moonshine" made from the "dregs".

In 1973, Giannola and Benito Nonino, of Friuli in Italy's north-east, did something small and new. They distilled the leftovers of one grape, the picolit, on their own, and used them only fresh and lightly pressed: the first grappa from a single grape. In Giannola's words, she and Benito "selected the best Friulian winemakers" to get it. One early doubter, she says, came round to be one of their strongest supporters. And six years before, the family says, the first of their test bottlings had their working printed on its label: the year, how much they'd distilled, how many litres came out, the bottle's number.

Nothing was rescued. Grappa was already being made. They only looked at it differently, one grape at a time, and I like to think Giannola could already smell what was in the picolit that nobody had kept apart long enough to find. Abroad, the laughing went on for nearly twenty more years. And not everything went the way the new grappa promised: most grappa is still drunk in Italy, and the traditional style has come back. I recognise you in that. Not right about everything, but right about the part that mattered, years before most people could see it.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Martini, that renowned stirred classic, with Nonino's grappa from a single grape in place of the gin. It's stirred with a pale, sweet French vermouth that has spent an hour with a fresh fig leaf. A fig tree is grown mainly for its fruit, and yet its leaves are highly fragrant. I chose it as a nod to the Noninos looking twice at something everyone already used. There's nothing on top: the grape reaches you first.

When you next see where someone's heading, show them what you saw, not just where you think they'll end up, the way the Noninos, as the family tells it, printed their working on the label: the evening they stayed behind, the small thing they fixed. Then they aren't carrying your hope. They're holding your reasons, and they can grow into them at their own pace. When they get there, they'll know they did it themselves. And you won't be the only one who can see it anymore.

anchors.fact: Sol Stoumen held the liquor licence of the Black Cat Café in San Francisco. In 1949 the state Board of Equalization suspended it indefinitely, ruling that the bar was a "disorderly house" because gay men and women met there. There was a second count too: beer sold to someone under 21 (S1).
anchors.meaning: The power in this story is a piece of paper, and it was his, not theirs. That's the kind of strength this guest has: something they hold that the people beside them don't.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: power over the situation, not over people; point 1 (Wren r3: point 2 = he went on serving them while the state came for the licence over it, scoped to 1951–63 per A4)

anchors.fact: Stoumen "fought this decision" (NPS) and hired the lawyer Morris Lowenthal; the case went to the California Supreme Court, which in 1951 ordered the licence reinstated. From 1951 to 1955 the bar did well with the same crowd (NPS, F13). Kamiya counts "Stoumen's 14-year battle", through a second revocation in 1956 and appeals he lost (S2, F6–F7).
anchors.meaning: No shouting, no scene. He answered with a lawyer, and after the win he went on serving them while the state came back. Holding the line quietly, and paying for it slowly.
anchors.speaksTo: hides: the effort; point 3; never raises their voice

anchors.fact: In 1951 the court ruled for him. With no evidence of illegal or immoral conduct, their meeting there was no ground to suspend the licence. Members of the public had "a right to patronize a public restaurant and bar" while acting properly (S1).
anchors.meaning: What he defended, a court then wrote down as theirs by right. The protection wasn't a favour he did them. It was making the world admit something that was already theirs.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: safety without a fight; guard: never "the small ones"

anchors.fact: In 1963 the licence was finally taken, just before the bar's Halloween party. The party went ahead with no alcohol: per NPS, Stoumen "decided to stay open and serve soft drinks". Kamiya has a witness who recalls hundreds still there at 6 a.m., "drinking only soft drinks and juices" (S2, S3).
anchors.meaning: The power ran out, and he stayed open for them and poured soft drinks (NPS's "decided", one page; never "until morning"). This is the day the guest fears, and it's the answer to it.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: powerless to protect; point 4; position: when you can't stop it, stay with them

anchors.fact: Whether he weighed giving them up, and why he fought, is on no page.
anchors.meaning: Signposted only ("I like to think…"), never a claim about him.

cocktail.closingLine: Take your time over the peel. When strength can't help, your time still can.
cocktail.glassware: a tall glass, filled with ice
method: Peel the whole lemon with a vegetable peeler in one long, unbroken spiral, from top to bottom, taking as little of the white as you can. Go slowly: if it breaks, it still works, but the one long piece is the drink.
Lower the spiral into a tall glass and hook its top end over the rim. Fill the glass with ice, which holds the peel against the sides.
Pour in 45 ml of cognac.
Top with 120 ml of cold ginger ale, then lift the drink once, gently, with a long spoon.
cocktail.name: In One Piece

recipe.note: for the peel only: one unbroken spiral
any VSOP; deeper than a VS, so you taste it under the ginger ale
not ginger beer, and not a sweet golden ginger ale

cocktail.tagline: You make people feel safe without making them feel small.

reading.epigraph: In honour of a night when the bar could pour only soft drinks.
whoYouAre: You walk into a room and it shifts a little. People notice you, and some of them are wary before you've said a word. So you've learned to go slowly and speak softly, and let them find out for themselves.

People assume you were born gentle. You weren't. You decide it, again and again, and you've never told anyone how often. There's a temper in you, and you know just what it could do, most of all when someone is picking on a person who can't answer back. So you don't shout. You go and stand beside them, and the room settles. When you're there, nobody has to fight.
And there's a fear you never mention: the day being strong isn't enough, when it's happening to someone who matters to you, and nothing you've got can stop it.
yours: In 1949, the California board that issued liquor licences ruled that the Black Cat Café in San Francisco was a "disorderly house". Its reason for that was who drank there: gay men and women met at the Black Cat. The bar's owner, Sol Stoumen, stood to lose his licence. He fought it with a lawyer. Morris Lowenthal argued that the Black Cat's customers had the right to gather there, and in 1951 the state's Supreme Court agreed: people behaving properly in a bar have a right to be served. A right, not a favour.

He went on serving them, and the state came back. One San Francisco writer counts the whole fight as fourteen years, and just before the bar's Halloween party in 1963, the licence was taken. The party went ahead without alcohol. One witness remembers hundreds of people still there at six in the morning, drinking only soft drinks and juices.

I like to think that night says more about Sol Stoumen than the court case does: the licence was his power, it was gone, and he stayed open for them and poured soft drinks. People rarely see that side of you. Not the strength. What you do once the strength has run out.

The cocktail I've made for you is a classic, the Horse's Neck. In turn-of-the-century Atlantic City it was simply ginger ale with a long, long twist of lemon, and many liked theirs with a "stick" of rye or gin in it. A leading drinks reference calls cognac with ginger ale a "winter warmer", so cognac it is: a deeper, older one, which still comes through clearly underneath, even with a pale, dry ginger ale leading nearly three to one. Strength, there the whole time, never raised. The whole lemon is peeled in one unbroken spiral and hung down into the glass: with only ginger ale around it, that was once the whole drink. We don't know which soft drinks were poured at the Black Cat that night. The soft drink leads this glass for that night's sake.

There will be a day when being strong isn't enough: trouble you can't stop, happening to someone you'd stand in front of. Don't go home. Stay until morning, and give them whatever you've still got, even if all that's left is being there. It was never your strength they came to you for. It was you.

anchors.fact: George Smith (1792-1871), a tenant of the Duke of Gordon, made whisky illegally in Glenlivet from at least 1815 (Oxford GLENLIVET pdf 917).
anchors.meaning: Made without anyone's say-so, on ground that wasn't his.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's point 1; the gift (made before anyone allowed it)

anchors.fact: The glen's illicit whisky already had a name: in 1822 the King's Chamberlain looked everywhere for "pure Glenlivet", not to be had outside the Highlands, and the king reportedly drank nothing else (Oxford pdf 917; Grant, *Memoirs of a Highland Lady*, 1898, p. 373). Glenlivet's, not Smith's by name.
anchors.meaning: The people who made the rules wanted the forbidden thing.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's point 2; the hidden doubt (good, or only good because forbidden?)

anchors.fact: Grant (at home in the Highlands, not in Edinburgh; her father sent word) had her store of it emptied for the king's household. It was "long in wood, long in uncorked bottles, mild as milk", with "the true contraband goût in it" (Grant p. 373): long-aged, gentle, and prized partly for tasting forbidden. Paraphrase in the reading; quote at most "mild as milk".
anchors.meaning: The doubt is on the page: some of its charm was that it wasn't allowed. Yet what she describes first is how it was made: time, and gentleness.
anchors.speaksTo: the hidden doubt; the position (it stands on its own)

anchors.fact: The duke pushed the 1823 Excise Act to bring illicit distillers into the law, urged Smith to apply, and in 1824 his was the first licensed distillery in Speyside (Oxford pdf 917).
anchors.meaning: The way in is offered by the people in charge, and he takes it.

anchors.fact: His former colleagues threatened him when he applied (Oxford pdf 917, his own words). No fire, no pistols.
anchors.meaning: Saying yes cost him with his own side.

anchors.fact: Within his first years as a licensed distiller, others were already trading on his whisky's name (Oxford SPIRITS MEASURE pdf 1879, "in the 1820s"). By 1844 it was being sold in London as "the Real Glenlivet", the first scotch promoted there; he opened a second distillery in 1840 and moved to Minmore in 1859 (pdf 917).
anchors.meaning: After the yes it was still wanted, in his lifetime: the thing stood on its own, without the wall.

anchors.fact: The Glenlivet 12, recommended: "subtle, even delicate", a benchmark (Oxford pdf 918); today's bottle is fruit-led, "pineapple, apricot, white grapes and peach" on the nose (Dwyer, *The Whiskey Wash*, 2025, secondary). Today's bottle, from the distillery he licensed; not his whisky.
anchors.meaning: Whatever the spark does, it draws out what's already in the malt.

cocktail.closingLine: Stir it for twenty seconds, then leave it be. It holds up on its own.
cocktail.glassware: a small tumbler, one large ice cube
method: Make the syrup ahead: stir the sugar into the hot water until it's completely clear, then let it cool.
Put the syrup, the elderflower liqueur and the bitters in a small tumbler. Pour in the whisky.
Add one large ice cube and stir for 20 to 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold. Don't stir longer: more melted ice would thin the whisky.

Peel a strip of lemon peel, about the length of your thumb, with as little of the white as you can. Hold it skin side down over the glass and squeeze it so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Asked In

recipe.note: from the distillery George Smith licensed in 1824; or any unpeated Speyside single malt that isn't sherry-cask
brings up the flowers already in the whisky

recipe.item: *for the syrup:* 100 g white sugar, 50 ml hot water
recipe.note: stir until clear and let cool; makes about 110 ml, keeps a month in a closed jar in the fridge

cocktail.tagline: You show people what better looks like while they're still saying no.

reading.epigraph: Before anyone made it legally, a king's chamberlain was looking everywhere for whisky from this glen.
whoYouAre: Tell you no, and you'll make it anyway. Usually you'd already started. The best things you've made began without anyone's say-so, often on ground that wasn't yours, and they turned out better than what was allowed. A no has never stopped you. If anything, it shows you where to begin.

It's the yes you don't trust. When the people in charge finally want what you made, something in you goes cold, as if being let in were the first step to being owned. And underneath sits a question you've never quite asked anyone: is it good, or only good because it isn't allowed? What I see is this. Much of what everyone takes for granted now, someone like you made first, before anyone agreed it could be done. You show people what better looks like while they're still saying no, and it matters to far more people than ever say so.
yours: By 1822, the whisky made illegally in Glenlivet already had a name. When the king visited Edinburgh that year, a woman whose family sent some wrote later that his chamberlain was looking everywhere for it. Her father sent word to her at home to empty her own store, and it went to the palace. She remembered it as whisky that had waited a long time in the cask and then in the bottle, "mild as milk", with the real taste of contraband in it. As if being forbidden were part of the flavour.

Since at least 1815, one of Glenlivet's illegal distillers had been George Smith, a tenant of the Duke of Gordon. The duke had done much to promote a new law, in 1823, that encouraged distillers like him to "go legal", and he urged Smith to take out a licence. Smith did. In 1824 his became the first licensed distillery in Speyside, and his old colleagues threatened him.

I like to think Smith faced the question you carry: was it ever good, or only good because it was forbidden? What's on the record is what he did: he went on making it, in the open. Being let in didn't make it disappear. It made it the one others copied: within a few years, people were trading on its name, and within twenty, London was being sold his as "the Real Glenlivet".

The cocktail I've made for you starts from the Old-Fashioned, a renowned classic. The whisky is The Glenlivet 12 Year Old, from the distillery he licensed: a subtle, gentle malt. It's stirred cold over a single big cube with a teaspoon of sugar syrup and orange bitters, then finished with the oil from a lemon peel. The one addition is a tablespoon of elderflower liqueur, to bring up the flowers a well-known cocktail book already tastes in this whisky: "elegant and floral", it says. Nothing smoky, nothing raw: none of it tries to taste forbidden, as a nod to a whisky that never needed to be.

Make something that isn't against anything: no rule in its way, nobody to prove wrong. Then show it to the people whose approval you've never wanted. If they want it, that isn't the moment you lose. It's the moment you find out it was good. And you'll still be the one who made it.

anchors.fact: On 1 April 1979 four friends from the Oxford University Dangerous Sports Club jumped from the Clifton Suspension Bridge in Bristol on elastic rope, Kirke in top hat and tails: theirs were the first recorded bungee jumps (GWR; NYT 2023). The costume is on record for Kirke only.
anchors.meaning: Something everyone called mad, done among friends, on April Fools' Day.

anchors.fact: The rope wasn't tested. Kirke, 2019: "We were called the Dangerous Sports Club, and testing it first wouldn't have been particularly dangerous" (GWR; NYT via BristolLive). He added that he was confident: clever friends had worked out how far the ropes would stretch (*Independent* 2023, via the *Bristol Post*).
anchors.meaning: The danger made into a joke, and a choice made with friends, not blind.
anchors.speaksTo: test 4; the gift (fear turned into a laugh)

anchors.fact: As he tipped off the bridge: "The main thing going through my mind was 'Whoooppeeee'" (NYT, via BristolLive 2019). None of them made any money from it (ITV West Country 2019; NYT).
anchors.meaning: For the feeling, not money or a cause.

anchors.fact: Police at first took it for an April Fool's joke, then arrested all four; by Kirke's account the police were "very good humoured about it" (ITV News 2019). Fined (GWR; "a small fine", NYT) and released on condition / the understanding that they'd never do it again (GWR; *Telegraph* obituary).
anchors.meaning: The sensible answer, on the page, and it came with a smile. A cost that ends in a laugh.

anchors.fact: Six months later Kirke and others from the club jumped from the Golden Gate Bridge (WaPo 2023; *San Francisco Chronicle* archive: 9 Oct 1979, four detained); the club repeated it across the US and the world (GWR; *Telegraph*).
anchors.meaning: Nobody else got to decide it was over. Wren to weigh: a promise to the police, broken.
anchors.speaksTo: the fear (the choice taken away); Wren's call

anchors.fact: Kirke on why the club existed (to *Vanity Fair*, 2013, relayed by NYT and WaPo): what they hated was formal sports' "little, important bourgeois instructors" saying you had to pass "five-part exams" first. **The club's reason, not the jump's.**
anchors.meaning: Who's in charge: other people deciding, sensibly, what you may do.
anchors.speaksTo: the hidden thing (it's about who's in charge)

anchors.fact: 2019, looking back: "I'd do it all again … Life is very long without those brief moments" (*Country Life*). Injury context stays out.
anchors.meaning: The managed days frighten more than the edge.

anchors.fact: Years later he said he was glad his stunts ("shenanigans") had given people a bit of fun (*Telegraph* obituary, reported speech).
anchors.meaning: What they give, said out loud.

anchors.fact: "The printed invitations had already been posted, so there could be no chickening out" (*Country Life* 2019, the journalist's narration, same paragraph as Clifton). **Who posted them, and to whom, isn't on the page.**
anchors.meaning: Their own way back, closed before anyone could close it for them, **as interpretation** ("I like to think"), not as their stated reason.

anchors.fact: Sloe gin: sloes (blackthorn, *Prunus spinosa*) steeped in gin **sweetened with sugar** (Oxford pdf 1814, 1573). It comes sweetened, so the drink adds no syrup. **Veto: `nuts` as a generic style** (stones sometimes crushed, almond sometimes added: *Difford's*; Sipsmith); veto-free only as a named bottle whose maker says otherwise.
anchors.meaning: Small wild cousins of the plum, already sweet before anyone adds a thing.

anchors.fact: Cynar, "the obscure Italian amaro" (*Proper* p. 68), has artichoke among its many flavourings and "a reputation as being extremely bitter" (*Codex* p. 260); plum is one of cooked artichoke's surprise pairings (*Flavor Matrix* pdf 32: the vegetable, not Cynar).
anchors.meaning: What makes people flinch becomes the part of the night everyone remembers. Never "it's milder than it sounds".

cocktail.closingLine: Strain it fine. Then send the invitations.
cocktail.glassware: a coupe, chilled
method: Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Pour the sloe gin, the gin, the lemon juice and the Cynar into a shaker. There's no syrup: the sloe gin comes sweetened already.
Fill the shaker with ice, close it, and shake hard for 10 to 15 seconds.
Empty the coupe, then strain the drink into it through a fine strainer, so no chips of ice get in. No garnish.
cocktail.name: Whoopee

recipe.note: a traditional British sloe gin of 25% or more; it brings the colour and most of the sweetness. Bought sloe gins may contain almond: if you avoid nuts, don't make this one
any London dry gin of 40% or more
squeezed just before
a bitter liqueur with artichoke among its flavourings

cocktail.tagline: You'll jump off almost anything. As long as it was your idea.

reading.epigraph: There's artichoke in this glass. Say so, and people pull a face. Then they taste it.
whoYouAre: The cold lake in March. The rope swing nobody else will try. The plan that sounded mad at dinner and is happening by morning. Your friends groan. Then they come, and it turns into the night they're still telling people about years later.

People think you're chasing the rush. It's plainer than that. In the second you let go, nobody is in charge of you: not the sensible voice, not whoever insists you need a course first, not the life that gets planned for you a little more each year. The drop is the one kind of helpless you choose. The other kind, padded and polite, where everything's decided and nothing's yours, frightens you more than any height. Said aloud, that would come out as a complaint, and you'd rather laugh.
And the laugh is what you give. You take what scares everyone and make it a game they can all be in. Around you, people remember they're allowed to feel alive. That's no small thing to give a person.
yours: On 1 April 1979, four friends from an Oxford club that called itself the Dangerous Sports Club gathered on the Clifton Suspension Bridge in Bristol, high over the river, and stepped off on elastic rope. Theirs were the first recorded bungee jumps. One of them, David Kirke, in top hat and tails, had covered his face so that his mother wouldn't recognise him in the papers next morning.

The rope hadn't been tested. Clever friends had worked out how far it would stretch, and Kirke said later that for a club with that name, testing it first "wouldn't have been particularly dangerous". What went through his mind as he went over, he said, was "Whoooppeeee". The police had at first taken it for an April Fool's joke. By Kirke's account, the police were very good-humoured about it. They arrested all four, and let them go with a small fine, on the understanding they'd never do it again. Six months later, Kirke and others from the club jumped from the Golden Gate Bridge.

A journalist who met Kirke wrote that the printed invitations had already gone out, so there was no backing out. Who posted them, we don't know. I like to think someone did it on purpose, closing the way back before anyone else could close it for them. That's you: not the jump, the invitations. Kirke once said the club was against "little, important bourgeois instructors" telling people they had to pass exams before they were allowed to try a sport. Not the danger. Who gets to decide. And years later he said he was glad his stunts had given people some fun.

The cocktail I've made for you is a sour, one of the great classic shapes: sharp with lemon, sweet just enough. It starts from sloe gin, made by steeping sloes, small wild cousins of the plum, in gin with sugar. That turns it red and leaves it sweet already, so I add no syrup. I shake it hard with London dry gin and fresh lemon, and pour it into a coupe, chilled first. Then the surprise: a small measure of Cynar, an Italian bitter with artichoke among its many flavourings, and a reputation for being extremely bitter. A cookbook of surprising pairings puts cooked artichoke with plum, and here it gives the sweet sloe the bitter edge it needs. I put it in for you: you're the one who turns what makes people flinch into the part of the night everyone remembers.

So I'd never tell you to stop jumping. I'd point you at a bigger drop. It isn't off a bridge. It's the plan for your life that somebody sensible drew up, a little at a time, that you've half stopped noticing you never chose. You don't have to tear it up. Take one piece of it back, the way you'd step off an edge: decide, tell people, send the invitations, so there's no backing out. Kirke said life is very long without those brief moments. I'd add one thing. The long part can be yours too.

anchors.fact: Under a 1919 treaty that limited cheap foreign spirits, local distilling in Nigeria was banned, and ogogoro stayed illegal after independence in 1960 (Oxford, OGOGORO pdf 1417). **The ban's start year is contested** (PUNCH 2022: "an era of prohibition that began in 1910"), so the reading gives no start year beyond Oxford's treaty, and never says imports flooded in.
anchors.meaning: One rule for the foreign spirit and another for the local one. The unfair thing that "those are the rules" kept standing.
anchors.speaksTo: the unfair thing; Wren's fear (told to leave it to the people in charge)

anchors.fact: In 1968 the educator and activist Tai Solarin (1922–1994), a teetotaller, "contrived to get himself arrested for possessing the spirit", to dramatise the injustice of banning a local spirit while allowing foreign ones (Oxford pdf 1417). The motive is Oxford's, relayed from its 1968 newspaper source. **Only what he did; nothing he said or wrote.**
anchors.meaning: Not their fight, broken where everyone could see who did it. His not drinking shows he had nothing to gain from it, never a virtue.
anchors.speaksTo: test 1, 2; the one true thing ("It's rarely your fight")

anchors.fact: He was charged: "Solarin Freed of Gin Charge", *Lagos Daily Times*, 14 Sep 1968, p. 3 (cited in Oxford's bibliography, pdf 1418; the paper itself is unread). The charge was printed as "gin". **No place, no arrest date, no sentence, no time in a cell is on any page**: never "risked prison", never a police station. The 14th is the paper's date, not the day he was freed.
anchors.meaning: The cost was his, and it was meant to be seen. He paid for doing something instead of doing nothing.
anchors.speaksTo: test 4; "You'd rather pay for doing something…"

anchors.fact: "That finally changed in 1968, when" he did it (Oxford pdf 1417). **Cause at "when" strength, no stronger**; no law and no date of the change. Contested by secondaries that date legality to independence (PUNCH 2022; Olúpàyímọ, *Yoruba Studies Review* 2017, pp. 204–205) or "the early 1960s" (*Vanguard* 2015). The 1968 gin charge shows the ban was still enforced in 1968, so Oxford stands, at its own strength.
anchors.meaning: It worked: it broke for everyone, not one case at a time. Also what they give: a rule shown to be movable.
anchors.speaksTo: test 3; the position (break it once, where it's seen, so it breaks for everyone)

anchors.fact: Ogogoro, also called "local gin", is Nigeria's national spirit, distilled from the sap of the raffia or oil palm (Oxford pdf 1417). Gin was "the preferred spirit around the Gulf of Guinea" (same page). PUNCH (Adaorah Oduah, 29 Jul 2022) says the British smeared it as a "knockoff" of British gin: **secondary, a guard for the reading, not a fact for it** unless attributed.
anchors.meaning: The local spirit was never a copy of anything.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink; Wren's guard (fairness, not victory)

anchors.fact: Pedro's Premium Ògógóró: 40%, unaged, distilled from fermented palm sap in villages in Delta and Ogun states, then redistilled in Lagos (*Difford's Guide*, product page, fetched 2026-10-01). £58.95 per 50 cl (Artifex Drinks, fetched 2026-10-01). Stocked in Lagos, London, Nairobi and Accra (PUNCH 2022). Founded by Lola Pedro and Chibu Akukwe in 2017, first bottle on sale 2019 (PUNCH). **There's also a 5-year aged version (Artifex): the spec names the unaged one.** Difford's taste notes include coconut, but they describe flavour, not an ingredient.
anchors.meaning: Buyable, branded and made properly. Recommended, never unbranded (the safety guard).

anchors.fact: Splitting a Martini's base between spirits keeps its form (*Cocktail Codex* p. 71, Dean Martin; the Vesper on the same page splits gin with vodka). **The Codex's splits are unequal; equal halves are ours.**
anchors.meaning: Gin and the local spirit at the same measure: one rule for both, neither taking the other's seat. The twist, tied to the story in one clause. Near *One Table*'s equal thirds (rye and cognac, the Vieux Carré): owned in Checks; theirs is two sides at the same weight, ours one rule for both.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; Wren r1 (equals side by side)

cocktail.closingLine: Equal measures, no more of either. Then pick the rule that isn't fair, and break it where it can be seen.
cocktail.glassware: a Nick & Nora, chilled
method: Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Measure 30 ml of the ogogoro and 30 ml of the gin into a mixing glass or a jar.
Add the vermouth, the half barspoon of demerara syrup and the dash of orange bitters.
Fill with ice and stir for 20 to 30 seconds, until the outside of the mixing glass feels very cold.
Empty the glass, strain the drink into it, then squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, and drop it in.
cocktail.name: Can't Watch

recipe.note: a Nigerian spirit distilled from palm sap, 40%. Buy the unaged Premium, not the 5-year aged bottling. If you can't find it: another branded, unaged West African palm-sap spirit, never a homemade or unlabelled one
any London dry gin of 40% or more
an Italian-style red vermouth
one part demerara sugar dissolved in one part warm water, cooled
squeezed over the top

cocktail.tagline: You can't walk past an unfair fight, even when it isn't yours.

reading.epigraph: In 1968, a non-drinker got himself arrested for one of the spirits in this glass.
whoYouAre: Someone sighs: it's a pity, but those are the rules. You've already stopped listening. You're working out which rule it is, who it's really for, and what it would take to get round it by Friday. Not for you. Usually it isn't even your fight.

People put it down to nerve, or a taste for trouble. It's neither. It's that you can't watch. Being told to wait, to go through the proper channels, to leave it to the people who run things while it carries on happening: that's the thing that truly frightens you. And there's a part you'd never say out loud: some of it is for you. Doing something, even something that costs you, is how you stop feeling helpless.

So you fix it, quietly, one person at a time: a rule bent just for them, a back way found. It works. What it gives people is real: with you around, "those are the rules" stops being the end of the matter, and that matters more than you let yourself think. But you know the other half. The rule is still there in the morning, and so is the next person it lands on.
yours: For decades, Nigeria's own spirit was against the law. Ogogoro is distilled from the sap of palm trees. In colonial Nigeria a treaty banned distilling spirits locally, while foreign spirits could still be sold, gin above all. People made it anyway, more and more of them, and it stayed illegal even after independence in 1960.

In 1968, a Nigerian educator called Tai Solarin got himself arrested for having some. He did it on purpose, to show everyone how unfair it was to ban a local spirit and allow foreign ones. That September, a Lagos paper's headline read "Solarin Freed of Gin Charge". The ban ended that same year. And Tai Solarin didn't drink.

How it went, we don't know. I like to think he simply made the rule do, where everyone could see, the one thing it couldn't defend. It was never his drink. He picked the fight up anyway, and made sure the charge landed on him. I recognise you in that. If putting it right has to cost somebody, you'd rather it cost you.

The cocktail I've made for you is built like a Martini, the classic that needs no introduction: stirred, ice-cold and strong, poured into a little stemmed glass, chilled first. It stands on two spirits in equal measure: Pedro's, a Nigerian ogogoro distilled from palm sap in villages and then again in Lagos, and a London dry gin. Thirty millilitres of each, and neither stands in for the other. I split them as a nod to the point Tai Solarin got himself arrested to make: one rule for both, so neither gets the bigger share, the way you'd always have it. Sweet vermouth brings them together, with a little demerara syrup, which sits well with the toffee tasters find in Pedro's, and a dash of orange bitters. The orange oils, pressed from the peel above the glass, belong to both.

You'll go on fixing things one person at a time, and you should. But once, pick the rule that keeps sending you back, and stop working round it on the quiet. Do it where people can see who did it, so the rule has to answer for itself. Not for the thanks. So it changes for everyone, and you get the thing you've wanted all along: never having to watch that one again.

anchors.fact: Chartreuse is a monastic herbal liqueur made under Carthusian supervision, "in the foothills of the French Alps for most of its history" (Oxford pdf 439).
anchors.meaning: Where the no was said.

anchors.fact: Chartreuse's cocktail "golden age" is the cocktail renaissance, and it "probably has never been more popular" (Oxford pdf 440, c. 2021).
anchors.meaning: The world wanted more, right when they stopped.

anchors.fact: In 2021 the monks decided **not to increase** production, and in January 2023 a letter from Chartreuse to its trade partners ("dear valuable partner") announced allocation (*Daily Pour* 2023, quoting the letter; VinePair).
anchors.meaning: The refusal, dated. "Not more", never "less".

anchors.fact: The letter's primary goal: "protect their monastic life and devote their time to solitude and prayer"; and the monks "are not looking to grow the liquor beyond what they need to sustain their order" (*Daily Pour*).
anchors.meaning: The no says what it's for. That's the reading's position.

anchors.fact: The same letter sets allocation to "core and historical markets" and protects bar channels (*Daily Pour*).
anchors.meaning: It's a trade letter too. The hype reading is owned as the bartender's own first thought, never denied and never claimed.

anchors.fact: Shortages in places, backorders, some bartenders using stand-ins (Aperol in "The First Word") (VinePair, anecdotal).
anchors.meaning: The price of a no, paid in other people's disappointment. The order's lost sales are never stated.

anchors.fact: Armagnac is "France's oldest commercial spirit", older than cognac "by at least 150 years" (Oxford pdf 137).
anchors.meaning: Our choice of base. The story claims nothing for it.

anchors.fact: One tablespoon (15 ml) of yellow Chartreuse supplies most of the sugar in an Armagnac Old-Fashioned (spec v2; Codex p. 29, a sweet liqueur in place of sugar).
anchors.meaning: "Only what's needed", in the glass: our nod, signposted.

anchors.fact: Yellow Chartreuse's flavour is "honeyed and herbal" (*Codex* p. 188); the drink at 31.3% / 7.11 g sits just under Arnold's built centre (spec v2, `balance.py`): "strong… only lightly sweet", never "dry".
anchors.meaning: The glass described in the source's terms.

anchors.fact: The letter covers "the Chartreuse liqueurs", plural (C7): yellow is under the same allocation. The 43% and the product list are *The Daily Pour*'s narration (C10), not the letter.
anchors.meaning: "A bottle that's hard to find" is true of the bottle in the glass.

cocktail.closingLine: One level spoonful of the Chartreuse, and no more. Then pour one for someone who's only heard you refuse.
cocktail.glassware: an old-fashioned glass, ice cubes
method: Make the syrup ahead: stir the sugar into the hot water until it's completely clear, then let it cool.
Fill a level tablespoon with yellow Chartreuse and tip it into an old-fashioned glass. Add the half teaspoon of syrup and the bitters, then pour in the Armagnac.
Fill the glass with ice cubes and stir for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Peel a strip of lemon peel about the length of your thumb, with as little of the white as you can. Hold it skin side down over the glass and squeeze it so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Kept

recipe.note: France's oldest commercial spirit, a grape brandy from Gascony; any blended VS or VSOP Armagnac at 40%. If yours is stronger, see the note below
the Carthusians' herbal liqueur, and most of the drink's sweetness. One spoonful, and no more

recipe.item: *for the syrup:* 100 g white sugar, 50 ml hot water
recipe.note: stir until clear and let cool; makes about 110 ml, keeps a month in a closed jar in the fridge
pour less of it and make up to 60 ml with cold water: 56 ml + 4 ml water at 43%, 53 ml + 7 ml at 45%, 50 ml + 10 ml at 48%, 46 ml + 14 ml at 52%, 43 ml + 17 ml at 56%

cocktail.tagline: You keep your promise to yourself, even when compromise sounds reasonable.

reading.epigraph: The makers of one bottle in this glass chose not to make more.
whoYouAre: Everyone at the table is nodding along to something that isn't true, and you can feel your face giving you away. Not because you love an argument. You can spot something put on, and you've never learned how to stop noticing.

Underneath sits a promise, made a long time ago, about the person you'd never turn into. You check on it more often than anyone would guess. What scares you is how gently the change would come: nobody forcing you, no moment you'd notice, only your own good reasons, one after another, until you're someone you once swore you'd never be.

You never got used to it, and the people who live and work beside you are better off for it. When you say so, they remember what they meant before they stopped noticing. Without someone like you, a room can talk itself into almost anything.
yours: Chartreuse is a monks' liqueur of herbs, made in the foothills of the French Alps. By around 2021 it had probably never been more popular. The new wave of cocktail bars had made it a favourite, and more and more people wanted it.

So, quietly, the monks decided not to make more than they already did. In January 2023, a letter from Chartreuse told the businesses that sell it that from then on there would only be a set amount for each of them. The first reason it gave was to protect the monks' life of solitude and prayer, and it said they had no wish to make more than the order needed to keep going. In many places, shelves emptied. Some bartenders who'd built drinks around it had to find stand-ins.

If you're suspecting a clever way to make a bottle more wanted, I wondered that too, at first. But the reason was put in writing, to the very businesses asking for more. Nobody was wrong to love it. I like to think the monks simply wouldn't turn into a bigger version of themselves, one with no room left for the life they'd chosen, and that their no wasn't there to push anyone away, only to hold on to something. I hear the same no in you.

So for you I chose the Old-Fashioned, as renowned as classics get, and built it on Armagnac, a French brandy older than cognac by at least a century and a half. Just one tablespoon of yellow Chartreuse goes in, and it does most of the sweetening, as a nod to the monks: one spoonful is all it needs. Stirred cold over ice with bitters, a strip of lemon peel squeezed over it at the end, it's deep, warm brandy with a honeyed, herbal edge: strong, golden and only lightly sweet. And a bottle that's hard to find goes a long way here.

Keep the promise. But most people know you by what you turn down. Let someone see what it's protecting: what you love, up close, before anyone gets the chance to argue. A refusal starts arguments. Something you love, shown to someone, tends to end them. And then you're known for what you love, not only for what you refuse.

anchors.fact: During the war, Rupert Grant, a Trinidad calypso singer whose stage name was Lord Invader, wrote the words of "Rum and Coca-Cola" (*Khan*, Finding 1; month conflicts across sources, so no month). It was a hit on the island, and the 1948 court says both soldiers and islanders sang it a great deal (*Baron*; "together" and "as much as" are not on the page: audit A1, my own shorthand struck).
anchors.meaning: A joke aimed at the people with the money, sung openly, and the people it was about sang along.
anchors.speaksTo: test 1; the one true thing (the joke gets a true thing past the people it's about)

anchors.fact: The 1947 judge read its chorus as a comment on a change in Trinidad's economy, too big for the calypso tents to leave alone (*Khan*). SFW p. 4: calypsonians called the American bases, slyly, "the American social invasion".
anchors.meaning: What it laughed at was the soldiers' dollars and what they were doing to the island. **Never the women, never the lyric's subject** (Wren).
anchors.speaksTo: test 1; the gift (the thing in charge seen at its real size)

anchors.fact: Mohamed Khan, who ran the tent Grant sang in, testified that calypsos had to go before a police-chaired board of censors before anyone could perform them, and that this one did (*Khan*).
anchors.meaning: Said under watch, and it still got through. **Khan's testimony about the tent's routine; nothing says the censors objected.**
anchors.speaksTo: test 1; what they hide (how much they mean it)

anchors.fact: Morey Amsterdam, an American comedian, came to Trinidad in September 1943 as a USO entertainer (*Baron*), heard it, took it home, and copyrighted it in 1944 as his own work (with Sullavan and Baron) (*Khan*; SFW p. 4). The Andrews Sisters' record was a hit, and its first 200,000 copies credited Amsterdam with the words and the music (*Baron*).
anchors.meaning: The joke taken by another joker, and sung back by millions who never heard what it was about.
anchors.speaksTo: test 2; the fear (the joke taken, sung back harmless)

anchors.fact: Many US radio networks at first refused to play it, as a song about an alcoholic drink (Oxford pdf 504). SFW p. 14 adds advertising and the lyrics.
anchors.meaning: The bite wasn't the problem: the drink was. **Never "banned for its bite".**
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's guard; test 2 only as the drink

anchors.fact: The New York court found that Grant wrote the words (Finding 1) and that the taking was "deliberate and intentional" (*Khan*; dossier only since v3, cut for length, not corrected). It accepted his own protest that he was the composer as the basis of the decision. **The plaintiff was Khan, who held the rights** (Grant on the stand: "I don't own no rights"). The tune was Lionel Belasco's 1906 "L'Année Passée", which Grant had learned and changed a few notes of (*Baron*).
anchors.meaning: It landed on the record as true: a court wrote down whose words they were. **"His words", never "his song" or "his tune"; never "he sued", "he won", "he got it back".**

anchors.fact: In January 1946, with the case still open, he recorded "Yankee Dollar" in New York. *Down Beat* called it "a sort of sequel" (SFW pp. 12–13). Its chorus makes his own hit the punchline: having sung "Rum and Coca-Cola" gets him nowhere without the dollars.
anchors.meaning: He didn't stop to grieve the stolen joke. He made a new one, partly at his own expense. **Chorus only; the verses are about women.** "At his own expense" is our reading.

anchors.fact: In March 1959 he recorded "Crisis in Arkansas" (Folkways FW 8733), aimed at Governor Faubus, who had kept nine Black students out of Little Rock's Central High in 1957. Its chorus teases the governor for wearing a black bow tie and tuxedo while he called Black people names (SFW pp. 23–24).
anchors.meaning: Years after the theft he was still laughing up, at a man in power, out loud. **Bow-tie joke only;** Wren rules on "political side today" (my view: segregation is history, not a party).
anchors.speaksTo: test 3; test 1; the one true thing

anchors.fact: The defendants didn't pay him until seven years later. Folkways letters show he was always short of money, even after the settlement (SFW pp. 4–5). He kept recording for Moses Asch until a last session on 6 June 1961, months before he died (SFW pp. 5–6; **death year conflicts inside SFW: no year**).
anchors.meaning: The ending holds, at a price: the court gave him the words, not a fortune. What he kept was the next song. **No dollar figure** ($132,000 vs $150,000).
anchors.speaksTo: test 5; the fear (powerlessness answered by the next joke, not by money)

anchors.fact: Rum with Coca-Cola is older than the song: it was already popular in Venezuela by 1911 (Oxford pdf 107). The Cuba Libre is "also known as" Rum and Coca-Cola (Oxford pdf 613). *Joy* says the song made it popular in the 1940s (pdf 71).
anchors.meaning: The everyday drink the song made famous. **Never "his drink" or "he named it".** Tomás: call it "rum and Coca-Cola" in the text.

anchors.fact: In the classic Cuba Libre, lime juice lifts a plain rum and Coke, because lime peel is a key ingredient in most colas: the juice brings that out and cuts the sweetness (*Codex* p. 213). *Joy* (pdf 272–273, under CUBA LIBRE): it needs at least an ounce of lime to balance the cola; seldom thought much of, but heavenly when made properly.
anchors.meaning: The sweet, cheerful drink everyone sang along to, made with the bite left in. **"Most colas" is the *Codex*'s scope: never "Coca-Cola's recipe has lime" or "what the cola was hiding"** (it's secret, card C2; audit A6). The *Codex* classic is white rum over three cubes: ours is a riff (aged rum, full glass, bitters, and the lime doubled from the *Codex*'s ¼ oz to 15 ml; *Joy* asks for at least an ounce, so never "twice the usual": audit v2 B1).

anchors.fact: Angostura bitters are made in Trinidad (*Codex* p. 14); there a bottle sits on every table, for cooking and as a condiment (Oxford pdf 111). The recommended rum, Angostura 1919, comes from the same company's distillery (rum from the 1930s, Trinidad Distillers from 1949: Oxford pdf 114); the substitute rum isn't Trinidadian, so the reading says "the rum I'd reach for" (audit A5).
anchors.meaning: The island's own bitter on top of the famous sweet drink. A joke always tastes of where it was made. **Our interpretation.**

anchors.fact: No page describes a Trinidad rum style. The only Trinidad rum page is one company's: Angostura's rums, column-distilled and aged in bourbon barrels (Oxford pdf 114), from a distillery founded in 1949, after the song.
anchors.meaning: If the base is Trinidadian it's a named, recommended bottle, never "a Trinidad-style rum".

anchors.fact: Two published historical Coca-Cola formulas (Beal's notebook, in the *Atlanta Journal-Constitution*, 1979; Pemberton's, via Pendergrast) list nutmeg oil (This American Life, "The Recipe", 2011). Coca-Cola says the real formula is still secret (Reuters via NBC, 2011). No library page either way.
anchors.meaning: The safe side was `nuts` (Tomás's call). Ruled none by Robin 2026-10-06 (D1): a published historical formula is not a stated ingredient.

cocktail.closingLine: Squeeze the lime and drop it in. If they sing it back wrong, write a new one.
cocktail.glassware: a tall glass, filled with ice
method: Fill a tall glass with ice and pour in the rum. Stir for three seconds.
Squeeze in the lime, then drop the squeezed half into the glass.
Pour the cola gently down the side, and stir once.
Shake two dashes of bitters onto the top, so the first thing you smell is the island.
cocktail.name: With the Bite In

recipe.item: Angostura 1919 aged rum (recommended), or any column-distilled aged rum, not spiced, about 40%
recipe.note: from Trinidad, made by the same house as the bitters
about half a lime; keep the squeezed half
fridge-cold, freshly opened
on top, last
dropped into the glass, not muddled

cocktail.tagline: Your jokes give people the nerve to question who's in charge.

reading.epigraph: A song made rum and Coca-Cola famous. The song was never really about the drink.
whoYouAre: There's a meeting, or a family dinner, or a rule nobody's supposed to question, and everyone's nodding along. Then you say something, lightly, and the table laughs, the person at the head of it too, a beat late. Nobody can quite tell you off. It was only funny. That was the idea.

Nobody notices that you chose it. The joke isn't a reflex, and it never punches down. It's aimed at whoever's at the head of the table, because that's the one place a plain sentence would be stopped. So you keep quiet about how much of it you mean: the moment they know, they stop laughing and start stopping you. A telling-off you can live with; it means it landed. What you dread is hearing your line from somebody else, everyone laughing, with the point quietly taken out.

And what you give is more than a laugh. When a room laughs at whatever's in charge, it sees how ordinary the thing really is, and fears it less. That's how you hand people their nerve back, and it's a real gift, whatever you call it.
yours: In wartime Trinidad, with an American base on the island, a calypso singer called Lord Invader set new words to an old tune by Lionel Belasco. Where he sang, songs had to get past the police commissioner's board of censors. His got through. It was called "Rum and Coca-Cola", it laughed at what the soldiers' money was doing to the island, and soldiers and Trinidadians alike sang it.

In 1943 an American comedian, Morey Amsterdam, heard it while entertaining the troops and took it home. The Andrews Sisters made it a hit, and the first 200,000 records named Amsterdam as the writer. A New York court later found that Lord Invader had written the words. The money reached him seven years late, and even then he was often short.

While the case went on, he recorded "Yankee Dollar", a follow-up that turned the joke on himself: the man who'd sung the hit, still without the dollars. Years later came "Crisis in Arkansas", which laughed at the black bow tie of the governor who had kept nine Black students out of a Little Rock school. I like to think he'd worked out what you know: someone can take a line, but never the place it came from.

The cocktail I've made for you is rum and Coca-Cola. It's older than the song, and simple, but made properly it's a classic worth asking for by name, long and cold over plenty of ice. The rum I'd pick is from Trinidad, from the same house as the Angostura bitters that go on last, so the island reaches you before anything else. And the lime, squeezed and dropped into the glass, to cut through the cola's sweetness. I doubled the lime in the recipe I started from, as a nod to the song: sweet enough for everyone to sing, and still sharp.

One day you'll hear a line of yours from someone else, to a big laugh, with the point gone. Don't spend the evening proving it was yours. Come up with another, and aim it a little higher than the last. A joke can be borrowed; the person it came from can't, and every room that laughed with you is a little braver for it.

anchors.fact: In 1879 Stevenson crossed the Atlantic and then the continent to reach Fanny in California (Sanchez, *Life of Mrs. R. L. Stevenson*, 1920, ch. V; the *Amateur Emigrant* dedication is signed 1879). He sailed from Glasgow and touched at Greenock; no port in the reading. He didn't go steerage: he took the second cabin, which sat in the middle of the steerage decks, so he'd have a table to write at (*The Amateur Emigrant*, "The Second Cabin", Gutenberg #627).
anchors.meaning: Going towards someone, at a cost, with no way back.
anchors.speaksTo: story test 1–2; the one true thing (rebels towards someone)

anchors.fact: His parents objected at first: not to her divorce, but to his choosing an American and a stranger. Once they saw his mind was made up for good, they gave way completely, promised an allowance and got ready to welcome her (Sanchez ch. V). His father's help after the wedding was generous and freely given (Colvin, intro to the *Letters*, Gutenberg #31809).
anchors.meaning: The world bent to a mind made up. One clause in the middle, never the ending (*Asked In* owns being let in).

anchors.fact: They went quietly "across the bay" and married on 19 May 1880 (the city is not on the page), with two witnesses, and took Fanny's son Sam, about twelve, with them (Sanchez ch. V).
anchors.meaning: The start of the life, not the end of the chase.

anchors.fact: That summer four of them squatted in an abandoned miners' bunkhouse on Mount Saint Helena. He called himself and Fanny the King and Queen of Silverado, Sam the Crown Prince, and Chuchu the dog (a setter crossed with a spaniel) the Grand Duke. Their first act of taking the place was cutting out the poison oak growing inside (*The Silverado Squatters*, "The Act of Squatting", Gutenberg #516).
anchors.meaning: A stop made on their own ground, and they crowned themselves in it.
anchors.speaksTo: test 3; Wren's position (stop where you choose)

anchors.fact: Why the mountain: his health and their purse. Fanny was told nothing else would save his life, and they couldn't afford a resort (her 1883 letter, via Sanchez ch. V; also the fog, same chapter). "Rent-free, into a ready-made house" is what tempted him, said of the idea and of another place (Pine Flat) first.
anchors.meaning: The reading gives no reason for the mountain and never says they went up to be free.

anchors.fact: They kept their wine in the old mine tunnel (*Silverado*, "Episodes in the Story of a Mine"); Nellie says the tunnel's mouth was the one place that was always cool (Sanchez ch. V).
anchors.meaning: The cold, dark place the wine waits in: the drink's overnight step.

anchors.fact: At night one candle stood in the neck of a pint bottle, and, seen from outside on the platform where he walked, the cracked old house seemed to burst with light through its chinks; you'd have taken it for a fire. A traveller on the far hills, if one had been there, would have stopped to watch it (*Silverado*, the book's last paragraph).
anchors.meaning: A life that stopped still looked, from outside, like something burning. The watcher is an "if": never "people saw".

anchors.fact: In Schram's cellar, "the oldest vineyard in the valley" (eighteen years old, Stevenson guessed), he tasted everything, including a "Hock" and a Golden Chasselas, while Fanny sat on the veranda with Mrs Schram (*Silverado*, "Napa Wine").
anchors.meaning: The wine of the place they'd chosen, on his own page.

anchors.fact: Oxford traces the Highball back to white wine and soda water, the Austrian Spritzer (HIGHBALL, pdf 1005). **Owned link, one clause:** Schram's "Hock" was a Californian wine sold under the German style name, and "hock" is the word Oxford uses for German white wine. We never say Stevenson drank wine and soda, a Spritzer or a Highball. Byron stays out (hangover cure: medicine; and the Thrill Seeker's backup).
anchors.meaning: Our long glass descends from a drink made with the kind of wine he tasted.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; "let the drink sound worth having"

anchors.fact: At sunrise and late at night the scent of sweet bay filled the canyon (*Silverado*, "Toils and Pleasures"); bay also among the afternoon smells in "The Act of Squatting". The page doesn't say which tree; our kitchen bay leaf is a stand-in, never "his bay", and never a reason to pick a wild leaf.
anchors.meaning: The scent of the place, put in the bottle before the pour.
anchors.speaksTo: the spark (Wren rules on the *Just Knew* echo)

anchors.fact: The marriage gave them "fourteen rich years" together, Nellie wrote, counting from the wedding (Sanchez ch. V). In Samoa, she says, "home" first meant something to them: they bought land near Apia, named the place Vailima ("five waters", for its stream) and set about clearing the forest, with hired Samoan workers, and building the house (ch. VIII, printed p. 167). To the end it was their custom (Sanchez uses the phrase in ch. VII and ch. VIII) that he brought her each morning's writing for her verdict (ch. VIII).
anchors.meaning: It holds past the page: they stopped again, on ground they chose, and the love didn't cool.
anchors.speaksTo: test 4; the Lover's fear (love going cold) answered

anchors.fact: Stevenson put a line of Cicero over the book (*De Officiis* I.xx). In Walter Miller's translation (Loeb 1913), such people living quietly in the country have kings' aims, "to be subject to no authority, to enjoy their liberty, that is, in its essence, to live just as they please" (§70). Counterweight: Cicero goes straight on to rank public life higher (§70–71).
anchors.meaning: Stevenson's own framing of stopping as freedom, his choice of where to cut, not Cicero's verdict.

anchors.fact: A colder liquid holds more dissolved CO2 at the same pressure (*Liquid Intelligence*, printed p. 289).
anchors.meaning: Why the wine waits cold.

cocktail.closingLine: Ice first, soda last. Then pour it where you mean to land, and unpack.
cocktail.glassware: a tall stemmed wine glass, filled with ice
method: The evening before, push one dried bay leaf into a bottle of dry California white, put the cork back in, and stand the bottle in the coldest, darkest corner of the fridge. The leaf stays in the bottle.
Put the soda water in the fridge too.
Fill a tall stemmed wine glass with ice.
Pour in 135 ml of the cold wine.
Top it with 45 ml of cold soda, poured gently so it keeps its bubbles, and give it one slow turn with a spoon.
cocktail.name: Rent-Free

recipe.item: dry California white wine (crisp and unoaked, a dry Riesling style), with a bay leaf left in the bottle overnight
recipe.note: he tasted one sold as "Hock" in a Napa cellar; kept cold in the dark, the way they kept theirs in the tunnel
goes into the wine bottle, and stays there

cocktail.tagline: You make choosing someone feel like choosing freedom.

reading.epigraph: Its wine spends a night in the cold, as two newlyweds kept theirs: in a mine.
whoYouAre: A one-way ticket. A job left on a Friday. A family dinner where you finally told them, and the table went quiet. You've chosen people, places and whole lives like that: all at once, and usually against advice. And every time, choosing and getting free felt like the same thing. Whoever you fell for was also the way out.

You'd never tell anyone how much you'd like to land somewhere. It feels like giving in. Being parked is the real fear: someone else deciding where you stop, and the life you ran towards slowly picking up the rules of the one you ran from.
And whoever you choose never has to guess. They know they were picked over everything else. Next to you, love looks like courage, and anyone watching starts asking what they'd leave for theirs.
yours: In 1879 a young Scottish writer, Robert Louis Stevenson, crossed the Atlantic and then the whole of America to reach Fanny, an American, in California. The next spring, they married. His parents had objected, because she was "an American and a stranger", and when they saw his mind was made up, they gave in completely.

After the wedding, they moved into an abandoned miners' bunkhouse high on a mountain above the Napa Valley, with Fanny's son and their dog, and lived there as squatters. What had tempted him was the idea of going "rent-free, into a ready-made house". He crowned the two of them "the King and Queen of Silverado", and his first job, to take possession, was cutting out the poison oak that had grown up through the floor. They kept their wine in the old mine tunnel, the one place on that hot hillside that stayed cool.

His book about that summer ends at night, with a single candle stuck in the neck of a bottle. From outside, he wrote, the old cracked house seemed to burst with light, and anyone out on the far hills would have stopped to watch. I like to think that's what stopping looks like for you: not being caught, but choosing the place, and making it as wild as the road. Years later, in Samoa, they bought land, set about clearing it and building a house, and called the place Vailima. Fanny's sister wrote that it was there "home" first came to mean something to them, and he was still bringing her each morning's writing to judge.

The cocktail I've made for you is a wine highball: white wine and soda, one of the long, light drinks the highball is traced back to. In a Napa cellar he tasted a wine sold as "Hock", the English name for German white wine, so here it's a crisp, dry California white. The evening before, one bay leaf goes into the bottle, and the bottle goes into the coldest, darkest corner of the fridge, as a nod to the tunnel, and to a canyon he wrote smelled of sweet bay at sunrise and late at night. Then it's poured over ice into a tall stemmed wine glass, and topped with soda straight from the fridge.

When the pull to go comes again, ask yourself what you'd be leaving. If it's someone deciding for you, go. If it isn't, stop, on purpose, in a place of your choosing, and make that the adventure. Being caught means someone else chose where you'd end up. Stopping means you did.

anchors.fact: The Gaja house in Barbaresco was founded in 1859. Angelo took over at 21, in 1961, and he's credited with bringing Barbaresco out of obscurity. In the 1980s his single-vineyard Barbarescos made a sensation (O'Keefe, *The Wine News*, 2006).
anchors.meaning: He built the very thing he would later take apart.

anchors.fact: As those single vineyards grew in prestige, the family's own Barbaresco, from fourteen vineyards and always the house's "historic wine", started being called "normale" or "basic" and seen as lesser, "which I never intended" (Gaja, to O'Keefe, 2006).
anchors.meaning: Something good dying politely: the house's oldest wine demoted by habit, and by his own success.

anchors.fact: In late 1999, starting with the 1996 vintage, he moved his single-vineyard Barbarescos out of Barbaresco's top classification to the wider regional name (Langhe Nebbiolo, per O'Keefe). He said it was "in support of Barbaresco", so the house would have "one Barbaresco only" (O'Keefe 2006).
anchors.meaning: He broke the thing he loved, on purpose, and said why.

anchors.fact: The move also let him add a little Barbera, which Barbaresco's rules prohibit. He said it was for freshness, which Nebbiolo sometimes lacks in hot years (O'Keefe 2006; Decanter 2019 twice; the percentage differs, 5% or "up to 15%").
anchors.meaning: Two reasons, both his. The reading never says it was only for the family wine. Say "a little Barbera", no number.

anchors.fact: It shocked the wine world. Rumours said he wanted foreign grapes, critics in Italy and abroad lamented Barbaresco's reputation, and he knew what journalists "have said and continue to say" (O'Keefe 2006).
anchors.meaning: Blamed for the break, not thanked for the reason.

anchors.fact: The predicted exodus after him didn't happen. Barbaresco's producers held firm on the wine's character, and O'Keefe judged that this gave Barbaresco "a sense of identity" (2006).
anchors.meaning: The thing he was blamed for damaging stood up for itself.

anchors.fact: From the 2013 vintage, Gaia Gaja and her siblings took the three single-vineyard wines back into Barbaresco, now all Nebbiolo, "thanks also to the support of our father"; "every generation has its own path to follow" (Decanter 2019). Still labelled Barbaresco DOP, 2020–2023 vintages (US importer's page, fetched 2026-10-01).
anchors.meaning: What grew back was the old thing itself, by the next hands, with his blessing, and it holds today.

anchors.fact: The syrup's wine, a young Langhe Nebbiolo, carries the very regional name Gaja moved his single-vineyard Barbarescos down to (O'Keefe 2006: "to Langhe Nebbiolo DOC"; Decanter 2019: "the 'Langhe' denomination"). Owned in one clause (audit v2, O1).
anchors.meaning: The plain name holds the drink: a coincidence, said as one, never as his choice.

anchors.fact: Grappa is Italian pomace brandy: the skins, seeds and stems left after grapes are pressed for wine. The young kind (giovane) rests at least six months in steel or glass. It's sold at a minimum of 37.5% (Oxford GRAPPA pdf 935).
anchors.meaning: The part the winemaker leaves behind, made into the drink's core.

cocktail.closingLine: Warm the wine, never boil it. Then take apart what you love, and leave room for someone to put it back.
cocktail.glassware: a heavy old-fashioned glass, one large cube
method: Make the syrup ahead. Put the Nebbiolo and the sugar in a small pan over low heat and stir until the sugar has dissolved. Don't let it boil: it should still taste of the wine. Let it cool, then bottle it and keep it in the fridge.
Put the syrup and the bitters in the glass. Add the grappa and stir to mix.
Add the large ice cube and stir about fifteen times, until the glass feels cold. Serve it straight away, with no garnish.
cocktail.name: For Its Own Good

preparations.text: (makes about 400 ml; keeps in the fridge for about a week, my estimate): 250 ml dry young Nebbiolo (a Langhe Nebbiolo) and 250 g white sugar.
preparations.title: Nebbiolo syrup

recipe.note: giovane or bianco, not wood-aged, 37.5-43% (a Piedmont grappa, if you can find one); Italy's spirit made from the skins, seeds and stems left once grapes are pressed for wine
a young Langhe Nebbiolo warmed with its own weight of sugar; it's the only sweetness in the drink

cocktail.tagline: You know when letting something end is how you keep it alive.

reading.epigraph: This glass's grape made one winemaker famous. Then he demoted his own famous wines.
whoYouAre: Someone says "but that's how it's always been", and you feel it before you can explain it. It's still standing, but it stopped being alive a while ago: the trip nobody enjoys any more, the group that meets because it always has, the way of working everyone defends and nobody would choose today. Sooner or later you're the one who says so. Then you're the one who ends it, and the one they're cross with.

You only ever break the things you love. Nobody fights that hard over something they don't care about. And afterwards you miss it, often more than the ones who were angry with you. You tell no one, in case it's taken for an apology. Your real fear is quieter than any row. It's something good being kept going out of politeness, year after year, until nobody remembers why it mattered, and you, who saw it, said nothing.

Because of you, the thing they loved gets a second life, the cross ones included. They rarely thank you at the time. But what grows back is usually better, and very often it's still theirs. That's love too: the kind that's willing to end things.
yours: Angelo Gaja's family house in Barbaresco, in north-west Italy, was founded in 1859. He's credited with bringing Barbaresco, a wine made from the Nebbiolo grape, out of obscurity. His single-vineyard wines became famous.

But as they grew famous, the family's own Barbaresco, always the house's "historic wine", started being called "normale", the lesser bottle. "Which I never intended," he said. So, starting with the 1996 vintage, he took those single-vineyard wines out of Barbaresco's top classification, down to a plainer regional name. In his words, it was "in support of Barbaresco", so that the house would have one Barbaresco only. It also freed him to add a little Barbera, which the rules didn't allow, for freshness, he said. So there were two reasons, and both were his. It shocked the wine world, and critics mourned Barbaresco's reputation.

I like to think the first reason was the one that mattered to him: his own famous wines taken down a rank, so the house's own would stop being second best. And look at what grew back. Barbaresco's other producers held to what it was, and a wine writer living in Italy judged that it gave Barbaresco a sense of identity. Then, from the 2013 vintage, his children brought those three wines back into Barbaresco, all Nebbiolo now, with his support. "Every generation has its own path to follow," his daughter Gaia said.

The cocktail I've made for you is a grappa Old-Fashioned: the famous classic, built on young grappa, Italy's spirit made from the skins, seeds and stems left once grapes are pressed for wine. Its only sweetness is a syrup of young Langhe Nebbiolo, warmed gently with sugar and never boiled. As it happens, that's the plainer name his famous wines were moved down to. I chose it as a nod to the family wine he put first, the one people had started calling basic: here, a plain young wine is what holds the drink together. Then orange bitters, two dashes, and one big cube; it's stirred only until the tumbler feels cold. No garnish. Strong and cold, with the red wine underneath.

When you next end something you love, say why while you're doing it: that it's for the thing's sake. Then leave the rebuilding to someone else, even if they bring back something that looks a lot like the old way. That isn't your break being undone. It's what it was for. And you get to love the thing again, without carrying it alone.

anchors.fact: Roy Olmstead, a Seattle police lieutenant fired after his 1920 arrest, became the biggest bootlegger on Puget Sound, with a business of bookkeepers, salesmen, drivers and lawyers (HL; LII facts: "not less than 50 persons"). (F2, F5)
anchors.meaning: He knew how things really get done, from the inside.

anchors.fact: He was no saint: as an officer he took bribes and sold probation recommendations, and as a bootlegger he paid off Seattle police and King County sheriffs; the Supreme Court's own facts record his promises of payments to officers (FJC pp. 7, 29; LII). (F3, F4)
anchors.meaning: Must be owned in one plain clause. The reading never implies he was clean; the mirror is the one rule, not the man.

anchors.fact: He did not allow his employees to carry guns, and told his men a lost shipment was better than a lost life (HL, reported speech; HW words it differently). In a trade HL calls "inherently hazardous and violent". (F5, F6)
anchors.meaning: A code stricter than his trade, set for his own people. **Paraphrase only, no quotation marks.** Not "it bound him first" (the rule is recorded for employees) and not "it cost him cargo" (no shipment recorded lost).

anchors.fact: The wiretaps that caught him were a crime under Washington law (1909 statute, a misdemeanor), which the Court's own majority quoted, then admitted the evidence anyway (LII, Taft; Brandeis "wire tapping is a crime"). (F11)
anchors.meaning: The system broke its own rules to catch him.

anchors.fact: The government's own brief, quoted by Brandeis: the Prohibition Unit "disclaims" wiretapping and the Justice Department "has frowned on it" (LII, Brandeis fn). (F12)
anchors.meaning: Even the people with the rulebook disowned the method they used. (Dossier or one clause.)

anchors.fact: Upheld 5–4 on 4 June 1928 (the evidence could stand); Holmes, Brandeis, Butler and Stone dissented (LII). (F14)
anchors.meaning: Not "two justices": four.
