anchors.fact: Brandeis: officials must be held to the same rules of conduct the law commands of the citizen; when the government breaks the law it breeds contempt for law (LII). Holmes: "dirty business"; better some criminals escape than the government play "an ignoble part". (F15, F16)
anchors.meaning: The person's grievance in the Court's own mouth: the same rule for the people who make it. Paraphrase Brandeis (the "Our government" sentence and our-words rule).

anchors.fact: HL: Seattle would "always" know him as "King of the Puget Sound Bootleggers". (F19)
anchors.meaning: Kills "the code is the part people remember".

anchors.fact: His cargo was Canadian whiskey from British Columbia (HL: "an unlimited source of good liquor in British Columbia"; "nearly 100 cases of Canadian whiskey"). (F2)
anchors.meaning: Base from his trade. HL says nothing about him never cutting his liquor; HW (2023 interview, single) says he didn't cut it "with toxins": legend-grade, signposted at most, never in the bottle as fact.

anchors.fact: Canadian blends came to be called "ryes" during and after Prohibition because so much bootleg came from Canada (*Joy* pdf 423). (E7)
anchors.meaning: Optional plain-language clause.

anchors.fact: Embury's CANADIAN: Canadian whisky, 2–3 dashes each of curaçao and Angostura, 1 teaspoon of sugar syrup; "Maple syrup is sometimes used in place of the sugar" (Embury, OCR highlight, E2 corrected). Embury held that cocktails should never have more than a hint of sweetness (Oxford pdf 719, E8). Oxford pdf 1226 (Soole): maple "can dominate a drink" (E6).
anchors.meaning: The maple is Embury's own noted variant of this very drink, at his teaspoon. In the reading: "the book notes" (Embury unnamed); the held-back measure rests on balance.py (6.25 ml OUT) and Soole's warning, the sweetness rule stays in the dossier. E4 is a different drink. The stir, coupe, 60 ml and peel are Tomás's.

cocktail.closingLine: Scrape the teaspoon of maple flat. Then show someone close where you draw the line.
cocktail.glassware: a coupe, chilled
method: Put the coupe in the freezer for 10 minutes so it's properly cold.

Measure the maple syrup into a mixing glass or jar: fill the teaspoon, then scrape the top flat with a knife. Add the curaçao and the bitters, pour in the whisky, and stir for a few seconds without ice, until the maple has dissolved. It's thick, and it won't dissolve once the drink is cold.
Fill the mixing glass with ice and stir for 20 to 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
Strain into the cold coupe.
Peel a strip of orange peel about the length of your thumb, with as little of the white as you can. Hold it skin side down over the drink and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Where You Stand

recipe.note: any blended Canadian whisky at 40% or a little above; the kind that filled his cases
a flat teaspoon, never heaped: a quarter-teaspoon more tips the drink too sweet. I like a dark one; any pure maple syrup, never pancake syrup
about three dashes, the top of Embury's "2 or 3"

cocktail.tagline: You know how things really get done. You also know what you'll never do.

reading.epigraph: A century ago, Canadian whisky was worth breaking the law for. On both sides of it.
whoYouAre: You know the difference between how things are meant to work and how they actually do: who to ask, what to say, which door opens if you knock the right way. When the official route stops answering, people come to you, and you sort it without a fuss, and without making them feel small for asking.

Behind all that, there's a line. You've got one, and you've never needed to write it down. There are things you won't do, whatever they'd win you, and you keep that to yourself, because out loud it would sound soft. But it's why the people near you feel safe. They may not know exactly where the line is. They know you won't cross it. That matters more than you'd guess: with you, nobody has to wonder where they stand.

What gets to you is the people who write the rules, break them when it suits, and call it procedure. Being pushed around by someone like that, with no say at all, is the nearest you come to being afraid.
yours: Roy Olmstead had been the youngest lieutenant in the Seattle police. In 1920 he was caught bootlegging Canadian whisky and dismissed. He understood the city from the inside: as an officer, he'd taken bribes. Soon, as the biggest bootlegger on Puget Sound, he was the one paying them.

He wasn't a good man by any law's measure. But in a trade that was dangerous and often violent, he had a rule of his own: his men weren't allowed to carry guns. Better to lose the liquor than a life, he told them. Then federal agents tapped his phones, though wiretapping was a crime in Washington State, and in 1928 the Supreme Court ruled, five votes to four, that the evidence could stand.

Justice Brandeis wrote, in dissent, that officials should be held to the same rules the law commands of everyone else, and that a government that breaks the law breeds contempt for it. I like to think you'd have nodded at that. Not because Olmstead was innocent: he'd enforced the rules while letting himself off, and you'd be the first to say so. Because it's what you've always known: whoever writes the rules keeps them too. And even in that trade, his men knew exactly where his line was.

The cocktail I've made for you is the Canadian, from *The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks*, a landmark book first published in 1948. It's straight Canadian whisky, the kind that filled Olmstead's cases, with orange curaçao, Angostura and a teaspoonful of sugar syrup. The book notes that maple sometimes takes the sugar's place. That's the version I've chosen: maple, for the country the whisky came from, one teaspoon exactly, scraped flat. A quarter-teaspoon over, and it tips too sweet. I stir it ice-cold and pour it into a chilled coupe, finished with orange peel. A line, held, in the glass.

You make more of the rules around you than you'd ever admit: who gets helped, and how, and what's never done. So let one person you trust in on where your line is, and let them hold you to it, as you'd hold anyone else. It costs you nothing you'd ever spend. And once someone else can see it, your line isn't a habit any more. It's your word.

anchors.fact: In 1965 Fritz Maytag bought control of Anchor, a failing San Francisco brewery whose beer had often gone sour. He brought his microscope in to work out why, and the brewery took ten years to show a profit. (F1, F8; Oxford ANCHOR DISTILLING pdf 103; Lucchesi, *SF Chronicle* Q&A 2015)
anchors.meaning: They saw it before it had a name, and they stayed with it while it was fragile.

anchors.fact: He came from the washing-machine family, and by his own account he spent his whole nest egg on the brewery. (F7; Abate, *SF Chronicle* 2010, his 2000 words to Ostler)
anchors.meaning: The risk was real and it was his. Say it once, plainly.

anchors.fact: Oxford calls what he made of Anchor the vanguard of craft beer. A San Francisco paper later called the brewery's beers the first drops of what became a flood of small-brewery beer, and by the 1980s other breweries were following his lead, Sierra Nevada among them. (F1, F18; pdf 103; Holbrook, *SF Chronicle* 2004; Abate 2010)
anchors.meaning: They give a new thing a shape that other people can follow.

anchors.fact: Even so, he kept his own brewery small. Around 1992 he decided it didn't have to keep growing, and in 1996 he said, emphatically, that he didn't want it to get too big. (F10; Burlingham, *Small Giants* 2016 ed.; Acitelli 2013; Stanford 1996 via *Alta* 2023)
anchors.meaning: The wave was other people's. The wheel they kept was their own. Wren's call; see N3.

anchors.fact: In 1993 he started a distillery in a corner of the brewery's warehouse, to make rye whiskey the way early American distillers had. Until the whiskey had aged and he knew it was good, it was a secret from all but a few employees. (F2, F6, F20; pdf 103; Abate 2010; Holbrook, *SF Chronicle* 2004)
anchors.meaning: The plan stays behind a door until it's right. Once the first edge had grown up, they went looking for the next one.

anchors.fact: Oxford calls Old Potrero the first modern small-distillery whiskey to reach the market, and says it was perhaps fired too early across the bows of the American whiskey industry. (F3; pdf 103)
anchors.meaning: Early isn't safe. They go anyway. Say it as a writer's judgement: Paul Clarke signs the entry (pdf 104), so "one drinks writer" in guest text (2026-10-06).

anchors.fact: A wave of new ryes from small distilleries began with Old Potrero, and by the 2010s rye's growth was being driven by the cocktail revival. (F4, F21; Oxford pdf 2165)
anchors.meaning: The edge they start goes mainstream in other people's glasses.
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: it grows up

anchors.fact: In 2010, at 72, he sold Anchor and stayed on as chairman emeritus. Of the new owners, he said "I plan to do whatever Keith says, to help them do well." (Keith Greggor was the new chief executive.) (F11, F12; pdf 103; Ross, *SF Chronicle* 2010)
anchors.meaning: Handing over the wheel, and offering a hand with it. His reasons for selling aren't on record; see N4.

anchors.fact: Thirteen years after he sold, the owners after him closed the brewery (July 2023). A new owner bought it in May 2024 and has promised it back. As of autumn 2026 the old labels are approved again, but no beer has been poured. (F14–F16; SF Chronicle 2026; SF Standard, May and Sep 2026; *American Craft Beer* Jul 2026)
anchors.meaning: The fear came true after them, and it isn't the end. Date it ("last I read, in 2026").
anchors.speaksTo: fear: tamed by the mainstream · Outlaw check: the ending holds today

anchors.fact: Old Potrero is still made from 100% malted rye in San Francisco. Today's core bottles are a six-year straight rye (48.5%) and a six-year toasted-barrel rye (51.2%), the second first sold as an 18th-century style. (F17; oldpotrero.com, 2026-10-01)
anchors.meaning: The edge they went to is in the glass. It's today's bottle, never his.

cocktail.closingLine: Mash the quince until no lumps are left. Then pick what you'll steer yourself, and let the rest run.
cocktail.glassware: a well-chilled coupe
method: Loosen the quince: put 30 g of quince paste (a slice about the size of a matchbox) in a cup with 30 ml of just-boiled water and mash it with a fork until no lumps are left. Let it cool. That's enough for three drinks, and it keeps in the fridge for a few days.
Put the coupe in the freezer.
Pour the loosened quince, the lemon juice, the Cointreau and the rye into a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about 12 seconds, until the outside is frosty.
Strain it into the cold coupe through the shaker's strainer and a small fine sieve held underneath, which catches any bits of quince.
Hold the orange peel over the drink, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top. Then lay it on the rim.
cocktail.name: Before It Had a Name

recipe.note: recommended; the Toasted Barrel bottling (51.2%) works too; or any straight rye of 40-51%
or any orange liqueur of the triple sec style, about 40%
squeezed the same day
plain membrillo (quince, sugar and lemon, with no nuts in the ingredients) mashed with an equal weight of just-boiled water; check the pack for a nut warning
squeezed over the top

cocktail.tagline: Your rebellions have a plan, and a future people can join.

reading.epigraph: Old Potrero began as a brewer's next idea, once other brewers had followed his lead.
whoYouAre: You catch it before anyone has a word for it: a sound, a look, an idea a few people keep circling. And you're the one who gives it a shape, a name, a place, a first version people can point at and join.

People see the rebel. They don't see the plan, and you prefer it that way, because wanting to steer sounds like the very thing you were all against. So you steer quietly. What worries you is what it turns into afterwards: run by people who never got it, smoothed out for everyone, your hands nowhere near it.
Most new things die young, talked out of it or copied badly. The ones you start tend to grow up, because someone was steering while they were fragile.
yours: In 1965, when factory beer ruled America, Fritz Maytag, from the washing-machine family, bought a failing San Francisco brewery called Anchor. Its beer, he admitted later, wasn't good: a lot of the time it was sort of sour. He brought in a microscope and, in his words, spent his whole nest egg on the brewery. It took ten years to make money.

What he'd started caught on: a San Francisco paper later called his beers the first drops of a tsunami. Others opened the breweries that followed. His own, he kept small. And in 1993 he set up stills in a corner of the brewery to make rye whiskey, a secret from all but a few of his staff. One drinks writer calls it an early, "perhaps too early", shot across the bows of American whisky.

When he sold, in 2010, the man who'd steered it for forty-five years said he'd do whatever the new boss said, to help them do well. Thirteen years later, under other owners, the brewery went quiet. A new owner has promised it back, though in the autumn of 2026 it still wasn't pouring. That's your fear, come true long after he'd let go. But look at what didn't stop: the small breweries everywhere, and a wave of new small-distillery ryes that the same book says began with his. I like to think that's why he could offer to take orders. He'd never needed the whole wave. Only to start it, and keep one part small enough to steer himself.

The cocktail I've made for you is a rye Sidecar, after the renowned classic of brandy, orange liqueur and lemon, shaken hard over ice, then strained twice, the second time through a fine sieve, into a well-chilled coupe. The rye is Old Potrero, the name his first rye was sold under, though today's bottles are aged longer than that first one, and there's more of it than anything else. Where some bartenders add a little syrup, I add quince paste instead, loosened with hot water. Quince is a fruit hardly anyone eats raw, so hard and mouth-puckering it takes real work, and then it's wonderful, with a strong perfume. I chose it as a nod to a sour beer he took on, and put right.

So let me steer, just once. When something you started takes off, don't try to hold on to all of it. Decide what you'll keep steering yourself, and do it properly. Let the rest run in other people's hands. That isn't it getting away from you. It's how you'll know it was real. And it leaves you free for the next thing nobody has a name for yet.

anchors.fact: An importer launched the Amaretto Sour in 1974 as amaretto and lemon juice, two to one. By the 1980s it was a standard drink, and most bartenders made it with bought sour mix. (F1–F2; Oxford pdf 97)
anchors.meaning: A drink everyone had stopped thinking about: the decision was made, and nobody argued.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: Powerlessness (the decision made before anyone could think)

anchors.fact: The Oxford entry calls that version flat: an easy drink that tasted of little but the liqueur. (F3; pdf 97)
anchors.meaning: The scorn had a point, and the case for the drink starts by saying so.

anchors.fact: On 9 February 2012 a Portland bartender, Jeffrey Morgenthaler, posted on his own website that he made the best Amaretto Sour in the world. It opens "No, really. I'm serious." (F6; post 2012)
anchors.meaning: The side nobody was on, taken on purpose, in public, and funny.
anchors.speaksTo: essence: spark debate and provoke controversy · tone: provocative

anchors.fact: The post agrees with the critics first: the usual ones are too sweet, and amaretto alone is too weak to hold its own. A sour has to be adjusted for this liqueur, he wrote, and his answer to the weakness is cask-proof bourbon. (F7; post 2012)
anchors.meaning: He argued for the thing by granting everything true that was said against it.

anchors.fact: Some readers ribbed him in the comments. One asked whether it was still an Amaretto Sour with bourbon in it, and another said he wouldn't call it one. (F9; post comments, 10–21 Feb 2012)
anchors.meaning: The price: a ribbing and the purist's question. Never "resented".
anchors.speaksTo: fear: being written off as contrary

anchors.fact: One reader remembered the old ones as "sickly sweet", and another, a bartender, wrote that he'd make it to restore public faith in amaretto. (F11; post comments, 2012)
anchors.meaning: The scorn he argued against, on the same page.
anchors.speaksTo: the room that had stopped thinking

anchors.fact: By 2021, the Oxford Companion's entry on the Amaretto Sour was his. It grants the old version's flatness and says the drink "can be greatly improved": lemon juice again, a little egg white, cask-strength bourbon. (F4–F5; pdf 97)
anchors.meaning: The argument became part of the drink's own record, won or lost. Told plainly: he wrote the entry.
anchors.speaksTo: goal: Liberation (a mark left) · driver: Leave a mark

anchors.fact: The *Cocktail Codex* (Death & Co's team) prints the Amaretto Sour among its classics: fresh lemon, less syrup, no bourbon or egg. (F13; *Codex* p. 114)
anchors.meaning: Another bar's book treats it as a classic. Never "his version became the classic".
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: the idea holds up

anchors.fact: Jim Meehan's Oxford entry on variations gives the bourbon added to an Amaretto Sour at a Portland bar, Pépé Le Moko, as an example of a bar's own deliberate twist. (F14; pdf 533; his bar per pdf 2269)
anchors.meaning: His addition is known to others by name. Never "a new standard" (that sentence is general).

anchors.fact: In 2014 he titled another post "Hot Toddies suck—long live the Hot Toddy". What Oxford takes from it is his way to keep a toddy hot, not just warm. (F16; Oxford TODDY pdf 2034, 2036)
anchors.meaning: The same move from the other side: knocked in the title, fixed in the body. Never "attacked the drink everyone loves" (the post is unread).
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: argues against what might be true

anchors.fact: Our glass follows his 2012 post for the amaretto (45 ml), cask-strength bourbon (22.5 ml), egg white, old-fashioned glass, fresh ice and lemon peel. The syrup is out, the lemon is cut from 30 to 22.5 ml and half a teaspoon of sherry vinegar is in: all three are ours. His own two printings differ on the syrup (15 ml simple vs 5 ml 2:1). (F4, F8, C1)
anchors.meaning: Ours, built on his fix. Never "his recipe" or "made his way".

cocktail.closingLine: Measure the vinegar, and be ready to defend it. Next time, let the view you defend be one you hold.
cocktail.glassware: an old-fashioned glass, fresh ice
method: Fill the glass with fresh ice and leave it to chill.
Separate a fresh egg. Whip the white with a fork for about 20 seconds, until it's loose and frothy, then measure one tablespoon. You won't need the rest.
Pour the amaretto, bourbon, lemon juice and sherry vinegar into a shaker. Add the spoonful of egg white last.
Fill the shaker with ice, close it, and shake hard for about 15 seconds.
Strain into the glass, over the fresh ice. A thin white foam will settle on top.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the foam, shiny side down, so its oils fall on the drink, then lay it on top.
cocktail.name: Hear Me Out

recipe.note: an Italian amaretto
bottled at or near barrel strength; 55% or stronger
the Spanish kind (vinagre de Jerez); measure it, don't guess
from a fresh egg; whip the white, then measure a spoonful
over the top

cocktail.tagline: You'll argue the other side. Sometimes it's even yours.

reading.epigraph: One bartender made the case for this drink by admitting what was wrong with it.
whoYouAre: Someone says it's settled, and something in you sits up. It isn't that you think they're wrong. Often you think they're right. But nobody has argued with it yet, and an idea nobody has argued with hasn't been tested. It's only been agreed with. So you take the other side.

You'd hardly ever admit how often you agree, or how glad you'd be to lose to a good answer. "Only playing devil's advocate" keeps your own view safe, where nobody can argue it down. The sigh is what you dread, the "there they go again": once your questions stop counting, you're stuck with decisions nobody was allowed to think about.

Nobody says thank you in the moment. They should. An idea that's survived you can survive almost anything, and when the real objection comes, from a boss, say, the others already have the answer, because you made them find it.
yours: In the 1980s the Amaretto Sour was a standard. An importer had launched it in 1974 as two parts of the sweet Italian liqueur to one of lemon juice, but by then most bartenders reached for bought sour mix instead, and the drink tasted of little but the liqueur.

Then, in February 2012, a Portland bartender, Jeffrey Morgenthaler, posted on his website that he made the best Amaretto Sour in the world. It opens: "No, really. I'm serious." And before he made his case, he gave the other side its due. Other Amaretto Sours were too sweet, he wrote, and amaretto on its own is weak. "It needs help." His help was cask-strength bourbon. Some readers teased him, and one asked whether it was still an Amaretto Sour at all.

That's the move I recognise in you. He never pretended the old drink was good. He granted the point, then showed what the drink could be once it was answered. Two years later he tried the move from the other end, with a post called "Hot Toddies suck—long live the Hot Toddy", and a better way to keep one hot. And by 2021, the entry on the Amaretto Sour in the *Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails* was his. I like to think the teasing pleased him: it meant someone was arguing back.

The cocktail I've made for you is an Amaretto Sour, a classic again, built on his fix: an Italian amaretto, cask-strength bourbon for backbone, fresh lemon, and lightly whipped egg white, a spoonful of it, shaken and strained over fresh ice, with lemon oil over its thin white foam. Then I argued with him, as you would. He said the others were too sweet, so I took him further than he went: no syrup at all, a little less lemon to match, and the amaretto doing all the sweetening. And there's sherry vinegar in it, half a teaspoon, an ingredient I'd have to defend in most bars, in honour of the side nobody takes. Vinegar is one of the best partners nuts have in the kitchen, and here it keeps the sweetness honest.

Here's my side, and I mean it. Keep testing everything: people are better for it, even the ones who sigh. But now and then, argue for something you actually love, and say plainly that it's what you think. No escape hatch, no "just for the sake of argument". Let them push back on you for a change. You may find your own ideas survive you too, and everyone else finally gets to argue with the real you.

anchors.fact: In Naples, someone having a coffee at the bar pays for a second one before leaving, for someone who can't afford one (NPR 2013; Mancini, Global Informality Project; *Euronews* 2020).
anchors.meaning: Kindness done as an ordinary purchase, at the price of one more coffee.

anchors.fact: Whoever comes in later asks whether there's a suspended coffee, and is served (NPR 2013; Mancini).
anchors.meaning: The one who asks is served as a customer. The question puts nobody in front of anyone.

anchors.fact: One Italian scholar (Mancini) reads the question as "a gentle query": a direct "Would you pay for a coffee for me?" would stress the economic difference between two people, so the coffee seems to fall "from the clouds", not from the giver's hands. Interpretation, his.
anchors.meaning: The custom's own wording treats the person as someone, not as a problem.
anchors.speaksTo: Respect; fear of Discourtesy and Indifference

anchors.fact: A city's custom with no known first giver. How old it is isn't known: the sources say about a century, or the end of the Second World War, or that one can only speculate.
anchors.meaning: Not one hero: ordinary people, one coffee at a time.

anchors.fact: The giver doesn't choose: the coffee is for "an unidentified future customer" (Mancini), whoever "entered later" (De Crescenzo to NPR).
anchors.meaning: Something left waiting for the ones you'll miss, stood on the one who walks in.
anchors.speaksTo: Altruism; not passing by on the other side of the road

anchors.fact: Espresso's texture "dies fairly quickly" and a *caffè shakerato* (espresso shaken with ice and a little sugar) "must be consumed very quickly" (*Liquid Intelligence* pp. 352–353). Ours adds brandy and no cream; Arnold warns that liquor throws off a shakerato's body (p. 354).
anchors.meaning: A cup can't wait; what waits is the payment. So the coffee is made only when someone is there.

anchors.fact: The *Flavor Matrix* lists coffee among the best pairings for root vegetables (celery root, parsnip, salsify), which are "most commonly roasted or boiled and puréed" (pdf 224).
anchors.meaning: The syrup is the part made ahead, for whoever comes later. Never a picture of people.

anchors.fact: The *Codex* pairs cognac with a coffee liqueur in a hot toddy, *In Hot Water* (Brittany Fells, 2014; p. 38).
anchors.meaning: Brandy and coffee is an established pairing.

cocktail.closingLine: Make the syrup before you know who it's for.
cocktail.glassware: chilled coupe
method: Ahead of time: peel and slice 250 g of parsnips and roast them at 200°C for about 35 minutes, until the edges are brown. Simmer them for 10 minutes with 250 g sugar and 250 ml water, let it cool, then strain, pressing on the parsnips. You'll have about 400 ml, enough for twenty-odd drinks. Keep it in the fridge.
Chill the glass.
When someone's actually there, pull one espresso. Never before: it loses its texture fast.
Put the brandy, the syrup and the salt in a shaker, then the espresso. Fill it with ice and shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Strain into the cold glass and drink it at once: the texture doesn't last.
cocktail.name: Whoever Comes In

recipe.note: an aged grape brandy, such as a VS cognac or a Spanish brandy
one shot, pulled only when you're about to shake; a stovetop moka pot works too, though the foam will be thinner
made ahead; the jar keeps about a week in the fridge
or a small pinch of salt

cocktail.tagline: You stop for the people everyone else has learned to walk past.

reading.epigraph: Part of this drink is made days ahead. The rest waits until someone's there.
whoYouAre: Most people pick up a knack from living among strangers: looking through someone. The person sitting by the cash machine with a paper cup, the one talking to nobody on the bus, the tourist turning the map round for the third time. Everyone else's eyes slide past. Your eyes stop. You say hello. You ask where they're trying to get to. For a minute, someone everyone had stopped seeing is just a person in the queue again.

What people miss is the cost. The ones you walk past, because you were late or tired, follow you home for longer than all the times you stopped. You'd hate to be called good. You're just more afraid of a street where everyone has stopped looking, where anyone could end up being stepped round, you included. The people you stop for get to be someone, not a problem. And everyone watching learns that stopping is normal.
yours: Naples has an old custom called the *caffè sospeso*, the suspended coffee. Someone having a coffee at the bar pays for a second one before they leave, for someone who can't afford one. Nobody knows how old it is, or how it began; the stories don't agree. It doesn't belong to anyone in particular. It's just something people there do, one coffee at a time.

Later, somebody comes in and asks at the bar: is there a suspended coffee? If there is, they're served like any other customer. One Italian scholar reads that question as the gentle part. Nobody has to say "would you pay for a coffee for me?", so the difference between the two of them never has to be said out loud. The coffee arrives, as the scholar puts it, "from the clouds", not from somebody's hand.

I like to think the people who keep it going see whoever walks in next the way you see a stranger: as someone, not a problem. And whoever pays never chooses who gets it. It's for whoever comes in. That's how your kindness works too: it starts with stopping, before you know a thing about them.

The cocktail I've made for you is built the way the custom works. Part of it is made days ahead, as a nod to the coffee paid for someone who hasn't come in yet: a syrup of roasted parsnips, sweet and a little earthy, with enough in the jar for twenty-odd drinks, waiting in the fridge for whoever's next. The rest is only made when someone's actually there, because espresso loses its texture fast. One shot, pulled fresh, shaken hard with brandy, the syrup and two drops of salt water, poured into a cold coupe and drunk at once. It starts from the Italian *shakerato*, espresso shaken with ice and lightly sweetened; I've added the brandy. Coffee is listed among parsnip's best pairings in the flavour book I trust most: think of carrot cake with a strong coffee.

You can't stop for every one. Nobody can, and the ones you miss will come back to you later. So leave something waiting for them: a coffee paid ahead at the place you go every morning, an hour given somewhere they'll come in after you've gone. Then, some morning when you're late and you hurry past, you'll know something's already there for them, and they won't follow you home.

anchors.fact: Born in 1955 in Tullibody, Scotland, near the Cambus distillery where his father worked; he started there at 17, in 1973 (Oxford Companion, NICHOL, pdf 1388). In his telling, you got a job there if your father or uncle already had one (*Difford's Guide*, 2015).
anchors.meaning: The gift grew inside the people he came from. It was never a way out.

anchors.fact: When Cambus closed in 1993 he went to Cameronbridge in Fife, making liquid carbon dioxide, then grain whisky and neutral grain spirit from 1996 (Oxford pdf 1388). His own words on that spirit: hardly appreciated, because it "tastes of nothing and smells of nothing" (*The Spirits Business*, 2013).
anchors.meaning: Years making the part of the drink nobody notices. Talent in a place you'd never expect to find it.
anchors.speaksTo: appearances can sometimes be deceptive; fear of Exclusion

anchors.fact: In 2005 he joined the team making gin and vodka at Cameronbridge, and within a year he was Tanqueray's master distiller (Oxford pdf 1388). Tanqueray has been made in Scotland since 1998 (Oxford pdf 1986), and in his time it was made at Cameronbridge (*Difford's Guide*; the Gin Guild; his own "two stills for Tanqueray", 2013).
anchors.meaning: The gift came out where he already stood. He didn't have to leave to be found.

anchors.fact: He's credited with developing the Rangpur (2007), producing the Old Tom (2014) and the Bloomsbury (2015), and with maintaining the London Dry (Oxford pdf 1388). In his words, he made "a few other gins for Tanqueray" (*Difford's Guide*, 2015).
anchors.meaning: The talent was real, and it was his.

anchors.fact: Oxford calls him a "passionate, even irascible" advocate of the idea that big distilleries don't automatically make worse spirit (pdf 1388).
anchors.meaning: He stood up for the place everyone looked down on, and for the people who worked there.

anchors.fact: He called the master distiller's job "a testament to my father" (*The Spirits Business*, 2013). He lived some forty years in Alloa, a couple of miles from where he was born (*Difford's Guide*, 2015).
anchors.meaning: He kept both: the gift, and the people he came from.

anchors.fact: In May 2015, as he retired, the Gin Guild gave him its Lifetime Achievement Award. He said it was "completely unexpected" and that his father would have been proud (the Gin Guild).
anchors.meaning: The moment the room sees it, and he thinks first of home.

cocktail.closingLine: Make it where everyone is, not in the other room. Someone will ask about the finish.
cocktail.glassware: plain kitchen tumbler (about 250 ml), three or four ordinary ice cubes from the freezer tray
method: Make the syrup: put the sugar, water and liquorice root in a small pan and bring it just to a simmer, stirring until the sugar is gone. Let it simmer gently for 5 minutes, then take it off the heat and leave it for 30 minutes. Strain out the root and let the syrup cool.
Put the syrup and the bitters in a plain tumbler first, then pour in the gin.
Add three or four ordinary ice cubes and stir for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold. Then stop: the cubes keep melting as you drink.
Nothing goes on top.
cocktail.name: Right Here

recipe.note: the gin Tom Nichol looked after; or any juniper-led London dry gin, 40% to 47%. If your bottle says 47% or more, use 50 ml
brings forward the hint of liquorice the gin is said to have already

recipe.item: *for the syrup:* 100 g white sugar, 100 ml water, 5 g dried liquorice root (about two finger-length pieces), chopped or snapped small
recipe.note: makes about 160 ml; keeps two weeks in a closed jar in the fridge. Dried liquorice root is sold in health-food and tea shops. Check the pack for a nut warning. Liquorice sweets won't do: they aren't the root

cocktail.tagline: You make something remarkable, then go back to being one of the gang.

reading.epigraph: Four plants flavour this gin, they say. The last you taste comes first here.
whoYouAre: There's something you're good at that doesn't match the picture people have of you. A cake nobody believed you'd made. A song you only sing in the car. A drawing on the back of a work envelope. When someone finds out and says "you never said", you laugh and change the subject. Part of you has always believed you had to pick: be good at it, or stay one of them.

You want both. When it shows, nobody you love thinks you've got above yourself. They're proud it's one of theirs who did it. That's your gift to them, more than the cake or the song: it shows them what someone like them can do.
yours: Tom Nichol grew up in Tullibody, in Scotland, near the distillery where his father worked. At seventeen he was dragged into it, screaming and shouting, he says: his father had set up the interview. For over thirty years he worked in whisky and in jobs nobody outside a distillery hears about, including liquid carbon dioxide and plain grain spirit. It gets little thanks, he said, because it tastes of nothing and smells of nothing.

In 2005 he moved to the gin team at the same distillery, where Tanqueray was made. Within a year he was Tanqueray's master distiller, in charge of the gin itself. He's credited with new Tanqueray gins of his own, and with keeping the everyday one as it should be. When he retired in 2015, the gin trade's guild gave him a lifetime award. He called it completely unexpected, and said his father would have been very proud of him.

He'd lived forty years by then a couple of miles from where he was born, and he argued one idea hard, sometimes short-temperedly: a big distillery doesn't have to make worse spirit than a small one. I like to think you'd recognise that: the talent turned up right where life had put him, and once it was noticed, he didn't leave the place behind; he stood up for it.

The cocktail I've made for you is a gin Old-Fashioned, the classic of spirit, sugar and bitters, built in an ordinary tumbler over ice from the freezer tray. The gin is Tanqueray London Dry, with nothing to cover it. It's said to be made with only four plants: juniper, coriander, angelica and liquorice, the hint that comes at the finish. So the sugar comes as a liquorice root syrup, in honour of a talent that was in that distillery long before anyone named it. The liquorice is the gin's own, they say: it only brings forward what was already there.

So show it to the people who knew you first, before strangers. Make the cake for your own table. Sing with the window down on the way to your family's. Nobody will think you've changed. You'll find out you never had to choose, and they'll get to be proud of something that's theirs too.

anchors.fact: He taught English at a Los Angeles high school, and after a 1970 trip wanted to live in Amsterdam, a place where, in his words, he "could really learn a lot about myself", but he didn't know how a public-school teacher could (*A Proper Drink* p. 79; Oxford Companion pdf 2260; *Drinks International*, 2017).
anchors.meaning: A safe job, and a wish to be somewhere else with no plan yet.

anchors.fact: He worked out the how on a road trip through Mexico: open something the city lacked, Mexican food. "My main goal was to support myself," he said (*A Proper Drink* p. 79; *Drinks International*, 2017).
anchors.meaning: The reason was small and plain: a way to live where he wanted, on his own pay.

anchors.fact: In 1976 he opened Café Pacifico in Amsterdam with little money, on a street where people told him they'd never come because it was "too dangerous"; within six weeks there were queues, as his partner Phil Bayly remembered (*A Proper Drink* p. 79; Oxford pdf 743; Bayly, CLASS, 2021). He had never been a bartender or a cook (his own account, via Bayly).
anchors.meaning: Starting from nothing, with what was on the record: no money, no trade.

anchors.fact: His partner's account of his rule for the staff: "Tight on bottom, loose on top": do the job well, and you could do it in your own style (Bayly, CLASS, 2021).
anchors.meaning: The freedom he left to find, he handed to the people who worked for him.

anchors.fact: In London (from 1982) young bartenders "having few places to go" found Pacifico, and Danny Smith spent ten years there making Margaritas for bartenders off their shifts (*A Proper Drink* pp. 79–80, 98). At La Perla, another of his London places, Dre Masso, a bartender Danny Smith brought along one night, told Smith "I felt like I was at home" (p. 80).
anchors.meaning: What he built for himself became where others belonged, in their words, not his.

anchors.fact: In 2017 he said he was handing his shares in London's Pacifico to the people who worked there, "a cooperative", keeping a minority stake because he wanted "to still be a bar owner – and be part of the community" (*Drinks International*, 2017).
anchors.meaning: He wanted to stay in it as one of them, not over them. (His words in 2017; how the handover ended isn't on record. His regret in the same answer, that he should have got out of the way about five years sooner, is used in y3 and y5; "ashamed" stays in the dossier.)

anchors.fact: Pacifico's Margaritas were made with Sauza Blanco and Giffard triple sec, "to Estes' specifications", according to Danny Smith (*A Proper Drink* p. 79); Estes's proportions aren't on record, so ours are the *Cocktail Codex*'s classic (p. 166). The Margarita is one of the drinks that have "indisputably achieved" classic status (Oxford Companion, CLASSIC COCKTAIL, pdf 473). Today's basic Sauza silver is a mixto (51% agave; Oxford SAUZA pdf 1743), and Giffard sells a 25% and a 40% triple sec. Ours are Sauza's 100% agave blanco and Giffard's 25% Triple Sec: his brands, not necessarily his bottlings.
anchors.meaning: The measured half of the glass is his half: the brands he chose, kept exact. The top is left to whoever makes it, as his partner remembered his rule.

cocktail.closingLine: Measure the bottom exactly. Then hand the top to someone else, and join the people you made room for.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail glass (about 200 ml), chilled, no salt
method: Put the cocktail glass in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you work.
Measure the tequila, triple sec, lime juice and syrup into a shaker. Measure them exactly: this is the tight part.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold comfortably.
Empty the glass and strain the drink into it. No salt.

Now the loose part. Cut a wide strip of grapefruit peel with as little white as you can, hold it skin-side down over the glass and squeeze it so its oils fall on the drink, then rest it on the rim. That's my top. If someone else is making it, the top is theirs: anything that goes on the drink rather than into it.
cocktail.name: Loose on Top

recipe.item: Sauza 100% agave blanco tequila (recommended; sold in the US as Sauza Signature Blue)
recipe.note: The brand Café Pacifico's Margaritas were made with, per one of its barmen; this is Sauza's 100% agave blanco, not Pacifico's exact bottle. Or any blanco tequila of 38-40%.
The brand Pacifico used, per one of its barmen. Giffard makes it at 25% and at 40% (Curaçao Triple Sec), and both balance. Or any French triple sec.
Squeezed the same day.
Equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear.
The loose top: oils squeezed over the drink, then rested on the rim.

cocktail.tagline: Your independence has a way of becoming a place other people belong.

reading.epigraph: One restaurant owner chose the brands in this drink. Whoever's pouring chooses the top.
whoYouAre: You started something of your own. Maybe a Sunday football team, a stall at the weekend market, a supper that turned into a monthly thing, or a whole business. When people ask why, they expect a big reason. The real one is smaller, and you rarely say it: you wanted to live your way, and pay your own way doing it.

There's something else you keep quiet. Somewhere along the line, other people started treating it as theirs. They turn up early, bring friends and save each other seats. And part of you worries about ending up in the corner, keeping the whole thing running for everyone else to belong to. The freedom you went out for always turns out to have room for other people in it.
yours: Tomas Estes taught English in Los Angeles and wanted to live in Amsterdam, a place where, he said, he could learn a lot about himself. He couldn't see how a teacher could manage it. A Mexican restaurant could. "My main goal was to support myself," he said, though one writer saw it differently: the restaurant was his way to freedom.

He opened Café Pacifico there in 1976, with little money, on a street people told him was too dangerous to visit. A second Pacifico opened in London, around a long bar. Young bartenders with few places to go for a proper cocktail found it, and one of its barmen spent ten years making Margaritas for the ones just off their shifts. At another of his London places, one bartender said he felt at home.

His partner Phil Bayly remembered his rule for the staff: "Tight on bottom, loose on top." Get the work right, then do it your way. I like to think that's the whole of him: he left to be free, then gave the same freedom away. In 2017 he said he was handing his shares in the London restaurant to the partners who worked there, keeping a minority share because he wanted to stay "part of the community". He added that he should probably have got out of the way five years sooner.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Margarita, a renowned classic. I made it with the two brands one of his London barmen said Estes chose, Sauza for the tequila and Giffard for the triple sec, shaken hard with fresh lime and served ice-cold, with no salt. The bottom is measured to the drop, as a nod to the tight half of his rule. The top is the loose half: I squeeze the oils of a grapefruit peel over it, and when someone else makes it, the top is theirs to choose. It only ever goes on the drink, never into it, so whatever they pick, the drink underneath still holds.

Don't leave it as late as he did. Whatever you've started, the team, the stall, the thing with your name on the door, hand someone the piece you've kept hold of and let them do it their way. It won't be how you'd do it. It'll be theirs, and that means it's working. Then turn up the way everyone else does: early, with a friend, for no reason except that you like it there. You went out on your own to be free. You don't have to stay on your own to keep it.

anchors.fact: Ralph Erenzo, a climber for about thirty years, had camped for about twenty-five of them on climbing trips to the Gunks, at a spot with no toilets, no running water and no management. That's why he decided to open a campground (his own account, Gunks Climbers' Coalition interview, c. 2015; card F4).
anchors.meaning: A shortcoming everyone had put up with for years, and the one who decided to do something about it.

anchors.fact: In 2001 he bought the old Tuthilltown gristmill property near Gardiner, NY, to run a campground for climbers visiting the Shawangunk Ridge. His neighbours objected (Oxford HUDSON pdf 1037; card F1).
anchors.meaning: The first go, made in public and blocked.

anchors.fact: Three years with no income and legal fees. One neighbour said the aim was to stall him until his money ran out and he had to sell. That's Erenzo's memory of it, and it's about the campground, not the distillery (GCC interview, c. 2015; card F5).
anchors.meaning: The doubters, out loud.

anchors.fact: Erenzo asked the local zoning officer what he could do with the land. He was told it lay in an agricultural district, where farming was his right, and that a winery counts as farming (GCC interview, c. 2015; card F6).
anchors.meaning: He was pointed in a direction. He didn't find the law (the Trailblazer fence).

anchors.fact: In 2007 the AP called Erenzo and Brian Lee "unlikely spirit makers". Erenzo had run a climbing gym in Manhattan, and Lee was a broadcast engineer. Lee joked that his only fermenting had been cinnamon buns with his kids (AP, 15 July 2007, via NBC News; cards F7–F8).
anchors.meaning: No title, no training, and a joke about it.

anchors.fact: Erenzo, 2007: about two and a half years "from a dead stop knowing nothing about it" to a working still. In 2017 he said he started with no prior knowledge, from instructions on the internet. Lee learned the fermenting and installed the still (AP 2007; *Whiskey Reviewer* 2017; cards F9–F11).
anchors.meaning: Learning the job while doing it, in plain view.

anchors.fact: Gable was recruited when the distillery was founded, while he was still at university. Ralph, recalling it in 2021: "I'm building a distillery – I need your help!" Gable learned distilling "from the ground up" (*Hudson Valley One*, 11 May 2021; card F13). The page calls it a "call for help". It never says the call was by phone, and it gives no reason for it.
anchors.meaning: Saying the second half out loud: "I need your help".

anchors.fact: Tuthilltown's first product was a vodka from New York apples. In 2007 came Hudson Manhattan Rye, 92 proof, from 100% New York rye (Oxford pdf 1037; card F3). The AP reported that the apple vodka kept a faint apple taste (card F21).
anchors.meaning: Their first go (apples) beside what they got good at (rye).

anchors.fact: June 2015: the state's agriculture department said Tuthilltown was "one of more than 100 craft distilleries" operating in New York, and its commissioner called it "a model for beverage producers across the state" (NYS Agriculture and Markets, 12 June 2015; card F16). It says nothing about cause, and nothing about the Act.
anchors.meaning: What they started reached others, as the state said it.

anchors.fact: Hudson Manhattan Rye was renamed **Do The Rye Thing** in 2020, with a new recipe: 95% rye and 5% malted barley. It is bottled at 46% and called a New York straight rye. The brand is wholly owned by William Grant & Sons (*The Spirits Business*, 15 Sep 2020; hudsonwhiskey.com, fetched 2026-10-01; card F22–F24).
anchors.meaning: Today's bottle descends from the amateurs' rye, but it isn't the 2007 bottle: never "100% New York rye" for today's bottle, and never "theirs".

anchors.fact: *Cocktail Codex* p. 22: pull back the base and add another spirit "like apple brandy, to accent the primary spirit"; rye and apple brandy are "a magical, crowd-pleasing combination".
anchors.meaning: The split base is craft as well as story. That's one book's praise, not "famously".

cocktail.closingLine: Make it before you've practised, with someone watching. Ask for a hand before you need one.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass, one large cube
method: Put a large ice cube in the rocks glass to chill it while you mix.
Pour the rye, apple brandy, vermouth, syrup and bitters into a mixing glass or a jar, and fill it with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass is very cold.
Strain it over the large cube.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top, skin side down, so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: I'll Do It

recipe.item: Hudson Do The Rye Thing New York straight rye (recommended)
recipe.note: the rye line those amateurs began, sold today under this name; or any straight rye, ideally one distilled in New York State
bottled-in-bond (50%) if you can find it; any American apple brandy of 40% or more works
a red Italian-style vermouth
equal parts demerara sugar and hot water, stirred until clear, then cooled
for the top

cocktail.tagline: You say yes before you know how.

reading.epigraph: The rye this drink calls for was first made in a barn, by amateurs.
whoYouAre: Someone says it in the pub, on the doorstep or in the group chat: somebody really ought to do something about it. The broken bench, the club with no treasurer, the school play nobody will run. Everyone nods. Before you can stop yourself, you've said "I'll do it", and only later, doing the washing-up, do you realise you've no idea how.

Nobody hears about the evenings: the videos, the forums, the cousin who might know. You're out of your depth most of the way through, and you know it. The words you dread are "who asked you?", and worse, the doubters turning out to be right. You go anyway, partly because if you thought about it any longer, you wouldn't. The thing everyone was waiting for somebody to fix gets fixed. And because you so plainly need a hand, people who'd never have volunteered end up holding the ladder. What was everyone's complaint becomes something they did together.
yours: For about twenty-five years, Ralph Erenzo had camped on climbing trips to New York's Shawangunk Ridge with no toilets and no running water. So in 2001 he bought an old mill near the ridge to give climbers a proper campground. The neighbours objected. One of them, as Erenzo remembers it, told him the aim was to stall until his money ran out.

When the campground stalled, Erenzo asked the town's zoning officer what he could do with the land, and heard that a winery counts as farming. So Erenzo and Brian Lee, a broadcast engineer, set out to make spirits instead. Neither had any idea how. Lee joked that the only fermenting he'd ever done was cinnamon buns with his children. By Erenzo's count it took about two and a half years, from knowing nothing, to switching the still on and making alcohol. He said later that he worked from instructions he found online. And right at the start, Erenzo had asked his son, Gable, too: "I'm building a distillery – I need your help!"

Their first bottles held a vodka made from New York apples. Later came their whiskeys, among them a rye from New York grain. By 2015 the state counted more than a hundred craft distilleries, and its agriculture commissioner called Tuthilltown a model for producers across the state. I like to think the best thing Erenzo made there wasn't in a bottle. It was that call for help: what he was about to try, and that he couldn't do it alone, in a single sentence, long before he knew how. You always say the first half. It's the second half you swallow.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Manhattan, one of the great classics: rye stirred with sweet vermouth (a red, wine-based aperitif with herbs) and bitters, then poured over a single large ice cube, and an orange peel pinched over it so its oils land on the drink. It's built for Hudson's rye, sold today as Do The Rye Thing, the line those amateurs began, if you can find it. Beside the rye there's a little apple brandy, as a nod to the apples they started with. It isn't their vodka. It's their first go, kept next to the thing they got good at, and one of my favourite cocktail books calls rye with apple brandy magical. It comes out deep and warm, a little sweet, and brighter for the apple.

So, when "I'll do it" next comes out of your mouth, finish the sentence: "and I'll need a hand." Say it at the start, while you still don't know how, and say who you'd like. You worry it'll show how out of your depth you are. It will, a little. It's also the reason they'll come. The job gets done sooner, nobody waits for the experts, and the thing you started ends up belonging to everyone who helped.

anchors.fact: Before the 1950s, the drink "appears to have been" called simply *pinga com limão*, cane spirit with lime. It's on record only from the mid-nineteenth century: "of no great antiquity" (Oxford CAIPIRINHA, pdf 383). F2, F3
anchors.meaning: An everyday thing named after its ingredients. Keep Wondrich's "appears". Never "centuries-old", "ancient" or "traditional for generations". **Sugar isn't in the mid-1800s record:** the name is cane spirit *with lime*. The first sugar on the page is Wells's refresco of "cachaça, lemon, sugar, and water", thirty years after 1856 (1880s). So the mid-1800s date goes with the lime only (audit v2, A6).

anchors.fact: In São Paulo, in the first half of the 20th century, the Batida Paulista showed American influence ("not only in its incorporation of ice"). Some versions used simple syrup, others added egg white and a "splash" of gin, which the poet Mário de Andrade called "sophisticated" in 1944, and these "would require mixing in a cocktail shaker" (pdf 383). F4
anchors.meaning: The fashionable improvement, on the page. Syrup was in *some* versions, egg white and gin in *others*: never syrup as every version's touch (A7). **The shaker is tied to the egg white and gin only** (Tomás's anchor, r3): the page gives no method for the syrup versions or for the third way. Andrade's word reaches us in Wondrich's English, in quotation marks, and his tone is unknown: never a sneer, never praise. The improvers aren't sneered at either (Wren's test 4).
anchors.speaksTo: the fashionable try to improve it

anchors.fact: "Some drinkers, however, rejected such innovations" (pdf 383). F5
anchors.meaning: Someone said no to the additions. **Unknown:** who they were, why, and whether they're the people who made the caipirinha (Wren's note a). Any link is signposted.

anchors.fact: "A third way, one that incorporated the ice from the new drink into a nostalgic, rustic preparation built simply in the glass" (pdf 384). F6. **Contested:** Oxford's CACHAÇA entry calls the Batida Paulista "better known by its alternate name, the Caipirinha" (pdf 380), and Wondrich himself says "Batida Paulista" "appears to have been" one of its original names (pdf 383). C1
anchors.meaning: The heart of the mirror: it took the one new thing that was better (the cold) and left the show. Told as Wondrich's account ("as one historian tells it"), or after "I like to think". "Built simply in the glass" is a five-word run of his: in guest text, our words ("made right in the glass", A8). The page names the ice as what the third way took. "Just one thing" is our reading, and it lives in y3's "I like to think". "Nostalgic, rustic" is his reading: attribute it or put it in our own words. Never claim as fact that it was a separate drink from the city one.
anchors.speaksTo: takes the one better thing, leaves the show

anchors.fact: *Caipirinha* comes from *caipira*, "a southern Brazilian epithet for a person from the rural hinterlands". The name was in occasional use by the 1950s and widespread by the end of the 1960s, by which time the drink "was known throughout Brazil" (pdf 384). F7
anchors.meaning: Said once, plainly: "a word for someone from the countryside" (Wren's ruling). Never "Little Hillbilly", "affectionate" or "proud". Nobody on record chose the name or reclaimed the word, so the guest makes that link alone.

anchors.fact: Abroad, "a strong vogue in Europe ... where it remains popular" (pdf 384). Non-Brazilians consider it Brazil's national drink (pdf 383). F1, F8
anchors.meaning: No decade (1970s or 1980s is contested, C1). Never "the one the world orders" or "everywhere" (C2: the vodka version travelled too, as Kenya's Dawa, pdf 631). "National drink" is said from the outside only.

anchors.fact: "Fashionable city dwellers found cachaça too rustic and backward-looking" and preferred vodka: the Caipiroska, which "first appears in the early 1980s" (pdf 384). F9
anchors.meaning: The fashionable kept the name and dropped the cane. Said gently, with no sneer at the city or at vodka drinkers. "Early 1980s" is the first appearance, not the year everyone switched.

anchors.fact: Decree 4.851 (2 Oct 2003): a caipirinha is "a bebida típica brasileira", made "exclusivamente com Cachaça, acrescida de limão e açúcar". Decree 6.871 (2009, art. 68 §5): may be called caipirinha when "elaborada com cachaça, limão e açúcar". Decree 12.709 (31 Oct 2025, art. 74, in force): "industrializada", "elaborada com cachaça, limão e açúcar". L1–L3
anchors.meaning: Brazil set down in law that the name goes with the cane, the lime and the sugar. That vindicates it **as plain**. **Scope:** the decrees regulate drinks made and sold as products ("industrializada"), not what a bar or a kitchen pours. "Only"/"exclusively" is 2003's wording alone: the 2009 text allows water and additives. Never "banned" or "illegal". Safe line: *Brazil's law defines a caipirinha as cachaça, lime and sugar, and has since 2003.*
anchors.speaksTo: vindicated as plain; the emperor moment

anchors.fact: Cachaça: by the end of the 19th century "both loved for its deep traditions and scorned for its perceived rusticity and backwardness" (Oxford CACHAÇA, pdf 379). By Brazilian law it's 38–48% ABV (pdf 379; *Codex* p. 112). F10, F12
anchors.meaning: Loved and looked down on at the same time: the guest's position, in a bottle. Our words only.

anchors.fact: Granulated sugar muddled with lime "abrades the zest of the lime and introduces the lime's essential oils to the drink" (*Joy* pdf 173; pdf 151: "far fresher-tasting", said of lemons, "also occurs in a Caipirinha"). The muddled lime stays in: "a pleasant limy flavor that builds toward the end", though the pieces "can get bitter" (*Codex* p. 137).
anchors.meaning: The taste reason for the sugar and the lime left in (Tomás's guard: never a history reason). "Fresher" is Regan's word for the effect. Our build in the glass with no shaker is **our** reading of "built simply in the glass", not a documented recipe. The *Codex* shakes its own version.

anchors.fact: *Codex* p. 115: the peel holds "the bitter pith"; "if a seedy piece of citrus is muddled, the drink can become quite bitter". *Joy* pdf 263: muddle limes and sugar in an old-fashioned glass, add crushed ice and cachaça, stir.
anchors.meaning: The seed step and the peel's bitterness are sourced. Muddling in the glass has a book behind it (*Joy*), so the build isn't only our invention; the third way's own method still isn't on any page.

anchors.fact: Ours: unaged cachaça (our choice; the law says only "cachaça", A9), a medium lime (6 of 8 pieces), granulated sugar, cracked ice, built and stirred in the glass.
anchors.meaning: It matches the law's three things plus the ice the third way kept. Never "the original recipe" or "the way Brazilians make it": no period recipe with measures is on the page. Never say our glass "meets the law" (the decrees cover products).

cocktail.closingLine: Leave the lime in. Then let the whole table see you enjoying it.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass (double old-fashioned, about 300 ml), filled with cracked ice
method: Cut the lime in half across the middle. Lay each half cut side down and cut it into quarters. Pick out any seeds you can see, because they make it bitter.
Put 6 of the pieces in a sturdy rocks glass and add the sugar. Keep the last 2 pieces for the next one.
Press each piece firmly with a muddler, or the end of a rolling pin, giving it a slight twist, until every piece is crushed and the sugar has mostly gone. Then stop.
Fill the glass with cracked ice. To crack it, wrap ice cubes in a clean tea towel and give them a few knocks with the rolling pin.
Pour in the cachaça and stir from the bottom for about ten seconds, so the sugar comes up into the drink.
Leave the lime pieces in. They keep flavouring the drink, and the peel can add a little bitterness, which is part of the pleasure.
cocktail.name: Good as It Is

recipe.note: white (prata or branca), any bottle of 38–45%: the cane spirit itself
cut across the middle, then each half into quarters; 6 of the 8 pieces go in
grains, not syrup: they grind the oil out of the lime skin, so you taste the skin as well as the juice
to fill the glass

cocktail.tagline: Impressing you is hard. Delighting you is easy.

reading.epigraph: In Brazil, the law spells out what goes in a caipirinha. It's a short list.
whoYouAre: At the wedding with seven courses and a little card for each, what you remember is the bread. Warm, with too much butter. You said so with your mouth still full, and you meant it. You know what the foam on the fish was meant to be. You've heard the words, and you can use them if you have to. You just liked the bread more.

What stings isn't being called plain. It's the half-smile that says you liked it because you don't know any better. So in some rooms you turn yourself down a notch, and more than once you've ordered the clever thing just to keep your seat at the table. That costs you more than it shows. What you're really afraid of is being let in as the sweet one, and never as one of them. But watch what happens on the nights you don't turn it down. Someone leans over and admits the bread was the best bit for them too. Then someone else does. With you there, people can stop performing and just enjoy it.
yours: Brazilians were already drinking cachaça, their spirit made from sugar cane, with lime by the middle of the 1800s. In the first half of the last century, the city of São Paulo gave it American touches: ice, and in some versions sugar syrup, or egg white and a splash of gin, which the poet Mário de Andrade described in 1944 as "sophisticated". Some drinkers turned the new touches down.

As one historian tells it, a third way came out of that: the old country drink, made right in the glass, taking the ice from the city version. It took the name caipirinha, from a word for someone from the countryside, and by the end of the 1960s it was known all over Brazil. Europe took to it later, and still loves it. Back home, the fashionable city crowd found cachaça too rustic and made the drink with vodka instead. Brazil's law, though, defines a caipirinha as cachaça, lime and sugar, and has since 2003.

I like to think the people who kept it plain knew exactly what the egg white and gin would do, and took the ice because cold is simply better, and left the rest because they liked it how it was. You choose the same way. You're not against new things. You take what's actually good and leave the show.

The cocktail I've made for you is the caipirinha, Brazil's famous classic, made with just three things, the same three its law names: cachaça, lime and sugar, and then the ice. The cachaça is an unaged one. I didn't add anything, as a nod to the people who kept it plain. I built it in the glass with no shaker, which is how I picture that third way. The sugar is crushed into most of a lime until it has nearly gone, and its grains scrub the oil from the skin, so you taste the skin as well as the juice. The sugar stays on the dry side, so the cane and the lime come through. The pieces stay in, peel and all, and if it's left to sit, the peel adds a little bitterness. It's cold, bright and sharp, with the cane spirit's warmth underneath.

A small dare, then. Next time a table goes quiet and careful over something clever, don't wait to hear what everyone else thought. Say what you loved, even if it was the bread. It'll be a better evening for it, and you'll learn how many of them were hoping someone would.

anchors.fact: Jeppson's Malört is a bitter, wormwood-based liqueur in a Swedish schnapps style; through the second half of the twentieth century it was a Chicago dive-bar rite of passage for locals and for out-of-towners willing to try it. (Oxford pdf 1103; F1, F2)
anchors.meaning: The bitter thing is offered, not forced: "willing" is the line holding.

anchors.fact: It is still "practically a rite of passage for residents and visitors" (WBEZ 2023). Visitors who let a Chicagoan order for them often pull a face, and the face has a name: the Malört face (*The Ringer* 2019; F4, F6; no coiner, M4).
anchors.meaning: Being got is how you're let in, and the newcomer agrees to it ("trusted").

anchors.fact: Sam Mechling, working as a bouncer at a wine bar, was dared by someone at work to try it; the colleague told him it tasted like a kitchen junk drawer, and it did. (WBEZ 2023; M1, M2)
anchors.meaning: He was got first. "Dared" is said of an adult who chose to try it, never aimed at the guest.

anchors.fact: He then introduced it to his friends at birthday parties and gatherings, obsessed with their first reactions; later, at the Malört nights he ran, he bought people's drinks with his own money and sold T-shirts to break even. (WBEZ 2023; M3, M5, M6)
anchors.meaning: He passed on the way he'd been let in. The paying is at his events, not the birthdays.

anchors.fact: The brand's owner, Pat Gabelick, turned up unannounced with her lawyer at the bar where he worked; the meeting was tense at first. He showed them a letter he'd tried to send her months before, saying how much he loved the drink, with a cheque from the T-shirt profits; the post office had returned it. (WBEZ 2023 only; M7, M8)
anchors.meaning: The fear of being shut out, made literal; then a plain letter, no joke. "The letter got him in" is Wren's "I like to think", not fact (though WBEZ does say the mood changed after it).

anchors.fact: Instead of suing him, she hired him. In his words, he went from expecting to be "financially destroyed" to "a dream job" in about five minutes. Looking back (2023), he said the drink gave him new friends. (WBEZ 2023; *The Ringer* 2019; M9, M10, M12)
anchors.meaning: Taken in by the very house his jokes were about. Never "she laughed"; T-shirts never called illegal (Scoundrel's ground). No years.

anchors.fact: A named reviewer found "clear grapefruit peel notes" in Malört itself (Drink Spirits, Geoff Kleinman, 2012), and one of the descriptions Mechling collected and liked best compared it to an aspirin wrapped in grapefruit peel (*The Ringer* 2019; B5, B6). Grapefruit juice is "bitter-tart" (*Codex* p. 120); small amounts of salt suppress bitter flavours (Oxford pdf 1721; B9).
anchors.meaning: The grapefruit is in the bottle's own taste, so it isn't forced on it. Salt softens both bitters.

anchors.fact: Grapefruit juice frozen into cubes and shaken with the spirit to slush, maple and salt, strained into a chilled coupe, after Arnold's Shaken Drake (*Liquid Intelligence* p. 149), whose spirit is kümmel, a German caraway liqueur (aquavit is its Scandinavian cousin), with a little vodka.
anchors.meaning: Our riff, never Arnold's recipe; ours swaps his kümmel for Malört.

anchors.fact: Jeppson's Malört, 35% ABV, sold as a liqueur (maker's page, B2); made in Chicago by CH Distillery (Oxford pdf 1103, B1); sold in 30 US states (maker, B8). Substitute style: a Swedish besk (bäsk) brännvin, the bitter wormwood schnapps the maker says Malört belongs to.
anchors.meaning: Named because the custom is this bottle (22 bartenders' affidavits, *The Ringer*; B3).

cocktail.closingLine: Freeze the grapefruit hours ahead. Pour it for someone new, and let that be the only setup.
cocktail.glassware: coupe, chilled
method: At least four hours before, squeeze and strain the grapefruit. Pour 30 ml into each of two spaces in an ice-cube tray and freeze.
Put the coupe in the freezer to chill.
Pour the Malört, the maple syrup and the salt into a shaker. Add the two grapefruit cubes and no other ice.
Close the shaker and shake as hard as you can for at least 30 seconds, until the cubes have turned to slush and you can't hear any lumps. The shaker will get very cold.
Strain it into the frozen coupe and serve at once. There's no garnish.
cocktail.name: Got You

recipe.note: recommended: the bottle the custom is about; or any Swedish besk (bitter wormwood spirit) of 35% or stronger
frozen hours ahead as two ice cubes: they're the only ice in the shaker
dark, robust; it rounds off the grapefruit's bitterness
salt tames bitterness, and this drink has plenty

cocktail.tagline: You only play jokes on the people you want to keep.

reading.epigraph: Built on Chicago's bitter liqueur for willing visitors. The face they pull has a name.
whoYouAre: You don't play jokes on just anyone. The new one at work, a friend's quiet cousin, the neighbour who's only just started coming to the barbecue: they're who you pick. Salt in the sugar bowl, a made-up house rule, a serious look held a beat too long. Then you watch. The moment their face cracks and they laugh is the moment they're in, and a week later they're telling it themselves: the day you got them.

Someone got you first, and you rarely mention it. That's how you got in, and every joke since has been you passing it on. You remember the one that didn't land, too: the face that never came round. It's why you can feel the line before you reach it. And there's a smaller worry you'd never admit: if nobody ever gets you back, you start to wonder whether you're really in. A stranger leaves with a story that makes them one of you. People feel claimed. That lasts a lot longer than the laugh.
yours: For decades, Chicago's dive bars have poured a bitter wormwood liqueur called Jeppson's Malört for anyone willing to try it, locals and visitors alike. It's practically a rite of passage. Visitors who let a Chicagoan order for them often pull a face, and it has a name: the Malört face.

Sam Mechling was got too. He was working the door at a wine bar when someone at work dared him to try it, and told him it tasted like the junk drawer everyone has in their kitchen. Then he did what you'd have done. He brought it to his friends' birthdays and gatherings, for the look on their faces. Later he ran Malört nights, buying people's drinks himself and selling T-shirts to cover it.

Then the drink's owner, Pat Gabelick, turned up, unannounced, with her lawyer at the bar where he worked. He expected to be, in his words, "financially destroyed". Instead he showed them a letter he'd tried to send her months before, saying how much he loved the drink, with a cheque from the T-shirt money. The post office had sent it back. Instead of suing him, she hired him, and long afterwards he said the drink had brought him new friends. I like to think the jokes got him noticed, but the letter got him in. That's you, I'd bet: the joke is how you show it, and underneath there's always a letter like that.

The cocktail I've made for you puts Malört up front, a full measure and nothing hidden, because nobody's being caught out tonight. It's shaken with grapefruit juice frozen into cubes hours ahead, a method I took from a book on how drinks work, so the cold comes from fruit instead of water. A spoon of maple and some salt go in too, and it's strained, ice-cold, into a coupe. Grapefruit is bitter as well, and the salt softens both, so each makes the other good. One reviewer even found grapefruit peel in the taste of Malört itself. I chose it as a nod to Sam, who kept bringing the bitter thing to his friends. It comes out sharp, bright and much friendlier than its reputation.

Keep playing your jokes. They work. But once, with someone you've decided to keep, do what that letter did: no joke to hide behind, just what you're glad they're here for. It feels more exposed than any prank. It's also the surest way to learn you're in, because people answer plain words in kind. And one day, one of them will get you back, properly.

anchors.fact: The Cohasset Punch (rum, sweet vermouth, lemon, a piece of preserved peach) was a Chicago fixture from the 1890s until 1986 (Oxford Companion, COHASSET PUNCH, pdf 549, David Wondrich).
anchors.meaning: The neighbourhood's own drink: there for ninety years, never needing to explain itself.

anchors.fact: As Oxford tells it, Williams, who kept a Chicago saloon, was a guest at a summer house in Cohasset, Massachusetts, when the party decided New England made the best punches. He "was not satisfied with the verdict" and wired his partner, Tom Newman, to make a new punch and ship a keg of it, express. It "rapidly won over the crowd" (Oxford pdf 549, citing a 1902 trade paper; later tellings differ on who mixed it, so the story is framed as Oxford's).
anchors.meaning: Not content to be the comfortable second thought: they sent something good, and it was picked.

anchors.fact: Newman's punch was "Medford Rum–based" (Oxford pdf 549). Medford is a Massachusetts town about five miles north of Boston, and by then its name stood for New England rum in general (Oxford, RUM, MEDFORD, pdf 1699). An early bar guide prints the Cohasset Punch with "New England rum" (Paul E. Lowe, *Drinks: How to Mix and How to Serve*).
anchors.meaning: The case against New England's punch was made with New England's own rum, and it won. Why he used it, and whether anyone noticed, is not on record: only "I like to think…".

anchors.fact: The punch was bottled from 1899 and printed in 1901, but the saloon's regulars agreed neither version "did the drink true justice". At the bar it came with a brandy-soaked piece of peach and was stirred "at length" (Oxford pdf 549).
anchors.meaning: The people who knew it best chose it made by hand, by someone who knew them, over its packaged self.

anchors.fact: Our version follows Oxford's printed spec (pdf 550: muddled lemon, amber rum, sweet vermouth, rich syrup, orange bitters, stirred, coupe, brandied or canned peach) at three-quarters size. The bar stirred it "at length" and served a peach soaked in brandy "and some liqueur" until soft (pdf 549). The full minute's stir and the spoonful of syrup in the peach jar are ours.
anchors.meaning: The familiar thing, given care ahead of time, made the way the people who knew it best liked it.

anchors.fact: In 1916 the drink passed to the Ladner brothers. After Repeal their bar put up a neon lighthouse sign: "Home of Cohasset Punch". The sign and the punch stayed a Chicago fixture until 1986 (Oxford pdf 549–550).
anchors.meaning: A drink a place was proud to be the home of.

cocktail.closingLine: Give the peach its few days in the brandy. Some things are worth being waited for.
cocktail.glassware: coupe, chilled
method: A few days ahead (at least a night; they keep a week in the fridge): cut a ripe peach, or drained canned peach halves, into eighths. Put the slices in a clean jar, cover them with brandy, add a spoonful of sugar syrup (or of the can's syrup), put the lid on and leave them in the fridge until they're soft right through.
Put a coupe in the freezer.

Cut about a third of a lemon into small pieces and press them hard in the bottom of a mixing glass or jar with a muddler (the end of a rolling pin works), so they give up their juice and the oil in the peel.
Add the rum, the vermouth, the sugar syrup and the bitters.
Fill the glass with ice and stir for a long time, a full minute. Stirring keeps the drink round and smooth. Shaking would make it frothy.
Lift a peach slice out of the jar and put it in the bottom of the cold coupe. Pour the drink over it through the strainer and a tea strainer, to catch the bits of lemon.
cocktail.name: First Choice

recipe.note: an aged rum made from molasses, the kind New England once made
half the drink, and most of its sweetness

recipe.amount: about a third of a lemon
recipe.item: fresh lemon, cut into small pieces
recipe.note: pressed in the glass for its juice and the oil in its peel

recipe.item: rich sugar syrup (2 parts sugar to 1 part water, by weight)

recipe.note: an eighth of a peach, soaked in brandy for a few days until soft right through

cocktail.tagline: People feel at home with you before they've even taken their coats off.

reading.epigraph: Chicago's answer to New England's punch was made with New England rum.
whoYouAre: Half past eight on a Friday, your phone lights up: "free tonight?" You know what it means. Something else fell through. And you nearly always are free, and you nearly always go, and ten minutes after you arrive they've kicked their shoes off and they're telling you about their week. People are at ease with you in a way they aren't anywhere else. Families take to you on the first visit. New people get brought to meet you first, because with you nobody has to try.

What you don't tell anyone is that you'd like, now and then, to be the plan and not the fallback. Not the easy option: the one somebody picked on purpose. You don't say it, because wanting something out loud feels like a fuss, and you've never wanted to be the one causing it. So you stay gracious, and part of you wonders whether you'll always be liked by everyone and picked first by no one. With you, nobody has to earn their place, and that was never a consolation prize.
yours: In the 1890s, the story goes, a Chicago saloon keeper named Williams was a guest at a summer house in Cohasset, Massachusetts, when the party agreed that New England made the best punch. Williams wasn't satisfied with the verdict. He wired his partner, Tom Newman, to make a new punch and ship it by the keg, express. It came, and it won the room over.

Chicago's answer to New England was made with New England rum, from Medford, a few miles north of Boston. Whether Newman meant anything by it, nobody can say: bar books of the day called for that rum by name. But I like to think that crowd was won over by something they'd known all along, in a glass they didn't expect.

Then it won Chicago. It was bottled, and its recipe printed, but the regulars agreed neither did it justice. They wanted it as the bar served it: stirred at length, with a piece of peach soaked in brandy until soft. Later owners put up a neon lighthouse that read "Home of Cohasset Punch", and the drink stayed for about ninety years.

A whole city felt at home with this drink, and in the story, it began because one guest wouldn't let the matter rest. The cocktail I've made for you is the Cohasset Punch, a Chicago classic: an aged amber rum and sweet vermouth (wine with herbs steeped in it, then sweetened) in equal parts, lemon pressed for its juice, a little syrup, orange bitters. That bar always stirred it, and at length, so I stir it for a full minute. The peach can start as an everyday tin. You cut it small and soak it in brandy for some days, until it's soft right through, like the slice they got at the bar, not the half peach the printed recipe usually turned into. I did it that way for the people who could tell the difference, and because something familiar, given a few days' care, is worth coming back for.

In that story, Williams was a guest in someone else's house. He could simply have agreed. Instead he sent for something better, and let the room decide. When you next notice you're someone's easy option, don't be gracious about it. Let them see you'd like to be first. Whoever picks you then won't be settling.
