They'll know exactly what they've got, and you can simply enjoy being chosen.

anchors.fact: Hawaiians traditionally roasted the big ti stems underground for several days, as agave is roasted in Mexico; roasting turns the starch to sugar (Oxford OKOLEHAO, pdf 1419; Alexander 1891 p. 157 describes the baking). F4
anchors.meaning: The skill and the plant were the islands' own before any still: comes first in the telling (Wren). **Never** the traditional ti "beer" (C1: Alexander p. 87 says Hawaiians used neither fermented nor distilled drink).

anchors.fact: Oxford: a still "jury-rigged" from "two discarded whaling ship blubber-boiling pots, with a gun barrel to draw off the spirit" (pdf 1419). Alexander 1891 p. 157, the earliest account: iron pots "procured from ships", a gun barrel as the tube. F5, F6
anchors.meaning: Cooking pots and a gun barrel doing a still's job: the wrong parts that worked. Pots and gun barrel on two sources; "discarded" and "whaling" are Oxford's alone (C3), so say them as Oxford tells it or leave them.
anchors.speaksTo: can fix anything, with whatever's to hand

anchors.fact: Oxford: William Stevenson, 1790s (pdf 1419). Alexander: distilling "is said to have been first practiced here by" him, "before the year 1800" (p. 157). F2, F3
anchors.meaning: Name him plainly, once, as the man the story credits ("the man usually credited"). Never "fugitive", "convict", "Australian". The guest isn't him: the fix, not the maker, is the point.

anchors.fact: *okole* = "bottom", *hao* = "iron" (Oxford pdf 1419). Why: Oxford, the twin pots looked like buttocks; Rowley 2014, they "were said to" and the nickname "stuck". F7
anchors.meaning: The bodge's own joke became the spirit's name: the mark it left. Meaning of the word is fact; the reason is "the story goes". "The name is Hawaiian", never "the Hawaiians named it". "Bottom" once, warmly.

anchors.fact: "At one time almost every chief had his still" (Alexander 1891 p. 157). F8
anchors.meaning: The makeshift wasn't a one-off: it was copied and kept. **Chiefs, not ordinary people**, and no date. Wren's limb 3 ("ordinary people used it for a long time") has no page for the still itself: what lasted on the record is the spirit and the name.

anchors.fact: Local Hawaiian distilleries make okolehao again from ti root with sugar cane (Oxford pdf 1421); Island Distillers' 100-proof cane-and-ti (Rowley 2014). F10
anchors.meaning: Made **again**, never "still": production broke off (pdf 1421, "only since 2012 … again"). The thing is kept, not replaced. Present tense on 2014/2021 sources; **no year** (C2); bottle availability is Tomás's to check.
anchors.speaksTo: "don't worry, we'll just get a new one" answered

anchors.fact: Oxford: the ti "is a relative of the agave", its stems roasted underground "as is done with agave piñas in Mexico" (OKOLEHAO pdf 1419); traditionally, mezcal piñas are roasted "in a conical earthen or stone-lined pit underground for several days" (MEZCALEROS pdf 1287). Joven mezcal is unaged (MEZCALEROS pdf 1290; *Codex* p. 165, "young"). F4
anchors.meaning: Why mezcal: the nearest relative, traditionally roasted the same way. **"Traditionally" stays** (R10): not every mezcal is pit-roasted today. **Never called okolehao** (Wren). Say "joven mezcal", never "joven" alone: a "joven" tequila can be a caramel-coloured gold (Oxford SAUZA pdf 1743). The bottle is a stand-in, so nothing about it is "his" or "theirs".
anchors.speaksTo: makeable from an ordinary kitchen; with what's to hand

anchors.fact: A label reading okolehao doesn't promise ti: the 1960s Hawaiian Distillers' was bourbon with ti extract (Oxford pdf 1421); in 2026 an attorney estimated nine label applications since 2015, "several" described as rums (Aloha State Daily, 24 Feb 2026, secondary). F11, F12
anchors.meaning: The dossier's reason the glass makes do. Guest text needn't say it; if it does, "a bottle by that name may not be what the story made".

anchors.fact: Oxford: marmalade "includes tangible pieces of peel" and "simultaneously provides sweetness and flavor" (MARMALADE AND JAM pdf 1240). *Codex* p. 77: a teaspoon of orange marmalade in Alex Day's Little Victory (2013) brings "a touch of sweetness and a pleasant bitterness".
anchors.meaning: Sweetness is on both pages; **the bitterness is the *Codex*'s, said of one drink.** "Does the bitters' job" is our reading, not a book's.

cocktail.closingLine: Strain it through the gap in the lid. Then leave the jar by the sink, and enjoy a room where nothing's broken.
cocktail.glassware: small tumbler, one large cube
method: Take a clean jar with a screw lid (about 350 to 500 ml). A marmalade jar that's nearly finished is best: leave about 1½ teaspoons in it and scrape the sides down. Otherwise, spoon the marmalade into any clean jar.
Pour in the mezcal. Stir with the spoon for about 20 seconds, scraping the bottom, until the marmalade has loosened into the spirit.
Fill the jar two-thirds with ice. Screw the lid on tight and shake hard for about 10 seconds, until the jar is too cold to hold comfortably.

Put the large cube in a small tumbler. Loosen the lid a quarter turn, hold it in place with your thumb and strain it through the gap: the lid holds the ice back. A few shreds of peel will come through. Leave them in.
cocktail.name: Good for Years

recipe.note: any joven mezcal from 40% to 50%; an espadín is the easiest to find
an ordinary one, not reduced-sugar: the sugar and a bitter edge in one spoon
for shaking
in the glass

cocktail.tagline: You find years of life in the things people were ready to throw away.

reading.epigraph: No shaker, no strainer, no syrup. Just the last of a jar.
whoYouAre: Someone's lamp has died, or the zip's gone on a coat, and they're already saying it's had its day. You've got the back off before they've finished the sentence. A hair grip, a folded bit of card, tape from the kitchen drawer: you use whatever's there, and it works. It looks a bit odd. It lasts for years.

At a party where nothing's broken, you're not quite sure where to stand, and a dripping tap in the kitchen feels like being let in. What gets to you is the shrug, and "just get a new one", because a world that throws things away has less room for you in it. When you mend something, people keep their own thing, the bike they learned on or a grandparent's lamp, and the piece of their life that comes with it. And you show them what was wrong, so the impossible turns out to be ordinary.
yours: In Hawaii, people had long known how to bring the sweetness out of the ti plant, a relative of the agave: they roasted its big stems underground for days. Then, before 1800, distilling arrived, and the man usually credited with it is William Stevenson. His still was a makeshift: iron pots off the ships, with a gun barrel to carry the vapour.

It caught on. One history from 1891 says that at one time almost every chief had a still. And the contraption left its mark on the name. The spirit is called okolehao, which is Hawaiian: *okole* means bottom, and *hao* means iron. The pots were said to look like one, and the nickname stuck. Distillers on the islands make it from ti root again today.

I like to think that's the best ending a makeshift can have: people copied it, made a joke of its looks, and named the whole thing after it. Your repairs go the same way. All over the place, things are still working because of you, held together with something they were never meant to have, and someone smiles at the tape every time they use them. They're smiling because the thing is still theirs.

The cocktail I've made for you isn't okolehao. A true one is hard to find outside Hawaii, and not every bottle with that name on it has been made from ti root. So I made do, as a nod to that still. It's a mezcal Old-Fashioned, the cocktail at its most classic: a spirit, a little sugar, something bitter. Mezcal's agave is traditionally roasted underground for days, just as the ti was. There's no syrup and no bottle of bitters: a spoonful of orange marmalade does both jobs, sweet from the sugar and bitter from the peel. And it's best shaken in the marmalade jar itself, the nearly finished one that was on its way to the recycling, then poured through the gap under the loosened lid. The jar is the shaker and the strainer. It comes out soft orange and a little smoky, with a bitter edge and a few shreds of peel.

Next time you're asked round and nothing's broken, leave the dripping tap alone. Stay in the room with everyone else; the tap can wait. They didn't invite you for what you can mend. They invited you because they like having you there. And for once, you can enjoy the evening too.

anchors.fact: In 2002 Nick Blacknell, who had worked with Ford at Seagram's, sent him to New York to hand-sell Plymouth gin. When Blacknell took the brand over, it was down to five thousand cases a year (*A Proper Drink* p. 109; card F3).
anchors.meaning: Sent in where nobody was waiting for him.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing (am I one of you?)

anchors.fact: Simonson: Ford "laughed after every other sentence and was hard to dislike" (p. 110; F4).
anchors.meaning: What they show: ease, a grin.

anchors.fact: Ford said he "never once sold a bottle". Instead he asked bartenders if he could teach them about his gin and about bartending (p. 110; F6). It's his own account of his method, not a sales figure.
anchors.meaning: The ask said out loud, not a trick.

anchors.fact: When Jim Beam took over Plymouth's distribution, they "wanted nothing to do with whatever a brand ambassador might be". Blacknell's deal: "Give him three months". "Ford stayed." (p. 111; F7). They rejected the role, not him by name.
anchors.meaning: Handled like a stranger, and someone who knew him vouched.

anchors.fact: Of the trips' cost, Blacknell said Ford "probably didn't tell me how much it cost" and "I didn't really mind; he was doing a good job" (p. 111; F9). It's Blacknell's guess, said afterwards.
anchors.meaning: Someone in charge suspected, and didn't mind.

anchors.fact: Ford convinced Plymouth to invite a handful of American bartenders to its distillery in England. A kind of travel followed in which "Humble drink-slingers" who'd never been offered "so much as car fare" were flown to Cognac, Kentucky, Jerez and beyond (p. 111; F8). Oxford: the model "was copied and employed across the liquor and bar industries" (pdf 828; F2). The page doesn't order the trips against Beam's takeover.
anchors.meaning: The rule bends for the whole table.

anchors.fact: Oxford gives two aims together: the brands' influence, and the bartenders' "education and professional standing" (pdf 828; F2).
anchors.meaning: Never only the generous half.

anchors.fact: Plymouth's revival: Murphy and Rolls's investors bought it in 1998 and restored it. Oxford credits Plymouth's "support for the modern cocktail revival", see FORD, SIMON (pdf 1541; P1). Ford's link to this gin is on the page. Today's ABV is unsourced (P2).
anchors.meaning: It's his gin, but not his rescue alone.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink: the story in the glass

anchors.fact: The French 75 is "essentially, a Champagne or 'Imperial' Tom Collins". The traditional recipe is strained "into a highball glass filled with cracked ice". Arnaud's flute (served up, with cognac) is "counter to the original recipe" (Oxford pdf 850–851; P4). The Codex: "Some bartenders prepare a French 75 in a tall glass with ice"; the Codex itself uses a flute and Plymouth (p. 142; P5).
anchors.meaning: The ice that makes someone wince was in the original. The legend gets granted, then corrected.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink; truth with a wink

anchors.fact: Until the 1840s champagne was "preferred sweet", and "If too sweet, it was best served almost frozen". The first recorded Champagne Cocktail (Panama, 1855) had ice (Oxford pdf 427; I1–I2).
anchors.meaning: Older than the rule people quote. Never "the rule is younger": no page dates a rule.

cocktail.closingLine: Ice first, whoever's watching. Then pour the rest of the bottle for the table.
cocktail.glassware: large wine glass (about 500 ml), filled with ice
method: Fill a large wine glass right to the top with ice. Yes, for Champagne.
Shake the gin, lemon and syrup hard with ice for about five seconds, just enough to chill it.
Strain it over the ice in the wine glass.
Pour in the Champagne slowly, then lift it once with a spoon to mix.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
Pour the rest of the bottle for whoever's with you.
cocktail.name: Just This Once

recipe.note: or any dry gin of 40–43% (for a 44% gin, use 45 ml)
or any brut (dry) sparkling wine; the rest of the bottle is for the table
squeezed over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: You charm a yes out of people, then bring your friends along.

reading.epigraph: The man sent to sell the gin in this glass said he never sold a bottle.
whoYouAre: It's ten past ten, and the kitchen closed at ten. You go up to the counter, make the cook laugh, and five minutes later there are chips for six. The doorman, the receptionist, the teacher at the gate: you've had a yes out of every one of them, and you asked to their face.

People say you get away with everything. You don't. You get let off, which is different: someone decided to, because it's you. Every "go on, then" is a small proof you're still wanted. What you dread was never the telling-off. It's the one who doesn't look up, says "rules are rules", and handles you like a stranger.

There's a code in it, though you'd laugh at the word: you only try it on someone who can afford to say yes. When a rule bends for you, it bends for everyone you came with, though you never get credit for it.
yours: When Nick Blacknell was brought in to save Plymouth gin, it was down to five thousand cases in a year. He sent an old colleague, Simon Ford, to New York to hand-sell it. Ford said he never once sold a bottle. He asked bartenders, "Can I teach you about my gin?" He was, by one account, hard to dislike.

An American whiskey company took over selling Plymouth and wanted nothing to do with whatever his job was, so Blacknell bargained for three months. Ford stayed. He talked Plymouth into flying a handful of American bartenders to its distillery in England. On the bills, Blacknell said: "Knowing Simon, he probably didn't tell me how much it cost… I didn't really mind; he was doing a good job."

That's the sentence I'd frame. Somebody guessed, and didn't mind. And those trips spread: bartenders who'd never been offered so much as a bus fare were flown to Cognac, Kentucky and Jerez, and the idea was copied across the trade. I like to think he never forgot who'd let him off. That's you. A yes you win is never only for you.

The cocktail I've made for you is a French 75, a renowned Champagne classic, made with Plymouth, the gin he said he never sold. It breaks a rule people love to quote: the Champagne goes over ice, a whole wine glass of it. Somebody will wince. They needn't. The original recipe went over cracked ice, in a tall tumbler. I've made it a little sharper and sweeter than the flute version, so it stays balanced as the ice melts into it. The rest of the bottle goes round the table, as a nod to those trips: when Ford got a yes, other people came along.

Keep asking. It works, and whoever says yes enjoys it more than they let on. But now and then, ask for something you're owed, plainly, with no grin and no "go on". Watch the yes come anyway. The people who let you off were never doing it for the charm. They like you.

anchors.fact: In 2014, Houston bar owner Bobby Heugel told a drinks magazine that limes are packed by size, and that the odd-sized leftovers go into what the trade calls packer's cases, sold, by his account, for 30-40% less (*PUNCH*, 2 Apr 2014; F5).
anchors.meaning: The saving was there all along. It took someone who knew how the trade packs its fruit to tell people to ask for it.

anchors.fact: He added that maybe they weren't so easy to find in Houston any more, because he'd been telling people about them (his account, with his "maybe"; F6).
anchors.meaning: Our reading only: he gave away an edge of his own.

anchors.fact: He said one of the biggest problems that year was the limes' quality, which was little talked about, and asked why bars didn't recommend a better drink made with lemon, and tell the customer why (*PUNCH*; F7). Lemon is historically the commonest citrus in cocktails, because limes weren't widely available until the 1930s (Oxford, CITRIC ACID, pdf 466; F15).
anchors.meaning: The honest recommendation, with the reason given. The lemon isn't the stand-in: in cocktails it came first.

anchors.fact: Of where he started ("undeveloped markets"), Heugel said there was nobody at all he could talk to about drinks (*A Proper Drink*, p. 293; F10).
anchors.meaning: Our reading only: he knew what it was to be left outside the conversation.

anchors.fact: Spring 2014: Mexican limes were scarce and dear; the magazine blamed a bacterial disease and bad weather (*PUNCH*, the magazine's narration; F1).
anchors.meaning: The moment ordinary drinkers were about to pay more for the same drink.

anchors.fact: The Jack Rose (applejack, lime, grenadine) was one of three popular drinks, with the Bronx and the Clover Club, that in the 1900s made it acceptable for a cocktail to contain citrus juice (Oxford, JACK ROSE, pdf 1089). Oxford calls it "a solid classic" (pdf 1090), and the *Cocktail Codex* prints it as a classic, made with straight apple brandy (p. 129). Card `jack-rose.md` F1, F7, F9; C1 (Oxford's base is applejack).
anchors.meaning: A classic in print by 1899: the kind you tell a friend how to make right.

anchors.fact: By 1913, as the drink spread beyond downtown New York, its mixed citrus gave way to straight lemon or the trendier lime (Oxford pdf 1089; card F6).
anchors.meaning: Lemon or lime was settled by taste and fashion in this drink's own past. Here it's settled by tasting.

anchors.fact: *Codex*: the lime is the counterpoint that cuts the grenadine's richness (p. 129; card F9). Tomás's balance: lime in range only at 17.5 to 22.5 ml (15 and 25 OUT), and grenadine OUT at 22.5 ml (spec sweeps, 2026-10-06).
anchors.meaning: Our reading, on Tomás's numbers: the jigger, not a count of fruit, is what makes it the same drink every time, from any size of lime.

cocktail.closingLine: Juice the odd-sized limes. Then make one for the friend who always guesses.
cocktail.glassware: coupe (about 180 ml), chilled in the freezer
method: Put a coupe in the freezer.
Squeeze a lime and a lemon. Taste a drop of each juice. Use whichever tastes better today, and if anyone asks, tell them why.
Measure 20 ml of that juice into a shaker with 17.5 ml (3½ teaspoons) of grenadine and 60 ml of apple brandy. Measured out, it makes no difference what size the lime was.
Shake hard with ice for about 12 seconds.
Strain into the cold coupe. No garnish.
cocktail.name: Word Gets Round

recipe.note: a Calvados or an American straight apple brandy, 40 to 50%; not applejack, which is blended with neutral spirit
measured, not counted: any size of lime will do, so buy the odd-sized ones if your shop sells them cheaper. Or use lemon, if the lemons taste better that day

made from pomegranate: equal weights of 100% pomegranate juice and sugar, shaken in a closed jar until the sugar has gone. If you buy it, check the label says pomegranate. Measure it as carefully as the juice

cocktail.tagline: Nobody near you pays extra for not knowing.

reading.epigraph: Limes are packed by size, a bartender said. Odd ones go cheap. Measures don't mind.
whoYouAre: Your neighbour's parking fine came back cancelled, because you knew which sentence the appeal needed. A friend got their money back from the airline in one call, with you beside them saying what to ask for. You know which form actually gets read, and that you're allowed to ask for a name. All of it matters on the day a letter arrives and someone you love goes pale.

You'd rather not admit that you like knowing. It's a kind of power, though you wouldn't use the word. And when someone offers you a seat where things get decided, you come up with a reason to say no. Knowing this much already puts you near the side of the counter that says no. One step further, and you're afraid your own people would start to see you as one of them.

Because of you, people who'd have paid full price, signed the wrong thing or taken no for an answer didn't. You put what you know on the side of the people nobody told. That counts for a great deal more than you let it.
yours: In the spring of 2014, limes in America suddenly got scarce and expensive. A drinks magazine blamed a bacterial disease and bad weather, and asked bartenders for advice. One of them was Bobby Heugel, who owned a bar called Anvil, in Houston.

He gave away a trick of the trade. Limes are packed by size, he explained, each case holding fruit that matches. The odd sizes left over, some as big as your fist, go into what the trade calls a packer's case, and by his account it sells for 30 to 40% less. Almost every distributor has them, he said, though maybe not so many in Houston any more, because he'd been spreading the word. Then he said one of the biggest troubles with that year's limes was their quality, and asked why bars didn't recommend a better drink made with lemon, and tell the customer why.

He wasn't a newcomer. He owned the bar, and he gave the saving away anyway: to his own city first, by his account, then to anyone who read the magazine. Of where he started, he once said there'd been nobody at all he could talk to about drinks. I like to think he remembered that. I think you would. You know what it's like to be the one nobody told, and you've made sure your own people never are.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Jack Rose, a classic worth knowing. I make it with apple brandy, fresh lime and grenadine, shaken hard, then poured into a coupe you've frozen first. It's rosy red, with warm apple under bright pomegranate and lime. The balance is narrow, so the lime and the grenadine are both measured, and the lime is never counted, as a nod to Heugel's trick: measured out, it makes no difference what size the lime was. Its grenadine is pomegranate juice with sugar dissolved in it. By 1913, the Jack Rose was being made with lemon, or with lime, the newer fashion, so that choice goes back a long way. If the lemons are better that day, use lemon, and tell whoever's drinking why.

Say yes when you're next offered a seat where things get decided. You're afraid it would put you behind that counter, on the side that says no. It needn't, as long as you keep telling your people everything you know. From there you'll have more to share, and more people to share it with.

anchors.fact: Sloe gin is a British drink: the berries of the blackthorn bush steeped in gin and sweetened with sugar, traditionally poured around Christmas and New Year. (A1, S1; Oxford SLOE GIN pdf 1814, PRUNELLE pdf 1573)
anchors.meaning: Something plain, made at home, kept for the time people gather.

anchors.fact: Rural households in Britain have made it since the 1800s; with damson gin, it was a standard thing to do at harvest. (A2, S11; pdf 1814)
anchors.meaning: Know-how that lives in ordinary homes, not in a trade or a school.

anchors.fact: It reached the newspapers in the 1830s, was being made to sell by the end of that century, and had a brief vogue in America in the early 1900s (the Sloe Gin Fizz by 1904). (A3, S12, S14; pdf 1814, FIZZ pdf 794)
anchors.meaning: The trade's moment came and went.

anchors.fact: After that it fell out of favour and was missing from drinks menus for decades, apart from a slight mid-century rise with the Fizz. (A4, S13; pdf 1814)
anchors.meaning: Dropped by the menus, never said to be dropped at home. Menus only, not "the trade"; the Fizz is never said to end.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: that it stops with them

anchors.fact: In Britain it is still made from traditional recipes handed down through generations of rural families. (A5, S15; pdf 1814, "continues")
anchors.meaning: What they were given goes on being handed down. Told beside the menu decades, order-neutral: never "kept it alive", "saved", "outlasted". No named giver exists; none invented.

anchors.fact: Every winter, countryside pubs and fairs hold contests to settle whose recipe is best in the area. (A6, S16; pdf 1814)
anchors.meaning: Folk know-how tested in public by the people who keep it, and a little funny.

anchors.fact: One, the World Sloe Gin Championships, was hosted by the George Inn at Frant, open to home makers and distillers. (A7, S17; Ellis, *Severn Bites* 2016, secondary)
anchors.meaning: A village pub giving itself a world title. Past tense: never "still held".

anchors.fact: In the 2016 blind tasting, the three judges scored the top six home-made entries above every commercial one. (A8, S17; Ellis, quoting the press release)
anchors.meaning: Plain know-how holding its own. Told once, never "beat the experts".

anchors.fact: A maker who says she won it twice wrote in 2016 that she was trying the way fruit liqueurs are made in Croatia, leaving her jars in the sun. (A9, S18; Ellis 2016)
anchors.meaning: What's handed on gets tried and changed. The page never says that batch won.

anchors.fact: The Blackthorn is a name, not one recipe: one 1947 bar guide printed five quite different drinks under it, one of them gin, sloe gin, dry vermouth and orange bitters. (B1, S19; Oxford BLACKTHORN COCKTAIL pdf 280)
anchors.meaning: Many versions, one kept. The measures are Tomás's, never "Trader Vic's recipe".

anchors.fact: Bartenders have made it different ways for more than a hundred years: in 1922 a London barman wrote that it was an old drink made two ways. (B2, S20; pdf 280, Vermeire)
anchors.meaning: The argument over the right recipe is old. Paraphrase, never Felten's "great Blackthorn debate".

anchors.fact: The sloe-gin version was credited in 1908 to William Smith, bartender at Honolulu's Royal Hawaiian Hotel; his had both vermouths and Angostura. (B3, S21; pdf 280, Boothby)
anchors.meaning: A name on the recipe, as the guest keeps names on theirs. Ours isn't Smith's.
anchors.speaksTo: the giver kept in the room

anchors.fact: Of the shapes on record, this one keeps the dry vermouth because the sloe gin is already sweetened. (B4; pdf 280 + Tomás's balance, ours)
anchors.meaning: Kept what worked, and said why.

cocktail.closingLine: Sixty between the two gins, whatever the bottle. When you teach it, say how you split the sixty.
cocktail.glassware: small stemmed glass (about 150 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Put the glass in the freezer for 10 minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you make the drink.

Pour a little of the sloe gin and taste it on its own. Every bottle is sweetened by its maker, and a home-made one is sweetened to its maker's taste, so this sets your measures: the sweeter it is, the less sloe gin and the more plain gin, choosing the line from the rule. The two always add up to 60 ml.
Pour both gins, the dry vermouth and the bitters into a mixing glass (or any tall, sturdy glass) and fill it with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the mixing glass feels very cold.
Empty the serving glass if it's holding ice, then strain the drink into it. No ice in the glass.
Hold the lemon peel skin side down over the drink and pinch it between finger and thumb, so its oils fall onto the top. Then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Tried and True

recipe.note: a traditional sloe gin: bought, made by someone you know, or your own. Sloe gins can contain almond, and some makers crush the stones: if you avoid nuts, don't make this one
any London dry gin, about 43% or stronger
French-style dry white vermouth; keep it in the fridge once it's open
about the length of a thumb, with as little of the white pith as you can

recipe.item: *the rule:* the sloe gin and the gin always add up to 60 ml (2 oz)
recipe.note: most sloe gins: 30 ml of each. Sweeter than most: 22.5 ml sloe gin, 37.5 ml gin. Sweet as a syrup: 15 ml sloe gin, 45 ml gin

cocktail.tagline: Your best advice keeps someone else's voice in the room.

reading.epigraph: In 1947, one bar guide printed five different Blackthorns. This glass is built on one of them.
whoYouAre: A friend starts a new job tomorrow and is sure they'll get it all wrong. You tell them what an old neighbour used to say: learn everyone's name on the first day, and the rest can wait. It's exactly right, and they write it down. Half of what you know came like that, with somebody's name on it, and you still hear their voice when you say it.

Some of what you were told turned out to be wrong, and you let those bits go quietly, because saying so would feel like letting them down. What's left, you've tried for yourself. You can't always say why it works, only who told you, and when someone asks for the reason, you doubt yourself. The real fear is the day nobody asks. If it stops with you, a little of them stops too.
But each time you say "as my neighbour used to say", that neighbour is in the room again, and someone leaves with something to use tomorrow. You do a kindness to two people at once.
yours: Since the 1800s, households in rural Britain have made sloe gin: the berries of the blackthorn bush, left in sweetened gin and poured at Christmas and New Year. Along with damson gin, it was simply something you did at harvest.

By the end of that century it was being made to sell, and America had a short fling with it. Then for decades it went missing from drinks menus. In the countryside, the recipes went on being handed down through the generations, and they still are. Every winter, pubs and fairs hold contests to settle whose is best. One pub, the George Inn at Frant, hosted one called the World Sloe Gin Championships, and in 2016 the judges, tasting blind, gave all of the top six places to sloe gins made at home. One maker, who reports winning it twice, wrote of trying the way fruit liqueurs are made in Croatia: leaving the jars in the sun.

That's my favourite part. A blind tasting can't ask who you got your recipe from. It can only ask whether it's good. I like to think every home-made gin on that table began as somebody else's and ended up as its maker's own. That's what you do with what you were given: every name attached, every piece tried, and only what survived handed over.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Blackthorn, a classic that a barman in London was already calling very old in 1922, when it came two different ways. Of the five a 1947 bar guide printed, I kept the one built from gin, sloe gin and dry vermouth, with orange bitters, because the sloe gin is already sweetened and the dry vermouth lets the fruit show. It's stirred until very cold, served small with no ice. At the end, a lemon peel gets one pinch over the glass, for the scent. Use a traditional sloe gin, bought or made by someone you know, and keep one rule: the two gins always make 60 ml between them. Taste the sloe gin first. The sweeter it is, the less of it and the more of the plain gin. I left that call to you as a nod to those pub contests: whatever the recipe says, your own taste decides.

You're afraid it ends with you. It doesn't. Somewhere, someone already starts a sentence with your name, and you just haven't been there to hear it. So don't wait for someone to ask, or until you're old. This year, teach one thing you were taught to someone who'll keep it, and tell them the bit you changed, and why. That's how you end up among the people you quote.

anchors.fact: James "Jimmie" Charters, barman at the Dingo in Montparnasse, Paris, from 1924 (he came "as assistant barman") (F2).
anchors.meaning: A real room with a real person running the bar: standing, not a title.
anchors.speaksTo: Authority on loan: the one everyone in the room looks to.

anchors.fact: His credo: success behind the bar comes from "an ability to understand the man or woman I am serving, to enter into his joys or woes", so they feel "the need of me as a person rather than a servant" (F1; *Joy* pdf 114–115 credits Cody's book).
anchors.meaning: The authority is spent on understanding people. Use a paraphrase in the reading and quote at most "joys or woes".
anchors.speaksTo: The one true thing: they give people a hearing.

anchors.fact: His job, as he listed it: "settle fights, listen to intimate confidences, prevent jealousies, arrange parties, and crack jokes. I never worked so hard in all my life" (F4).
anchors.meaning: Listening sits right next to settling fights, and he calls it work.
anchors.speaksTo: Hidden: the patience takes effort and isn't temperament.

anchors.fact: Fights were "to be avoided at all costs". He could "usually" smell one coming (his "usually") and would try jokes or a drink on the house. "Usually the free drink works": they "forget their quarrel and drink to each other, or both drink to me, or in some way forget to be angry" (F5).
anchors.meaning: He answers heat with a welcome, not force, and the angry ones stay. ("Usually" is his word: keep it, it isn't "always".)
anchors.speaksTo: Gift: even the angry one leaves still welcome. Fear: chaos on their watch.

anchors.fact: He couldn't stop a regular's credit "for fear he will be angry, walk out, and everything will be gone" (F7).
anchors.meaning: Keeping people in the room cost him money and nerve.
anchors.speaksTo: It visibly costs them something. The private fear is that it comes apart anyway.

anchors.fact: It didn't always work: once he "had to carry" the brawlers "out, one at a time" (F9).
anchors.meaning: A calm that sometimes failed. It isn't a saint's story.
anchors.speaksTo: "I listened too long and it came apart anyway": honest, and gentle.

anchors.fact: When customers bought him drinks, he kept look-alikes under the bar (bitters and water, cordial and water) and raised "the appropriate glass", because "I believe in always drinking what the client drinks!" (F12).
anchors.meaning: He matched them glass for glass while keeping a clear head. *Our reading:* the steady face kept for everyone.
anchors.speaksTo: Hidden: people check their face first, so they keep it steady. **Guard C8:** never "fooled them".

anchors.fact: A cocktail he invented at the Dingo: cognac, with a sixth each of Pernod, Amer-Picon, Mandarin and sweet cherry brandy, shaken, "either drunk straight or diluted with a little soda" (F11). The cognac share is OCR-garbled; 2/6 is our inference.
anchors.meaning: A real house drink to riff from. Only "a cocktail he invented at the Dingo" is fact; the proportions are not his unless confirmed, and anything we change is ours.

anchors.fact: Arnold's "Languishing Ice Manhattans" (*Liquid Intelligence* pp. 87–88): one Manhattan stirred 15 seconds, then left on its ice 90 seconds before straining, came out "almost identical" to one stirred and strained at once. He says letting ice sit "for upward of 2 minutes won't ruin the drink"; the extra dilution is "remarkably negligible" (rye, not rum: applying it to our drink is Tomás's craft call). Condition (p. 87): "reasonably short (a couple minutes)" and ice "fairly large (not shaved)".
anchors.meaning: The stirred drink can wait while someone finishes.
anchors.speaksTo: The one true thing: let them finish.

anchors.fact: He had boxed professionally (F3).
anchors.meaning: One clause at most: the Gentle Giant's shape (*In One Piece*).

anchors.fact: The Bob/T scene (fists unclenching, "Have a drink… Make it a whisky and a Pernod, Jimmie") is Bob's calm, not Jimmie's (F13).
anchors.meaning: Never told as Jimmie's act.

cocktail.closingLine: Let it wait on the ice until they've said everything. Then strain it, and give your answer.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail glass (about 180 ml), chilled
method: Chill the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Put the cognac, sweet vermouth, mandarin liqueur and bitters in a mixing glass or jar. Fill it with ordinary ice cubes (not crushed).
Stir for about 15 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
If someone's still talking, stop stirring and leave the spoon where it is. The drink can sit on its ice for a minute and a half or so without getting watery.
When they've finished, empty the serving glass and strain the drink into it.
Squeeze the mandarin peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Go On

recipe.note: any VS or VSOP cognac, 40% or stronger
any mandarin liqueur made on brandy or cognac; for the Mandarin in the cocktail Jimmie invented at the Dingo
squeezed over the top, then dropped in; a clementine works

cocktail.tagline: Most of the fights you've stopped never happened.

reading.epigraph: This drink can sit on its ice while someone finishes talking. Someone once timed it.
whoYouAre: You hear it before anyone else does. A joke at dinner that lands a little too hard. A voice going up half a note in a meeting. A group chat going quiet in the wrong way. By the time the others notice, you've already pulled up a chair, asked the one who's upset what they meant, and let them say all of it.

People take you for easygoing. You aren't. You're listening the whole time, because when people are in your care, you'd rather hear the hard thing tonight than watch it break something later. You could settle most of it with one word, and you rarely use it. You'd rather they finish. People say the real thing around you, because they're sure you'll hear all of it. You never mention how hard you work at it, or the fear underneath: that the one time you miss it, it all comes apart, and someone you were looking after pays for it.
yours: In 1924, a barman called Jimmie Charters started at the Dingo, a bar in Montparnasse, Paris, as the assistant. Years later he told his story to a writer, Morrill Cody, and the job he described went a long way past the drinks. He was there to settle fights, to listen when people confided in him, to stop jealousies before they started, and to crack jokes. He'd never worked so hard in his life, he said.

Fights, he said, were to be avoided at all costs. He could usually smell one coming, and then he'd do anything to stop it. He'd try a drink on the house, and usually, he said, the free drink worked. And this is what gets me: the two who'd been about to fight would drink to each other, or both drink to him, or one way or another forget to be angry. It didn't always work. Once a fight broke out anyway, and he had to carry one side out, one at a time.

I like to think the drink was never the point, and that he wasn't deciding who was right. He was turning two people back towards each other before anyone got hurt, and that's what you do. He also admitted what it cost him. When a regular ran up a big tab, he couldn't stop the credit, for fear they'd get angry, walk out, and everything would be gone. I think you know that fear. It's the no you swallow to keep the room together.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Manhattan, one of the most famous classics, the one so many others were built on. I've made it on cognac instead of whiskey, with a small spoon of mandarin liqueur and the oil from a mandarin peel, as a nod to the cognac and the Mandarin in the cocktail Jimmie invented at the Dingo. It's rich and warm, and the first thing you'll smell is mandarin. And it's stirred on purpose. Dave Arnold, who wrote a whole book on the science of cocktails, once left Manhattans sitting on their ice for a minute and a half before straining them, and could find almost no difference. So this one can wait a minute or two on its ice while someone finishes what they're saying.

You're right to hear people out, and they're right to trust you for it. But one day the kind thing will be the no: the tab stopped, the plan called off, the decision made before everyone agrees. Say it plainly, once they've finished. The people you listened to won't walk out. They stayed because you listened, and that's exactly why your no will hold.

anchors.fact: Wayne Collins (b. 1970), British bartender from Camden, North London; began pulling pints at a relative's pub in Hoxton in the late 1980s (Proper p. 102; Oxford COLLINS, WAYNE, pdf 557). F1
anchors.meaning: A working bartender behind the bar, not a critic at a desk.

anchors.fact: He "hated the fruit Martini" and wrote an article in *Class* "bashing it" (Proper pp. 101–102). The page gives **no date** for the article; it sits in the chapter's late-1990s London. It doesn't say the article was aimed at LAB or at any one drink. F2
anchors.meaning: A public no to the drink the room loved. The cost on the page is the stand itself. Anything about it costing him warmth is "I like to think".

anchors.fact: *Proper* p. 39: the "red-hot Met Bar" in London "was all about fresh-fruit Martinis"; LAB ("pivotal… in the late 1990s") had its own. p. 98: the Met Bar's fruit "Martinis" "were greeted like a revelation". *Class* was a magazine, published by Simon Difford (p. 39). **Counterweight:** the fruit "Martinis" "made the Martini purists livid, but it kept the cocktail's name alive", and Difford himself argued that the name made it a serious drink (p. 39). F13 (r4, audit R1/R2)
anchors.meaning: The hottest bars poured them, and people loved them. Never "everywhere", and the setting never dates the article. The other side had a case, so nobody is a villain.

anchors.fact: His stated reason: "I didn't like that it was called a Martini" (Proper p. 102, Collins on the record, 2014). F3
anchors.meaning: The objection is to the **name**: a careless thing carrying a name meant to stand for something. Never say he wrote the article for the guests.

anchors.fact: His cocktail schooling came from Lee Chappell (p. 102). In Collins's own quote: "Why would anyone drink gin and vermouth? He'd say, 'You better start liking it. It's not about you, is it? It's about the guests.'" **Speaker:** the outer quote has no tag, but "He'd say" is Chappell, so the voice asking is Collins's, recalling. Tell it as "the way Collins remembers it". "He'd say" is habitual, so no single scene, no date, and no "young" (the page gives no age). F4
anchors.meaning: The standard he later defended wasn't his taste. It was handed to him against his taste, for whoever would drink it, and given with its reason.
anchors.speaksTo: the reason is care, not vanity

anchors.fact: Chappell ran the Long Island Iced Tea Shop in Covent Garden, which served bottled cocktails "at a time when no one else did"; Collins likened him to Bryan Brown's character in *Cocktail* and said he knew five hundred recipes (p. 102). F5
anchors.meaning: The man who taught the gin-and-vermouth rule ran a shop named for a party drink. The standard isn't snobbery. If used, "our reading".

anchors.fact: He kept reading old cocktail books and studied Peter Dorelli (Savoy) and Salvatore Calabrese (Lanesborough) (p. 102); he "grabbed what he could find at book fairs" (p. 60). F6
anchors.meaning: The standard was learned, slowly, out of sight.

anchors.fact: In 2000 chef David Cavalier hired him as bar manager at High Holborn, a forty-seat bar. His menu of classics had "Manhattans, Daisies, and Punches": "I looked for drinks that I found in books that were not on lists around London" (p. 102). F7
anchors.meaning: Say "weren't on other London menus", never "couldn't get anywhere else" (audit R4). Daisies are named as a kind; the whiskey one isn't (R7). The refusal came with a yes: the real one, put in front of people. The position's ground.

anchors.fact: Simonson: "In a time when most London drinkers had never been served a cocktail without ice", Collins was "stirring perfect Sazeracs" in "expensive glassware" (p. 102). The claim is Simonson's, and the glassware is the **Sazeracs'**. F8
anchors.meaning: A Daisy served up in fine glass is **our** choice, said as ours ("the way he served his Sazeracs"), never his Daisy. "Without ice" carries "up"; it doesn't carry "very cold" or "stemmed" (audit R9).

anchors.fact: Of High Holborn: "it influenced a lot of people" (Tony Conigliaro); "An amazing bar to work in" (Sebastian Reaburn, one of his bartenders) (p. 102). The subject is **the bar**, not Collins alone. F9
anchors.meaning: Other people's work got better near it. Robin's rule: say the gift once, plainly.

anchors.fact: Oxford: a key role in the UK bar renaissance of the 1990s, "driving up service standards and improving product knowledge in the industry" with the Mixxit training and education programme he developed (pdf 557). Name Mixxit only as a training programme; the page doesn't date it, so no "went on to" (audit R6). Say "in the trade" or "the industry", not "across the UK". F10
anchors.meaning: The standard became something others were trained to meet.

anchors.fact: Oxford DAISY (pdf 627): "a sour sweetened with a liqueur or flavored syrup, lightened with a splash of sparkling water, and served in a cocktail glass", an American drink of the 1870s, first in print in 1876. In those first printed Daisies the orange cordial is "intended as an accent, not as the main sweetener" (*Imbibe!* pdf 105–106). So by the *Codex*'s structure (p. 106: a small liqueur is seasoning) ours is a **sour, Daiquiri family**. Oxford calls the old Daisy "one of the progenitors of the Sidecar and the Margarita". Daisies were on his High Holborn menu (Proper p. 102). Never the *Codex*'s modern-daisy definition, and never "a Sidecar". Tomás owns the recipe; never "his recipe". F11 (fixed r3, audit H1)
anchors.meaning: Why the drink is an old Daisy: it's the one on his menu that no sibling pours.

anchors.fact: Oxford pdf 627: "Neither version… has been prominent in the twenty-first-century cocktail renaissance" (the book's judgement, 2021). F12
anchors.meaning: Even now it's rarely on a list. Never "nobody makes it".

anchors.fact: Tomás's two teaspoons of vermouth: Chappell's answer to "Why would anyone drink gin and vermouth?" was "You better start liking it" (p. 102). The page never says Collins came to like it, never says *dry*, and the lesson is about gin. The tie is our reading. Taste: Tomás's numbers support "drier" (7.03 → 6.62 g sugar), but not "sharper" (acid 0.828 → 0.793%). (audit T8, R10)
anchors.meaning: The taste he was told to start liking, for someone else.

cocktail.closingLine: Measure the vermouth: it's only two teaspoons. And when you turn something down, add the why.
cocktail.glassware: fine stemmed cocktail glass (about 210 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Chill the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Put the bourbon, lemon juice, simple syrup, curaçao and dry vermouth in a shaker. Fill it with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds, until the outside of the shaker is almost too cold to hold.
Empty the glass. Strain the drink into it, pouring through a small sieve as well so no chips of ice get in.
Pour the tablespoon of cold soda water on top. No garnish.
cocktail.name: On Their Behalf

recipe.note: any bourbon of 45% (90 proof) or stronger
equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear
an accent, not the main sweetener, as in the first printed Daisies
a little vermouth, for the gin and vermouth Collins remembers his teacher telling him to start liking: it was for the guests, not for him
added last

cocktail.tagline: Your standards are a promise to the person who'll never know what you turned down.

reading.epigraph: Two teaspoons of vermouth went in, for a taste one bartender was told to start liking.
whoYouAre: You notice the thing that's slightly off. The line on the page that sits a millimetre low. The dish that should have come out hot. The word on a menu that doesn't mean what it says. Most people let it pass. You can't, and you'd rather seem cold than let it go out like that.

People take it for pride, or for your taste. It isn't, mostly. At the end of every piece of work there's someone who'll never know what you turned down for them, and they're who you're thinking of. You hardly ever mention it, because it sounds like asking to be thanked. So your no arrives alone, without its reason. What you fear is something careless going out under a name that was meant to stand for something. Around you, good becomes normal. People raise their own bar near you, often without noticing they have, and whoever's at the end gets it as it should be.
yours: In 1990s London, the hottest bars were pouring fruit "Martinis". People loved those drinks, and plenty still do. A bartender from Camden called Wayne Collins hated them, and wrote an article against them in a magazine called *Class*. His quarrel was with the name. As he told Robert Simonson in 2014, he didn't like that it was called a Martini.

The way Collins remembers it, he'd ask why anyone would drink gin and vermouth, and his teacher, Lee Chappell, would tell him he'd better start liking it, because it was for the guests, not for him. Chappell, by the way, ran a place in Covent Garden called the Long Island Iced Tea Shop. Nobody in this story is a snob.

I can't know what was in Collins's head when he wrote that article, but I like to think it was Chappell's lesson: not his own taste, but a promise made to someone else, about what a name should mean. He didn't stop at no, either. In 2000, as bar manager at High Holborn, he put on a menu of drinks he'd found in old books, ones that weren't on other London menus. That bar, as one London bartender put it, influenced a lot of people, and the training programme he built, Mixxit, is credited with driving up service standards in the trade. That's the shape of what you do: the no comes with a better yes behind it, and people around you start holding the same line.

The cocktail I've made for you is a whiskey Daisy. Daisies were on his High Holborn menu, and I've made this one the old way: whiskey (bourbon, here), fresh lemon, some sugar, just a touch of orange curaçao, then only a splash of soda. It's an old classic you'll still rarely find on a list. I serve it very cold, in a fine stemmed glass. Like his Sazeracs, it comes in good glassware with no ice in it. And I've added two teaspoons of dry vermouth, as a nod to the gin and vermouth Collins was told to start liking, for the guests. You won't taste it as vermouth. You'll taste a drier, rounder drink because of it.

I wouldn't ask you to lower the bar. Please don't, for anyone. But from now on, when you turn something down, add the why, the way Chappell did. A no that comes with its reason stops sounding cold. It sounds like care, because that's what it is. And the reason travels where you can't: people start keeping your standard in rooms you'll never walk into, because at last they understand why.

anchors.fact: Norman Hobday (1933-2011) opened Henry Africa's in San Francisco in 1969 (Oxford pdf 995; *Proper* p. 51: Broadway and Polk; he "helped kick off the fern bar movement"). F1, F2, F22; A7
anchors.meaning: The one who changed the room. Never "the first fern bar" (C1: the Trident was three years earlier).

anchors.fact: By his own account (Chronicle 2011), when he found the place it was a bar with blackened windows. F13; A8
anchors.meaning: The old room as it was. Told as his account. Never say he changed the windows.

anchors.fact: "There wasn't enough money to remodel", so he brought in plants: they "did a hell of a job for what they cost" (Chronicle 2011, his words). F14; A9
anchors.meaning: The sensible reason, said out loud. On the record, so the bartender grants it ("I believe him").
anchors.speaksTo: the practical argument that hides the love

anchors.fact: "It was bright and cheery. People started swarming in there" (Chronicle 2011). Fern bars made barrooms bright places where "both sexes could mingle on equal terms" (Oxford pdf 770). F6, F15; A2, A10
anchors.meaning: More people let in. Women on equal terms is the story's change, never a point about the guest.
anchors.speaksTo: more people in the shared place

anchors.fact: Many singles bars were dressed like 1890s Gilded Age lounges ("brass rails, Tiffany lamps, and potted plants"), lounges that "had often banned unescorted women"; the change was made by "nostalgists" as well as feminists and ecologists (Oxford pdf 995, 770). F4, F5, F7; A3, A4
anchors.meaning: The old look brought back, holding everyone. It's a look revived ("fancifully resurrected"), not furniture kept, and the movement's nostalgia isn't Hobday's stated motive.
anchors.speaksTo: the old form kept, the welcome changed

anchors.fact: Hobday "loved his bar as much as his customers did", legally took its name, Henry Africa, a few years before it closed, and kept it until he died (Oxford pdf 995; Chronicle 2011). F12, F17; A11
anchors.meaning: The love shows in staying, not in what he said. "I like to think it was never the whole reason" is the one signposted sentence. Dossier only: in his telling the name came from his mother's condition (F16).

anchors.fact: Fern bars are credited with bringing the American saloon back from the dead (Oxford pdf 770, paraphrased; never its eight-word run). F8; A5
anchors.meaning: The change saved the old thing.

anchors.fact: Henry Africa's closed in 1986 (Oxford pdf 995). By the early 2000s, the craft movement's principles included keeping "the gender-inclusive bars" and the women behind the bar (Oxford pdf 1332). F10, F11; A6, A13
anchors.meaning: The bar closed and the change didn't. The movement was "people", drinkers and bartenders together, not "a new generation of bartenders".

anchors.fact: The Lemon Drop, Hobday's "most enduring original cocktail" (Oxford pdf 995); the original was "a more elegant affair", served up in a sugar-rimmed cocktail glass, before it became a shot. His bar used fresh juices to order (pdf 1175). F18-F20; A14-A16
anchors.meaning: Made the elegant way it began. Never "his recipe" (C2: *Proper* p. 52 adds triple sec) and never "his lemon" (C3). The ratio and the outside-only rim all the way round are ours. No "mask".

anchors.fact: James C. Maloney's *20th Century Guide for Mixing Fancy Drinks* (Chicago, 1900) prints a family of Bell-Ringers whose glass is coated inside with "Eagle Creme D'Apricot" ("abricotine"), red, before the drink goes in; half a teaspoon in the Gin and Manhattan ones; also in the *Police Gazette* 1902-03. B1-B7; A17
anchors.meaning: The old era's gesture around the new drink. Date: "1900", never "1890s" (C6); "close to" or "at the very end of" the era the fern bars dressed up as. His was a sweet red liqueur. "Tip nothing out" is ours (B2).
anchors.speaksTo: the old form kept, holding the new

anchors.fact: Dry apricot eau-de-vie in place of his liqueur: "less sweet and more delicate" (Oxford pdf 133, "little residual sugar"). Apricot pairs with citrus and fruit brandy (*Flavor Matrix* pdf 236, rendered). B8; A18
anchors.meaning: Our swap, said as ours: the glass smells of apricot without being any sweeter. Veto-free under Robin's evidence rule (2026-10-06): no page names kernels in the eau-de-vie (Oxford pdf 133: apricots and pomace).

cocktail.closingLine: Coat the glass before you pour. And before you change anything, say what you're keeping.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail coupe (about 200 ml), chilled, coated inside with apricot eau-de-vie, fine sugar on the outside of the rim
method: Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes.
Pour the half teaspoon of apricot eau-de-vie into a saucer, and spread a little fine sugar on a second saucer.
Turn the cold glass upside down and roll the outside edge of its rim through the apricot spirit, then through the sugar, until a thin band of sugar runs all the way round the outside.
Pour what's left of the apricot spirit into the glass and turn the glass slowly until the inside is coated. Leave it there. Nothing gets tipped out.
Put the vodka, lemon juice and simple syrup in a shaker, fill it with ice and shake hard for 10 to 15 seconds.
Strain it into the glass.
cocktail.name: Not the Same

recipe.note: any plain, unflavoured vodka of 40% or stronger; not a citrus vodka
squeezed just before you mix
one part sugar dissolved in one part warm water, cooled

a clear, dry apricot brandy (Hungarian barack pálinka or Austrian Marillenbrand style), not the sweet apricot-flavoured kind. It coats the glass, the way a Chicago bartender coated his glasses in 1900
on the outside of the rim only

cocktail.tagline: You change the things you love so more people get to love them too.

reading.epigraph: A Chicago bar guide of 1900 says to coat the glass. The drink came decades later.
whoYouAre: Every summer there's the same street party, and every summer a few more people find a reason to miss it. You're the one who suggests the Saturday instead of the Sunday, and the neighbours nobody ever thought to knock for. You keep the food everyone brings, the old songs, the raffle with the terrible prizes. Someone who's been coming for thirty years tells you it won't be the same. It isn't. The next summer, the street is full.

Nobody guesses that you love the old version more than the people defending it. You argue with dates and numbers, because "I'd hate to lose this" sounds soft, so the ones who love it too can hear someone wrecking it. The row doesn't scare you. What does is the change you pushed for turning out to be what finishes it off, and everyone remembering it was you. And look what you leave instead: the things people love are still there, with more people in them, because someone cared enough to change them. Nobody says so at the time. Someone should.
yours: Before he opened Henry Africa's in San Francisco in 1969, Norman Hobday found the place, which he remembered as a bar with blackened windows. There wasn't enough money to remodel, he said later, so he brought in plants. As he put it, they did "a hell of a job for what they cost". It was bright and cheery, he said, and people started swarming in.

Hobday loved the place as much as his customers did. A few years before it closed, he legally changed his own name to the bar's, Henry Africa, and kept it until he died. Many bars like his were done up with brass, Tiffany lamps and ferns, like the lounges of the 1890s, which had often turned away women who came on their own. Now women and men came in on equal terms. Fern bars are credited with bringing the American saloon back from the dead.

He gave the cheap reason, and I believe him. But I like to think it was never the whole reason: nobody takes a bar's name for the rest of their life over a cheap fix. You'd know that move. You give the sensible reason out loud, and the love shows in how long you stay. And what you change tends to outlive the place. Henry Africa's closed in 1986. The change didn't. When the bar world went back to the old craft in the early 2000s, it chose to keep, among other things, the bars where women drank on equal terms, and the women working behind them.

The cocktail I've made for you is Hobday's most enduring drink, the Lemon Drop, made the elegant way it was first served, before it shrank into a shot: up, in a sugar-rimmed glass. Mine is a chilled coupe, and I take the sugar all the way round. The lemon is squeezed fresh, the way his bar made its juices, to order. It tastes of the lemon candy it's named after, sweet and bright. The change is in the glass. In a Chicago bar guide from 1900, James Maloney gave a set of drinks that went into a glass coated inside with apricot liqueur, a sweet red one. I do the same with a clear, dry apricot brandy. Half a teaspoon is enough to coat the glass and hold the rim's sugar in place, and I tip none of it out. It's there as a nod to what you do: the old thing kept on purpose, holding the new one. The apricot reaches you first, then the lemon.

You keep the love behind the sensible reasons, and that's why the people defending the old version hear an enemy. Let them hear the love first, before the dates and the numbers. They'll find someone on their side, because you always were. And once the place is full again, don't stand by the wall checking that it held. Go in and enjoy it. It was always as much yours as theirs.

anchors.fact: (Oxford: the Old Tub name "gained some distinction through the late 1800s", F2, so say "by the late 1800s" and no place.) At Repeal, late 1933, aged sixty-nine, he brought his brother Park, Park's sons Carl and Earl, and his son T. Jeremiah back to work (Oxford pdf 1105: "gathered his family"). Cowdery says the brothers and their sons reopened the distillery. F6
anchors.meaning: A place kept for named others, more than one, after everything had stopped. In our words, never the family-tradition line (C5), and never "he alone" (C4).

anchors.fact: Oxford: to his "chagrin" he learned he had lost the rights to the family's old name, Old Tub. Cowdery: there were problems over who owned that name. F8
anchors.meaning: The private wince, in the record's one word for a feeling. The name was lost, not given (C2). Why it went isn't known.

anchors.fact: By the following August building had begun, and distilling started 120 days later (Oxford pdf 1105, F7: say "by the next August" and "about four months", never "summer" or "a new distillery"; Cowdery has it rebuilt). The whisky went out under his own name instead, and soon became the familiar Jim Beam (Oxford pdf 1105; Cowdery). F8
anchors.meaning: **Our reading** (signposted): he carried on without the old name rather than stop, and kept them working. No motive is on record (C8). Never "Colonel" (C6).

anchors.fact: After he retired in 1944, his nephew Carl and his son T. Jeremiah ran the work (Oxford). When the company was sold in the 1940s, the new owners "kept the name, and the family" (Cowdery). F9, F10
anchors.meaning: The promise held past him. Name only these people and these roles (C7). Who owned what stays out (C1).

anchors.fact: "The best-selling bourbon" (Oxford, sources accessed 2021). Beam descendants "still have a large say" (Cowdery, 2024). F11, F12
anchors.meaning: Lets the drink sound worth having. Present tense ("still"), never research talk (Q145, 2026-10-06: "last I read" cut, "today" not added). Cowdery May 2024 is the latest page read, so re-check before publishing. Say "the family's descendants", not "his" (Cowdery counts the whole Beam line).

anchors.fact: Oxford's Jim Beam white label: "a four-year-old 80-proof whisky" (40%), sources accessed 2021 (pdf 1106). F11
anchors.meaning: A named bottle, recommended. Its strength is on the page only as of about 2021, so give a dated or style-level ABV. Substitute: any Kentucky straight bourbon.

anchors.fact: Oxford: the New York Sour is a whisky sour "with a float of red wine layered on top", dating to the 1880s, "first attested to Chicago". It was known elsewhere as a "Southern" or "Continental" Sour and called "New York" in Boston, from 1885 (pdf 1387). *Imbibe!*: "the name it finally settled on after Prohibition" (pdf 96). Oxford's recipe uses straight rye in a cocktail glass. The *Codex* gives it as bourbon, lemon and simple syrup, "shaken and served in a coupe with a float of juicy red wine" (p. 257).
anchors.meaning: Name it as a renowned classic. The name's history stays out: it would be a second name story beside Old Tub. Bourbon is on a page (Codex); the wine glass and the 20 ml of syrup are Tomás's, so never "the classic way".

anchors.fact: An 1883 Chicago bartender told a reporter that "the claret makes the drink look well and it gives it a better taste" (*Imbibe!* pdf 96; Oxford pdf 1387, *Chicago Tribune* 25 Nov 1883). He also claimed to have invented it, and Wondrich is sceptical: another Chicago bartender topped a sour with claret the same year.
anchors.meaning: The proof line, with its channel: "a Chicago bartender told a reporter in 1883". In the epigraph, it's "his sours", never a bare "it" that makes our glass the one he praised. Never "the man who invented it". Our reading: the one thing allowed to show makes the whole better.
anchors.speaksTo: let them see you mind, once

anchors.fact: Oxford: egg white and ice "blur the sharp line" between the sour and the float (pdf 1387).
anchors.meaning: Up, with no egg and no ice. The line stays sharp.

anchors.fact: Tannins in grape skins and seeds give red wine its tannic flavours, and many polyphenols are astringent (*LI* p. 265).
anchors.meaning: A taste claim, labelled as taste: a small dry pucker on the first sip, then the sour.

anchors.fact: The *Flavor Matrix* lists red wine among corn's surprise pairings (pdf 88). Bourbon must be at least 51% corn by US regulation (Oxford CORN pdf 583).
anchors.meaning: The classic float is also the Matrix's pairing, so the classic is kept because the float is the point. Say "bourbon is mostly corn", never Jim Beam's own mash bill (not on a page).

cocktail.closingLine: Float the red so it shows. Once in a while, so should the cost.
cocktail.glassware: small stemmed wine glass (about 250 ml), chilled, no ice in the glass
method: Chill the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Put the bourbon, lemon juice and simple syrup in a shaker. Fill it with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds, until the shaker is frosty on the outside.
Empty the glass. Strain the drink into it, through a small sieve as well, so no chips of ice get in. Let it settle for a few seconds.
Hold a spoon upside down just above the drink, and pour the red wine slowly onto the back of it, so the wine spreads out and rests on top as a thin red layer. Don't stir. No garnish.
cocktail.name: A Place Kept

recipe.item: Jim Beam bourbon (white label, 40% as of about 2021)
recipe.note: recommended: the whisky that took his own name. Or any Kentucky straight bourbon of 40% or stronger
equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear
a young, dry, juicy red such as a Cabernet Sauvignon. Floated on top, never shaken in

cocktail.tagline: When you say there's room for everyone, there is.

reading.epigraph: Red wine floats on this sour. In 1883, a bartender said wine made his sours better.
whoYouAre: When you tell people there's a place for them, they stop worrying. They can, because you've taken the worrying on yourself. You keep your word the way other people keep a house: every day, mostly unseen, and without asking whether it suits you this week.

You said there'd be a place for all of them. You never said what it cost you. Something of yours goes missing along the way, a plan, a weekend, the thing you'd hoped to put your name to, and you act as if it were the obvious thing to do. Partly because it is. Partly because you're afraid that if they saw you mind, they'd ask themselves whether the promise still holds. It does. Because of you, the ones who rely on you get to stop worrying about tomorrow, and most people go a whole life without that.
yours: Old Tub was a good name for a bourbon. Through the late 1800s it made something of a name for itself, made by Jim Beam's father and grandfather, and in 1892 Jim took over running it, with his brother-in-law. Then Prohibition shut everything down. When it ended, late in 1933, Jim was sixty-nine.

He gathered the family: his brother Park, Park's sons Carl and Earl, and his own son, T. Jeremiah. The family still remembers him telling them it was time they all went back to work. By the next August, building work had begun, and about four months after that the stills were running. Along the way he found out that the right to the Old Tub name had been lost. He minded. The word used for it is chagrin, which is the polite word for a wince. The whiskey went out carrying his own name instead. You've almost certainly seen it.

After he retired in 1944, his nephew Carl and his son T. Jeremiah ran it, and the family's descendants still have a big say in how it's made. We don't know what Jim told them about the name, but I like to think he said very little: there was work to do, and he'd promised them a place in it. I recognise that in you. You keep the place you promised, and when something of yours is lost along the way, you carry it quietly and go on.

The cocktail I've made for you is a New York Sour, a renowned classic. Mine is bourbon, fresh lemon and sugar, shaken cold and poured without ice, sharp and clean. I'd make it with Jim Beam, since it carries the name he ended up with, though any Kentucky straight bourbon will do. Then one thing goes over the top: a float of dry red wine, a thin red band above the tawny sour. Only the wine shows, and it brings a little dry pucker to the bright sour. Back in 1883, a bartender in Chicago told a reporter the wine made the drink look good and taste better. I put it there for the one thing in this story that stung.

When keeping a promise costs you something, say so, once, to someone you kept the place for. The promise won't look any weaker. It'll look exactly like what it is: something you care about enough to pay for. And they'll finally get the chance to thank you, which you so rarely allow.

anchors.fact: Chalker's brief for Gin Palace (Melbourne, 1997): "I wanted it to look like it had always been there", a Budapest bar of the 1890s, renovated in the 1950s and still going; a sleek bar among heavy old sofas and armchairs (*Proper* p. 141). F1, F5, F6
anchors.meaning: He didn't ask for one good thing. He asked for the whole picture, down to the room's age. Fences: "outlandish" is Simonson's word; no "canoodling".
anchors.speaksTo: The lighting, the table, the song: it must be right

anchors.fact: His reason, in his words as Simonson reports them: the Martini and the Gin & Tonic "are the two best drinks ever made." "Let's work with that." (*Proper* p. 141). F3
anchors.meaning: The insistence came from delight. Fence (F2): he drank vodka "like everyone" and chose gin partly because vodka had been done: never "he loved gin all along", and that reason gets one clause at most (Trend Setter's ground).
anchors.speaksTo: a pure belief that life should be beautiful

anchors.fact: He thought "Gin Palace" sounded funny, fun and "a bit overblown" (*Proper* p. 141). F4
anchors.meaning: He said it was a bit much before anyone else could, and went ahead. "Overblown" is about the **name**: Simonson's extension to the man, and the "camp" quote after it, never appear.

anchors.fact: He bought every gin he could find, about fifteen in 1997, driving out of his way for some; the first list had ten Martinis, from the old books and his own fancy, two of them made with vodka (*Proper* p. 141). F7, F8
anchors.meaning: No reason to accept less, and the vodka drinkers weren't left out: they got a Martini made with the same care. Our reading for the gift. Fences: no price; no "two hundred" unless dated to 2016.
anchors.speaksTo: sees no reason to accept less

anchors.fact: Simonson: "bizarre. And it was an instant success." Orders split evenly between gin and vodka where, Chalker said, most bars sold nine vodkas to one gin (*Proper* p. 142). F9, F10
anchors.meaning: People had stopped expecting it, and came for it anyway. "Bizarre" stays with the bar and stays the author's; the ratio is Chalker's own account. Not everyone drank gin: never "won the city over".

anchors.fact: Jacob Briars, then a bartender at Matterhorn in Wellington, New Zealand, remembered Gin Palace as the first time he'd seen anyone use more than a dropper of Noilly Prat, and the first time he'd seen orange bitters (*Proper* p. 142). Noilly Prat's dry vermouth had been exported "as far as Australia" by 1862 (Oxford NOILLY PRAT, pdf 1395). F11, F12
anchors.meaning: The good vermouth had been in the country for over a century, used a drop at a time; here it was poured as if it mattered. Fences: Briars's own experience, never "nobody in Australia"; he was *working* in New Zealand, his nationality isn't on the page (never "from New Zealand"); the page names no Gin Palace recipe or ratio. Tomás owns whether Noilly Prat is named.
anchors.speaksTo: sees no reason to accept less

anchors.fact: Two parts gin to one of vermouth was the Martini's standard by the 1910s; by 1954 a Martini meant at least five-to-one, an Extra Dry meant no vermouth at all, and 1952 had a run of jokes about the least vermouth you could add (Oxford MARTINI, pdf 1247). F13
anchors.meaning: The dropper had a history: for decades the joke was how little vermouth you could get away with. Asking for a real pour of it is asking for the drink as it was meant. Fences: American drinking, not Melbourne's; never "Chalker's ratio" (not on the page).
anchors.speaksTo: sees no reason to accept less

anchors.fact: Gin Palace's first list had a Martini "with more vermouth than gin" (*Proper* p. 141). The old reverse-proportion Martinis used sweet vermouth and Old Tom (*Imbibe!* pdf 198-199, Martinez 1887). F8, F14
anchors.kind: proportion (if B, more vermouth than gin)
anchors.meaning: "The kind of Martini on his first list", never "his recipe" (no ratio or vermouth on the page). Never "the original Martini" or "the old way" with dry vermouth: the old ones were sweet.

anchors.fact: Noilly Prat Original Dry is "considered the archetype for dry vermouth"; Extra Dry was made for the US market in 1955 (Oxford NOILLY PRAT, pdf 1395). F15
anchors.meaning: If Tomás names Noilly Prat, either version is honest, but neither is "the bottle Briars saw": the version isn't on record.

anchors.fact: Tokaji is a rich, sweet wine from Hungary's Tokaj region (Wikipedia, "Tokaji", 2026-10-01; secondary, low). F16
anchors.meaning: Our reading: a measure (20 ml) of Hungary for Chalker's imagined Budapest bar. Signposted ("I like to think"), never "what they drank in 1890s Budapest". Out: "King of Wines", royal gifts, "noble rot".
anchors.speaksTo: the lighting, the table, the song

cocktail.closingLine: Pour more vermouth than gin. Make the joke yourself, then ask for it anyway.
cocktail.glassware: large V-shaped cocktail glass (about 250 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Put the glass in the freezer for 10 minutes.
Pour the vermouth, gin, Tokaji and bitters into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir for about 15 seconds, until the outside feels very cold.
Strain into the cold glass. There's no ice in the glass.
Twist the lemon peel above the glass so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Say So

recipe.note: Or any French dry vermouth. Here it's poured, not dropped in.
Any London dry gin of 40% or stronger.

(5 puttonyos: my label guidance, unsourced.) A rich, sweet wine from Hungary's Tokaj region, as a nod to the Budapest bar Chalker imagined. Not a dry Tokaji. Or any sweet white wine made from shrivelled grapes, in the Sauternes style.

cocktail.tagline: You won't settle for fine. Not with wonderful right there.

reading.epigraph: The bar behind this Martini was built to look as if it had always been there.
whoYouAre: You walk in and you know at once. Wrong table, the light's too harsh, and that song isn't helping. So you say so, kindly, usually. If nothing happens, a little less kindly. And it's never only your own evening you're asking for. You want all of it right: the room, the glass, the music, everyone at their best.

People hear a demand. What you're really saying is that you still think it can be lovely. Most people stopped expecting that years ago. You didn't. You rarely let that part show, because hope is easy to laugh at, and a demand at least sounds strong. And you mind being called difficult more than you let on. What you dread is asking, watching nobody move, and then the whole thing sliding, bit by bit, into a mess. Because you said something, everyone gets the better night, including the ones who'd never have asked. Most of them wanted it too. It matters more than anyone thinks to tell you.
yours: In 1997, Vernon Chalker opened a bar on a laneway in Melbourne and built it around gin. It was an odd choice then. Chalker drank vodka himself, like nearly everyone, and hardly anybody cared about gin. But he reckoned the Martini and the gin and tonic were the two best drinks ever made, and he meant to work with that.

What he asked for was the whole picture. In his words, he wanted it to look like it had always been there: a Budapest bar of the 1890s, done up in the 1950s and still going. Heavy old sofas went in around a sleek bar. He bought every gin he could find, about fifteen back then, and drove out of his way for some of them. He called it Gin Palace, because he thought the name sounded funny, fun and "a bit overblown". The writer who tells the story calls the bar bizarre. It was also an instant success.

This is the bit I like best. He called his own bar's name a bit overblown, first, and then went ahead anyway, right down to the age of the furniture. And people came. By his account, almost every bar then sold nine vodkas for every gin. At his, orders split down the middle, and even the vodka drinkers had two Martinis of their own on the list. I like to think that's insisting done for the right reasons: nobody gets left out of the better version. It's what you do too.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Martini, one of the two classics he built that bar on, made the generous way: more vermouth than gin, like one of the ten Martinis on his first list. (Vermouth is wine steeped with herbs and spices, with a little spirit added.) A bartender then working in New Zealand, Jacob Briars, remembered Gin Palace as the first place he'd seen anyone use orange bitters, and also the first time he'd seen anyone use "more than a dropper" of Noilly Prat, a French dry vermouth. So both are here. Then one thing of mine: a small pour of Tokaji, a rich sweet wine from Hungary. His Budapest bar was only ever imagined, and I like to think it would have poured some, so this is my nod to it. It softens the dry edge, so the drink comes out gentler and silkier than most Martinis. It's stirred over ice, poured into a big, chilled V-shaped glass, with a lemon peel pressed above it, so its oil mists the top.

So keep asking. Please don't stop. But borrow Chalker's trick. You and I both know it isn't too much. Make the joke anyway, with a grin, before you ask: "I know, it's a bit much." Then ask. It's hard to call someone difficult when they've laughed first, and once people are laughing with you, they'll help you get it right. And when it's right, enjoy it as much as you knew you would.

anchors.fact: A school for bartenders, opened in 1996, was so short of money that it was always one student short of affording the next course; the founders worked bar jobs at night (whose bars, the page doesn't say) and taught in the morning. It went bust (*Proper* p. 99, Turner on the record; F2–F4).
anchors.meaning: A real failure, not a hiccup: it could have ended the whole thing.
anchors.speaksTo: the setback that could have ended it

anchors.fact: Its founders opened a bar under the same name; the book says it was meant as a living advertisement for the school, and one founder said they opened it because the school didn't work out. The school didn't survive; the bar did (p. 99; F5). Order-neutral only.
anchors.meaning: The party had a plan inside it from the first night: it was there to sell something.
anchors.speaksTo: fun and control at once; a party with a purpose

anchors.fact: The owners chose what kind of bar it would be: a party bar, loud and busy, not a quiet temple to the craft (p. 99, Simonson's narration; F6).
anchors.meaning: The fun was decided, not stumbled into. The steering shows as a choice.
anchors.speaksTo: the steering, as an uncontested decision

anchors.fact: Douglas Ankrah, one of its founders, said other bars were "very, very passively boring" (*quotable*, p. 100; F7). Past tense: he died in 2021 (*Spirits Business*, 17 Aug 2021; F16).
anchors.meaning: Dull is the enemy, in the founder's own mouth.
