anchors.fact: One of its bartenders, Jamie Terrell, said they wanted to make "the best drinks in the world" (*quotable*, p. 100); he and Ankrah wrote five cocktail menus together, each with two hundred drinks (F9). Never "a thousand".
anchors.meaning: Ambition inside the noise: the party was going somewhere. Shown as an aim, never as hours nobody saw.
anchors.speaksTo: the steering as an aim; going somewhere

anchors.fact: Someone who saw it remembered the bartenders tasting through a straw and then adding a little more mint, a little more sugar, a dash of bitters, adjusting the drink (the page says "the drink", never "each" or "every") (Simon Ford, pp. 100–101; F11, cut before "free pour", C1). Plural, never Ankrah alone.
anchors.meaning: The hand on the wheel in a loud room: control as constant small corrections.

anchors.fact: At first nobody took much notice; the first months of 1999 were slow, until good press turned it (p. 101; F13). The service could be slow too: a founder who had left joked you should order a beer with your cocktail, to have something to drink while you waited (Turner, p. 101; F12).
anchors.meaning: It could have gone dull, or tipped into a mess, and nearly did.

anchors.fact: One bartender said everybody in the trade used to be there: to be hired, to hire, to meet a drinks firm's rep (Conigliaro, p. 101). The book credits it with helping knit London's bartenders together and with making bartenders (the page doesn't limit it to London's) celebrities rather than wage slaves (F14); Oxford calls it a breeding ground for new talent (pdf 119; F15).
anchors.meaning: People came in numbers, willingly, and went further than they would have alone.
anchors.speaksTo: people followed because it was exciting; the gift

anchors.fact: Many of its drinks came in a big glass of crushed ice, about 14 oz (Turner, who had left before the bar opened, says "everything", p. 100; the same pages mention its Martinis, p. 101, so never "everything"), built on vodka and fresh fruit, with "mountains of ice" (Simonson, p. 100; F10).
anchors.meaning: Loud and generous on top; Tomás's exact balance underneath.

anchors.fact: The three corrections Ford remembered are on the page in this order: a bit more mint, a little more sugar, a dash of bitters (pp. 100–101; F11). The guest's taste-and-adjust step at the table uses exactly these three.
anchors.meaning: Steering done in the open, as fun, at the table: the change of plan as something the guest does, not hidden work.
anchors.speaksTo: the steering, seen; control inside the fun

anchors.fact: Raspberry and the toasted-cumin pinch are ours. The pages never name a LAB fruit beyond the general vodka-and-fresh-fruit base and Reed's backbar "like a greengrocer" (p. 100; F10). *Flavor Matrix* BERRY (pdf 52): raspberry is a listed subtype; cumin is one of four surprise pairings for the berry family as a whole.
anchors.meaning: Say it as our choice ("I chose raspberry"), never "LAB's raspberry" or "the way LAB made it".
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; the twist tied to the story

anchors.fact: Few of its cocktails outlived its heyday (p. 101; F14). The jiggers are contested (C1).
anchors.meaning: Keep the reading off "its drinks lasted" and off any measuring claim.

cocktail.closingLine: Taste it through the straw and make one call. Then pass the glass to whoever hasn't made a call yet.
cocktail.glassware: a big glass (about 400 ml, a 14-oz highball or double old-fashioned), chilled in the freezer, packed with crushed ice and a straw
method: Make the syrup ahead. Warm half a teaspoon of cumin seeds in a dry frying pan, shaking it, until they smell nutty, then crush them lightly with the back of a spoon. Blend them cold with 100 g fresh raspberries and 100 g white sugar until the sugar has gone. Leave it for 30 minutes, then press it through a fine sieve to take out all the seeds. Keep it in the fridge.
Put the glass in the freezer for a few minutes.
Put the vodka, lime juice, syrup and mint leaves into a shaker with just a few pieces of crushed ice. Shake for about five seconds, only enough to mix it. The ice in the glass does the rest.
Pour everything, leaves and all, into the cold glass. Fill it four-fifths with crushed ice and stir up and down with a long spoon for a few seconds. Then pack in more ice, piled up above the rim.

Put a straw in and taste it. Then make one call: a few more mint leaves pushed down if you want it fresher, half a teaspoon more syrup if it's sharp, or a dash of Angostura if you want it deeper. Stir once more.
Top with the mint sprig and two raspberries.
cocktail.name: Who's In?

recipe.note: any unflavoured vodka from 37.5% to 45%
homemade: fresh raspberries, the same weight of sugar and a little toasted cumin, blended cold and sieved. Keeps a week in the fridge
they stay in the glass

recipe.item: 3 or 4 more mint leaves, or ½ tsp (2.5 ml) more syrup, or 1 dash Angostura bitters
recipe.note: your call, after you've tasted it through the straw
lots of it: more ice than drink

recipe.item: a mint sprig and two fresh raspberries
recipe.note: on top of the ice

cocktail.tagline: People follow your lead because it feels like joining the fun.

reading.epigraph: A bartending school went bust. Its party bar didn't. This drink comes in its big glass.
whoYouAre: The last train's cancelled, and there are twelve of you on a cold platform. Someone sighs. You make a joke, it lands, and somewhere in the middle of it there's a plan, and everyone hears it: the café that's still open, the walk across town, a bet on who gets home first. Years later, it's the night everyone brings up.

Nobody calls it being in charge, because to them it feels like being asked along. You like it like that. Being obeyed bores you, and it would turn you into the boss. You seldom admit how much you enjoy having your hand on the wheel, and that when you make that first joke, you don't yet know it'll work. What you dread is the night it gets away from you, or the night the fun runs out and you're just someone telling people where to go. Around you, a plan falling apart is where the good part begins. People go further than they ever would on their own, and they come back glad they went.
yours: Six hundred pounds bought you three weeks at the London Academy of Bartenders. It opened in 1996, and it never had enough money. One of its founders, Alex Turner, said they were always one student short of being able to run the next course, so the founders worked bar jobs at night and taught in the mornings. Eventually the school went bust.

The name didn't. Douglas Ankrah and Richard Hargroves had a bar called LAB as well, meant, by one account, as a living advertisement for the school. The school didn't survive. The bar did, and it was never a quiet advert. Its owners wanted a party bar, loud and busy every night. Ankrah said other bars were "very, very passively boring". Jamie Terrell, whom Ankrah brought in, remembered what they were after in all that noise: "the best drinks in the world". The two of them wrote five cocktail menus together, with two hundred drinks on each.

It could have gone quiet. Early in 1999 it was slow, and hardly anyone noticed the place until good press turned it. After that, one bartender said everybody in the trade used to be there, to hire, to get hired, or to meet the drinks firms' reps, and it helped make bartenders into names people knew. Someone who saw it remembered the bartenders sipping a drink through a straw, then adding "a bit more mint, a little more sugar, a dash of bitters". My favourite detail: in a room that loud, someone was still tasting. I like to think you'd have got on with them. When a plan falls through, you don't mourn it. You throw the party, and you mean the party to get somewhere.

The cocktail I've made for you is a vodka Daiquiri, built like a Mojito, in the kind of big glass LAB served so many of its drinks in, with crushed ice heaped above the rim. I chose raspberries for it, blended cold into a syrup, so the bold red comes from the fruit alone, with a pinch of toasted cumin in the syrup, a turn you won't see coming that works out, and lime and mint leaves that stay in: bright and generous. Then it's over to you. When you make it, taste it through the straw and make one of those three calls: a few more mint leaves, a little more syrup, or a dash of bitters. That step is there as a nod to those bartenders tasting in all that noise, and the drink is built so that whichever call you make, it holds.

Somewhere near you is someone who never makes the first joke, because you always do. When the evening next falls apart, wait a moment. Leave it to them, and follow wherever it goes. You won't lose the wheel. What you'll get is something you almost never have: the fun of not knowing where you're going while someone else steers.

anchors.fact: Ciro Capozzi (1855–1938), a sea captain's son from the Bay of Naples, head bartender of a small American bar facing the Monte Carlo casino from about 1885; his own bar from 1888 (pdf 460–461). F1, F2, F5
anchors.meaning: A barman, behind the bar, not a host on a stage. "About 1885", never a bare year.

anchors.fact: Where other European bars poured fantasies with names like "Heaps of Comfort", he served drinks "far simpler", and brought Europe the Manhattan (pdf 460). F4
anchors.meaning: Nothing showy: the hold was the person and the care, not the trick.

anchors.fact: His guests were "very strongly English", among them the prince of Wales, who would show him cocktails he had learned; with him and the newspaper owner James Gordon Bennett as regulars, the best of the season's society followed (pdf 461). Habitual, undated, no drink named. **Counterweight:** the prince already liked American drinks when most of his circle didn't (pdf 491), so never "won him over". F6, F7
anchors.meaning: The most watched man in the room brought something of his own to the bar. Around this guest, people feel free to offer something. Any "relaxed" or "at home" is "I like to think".

anchors.fact: Oxford: "charm, skill, and hospitality" gave him the leverage to move the culture; to say he made the cocktail fashionable in Europe "might be an exaggeration", "but it would not be much of one" (pdf 462). F12
anchors.meaning: The warmth worked, and it changed what a whole society drank. Keep the hedge whenever the claim is made. Paraphrase in the reading; "charm" is never praise of the guest.

anchors.fact: His wife Clotilde ran the till and his brother Salvatore the bar; it "ran smoothly" until 1911 (pdf 461). F8
anchors.meaning: Optional. The room rested on him, but others held it too.

anchors.fact: In 1911 he sold to London investors and retired to his villa nearby, living quietly for another twenty-seven years (pdf 461). F9
anchors.kind: the stepping away (not in reading v2)
anchors.meaning: He stopped. The question the guest never asks, answered once in the record.

anchors.fact: The new owners kept "the same formula" and opened in Paris in 1912, an instant success (pdf 461); the Monte Carlo house itself ran until "the immediate postwar years" (pdf 462), some three decades after he left (our arithmetic; the war is read from context). F10, F11
anchors.kind: what kept going (not in reading v2)
anchors.meaning: They kept coming after he'd gone. Never say he watched, or that it was the same without him; never "after him" from Oxford's kings sentence (C2).

anchors.fact: (Reading v2: ours is rye, sweet vermouth, bitters; no page says what Ciro's Manhattan was made with, so the recipe is said as mine, audit v2 H2.) The Manhattan had reached Monte Carlo by the end of the 1880s (pdf 1224); he was introducing it to Europe (pdf 460). F4, F16
anchors.meaning: Why a Manhattan, plain. Tomás owns the recipe; never "his recipe" for our riff.

anchors.fact: His own Cocktail, 1898: bitters, a half barspoon of orange curaçao, a little rich syrup, genever, cognac or American whiskey, stirred, up, lemon twist (pdf 491–492, Wondrich's measures). F15
anchors.meaning: Optional source for the spark or the twist: something from his own glass. Tomás's call.

anchors.fact: The prince had a cocktail of his own: a London paper of July 1887 describes "the drink the prince concocted" (Oxford PRINCE OF WALES, pdf 1562), and a 1901 book says he "is credited with having composed" it (*Imbibe!* pdf 231). Rye, a small piece of pineapple, Angostura, lemon peel, a little maraschino and champagne, sugar. Our glass takes only the pineapple. F17
anchors.meaning: What the guest brought to the bar, in the glass. **Signpost the link:** the page says he showed Ciro "cocktails he had learned" (pdf 461), never which, so "I like to think this one was among them". Never "his recipe" or "the prince's cocktail" for ours. In guest text, say "a cocktail of his own" with its channel ("as a London paper had it in 1887", one paper, the *Evening Telegraph*; or "it was credited to him"); never cite the 1901 book's title (a royal word), and don't name the drink by its title (the prince appears once). F18

anchors.fact: In 1887 pineapple was "extraordinarily costly", and Oxford reads the prince's drink as "conspicuous consumption" (pdf 1562). Wondrich files it as a variation on the Improved Whiskey Cocktail (*Imbibe!* pdf 230). F17, F19
anchors.meaning: The pineapple was the showy part of *his* glass, so never call it humble or modest. In ours it's hidden at the rim: that's our change, said as ours. Never "Improved" in our lineage (*Beside the First*).

cocktail.closingLine: Strain the pineapple out. It's still there at the rim. So are you, even when you're not trying.
cocktail.glassware: stemmed cocktail glass (about 180 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Put the cocktail glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Put the pineapple and the syrup in a mixing glass or jar. Press the pineapple with a muddler or the end of a rolling pin until its juice runs.
Add the rye, the vermouth and the bitters. Fill the mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
Empty the cocktail glass. Strain the drink into it through a small tea strainer, so no pineapple gets through.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Up Close

recipe.note: cut from near the base, where it's sweetest; no bigger, or the drink turns sharp
2 parts sugar to 1 part water, stirred until clear
any straight rye, 40% or stronger; the numbers were run on 50%
a red Italian-style vermouth
or any aromatic bitters
squeezed over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: People remember how you made them feel because you remember who they are.

reading.epigraph: A Monte Carlo barman kept his Manhattans plain. This one borrows from a regular's cocktail.
whoYouAre: Someone comes back after a year away, and you ask about the interview they were dreading. You remember their sister's name. You stay with them a second longer than they expect. They go home feeling remembered.

You know exactly what your attention does, and you give it on purpose, because a lot holds together when you do. People who watch from further off call it charm, and sometimes mean it as a warning. They've got it backwards: it works because you mean it. You hardly mention what it costs, or the question underneath: if I stopped, would they still come? The fear is the evening it doesn't land, when someone looks past you and everything quietly drifts. People leave feeling they were the one who mattered, and sure enough to offer something of their own. On an ordinary evening, nobody expects to be given that.
yours: In about 1885, a sea captain's son from near Naples was made head bartender of a small bar facing the casino in Monte Carlo. Ciro Capozzi had actually tended bar in America, and where other bars poured inventions called things like Flip Flaps, he served far simpler drinks, the Manhattan among them.

His own bar opened in 1888, just off the casino square, and among its regulars was the Prince of Wales, who would show him cocktails he had learned. He liked American drinks already, so Ciro never had to win him over. He kept coming back, with what he knew. I like to think Ciro treasured that: the most watched man in Monte Carlo, at ease enough to teach the barman.

People look for the trick in you, and there isn't one. The plainness is the point: someone paying real attention, and meaning it. And the best of it was never that people are charmed. It's what they bring you once they feel seen. Anyone can be charming for an evening. You remember, you return to it, and so people offer you their best.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Manhattan, the renowned classic Ciro was pouring in Monte Carlo. Mine is rye, sweet vermouth and bitters, stirred until ice-cold, then brightened with lemon peel. To it I've added a small square of fresh pineapple, from a cocktail of that regular's own, as a London paper had it in 1887. I like to think his own was among the ones he showed Ciro. Back then a pineapple was hugely expensive, and his drink showed it off. In this glass it goes quiet: pressed with a touch of syrup, then strained out again, as a nod to what a regular brings to the bar. It still looks like a plain Manhattan. You only find the pineapple up close.

Soon, for once, don't be "on". Let someone else carry the conversation, and let them show you something they've learned. Then you'll see whether they'd still come, and I hope the answer surprises you, in the best way.

anchors.fact: An Irish-born New York bartender who rose from bellboy to head bartender at the Ashland House, and later wrote under the name Patrick Gavin Duffy (Oxford pdf 687; *Imbibe!* pdf 91). F1
anchors.meaning: Someone with a past in the trade, not a newcomer. Pseudonym's reason unknown: no guess.

anchors.fact: He had been out of the trade for years, in Ireland and then running rooming houses in Brooklyn (Oxford pdf 687; *Imbibe!* pdf 91–92). No year for leaving (C1). F4
anchors.meaning: The quiet years, without a date to argue over.

anchors.fact: In December 1933 he told a reporter he had watched drink coming back for three years, with little to do but look after his two houses, and so began gathering recipes, thinking of a trade whose old hands had gone (*Brooklyn Daily Eagle*, 1 Dec 1933, p. 2). F5
anchors.meaning: His own account, so it may be told as fact, as reported. He saw it coming before it came.

anchors.fact: The *Eagle* reported the book out on 1 December 1933; the publisher had announced it for 5 December, the day Repeal took effect (*Eagle* 1 Dec "out this week"; *Florida Times-Union* 10 Dec; *Joy* pdf 62). F8, F11
anchors.meaning: Ready when the moment came. Say "as the ban ended" or "by the time the ban ended"; never "days before" alone, since the announced date is the day itself (A11). Prohibition is this one date clause.
anchors.speaksTo: the right words at the right time

anchors.fact: He included the dry-era mixtures because people asked for them, but marked the wilder ones (the reporter's "more fantastic") with a small circle as ones he wouldn't recommend; a launch report says he starred the ones he thought in the best tradition (*Eagle* 1 Dec 1933; *Florida Times-Union*, 10 Dec 1933, p. 37). F7, F8
anchors.meaning: Judgement given in plain marks: structure for a confused trade, without lecturing.

anchors.fact: Wondrich ranks it among the few books that did most to bring the bar's craft back after Repeal; Oxford says it stayed in print for forty years (*Imbibe!* pdf 92; Oxford pdf 687). F13
anchors.meaning: Words others stood on, judged by others. "His book", never "his recipes".

anchors.fact: His Herald Punch: dedicated to the *New York Herald* in 1901, rye with orange, a little sugar and a little St. Croix rum, shaken and strained into a sour glass (*Imbibe!* pdf 92). F14
anchors.meaning: His one drink that caught on, given to a newspaper. Whether the Manual prints it is unchecked: never "from his book".

anchors.fact: The Manual borrowed heavily (Ensslin's 1916 book, Craddock's Savoy book), and Duffy said himself he "read up on the subject" (*Imbibe!* pdf 241; *Joy* pdf 63–64; *Eagle* 1933). F6, F12
anchors.meaning: Never "his recipes", "his words" or "from memory" for the contents. What's his: the order (by base spirit), the marks, the judgement. Ensslin and Craddock stay in the dossier.

anchors.fact: Out of the guest text: the highball claim (highball.md F8), the Sullivan–Morgan meeting, his views on women bartenders and mixed drinking, liquor as a cure (F16), "a gentleman's drink" (gendered), any recipe count.
anchors.meaning: Counterweights carried openly; none is softened into praise.

anchors.fact: Year 1933, settled by the December 1933 press (F10). *A Place Kept* says "late in 1933" for Beam: our clause is the ban ending, never "shut everything down" or "late in 1933". *Anyone Would Have* (Firefighter) owns "nobody behind the bar could make it": our story is his foresight, not the skill gap.
anchors.meaning: Apart from the siblings in wording.

anchors.fact: Ours, not Duffy's: the orange juice brought up to lime strength with citric and malic acid, Arnold's method (*LI* p. 60: 32 g citric and 20 g malic per litre of fresh juice). Plain orange juice is about 0.8% acid, lime 6% (*LI* p. 137); Arnold says orange alone isn't acidic enough for a proper sour (p. 60).
anchors.meaning: The softest thing in the glass made to hold: **our reading, signposted**. Arnold's own reason was a glut of oranges, not strength. Never "his recipe" for the riffed drink.

anchors.fact: Blood orange, if Tomás uses it: Oxford CITRIC ACID (pdf 467) gives a deep red colour and slightly acidic juice, available mainly in winter; Wondrich suggests it for the "rich orange" he can't identify (*Imbibe!* pdf 92).
anchors.meaning: Seasonal: Wren's call whether "its moment comes in its season" is worth one clause. "Rich orange" is unidentified: never say what Duffy meant.

anchors.fact: The rum: Duffy wrote "enough St. Croix to flavor"; the half ounce is Wondrich's bracket, taken from a Paris "jury" he quotes without date or source (*Imbibe!* pdf 92). Today's St. Croix rum is column-still and "nothing like" the old Santa Cruz style (Oxford pdf 1732–1733).
anchors.meaning: Never "his half ounce", never "the rum he used", never "argued" or "fixed" for the jury. A Virgin Islands rum is a style choice.

anchors.fact: Oxford lists other original recipes of his (Brandy Punch, which it says his Manual describes; the Blinker and others, pdf 687). Wondrich: the Herald Punch was the one that caught on with the public (pdf 92).
anchors.meaning: Never "his only recipe" or "the one drink that's his". The Brandy Punch is a bowl (other pours' ground): out. Whether the Manual prints the Herald Punch: unchecked (library gap).

anchors.fact: The book was loose-leaf and waterproof, with supplements promised for a year (*Florida Times-Union* and *Plain Dealer*, 10 Dec 1933). F8
anchors.meaning: Never a cloth-bound book in the image or the text.

cocktail.closingLine: Sharpen the orange before anyone's thirsty. Then say it early, while nobody else is worried.
cocktail.glassware: stemmed sour glass (about 240 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Sharpen the orange. Squeeze about 4 oranges for 250 ml of juice, on the day you'll serve it, and strain it: many navel oranges turn bitter if the juice sits. Weigh in 3.4 g of citric acid and 2.1 g of malic acid, and stir until both have dissolved. If you only have citric acid, use 5.5 g. If your scale only weighs whole grams, make twice as much: 500 ml of juice, from about 8 oranges, with 11 g of citric acid. Keep it in the fridge until the first drink.
Chill the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Put 60 ml of the sharpened juice and the sugar in a shaker, and stir until the sugar has dissolved.
Add the rye and the rum, fill the shaker with ice, and shake hard for about 12 seconds, until the outside is frosty.
Empty the glass. Strain the drink into it, through a small sieve as well so no chips of ice get in.
Hold a strip of orange peel over the drink, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top. Then lay it on the rim.
cocktail.name: The Long View

recipe.note: 43% or stronger; 50% is ideal

recipe.item: Virgin Islands (St. Croix) rum, lightly aged
recipe.note: a style; Duffy asked only for enough to flavour it, and half an ounce is Wondrich's measure. Any lightly aged rum of about 40%, not spiced
fresh orange juice with a little citric and malic acid stirred in (see step 1); in winter, try blood oranges
stirred into the juice first

cocktail.tagline: The worse it gets, the clearer you are.

reading.epigraph: Rye and orange, after a bartender whose book came out as the ban ended.
whoYouAre: On an ordinary day you can seem like too much. You take the long view when the rest of the room is busy with the week, and you mention what could go wrong before anyone else is worried. People nod, and talk about something else. Then the worst day comes, the one where everyone else is lost for words, and they all look at you. You've had the words for a while.

You don't say how much the quiet stretches sting. Seeing it coming isn't much comfort while nobody's listening. And part of you, a part you'd rather not mention, steadies in a crisis, because at last you make sense. What you lie awake over is being the one in charge on the day the storm wins, and being remembered for that. So you work out what you'd say long before anyone asks, and on the day people have nothing left to stand on, you hand them a sentence that holds. People get through their worst days because of how you talk them through it.
yours: In the 1890s, Patrick Duffy was head bartender of New York's Ashland House. Someone at the time described his waxed moustache and the carnation in his lapel. Then he left the trade. Years later he was running rooming houses in Brooklyn.

In December 1933 he told a reporter how his book came about. He'd been watching drink coming back for three years, and with not much to do but look after his two houses, he'd started gathering the recipes. The book was on sale by the time the ban ended, and it holds the detail I love most. The mixtures people had got used to in the dry years went in, because people asked for them, but the wilder ones got a little circle: he wouldn't want it said he'd recommended them. The ones he thought belonged to the best tradition got a star. A cocktail historian puts it among the few books that did most to bring the craft back.

Maybe the circles were only good manners. I like to think they were more than that: a man who knew the day had come, cared what would be said about it afterwards, and made sure nobody could say he'd let it slide. You'd have drawn those circles too. You know a moment like that gets remembered, and you want to be remembered for what you stood behind.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from his Herald Punch, the one drink of his that caught on, which he dedicated to a newspaper, the *Herald*, in 1901: rye, orange juice, a spoon of sugar and just enough rum to flavour it, shaken well and strained into a sour glass. The same historian calls it a corker. Orange on its own is too gentle to hold a sour up, so I sharpen the juice, about halfway to lime, with a little of the acids that make lemons and apples tart. You still taste orange, bright and fresh, with the rye's dry spice through the middle and the rum warm underneath. It just holds. I did that as a nod to the work he did before anyone needed it.

The quiet years aren't the wait. They're where the words come from. Next time you see something coming and nobody's listening, mention it anyway, once, plainly, and early. You don't need everything to go wrong to be worth hearing. And if the day does come, you'll find people already listening.

anchors.fact: He came from the club world, where he could turn out seven vodka drinks in fifteen seconds. On his first visit to a slow New York craft bar he was handed a Daiquiri served up, and he'd never had anything like it. Yet, in Simonson's telling, he didn't think the place would amount to much: a quarter of an hour for one round seemed laughable. He offered to bartend there one night a week anyway, to give Petraske a break, thinking he might learn something (*Proper* pp. 92–93; F3–F4).
anchors.meaning: Won over before he won anyone over. He knew the replacement from the inside before he argued for it.
anchors.speaksTo: who this is: had the replacement ready before the argument was over

anchors.fact: In 2007 The Violet Hour opened with him behind the bar, in a city Simonson sums up as beer, whiskey and nothing fancy. It had no vodka, no olives, small coupes, house rules of manners, and in his words "everything fresh, everything measured right". A month later the Drawing Room opened, and between them Chicago suddenly had a cocktail scene (*Proper* pp. 280–282; Oxford pdf 522; F6–F11).
anchors.meaning: A real overturning of how a city drank, and not done alone.

anchors.fact: Looking back, he says they had to be serious at the start, and that without that seriousness he doesn't think "this" would exist. The page doesn't say what "this" is (*Proper* p. 282; F12).
anchors.meaning: He doesn't apologise for the strictness. He liked holding the line and still says it was needed. Our reading: "this" is what Chicago's bars became.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: likes being in charge, and always did

anchors.fact: He hired the bar's staff (Mike Ryan, 2008), and Charles Joly says Chicago's bartending family trees split into two: Bridget Albert's protégés and Toby's (*Proper* p. 283; F13–F14).
anchors.meaning: He stayed for the dull part, so the change had people to carry it.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: makes change real, still there on Monday

anchors.fact: Looking back, he cringes at some of what he did then, such as refusing to make a vodka Martini because he thought it beneath him (*Proper* p. 282; F12), when he'd once made vodka drinks by the seven (F3).
anchors.meaning: The irony, told kindly and by him first. Our reading: the one who changed how a city drank once turned down what it ordered.

anchors.fact: One of his protégés went back to his home city and co-wrote a small, self-published book, a reaction (in his co-author's words) to how boring a lot of cocktail bartenders were, with bitters and bitter liqueurs at the base of the drink. Maloney was among the bartenders who contributed to it (*Proper* pp. 283, 286–287; F15–F17).
anchors.meaning: When the next rebels came, he was in their book. The page doesn't say what he gave.
anchors.speaksTo: fear → position: ask what they'd put in its place, and listen

anchors.fact: That book's Gunshop Fizz began from The Violet Hour's Pimm's Cup template of muddled strawberry and cucumber, with Peychaud's bitters where the Pimm's had been (*Proper* p. 289; F18, F25).
anchors.meaning: The challengers kept his template and changed the heart of it.

anchors.fact: Pimm's No. 1 is a bottled gin cup: in Oxford's words essentially a bottled British Gin Sling, minus the citrus and the fizz. Only its 1912 trademark is confirmed, and no document shows James Pimm made it (Oxford pdf 1514; F21–F22).
anchors.meaning: The template was itself an old order the rebel's bar kept and served.
anchors.speaksTo: the old way kept inside the new one (Tomás's shape 2)

anchors.fact: A Pimm's Cup is customarily served tall, lengthened with lemonade or soda (Oxford pdf 1514); *Joy* builds it with 5 to 7 oz of soda, and the more traditional English way garnishes it with a sliver of cucumber (pdf 365–366). The Violet Hour's small coupes (*Proper* p. 282) are only an image prop now.
anchors.meaning: The guest's old order, served the way it has long been served. Never vodka in this pour: that was the bar's first line.

anchors.fact: Peychaud's is a bright-red bitters with a secret recipe. Oxford describes anise, nutmeg and clove *notes*, not listed ingredients (pdf 1502). It's the bottle that took the Pimm's place in the protégés' drink (*Proper* p. 289).
anchors.meaning: One spoonful of the next one's change, let into the guest's own glass.
anchors.speaksTo: fear → position: the drink as proof

anchors.fact: Clapping a sprig once between the hands to release its scent was pioneered by Maloney, "a showman's flourish" (Oxford pdf 1853).
anchors.meaning: What the old hand brings to the next one's drink (our reading; never what he gave the book, A5).
anchors.speaksTo: gift: give them something towards it

cocktail.closingLine: Spoon the bitters in before the soda. When the next one comes, ask what they'd put in its place.
cocktail.glassware: Collins glass, filled with ice
method: Put the strawberries and cucumber slices in the bottom of the Collins glass with the lemon juice, and press them with a muddler until the strawberries are pulp.
Add the Pimm's, then spoon in the Peychaud's.
Fill the glass with ice, top with the soda water, and stir gently, lifting the fruit up from the bottom.
Lay the mint sprig on one palm and clap your hands together once, just hard enough to release its smell without tearing it. Set it in the glass beside a cucumber slice.
cocktail.name: Had to Be Serious

recipe.item: Pimm's No. 1 Cup, recommended, or any gin-based fruit cup of about 25%
recipe.note: The cup the template was built on.

recipe.item: Peychaud's bitters, recommended, or a bright-red aromatic bitters
recipe.note: The bitters the next book swapped in for the Pimm's. Here they go in beside it.
Muddled.
Muddled.
To top.
Clapped once, to garnish.

cocktail.tagline: You didn't just tear it down. You stayed to run it.

reading.epigraph: In one rebel drink, these bitters replaced the Pimm's. In this glass, they share it.
whoYouAre: You were the one who said the old way was finished. People laughed. Then they let you try, it worked, and the new way was yours to keep going: the rota, the budget, the wet Tuesday when nobody remembers why anything changed. Most people who start a fight are gone by then. You stayed.

You'd rarely admit it, but you never wanted a free-for-all. You wanted it run properly, by you, and you had the plan for afterwards before the argument was over. The day you dread is someone new standing where you stood, saying what you said, and you hearing yourself answer the way they once answered you. But staying is the hard part, and hardly anyone thanks you for it. You make the better way real, and keep it real, so the people who wanted it actually get to live in it.
yours: Toby Maloney came from the club world, where he could turn out seven vodka drinks in fifteen seconds. A tiny New York bar where one round took fifteen minutes struck him as laughable. He took a night a week behind its bar anyway, thinking he might learn something.

In 2007, The Violet Hour opened with him behind the bar, in Chicago, then mostly a city of beer and whiskey. Later, one bartender said the city's bartending family trees ran back to two people, and he was one.

He has since said he cringes at some of it, like refusing to make a vodka Martini because he thought it was beneath him. He also said he doesn't think any of this would exist without that seriousness. He kept both halves. A few years on, one of his protégés co-wrote a small book of radical recipes, a reaction, his co-author said, to how boring a lot of cocktail people were. Maloney contributed to it.

That's you in one life: the newcomer who laughed, the strict one who held the line, the old hand who gave something to whoever came next. You know the cringe at how hard you once had to push, and you'd still never say it was wrong to push. And one day, years in, someone younger looks at what you built the way you once looked at the old way.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from the Pimm's Cup that one of that book's recipes began with, a British summer cooler: muddled strawberry and cucumber, the Pimm's left in, a little lemon, and soda. Then one spoonful of the bright red bitters their book swapped in for the Pimm's. The measures, the lemon and one more touch are my own: a sprig of mint, clapped once between the palms, a trick Maloney pioneered, as a nod to what you bring to whatever the next one makes. Your order is still the glass. Their change is in it.

When someone you've taught comes back and tells you it's all got a bit boring, don't defend it first. Ask what they'd do instead, and give them something towards it. You had your answer ready once. So might they, and whatever they build will carry some of you in it.

anchors.fact: New Orleans "was a Brandy Julep town" before the Civil War. In the decades after it the city "became much more Americanized", and an 1885 *Times-Democrat* interview had a bartender calling "brandy drinking in New Orleans… a thing of the past": whisky had "displaced it" (*Imbibe!* pdf 182). F9
anchors.meaning: The city's own drink was replaced by the newcomer's. The split is a change in what the city drank, told through the drinks, never through groups of people. It's 1860s–1885, about fifty years before the glass: never a live quarrel at the bar (C2).

anchors.fact: Walter Bergeron (1889–1947), then head bartender at the Monteleone Hotel, who "had worked at the bar before Prohibition and returned upon Repeal" (Oxford VIEUX CARRÉ, pdf 2102). F2
anchors.meaning: Someone with standing behind the city's bar. His own background and side aren't on record (C1). Say "the Monteleone's bar", never "the Carousel Bar" (C11). He's never Victor "Trader Vic" Bergeron (C8).

anchors.fact: He created the Vieux Carré "in the 1930s" (Oxford pdf 2102; *Joy* pdf 402). The 1937 recipe: ⅓ jigger each of rye whiskey, cognac brandy and Italian vermouth, with ½ tsp Bénédictine and a dash each of Peychaud's and Angostura (Arthur 1937, 1984 reprint, archive.org OCR highlight). Oxford's modern spec: 30 ml each, 5 ml Bénédictine, 2 dashes each bitters; *Proper* p. 255: ¾ oz each. F3, F5, F6, F10
anchors.meaning: **Our reading** (signposted): the whiskey the city had taken up and the brandy it used to drink, poured at the same measure in one glass, neither cut below the other. It's **three** equal parts (vermouth too), never "half and half" (C4). Whether "full strength" or "the same measure" is Wren's call; "same measure" is the literal page. No reason for the pairing is on record (C7 revised); the drink's motive is the next row but one.

anchors.fact: "named for the French Quarter"; it "translates as 'old square'" (Oxford pdf 2102; *Joy* pdf 403). F4
anchors.meaning: The glass carries the old quarter's name. **Who chose it isn't on record** (C3): "it carries the old quarter's name", never "he named it". Our reading: the newcomer's spirit sits under the old city's name.

anchors.fact: Arthur 1937: Bergeron "takes special pride in mixing" it; "He originated it, he says, to do honor to the famed Vieux Carré, that part of New Orleans where the antique…" (archive.org OCR highlight of the 1984 reprint, matched in Pearce 2017). F12
anchors.meaning: His reason for the drink, in his words as Arthur relays them: to honour the old quarter. Tell it with the channel ("he told the man who first printed it" or "he said"). It gives **no** reason for putting the two spirits together: that stays "I like to think".

anchors.fact: Its recipe "first appeared in print in 1937" (Oxford pdf 2102, citing Stanley Clisby Arthur). F3
anchors.meaning: Say "the 1930s". Never "1938" (C6).

anchors.fact: Oxford: "A Manhattan variant" (pdf 2102). F1
anchors.meaning: One clause at most (Wren's guard: Ciro's Manhattan is the Magnetic Leader's).

anchors.fact: Oxford: "typically served on the rocks", over fresh ice in a large rocks glass; "serving it up makes for a lovely presentation" (pdf 2102). F5
anchors.meaning: Both serves are on the page. Tomás's choice. Never "the way Bergeron served it" (C13).

anchors.fact: Cardamom on both the Grain wheel (p. 127) and the Grape wheel (p. 131) of the *Flavor Matrix*, rendered (F14). Steep scaled from *Codex* p. 288 (10 g/750 ml, ~12 h, room temperature; p. 95 on vermouth-strength liquids) (F15).
anchors.meaning: Our addition, said as ours: the shared part of the glass (the vermouth) changes, and neither spirit does. Scope: "the grain behind the rye and the grape behind the cognac", never "rye and cognac pair with cardamom". Never Bergeron's.

anchors.fact: Peychaud's and Angostura are both in the 1937 recipe (F6).
anchors.meaning: Name them as ingredients only. The pairing of both bitters is also O'Reilly's Sazerac (*Imbibe!* pdf 182): no Sazerac (C9).

cocktail.closingLine: Put the cardamom in the vermouth, never in either spirit. Next time you cross over, bring all of yourself.
cocktail.glassware: large rocks glass (about 300 ml), one large ice cube
method: The night before, put about 3 g of whole green cardamom pods (roughly 15) into 250 ml of sweet vermouth in a clean jar. Leave it at room temperature for about 12 hours, then strain it back into its bottle and keep it in the fridge. It's enough for eight drinks.
Pour the rye and the cognac into a mixing glass or jar, just as they come from the bottle.
Add the cardamom vermouth, the Bénédictine and both bitters. Fill the mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
Put one large ice cube in the rocks glass and strain the drink over it.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: One Table

recipe.note: 40% or stronger; a 50% bottled-in-bond rye is what the numbers were run on
any VS or VSOP cognac, 40% or stronger

cocktail.tagline: You give both sides a place at a table they thought they couldn't share.

reading.epigraph: A city gave up brandy for whiskey. Years later, one glass poured both.
whoYouAre: A family stops speaking over a seating plan. A team splits down the middle over who did the work. Two neighbours each want you to say the other one's wrong. Everyone waits to see which table you'll sit at. You go and sit with the people who expected you not to, and you have whatever they're having.

You don't do it with a speech. You've never won anyone round with an argument, and you don't try. You just turn up on their ground and mean it. From outside it can look like sitting on the fence. It isn't. You have a side, and you know your own mind. The hardest question you get doesn't come from the other side. It comes from your own: whose side are you on? What you fear is being made to choose, and the day a row stops being a row and becomes the way things are. Because of you, nobody has to pick a table. Both halves end up in one room, and neither had to give itself up to get there.
yours: Before the American Civil War, New Orleans was a brandy town. Its juleps were made with brandy, and that was how the city drank. Then the city changed. By 1885, a bartender was telling a New Orleans newspaper that brandy drinking there was over, and that whiskey had taken its place. The city drank it in whiskey cocktails and in the new Manhattan.

By the 1930s, the Hotel Monteleone's head bartender was Walter Bergeron. He'd worked that bar before Prohibition and returned when it ended. The drink he created there became the hotel's signature. It's a Manhattan at heart, but where a Manhattan has whiskey, his has two spirits: rye whiskey and French cognac. They go in at equal measures, level with the sweet vermouth, plus two different bitters and a touch of a herbal liqueur from France, Bénédictine. Its name is the old quarter's: Vieux Carré, "old square".

He said he made it to honour the old quarter. Why he put those two spirits side by side, he didn't say. But I like to think it's the city's whole story in a single drink: the brandy it drank first and the whiskey it turned to, together in one glass, neither poured a drop less than the other. That's what you do. When people split, you don't rule on which half was right. You bring both in, at the same weight, and you call it by a name everyone already shares.

The cocktail I've made for you is the Vieux Carré, a renowned New Orleans classic, with the proportions of its first printed recipe: rye, cognac and sweet vermouth in three equal measures, none cut back for another. I didn't change either spirit. I steeped the vermouth overnight with green cardamom, as a nod to the ground the two sides share: of the three measures, the vermouth is the one that belongs to neither, and cardamom goes with both the grain behind the rye and the grape behind the cognac. It's stirred, rich and deep, with the rye's spice and the cognac's softer fruit each as clear as the other, and the cardamom warm in the vermouth between them.

When you go over to the other side, you tend to leave a little of yourself at the door, so they feel safe. Your own side notices, and that's where the question comes from. Don't pour less of yourself. It was never your quietness they trusted. It's that you came as you are and stayed. And when your own side asks again, you'll have your answer: both, and still me.

anchors.fact: In the 1830s Lowland distillers took up continuous stills and made a light, clean grain whisky cheap enough for city factory workers (Oxford pdf 2149; card F1).
anchors.meaning: The case starts with the bottle the least-heard drinker could afford.
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: the quietest person gets the same answer as the loudest

anchors.fact: The old pot-still malt makers said the new spirit wasn't whisky at all; the argument was heated (pdf 2149; F2), and not only in Scotland (the Dublin distillers, pdf 541; F12). The pot-still makers are the "traditional" side (pdf 70).
anchors.meaning: One side had age and craft on its side; the comfortable story was "only ours is real".
anchors.speaksTo: the comfortable story nobody bothered to check

anchors.fact: A British commission took evidence in person in 1908 from across the spirits trade (pdf 317, 1697, 875; F6).
anchors.meaning: Everyone heard before the call.

anchors.fact: It set definitions and labelling rules, banned neither blending nor the word whisky on column-still spirit (pdf 70; F4); the definition later books quote rests on grain and malt and names no still (F5, secondary).
anchors.meaning: A decision, not a split: the newcomer was whisky, and the name now had to mean something.
anchors.speaksTo: a decision, not a compromise; clear rules protect people

anchors.fact: The grain side was the larger one: in 1877 six of the largest Scottish grain distillers formed an alliance (pdf 666; F7). The page gives size, not money.
anchors.meaning: Never the underdog's win: it was the drinker, not the distiller, who had less. Keeps the reading honest.

anchors.fact: Oxford hedges it: settled "legally, anyway" (pdf 2149; F3); and in the decades after, the authenticity argument won the public through marketing (pdf 70; F8).
anchors.meaning: The ruling stood; being liked for it didn't follow.
anchors.speaksTo: what they hide: it costs them; they don't owe the room its agreement

anchors.fact: Grain whisky's acceptance as its own category goes back to the commission, and today it is most often used to make blended whisky (pdf 2149; F9).
anchors.meaning: The call stood: blended Scotch in this glass is honest and legal, not a lesser bottle.

anchors.fact: Blended Scotch is malt and grain whisky together (Oxford pdf 2132, 209; F11), and blending pot- and column-still spirit had been legal since 1860 (pdf 284; F10).
anchors.meaning: The glass holds both sides of the argument.
anchors.speaksTo: the decision stood; one rule for both

anchors.fact: The definition later books quote asks that the grain's starch be turned to sugar by malt (F5, secondary). Malt is one requirement among others (cereal grain, distillation); no still is named.
anchors.meaning: The malt syrup is the definition in the glass. Never "the one thing", never "the law" (C2).
anchors.speaksTo: tie the twist to the story in one clause: one rule, whichever side

anchors.fact: Malt sits on the Grain flavour wheel (Matrix pdf 137); citrus is a Grain best pairing (pdf 136), hence the orange peel.
anchors.meaning: A place on the wheel, not a taste claim.
anchors.speaksTo: the spark is sourced, not decoration

anchors.fact: If Robin takes the veto-free version: honey is a Grain best pairing (Matrix pdf 136; the subtypes are wheat, barley, oats, farro and quinoa; corn is its own entry, pdf 88, with no honey), and saffron steeped in spirit gives a bright yellow (Oxford pdf 1072).
anchors.meaning: Honey goes with grain (barley on the page), which is where the definition began, not the still. Never "for both whiskies equally" (grain whisky is often corn, pdf 2149).

cocktail.closingLine: Stir until you can't see the malt. Then say what you've decided, and let the argument go on without you.
cocktail.glassware: old-fashioned glass (rocks glass, about 300 ml), filled with ice cubes
method: Make the malt syrup: stir 1 tablespoon of barley malt syrup into 2 tablespoons of rich sugar syrup (2 parts sugar to 1 part water by weight, dissolved warm) until no streaks are left. It keeps in the fridge for weeks.
Put the malt syrup and the bitters in the glass, add the whisky, and stir to mix.
Fill the glass with ice cubes and stir for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass is cold.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Either Way

recipe.note: any blend, 40-43%: malt and grain whisky together
1 part barley malt syrup (from a jar, the baking shelf) to 2 parts rich sugar syrup, stirred smooth; up to 1¾ tsp if your malt syrup is dark
squeezed over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: You want a fair answer, even when it means changing your mind.

reading.epigraph: There's whisky in this glass that rival distillers once insisted wasn't whisky at all.
whoYouAre: Two friends fall out, and sooner or later each of them tells you their side. You hear both out to the end, and you ask for the bits that don't flatter them. Then you tell them plainly what you think happened, and it's rarely what either of them hoped. When trouble comes round again, it's the one you disagreed with who calls first.

People assume plain speaking is easy for you. It isn't, not once. You want to be liked as much as anyone, and later, alone, you replay the conversation, half hoping someone will show you what you missed. What you won't put up with is the kind-sounding fudge, the "let's not make a fuss", because you know who pays for it, and it's never the person saying it. It's the quietest one there. With you, the quietest voice gets the same answer as the loudest, and it matters more than they ever tell you.
yours: For decades, distillers argued about a word. In the 1830s, whisky makers in the Lowlands took up a new kind of still, one that could run without stopping, and made a light, pure grain whisky cheap enough for city factory workers. The makers of malt whisky, from the old pot stills, said the new spirit wasn't whisky at all. They had age and tradition on their side. The grain side had the size: in 1877, six of the biggest grain distillers joined forces.

In 1908 a British commission sat and took evidence in person from across the spirits trade. Where it landed was plain. Whisky was a spirit distilled from cereal grain, its starch turned to sugar by malt, and nothing in that said which still. The new spirit was whisky. Blending stayed legal, and the commission set out what a label could claim.

That settled the law, not the argument. Over decades of marketing, the idea that the older whisky is the real one has largely won people over. The ruling stood anyway. That will be familiar to you: a call that went against the side with age and tradition, and then held, liked or not. I like to think the people it looked after most weren't in the room at all: whoever was buying the cheaper bottle.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from one of the most renowned classics of all, the Old-Fashioned. I make it with blended Scotch: malt and grain whisky together, the two whiskies that argument was about. Only the sugar is different. I sweeten it with a syrup made partly from barley malt, which the commission's definition asked of every whisky, whatever still it came from. That's as a nod to how you treat people: one rule, whichever side they're on. The malt makes it rounder and warmer than plain sugar would. Angostura goes in as well, the glass is a heavy one packed with ice, and last, orange peel is squeezed above it for its scent.

Once everyone's been heard and you've made the call, you've done the fair part. You don't also owe the room its agreement. Some of them will never come round, and that doesn't make the call any less fair. If the evidence ever changes, it'll find you, because you're the one who always asks for it. Until then, take the evening off from deciding. You've earned the nights when nobody needs an answer from you.

anchors.fact: Brian Rea (1927–2021) was an American bartender, collector and historian of the bartender's craft. His career got going properly when the 21 Club in midtown Manhattan hired him. Source: Oxford REA, BRIAN, pdf 1614 (primary tier).
anchors.meaning: The student is real and on the record.

anchors.fact: Jerry Berns (1907–2006) taught Rea the bar and restaurant business. Oxford's verb is "schooled", and it calls Rea "enthusiastic" (pdf 1614). Nothing on the page says how Berns taught him, what he said, or how he felt about it.
anchors.meaning: The teaching is a fact. Feelings and lessons are not: (3) is signposted only, and (4) is never a story event.

anchors.fact: Rea worked his way up to head bartender at 21, in years when Oxford calls it "arguably" the most famous bar in the world (pdf 1614). Those years are undated. His first bar job was in 1947 (somewhere else) and his West Coast years were in the 1960s.
anchors.meaning: He learned in the best-known room there was. Then he left it. Keep "arguably", and never date his 21 years.

anchors.fact: In 1969 Rea came up with a new hospitality job, the beverage director, which would run bar and drinks separately from food (pdf 1614).
anchors.meaning: Our reading, signposted: he was taught the bar and the restaurant as one business, and his own idea split them apart. The student went somewhere the house hadn't. Oxford never links the idea to Berns.

anchors.fact: He talked to six big hospitality companies. One of them, Host International, was willing to try it and made him its director of beverage services (pdf 1614).
anchors.meaning: The success is plainly his. Say "talked to six" and "one said yes". Never "five turned him down" (not on the page). Host's title for him was "director of beverage services".

anchors.fact: Berns died in 2006. Rea's 1969 job and everything after it fall within Berns's lifetime (pdf 1614 gives both men's dates).
anchors.meaning: This makes a signposted "I like to think Berns heard about it" honest. No page says he heard, or was glad.

anchors.fact: The Southside is a tall drink of gin, lemon, sugar, mint and soda. Oxford says it has "for many years" been the 21 Club's house drink (SOUTHSIDE, pdf 1851), with no dates.
anchors.meaning: The glass belongs to the house where the teaching happened, not to Rea. Never "the drink Rea learned" or "poured". Use "long the house drink", never "still is".

anchors.fact: Oxford's build: 45 ml gin, 30 ml fresh lemon, 22.5 ml simple syrup and about six mint leaves, shaken hard with ice, strained into a highball glass over ice, a short top of soda, a quick stir and a mint sprig (pdf 1851). Its other two versions: a mint-steeped "mix" left in the fridge for two to three days, and rum in place of gin in Maryland's Hunt Country.
anchors.meaning: Tomás's baseline. The make-ahead mix is fenced (Wren).

anchors.fact: Oxford calls the Southside the country-club drink of New York's "plutocrats". It adds that 21 being its home did nothing to change that reputation (pdf 1851). The Chicago-speakeasy origin is a rumour, and Oxford says it's wrong.
anchors.meaning: One wry clause at most (Wren). The Chicago rumour stays out (it's the Connoisseur's correction shape).

anchors.fact: Rea wrote *Brian's Booze Guide* (1976) and *Brian's Bartender Guide* (1978). Oxford says both show his humour, common sense and strong technique. *B.A.S.T.A.R.D.S.* came out in 2017 (pdf 1614–1615). I found nothing in his own words about Berns.
anchors.meaning: (3) and (4) stay where Wren put them. Library gap raised (below).

cocktail.closingLine: Put the two sprigs in together. Then find out what one of them knows now that you don't.
cocktail.glassware: highball glass, chilled, filled with ice
method: Put the highball glass in the freezer for ten minutes, then fill it with ice.
Put the gin, lemon juice, simple syrup, mint leaves and tarragon leaves in a shaker. Fill it with ice and shake hard but briefly, about five seconds, so there's room left for the soda.
Pour it through the shaker's strainer and a small tea strainer into the glass, so no bits of leaf get through.
Add the cold soda water and give it one quick stir.
Clap the mint sprig and the tarragon sprig once between your hands to wake their scent, then set them in the glass together.
cocktail.name: Further Than Me

recipe.note: ideally 43% or stronger; 40% works, just a touch lighter
lemon, as Oxford's Southside has it
equal weights of sugar and water, stirred until clear
shaken in and strained out
about the tip of one sprig; shaken in beside the mint, strained out
added last

recipe.item: sprig of mint and sprig of tarragon
recipe.note: to finish, set in together

cocktail.tagline: You teach people to trust their own judgement, even when it takes them beyond yours.

reading.epigraph: The 21 Club's house drink for many years. The second herb in it is mine.
whoYouAre: Someone rings with a decision they can't make and asks what you'd do. You could tell them. Usually you don't, at least not at first. You ask what they've noticed so far, you say what you'd keep an eye on, and you let them get to the end of the sentence themselves. It takes longer. The one thing you couldn't live with is someone following you into a wrong answer. What they work out for themselves is theirs, to keep or to change.

Then one day they stop ringing. They've got it. Years later they explain something to you, faster and better than you'd have managed, and you feel two things at once: very proud, and slightly left behind. You only ever mention the first. That's better than any answer you could have handed them: they leave able to manage on their own, and sure they always could.
yours: There was a time when New York's 21 Club was arguably the best-known bar anywhere. Brian Rea was hired there, and Jerry Berns schooled him in running a bar and a restaurant. Rea was an enthusiastic student. He became head bartender. Then he left.

Another bar followed, then the West Coast. In 1969 he dreamed up a new job, the beverage director, who would run the bar and the drinks separately from the food. He talked to six big hospitality companies about it, and one said yes. I like to think the lessons took precisely because he carried them somewhere else: taught the bar and the restaurant as one business, he made a job out of setting them apart.

Berns lived until 2006, so that new job came well within his lifetime. We don't know if Berns followed it. I like to think he did, and that he was glad the idea wasn't his. That's what I recognise in you. You've never wanted anyone to turn into a copy of you. The day someone you helped goes past you is the day you know it worked.

The cocktail I've made for you is the Southside, a classic and, for many years, the 21 Club's house drink: gin, fresh lemon, sugar and mint, shaken, poured over ice in a chilled highball glass and lifted with soda. It's crisp and bright, the way a long drink should be. And I added one thing of my own, a few leaves of tarragon shaken in beside the mint, as a nod to the student who took what he was taught somewhere new. Tarragon shares some of what makes lemon smell of lemon, so it belongs with the rest, and still it brings something of its own. To finish, a sprig of each goes in together, both standing tall, neither one hidden behind the other.

Think of someone you once helped who has gone further than you, in the very thing you helped them with. Don't wait for them to ring. Get them to explain it to you, and this time let them get all the way to the end of the sentence. It isn't a debt they're paying back. It's the proof you were right about them.

anchors.fact: The word "rickhouse" comes from "rick", the name for the wooden structure that holds up the barrels. (A1, F1; RICKHOUSE pdf 1665)
anchors.meaning: The place is called after what carries the weight, not after its walls.

anchors.fact: In Kentucky, whisky ages in tall warehouses where the barrels rest in wooden racks. (A2, F2; BARREL STORAGE SYSTEMS pdf 219) No floor count (C1).
anchors.meaning: Still how it's done today: a structure that stands.
anchors.speaksTo: story: build it so that it stands

anchors.fact: In the simplest of them, the racks are joined into the core of the building, the floors are fixed to the racks, and the walls are only a covering put round it all. (A3, F4; pdf 219-220) Never "every rickhouse".
anchors.meaning: What holds it up is inside, out of sight; the visible part carries nothing.
anchors.speaksTo: story: the beam that was never really load-bearing (turned inside out) · fear: Deception

anchors.fact: That covering can be brick, wood or corrugated tin. (A4, F4; pdf 220)
anchors.meaning: The covering could be any of the three, and it isn't what carries the weight (v2: "it doesn't matter" was mine and went too far; the page never says the covering is irrelevant to the whisky).
anchors.speaksTo: the decorative part can belong to anyone (Wren r1)

anchors.fact: The barrels lie side-on to the aisles, so any one can be rolled out and moved, say from the hot top floor to the cooler bottom. (A5, F5; pdf 220) "Can", never "are": rotation is not widely used (C2, pdf 218).
anchors.meaning: Built so it can be adjusted later, whether or not anyone does.
anchors.speaksTo: story: test it in their head

anchors.fact: A great deal of air moves through a rickhouse, and that air, like the option of moving barrels, helps the whisky age evenly. (A6, F6; pdf 220; v2: the page credits the air to the rickhouse, not to "open racks", and says it helps, not that it's "what lets")
anchors.meaning: The space is part of how it works. Built in with the racks, not left by chance; it serves the whisky, it holds nothing up (G4).

anchors.fact: A newer way stands barrels upright on pallets, packed tight. It saves room and gives up the air. Irish and several Canadian distillers use it more and more. (A7, F7; pdf 220)
anchors.meaning: The tidier version, with a real trade-off. Never a failure or cheap; tight single-story warehouses are another sound route to even ageing (F10, pdf 218).
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's shadow: packing it too tight

anchors.fact: No designer or date is on record for the rickhouse; the page's only date is the older pyramid stack's. (A8, F8, G1; pdf 219)
anchors.meaning: Limb (1), a frame laid out before it was filled, is our inference: it lives in the guest's own scene, never "someone drew it".

anchors.fact: Bourbon must age in new, charred oak; in Kentucky's hot, fairly dry summers it generally gets stronger as it ages, as water leaves before alcohol. Bourbon need not be made in Kentucky, but most is. (A9, F12-F13; WHISKY, BOURBON pdf 2138, 2140)
anchors.meaning: Why the glass holds bourbon: it's what the racks hold. Tomás's to use or not.

cocktail.closingLine: Add the water and the peel, and that's your last job tonight. Then be a guest at your own evening.
cocktail.glassware: small coupe, chilled, no ice
method: The night before, stir the bourbon, popcorn syrup and bitters together in a small plastic bottle, or a jar with plenty of space at the top (glass can crack in the freezer if it's too full), close it and put it in the freezer. With no water in it yet, it won't freeze.
Ten minutes before serving, put the coupe in the freezer too.
Fill a jug with water and ice, and measure out 30 ml of the cold water, leaving the ice behind.
Pour the jar into the cold coupe, add the water and stir three or four times with a spoon.
Squeeze the peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then lay it on the rim or drop it in.
cocktail.name: What It Rests On

recipe.note: any, 40 to 45%; if yours is 46 to 50%, use 40 ml of water below instead of 30

100 g demerara sugar dissolved in 100 ml hot water; off the heat, stir in about 20 g plain popcorn (2½ cups, from about 2 tablespoons of kernels, popped dry or in a little plain oil, with no butter), cover for 30 minutes, then press it through a sieve. Makes about 120 ml; keeps a week in the fridge. If you use bought popcorn, check the pack: butter is dairy, and coconut oil counts as nuts
measured from a jug of water and ice, with no ice going in
whichever you have

cocktail.tagline: People lean on what you make without ever wondering why it holds.

reading.epigraph: Bourbon's grain is at least half corn. This glass hides a little more in the syrup.
whoYouAre: By the time you say "that'll work", you've already watched it fall down a dozen ways. The trip for twelve, the move, the kitchen that has to feed everyone at once: you've walked through it in your mind, found where it gives, and fixed it while everybody else was still choosing dates. So your calm yes has a whole night of no behind it, and nobody ever hears that part.

You don't much mind how something looks. Someone else can pick the colours and the name. What you can't trust is a thing that only looks sound: the confident arrangement nobody has tested, the promise with nothing underneath. You'll say "not yet" to something everyone loves before you'll watch people stand on it.
Nothing goes wrong, so nobody asks why. They get to enjoy the evening without once thinking about the floor, and that is care, even if it never gets called that.
yours: In Kentucky, where most bourbon is made, barrels age in tall warehouses called rickhouses. The name comes from "rick", the word for the wooden structure the barrels rest in. In the simplest rickhouses, the racks aren't just inside the building. They are the building: joined into one frame, with the floors fixed onto it and the walls only a covering wrapped round the outside. It can be brick, wood or tin, and none of them takes the weight.

A great deal of air moves through a rickhouse, and that air helps the whisky age evenly. Each barrel lies side-on to the aisle, so it can be rolled out and moved if it ever needs to be. There's a newer, tidier way: barrels stood upright on pallets and packed tight. It saves plenty of space, at the cost of the air, and it's a fair trade for the distillers who choose it. But I like to think the open racks hold a lesson: their gaps were built in from the start.

I see you in that building. People notice the walls: the easy evening, the trip where nothing went wrong. Nobody sees the frame you set up underneath it in the nights before, with every weak spot already found. And you're happy to leave it unseen. Admiring the racks was never the point. They just have to take the weight.

So the cocktail I've made for you is a bourbon Old-Fashioned, the renowned classic, with what carries it hidden inside. By law, at least half of bourbon's grain is corn, and none of it shows in the glass. As a nod to the frame nobody sees, I steeped the sugar syrup with popcorn, so a toasted corn note sits quietly under the whiskey. It's mixed the night before and kept in the freezer, and its water is measured out rather than left to the ice, so what you pour is exactly what you meant. The only thing on show is a strip of peel, orange or lemon, whichever you have. Like the walls, it's the part that could be anything.

When it's for people who matter to you, you fill every gap, because a gap is one more thing that could go wrong. Next time you lay out a weekend for them, check every part as usual, and then put the gaps in yourself, as carefully as anything else: a chair nobody's been given, an afternoon with no name on it. You'll simply have given them some air, and in my experience that's where the best of a weekend usually happens.

anchors.fact: In 1824 Samuel Morewood wrote that the traveller Engelbert Kämpfer had credited the spirit's discovery to "Professor Sylvius of Leiden". Through that essay the attribution entered mainstream drinks history. (A1; F2-F3; Oxford SYLVIUS pdf 1968)
anchors.meaning: The neat answer arrived complete: a name, a title, a city. Leiden is Morewood's word, not the narrator's (G2).
anchors.speaksTo: essence: being fooled by an easy answer

anchors.fact: Oxford calls Morewood the founder of the field and his essay pioneering; it held the first comprehensive history of distilling, and some of its sections haven't been entirely replaced since. He was probably right that the spirit Kämpfer named was ordinary genever. (A2; F2, F4, F7; pdf 1968, SPIRITS WRITING pdf 1884)
anchors.meaning: The answer came from the most careful person in the room, who got the hard part right. Grant him before anything else (Wren b). Keep "probably".
anchors.speaksTo: Sage goal: Wisdom · Wren (2): someone careful, not a fool

anchors.fact: Kämpfer seems to have meant Sylvius's own version of the traditional Dutch spirit; Morewood took it to mean Sylvius fathered the spirit itself. (A3; F6, F8; pdf 1968) What the 1691 conversation was about stays out (G1), and Kämpfer did call the spirit newly invented, so never "he never said so" (G3).
anchors.meaning: Going back to what was actually said makes the claim smaller: one man's recipe, not the spirit. The second look narrows the name; it doesn't swap in a new one (C3). "Seems" stays in the reading.
anchors.speaksTo: story: the truth is always one layer deeper · Wren (4)

anchors.fact: Most nineteenth- and twentieth-century writers followed him without question; he is still cited so widely that historians despair of removing the title, and they have only recently begun to correct it. (A4; F1, F9; pdf 1968)
anchors.meaning: It held because it was satisfying. That motive is not on the page: "I like to think" only. No span of years in the epigraph (Wren f); "most", never "everyone" (G4).

anchors.fact: Genever goes back at least to the late 1400s. A 1495 Dutch cookbook by an unknown, clearly wealthy author has a recipe seen as the first mention of a juniper spirit drunk for pleasure: distilled wine with the costliest spices of the day, juniper one of the cheap ones. Sylvius was born in 1614. (A5; F10-F11; pdf 1968, GENEVER pdf 872-873)
anchors.meaning: Under the one name is something older and bigger, from more than a century before him. The author's name is unknown: one clause at most, never the landing (Wren a; G7).
anchors.speaksTo: position: what's underneath is older and bigger (Wren r1)

anchors.fact: That early spirit was distilled from wine; by 1588 grain had replaced grapes. Today's genever is built on malt wine, a grain spirit distilled at least three times. (A6; F12, F17; pdf 570, 873-874)
anchors.meaning: The glass holds the grain descendant, not the 1495 recipe: never "the same spirit" or "the original" (Tomás's fence).

anchors.fact: After a Dutch king took the English throne in 1688, English distillers copied genever without its grain or skill, made up the flavour with more botanicals and sugar, and shortened the name too: "geneva", from jenever, became "gin". (A7; F13; GENEVER pdf 873, GIN pdf 890)
anchors.meaning: The short, familiar word sits on top of the older spirit; the guest's glass holds the elder. Not "stripped" (*Half a Rim*).
anchors.speaksTo: Wren r1: the older, bigger thing under the neat name

anchors.fact: Oude ("old") genever must hold at least 15% malt wine, at most 20 g sugar a litre, at least 35% ABV; no genever has to be aged, whatever it's called. After 1945 the lighter jonge style almost killed oude off; the cocktail revival since the 1990s brought it back. (A8; F15-F16; pdf 874-875)
anchors.meaning: Even "old" is an easy answer: it means the older style, not years in a barrel. Never "aged" (G6). Tomás's to use or not.

anchors.fact: Holland gin and brandy were by far the most popular spirits for the early Cocktail (the page sits beside an 1833 recipe). By the 1880s drinkers were asking for cocktails the "old-fashioned" way, with spirit, lump sugar and ice and nothing added (the 1882 Chicago report names whisky). In 1895 the New York bartender George Kappeler printed it as sugar, two dashes of Angostura, ice, lemon peel and spirit, with a Holland gin version among others. Dutch gin began to disappear from American bars with the Dry Martini in the 1890s. (A9; F14, F18; *Imbibe!* pdf 68, 175, 185-187; GENEVER pdf 874; v2: the early-Cocktail popularity and the 1880s requests are two eras, never one sentence)
anchors.meaning: The plain build is how this spirit was drunk before it went out of fashion.
anchors.speaksTo: drink: the build isn't a bridge

anchors.fact: Caspar Coolhaes (1536-1615) took a professorship at Leiden in 1574, became a distiller after his excommunication in 1582, and in 1588 wrote the earliest known book to confirm grain had replaced grape, disapproving of the change. (A10; F19; COOLHAES pdf 570)
anchors.meaning: There was a Leiden professor in genever's real story, and he grumbled about the very change that made it. **Fence:** never "the real inventor"; offering him as the answer is Morewood's step again (C3). Wren's call; dossier by default.

cocktail.closingLine: The brandy goes in before the genever. Love the next neat idea, then learn what it started as.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass (about 300 ml), filled with ice cubes
method: Pour the brandy into the rocks glass first.
Add the syrup and the bitters, then pour the genever on top.
Give it a quick stir, fill the glass with ice cubes, and stir again for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Look Again

recipe.note: any VS cognac or Armagnac, about 40%. It goes in first
Dutch or Belgian: look for "oude" on the label, not "jonge" (young). "Oude" means the older, maltier style, not aged. 35% or stronger
2 parts sugar to 1 part water, by weight, stirred until clear

cocktail.tagline: The more you like an answer, the harder you look at it.

reading.epigraph: "Gin" began as a short form of the name of the spirit in this glass.
whoYouAre: Over dinner, a friend explains a lovely theory about how something famous really began. It's neat, it has a name and a date in it, and you love it at once. Hours later you're still in your chair, turning it over. People take that for doubt. It's closer to the reverse: you fall for ideas faster than anyone you know, which is exactly why you check the ones you love.

What worries you is your own delight: a lovely idea, passed on with confidence, that turns out to be wrong. And when a favourite doesn't survive a closer look, you let it go without a fuss. Nobody sees what that costs you.

You take other people's ideas as seriously as your own. Someone floats a half-thought, and you follow it further than they dared, and they leave feeling cleverer than they came. It's respect, and it means more to them than you know.
yours: There's a famous answer to who invented gin, repeated so widely that drinks historians despair of ever shifting it: a chemist in Holland called Sylvius. It took hold in 1824, when Samuel Morewood wrote that a German traveller, Engelbert Kämpfer, had credited the spirit's discovery to "Professor Sylvius of Leiden". Morewood was nobody's fool. He's been called the founder of the field, and his history of distilling was the first full one. He was probably right, too, that the spirit Kämpfer meant was genever, the Dutch spirit gin grew out of.

Maybe Sylvius did make a fine one. Kämpfer seems to have meant just that: Sylvius's own version of a spirit the Dutch were already making. Morewood read it as the invention of the spirit itself, and most of the writers who came after him took his word without question. Historians have only recently begun to correct it. Genever goes back at least to the late 1400s, more than a century before Sylvius was born, and the author of its earliest known recipe is unknown.

I like to think the answer lasted because it was such a good one: a name, a title, a city. It's exactly the kind of answer you'd love. And you're also the one who'd go back to the traveller's words late at night, and find the claim smaller than it looked, and the spirit under it older and bigger. I see both of those people in you: the one who loves the neat answer, and the one who goes back anyway.

So the cocktail I've made for you is built on the older spirit. It's that classic of classics, the Old-Fashioned, made after a New York bartender's recipe of 1895, which came in a Holland gin version too: a little sugar, Angostura, lemon peel, ice. The spirit is oude genever, the old style (the word names the style, not years in a barrel): rich, malty, closer to a whisky than to the gin you know, which took its short name from it. Under it, poured in before the genever, is a little French grape brandy, distilled from wine, as a nod to the wine Dutch distillers made their spirit from before they turned to grain. Once it's stirred you can't find the layers. The older one is in every sip.

So keep loving the neat answers. Don't change that. Just, next time one delights you, don't save the going back for midnight and your own chair. Go back with the friend who brought it: "I love that. Want to see what's underneath?" Most of the time, what the two of you find is older and bigger than the story you started with, and it's theirs to keep too. Going back stops being the lonely part, and becomes what the evening was for.

anchors.fact: By the late 1990s, worn out, he sold his company and turned to property.
anchors.meaning: The story starts with a step away from what he was good at, not with a plan revealed.

anchors.meaning: The payoff on record is the city's cocktail scene turning, in one hedged witness account beside the book's "made the difference". Not downtown revived, not his fortune, not him being proved right.

cocktail.closingLine: Swirl it once the coffee starts to show. When you miss one, make the next move just as steadily.

Squeeze the peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
