cocktail.tagline: You see far enough ahead to let a quick win go.

reading.epigraph: Rye, sugar, bitters, peel. The coffee is in the ice, and arrives later.
whoYouAre: You turned down the offer everyone said you'd regret. Or you let the first chance go by, or gave up a point in an argument you could easily have won. People shook their heads, kindly, and it looked as if you'd got it wrong. You let it look that way. You couldn't prove it yet, and you won't promise what you can't show.

It costs you, too. Letting go of the sure thing never feels clever. It's a loss, and you carry it, saying nothing, until the move plays out. You don't mind looking as if you've got it wrong for a while. What you mind is the move you didn't see, after people trusted you to have read it all.
When everyone wants the quick win, you can sit through the slow one, and whoever is with you can stop panicking. That steadiness is a kindness, even on the days it gets called stubbornness.
yours: By the late 1990s, Cedd Moses had worn himself out at work and sold his company. He turned to property. Going out to bars and restaurants in Los Angeles had left him in love with the city's rundown old centre, which one book calls dead. He says he went downtown to open bars and bring the area and the city's cocktails back, out of pride in the city and a love for its old buildings. He started buying property there while it was cheap. "Everyone at the time thought I was insane," he remembers.

His first bar was Golden Gopher, but the same history says it was a later one, Seven Grand, that made the difference: mostly a whiskey bar, where a lot of promising bartenders worked. Chuck Taggart, an early cocktail lover in the city, called its opening the big turning point, "to me": it wasn't the first, he said, but it seemed to set off so many others. Moses kept opening bars after that.

We don't know how it felt to him while he was buying. I like to think the buying didn't feel clever then, more like a price paid early, with nothing yet to show for it and everyone shaking their heads. That's the piece of this story I'd hand you: the move made before it could be judged, the stretch of looking wrong, and a first try that came before the one that made the difference. I like the size of the ending, too. We don't know whether he ever got everything he went downtown for. The record is smaller: a history that says Seven Grand made the difference, and one man who calls it, "to me", the turning point. I suspect you trust that ending more than a triumphant one.

The cocktail I've made for you is a famous classic, the Old-Fashioned, built strong on a barrel-proof rye, because Seven Grand was a whiskey bar (the rye is my choice). It's sweetened with demerara, seasoned with Angostura, stirred cold, poured over one block of frozen black coffee, with the oil of an orange peel added last. Anyone who knows an Old-Fashioned may think I've got the ice wrong. The first sips are the Old-Fashioned alone, strong and good on their own. Then, as the block melts, the coffee gathers in a dark ring around it, and one slow swirl brings it in, its roast meeting the toasted side of the grain. The coffee is in the ice because of those years downtown: the move is made first, and nobody can taste it yet.

One day there'll be a trap you don't see. Not because you weren't paying attention: you were, more closely than anyone at the table. Some things can't be read from where anyone is sitting. When it happens, it doesn't mean the people who doubted you were right. Take that loss as plainly as you take the ones you choose, and carry on. You'll have lost a piece you didn't mean to give. You'll still have everything that made you good at this.

anchors.fact: A Berlin chemist, Mitscherlich, had written that the salts of tartaric acid and of its strange twin from a tartaric-acid works were alike in crystal form and make-up, yet only one turned polarised light. It seemed beyond men like Mitscherlich and Biot.
anchors.meaning: The older answer was an honest miss, not a bluff.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's (4): an earlier senior answer, wrong on the record

anchors.fact: At 25, just made a doctor, Pasteur noticed tiny facets on the crystals that Mitscherlich had missed. His first idea about them failed (the twin's crystals had them too), but they came in two forms, mirror images like a left and a right hand, and he sorted them by hand into two piles; each pile turned the light the opposite way.
anchors.meaning: What they knew was something they saw for themselves, by looking closely at what others had looked past. (v1.2: "harder than anyone thought worth it" was mine, not on the page.)
anchors.speaksTo: essence: knows more than you'd expect them to · story: a mind that runs ahead with wide-open eyes

anchors.fact: Biot, 74, who had studied this kind of light for thirty years, asked "Are you quite sure?" and said he'd like to investigate "that young man's results". His biographer says he found it hard to believe someone so new had managed it.
anchors.meaning: The doubt was about who was saying it.

anchors.fact: Pasteur wrote asking to see Biot, wanting to convince him (biographer); Biot offered to verify the results. Biot used his own acid, had the salt made in front of him, set the dish in a corner of his room where nobody could touch it for two days, then made up the solutions and read the result himself.
anchors.meaning: Being checked is being taken seriously: Pasteur answered by showing. (v1.2: "asked to be checked" and "hid" were mine.)

anchors.fact: When it came out as Pasteur said, Biot took his arm and, as Pasteur told it, called him "my dear child" and said he had loved the sciences so much that this made his heart beat. (French "mon cher enfant", our translation.)
anchors.meaning: The words that usually sting were said by the one who had checked, as a blessing.
anchors.speaksTo: story: the delight never went out of it

anchors.fact: His biographer says that when he explained his work, no question surprised him and he never laughed at not knowing.
anchors.meaning: They give everyone the respect they once had to wait for.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: Being patronised (turned into what they give)

anchors.fact: Tartaric acid is the main acid of grapes, first found in the crust inside wine barrels. The twin Pasteur sorted split into a right-hand acid, like the grapes' own, and a new left-hand one, and Biot read the left one first. (A7, L1, F3, F8, F18) Never "grapes make only one form" (F19) and never which hand is in a jar of powder (G2).
anchors.meaning: The grapes' own acid was the familiar half; what nobody had seen was its other hand.
anchors.speaksTo: goal: Wisdom/Knowledge · essence: knows more than you'd expect them to

anchors.fact: Verjus is pressed from wine grapes before they've ripened, bottled unfermented, and the *Codex* uses a lot of it as the acid in stirred sours. Grapes' acids are tartaric and malic. (A8, L4; *Codex* p. 187, *LI* p. 61) The grapes are picked unripe on purpose.
anchors.meaning: The sour in the glass comes from the grape itself, the fruit whose acid he took apart (our reading; never about the guest's age, and nobody called the grapes "not ready").
anchors.speaksTo: story: a mind that runs ahead with wide-open eyes

cocktail.closingLine: Stir it until the outside is ice-cold. Next time you know something, leave off the "I think", and let them check.

method: Put the coupe in the freezer for 10 minutes, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Pour the pisco, orange liqueur, blanc vermouth, verjus and syrup into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside feels ice-cold. Don't shake it: shaking waters this one down too far.
Empty the coupe and strain the drink into it, with no ice.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Nothing Escaped You

cocktail.tagline: You know more than people expect, and make them glad they asked.

reading.epigraph: A Sidecar without its lemon. The sour comes from the grape itself.
whoYouAre: Someone is explaining your own subject to you, slowly, as if to a child. You've known it for years, better than they do. You smile, you let them finish, and you put "I think" in front of the part you're sure of. You learned that early, along with everything else: people hear who's talking before they hear what's said.
Being doubted doesn't hurt. A real "show me" is a kind of respect. The pat on the head does, from someone who never looked, and so does finding out that the confident voice was bluffing all along.

And the delight never went out of it. You give everyone the thing you once had to wait for: you never talk down to anybody. Ask you anything and you answer the real question. People leave a conversation with you feeling cleverer than before. Nobody forgets how that felt.
yours: In Paris in 1848, Louis Pasteur was a chemist of twenty-five, just made a doctor. A senior Berlin chemist, Mitscherlich, had written about two salts. One came from tartaric acid, the main acid of grapes, the other from a strange twin found at a tartaric-acid works. Their crystals looked alike, yet in water only the first turned polarised light (light that vibrates in one direction) to one side. Pasteur noticed tiny facets on the crystals that Mitscherlich had missed. His first idea about them didn't work, so he looked closer: the twin's crystals came in two shapes, mirror images, like a left hand and a right. He sorted them into two piles, and each turned the light the opposite way.

Jean-Baptiste Biot, seventy-four, was an authority on that kind of light. "Are you quite sure?" he asked, and said he'd like to investigate "that young man's results". His biographer says Biot could hardly believe someone so new had managed it. Pasteur wrote and asked to show him. Biot offered to check it, brought his own acid, watched the salt being made, put the dish out of reach for two days, then made up the solutions and read the result himself. It was as Pasteur said. Biot took his arm and, as Pasteur told it, said: "My dear child, I have loved the sciences so much in my life that this makes my heart beat."

My dear child. Those are the words you've been talked down to with, and here they come from the one person who had checked, as a blessing. I like to think that's what you've been hoping for since you were small: not to be believed on sight, but to be looked at properly. The doubt was never the insult. The insult is someone who never looks, and you've learned to tell the two apart faster than most. You've had plenty of practice. Pasteur's biographer adds that when he explained his chemistry, no question surprised him, and he never laughed at anyone for not knowing. That part is you as well.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Sidecar, a renowned classic, built on pisco, South America's clear grape brandy, with a little blanc vermouth (the pale, lightly sweet kind) and an orange liqueur. The change that matters: the lemon is gone, and white verjus, juice pressed from wine grapes before they ripen, gives the sour instead. I swapped it as a nod to Pasteur: the sourness is the grapes' own acid, and its tartaric is the familiar one of the two hands he sorted apart. It's stirred very cold and served up, bright and winy, with orange peel to finish.

So when someone doubts what you know, don't shrink and don't argue. Show them, the way he did, and let them look for themselves. The ones worth keeping will look. You've waited long enough to be believed. You don't have to wait to be heard. And I hope that more than once in your life, someone who checked takes your arm.

anchors.fact: Journalists founded the Clover Club in Philadelphia in the 1880s; judges, lawyers and bankers made up the other half. It dined once a month at a Philadelphia hotel, and it had set out to enjoy good eating, deep drinking and giving politicians a hard time.
anchors.meaning: Insiders at a grand table, with permission to tease the powerful. The licence came with the seat.
anchors.speaksTo: essence: reveals the truth using humour · Wren (2) aimed up

anchors.fact: Politicians were at the table, invited. In the club's first two years its guests included two former governors and an attorney-general, alongside generals, judges and actors.
anchors.meaning: The joke was made to the face of the person it was about, at a dinner they had been asked to. Their audience was the king, not the crowd.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren (3) from the inside, with licence

anchors.fact: At every dinner, after the oysters, the president stood and drank to "Our Guests" from a silver loving cup. The guests then drank from it standing, while the members stayed seated.
anchors.meaning: The guests were honoured, and on their feet, before anyone teased them. The welcome came before the wit. Signposted only ("I like to think"): the book gives no reason for the custom.
anchors.speaksTo: give: someone can be wrong and keep their dignity

anchors.fact: The club's own book (1884) says a battle of wits started with the speeches, before the coffee, and that it sprang from the wine. It claims the wit was kindly meant, taken in good part, and seldom fell on barren ground.
anchors.meaning: By their own account, the jokes were meant to land and to grow. That's the club's claim about itself, made once in print: tell it as "the book claims", never as a habit ("they liked to say") and never as proof that anyone changed their mind.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren (4) the point stuck (claimed) · fear: Deception

anchors.fact: Each new member was welcomed with some ceremony, and after a few meetings the club got a baby's chair and a rattle for it; the book lists the members who sat, or should have sat, in the chair. And the club made a rule against any rule that smacked of formality or foolishness.
anchors.meaning: They made themselves the silly ones first. The licence to tease the guests started at home.
anchors.speaksTo: hide: cleverer than they let on · Jester goal: Humor

anchors.fact: The club had its own cocktail. Its recipe first turns up in 1901, when the head bartender at the Waldorf-Astoria gave it to a paper, the *New York Press*: gin, lemon, raspberry syrup and egg white. By 1910 it was everywhere.
anchors.meaning: A frothy pink drink over a full measure of gin. It looks like the least serious thing on the menu, and it isn't (Wren C6, signposted, never a fact).

anchors.fact: It didn't come back after Prohibition, and in 1934 *Esquire* named it one of the ten worst cocktails.
anchors.meaning: The drink's own story, laughed at. Never a verdict on the guest (Wren C3), and never "the worst".
anchors.speaksTo: Jester fear: being taken for the merely silly

anchors.fact: It was more or less forgotten until the late 2000s, when a new bar took its name and gave it a second life.
anchors.meaning: One clause, the drink's story only. No bar, no name, no "proved right".

anchors.fact: Wine was on the club's own table: members paid for their own wine, and the club's book mentions its wine and its champagne. The 1901 recipe has no wine in it.
anchors.meaning: The wine in the raspberry comes from the club's table, not from its recipe: a riff on the drink, drawn from the dinner. Ours, never "their recipe", and never "red" for what they drank.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof · the spark (Tomás)

cocktail.closingLine: Froth it before the ice goes in. Then tell one joke tonight that's for nobody's good.
cocktail.glassware: coupe, chilled in the freezer, no ice in the glass
method: Up to a week ahead, make the syrup. Put the raspberries, sugar and wine in a blender and blend on low until you can't feel any sugar grains, about a minute. Leave it 30 minutes, then press it through a fine sieve to take out the seeds. Jar it and keep it in the fridge.
Put the coupe in the freezer.
Crack an egg, keep the white, and whisk it lightly with a fork for a few seconds so it pours. Measure 15 ml.
Pour the gin, lemon juice, syrup and egg white into a shaker. Close it and shake hard with no ice for about 10 seconds, so the white turns to froth.
Open it, fill it with ice, and shake hard again for 12 to 15 seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold comfortably.
Strain it into the cold coupe through a small tea strainer held over the glass, so the froth comes out smooth.

squeezed the same day

cocktail.tagline: Your jokes let people change their minds without losing face.

reading.epigraph: A club that teased politicians over dinner had a drink of its own. It was pink.
whoYouAre: Someone at the table has started to believe their own story. A boss, an old friend who's done well, the relative everyone humours. You don't correct them. Correcting them would cost them something with everyone watching. So you make it funny, carefully, aimed at them and not at the room, and they're the one laughing hardest. Nothing else happens that night. A week later, quietly, they've dropped it. Nobody mentions the joke, least of all you.

It sounded like a quip. It took you most of the evening. Nobody guesses how much the untrue thing bothered you while you were smiling: you can sit with almost anything except a story everyone has agreed to believe. The room that frightens you is the one where nobody's allowed to laugh, because that's where it stays true for good. And there's a cost you rarely mention. When you mean something about your own life, people are still waiting for the funny part.
You let people be wrong and keep their dignity. It's kinder than honesty on its own, and much harder.
yours: In Philadelphia in the 1880s, some journalists started a dining club, the Clover Club. Once a month they had dinner at a hotel there, and they had set out to enjoy good food, plenty of drink and teasing politicians.

Politicians were at the table. They'd been invited: in its first two years the club's guests included two former governors and an attorney-general. The guests were toasted from a silver loving cup, then drank from it standing while the members stayed seated. Then came the speeches, and what the club's own book called a "war of wit". The book claims it was kindly meant and well received. And after a few meetings, the club got a baby's chair and a rattle for welcoming each new member.

I recognise you in that. They didn't shout from outside. They asked the powerful to dinner, honoured them first, and they'd already made themselves look ridiculous with a rattle. I like to think that's why a guest could laugh along: nobody at that table had to lose face to hear it. You do the same. You go first as the silly one, so the person it's about can take it home.

The club had its own cocktail: gin, lemon, raspberry syrup and egg white. Its recipe first turns up in 1901, when the Waldorf-Astoria's head bartender gave it to a paper, the *New York Press*. In 1934 *Esquire* named it one of the ten worst cocktails, and it was all but forgotten until a new bar named itself after it, late in the 2000s, and poured it as its own. It's a classic again, and the cocktail I've made for you is a Clover Club, with a syrup of my own: I make the raspberry syrup with red wine instead of water, as a nod to those dinners, where the wit came with the wine. It looks like the least serious thing you could order, pink under a soft cap of froth. Underneath is a full measure of gin, and the raspberry tastes deeper, of fruit and wine rather than sweets. You only find that out by tasting it. I like to think your best jokes work the same way.

Keep telling the truth like that. The people who've been wrong around you are luckier than they know. But every joke of yours is working for something: the truth, the face, whoever it's about. Now and then, make one that carries nothing at all, daft from start to finish, just because it makes you laugh. That club kept a baby's rattle, after all.

anchors.fact: The Rob Roy's most credible origin is a bar by the Hoboken ferry in the mid-1890s: a salesman asked for a cocktail made with his new scotch, when scotch wasn't used in cocktails, and bartender Henry August Orphal invented one on the spot.
anchors.meaning: Someone listened, so that a stranger's taste could be understood: the Lover half, connection through understanding.

anchors.fact: An earlier Rob Roy (1873) was lost to a garbled newspaper recipe. The surviving story is known because Orphal's brother wrote it down in 1941. A grand hotel (the Fifth Avenue) served it as "new" in 1897, when it was already about two years old.
anchors.meaning: The true story over the famous one; getting it right is a way of caring: the Sage half, and the fear of deception answered.
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: Honesty · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: Stirred, not shaken: shaking beats in air bubbles and clouds the drink, stirring keeps it clear.
anchors.meaning: Nothing hidden; you can see all the way through it.

anchors.fact: Dry oloroso matures in a solera: the oldest barrel is drawn from but never fully emptied, then topped up from the next oldest.
anchors.meaning: Every glass keeps a little of what came before: patience, depth.

anchors.fact: Two sherries, one dry (walnut aroma, no nuts) and one sweet (PX, raisin), stay distinguishable in the glass.
anchors.meaning: Discernment is the gift. Two voices you can tell apart, not an unresolved blur (Sage fears ambiguity).

anchors.fact: Early Rob Roys were scotch, vermouth and orange bitters (often equal parts). This one keeps the orange bitters.
anchors.meaning: A nod to the first version: respect for origins.

anchors.fact: Sage is a surprising pairing for both citrus and honey.
anchors.meaning: Chosen for flavour alone.

cocktail.closingLine: Sip it slowly. It was made to be understood, not finished.
cocktail.glassware: Nick & Nora
method: Chill a Nick & Nora glass.
Stir the scotch, vermouth, both sherries and the bitters with ice until very cold.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then set it aside.
Slap the sage leaf once between your palms and lay it on the surface.
cocktail.name: A Brother's Care

recipe.note: a little of what came before
how it was first made
for the taste, nothing else

cocktail.tagline: You know why something is wonderful, and who you want to share it with.

reading.epigraph: Nothing in this glass is pretending. You'd know if it were.
whoYouAre: You're a scientist of the senses. You notice what other people miss: the second flavour hiding behind the first, the moment a drink changes in the glass. And you've taught yourself to put it into words.

Among your friends, you're the one people ask before they choose: the restaurant, the song, the gift, the place to go. It isn't because yours is the loudest opinion. It's because you can always say *why*. That's your gift. You don't just know that something is good, you know what makes it so. It's also how you love people. When you find something wonderful you can't keep it to yourself, and nothing makes you happier than watching someone discover it through you. What you can't forgive is being fooled: the label that promises too much, the story told only to impress.
yours: You may know a story about this drink's ancestor, the Rob Roy. It's usually told with a grand New York hotel in it. The hotel did serve it, but only once the drink was already a couple of years old. The truer story is more specific and more niche. In the 1890s a salesman walked into a working bar by the Hoboken ferry with a new scotch and asked for a cocktail made with it. Nobody mixed scotch back then. The bartender could have said no. Instead he listened, and invented something on the spot, so that a stranger's whisky could be understood.

That story nearly didn't survive. An earlier Rob Roy, twenty years before, was lost when a newspaper printed its recipe wrong. This one lasted because the bartender's brother took the trouble, nearly fifty years later, to write down what really happened. That's you, isn't it? You're the one who takes the trouble. You'd rather have the true story than the famous one, because for you, getting it right is a way of caring.

So I made it the way it would resonate with you: the purest truth, with no frills for show. It's stirred rather than shaken, so it stays perfectly clear and you can see all the way through it. There are two sherries in it: a dry one that smells of walnuts, though there isn't a nut in the glass, and a very sweet one that tastes of raisins. They don't blur together. You'll be able to tell them apart, and for someone like you, that's the pleasure. The dry sherry is aged in rows of barrels where the oldest is never completely emptied, so every glass keeps a little of what came before. And a single sage leaf, because sage goes surprisingly well with orange and honey.

Here's what I'd ask of you. When you do have this in front of you, take the first sip without naming anything. No notes, no verdict. Name it all on the second, if you still want to. Then try the same thing the next time anything delights you: a meal, a song, a person. Let the first moment go unexplained. You've spent years making sure pleasure tells you the truth. It will. You can put the notebook down.

anchors.fact: Michael Jackson (1942–2007) was an English journalist, not the singer. At sixteen he began a series of pieces about pubs for weekly papers in West Yorkshire.
anchors.meaning: An ordinary beginning: pieces about pubs in weekly papers, not a stage. The scale starts small.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren trap: write the scene small · not the singer, one clause

anchors.fact: Apart from a handful of earlier books, publishers hadn't imagined anyone would want to read more about whisky than a label. His 1977 beer book stood out for treating beer thoroughly and seriously.
anchors.meaning: The "before" his work changed: nobody thought there was more to say.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren (4) the "before" · essence: using knowledge to transform the world

anchors.fact: His 1977 *World Guide to Beer* introduced the idea of beer "styles": ways of grouping beers and showing how they relate, like pale ale, porter, pilsner, bock and India pale ale.
anchors.meaning: A way of seeing, not a verdict. Once you know how beers are grouped, you can place one you've never tried, by yourself (our reading, signposted).
anchors.speaksTo: gift: a way of looking, not something to obey · goal: Wisdom

anchors.fact: Ten years later, his *World Guide to Whisky* (1987) did the same for whisky, laying a foundation for a new way of looking at it by showing how the world's whisky types relate to one another.
anchors.meaning: How things relate is what the glass holds: two whiskies from two countries, related (the pair and the link are ours, never his).

anchors.fact: His influence reached writers, readers and drinkers, and just as far among distillers and brewers, many of whom counted him as an inspiration or simply a friend.
anchors.meaning: It spread through people who then used it for themselves.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: being followed into a mistake (inverted) · driver: leave a mark

anchors.fact: Oxford suggests the greatest tribute to his influence is that his books, unique in their day, now seem common and obvious.
anchors.meaning: The word "obvious" is spent here, once, as Oxford's tribute, never as the guest's trait.
anchors.speaksTo: story: make it so simple it seems obvious (spent once)

anchors.fact: No source I read records his doubt, or any check before his styles spread.
anchors.meaning: Signposted only: "I like to think he worried…". Never told as an event.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: a revolution built on a flawed idea · Wren (4), signposted

anchors.fact: Two whiskies called rye, from two countries. Canadian whisky is often called rye, though corn is usually its main grain, with a little rye for flavour. American rye whiskey must be made from at least half rye.
anchors.meaning: Same name, two countries, the grains usually the other way round: a relationship the guest can see at once. The pairing is ours, never his.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: a new way of looking · the drink as proof

anchors.fact: In *The Flavor Matrix*, tamarind sits in the Sour segment of both the Corn chart and the Grain chart.
anchors.meaning: A flavour that goes with both grains, found in a book that charts how flavours relate. The tie to Jackson is our reading (signposted), and the book is about the grains as food, not the whiskies.
anchors.speaksTo: Robin: a spark tied to the story in words

cocktail.closingLine: Put it out there. They'll pick it up with their eyes open.
cocktail.glassware: small tumbler (about 200 ml), chilled in the freezer, no ice
method: Put the tumbler in the freezer for 15 minutes.
Pour both whiskies, the demerara syrup, the tamarind water and the bitters into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir quickly for about 15 seconds, until the outside is very cold.
Strain into the cold tumbler. No ice in the glass.
Hold the orange peel over the drink, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top. Rub it once round the rim and drop it in.
cocktail.name: Plain to See

recipe.note: Any blended Canadian whisky made mainly from corn (most are), 40% or a little stronger; not a 100% rye Canadian. Canadian whisky is often called rye, though corn is usually its main grain, with a little rye for flavour.
Any straight rye, 40-55%. This is the one made from at least half rye: the same name, and in a typical bottle the grains the other way round.
Equal parts demerara sugar and hot water, stirred until clear, then cooled.

Break 25 g of sour, seedless tamarind pulp (a block from the world-food aisle; not "sweet tamarind") into a bowl, pour on 60 ml of just-boiled water, leave 30 minutes, mash with a fork and press through a sieve. Keeps a few days in the fridge. Blocks vary: if yours is very sour, use 1 tsp; if it's mild, 2.

cocktail.tagline: You take a yes more seriously than a no.

reading.epigraph: Two countries, two whiskies, both often called rye. One usually holds only a little rye.
whoYouAre: You've seen how something could work better: the way the team runs its week, how the family shares out the holidays, the fix a friend has needed for years. You can see it whole. And before you say a word, you walk back through it, more than once, until you can explain it in a sentence. From outside it looks like confidence. It's closer to care. You know that if they like it, they'll actually do it.
What keeps you up is the yes: everyone's, and then finding out you were wrong. A mistake you make alone stays with you. A mistake people take up because of you travels with every one of them.

So you never hand anyone an answer to obey. You give them a way of seeing it, plain enough to use without you, and to notice if you've slipped. You never asked anyone to believe you. You showed them how to look. That's generosity, and not the usual kind: people leave you more capable, not more in need of you.
yours: In 1977 an English journalist called Michael Jackson (no relation to the singer) published a guide to the world's beer. He'd started at sixteen, writing about pubs for weekly papers in West Yorkshire. His book took beer thoroughly and seriously, and it brought in an idea: beer "styles". Pale ale, porter, pilsner, bock, India pale ale: groups of beers, and how each one relates to the others.

Ten years later he did the same for whisky, with a book that showed how the world's whisky types are related. Before then, apart from a handful of earlier books, publishers hadn't imagined anyone would want to read more about whisky than a label. His influence reached writers, readers and drinkers, and brewers and distillers too, many of whom counted him an inspiration, or simply a friend. Perhaps the best tribute to him is that his kind of book, new in its day, now seems obvious.

Did it ever keep him up at night? I can't say. But I like to think it did, and that it's why his big idea was a way of grouping, not a verdict: with a style in your head, you can place a beer you've never tasted, by yourself. I see you in that. You don't want people simply following you. You want them to see what you saw, and carry on from there without you.

So the cocktail I've made for you is a renowned whiskey classic, an Old-Fashioned, with its whisky drawn from two countries. Canadians often call their whisky "rye", a name from the days when it was wheat whisky flavoured with rye; today most of it is made mainly from corn, usually with a little rye for flavour. American rye whiskey must be at least half rye. Same name, the grains usually swapped, side by side in one glass. To honour his guide to how whiskies relate, I used a guide of my own, a chart of which flavours go together, and looked for a flavour that goes with both grains. I found tamarind, dark and sour, and it gives the drink the sourness it needs to balance. Stirred with ice in a jar, it's strained into a frozen glass with none, and finished with oil pressed from orange peel.

You keep the next idea back until you're sure, and you'll never feel quite sure enough. But look at what you've already done to it: you've made it simple enough to see through. People who take up an idea like that aren't following blindly. So share it before it's big. A flaw found among a few friends costs a laugh. And if there's no flaw, you get what you were after all along: people doing something better, their own way, because of what you showed them.

anchors.fact: Joseph James Forrester, born in Hull in 1809, went to Oporto in 1831 to join his uncle's port house, Offley, Forrester & Webber; the DNB calls him a merchant and wine shipper (F1, F2).
anchors.meaning: He spoke from inside the trade, about wine he shipped. What he said came from what he'd seen, not from a theory.

anchors.fact: In 1844 he published a pamphlet on the port trade without his name on it, *A Word or Two on Port Wine*; eight editions ran out fast (F4, C1).
anchors.meaning: Plenty of people wanted a copy. That says there was demand, not that anyone agreed.
anchors.speaksTo: Not afraid to share what they have discovered and what they know

anchors.fact: The DNB says he blamed abuses in how port was made and handled, and the Douro Wine Company's monopoly (created 1756), with its heavy export taxes and its limits on what could be shipped, for the slump in the trade (F5, F6).
anchors.meaning: He named the way things were officially run, not a rival.
anchors.speaksTo: challenges conventional wisdom · a comfortable lie becoming the official truth

anchors.fact: He was easily identified as the author, and "bitterly attacked by the persons interested", meaning people with a stake in the trade as it was (F7). The people of the wine country backed him warmly (F8, one clause at most).
anchors.meaning: Leaving his name off didn't keep him out of it. The attack came from those with something to lose; it says nothing about whether he was right.
anchors.speaksTo: everyone important wants them to stop

anchors.fact: In May 1852 he gave evidence, as Mr. J. J. Forrester, to the Commons Select Committee on Import Duties on Wines, setting out at greater length every abuse the pamphlet had summarised (F10–F12). A bibliography lists more of his writing on the same subject in 1845 (F13).
anchors.meaning: After the attack he said it again, with more of it, under his own name and on the record.

anchors.fact: Oxford: elderberries were used to darken port and add fruit, and by the 1840s Forrester railed against them (F14). Whether his charges held is disputed (C3).
anchors.meaning: What he wrote about was in the glass itself. We tell what he said, never that he was proved right.

anchors.fact: He had a stake too: he shipped port, and a 2011 history counts him among the people in the 1852 debate on Britain's wine import duties who weren't disinterested (C4).
anchors.meaning: He wasn't a saint and needn't be. A person can be right, or partly right, and still have something to gain.
anchors.speaksTo: (for Wren: the crank and purity traps)

anchors.fact: No source gives a reason for the anonymity (L1).
anchors.meaning: Signposted only: "I like to think he hoped the pages would be judged on their own."

anchors.fact: *Codex* p. 250: port is a fortified wine from the Douro Valley, a blend of several Portuguese grapes, fortified with young grape brandy partway through fermentation; red styles are ruby, vintage, late-bottled vintage, tawny, colheita.
anchors.meaning: Port is his subject, so it's the core, not a seasoning (plan).

cocktail.closingLine: Ruby first, then twice the tawny. Make the second pour the bigger one.
cocktail.glassware: small stemmed port glass (about 150 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Make the tea: steep 2 bags of plain black tea in 150 ml of just-boiled water for 8 minutes, twice as long as for a cup, so it comes out strong and a little drying. Lift the bags out, let it cool, and keep it in the fridge (it lasts two days).
Put the glass in the freezer for 10 minutes.
In a mixing glass or a jar, pour the ruby first, then the tawny, then the cold tea.
Fill with ice and stir for about 15 seconds, until the outside of the glass is cold.
Strain into the chilled glass, with no ice.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then set it aside.
cocktail.name: On the Record

recipe.note: a young, non-vintage ruby
any tawny with "10 years old" on the label
plain black tea (not Earl Grey or any flavoured tea), no sugar, no milk: 2 tea bags in 150 ml just-boiled water for 8 minutes, then cooled in the fridge

cocktail.tagline: You say what you've found, and give the next person courage to say it too.

reading.epigraph: Port goes in twice here: once in short, then again at greater length.
whoYouAre: You looked into it properly: the figures behind the plan everyone's excited about, the story the family has told for years, the way things have always been done at work. And it doesn't hold. So you said so, plainly, with what you'd found. The room went quiet, and not the good kind.

Here's what you don't show. You don't enjoy standing there on your own, not at all. Part of you hopes you're wrong, because being wrong would make life simpler. So you check it again, usually late, and it's still there. Then you say it again, with more of it. What you can't live with is the comfortable version becoming the official one, with nobody having said a word.

And often, later, someone finds you, a little quietly, to say they'd wondered the same. Because you said it first, they get to say it second. That's a gift, though it rarely feels like one at the time.
yours: In 1831 a young man born in Hull, Joseph James Forrester, went out to Oporto, in Portugal, to join his uncle, a partner in a port house there. He became a merchant and wine shipper, and over the years he came to believe the trade was being badly run: port mishandled in the making, and the Douro Wine Company, which held a monopoly dating from 1756, taxed exports heavily and limited how much could be shipped. He blamed both for the slump the port trade was in.

In 1844 he set it out in a pamphlet, without his name on it. It ran through eight printings fast, so plenty of people wanted a copy. He was easily found out anyway, and bitterly attacked by those with a stake in the trade as it was. I like to think he'd hoped the pages would be judged on their own.

What he did next is why I thought of you. He didn't go quiet. By the next year he had more on the same subject in print. And in 1852 he gave evidence to a committee of the House of Commons, under his own name this time, setting out at greater length every abuse his pamphlet had summed up. He wasn't on his own: the people of the wine country backed him warmly. He had a stake too: he shipped port himself, and what that committee was weighing was Britain's duty on wine. And not everyone since agrees he was right about all of it. But what stays with me is the order of things. First the attack, then more of the argument, not less. Most people only ever see the first time you say something. They don't see you checking it again, and coming back with more.

So the cocktail I've made for you is port, twice. It's stirred and served like a Martini, with port where the gin would be: first a short measure of young ruby, fresh and fruity, then twice as much tawny, a blend of wines from several years. The same kind of wine, said again at greater length, as a nod to the way he kept saying it. Port tends to be sweet, and rather than add anything to make it go down easier, I dried it with strong, cold black tea. On the flavour chart I work from, port and tea sit in the same family of aromas. Orange oil goes on top, and it's served with no ice, in a small, chilled port glass.

When a room goes cold on you, it's tempting to read it as an answer. On bad nights it feels like proof you're wrong. On good ones, like proof you're right. It's neither. Forrester was attacked by the people with a stake and backed by the people of the wine country, and neither of those settled whether he was right. So the next time it goes quiet, let it, and go back to what you found. If it's still there, say it again, with more of it. And if one day it isn't, you'll be the one who says so, out loud. That's exactly why people can trust what you tell them.

anchors.fact: The Sauza name, founded in 1873, left the family and passed from one company to the next: a Spanish firm, then Allied Domecq, Fortune Brands, Beam and Suntory. (A1, F1-F2; Oxford SAUZA pdf 1742) No year of sale (C1); never "sold six times".
anchors.meaning: A lot of business went on around a name.
anchors.speaksTo: story: everyone around the Dude is scheming, shouting

anchors.fact: By his own account, when the business, its two industrial distilleries and most of the fields were sold, his grandfather kept the estate in Tequila, with growing agave and an old distillery he had made into a museum. (A2, W2; *Distiller* 2025) The grandfather's reason isn't on record (card W2 note): never "kept it for him".
anchors.meaning: What stayed was small, and at the time it was a museum, not a business.
anchors.speaksTo: story: the rug that really tied the room together

anchors.fact: In his words: he felt the tequilas on sale had lost something next to the ones he drank with his grandfather, and thought getting the old distillery going again would be a fun project. (A3, W3; *Distiller* 2025) Taste judgement attributed to him.
anchors.meaning: He went back to what he knew from living it, and he didn't frame it as a crusade.
anchors.speaksTo: essence: True wisdom is keeping things real · story: Everything this person knows was learned by living

anchors.fact: Oxford: barred from using the family name, he chose Los Abuelos for his forebears, then a rum's trademark forced him to rename it Fortaleza; the brand has no tie to Sauza. (A4, F6; pdf 1742-1743) "Barred", "forced" (G1). The old distillery was called La Fortaleza (W2): two facts side by side, no "because" (G7).
anchors.meaning: He was refused one name and forced off another, and neither was his choice; the tequila never carried the first (v1.2: "the name was lost twice" was mine and went too far). The tequila didn't depend on its name.

anchors.fact: Sauza's basic line is mixto, at least 51 percent agave, and its agave goes through a diffuser: shredded raw, broken down with steam and chemicals. Diffusers came in around 1999-2003 to answer a real agave shortage. (A5, F3-F4; pdf 1743-1744, MIXTO pdf 1338, DIFFUSER pdf 647) Sauza also has 100% agave lines.
anchors.meaning: The fast way exists for a reason; he took the slow one. No sneer at anyone's bottle.

anchors.fact: A tahona is a big stone wheel pulled round a stone bed to crush the cooked agave; the type of mill goes back to ancient Greece and Rome, and reached Mexico probably in the 17th century. (A6, F7; TAHONA pdf 1971) Other tequilas use one too (F8).
anchors.meaning: Plain and old, and by his own account less efficient than a modern mill (v1.1: "heavy and slow, and it works" was mine, not on any page).
anchors.speaksTo: imagery: everyday objects, comfort and honesty, minimal polish

anchors.fact: In his words, the stone wheel is considerably less efficient than modern mills, and their year's output is a day's work for a big factory, so they won't make the most tequila or earn the most from it. (A7, W5, W10; *Distiller* 2025)
anchors.meaning: What he passed up was on the record, as his own choice.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: Deception (turned: no pretending it's the efficient way)

anchors.fact: As of 2025, more than twenty years after he started, they still cook in a brick oven, crush with the stone wheel, ferment in small wooden vats and distil in small copper pot stills, on the family's estate; they grow some agave there and buy the rest. (A8, W3, W5-W6; *Distiller* 2025) Bartenders' praise and "best" stay his words (G5).
anchors.meaning: It held. Wren's condition 3, met as a dated fact; quality claims stay his.

cocktail.closingLine: Pinch the oregano once and lay it on the ice. It's the smallest thing in the glass, and the one you'd miss.
cocktail.glassware: tall highball glass (about 300 ml), three ice cubes
method: Pour the tequila into a tall glass and add three ice cubes.
Stir for three seconds, just enough to chill it.
Pour in the cold soda water and stir once.
Pinch the oregano sprig once between finger and thumb to wake its scent, and lay it on the ice.
No lime, no sugar. The soda turns the tequila citrusy by itself.
cocktail.name: Whatever They Call It

recipe.item: Fortaleza Blanco tequila (the standard one, not the Still Strength), recommended
recipe.note: it can be hard to find: any blanco tequila made with a tahona, the old stone wheel, does the same job
straight from the fridge
pinched once, laid on the ice

cocktail.tagline: You let almost everything go. Just not the part that matters.

reading.epigraph: Built for a tequila that had to find a name twice. Stone still crushes its agave.
whoYouAre: Two hours into the evening, the table is arguing about something that sounds important: who said what, whose fault it was, what to call it. You've let all of it go. It isn't that you can't follow it. You followed it once, a while back, and found out how little of it was worth the heat. But buried in all that noise there's one small thing nobody else noticed was the point, and that one you won't let go.

Your ease took effort, though nobody sees it. You've been pulled into someone else's story before, and found yourself carrying part of something that wasn't true. So now you step back early. And because you step back, people sometimes decide you don't care. You do. You care about very few things, and you care about those all the way.
That gives people something, and they rarely say it: with you, nobody has to win. The temperature drops. When someone wants an argument to go quiet, they bring it to you.
yours: Sauza was founded in 1873, and the name grew into one of the biggest in tequila. Then the business was sold, and the name passed from one company to the next: a Spanish firm, then Allied Domecq, Fortune Brands, Beam and Suntory. Today its agave goes through a diffuser, a big industrial machine that breaks it down with steam and chemicals. It came in when agave ran short, and it gets more out of every plant.

One piece stayed in the family. As Guillermo Erickson Sauza, the founder's great-great-grandson, tells it, his grandfather kept the family estate in the town of Tequila, and on it an old distillery he'd turned into a museum. Guillermo felt the tequilas he could buy had lost something next to the ones he'd drunk with his grandfather, and he thought getting the old place running again would be a fun project. He wasn't allowed to put the family name on it. He called it Los Abuelos, for the grandfathers before him, and then a rum's trademark forced him to change that too. The name it ended up with was Fortaleza. The old distillery had been called La Fortaleza. Maybe one led to the other. I like to think so.

A name is what everyone fights over. Guillermo lost two, and kept the old way going. Over twenty years later, they still cook the agave slowly in a brick oven and crush it with a tahona, a big stone wheel pulled round and round a stone bed, which he'll tell you is far less efficient than a modern mill. As he puts it, they won't make the most tequila, or earn the most from it. I like to think the name was never the part he cared about most.

You'd have understood Guillermo straight away. Everyone else was busy with the name: who owned it, who could use it, what to put on the bottle instead. What mattered to him was smaller than all that: a piece of land, an old stone wheel, and a taste he remembered from drinking with his grandfather. You know that kind of small.

So the cocktail I've made for you is the simplest long drink there is, and one of the best: Fortaleza Blanco, or another blanco made with a stone wheel, with cold soda and nothing else poured in. No lime, no sugar, nothing covering it up. With soda, a blanco tequila turns bright and citrusy all by itself. The one extra is a sprig of oregano, pinched once and laid on the ice, as a nod to the small thing nobody thought to pick. It shares a note with the tequila, so it brings out something already there.

Your way has one cost, though. Because you let so much go, people take your ease for not caring. Next time the table's arguing and the thing you care about is caught in the middle of it, don't just keep hold of it quietly. Tell them, out loud, that it matters to you. The people who thought you were easy about everything will be surprised. Then they'll trust your ease even more, because they'll know it was always your choice.

anchors.fact: Alfred Barnard (1837–1918), an English journalist, is regarded as the first whisky writer (Oxford BARNARD pdf 211).
anchors.meaning: Keep "regarded as". Warmth and humour come with him (A8), so he is never a cold figure.

anchors.fact: In 1885 a London trade journal, *Harper's Weekly Gazette*, commissioned him to tour all the whisky distilleries; the reports were published two years later, in 1887, as *The Whisky Distilleries of the United Kingdom* (pdf 211; 1887 also pdf 402, 1079, 2153, 2177).
anchors.meaning: He was sent by the trade, not independent. "Sent to visit every distillery" is the commission's aim; no page counts the ones he reached. Never the 1889 edition as the first (C2).

anchors.fact: His tour took in Ireland: 28 distilleries working there in 1887 (pdf 2153; 18 in today's republic, 10 in the north, pdf 1079).
anchors.meaning: Say "Britain and Ireland", not Oxford's loose "Britain".

anchors.fact: Oxford notes the precision of his writing about the small details of much of the equipment at each distillery (pdf 211).
anchors.meaning: Wren's (1): the dull detail on show. "Much of", not all.

anchors.fact: Later Oxford entries measure change from his 1887 figures (pdf 1079: 18 in the republic in 1887, three by the 1960s; pdf 2153); his still-house pictures are captioned as he found them in the 1880s (pdf 2150, 2168); Oxford calls it the earliest and most accurate account, and the template for many later books (pdf 211); reprinted 1987 (pdf 212).
anchors.meaning: Wren's (2): later writers still count from his figures. Not "everyone trusts it". The fall needs its date, "by the 1960s" (audit v1 H1). "Most accurate" is Oxford's judgement, attributed.

anchors.fact: Oxford says his book barely mentions casks (pdf 211). Single source, Oxford's characterisation; the book itself is unread (library gap).
anchors.meaning: Wren's (3): our reading only: even this record has a gap, and later writers still count from it. No reason given (C1), no "missed", no "never".

anchors.fact: Oxford's reason for the gap (casks thought unimportant, pdf 211) is contradicted by PAXARETE pdf 1483 (19th-century producers prized ex-sherry casks).
anchors.meaning: Kept out of guest text. Paxarete never appears: pairing it with the gap makes a miss (G1), and sherry is the Connoisseur's.

anchors.fact: Oxford pairs his fussy love of detail with a sociable, funny man, whose accounts are dotted with lively scenes from the journey and read as a travelogue (pdf 211).
anchors.meaning: Wren's (4), on the page. Paraphrase only: Oxford's phrases are copy risks.

anchors.fact: He was in the end a freelance journalist who also wrote shorter pieces for individual distilleries (pdf 211).
anchors.meaning: Guard: never "independent"; the distillery names stay out.

anchors.fact: In Britain, whisky and soda took over from brandy and soda, becoming the standard once vine disease hit the cognac supply in the second half of the nineteenth century (HIGHBALL pdf 1005).
anchors.meaning: One clause at most, never the reason for the drink. Date it "the second half of the century", the page's span; the standard among soda drinks, not Britain's standard drink (audit v1 H4).

anchors.fact: Vanillin is among the compounds an oak barrel gives a spirit (MATURATION pdf 1265; BOTANICAL pdf 321).
anchors.meaning: Supports Tomás's vanilla as a nod to the cask. Never "the vanilla is the cask".

cocktail.closingLine: Ease the first cube in slowly. Then leave the hunch in the margin, where someone will find it.
cocktail.glassware: tall highball glass (about 300 ml), chilled in the freezer, 1-inch ice cubes added one at a time
method: Put the glass in the freezer for at least 15 minutes, and the soda in the fridge.
Pour the whisky and the vanilla into the cold glass.
Lower one ice cube in with a bar spoon so it doesn't crack, and wait about 10 seconds.
Stir slowly until drops form on the outside of the glass, about 10 seconds.
Add one or two more cubes, until the ice is two-thirds of the way up, and stir briefly.
Pour in just enough soda that the ice doesn't float. Push the spoon to the bottom, raise the lowest cube about an inch, and lower it again: that mixes it without knocking out the bubbles.
Add a last cube and the rest of the soda. Stir once, a single turn, and serve straight away.
cocktail.name: Note to Self

recipe.item: unpeated Highland single malt Scotch whisky
recipe.note: ideally one whose label says it was aged in bourbon casks, with no sherry or wine finish
the real thing, not "vanilla flavouring"; oak casks give whisky some of the same flavour

recipe.item: soda water or seltzer, very cold
recipe.note: straight from the fridge; two parts soda to one of whisky

cocktail.tagline: Impressive is easy. Exact is what you're after.

reading.epigraph: A careful 1887 book on whisky hardly mentions casks. The vanilla here is for them.
whoYouAre: You know when the boiler was last serviced, what the meter read in March, and how long bread really takes in your oven, not what the packet says. When an argument starts about how things used to be, you don't join in. You fetch the notes.

Some people mistake that for coolness. It isn't. Writing it down is how you keep a messy world still enough to think in. And, though you rarely admit it, it's one of the things you enjoy most. You're better company than your notebook suggests.

What haunts you is the thing you never thought to write down, the one that mattered after all, in a column you didn't make. But when someone needs to know what really changed, nobody has to guess. They count from your numbers, and the count holds.
yours: In 1885 a London trade paper sent a journalist called Alfred Barnard to visit every whisky distillery in Britain and Ireland. Two years later his reports came out as one book, *The Whisky Distilleries of the United Kingdom*. He's regarded as the first whisky writer. He set down the small details of much of the equipment at each distillery, and a modern reference book on spirits calls his book the earliest and most accurate account of the industry in its day.

Writers still count from his numbers. In 1887 he found eighteen distilleries working in what is now the Republic of Ireland. By the 1960s there were three, and that fall is still measured from his eighteen. Old pictures of still houses are captioned as he found them. And yet his book hardly mentions the casks. We don't know why. For all his fussing over detail, he was sociable and funny, and he dotted his reports with scenes from the journey, so the book reads as a travel story too. A hundred years on, it was reprinted.

I like to think two things kept it on the shelf: everything he did write down can be checked, and you can tell he was enjoying himself. I see you in both. Your notes will have a gap somewhere. Everyone's do. His gap hasn't stopped people counting from his book.

So the cocktail I've made for you is a true classic, the whisky highball: whisky and soda, which took over from brandy and soda in Britain in the second half of the nineteenth century. It's an unpeated Highland single malt, ideally one whose label says it was aged in bourbon casks, lengthened with two parts very cold soda. It's built step by step, and every step has a reason. A frozen glass and cold soda keep the bubbles. The first cube is lowered in slowly, so it doesn't crack. The bottom cube is lifted once, to mix it without knocking out the fizz. I've added one touch: a little real vanilla, as a nod to the casks his book hardly mentions, since oak casks give whisky some of that same flavour. It's there in the recipe, like everything else.

Keep the readings, the dates and the bread times exactly as you do. But put yourself in the notes too: the joke, the hunch, the part you loved. The numbers are what people will check. You are what they'll want to read.
